text:
As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

Researchers from MIT and Georgia Tech studied future situations in which the build-out of solar and wind farms has scaled up enough that 80 percent of the electricity supplied to customers in the U.S. is generated from renewable sources. They modeled systems with different mixtures of wind and solar power capacities.

They found that solar and wind farms could produce as much as 10 percent more power than the grid could immediately use or store in electricity systems that cost-effectively meet demand with 80 percent renewable energy. If not utilized, this excess electricity would go to waste.

This finding holds true even when the cost of energy-storage devices like batteries is low, and it remains largely consistent across the U.S. in many future scenarios.

The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available. It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.

This predictability presents an opportunity for some industrial processes that, with the right scheduling and capacity scaling strategy, could use this otherwise excess energy. Examples include raw materials grinding and even electrified steel production. The excess could also be tapped to help meet the growing electricity demands of data centers.

While it can be more challenging to run industrial processes intermittently than continuously, the predictability of potential excesses helps, the authors say. Additionally, strategies like designing less-capital-intensive machinery, or even sharing equipment across manufacturing sites, could also be useful.

“In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses. Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now,” says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study.

She is joined on the paper by lead author Micah S. Ziegler, a former IDSS postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Aliza Khurram, a former IDSS postdoc now at the Toyota Research Institute; and Shannon Y.S. Hwang a PhD student in IDSS. The research appears today in Joule.

Examining excess

Wind and solar energy are variable resources because they are dependent on weather. During periods when supply exceeds demand, operators often take measures to either store the excess or reduce energy production altogether.

But “another way to think about that curtailed energy is as an opportunity to use this excess electricity for some other processes,” Trancik says.

“Excesses could instead be used productively in a range of processes including making materials and training AI models,” Ziegler adds.

To help engineers design processes to utilize this resource, the MIT researchers modeled the dynamics, durations, and frequencies of excess energy events.

They used an energy systems model to study systems that combine wind, solar, and energy storage to meet different percentages of electricity demand in many future scenarios. The model can also simulate how these systems might operate hourly over decades.

They fed this model 40 years of data that captured weather extremes and fluctuations in wind and solar resources across the United States. They also incorporated technology-related factors, such as the cost of building different types of batteries or other kinds of energy storage, as well as electricity demand profiles for specific regions.

“All these costs are changing, so we wanted to study many different combinations of technologies to help people plan amid all this uncertainty about what the future power system is going to look like,” Trancik says.

They designed the model to handle this enormous amount of data, while balancing the level of detail so the problem was computationally tractable.

In the end, the researchers found that significant amounts of excess energy would be generated in electricity systems that meet a significant portion of demand with renewable energy. Even when systems are designed to minimize the costs of delivering renewable energy, the amount of potentially excess power available would regularly double the amount used to meet demand.

“We found that considerable excess energy could be available even in systems with very low-cost storage, including at costs an order of magnitude lower than what battery storage costs today,” Ziegler explains.

“There is a huge amount of renewable energy that might be wasted in these cost-optimal systems, and there is not as much sensitivity to location as one might have thought. This energy is broadly available across the U.S.” Trancik says.

The model shows that the greatest potential periods of excess energy would occur in the spring, with smaller amounts of excess available in the mid- to late fall. These excess periods typically continue for seven to 12 hours, usually occur midday through the afternoon, and sometimes last for multiple days.

Leveraging surplus energy

Because these excess energy patterns are somewhat predictable, scientists and engineers could design processes to capitalize on this resource, Trancik says.

“In many of the scenarios, excess energy was often available for seven to 12 hours continuously, which suggests this duration could be a good target for technology developers and system planners when they design and schedule processes,” Ziegler explains. “When the same characteristic is found consistently across a wide range of possible energy systems, it can be considered more robust to our uncertainty about the future.”

For example, some industrial machinery, like electric arc furnaces in steel production or mills for grinding raw materials, could be switched on and operated during these times.

This electricity could also power equipment to manufacture products used seasonally, like fertilizer or concrete, which tend to be used more during spring, summer, and fall, and less during the winter. This coincides with several periods where more excess electricity is available. The energy could also power flexible computing, such as AI training processes that can be scheduled for times of day, or even months, when excesses are more likely available.

The researchers hope these results inform the development of technologies designed to utilize excess renewable energy, like periodic manufacturing processes that efficiently operate for a few hours at a time.

In the future, they plan to study the costs of developing infrastructure, equipment, and technologies that can benefit from these excesses.

“In many places today, we enjoy inexpensive electricity, but there could be more constraints on the system going forward. This excess renewable energy could be a resource that we might utilize to meet increasing demands,” says Trancik.

“If we can develop cost-effective ways to use this excess energy, we could potentially reduce some costs of transitioning to low-carbon energy resources,” Ziegler adds.

This research was funded by the MIT Climate Grand Challenges as part of the Weather and Climate Extremes project, and by the MIT Portugal Partnership Research Seed Fund Program, the MIT Technology and Policy Program, Georgia Tech, the MIT Energy Initiative, and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) released the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which passed in the U.S. Senate on November 19th and is anticipated to come up for a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives.

“I am a strong NO on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act when it comes to the House.

“Tribes, environmental organizations, and community groups appealed to the sponsors of the BAAJA, asking them to remove or modify provisions that would undermine Tribal sovereignty and roll back key environmental laws. The Senate-passed bill functionally addressed none of those concerns. This bill rolls back environmental protections, catastrophically undermining the Clean Water Act, and allowing new offshore drilling. This bill would also create ‘forever permits’ for data centers. Voters made their opposition to data centers clear and now is not the moment to let Donald Trump hand a blank check to developers who want to continue building these sites in communities across the country.

“This bill completely disregards Tribal sovereignty. Especially in a moment of democratic backsliding, Tribal consultation and collaboration must remain a meaningful and enforceable component of federal decision-making. Protections for sacred sites are not bargaining chips to be traded. Democrats are ready to accelerate the clean energy transition — BAAJA is not how we reach that, though. I am proud to be one of 164 members who support the Energy Bills Relief Act, legislation that we should quickly pass next Congress.

“Waiting until the next Congress to pass permitting reform would provide a real opportunity to negotiate that never occurred with the current bill. I urge my colleagues to vote NO on this bill and listen to the resounding call of voters across the country to fight for our agenda, not fold.”

text:
Q: What are the primary grid stability challenges facing Latin American electricity markets like Mexico as renewable penetration grows?

A: The main challenge is integrating rising solar and wind capacity into grids capable of managing variable generation without sacrificing system stability or power quality. Higher renewable shares increase demand for frequency and voltage control, rapid disturbance response, and reliable operation across more dynamic networks.

For developers and investors, grid stability is central to the energy transition because it directly affects project bankability, availability, and long-term asset value. Evaluate grid conditions, interconnection rules, and voltage or frequency support requirements from the earliest design stages to reduce connection risks and avoid costly retrofits. In Mexico, pairing solar PV with energy storage and advanced power conversion allows developers to curb curtailment and transform renewable plants into flexible assets that actively support the grid.

Q: How do battery energy storage systems (BESS) and advanced inverters help stabilize high-renewable grids?

A: Storage systems allow operators to shift energy dispatch, reduce curtailment, manage demand peaks, and backstop grid services. By doing so, BESS turns variable renewable generation into a predictable, dispatchable resource that strengthens both grid reliability and project revenue models.

Advanced inverters complement storage by delivering the fast, precise regulation needed to manage grid interaction, including active frequency and voltage support. Combining BESS, advanced power conversion, and intelligent plant-level controls shifts a project from being a passive power generator to an integrated grid-stability asset.

Q: What role does grid-forming technology play in this context, particularly in weak or isolated networks?

A: Grid-forming capabilities allow inverter-based systems to actively establish and stabilize the grid’s electrical references rather than merely following them. This becomes critical as conventional synchronous generation declines across power systems.

Grid-forming functions provide voltage and frequency support, synthetic inertia, and fast response during grid disturbances. These capabilities are especially valuable in weak grids, isolated systems, or areas with high renewable penetration where stability constraints would otherwise block new capacity additions.

Q: How is utility-scale solar-plus-storage design evolving, and what advantages does a DC-coupled architecture offer over conventional configurations?

A: The industry is moving away from standalone PV and BESS installations toward unified hybrid power plants designed as a single energy system. Developers need to capture more generation, manage clipping and curtailment, optimize CAPEX, and unlock new revenue streams without adding unnecessary operational complexity.

The SMA Stability Enhanced DC Coupled Hybrid Solution addresses this shift by integrating PV generation, battery storage, power conversion, and plant control within a single coordinated architecture. Connecting solar PV and batteries on the direct-current (DC) side eliminates intermediate conversion stages, reducing conversion losses and simplifying equipment and balance-of-plant infrastructure. Compared with conventional AC-coupled designs, this streamlined layout lowers initial CAPEX without compromising technical performance.

Q: Beyond CAPEX optimization, how does this integrated architecture improve energy yield and overall project performance?

A: Combining a DC-coupled architecture with Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFET semiconductor technology achieves conversion efficiencies of up to 99.5% on the DC side and 99.45% on the AC side. In addition, direct DC integration captures solar energy that would otherwise be lost to inverter clipping, storing it for later dispatch through energy-shifting strategies.

For utility-scale developers in Mexico and across Latin America, this architecture maximizes usable energy yield while equipping plants with grid-forming and coordinated control capabilities to meet increasingly strict operational requirements.

Q: What technical and regulatory changes are needed across Latin America to accelerate the adoption of hybrid and grid-forming technologies?

A: Grid codes and regulatory frameworks must evolve to establish clear, verifiable, and consistent technical standards for solar PV, BESS, and grid-forming functions. Regulatory clarity reduces development uncertainty and enables engineers to design compliant plants from the outset.

At the same time, electricity markets need formal mechanisms to recognize and remunerate ancillary services such as frequency regulation, voltage support, spinning reserves, and synthetic inertia. Monetizing these services creates new revenue streams for storage, improves project bankability, and accelerates private investment in grid reliability.

Q: Which technological trends and operational factors will define grid reliability in the region over the coming years?

A: Three technological trends will shape Latin America’s power sector: deeper integration between solar PV and storage, wider deployment of grid-forming inverters, and increasingly intelligent plant-level control systems. Together, these technologies maximize energy output, manage grid constraints, and deliver essential stability services.

Achieving that potential also requires early collaboration among developers, grid operators, and regulators so project designs align with evolving system needs.

title: Wake County buildings move toward a cleaner energy future
description:
Across Wake County operations, public buildings are becoming more energy efficient as the County expands solar power, modernizes building systems and incorporates cleaner technologies into new construction and renovations.
The new Wake County Public Health Center, the County’s latest flagship facility, uses 65% less energy than the building it replaced.
This facility is one of the latest projects supporting Wake County’s Clean Energy Resolution and its goal of achieving 100% clean energy by 2050.
Clean energy projects across Wake County Several County facilities demonstrate how these strategies work together.
Wake County, Wake County Public School System, and Wake Tech each have clean energy guidelines designed for their specific facilities and operations and provide annual progress updates.
text:
Across Wake County operations, public buildings are becoming more energy efficient as the County expands solar power, modernizes building systems and incorporates cleaner technologies into new construction and renovations. Together, these investments support reliable public services while lowering energy use and advancing the County’s long-term clean energy goals.

The new Wake County Public Health Center, the County’s latest flagship facility, uses 65% less energy than the building it replaced. Its energy-efficient design is complemented by a 625-kilowatt solar installation, which will generate about 20% of the building’s electricity and further reduce its reliance on traditional power sources.

This facility is one of the latest projects supporting Wake County’s Clean Energy Resolution and its goal of achieving 100% clean energy by 2050.

Clean energy projects across Wake County

Several County facilities demonstrate how these strategies work together. At Beech Bluff County Park, an energy-efficient building combines geothermal heating and cooling with a 58.5-kilowatt solar installation. The facility was able to offset 80% of its energy from clean sources last year.

At West Regional Library, improvements to lighting, heating and cooling equipment and building controls have cut energy use per square foot by more than 50%. The Sandy Plains Public Safety Station takes another approach, with an all-electric design that uses heat pumps for heating, cooling and water heating, along with a 90-kilowatt solar installation.

In addition, facilities that are in the design and construction phase also demonstrate multiple strategies including Cary Main and Five Points EMS stations, Crowder Park and Lake Crabtree, and the Wendell North Public Safety that are being designed or built with heat pump heating and cooling systems and solar installations where feasible.

Expanding solar power and planning for the future

Solar power is another growing part of the effort. Wake County has solar installations at 23 buildings and facilities, with the capacity to generate more than 1.4 megawatts of electricity and more projects are underway.

GSA and FD&C are also looking to find ways to make the upcoming projects more efficient. With two large projects at the Detention Center and the future campus at the Wake County Office Park, there is significant potential for demonstrating the County’s efforts toward the Clean Energy goal.

“Every project gives us another opportunity to improve how our buildings use energy,” Davidson said. “We’re looking at what we can do in existing facilities and making energy efficiency and clean energy part of the conversation as we plan for the future.”

Tracking progress toward clean energy goals

The County’s Energy Advisory Commission also helps guide the effort by providing input on projects and monitoring progress. Wake County, Wake County Public School System, and Wake Tech each have clean energy guidelines designed for their specific facilities and operations and provide annual progress updates.

text:
A U.S. Senate megabill centered on permitting reform to streamline a wide range of federally-funded projects — called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — is dividing Vermonters.

The bill — introduced Sept. 30 and sponsored by U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-West Virginia, and U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, along with Energy and Natural Resources Chair U.S. Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico — is aimed at advancing energy and transmission line development and modernizing project permitting.

Developers, the business community and energy transition advocates say the legislation would expedite energy, housing and other infrastructure projects that get bogged down by a prolonged permitting process and make life more affordable.

“A strong permitting process should provide meaningful opportunities while also ensuring decisions are made within a reasonable timeline,” said Amy Spear, the president of the Vermont Chamber of Commerce, which signed on to a letter of support for the bill spearheaded by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. “Those objectives shouldn’t be mutually exclusive.”

Meanwhile the conservationist, historic preservationist and tribal groups say the rollback of bedrock laws protecting environmental and historic resources should not come at the expense of development.

Some of the controversial provisions of the nearly 500-page bill are broader exemptions of projects from review under the National Environmental Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The bill would truncate timelines for public and tribal feedback and legal appeals against federally funded projects.

“I think that there would be an incredible loss of resources if this bill were passed,” said Giovanna Peebles, the former longtime Vermont state archeologist and state historic preservation officer. “It would be an existential threat to historic preservation, and certainly to archeology.”

To illustrate what’s at risk, Peeples pointed to the Chittenden County Circumferential Highway project — a proposed 16-mile limited access beltway — which was scrapped after historic preservation review led to the archaeological discovery of dozens of indigenous sites. And, Peebles said, there are similar discoveries yet to be unearthed in Vermont.

The U.S. Senate advanced the legislation for discussion and amendments when the legislative body reconvened on Nov. 9, and the Senate voted on Monday in favor of an amendment, sponsored by Sen. Capito that included a package of updates to the bill. U.S. Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Peter Welch, D-Vt., voted “nay” in both procedural votes.

Sponsor Sen. Whitehouse said the bill’s chance of passing in the Senate seemed favorable, and he did not think certain House members’ critiques of the bill diminished the chances of it passing in the lower chamber, according to reporting from The Hill.

The nation needs to build clean energy infrastructure more efficiently to mitigate climate change and reduce Vermonters’ utility bills, Welch wrote in a statement to VTDigger, but “there are several issues with this permitting reform package that prevent me from supporting it in its current form.”

Welch wants to work with colleagues to resolve what he perceives as issues with the bill, including the undercutting of the National Environmental Protection Act and “provisions that could open the government up to unprecedented financial liability,” according to the statement.

‘Compromise bill’

Industry leaders such as Spear argue that the permitting reforms laid out in the bill would create a predictable and efficient regulatory environment, prevent costly project delays and allow developers to build more housing, affordable energy and modern infrastructure.

Predictability doesn’t mean limiting public participation, as that involvement is part of responsible development, said Spear, the Vermont Chamber of Commerce president, and the bill still can be amended by the Senate to better achieve that balance.

Some environmentalists think that the streamlining of federally-funded projects is necessary to hasten a green energy transition.

“It’s a compromise bill,” said Jennifer Durgin, Vermont state coordinator for Citizens’ Climate Lobby, and it has received bipartisan support. She said the trade-offs are worth it to see the expansion of green energy projects and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

“It’s also important to remember that no action is an action,” Durgin said. “The consequences of not taking any action mean that the planet gets warmer every year. It continues to drive erratic and extreme weather, such as the catastrophic floods, you know, that we have experienced in Vermont.”

A consistent, timely and predictable process that caps the timeline for legal challenges to energy projects at 150 days compared to a window of several years would be a boon to the state’s green energy developers and bring affordability for energy consumers, said Norwich Solar CEO Jim Merriam.

The bill has gained bipartisan support because developers such as Merriam have experienced a “misuse of the system” by people opposing and appealing projects that otherwise would go forward, delaying construction and adding unforeseen costs into projects, he said.

Jonathan Dowds, deputy director of Renewable Energy Vermont, said that the organization is supportive of the bill conceptually, but the federal permitting reform is “not likely to have an immediate impact on the Vermont energy mix.” Permitting reform is necessary at the state and local level to roll out more clean energy projects in Vermont, Dowds said.

‘Pretty devastating’

The bill is “pretty devastating” for environmental assets and historic sites, said Britta Tonn, the Vermont director of cultural resources for the engineering firm Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc. The bill would “gut” the National Historic Preservation Act and other federal regulations established decades prior, she said, allowing federal agencies to take a “top-down approach” on projects regardless of the implications on a local community.

The bill presents a false dilemma in asking the public to choose modest emission reductions in exchange for weakening the National Environmental Protection Act, the Endangered Species Act and the Clean Water Act, said Zack Porter, executive director of the public lands advocacy organization Standing Trees.

“We are being asked to give up, you know, decades and decades and decades of hard-fought measures to protect clean air, clean water, endangered species,” as well as “the public’s right to know what the government is doing and to weigh in,” Porter said.

The federal permitting process for energy projects is complex, and there could be ways to improve the system, said Jenna Lapachinski, field service representative with the Preservation Trust of Vermont, but she argued the bill falls short of creating predictable outcomes for development.

It would be more beneficial to invest in personnel to facilitate reviews with stakeholders of federally-funded projects at federal agencies that have been understaffed and underfunded for a while, especially after massive job cuts under the Trump administration, she said.

The bill “puts a lot of power into the hands of the federal agencies to make unilateral decisions about what’s an adverse impact,” Lapachinski said. “We’re thrusting even more responsibility onto agencies that are just, you know, despite their best efforts, probably not well positioned to take that on.”

The bill is being “rushed through the lame duck session,” said Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, and the bill’s sweeping changes should be considered by the newly elected Congress after they are sworn in.

If passed, the legislation would bar legal challenges during the duration of project development, which Campbell said would likely spawn litigation against the federal government if the bill is enacted in its current form.

The amendment the Senate approved Monday included provisions allowing tribal groups and states to serve as lead agencies on projects and requiring data center operators to pay for their share of electricity costs. Data centers will also benefit from streamlined permitting though, said Tonn.

Tribal advocacy groups say the amendment does not address concerns about meaningful consultation, and the bill would shorten the timeline for consulting tribes and cut back protections for sacred sites, among other concerns.

While Vermont is not currently home to a federally recognized tribe, southern parts of the state are the ancestral homelands of the Mohican tribe, and the tribe is consulted by federal agencies for projects in that area, said Vermont State Historic Preservation Officer Laura Trieschmann.

Trieschmann said that she would expect reviews of federally-funded projects to be minimal if the bill passes in its current form given limitations on what is considered an adverse impact, so “even the most obvious of historic resources would be lost because (the federal government is) just not looking.”

Historic preservationists have previously found success after weighing in on a plan to demolish a “cornerstone” historic former hotel in St. Johnsbury through the historic review process laid out in the National Historic Preservation Act, said Lapachinski. As a result, the building instead was restored and converted into apartments for $17 million in 2022.

“We historic preservationists know the significance of climate change and weatherization, and how our buildings live and breathe,” Trieschmann said. “We want to be part of those conversations, and I think there’s ways to make it happen where there’s everyone at the table.”

If the Senate passes the bill, the legislation will then move to the House of Representatives.

title: Recycle BC, Miller Waste Systems break ground on new MRF
description:
Recycle BC, Miller Waste Systems, Orion Construction and Astria Properties have announced a joint venture to construct a new materials recovery facility (MRF) in Delta, British Columbia, and construction is underway.
North Vancouver, British Columbia-based Recycle BC says the new facility is part of its broader investment in recycling infrastructure, following its transition to managing postcollection services directly in June.
The facility will be operated by Markham, Ontario-based Miller Waste Systems, with Langley, British Columbia-based Astria Properties providing development management, design coordination and permitting, and Langley-based Orion Construction serving as construction partner.

text:
Recycle BC, Miller Waste Systems, Orion Construction and Astria Properties have announced a joint venture to construct a new materials recovery facility (MRF) in Delta, British Columbia, and construction is underway.

The 145,000-square-foot facility will be designed to process a base capacity of approximately 120,000 metric tons of residential packaging and paper annually, with opportunity for future growth. Expected to be completed in 2028, the companies say the project will strengthen British Columbia’s recycling network, improve processing efficiency and support up to 200 jobs across construction and ongoing operations, including 60-70 permanent positions.

Built on a 10.6-acre former construction and demolition landfill, the companies say the facility will incorporate energy-efficient technologies and sustainable design features, including processing motors, electric forklift capabilities and six electric vehicle charging stations.

North Vancouver, British Columbia-based Recycle BC says the new facility is part of its broader investment in recycling infrastructure, following its transition to managing postcollection services directly in June.

The facility will be operated by Markham, Ontario-based Miller Waste Systems, with Langley, British Columbia-based Astria Properties providing development management, design coordination and permitting, and Langley-based Orion Construction serving as construction partner.

“This facility is an important part of how we’re strengthening B.C.’s recycling system for the long term,” Recycle BC Executive Director Sam Baker says. “By taking a more direct role in managing postcollection services and strengthening the infrastructure that supports them, we can improve how materials move and are tracked through the system, respond to changing recycling needs and ensure British Columbians continue to have access to reliable recycling services close to home.”

Miller Waste Systems, a Canadian-owned company with approximately 65 years of experience in waste collection, recycling and material recovery, is leading the design, construction and future operation of the MRF. According to the companies, nearly all processing equipment will be designed and fabricated in Canada, including technology supplied by Machinex Industries, a Canadian recycling equipment manufacturer with more than 55 years of industry experience.

“Designing a facility of this scale means thinking about both what the recycling system needs today and how those needs may change over time,” says Blair McArthur, CEO of Miller Waste Systems. “We’re drawing on decades of industry experience and Canadian manufacturing expertise to build a facility that can process materials efficiently, recover high-quality recyclables and adapt as packaging and collection systems evolve.”

The companies say the project will create opportunities for local contractors, suppliers and service providers throughout construction and ongoing operations, supporting economic activity in the region.

“This project represents a significant investment in the local economy, creating jobs and opportunities for businesses across the region,” says Joshua Gaglardi, president of Orion Construction. “From the skilled trades and local contractors helping bring the facility to life to the permanent jobs it will support once operational, this is the kind of infrastructure investment that delivers lasting benefits for our communities.”

The facility also will feature a dedicated 1,000-square-foot education space, where visitors will be able to observe recycling operations through an elevated viewing platform and camera systems. The companies say education opportunities coordinated through Recycle BC will offer British Columbians a firsthand look at how recyclable materials are sorted, processed and prepared for new uses.

“Behind investments like these are teams with complementary expertise working toward a shared goal,” says Astria Properties President David Basche. “Bringing this facility to life takes close collaboration across industry, local government and the project team. It’s rewarding to see that collective effort taking shape in infrastructure that will serve British Columbians for years to come.”

The facility will incorporate optical sorting and artificial intelligence-enhanced technologies to improve material identification, sorting efficiency and recovery. Designed to accommodate both single-stream and multi-stream recyclables, the companies say it will process materials through multiple sorting stages to help ensure collected material meets the quality standards required by verified recycling end markets. Real-time monitoring systems will support ongoing improvements in processing efficiency, while flexible facility design will allow operations to adapt to evolving packaging materials and collection systems.

The Delta facility is part of a broader effort to strengthen British Columbia’s recycling network, alongside upgrades to existing processing facilities in New Westminster and Kelowna.

text:
How a Vietnamese conglomerate is extending its industrial, technological and green mobility capabilities across Asia, creating new opportunities for regional development and a better life for people.

NHA TRANG, VIETNAM – Media OutReach Newswire – 24 November 2026 – Asia is entering a defining era of transformation. Rapid urbanization, growing demand for mobility, the transition to cleaner energy and accelerating technological change are reshaping the region’s economies and societies. The next chapter of development will depend not only on the ability to adopt new technologies, but also on building the industrial capabilities, infrastructure and ecosystems that can translate innovation into meaningful progress.

This was the vision behind “Building the Future of Asia”, the theme of V-Creator All Star Summit 2026 in Vietnam. Bringing together nearly 500 international journalists, content creators and community representatives, the summit offered a closer look at how Vingroup, one of Vietnam’s leading conglomerates, is seeking to contribute to this transformation through manufacturing, technology and green mobility.

For Vingroup, this ambition is rooted in a broader purpose: “To Create a Better Life for People”. Its development is not simply about expanding businesses or entering new markets. It is about building capabilities that can contribute to economic progress while making the benefits of development more accessible to people across the region.

From Vietnam’s industrial rise to new frontiers

Over more than three decades, Vingroup has evolved from its origins in Ukraine in 1993 into a diversified business group spanning real estate, hospitality, healthcare, education, manufacturing and technology. Its businesses, including Vinhomes, Vinpearl, Vinmec and Vinschool, have contributed to the development of modern urban communities and the expansion of essential services in Vietnam.

In recent years, the Group has increasingly focused on sectors that require deeper industrial and technological capabilities. VinFast’s transformation into an all-electric vehicle manufacturer is a defining example. It represents a significant step from traditional consumer-facing businesses into engineering, research and development, advanced manufacturing and participation in the global automotive industry.

This direction reflects the long-term vision of Vingroup’s founder and Chairman, Pham Nhat Vuong, to take on challenging sectors and build capabilities with lasting value. More importantly, it has laid the foundation for an ecosystem in which different businesses can reinforce one another.

The transition to electric mobility illustrates this approach. VinFast develops and manufactures electric vehicles; V-GREEN builds charging infrastructure; and GSM brings electric mobility into everyday transportation through technology-enabled services. Together, they address a fundamental challenge facing the EV transition: making cleaner transportation not only available, but also convenient, accessible and commercially viable.

This integrated model is now being extended beyond Vietnam, with Indonesia, the Philippines and India emerging as important markets in Vingroup’s regional strategy.

Taking industrial capabilities across Asia and closer to people’s lives

The significance of Vingroup’s international expansion lies not simply in introducing Vietnamese brands to new markets, but in adapting its capabilities to local development needs.

In Indonesia, VinFast has moved beyond vehicle distribution to establish a local manufacturing base. Its Subang facility in West Java, inaugurated in December 2025, has an initial designed annual capacity of 50,000 vehicles. The investment supports Indonesia’s ambition to develop its domestic EV industry, while creating opportunities for local employment, supplier participation and technical skills development.

The industrial ecosystem is complemented by V-GREEN’s expansion of charging infrastructure and GSM’s all-electric mobility services. Green SM is bringing electric taxis into everyday transportation, while its Green Limo service and vehicle partnership programmes create additional opportunities for local drivers and fleet operators. The result is a model that connects manufacturing with the infrastructure and services needed to make electrification part of daily life.

In the Philippines, VinFast is gaining a strong foothold in the rapidly evolving electric vehicle market. According to sales data reported by the Chamber of Automotive Manufacturers of the Philippines, Inc. (CAMPI) and the Truck Manufacturers Association (TMA), VinFast has maintained its position as the country’s leading battery electric vehicle (BEV) brand across multiple reporting periods. This growing market presence is underpinned by an expanding portfolio, a broader dealer and after-sales network, and ownership initiatives designed to make electric vehicles more accessible.

India presents another important opportunity. As one of the world’s largest automotive markets, it combines significant consumer demand with a strong emphasis on domestic manufacturing. VinFast inaugurated its electric vehicle manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu in August 2025, with an initial designed capacity of 50,000 vehicles annually, scalable to 150,000. Beyond serving the local market, the investment supports industrial localization, workforce development and the growth of a domestic supplier ecosystem.

The wider mobility ecosystem is developing alongside it. VinFast is expanding its distribution and service networks; Green SM has commenced electric ride-hailing operations in Delhi NCR. Each initiative addresses a different part of the mobility value chain, bringing products, infrastructure and services closer to consumers.

The three markets have distinct conditions and priorities. Indonesia offers opportunities to strengthen local manufacturing; the Philippines provides scope for partnership-led fleet electrification; and India combines a vast consumer market with significant industrial potential. Yet the underlying ambition is consistent: to contribute to local economies, support businesses and workers, and make cleaner, more convenient mobility accessible to more people.

This approach also reflects a broader understanding of sustainable development. Industrial investment can create jobs and strengthen local capabilities. Infrastructure can remove barriers to new technologies. Partnerships can open up business opportunities for local enterprises and individuals. Ultimately, the value of expansion should be measured not only by commercial growth, but also by the positive changes it brings to the communities in which businesses operate.

Building Asia’s future, creating a better life for everyone

Vingroup’s ambitions extend beyond mobility. Investments and development initiatives in artificial intelligence, robotics, automation and major infrastructure reflect the Group’s interest in technologies and systems that will shape the next phase of economic development. These are complex fields that demand long-term investment, technological expertise and sustained execution, but they also offer opportunities to improve productivity, connectivity and the quality of services available to society.

The future of Asia will not be defined solely by economic growth, industrial capacity or technological breakthroughs. Its true measure will lie in how these advances translate into better opportunities, more accessible services, sustainable communities and improved quality of life.

For Vingroup, contributing to Asia’s development and creating a better life for people are not separate ambitions. They are intrinsically connected. A stronger industrial ecosystem can create opportunities for communities; cleaner mobility can contribute to healthier urban environments; and technological innovation can make everyday services more efficient and accessible.

From Vietnam to Indonesia, the Philippines and India, Vingroup and its businesses are working to bring these benefits closer to people in the markets they serve. The same spirit of connection is at the heart of V-Creator. By bringing together people who inform, influence and shape public conversations across markets, the platform seeks to create connections that extend beyond a single event – fostering the exchange of ideas, encouraging a deeper understanding of regional developments and enabling new perspectives to emerge. More than a gathering of media professionals and creators, it reflects the belief that building Asia’s future is a collective undertaking, one that requires not only investment and innovation, but also shared knowledge, dialogue and collaboration.

Ultimately, building the future of Asia means building a future in which progress creates a better life for everyone.

text:
Paying for groceries, filling the car, and keeping a roof overhead can leave little room for another surprise. When events far away push up essential costs, families must adjust budgets they thought were settled.

I believe that vulnerability belongs at the center of the climate debate. Congress should amend the Clean Air Act to make protecting households from climate-related harm an explicit, lasting responsibility.

This year’s Middle East conflict illustrates how disruption reaches household budgets. In March, the International Energy Agency reported that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carried oil equivalent to around 20 percent of global consumption, had slowed dramatically.

Read More on Leadership Insights

The resulting supply shock pushed crude prices above $100 a barrel. Those figures describe a global market, but the consequences reach people buying fuel and businesses transporting everyday goods.

COVID-19 offered another lesson. Empty shelves and delayed deliveries exposed how much daily life depends on supply networks functioning together.

Federal Reserve researchers found that pandemic bottlenecks reflected both reduced supply capacity and a rapid shift toward buying goods instead of services. Supply disruption was not the only cause of inflation, but it helped turn an international emergency into a household affordability problem.

Climate change creates another source of pressure on essentials. In a 2025 analysis, European Central Bank economists identified extreme weather as a threat to food supply chains, pointing to drought-related olive oil price increases in Spain.

This does not mean every expensive grocery bill can be blamed on warming. It means climate risk belongs in any serious effort to protect purchasing power.

We cannot predict precisely when every disruption will arrive. We can decide whether to limit a source of future harm. For me, that is the affordability case for reducing greenhouse gas emissions: helping prevent avoidable pressures from accumulating around necessities that families cannot simply stop buying.

Federal policy is moving in the opposite direction. In February, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded its 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding and repealed associated vehicle emission standards.

Its stated reasoning included an interpretation that the relevant Clean Air Act provision does not authorize regulation addressing global climate change.

In September, the agency finalized a repeal of most of its 2024 greenhouse gas requirements for fossil fuel-fired power-plants.

The repeal took effect on November 16. In a separate proposal, the EPA argues that Section 111 of the Clean Air Act does not authorize it to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants to address global climate change.

How Congress Could Strengthen Climate Protections

Congress should answer this dispute over authority with clearer legislation. I propose an amendment explicitly adding carbon dioxide as a criteria pollutant and requiring climate protections informed by current science, including evidence developed since 2009.

The law should state what the EPA must regulate, establish deadlines, and require periodic scientific review.

The existing air-quality framework provides a starting point. Its primary standards protect health, including vulnerable people; secondary standards protect public welfare, including crops and buildings.

But adding carbon dioxide would require careful design. A globally accumulating gas cannot be addressed simply by copying a local pollution limit. Congress should specify how climate-based standards translate into enforceable U.S. emission reductions.

The cost objection deserves an honest answer. Climate policy can impose expenses, and households with little financial flexibility need protection. An amendment should require transparent implementation schedules, assessment of household impacts, and measures to help those least able to absorb transition costs.

If lawmakers choose carbon pricing, they should explicitly authorize its design and decide how revenue would support households.

Such legislation would not lower next week’s grocery bill or prevent every disaster. Its value would be a more durable legal foundation for reducing future risks, alongside clearer expectations for investment. Without that foundation, families remain exposed while businesses face another cycle of changing federal requirements.

The next Congress should begin with hearings that examine climate-related household costs alongside compliance costs, then draft an amendment and seek recorded votes.

Passage may be difficult, but lawmakers should explain which protections they support and how they would deliver them.

Families deserve a climate policy that helps them plan, rather than another promise made between emergencies.

Gary Yohe is an economics and environmental-studies professor at Wesleyan University whose research focuses on climate impacts, adaptation and mitigation, and the views expressed are his own.

text:
CSIRO scientists urged Australia to build a battery manufacturing industry instead of exporting critical minerals. A CSIRO report released in early November identified local manufacturing capabilities that could produce battery components.

Why it matters

Australia is the world's number one lithium producer, yet it exports raw minerals and ships end-of-life batteries overseas for materials recovery. Building domestic capacity could capture more value from resources the country already holds.

More than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under a federal scheme since July 2025. Electric vehicle sales have risen rapidly since March, though the report does not quantify the growth rate.

The players

CSIRO

The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation is Australia's national science agency, conducting research across industry and environmental fields.

The details

Australia has nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper and graphite, but exports them as raw materials for overseas processing. A CSIRO report released in early November found Australia could manufacture battery casings using aluminium aerosol can expertise and copper foil from scrap wire.

Timeline

July 2025: Federal home battery scheme began installations.

March: Electric vehicle sales began rapid growth.

Early November: CSIRO released its battery manufacturing report.

Tuesday: CSIRO scientists delivered the battery manufacturing warning at an event.

Related coverage

Nov. 22

Nov. 6

Energy

Nov. 23

Roadmap

The federal home battery scheme, operating since July 2025, has installed more than 600,000 units and created domestic demand for batteries. The CSIRO report asks whether that demand can support local manufacturing rather than continued reliance on imported finished batteries.

Local battery manufacturing could affect the price and availability of home and electric vehicle batteries over time. Households already using the federal scheme may see the supply chain behind their installed batteries change as domestic capacity develops.

The takeaway

Australia's mineral wealth gives it a head start in battery production, but capturing that value depends on processing and manufacturing at home. Tracking the CSIRO report's proposals will show whether local industry follows.

text:
North Carolina regulators approve additional solar, battery storage, natural gas capacity and continued nuclear development as Duke Energy plans for rising electricity demand.

Duke Energy is advancing plans to expand electricity generation and infrastructure in the Carolinas following an order from the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC) on the company’s 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan. The plan outlines how the company intends to meet growing electricity demand while keeping customer costs in focus.

“We know families and businesses are watching their energy bills closely, and we take that seriously,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina president. “The plan reflects an all-of-the-above approach – natural gas, solar, batteries and new nuclear – shaped by our customers and many partners across the state. We appreciate the commission’s careful review, and we’re committed to working together to keep the lights on, support economic development and hold down costs as the Carolinas grow.”

The plan combines natural gas generation, solar, battery storage and continued nuclear development, along with energy efficiency and demand response programs. Duke Energy said the approach is intended to address regional growth, reliability needs and infrastructure costs.

The resource plan was developed through a process involving the North Carolina Public Staff, customers, community and business leaders, and other stakeholders. Duke Energy said it will continue working with state leaders and stakeholders to address reliability, economic development and cost allocation, including ensuring large new energy users contribute toward the infrastructure required to serve them.

Some projects included in the order are already under construction, while others will require additional project-specific review and approval, with opportunities for public input.

Planned generation and storage additions

The NCUC order advances the following resources beyond those included in its 2022 and 2024 resource plan orders:

Solar: An additional 2,300 megawatts (MW), bringing planned solar capacity to 8,100 MW by 2034.

Battery storage: An additional 2,700 MW, bringing planned battery storage capacity to 5,400 MW by 2034.

Combined-cycle generation: An additional 2,720 MW from CC4 and CC5, on top of the previously approved 3,920 MW from CC1-3, for five combined-cycle units by 2033.

Combustion turbines: An additional 1,111 MW from CT5-7, beyond the previously approved 1,700 MW from CT1-4, for seven combustion turbines by 2032.

Nuclear development

The order authorizes continued development work supporting either small modular reactors or large light water reactor generation. Duke Energy is authorized to develop and submit amendments to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for two AP1000 units at the W.S. Lee site in Cherokee County, South Carolina, and revisions to the combined license application for two AP1000 units at the Shearon Harris site in Wake County, North Carolina.

The NCUC also opened a new nuclear docket requiring quarterly updates on development progress. The docket will inform the commission’s evaluation of reactor technology, costs, financing, execution risks and customer protections before a decision is made on whether to build a new nuclear plant.

Planning for regional growth

North Carolina and South Carolina are experiencing population and business growth that is increasing electricity demand. Duke Energy said its resource investments are intended to address rising demand, replace aging infrastructure and maintain reliability for approximately 4.8 million customers across the Carolinas.

Cost-reduction efforts

Duke Energy said changes to the 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan reflecting state and federal policy updates reduced projected customer costs over the next decade by nearly half compared with the resource plan approved in 2024.

The company also identified several initiatives intended to help manage future costs:

Utility combination: Combining Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, effective Jan. 1, is projected to save customers $2.3 billion between 2027 and 2040.

Tax credits: Nuclear and solar production and investment tax credits are estimated to generate $2.7 billion in net tax credits in the Carolinas from 2025 through 2028.

Federal grants: More than $110 million in U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) grant funding is intended to support reliability through transmission upgrades and power plant refurbishments.

Federal loans: Duke Energy has applied for DOE loans that could provide billions of dollars in additional customer savings.

Project construction and development

Construction is underway at facilities including the Person County Energy Complex and a second battery storage facility replacing the retired Allen Plant. Construction on the approved Anderson Natural Gas Project is expected to begin in 2027.

Duke Energy completed three solar projects in the Carolinas over the past year totaling 151 MW, with construction expected to begin on three additional projects totaling 192 MW. Regulators also approved planned combustion turbines at the site of the former Buck coal plant.

Duke Energy said it will continue working with the Public Staff, state and local officials, customers, and community and business partners as projects progress. The company also plans to continue offering energy efficiency programs and payment assistance to help customers manage their bills.

text:
Chinese new energy giant BYD is in talks to buy 4×4 manufacturer Ineos’s French factory.

The move to acquire the Hambach plant would give BYD a second passenger car manufacturing plant in Europe and help it circumvent heavy import tariffs imposed by the EU on Chinese car makers.

It would also help with the brand’s stated plans to develop and build cars in Europe to meet European tastes rather than simply reengineering cars designed for the Chinese market.

If the deal goes ahead, production of BYD models in France is unlikely to begin before 2028 at the earliest.

In June BYD announced it would begin manufacturing the Dolphin Surf at its plant in Szeged in ​southern Hungary before the end of this year, and said it was actively looking at other sites around Europe.

Earlier this year BYD’s ​special adviser for Europe, Alfredo Altavilla, said it would need three vehicle factories and a battery manufacturing plant in the region to achieve its target sales volumes and comply with European regulations.

Now, BYD has confirmed it is in exclusive talks with Ineos as the 4×4 specialist looks to move its manufacturing operations to the United States.

The Jim Ratcliffe-owned car maker caused controversy in 2020 when it acquired the Hambach site from Smart, having previously pledged to build its Grenadier in Wales. Now it plans to shift production to the US, where it sells 70% of its Grenadier and Quartermaster models.

BYD’s executive vice president Stella Li said its plans for Hambach would protect jobs in the north-eastern region and realise BYD’s aim to build vehicles designed specifically for European drivers.

She commented: “Our commitment to Europe is long term. Our proposed investment in Hambach reflects our confidence in France and our ambition to keep growing in Europe. We want to give European consumers the choice of vehicles built in France that bring our technology and our innovations in electric mobility closer to home.”

text:
Background

Ranking Member Huffman outlined five critical fixes in the jurisdiction of the Natural Resources Committee needed to earn his support for the Senate-passed permitting bill:

Respect Tribal sovereignty. Preserve Tribal consultation obligations, treaty rights, and the ability to enforce those rights in court.

Protect communities’ access to justice. Ensure people can challenge illegally approved projects and judges can stop damaging construction before the harm is done.

Close “forever permit” loopholes. Preserve future administrations’ ability to address illegal approvals and adopt health and environmental safeguards without forcing taxpayers to compensate corporations.

Protect endangered wildlife. Ensure decisions about endangered species follow the best available science.

Protect public lands and sacred places. Preserve protections for America’s special places like the Boundary Waters, Chaco Canyon, and America’s Arctic, and block giant AI data centers on public lands.

Full video transcript below:

"Let’s talk about where things stand in the final three weeks of this Congress on BAAJA, a huge 500-page permitting reform bill that passed the Senate last week. I want to be clear on exactly what is in this bill, why I oppose it in its current form, and how we can fix it – either now, if the bill’s supporters will negotiate reasonable changes, or six weeks from now, when Democrats hold the gavels in the next Congress.

Like most members of Congress, I support responsible permitting reform. I want our government’s approval processes for all types of projects to be faster and better for everyone involved – for companies who build things, workers who need jobs, and communities who deserve a say in projects that impact them. And I’m willing to support significant changes to make that happen.

But there’s a lot more going on in BAAJA than just streamlining the permitting system. As drafted, this bill is the most sweeping rollback of environmental laws we’ve ever seen – dramatically weakening protections for public lands, clean air and water, endangered wildlife, and sacred tribal sites.

The bill fundamentally changes federal reviews and approvals for all types of projects – not just power lines, but everything from data centers to pipelines and LNG terminals, uranium mines, ICE detention centers, and even President Trump’s vanity projects.

And it dramatically curtails the ability of impacted communities to engage in the review process – including native American tribes, sportsmen who hunt, fish and recreate on public lands, and conservation groups. And when they do, it makes it virtually impossible to force changes or to stop harmful projects in court, even when laws are broken.

Now, in a normal legislative process, especially for a huge complex bill like this, you would see public hearings with testimony from experts and careful deliberation. And legislators would have a chance to vote on amendments to fix major problems. But the Senate didn’t allow any of that with BAAJA – which is why two-thirds of Senate Democrats voted No.

And Republicans now want to rush it through the House and get it to President Trump’s desk before the end of the year.

I stand with a growing majority of Democrats who are drawing a principled line and refusing to be jammed – we will not support BAAJA unless there are fixes to the most glaring problems. We support responsible permitting reform – and there’s just too much at stake here for a rush job, just to get a deal done before the next Congress takes over.

Some have suggested that Democrats are just opposed to reaching ANY deal with Republicans and the Trump administration. And that’s not true – certainly not on this issue.

So let’s be specific. The most controversial and problematic parts of BAAJA fall under the jurisdiction of the Natural Resources Committee, which I hope to be chairing when the new Congress convenes a few weeks from now. I will tell you the specific changes that would remove my opposition and get me, and I believe many other Democrats, to “yes” as soon as next week.

Respecting Tribal Nations comes first. When a project threatens a Tribe’s water, treaty rights, or sacred sites, the federal government has obligations it must honor. The changes to the NHPA and CWA in BAAJA strip tribal nations of their seat at the table and their rights in court. That has to change.

The same goes for other impacted communities who deserve a fair chance to voice concerns about projects that could be harmful to them and – if the government breaks the law in approving a data center, mine, a pipeline or other project – to sometimes challenge that decision in court. BAAJA not only makes it much harder for impacted communities to bring a case, it blocks judges from issuing orders to change or stop a project even if it’s found to be illegal. That must change.

BAAJA also has loopholes that create “forever permits.” In other words, the permits the Trump administration hands out to their buddies over the next two years – even if they are found to be destructive or illegal – could be locked in for good. The extreme, unpopular policies and corruption we’ve seen from this administration are going to end when Donald Trump leaves the White House two years from now. But on energy and environmental policy, BAAJA essentially legislates a third term for Trump by tying the hands of future administrations regarding Trump’s decisions and putting taxpayers on the hook for massive damages if new health or environmental safeguards are placed on polluting projects.

BAAJA includes a radical rollback of the Endangered Species Act that goes far beyond anything that could be justified in the name of permit streamlining. The ESA is our most important safeguard for protecting America’s wildlife and habitat endangered species need to survive. BAAJA provisions that undermine the independence and quality of the science to skew ESA decisions against protection of wildlife must be removed.

Finally, data centers on public lands. I don't think there should ever be data centers on public land, but it's a real threat. This administration is pushing over a dozen giveaways of public land for huge data centers. At a minimum, if Donald Trump is going to propose data centers on our public lands that belong to all of us, there has to be a full and complete environmental review with a chance for everyone to participate in that process, and for those who may be impacted by it to challenge it in court.

The changes I’ve outlined won’t solve every problem with the bill. But we deserve at least this much to protect the basic interests of our environment, tribes, and communities all over the country.

We have specific legislative text ready to go to make these changes happen, and that is being shared with the sponsors of BAAJA. If the bill’s backers are open to compromise and will work with us on these changes – we can still pass the bill in this Congress, despite the terrible process that brought us to this point.

But if they continue the “take it or leave it” ultimatum approach, I’ll do everything I can to stop this bad deal. And six weeks from now, when Democrats are in charge, we will get to work on a strong, responsible permitting reform that everyone can get behind.

The American people, including the people’s House, deserve a say in this bill, and House Democrats – especially after the recent election – are going to insist on that.

So, for those who want to pass BAAJA now, I’ve told you how to fix it and I’m ready to work with you to make that happen. But if it can’t happen in the remaining three weeks of this Congress, that’s not the end of the story. Because if BAAJA doesn’t pass, I guarantee you House Democrats will keep working on this and we’ll deliver a much better deal – responsible permitting reform that helps build the things we need faster and more affordably without throwing tribes, local communities and the environment under the bus.”

text:
The U.S. Senate voted 62-33 on November 19, 2026, to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), using H.R. 2347 as the legislative vehicle. The Senate-passed measure now goes to the U.S. House of Representatives, where lawmakers must either approve the Senate text or make changes that would require further Senate action.

Senate passage marks the legislation's most significant advance to date and puts the House in a position to send the package to President Donald Trump, who has expressed support for the deal, before the current Congress is scheduled to adjourn before Christmas.

Manager's Package and Negotiated Updates from October Version

In the month following committee passage, Senate negotiations on the package focused on four areas: revisions to sections covering requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), historic preservation, project certainty and consultation, and treatment of transmission and data center projects. Emboldened by the outcome of the midterm elections, Democrats' negotiating positions strengthened into November. Democrats pushed for concessions to ensure greater protections for Tribes and historic preservation, while Republicans sought to preserve the prioritization of expedited project approvals.

Negotiations culminated in the development of a bipartisan manager's amendment to the committee-passed legislation, which was adopted on the Senate floor during the week's consideration. The cloture vote to advance the package was 70-27 – the most decisive vote in the Senate's process over the course of the week – demonstrating that the package initially garnered broad bipartisan support, including most Republicans and a coalition of 21 Democrats. The manager's amendment, offered by lead Republican negotiator Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as S.Amdt. 6883, was adopted on November 18, 2026, by a subsequent vote of 69-27, with expectations that additional amendments might tweak the agreement. Support, however, eroded significantly between November 16, 2026, and the chamber's narrow final passage, as discussed further in the following section.

A brief overview of agreed-upon changes folded into S.Amdt. 6883 as adopted on November 18 is below.

NEPA

Requires concurrent review where possible

Expands exclusions to federally funded broadband deployment on previously reviewed rights-of-way

Reinstates Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (TIFIA) and Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing (RRIF) financing under the review process, eliminating loan and loan guarantee exclusion

Historic Preservation

Increases annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund to $300 million per year

Requires agencies to seek info from states, local governments and Tribes for "undertakings," which include U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) projects receiving more than $10 million from DOT and other federal projects as determined

Requires agencies to follow program alternatives where available

Consolidates reporting requirements

Instates a corrective action process for Tribes

Project Certainty

Narrows the applicability of project certainty provisions to projects that have received final approval

Requires greater disclosure of project permits

Transmission and Data Centers

For transmission projects, requires disclosure of landowner rights in written notices and includes standards of conduct and recordkeeping requirements for communications

For transmission projects, eliminates simultaneous processing of applications for large projects

Excludes telecommunications utilities providing internet and cable from data center provisions

Requires data center permits and authorizations to be made public

Floor Debate and Amendments

As noted above, the Senate adopted S.Amdt. 6883 by a 69-27 vote on November 18, 2026, and passed H.R. 2347 as amended the following evening.

No additional amendments were adopted before final passage. An effort to establish votes on a negotiated slate of amendments broke down after Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) objected. As a result, a final proposed manager's package, which would have further revised historic preservation provisions to address Tribal concerns, addressed transmission-related eminent domain concerns and tightened an exemption from the data center ratepayer protections, which were not included in the Senate-passed text.

The failed amendment process leaves several issues unresolved, particularly concerns regarding Tribal consultation and the National Historic Preservation Act, which helped drive opposition from a number of senators who otherwise support permitting reform. Senate negotiators on the permitting reform bill are still committed to adopting the revised version of S.Amdt. 6883, which they believe improves the bill. They are seeking to include it in any "must pass" legislation before the end of the year and have pointed to the continuing resolution that Congress will have to pass before the December 11, 2026, deadline as a potential vehicle.

Tribal Implications

Since BAAJA's introduction, Tribes have focused their concerns on Title III, Section 2301, which would substantially rewrite Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. As introduced, Section 2301 moved much of the Section 106 process and narrowed key definitions, including "undertaking," "adverse effect" and "property of traditional religious or cultural importance." It made consultation discretionary when identifying historic properties, gave consulting parties 30 days to object to an agency's Section 106 report, allowed the secretary of the Interior to take over Tribal Historic Preservation Office (THPO) functions, cut the time to sue from as much as six years to 150 days, and limited court remedies.

S.Amdt. 6883 as adopted struck the discretionary consultation provision, required Tribal review of every finding and extended the objection period to 45 days. It replaced the THPO takeover with corrective action plans and technical assistance, including at least 180 days to submit a plan, and required notice of the final decision to every consulting Tribe, with the deadline to sue running from that notice.

Despite these edits, Title III's structural changes to Section 106 largely remain. The bill still narrows "undertaking" and "adverse effect," excluding many projects and harms to cultural landscapes from review; brings Tribes in only after agencies set the review boundary and make initial findings; and lets agencies reject feasible mitigation based on undefined "other considerations." Tribes still face shortened response deadlines, and missing one forfeits reconsideration of earlier findings or an agency response. The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation may still act in place of a THPO, THPOs still face mandatory evaluations and grant suspensions, and court remedies are largely limited to remand without vacatur.

The Senate passed the bill as amended by S.Amdt. 6883 without adopting any of the filed amendments that would have struck Title III or addressed specific Tribal historic preservation concerns. As a result, Tribal sovereignty concerns continue as the bill moves to the House.

Next Steps in the House and Political Landscape

Confirmed Next Steps

House consideration is expected after the Thanksgiving recess. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has indicated that he will first try to move the Senate bill under an expedited procedure known as "suspension of the rules" requiring a two-thirds vote and barring floor amendments; if that effort fails, he has said he would pursue a standard rule requiring a simple majority.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) endorsed the Senate-passed package on November 20, although Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.) urged leadership to promptly bring it to the floor. At the same time, House Democrats remain divided: Rep. Peters and other permitting advocates support action this year, while Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) and Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) have raised concerns about the Senate text and called for greater House input.

Political Outlook

The Senate vote demonstrates a viable bipartisan coalition, but House passage is not automatic. The cleanest path is approval of the Senate text without changes; any House amendment would send the measure back to the Senate and increase the difficulty of completing action during the compressed year-end schedule.

description:
Six Bills Sail Through the House H.R.
3978: The Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act Representatives Bob Latta (R-OH) and Scott Peters (D-CA) introduced the Nuclear REFUEL Act with overwhelming bipartisan support.
