text:
Earlier this month, the House passed six bills to develop domestic nuclear energy. The House took up these bills at the outset of the lame-duck session, passing four on its first day back after the midterm elections and passing two more two days later. Framed as an opportunity to reduce energy costs for Americans, the bills reduce narrowly defined regulatory requirements, refine the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) approval and licensing requirements, and increase transparency around Department of Energy (DOE) decisions related to nuclear energy.

Six Bills Sail Through the House

H.R. 3978: The Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act

Representatives Bob Latta (R-OH) and Scott Peters (D-CA) introduced the Nuclear REFUEL Act with overwhelming bipartisan support. Nuclear fuel recycling technology, known as pryoprocessing, creates a uranium-transuranic mixed fuel that advanced fast reactors can use to make energy while reducing nuclear waste. Currently, there are no commercial reprocessing facilities operating in the United States, and the NRC does not clearly state which regulatory pathway would apply to recycling facilities that do not separate plutonium. This bill explicitly excludes reprocessing facilities from the definition of “production facility.” As a result, the facilities would follow the same one-step licensing process as other fuel cycle facilities, rather than the two-step process used for production and utilization facilities that produce nuclear material in quantities significant for national security.

H.R. 9612: The American Enrichment Deployment Act

By a 394-3 margin, Representative Russell Fry’s (R-SC) American Enrichment Deployment Act, cosponsored by Kim Schrier (R-WA) and Erin Houchin (R-IN), passed the House. This bill amends the Atomic Energy Act (AEA) to allow uranium enrichment facilities to be constructed under the same terms and conditions as other fuel cycle facilities. If enacted, the bill would no longer require a license to construct a uranium enrichment facility; however, the NRC would still have to license facilities to process and handle special nuclear and source material. The bill does not alter NRC licensing authority, which includes its ability to deny an application for a license. It also preserves the applicability of the National Environmental Policy Act, hearing rights under AEA, and NRC’s inspection rights. The NRC would be responsible for promulgating regulations to implement the act, if passed.

H.R. 5549: The Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act

Representative Morgan Griffith (R-VA) introduced the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act, which Representatives Schrier and Marc Veasey (D-TX) cosponsored. House Bill 5549, which passed the House on a voice vote, amends the AEA by removing the automatic hearing requirement for construction permits, operating licenses, combined construction and operating licenses, and certain licenses to possess and use special nuclear material. Instead, a public hearing would be required only if a license is contested by an affected party. The public hearing would also use informal, rather than formal, adjudicatory procedures. If the NRC determines an application for an amendment to a construction permit, an operating license, or a combined construction permit and operating license involves no significant hazards, it could dispense with the 30-day notice and publication requirement. This amendment would apply to all applications and proceedings pending before the NRC on the date of enactment.

H.R. 9613: The Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act

Representatives Diana Harshbarger (R-TN) and Craig Goldman (R-TX) introduced a bill to update the role of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS), which passed the House by voice vote. ACRS is an independent expert panel that reviews reactor safety. Currently, the ACRS must review and report on every safety study and license application the NRC refers to the Committee. This bill, if signed into law, would amend the AEA to modify the ACRS’s role. Specifically, the ACRS’s actions—such as reviewing facility licenses and safety studies or advising the Commission on reactor hazards—would focus on reactor design, safety significance, novelty, and new actions before the ACRS. The Committee would have the flexibility to not review license applications when no novel or unique issues arise. The bill would also limit Committee appointments to two four-year terms unless the NRC determines that there is a compelling reason for a Committee member’s continued service.

H.R. 9614: The NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act

Representative Rob Menendez’s (D-NJ) NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act likewise sailed through the House by voice vote. House Bill 9614 amends the AEA to provide the NRC Commissioner discretionary authority to increase Senior Executive Service appointees’ pay by up to ten percent above the annual rate. If enacted, the bill would align pay authority to career employees and more adequately compensate employees monitoring licensing applications and safety oversight.

H.R. 9084: The Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act

Representatives Kathy Castor (D-FL) and Mariannette Miller-Meek (R-IA) introduced the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act. Through a myriad of disclosure tools, House Bill 9084, approved by the House in an easy voice vote, would bring new public visibility to nuclear projects DOE authorizes. The bill requires the Energy Secretary to publicly disclose and summarize any alteration to directives or safety standards that apply to DOE-covered nuclear facilities. Furthermore, within 24 hours of issuance, the Secretary must post preliminary and final documented safety analyses, though commercially sensitive information may be excluded. Within the same timeline, the Secretary must share any agreement authorizing a covered DOE nuclear facility. Aside from these public disclosures, the Secretary must also submit an annual report to Congress—specifically the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources—detailing the Agency’s nuclear-related activities taken during the previous calendar year.

The Senate’s Permitting Reform Bill Moves to the House

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) passed in the Senate on November 19, 2026, with a 62-33 vote, incorporates versions of four of the six House bills: H.R. 9612, H.R. 5549, H.R. 9614, and H.R. 9084. There is one key difference to note. The Senate married licensing-reform provisions from the American Enrichment Deployment Act (H.R. 9612) and the Senate’s MORE American Fuel Act of 2026 (S. 5249). Specifically, BAAJA requires applications before the NRC to provide notice of construction to state, local, and tribal governments no fewer than 15 days before commencing construction, a requirement which was not in the House bill. Additionally, BAAJA exempts certain federal authorizations for nuclear facilities from the otherwise more stringent permitting deadlines that the bill imposes.

The Nuclear REFUEL Act and Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act were not incorporated into BAAJA. This omission likely stems from the two House bills’ focus on changes to nuclear-energy licensing and not the broader permitting reform BAAJA looks to accomplish.

Whether BAAJA passes the House during the 119th Congress remains to be seen. Even if BAAJA does not, however, nuclear-energy reform appears to be an issue with momentum that the 120th Congress could tackle with bipartisan support.

The Trump Agenda and the Near-Term Outlook

President Trump, meanwhile, has made promoting development of domestic nuclear power a significant part of his second-term agenda. He signed four executive orders promoting nuclear energy on May 23, 2025. His administration has focused on licensing, advanced reactor demonstrations, financing, existing plant restarts, domestic uranium enrichment, and advanced fuel development—all toward a goal of quadrupling U.S. nuclear capacity by 2050.

Further development of America’s nuclear power generating capacity has been hampered for decades by strident opposition from communities and activists, in part due to fears that followed incidents at Three Mile Island, Pennsylvania, Chernobyl, Ukraine, and Fukushima, Japan. The recent convergence of bipartisan interest has been driven by desires to move away from fossil fuels, better reactor designs, and the sharp uptick in demand for electricity caused in large part by the artificial intelligence revolution.

Covington advises stakeholders to watch developments closely to and be prepared for fast-moving developments. Regulatory activity is ongoing, but additional statutory changes are possible as well. Congress has a well-earned reputation for moving slowly, but when interests align as they have in this area, the legislative process can move very quickly. Companies with particular exposures or policy goals in this area should engage as early in the process as they can. Covington’s Public Policy and Energy and Environment practices are monitoring these developments closely and are available to help clients navigate this rapidly evolving landscape. Whether you are assessing the implications of new legislation, navigating regulatory and licensing considerations, or pursuing broader policy or business objectives in the nuclear sector, we encourage you to contact us to discuss how we can help.

The ill-fated Tesla Cybertruck has been roundly excoriated for its dumpster-adjacent profile, but it looks pretty good compared to the EVs rolling out of the shop at the Missouri-based startup Intramotev. However, looks are not everything. Intramotev is on a mission to chase diesel fuel off the nation’s nation’s rail freight system, and its “TugVolt” autonomous electrified freight cars get the job done, aesthetically pleasing or not.

EVs On Rails, What A Concept

Intramotev surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar back in 2023 with two retrofit products. One is the ReVolt, a battery pack that can be slotted onto existing railcars hauled behind a locomotive, with the aim of saving diesel fuel. The other, more interesting retrofit is the TugVolt, an autonomous, electrified system that enables railcars to go about the business of hauling freight on their own, without a locomotive.

While the battery packs in each TugVolt have a limited range, that’s more than enough to accomplish a good day’s work including “first mile” loading duties. Once loaded up, they can hitch a ride on locomotives for long-distance travel, then split off to unload.

In addition, a freight yard that hosts a full complement of autonomous railcar EVs would require little, if any, participation from diesel-powered switcher locomotives. In addition to hauling its own freight, each TugVolt can also operate as a switcher, ferrying conventional railcars into position behind a locomotive.

The technology also has significant implications for decarbonizing highway freight as well. The closer an electric railcar can get to its destination, the less need there is for a diesel-fueled truck to pick up the slack. In particular, Intramotev is focusing on captive or short line routes, many of which have seen their rail traffic shrink in the face of competition from the trucking industry.

Intramotev On The Move

Intramotev has been rather busy over the past three years. In one particularly interesting development, in June Intramotev lent a TugVolt to a US Army Reserve Training exercise at the Camp Shelby Joint Forces Training Center in Mississippi, billed as the largest training exercise in the history of the Army Reserve.

“Soldiers, according to Intramotev, trained on and operated the TugVolt system under company supervision throughout the exercise and quickly became proficient with the technology, a detail that matters because military rail operations have traditionally required specialized rail crews, a category of personnel the Army has struggled to maintain at sufficient strength given how infrequently large-scale rail movements occur outside major deployment exercises,” reports the independent news and analysis organization Defence Blog.

As noted by Defence Blog, the exercise went off script when railcars loaded with military supplies arrived at the site. However, with their training freshly in hand, the participants were able to deploy the TugVolt to organize the incoming railcars for unloading.

More EVs For Texas

It’s no surprise to find Intramotev in Texas, too, considering the state’s reputation as a hot EV market. On November 3, the company expanded its ongoing relationship with Watco, a holding company specializing in short line railways.

The new arrangement calls for TugVolt to pull zero emission switcher duty at a to-be-named industrial facility in Seadrift, Texas. As noted by Railway Age, the Texas assignment adds to Intramotev’s EV footprint in the US, which also includes Michigan as well as the Army demonstration in Missouri, and a forthcoming agreement in Kentucky.

Railway Age further notes that in April, Intramotev lent itself to electrification efforts in Austria. That’s a particularly significant development because the client is ÖBB, the national railway of Austria, making it the first deployment of TugVolt technology under regulation, in addition to Intramotev’s first overseas client.

The agreement is also significant considering ÖBB’s sprawling footprint in Europe, consisting of more than 1,000 freight trains ranging across 18 countries every day.

Somebody Missed The EV Memo

Even more significant, at least from a policy perspective, is a $16.3 million grant from the Federal Railroad Administration branch of the US Department of Transportation. US taxpayers will shoulder the bulk of the cost-sharing arrangement, which is designed to model best practices for introducing EVs into the nation’s railway system. The project is hosted by the Columbia Terminal Railroad, a city-owned, 21.4 mile line that links two cities in Missouri, Columbia and Centralia.

“The project will deploy autonomous railcars on the line to produce the first documented safety record for autonomous railcar operation and create a workforce training curriculum,” FRA emphasizes.

“The proposed project was selected for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction and involves research and workforce development activities to conduct a phased autonomous rail technology and short-line infrastructure modernization program,” FRA elaborates, further noting that the EV project “aligns with the selection criteria by improving system and service performance,” with the ultimate goal of enabling freight to run more frequently and, ultimately, autonomously.

Of note, the grant of up to $16 million or so is part of a $2.3 billion railway CRISI modernization package, with CRISI being short for Infrastructure and Safety Improvements. Among other purposes, CSRISI “provides a Federal funding opportunity to “mitigate congestion at both intercity passenger rail and freight rail chokepoints to support more efficient travel and goods movement.”

Citing Intramotev official Don Soffer, the local news organization News Tribune notes that “more than 600 short lines in the U.S. have declined in use in recent decades due to their relative inefficiency.”

“Cross-country hauling is more profitable for companies, whereas short lines require very large hauls to justify the quick trip. The Columbia Terminal Railroad (COLT) does not operate on a set schedule, instead hauling whenever enough goods are collected,” the News Tribune continues.

Given that context, if the CSRISI grant is not a decarbonization program for short line railways and associated highway traffic, I’ll eat my hat. It’s also worth noting that practically the entire locomotive fleet of the US runs on a diesel-electric platform, meaning electric motors powered by an on-board generator. While fossil energy is still in play, the diesel-electric configuration is more energy efficient than sending fleets of diesel trucks onto the nation’s highways.

The nation’s trucking industry has also been wrestling with an ongoing driver shortage, providing further motivation to move more freight onto rails, EVs or not.

Stay tuned for updates on that Missouri project. FRA announced its selection for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction in October, so there are still steps to take before the TugVolt begins running.

Meanwhile, circling back around to that Army demo in June, more likely than not the hookup with the US DoD will not be a one-off. The Army has been notoriously slow to adopt EVs, and last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy did not help. Still, the Army has been sending out EV signals through its use of new “anti-idling” kits for ground vehicles, alongside a new contract with the US branch of the firm Rheinmetall for a fleet of crewless hybrid cargo haulers. Again, looks are not everything…

text:
California-based Energy Vault has closed $78 million in non-recourse construction and bridge financing for the SOSA Energy Center, a 150 MW / 300 MWh battery energy storage system under construction in Madison County, Texas.

The two-hour duration facility represents an approximately $100 million total investment and is the first energy storage project acquired and placed into development under Asset Vault, Energy Vault’s platform for owning and operating storage and data center power infrastructure.

The site is already under construction, and as part of the deal, the bridge loan will be repaid upon project completion using previously committed funds, including a $80 million preferred equity investment. Energy Vault did not disclose the names of the banks and financiers involved

Costs, revenues

Once commissioned, SOSA will operate on the ERCOT market on a merchant basis, making it a notable new project given tightening markets. The site will also provide power and ancillary services, and Energy Vault indicated it is flexible with its asset, and may elect to enter a contracted offtake agreement “as market conditions evolve.”

Energy Vault projects the asset will deliver $250 million to $300 million or more in long-term revenues while generating recurring EBITDA margins of 65% to 75%, in line with its broader Asset Vault portfolio targets. The company didn’t specify an operating timeframe for the revenue projection (15 or 20 years, for example).

Construction at SOSA began in the fourth quarter of 2025, with Energy Vault self-performing engineering, procurement, and construction. Civil work is complete and a substation has been installed, with major equipment expected on site in the coming months ahead of targeted commercial operations in the third quarter of 2027.

From all of these data points, the implication of the approximate $100 million spend is a capex of around $333/kWh including substation and the internal EPC work.

“Storage earns its place in a portfolio the way any infrastructure does, by being financed on its fundamentals,” said Cory Magnuson, president of Asset Vault at Energy Vault. “A bank, a strategic partner and an institutional investor have each backed SOSA on those terms.”

“We cannot solve our air pollution crisis in a place like Los Angeles unless we meaningfully and significantly drive down pollution from ships,” Martinez said.

They’re expecting to nearly double that number as new requirements of the at-berth regulation are set to take effect in Northern California.
text:
And some of the densest neighborhoods in the region are right nearby.

“Long Beach, Wilmington, San Pedro,” said Earthjustice attorney and longtime clean air advocate Adrian Martinez. “In those communities, you have people literally living right next to where these ships were belching out really toxic pollution.”

Those fumes, largely from burning diesel fuel, have been linked to higher rates of cancer.

“We cannot solve our air pollution crisis in a place like Los Angeles unless we meaningfully and significantly drive down pollution from ships,” Martinez said.

The effort to revoke California’s clean ship rule

That’s why, back in 2007, the state approved the first version of what’s called the ocean-going vessels at-berth regulation. In general, the law requires certain ships to either turn off diesel engines and plug in to electrical power at the port when they’re unloading or capture the pollution that comes out of their smokestacks.

Container ships, passenger ships and refrigerated-cargo ships have been phased into compliance since 2014, reducing smog-forming emissions from those sources by 80%, according to the California Air Resources Board. Since 2023, the rule has expanded to include more stringent emissions standards and more types of vessels.

“It's really one of the most important public health measures,” Martinez said.

Still, work remains to cut pollution. Southern California regularly exceeds federal air quality standards for fine particulate matter and ground-level ozone.

But one of the key tools to cut such pollution, the at-berth rule, has gotten caught in the crosshairs of the Trump administration’s attacks on California’s clean air regulations. In September, the Republican-controlled House voted to revoke California’s at-berth clean ship waiver.

Now the issue rests with the Senate. It’s unclear whether the Republican-dominated Senate will take up the issue in the lame duck session — or whether it will fall to the incoming Democratic majority when the 120th Congress convenes Jan. 3.

Those fighting the at-berth regulation argue that it increases costs, which get passed on to consumers, and that the technology just isn’t ready.

Capturing at-berth pollution

The ability for ships to connect to power at dock, called shore power, is slowly growing. But most ships still don’t have the ability to connect to that power, and there’s still not enough renewable energy to support it.

Plugging into clean electric shore power is the ideal solution, Martinez said, but ”the public health crisis from shipping is so great that we need all sorts of solutions.”

That’s why a handful of companies, including Stax Engineering, have invested in pollution capture.

At the company’s berth at the Port of Long Beach one recent morning, two huge neon green barges were docked. Each had a massive, folded mechanical arm that can extend more than 250 feet to connect to the smokestacks of ships.

“It's like a big elephant nose at the end, and it connects to the stack,” said Mike Wallace, Stax’s chief executive.

The arm directs soot and smog-forming nitrogen oxides, or NOx, into a processing unit inside three 20-foot containers. There, fine particulate matter is filtered, and a catalyst breaks apart the nitrogen oxides, releasing them back into the atmosphere as nitrogen and oxygen, the components of the air we breathe.

The process captures about 95% of smog-forming NOx and 99% of particulate matter, Wallace said.

It has yet to help with planet-heating emissions like carbon dioxide, and small amounts of carbon dioxide are released as part of the process. In terms of pollution from the barges themselves, Wallace said, the company works to limit their emissions through the use of low-carbon fuels like biodiesel.

The company is also expanding into carbon capture. That’s more of a challenge to implement because captured carbon needs to be used or disposed of somewhere, Wallace said.

“Longer term, what people are trying to do is reduce carbon across the entire shipping process,” Wallace said.

Stax has partnered with the London-based company Seabound to demonstrate how to capture carbon and other pollutants while ships are at sea.

A growing industry that doesn't drive up costs

Meanwhile, Stax Engineering continues to grow its efforts to capture NOx and particulate matter. The company has eight pollution-capturing barges, with three more coming online soon. The goal is to have 18 operating in the coming years.

Stax employs about 200 people, mostly union jobs. They’re expecting to nearly double that number as new requirements of the at-berth regulation are set to take effect in Northern California. With strong backers, including actor Edward Norton, the company’s chief strategy officer, Wallace said the company is well-positioned to meet the state’s evolving at-berth regulations.

“The reality is we're not going to have [cleaner] alternative fuels for 30 years at scale,” Wallace said. “So are we just going to pretend those emissions for the next 30 years don't need to be captured? When those alternative fuels come, we're going to have to find another line of business, which we're good with.”

Across the water from the company’s berth, far on the other side of the port, Wallace pointed to another Stax barge attached to a massive auto-carrying cargo ship. Instead of dark diesel exhaust spewing from the smokestack, there’s just the green arm of the Stax barge.

“You'd be seeing black exhaust, diesel exhaust,” Wallace said. “The numbers are somewhere between 20 [thousand] to 60,000 cars' worth of emissions a day coming out of those vessels.”

The federal government estimates this could add $7.66 to the price of the cars on that ship. For consumer goods, it adds fractions of pennies on the dollar.

That’s why Walker says the argument that the at-berth rule is a significant factor in high prices is "ludicrous.”

“It's kind of what the marching orders are to go against this regulation,” Wallace said, “but the math just doesn't add up.”

After the blue wave in the midterm elections, and with other priorities on the minds of Congressional Republicans, Wallace hopes the clock on revoking the at-berth regulation waiver just runs out.

By Victor Oloo • Tuesday, November 24, 2026 • 2 min read

On November 24, 2011, President Yoweri Museveni launched the Kiira EV, Uganda’s first homegrown electric vehicle, at Makerere University.

The two-seater battery-powered prototype was developed by students and staff under the Centre for Research in Transportation Technologies (CRTT) at Makerere University’s Faculty of Technology, now the College of Engineering, Design, Art and Technology (CEDAT).

What began as an extracurricular university research initiative had grown into an ambitious attempt to demonstrate that Ugandan engineers could design and develop an electric vehicle locally.

Although the original Kiira EV was designed as a proof-of-concept rather than a commercially produced vehicle, its launch laid the foundation for a much bigger industrial ambition. In 2014, Kiira Motors Corporation (KMC) was incorporated as a state enterprise jointly owned by the Government of Uganda and Makerere University.

The project subsequently expanded beyond the original two-seater prototype to include other vehicle concepts, among them the four-seater Kiira EVS and solar-powered bus developments. These projects helped move the initiative from university laboratories towards industrial vehicle engineering.

The most significant expression of that ambition is the Kiira Vehicle Plant in the Jinja Industrial and Business Park. Designed with an annual production capacity of up to 5,000 vehicles, the facility features dedicated body, paint, chassis, trim and final assembly shops, alongside quality inspection facilities. It is designed to support large-scale vehicle manufacturing rather than merely assembling imported components.

Kiira Motors has also moved towards commercial production through its Kayoola electric vehicle range, particularly electric buses intended to support cleaner public transport. The company has outlined plans to expand deployment across Ugandan urban centres while pursuing opportunities in regional markets.

Its longer-term ambitions include increasing local content in vehicle production, developing domestic component supply chains and exploring electric vehicle battery manufacturing. Plans to diversify into additional vehicle categories, including pick-ups, SUVs and commercial vehicles, also point to the broader industrial ambitions attached to the project.

Gavin Catto, chief executive of Green Cat Hydrogen (GCH), said it was a "major milestone" for its project at Chapelcross near Annan which would create dozens of jobs.

A plan for turning the area into a "green energy hub" was unveiled in 2024, backed by funding from the Scottish and UK governments.

Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using renewable energy through a process called electrolysis.

The hydrogen it produces can then be used as a fuel where the main byproduct of burning it is water.

title: BAAJA Permitting Bill Passes Senate - Rigzone
description:
“The bill limits the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act and expedites environmental reviews,” the summary states.
“Additionally, the bill addresses numerous aspects of energy infrastructure permitting,” the summary says.
“BAAJA offers a generational opportunity to cut through permitting delays and lower costs across America without compromising critical environmental protections,” Bradbury added.
“A more efficient and reliable permitting system will help attract investment, support good-paying American jobs and bring more energy projects online,” he added.
A statement posted on the Independent Petroleum Association of America’s (IPAA) X page commenting on the BAAJA Senate passage noted that “with bipartisan, bicameral, and presidential support, meaningful reform is closer than ever”.
text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), also known as S. 5653, has passed the Senate with a vote of 62-33, the National Association of Counties (NACO) website revealed.

The bill still needs to pass the House and go to the President to become law, according to the Congress.gov site, which highlighted that the bill is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats.

A summary of the bill included on the Congress site states that S. 5653 modifies federal permitting processes, including environmental reviews, to expedite a wide range of projects.

“The bill limits the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act and expedites environmental reviews,” the summary states.

This includes “further limiting the types of federal actions that trigger environmental review, narrowing the range of alternatives that must be considered in environmental reviews, and exempting additional types of projects from environmental review,” the summary outlines.

The summary notes that the bill also establishes deadlines for issuing permits once an environmental review is complete and limits permit obligations under the Clean Water Act.

This includes “narrowing the scope of review for water quality certifications, extending the term for permits issued under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, and limiting the time period for review of permits for discharges of dredged or fill materials,” the summary states.

The summary goes on to note that the bill also modifies requirements concerning threatened or endangered species to expedite the review of federal permits, including by shortening the timeline for certain consultations.

“Additionally, the bill addresses numerous aspects of energy infrastructure permitting,” the summary says. This includes “expanding the authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue construction permits for certain interstate electricity transmission projects; directing FERC to establish ratepayer protections related to certain large computational loads (e.g. data centers); removing permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land; and accelerating renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, or offshore energy projects,” the summary adds.

This bill also limits the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act, including by limiting what types of projects trigger review, the summary concludes.

In a statement sent to Rigzone, the American Exploration & Production Council (AXPC) applauded the Senate “for taking decisive action to address America’s affordability challenges by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act”.

“With Americans demanding common-sense solutions to lower costs, AXPC urged the House to build on this bipartisan momentum and pass comprehensive permitting reform before the end of the year,” the AXPC added.

In this statement, AXPC CEO Anne Bradbury said, “AXPC applauds the Senate for taking decisive bipartisan action to remove longstanding barriers to American energy and infrastructure development”.

“BAAJA offers a generational opportunity to cut through permitting delays and lower costs across America without compromising critical environmental protections,” Bradbury added.

“With meaningful relief for American families within reach, we respectfully urge the House to send BAAJA to the President’s desk before the end of the year,” Bradbury continued.

In another statement sent to Rigzone commenting on the Senate passage of BAAJA, National Ocean Industries President Erik Milito said the bipartisan Senate vote “is a major step toward making energy and everyday goods and services more affordable for American families and businesses”.

“Permitting delays drive up project costs, discourage investment and make it harder to bring new energy supplies online,” he added.

“Modernizing the permitting process will help meet growing energy demand while easing cost pressures throughout the economy. We applaud Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich for their leadership and commitment to finding common ground on an issue that affects every American,” he continued.

Milito went on to state that permitting certainty means investment certainty.

“Whether it’s offshore oil and gas, offshore wind or other major energy projects, companies need a predictable process and confidence that federal decisions will hold up over time,” he noted.

“A more efficient and reliable permitting system will help attract investment, support good-paying American jobs and bring more energy projects online,” he added.

“We urge the House to quickly send meaningful permitting reform to the President’s desk. This is an opportunity to lower costs for American families and businesses, strengthen domestic energy production and create jobs across the country,” he continued.

In a statement on the BAAJA Senate passage posted on the American Petroleum Institute (API) website, API President and CEO Mike Sommers said the bipartisan Senate vote “marks a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure”.

“We thank Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich for advancing long-overdue reforms,” he added.

A statement posted on the Independent Petroleum Association of America’s (IPAA) X page commenting on the BAAJA Senate passage noted that “with bipartisan, bicameral, and presidential support, meaningful reform is closer than ever”.

“It’s a chance to unlock investment, build critical infrastructure, strengthen energy security, and make progress on affordability for American families,” the statement added.

In a statement posted on its website, the Sierra Club criticized the Senate passage of BAAJA citing “little debate and an insufficient amendment process” and urged the House to reject the bill.

text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul is going nuclear on New York’s looming energy shortage — too late to head off disaster.

Last week, she rolled out her Comprehensive Advanced Nuclear Master Plan, calling to add 5 gigawatts of nuclear-power generation to the state’s existing 3.4 GW.

Nuclear power “is the most sustainable, the most reliable, and ultimately . . . most affordable way we can power our state,” Hochul argues.

She’s largely right about nuclear’s virtues; it can reliably produce energy while emitting no carbon at all.

Then again, people have a habit of freaking out over nearby nuke plants: Westchester hysteria prompted the premature shutdown of Indian Point, while fearful Long Islanders got Shoreham shut down before it ever opened — though the locals are still paying off the costs.

So the gov’s admirably ambitious in aiming to build out more nuke-generated power than the entire country has managed in the past 30 years.

Except that she can’t possibly get it built in time to head off New York’s coming energy trainwreck.

Under the 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, the state’s been racing to eliminate fossil-fuel power with no real replacement juice, even as it passes laws requiring more electricity.

Indeed, the New York Independent System Operator just warned that in six years the state won’t generate enough power to meet demand.

Nuclear plants take a decade or more to build — and Hochul’s plan has neither the federal OKs nor the financing to even start that clock.

Plus, the New York City metro area is already running short: Last summer, The Bronx, Brooklyn and Westchester endured rolling blackouts over a 72-hour period, thanks to insufficient power generation, as Syracuse.com reported.

Plus, aging power plants statewide will be shutting down in coming years, even as Albany still discourages (at least!) new fossil-fuel-plant investment.

That leaves renewables to fill the gap, with scant hope of getting remotely enough wind and solar online in time.

And the Empire State has nowhere near enough battery capacity to store power for when the winds don’t blow or the sun fails to shine — and lacks the transmission lines to get alternative energy where it’s needed.

Give Hochul credit for pushing nuclear despite strong opposition from enviro-radicals.

Every gigawatt will be needed, whenever it gets built; President Donald Trump should do what he can to help speed up the permitting.

But Hochul & Co. need to face reality: Climate mandates, like the city’s Local Law 97, and economic growth (think: data centers) boost the demand for electricity while other climate laws restrict the supply.

That’s a recipe for blackouts — and higher utility rates.

Hochul’s nuclear plan shows she at least understands the problem; it’s no solution, but surely deserves Trump’s help.

text:
Algeria has announced plans to build its first lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant, with a production capacity of five gigawatt-hours, under the leadership of Algerian-born expert Karim Zaghib, who has returned to the country after a career abroad.

The project is part of Algeria's broader efforts to facilitate technology transfer and develop a modern automotive industry. A meeting was held at the presidency to approve the project's next steps, with President Abdelmadjid Tebboune appointing Professor Zaghib, an internationally recognised expert in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology, as project director.

Zaghib will oversee the technical and technological stages of the plant's construction, which will operate under Sonelgaz International, with supervision from the Ministry of Energy.

Speaking after meeting Tebboune, Zaghib, who received Canada's Lionel-Boulet Award in 2019, described the project as vital for Algeria, which he said had all the necessary resources and capabilities, including minerals, iron and chemicals.

"The aim is to accelerate the production of an iron and phosphate alloy that can then be transformed into lithium-ion batteries," he said.

Zaghib explained that lithium batteries were not only used in electric vehicles but also for energy storage. He said Algeria could potentially develop projects to meet domestic demand while also opening up opportunities in international markets across Africa, Europe, North America and Asia, particularly China and other countries.

Developing the technology domestically could create 50,000 jobs, he added.

The Algerian government first considered the development of a domestic lithium industry in November 2025, when it established an inter-ministerial committee bringing together the ministries of hydrocarbons, renewable energy, industry and higher education.

The committee was tasked with developing a vision and strategy for the lithium sector, which the government considers a key component of the country's energy transition and efforts to strengthen industrial and technological sovereignty, make better use of strategic national resources and develop high-value industries of the future.

Since then, Algeria implemented projects to explore lithium deposits, particularly through field studies in the southern provinces of Tamanrasset and In Guezzam, in cooperation with Chinese company Ganfeng Lithium.

The studies revealed promising indications of lithium deposits and several other rare minerals, prompting the government to begin preparing a comprehensive national roadmap covering exploration, extraction and chemical processing.

Pilot projects have also been set up to manufacture the active materials used in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, in partnership with Algerian specialists and experts based abroad.

A strategy announced by Algeria's Ministry of Energy in November 2025 identified developing the lithium industry as a strategic priority, given its direct links to renewable energy and electric transport.

The initiative also aligns with the country's energy transition objectives, which include reducing its carbon footprint, diversifying sources of national income and building a knowledge-based economy centred on clean technology.

text:
This story was produced and originally published by Wisconsin Watch, a nonprofit, nonpartisan newsroom. It was made possible by donors like you.

Wisconsin’s electricity needs are on track to skyrocket. Utilities plan to spend billions of dollars to keep up, and ratepayers — residents, businesses and data center operators — will pick up the bill.

The three-member Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, is responsible for guarding ratepayers’ wallets from unreasonable spending, but Wisconsin law gives it relatively little sway over how utilities plan for the future.

The commission can review proposed power plants on a case-by-case basis, but not as part of a broader blueprint for keeping the lights on as affordably as possible.

That hasn’t always been the case. Bureaucratic gridlock and a near-blackout prompted Wisconsin lawmakers to scrap a more hands-on approach to energy planning three decades ago.

Utilities don’t mourn its loss. Ratepayer advocates, however, argue the hands-off approach that followed caused Wisconsin’s electricity prices to climb faster than necessary.

A flurry of new power plant projects spurred in part by the data center boom is pushing that once-arcane disagreement into the public eye, and regulators themselves are now taking a side.

Wisconsin once gave regulators broad planning power

Investor-owned utilities generally operate as regulated monopolies: State and federal commissions grant them exclusive rights to sell electricity to consumers within a defined territory in exchange for government oversight of their rates and infrastructure projects.

That basic model dates back more than a century in Wisconsin, which formed its Public Service Commission — among the nation’s first utility regulators — in 1907.

The mass adoption of air conditioning and the rise of nuclear power complicated the picture in the mid-20th century.

Wisconsin lawmakers responded in the 1970s by empowering the Public Service Commission to take the lead on energy planning, hoping to steer utilities toward the most cost-effective path to meeting skyrocketing electricity demand.

Those powers took shape as the “Advanced Plan”: 20-year road maps for utilities to meet electricity needs. Working in two-year cycles alongside consumer advocates and other players, the commission could revise the road map to fit its priorities, and especially to save ratepayers money.

“This approach requires that the utilities focus on the most cost effective means of meeting customers’ energy service needs,” the commissioners explained in a 1987 biannual report.

Utilities have a strong incentive to build new power plants. Ratepayers pay for newly built plants, along with a commission-approved “rate of return” on every dollar spent on the projects, passed along to the utility’s shareholders. The commission could use the Advanced Plan to reconfigure utilities’ construction plans in search of savings. Later iterations embraced demand-side fixes, trimming future energy needs by incentivizing customers to switch to energy-efficient appliances or run factories at off-peak hours.

The PSC used its planning power to chip away at utility monopolies in 1989 by beginning to open utility-owned transmission lines to other power producers. Wisconsin was an early adopter of an open transmission system, hoping to keep prices in check by encouraging competition in the electricity market. State lawmakers later directed utilities to pass control of their transmission infrastructure to a new, independent company to protect other power producers’ access to the grid. That company, now called the American Transmission Company, was the country’s first multi-state, transmission-only utility.

The PSC went further in 1993, inviting third-party developers to bid for power plant projects outlined in utilities’ long-term plans. Commissioners awarded a natural gas plant in Whitewater to a New York-based developer later that year, saving We Energies’ customers an estimated $66 million.

Other states deregulated their electricity markets entirely. Chaos ensued, most notably in California, where flawed execution, price gouging and a drought caused regional blackouts, a major utility bankruptcy filing and billions of dollars in economic losses.

Lawmakers let utilities take the lead

Wisconsin didn’t copy California’s experiment. It did, however, scrap the Advanced Plan.

Utilities argued comprehensive planning was cumbersome and prone to gridlock, blaming it for a slowdown in power plant and transmission construction in the mid-1990s. Some commission staff also recognized the Advanced Plan’s deficiencies.

“It became an anti-utility regulatory mechanism that put electric reliability at risk,” recalled Randel Pilo, the PSC’s chief energy economist through much of the 1990s.

A close call in the summer of 1997 pushed Wisconsin’s political and business leaders, and even some ratepayer advocacy groups, to rethink the state’s approach. With nuclear power plants in Wisconsin and Illinois unexpectedly offline for repairs, utilities warned that summertime air conditioning use might stretch the state’s supply past its limits and trigger widespread blackouts.

State lawmakers abolished the Advanced Plan the following year. They replaced it with what Pilo called a “regulation-lite” approach, leaving planning for Wisconsin’s energy future mostly in utilities’ hands.

The PSC still considers the cost of and market justification for new power plants, but not as part of a broader strategy for balancing affordability and reliability.

Utilities made the most of the new landscape. We Energies embarked on a $7 billion “Power the Future” construction spree only a few years later — the largest energy buildout in Wisconsin history. The present power plant construction boom may surpass that record if projections of data centers’ energy needs prove accurate.

Shift to ‘regulation-lite’ approach

Ratepayer advocacy groups and some independent energy developers argue the “regulation-lite” approach to energy planning is taking a toll on Wisconsinites’ budgets.

“Without a robust planning process, we don’t have balance and we’re left with higher bills,” said Tom Content, executive director of the Wisconsin Citizens Utility Board. Under the current system, he argues, “utilities present their spending plans to investors eager for the higher profits that come from their build-build-build agenda.”

Had regulators retained greater energy planning authority, Content believes they might have more closely scrutinized We Energies’ investments in coal-fired generators just before the fracking boom made natural gas cheap and abundant in the late 2000s. Wisconsin’s average electricity rates — the second-lowest in the Midwest in 1998 — soared during the Power the Future buildout. They are the region’s second-highest as of August.

Former Republican Sen. Robert Cowles, a longtime ally of ratepayer advocacy groups who chaired the Senate’s energy committee at several points in his 38-year Senate tenure, voted alone against the 1998 bill. He told Wisconsin Watch that preserving advanced planning could have curbed some of those rate hikes by reducing demand through energy efficiency programs.

“To the extent that we can avoid building additional capacity, it saves us money,” he said.

Skeptics of the current system don’t uniformly oppose construction. A 2026 study by Advanced Energy United — a clean energy trade group that supports comprehensive planning — estimated that We Energies’ customers could have saved roughly $150 per year between 2021 and 2024 had the utility replaced its Elm Road plant with renewables and battery storage, in part by avoiding the cost of fueling and maintaining older coal and natural gas plants.

Utilities maintain that the PSC already has sufficient authority to protect ratepayer interests.

“State regulatory staff, intervenors and the public thoroughly evaluate our projects, including their costs compared to alternatives, environmental impacts, and the actual need for these new generation resources,” We Energies spokesperson Brendan Conway wrote in an email. “This robust review process ensures customers are protected every step of the way.”

How Wisconsin compares to neighboring states

Wisconsin’s current approach to energy planning sets it apart from most neighboring states — and most of the country.

Minnesota’s Public Utilities Commission has required utilities to develop comprehensive plans since the early 1990s. Illinois adopted the practice earlier this year, and Michigan lawmakers re-introduced comprehensive planning a decade ago during a transitional period in the energy sector.

“We knew that there were a number of plants that were scheduled for retirement,” said Michigan Public Service Commission chair Dan Scripps, and “a better planning process was needed” to replace them.

Michigan’s residential electricity prices nevertheless remain the highest in the Midwest, but supporters of the state’s planning approach argue other factors obscure the policy’s positive results.

“Michigan’s energy bills are driven much more by distribution system upgrades than by generation costs,” said Michigan Energy Innovation Council President Laura Sherman, citing years of deferred power line maintenance for power lines. “Without the long-term planning and competition,” she added, “I think we’d see higher generation costs as well.”

“It is effectively impossible to know what rates would be” had Michigan not adopted comprehensive energy planning, said Jonathan Kim, a Chicago-based researcher with the watchdog Energy and Policy Institute. Any number of variables — even weather — can skew comparisons between states that take a hands-on approach to planning and those that do not.

Iowans, for instance, pay the lowest retail electricity prices in the Midwest even without a comprehensive energy planning process. Kim attributes those low prices to Iowa’s early and speedy adoption of renewables, which spare the state’s ratepayers from “fossil fuel price instability.” Renewables, and especially wind turbines, account for roughly 60 percent of Iowa’s in-state electricity generation, compared to about 12 percent in Michigan and Wisconsin.

Kim also underscored that utilities can take advantage of the long-term energy planning process at ratepayers’ expense.

“We’ve seen utilities routinely overproject demand growth or need for new projects so that the amount they have to build seems greater,” he said. If regulators approve a utility’s construction to-do list in one go, Kim added, “the incentive for utilities to cheat the system, as well as the need for heightened scrutiny and rigorous ratepayer advocacy, grow even stronger.”

Data center boom revives planning debate

With a massive energy buildout on the near horizon, even Wisconsin’s regulators are joining the push to rethink the state’s energy planning paradigm.

The Public Service Commission’s most recent draft strategic energy assessment — a biennial forecast introduced as a nonbinding Advanced Plan substitute — projects Wisconsin’s energy use will climb by roughly 40 percent over the next five years, driven mostly by new data centers.

We Energies’ parent company alone expects to spend nearly $47.5 billion on new infrastructure over that time frame.

Those plans await commission approval on a project-by-project basis. Among them: a pair of natural gas plants in southeastern Wisconsin.

We Energies isn’t building the plants itself. That responsibility falls to Invenergy, the nation’s largest independent energy infrastructure developer.

The same 1998 law that axed the Advanced Plan also streamlined permitting for independent “merchant plants” built to sell electricity on the wholesale market — a move lawmakers believed would spur competition. Invenergy’s proposed plants in Kenosha and Walworth counties qualify for that streamlined review, preventing commissioners from scrutinizing their price tags.

Invenergy brought the plants to the commission for approval last year. We Energies promptly applied to buy the facilities to power its data center customers for a combined $2.3 billion; that price tag has since climbed to roughly $2.8 billion.

While We Energies must still prove the natural gas plants would provide more reasonable prices than generators powered by a different fuel, it need not demonstrate that Invenergy offered a better deal than competing developers. Microsoft, which plans to “subscribe” to the Kenosha County plant’s power and pay for its purchase, declined to comment.

Wisconsin utilities have used the same maneuver at least a half-dozen times since 2018, mostly to develop solar and wind farms.

“When developers like Invenergy develop a project, they take on all the risk and responsibility of making that project viable, that protects our customers,” Conway wrote.

Commission Chair Summer Strand isn’t convinced. Speaking at the commission’s Oct. 15 hearing on Invenergy’s applications, Strand argued Wisconsin’s “piecemeal, often whack-a-mole approach” to energy planning enables the end-around.

Strand and her fellow commissioners emphasized that current law leaves them unable to consider the We Energies-Invenergy deal as a package, even if doing so could help identify a more cost-effective alternative. The commission approved Invenergy’s permits last month; it has yet to weigh in on We Energies’ purchase plans.

“The deficiencies in the current framework are ripe for legislative action,” Strand said.

Outgoing Gov. Tony Evers proposed granting the PSC comprehensive planning powers in his most recent draft budget, but the Republican-controlled Legislature rejected the provision. The question now falls to Gov.-elect David Crowley and a new Democratic-majority Legislature.

Pilo likewise believes Wisconsin’s energy planning model needs “modest reform,” even as he recalls the Advanced Plan’s flaws. In his view, a “major transformation” in Wisconsin’s energy sector calls for a planning model more focused on affordability, competition and “public stewardship.”

Ratepayer groups enthusiastically agree.

“It’s long overdue that we give the state the tools it lacks,” Content wrote in an October press release. “Until we do, the PSC is trying to guide the state down the ‘energy future highway’ without a GPS, or even a map.”

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct a figure related to planned infrastructure spending. WEC Energy Group, the parent company of We Energies, plans to spend $47.5 billion across its portfolio. A previous version incorrectly attributed that figure to We Energies alone.

text:
There are gaps in Australia's battery capability, a CSIRO engineer says. Photo: Dan Himbrechts/AAP PHOTOS

Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products.

Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries.

The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March.

Around 600,000 home batteries have been installed across Australia since 2025. (Simon Dallinger/AAP PHOTOS)

Speaking at an event called Australia's Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials.

"We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries - we're the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it," she said.

"However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we're actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries."

Advertisement

Ad

The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them.

Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said.

Australia is on a path to a bright future with energy security, a scientist says. (Simon Dallinger/AAP PHOTOS)

The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil.

"We do have some gaps in Australia's capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone," Mr de Looze said.

text:
The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands.

The reality is different. As it became clear toward 1945 that the second world war was moving toward complete allied victory, the leaders of the three great allied powers —Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin — naturally devoted more of their attention to the delineation and security architecture of postwar Europe. Understandings reached on the postwar status of European countries occupied respectively by the Western allies and the Soviet Union served mostly to ratify existing facts on the ground.

It was a concession to reality, not to Stalin, to acknowledge that the Soviet army, by defeating the German army in the East, had already gained control over most of Eastern Europe whether Western leaders recognized this control or not — and, alas, whether the populations of eastern Europe liked it or not.

Short of a new war with the USSR — that U.S. and British populations and soldiers would have categorically rejected and that they would probably have lost — FDR and Churchill had no ability to challenge, let alone attempt to reverse, Moscow’s assertion of a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe. Recognition of that assessment should therefore be seen not as a betrayal but as both inevitable and an act of prudence. Yalta was a first step towards establishing the geopolitical guardrails that later helped prevent the Cold War in Europe from spiraling into open and cataclysmic conflict and laid the foundations for U.S. containment strategy that prevented further Soviet expansion without recourse to war.

The Yalta comparison is also a false, and even ridiculous description of what is being discussed today. Russia would be completely incapable of occupying eastern Europe, even if it had any desire to do so, which it does not. The Russian army has proved incapable of conquering most of Ukraine. The only Russian demand for additional territorial control is the 2,000 square miles of the Donbas still occupied by Ukraine. That really does not compare to Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the other states subjected to Soviet communism after World War II.

Nor is China in any position to imitate the U.S. in 1945 and occupy Japan, South Korea and the Philippines. The cliche "if you're not at the table, you're on the menu” that so often accompanies the contemporary “Yalta 2.0” discourse is therefore obviously untrue.

Even during the Cold War, Yugoslavia, India, as well as swathes of Africa and the Middle East were able to practice non-alignment — effectively opting out of having to choose a side in the bipolar competition — without being carved up by Washington or Moscow. That is very much the desire, and the ability, of most states in the world today, including for example former Soviet states in Central Asia, which have no desire at all to choose between Russian, Chinese or U.S. hegemony. Their declared strategy is a “multi-vector” one.

Let us grant, for the sake of argument, the fantastical notion that the White House is keen on somehow “handing over” former Soviet and Warsaw Pact countries to Russia or East Asian states to China. Who in these two regions would possibly go along with such a scheme, and how can they be compelled to do so in the absence of military conquest?

The Russian demand for the withdrawal of NATO forces to the lines they occupied in the 1990s does not require the new NATO members of eastern Europe to leave NATO, or to disarm their own forces, let alone that they submit to regime change and Russian political control ( in any case a ridiculous idea, for anyone who knows the Poles and the Balts).

It should rather be seen as the first move in a new disarmament process; and NATO, instead of rejecting it out of hand, should come back with proposals of its own whereby limits in NATO forces on Russia’s borders should be matched by strict reciprocal limits on Russian forces in Belarus and Kaliningrad.

The model and inspiration should be seen not as “Yalta” but the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaties of the 1990s. The common NATO line is now that “Russia has no say in European security.” No sane person would have said that during the Cold War, and today, alas, hundreds of thousands of dead in Ukraine also demonstrate the opposite.

In any case, the Trilateral summit in Shenzhen did not talk about any of these issues. The official statement that followed the talks contained just two elements, both of which should be seen as valuable for humanity. The summit’s call for new nuclear limitation agreements, however vaguely formulated, should be seen as a tentative first step to a restoration of the treaties agreed by the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. in the later years of the Cold War — not to end that war, but to try to ensure that it did not escalate into universal catastrophe.

More generally, the summit symbolized a truth of vast significance: that if basic peace and order in the world is to be secured, then this will depend above all on reasonably peaceful relations between the world’s most powerful states, secured by agreements regulating those relations.

So if there is a legacy of the Cold War to which we should look, it is that of great powers assuming a degree of shared responsibility for maintaining a stable, working international system to be passed down to future generations. The Shenzhen summit represents a significant first step in that direction.

Finally, on the score of spheres of influence, it is perhaps worth noting that one is tacitly accepted by virtually the entire world, including China. Nobody is challenging the U.S. insistence on absolute military hegemony in Central America and the Caribbean, because they know that any attempt to do so would bring ferocious U.S. retaliation. Nor have the Europeans, for all their supposed commitment to a “rules-based order” pushed back in any way against the extreme hardening of the Monroe Doctrine under Donald Trump, as witnessed with regard to Venezuela, Cuba, and alleged drug traffickers.

Fortunately, there is no chance whatsoever of Russia or China being able to follow this particular U.S. rule.

Schumer went on to criticize the President for not securing any concessions from his counterparts, including on curbing Chinese espionage or preventing Beijing and Moscow from helping Iran target American troops.

The emphasis of Schumer’s remarks was striking given that dissatisfaction with Trump’s foreign policy and its economic ramifications helped propel Democrats back into the Senate majority earlier this month.

As Democrats debate whether their electoral victory presents an opportunity to rethink the party's foreign policy, Schumer's remarks suggest that some of its longtime leaders remain wedded to an older approach.

That tension is also emerging as a central dividing line in the contest to lead the new Democratic majority. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who announced last week that he would challenge Schumer, has made their disagreements over foreign policy, and in particular over how to approach the issues in the Middle East, as central to his pitch.

The two senators represent competing visions of the Democratic Party’s future. Faiz Shakir, a senior advisor to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has supported Van Hollen’s challenge, recently described him to NPR as a“pragmatic progressive” who is “going to know what the people of this country are asking us to do at this moment” and “can bring a lot of factions of the party together.”

Much of the debate is over how Democrats should approach using their power of the purse to cut off funding for the war in Iran before the new Congress is seated in January. Van Hollen and a number of his Democratic colleagues have called on the party to insist on a government funding bill that excludes money for the Iran war, which they say will force Trump and the Republicans to decide whether to risk a shutdown to continue the war. Other Democrats argue that a shutdown would be politically risky for the party, and that Democrats should wait until they are in the majority to force the issue.

Schumer, for his part, has not clarified his stance, as he continues to say that the war must end and a shutdown must be avoided.

Schumer's reluctance to say that he will prioritize ending the war has renewed scrutiny on his longstanding hawkishness toward Iran. Many foreign policy analysts and congressional critics have highlighted his place as one of a few Democratic opponents to the Obama-era Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), commonly known as the Iran nuclear deal, as one clear example.

Van Hollen has made this contrast central to his leadership campaign. “I don't see how after an election like this where ending the war and bringing down prices was a priority, we can cast a vote to fund the war,” he said recently. “And of course, Senator Schumer was one of the folks who originally opposed President Obama and the JCPOA, but I think the caucus wants to bring this war to an end,”

Progressives have also condemned Schumer’s approach in the lead-up to the war, during which he attacked Trump’s diplomacy with Tehran and, critics say, did not act quickly enough to slow the president’s march to war in February.

On Thursday, during his floor speech, Schumer questioned what “commitments” Trump made and what he “gave away” over dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, echoing his controversial June 2025 accusations that Trump was negotiating “side deals” and “folding on Iran.”

The disagreements extend beyond Iran. Van Hollen has taken a leading role in the effort to remove provisions of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would deepen military and intelligence cooperation between the United States and Israel.

“The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology,” Van Hollen and 11 Senate colleagues wrote in a recent letter to congressional leadership. “If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement.”

The letter further argues that the provisions would shift U.S. military assistance to Israel to more “opaque, less discernible avenues,” which the Senators call particularly troubling given Israel's conduct in Gaza, the West Bank, and elsewhere in the region.

Schumer has not publicly commented on these provisions, but is seen as one of Israel’s strongest supporters in Congress. In 2025, he told the New York Times that his “job...is to keep the left pro-Israel.” He has repeatedly called himself a “guardian of Israel” throughout his congressional career, which spans 45 years.

Their perspectives on the U.S-Israel relationship appears to be a key dividing line between the two senators. Van Hollen was first elected as an establishment-supported, Israel-friendly candidate, but his views have shifted. “Times have changed in a lot of ways, where the Democratic base has changed in a lot of ways, and he has changed along with it,” Yousef Munayyer of the Arab Center recently told The Intercept. “I don’t know that the same can be said for a lot of other folks, like Chuck Schumer.”

Independent trackers show that the sitting minority leader currently has more support, though the tallies remain close. The vote for majority leader is expected to take place in a secret ballot on Dec. 1.

But what a difference a year can make with Trump. On October 21, U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel publicly described the relationship as experiencing “turbulence.” Lee’s government, for its part, has tried to downplay recent tensions, arguing that overheated domestic politics in both countries need not undermine the strong foundation of the alliance. As South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told Parliament in late October, “When you’re in turbulence, fasten your seat belt and it won’t be a problem.”

In truth, some of the turbulence is of Seoul’s own making. In March, for example, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly identified a North Korean uranium enrichment facility, potentially compromising sensitive sources and methods. The Lee government insists that the information was already public, but Washington disagrees and has retaliated by restricting certain satellite-derived intelligence about North Korea and excluded Seoul from a trilateral meeting on North Korean cyber threats.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has complained about intelligence sharing broadly with Seoul, and South Korean Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha acknowledged as recently as last month that his government had not fully addressed Washington’s concerns.

South Korea has also been slow in deciding how to invest its pledged $350 billion, angering Trump in the process. For instance, Trump wants Seoul to invest roughly $54 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project, but Lee’s government has questioned its commercial viability. Although he has expressed confidence that South Korea will eventually follow through, Trump has made vague threats to resume tariffs if the deals remain stalled.

Separately, South Korean regulators imposed a fine of $423 million on Coupang, a U.S.-listed e-commerce company, following a massive consumer data breach. The Trump administration and congressional Republicans were outraged by the move, calling it discrimination against American companies, while the Lee administration justified the measure to protect consumer privacy data.

But the Trump administration shares much of the blame for the increasingly contentious bilateral relationship. For one thing, even though Washington and Seoul already agreed in June 2025 to reduce tariffs from 25% to 15% in 2025, Trump periodically threatens to raise tariff rates again to 25% when he gets angry about something. This has surprised and frustrated South Korean officials, who may no longer see Washington as a reliable strategic ally. And perhaps neither do the South Korean people. According to a Pew Research survey from August, 55% of them hold an unfavorable view of the United States — the highest such mark in more than 20 years.

North Korea poses a bilateral challenge as well. To be sure, both Trump and Lee want to prioritize renewed engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un rather than deterrence. But the Trump administration’s preferred approach differs from Seoul’s. Trump surprised South Korea by shortening the annual bilateral military drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Guardian, just hours before they began. He argued that they were unnecessarily provocative toward Kim, whom Trump hopes will join him in a summit.

Although he publicly accepted Trump’s decision to cut back combined military exercises, Lee would rather derive diplomatic leverage from enhanced military preparedness against North Korea, and the deterrence that comes with it, prior to negotiations. Trump further blamed South Korea for not contributing to the U.S. naval operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, in turn questioning why Washington continues to defend South Korea on the peninsula.

Deepening disagreements over China represent yet another irritant. The Trump administration clearly seeks greater “flexibility” in how it uses the approximately 28,500 U.S. troops deployed to South Korea. Rather than focusing exclusively on North Korea, Washington has publicly intimated that China could be the target of their future military operations, and that Seoul would be expected to support that mission.

Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge “Bridge” Colby, for example, visited Seoul in January and gave a speech at the Sejong Institute that curiously did not mention North Korea at all, and instead, replaced it with multiple references to countering China. To the shock of South Korean officials, Trump’s National Security Strategy, released last November, neglected to mention North Korea either and focused instead on the need for South Korea to help the U.S. and Japan secure the First Island Chain — a clear reference to containing China. Although Trump’s National Defense Strategy from January did reference North Korea, it avoided stating that denuclearization was still a U.S. priority and put the responsibility to deal with the regime more squarely on Seoul, with limited American support.

Trump’s submarine and shipbuilding deals are also in limbo. On the submarines, Trump wants them built at the South Korean defense firm Hanwha’s shipyard in Philadelphia, but the Lee government argues that South Korea offers more appropriate shipyards because they are already outfitted with advanced submarine-building capabilities. There is also the question surrounding the enriched nuclear fuel and associated sensitive technologies, which Seoul wants Washington to provide. But rules governing the bilateral relationship currently do not permit such transfers without specific exemptions or additional authorizations.

When the submarine deal was first announced in October 2025, none of these issues had been properly considered by the Trump administration, provoking the current disputes. And on broader shipbuilding, South Korea’s $150 billion financial commitment has largely stalled. Indeed, the president’s Make American Shipbuilding Great Again (MASGA) initiative has yielded zero concrete projects, embarrassing Trump, who wants to reenergize the U.S. defense industrial base and add manufacturing jobs. Progress on MASGA has also been hampered by a mix of legal, political, and financial obstacles.

Finally, the fallout from the September 2025 ICE raids on South Korean workers at the Hyundai-LG battery plant in the United States continues. Although Seoul wrapped up its internal investigation without retaliating against the U.S. government, attorneys representing more than 300 of the workers, who were allegedly shackled and abused during the ordeal, are now pursuing administrative damages, possibly a precursor to civil lawsuits, against the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI, and others. The political rhetoric surrounding the case became heated on both sides as the legal process continues to unfold.

Despite the growing tensions between them, South Korea and the U.S. remain staunch allies, and in fact, the Trump administration has referred to Seoul as a “model ally,” especially because of its increased defense spending. Lee and Trump reportedly spoke about future diplomatic engagements on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China this week. But difficulties remain, and the next two years under Trump and Lee could prove even more turbulent when it comes to trade, investment, military cooperation, and foreign policy.

Additionally, while many have interpreted the midterm elections as a rebuke of Trump’s foreign policy, they are unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea relations in substantive ways. The president typically has the lead on foreign policy, and lame-duck presidents tend to intensify their focus on it to secure their legacy. For South Korea, this likely means more, not less, of Trump, adding to Seoul’s urgency to somehow figure him out and stop making unforced errors.
