This leaves these firms two options: interconnect into a grid that can and will achieve these high reliability standards (without risk of curtailment) or build their own power off-grid. While the economics of building enough generation with the necessary redundancy for maintenance and unscheduled downtime is expensive compared to on-grid power, in comparison to other capital expenditures of hyperscalers, it is marginal.

If ERCOT can maintain reliability without threat of curtailment, and provide power quickly enough, it can offer a much better deal for both hyperscalers and consumers than islanded data centers. Data centers that bring revenue for reliable generation on the grid will lower costs in the long run for all consumers (due to economies of scale) while also ensuring that the proper investments are made in resource adequacy, transmission and distribution, and grid resiliency.

The best outcome, for the facility, the grid, and ratepayers alike, is not a choice between these poles but a hybrid of them: data centers that interconnect and bring firm generation and storage with them. The facility gets the reliability and speed the queue alone cannot yet deliver; ERCOT gains capacity it can call on during scarcity rather than losing it behind a fence; and ratepayers get grid reinforcement financed by private capital instead of socialized across the rate base. Texas policy should treat this hybrid posture as the default to enable—not a concession to tolerate—and measure every interconnection rule against whether it makes that posture easier or harder to choose.

ERCOT’s Batch Zero process, established through PGRR 145 (ERCOT, 2026e) and NPRR 1325 (ERCOT, 2026f) and approved by the PUCT in June 2026, was designed as a one-time, transitional framework that replaces ERCOT’s old case-by-case study with a single, system-wide batch study—a triage mechanism for an interconnection queue that has swelled to more than 470 GW. It also carries forward the flexible interconnection principles of PGRR 134, giving dispatchable and self-supplied loads a faster path to energization (Sharma Frank, 2025). These are real improvements, but the process asks developers for substantial commitments amid substantial uncertainty: a financial security deposit of $50,000 per MW, capacity allocations that may come in below requested levels, and energization timelines that can vary by years and remain subject to curtailment obligations.

The implementation of these changes is also more uncertain due to the ongoing data center audit. ERCOT suspended the Batch Zero study before issuing project classifications, and the PUC granted the good-cause exceptions needed to depart from the original schedule. ERCOT now expects to verify roughly 250 to 300 projects by December 2026 and has said it will not meet its April 2027 deadline to deliver the batch study results (ERCOT, 2026d). More fundamentally, Batch Zero can allocate capacity on paper, but it cannot by itself build the generation and transmission needed to serve the load. It is a procedural reform—a necessary one—but it is not a substitute for the physical buildout that SB 6’s reliability goals ultimately depend on, nor for permanent interconnection rules that can outlast a single batch.

It is precisely this reliability imperative that makes the interconnection question so consequential for the rest of ERCOT’s customer base. A recent Bloomberg New Energy Finance analysis found that 100 GW of on-site gas-burning capacity—equivalent to 18% of all existing U.S. natural gas generation—is planned to power data centers across the country (Rissman and Gimon, 2026). Hyperscalers are not pursuing private generation out of indifference to the grid; they are pursuing it because the grid has not kept pace with the speed and reliability their operations require.

Residential electricity users in Texas would benefit tremendously if this massive thermal generation buildout was integrated into the broader ERCOT grid. Not only would reliability increase to the extremely high standards data centers require, but consumers would also benefit from reliable power and transmission brought to their grid at the expense of hyperscalers. The lesson is not that off-grid gas should be banned or discouraged; it is that when interconnection cannot match the speed and certainty hyperscalers require, the generation gets built anyway—but outside the framework where it could support ERCOT during scarcity. The policy goal should be to make grid-connected development the path of least resistance, so that data center demand leads to more reliable generation on the grid, rather than permanently off it, while also facilitating better management of existing variable generation.

Policy Recommendations

The preceding analysis establishes that data centers can be either significant assets or significant liabilities to the ERCOT grid depending on how they are integrated. This section will translate that analysis into specific, actionable policy recommendations.

Recommendation 1: Reform ERCOT’s Load Forecasting Methodology and Plan for Long-term Demand

ERCOT’s planning challenge is a two-sided one: avoid underbuilding for facilities that will consume every megawatt they contract and likely more, while avoiding overbuilding for projects that never break ground.

An estimated 10–20% of proposed data centers ultimately get built on the schedules reflected in interconnection queue filings. ERCOT already models scenarios that count only 50%—or none—of unsigned “officer letter” load, and reduced large-load projections by roughly 50–55% in its 2025 adjusted forecast (ERCOT, 2025c; Watson, 2025). In that forecast, ERCOT reduced data-center load requests to 49.8% of submitted value and officer-letter load to 55.4% (ERCOT, 2025d). While applying a discount factor based on historical experience is a good start, we recommend an evolving, probability-weighted queue forecast rather than a static discount factor.

Here is how this refinement could work. Each project in the interconnection queue would carry a realization probability that updates as it clears observable, verifiable milestones: executed site control (ownership or lease rather than options), interconnection agreement execution with financial security posted, air and water permits, long-lead equipment procurement (transformers, turbines, and switchgear are the binding constraints), committed equity and debt financing, and construction notice-to-proceed. An early-stage filing with none of these commitments might carry a 5–10% weight; a project with an executed interconnection agreement, posted security, and equipment on order approaches certainty.

ERCOT is already beginning to collect much of this information through the Batch Zero eligibility criteria, which distinguish projects by maturity and commitment, so the incremental data burden of maintaining such a forecast is modest. Publishing the result as a probability-weighted band, updated quarterly, would give transmission planners, generators, and policymakers a shared, defensible view of demand that neither overreacts to speculative filings nor underestimates committed load.

Equally important, ERCOT should not assume that efficiency improvements will meaningfully reduce the electricity consumption of data centers over time. While individual chips and cooling systems are becoming more efficient, the history of computing suggests these gains will not lead to lower per-site demand. As power-per-rack falls, operators increase rack density, deploy more capable next-generation chips, and expand total computing capacity to chase increasing demand.

Efficiency gains have historically moderated projected consumption growth without reducing absolute consumption, and there is no reason to assume this pattern will change with the current wave of new load. ERCOT’s planning models should reflect this reality by assuming that contracted load will be fully utilized, and in many cases exceeded in the future, as facilities scale into their buildout and adapt to power-intensive new chips to remain commercially viable. Striking this balance is critical to avoid unnecessary costs and ensure long-term reliability.

Recommendation 2: Market Reform to Support Firm Generation and Load Flexibility

The current ERCOT market structure inadequately compensates firm, dispatchable generation, a structural flaw that predates the data center boom but is acutely exposed by it. The solution is not to force data centers into curtailment frameworks designed for aluminum smelters or other flexible loads; it is to reform the market so that the thermal generation data centers require is financially viable to build and operate within ERCOT.

ERCOT and the Texas Legislature should pursue two parallel tracks. First, market reforms should ensure that firm, dispatchable generation—primarily natural gas—receives adequate compensation for the capacity and reliability services it provides. To accomplish this goal, either the energy market must be modified to end the practice of paying all resources, whether dispatchable or variable, the same market price, or a program must be developed to ensure all resources in the energy market meet the same reliability standard. Texas has roughly the same amount of combined gas, coal, and nuclear capacity that it did 10 years ago, despite substantial demand growth (ERCOT, n.d.). Data center load is the demand signal that can justify the upfront cost of that investment, but only if the market structure rewards it.

Natural gas is what makes the first track practical on data center timelines. It is the only firm resource that can be developed at the speed and scale this load requires, and Texas’s in-state supply, pipeline network, and services workforce give it an advantage no other market can replicate. The binding constraint is not fuel but equipment: gas turbine order books now stretch years into the future, which means the projects that will serve load late this decade must reach commitment now—and developers will not commit amid regulatory uncertainty. Policy certainty around interconnection treatment, netting rules, and cost allocation is, in effect, generation policy. Structured to interconnect rather than island, this gas fleet also does double duty: serving its facility day to day while standing as capacity ERCOT can call on during emergency conditions, exactly as SB 6 contemplates.

Second, large load customers should be permitted and encouraged through price signals to self-manage grid stress through resources such as battery storage and additional on-site generation as an alternative to traditional curtailment obligations. A data center that can ride through a two-hour peak event on batteries or internal workload shifting via portable agreements will impose less stress on ERCOT than one that either curtails inference or demands uninterrupted grid power with no flexibility at all. Facilities with these redundancies in place should be given priority over those who are unable to manage load during peaks or outages.

Energy storage is the hinge that makes both tracks work and is a necessary component of the data center energy stack given the rapid demand fluctuations and high reliability needs that AI data centers present. On the generation side, batteries bridge the seconds-to-minutes gap between a grid disturbance and turbine response, allowing a gas-anchored facility to meet Tier IV reliability without overbuilding turbines for redundancy alone. On the load side, storage is what turns flexibility commitments from a workload risk into an engineering specification: a facility with hours of on-site storage can ride through a curtailment window or a peak event without touching inference workloads, which is precisely why hyperscalers will accept flexible interconnection terms they would otherwise refuse. Storage also supplies fast frequency response and other stability services the grid needs more of as thermal inertia declines. Every element of the framework this paper recommends—flexible interconnection, bring-your-own-power, demand volatility management—becomes more credible and cheaper to deliver when storage is part of the stack, and qualification and cost-allocation rules should treat co-located storage accordingly.

This dual approach of firming the grid through market reform while allowing data centers to contribute flexibility on their own operational terms aligns private investment incentives with public reliability needs more effectively than any mandatory curtailment regime could. Hyperscalers will build firm generation when the market rewards it and when doing so is cheaper than the alternative of full islanding. ERCOT’s job is to make sure that calculus points toward the grid.

Recommendation 3: Direct Cost Assignment for Transmission Triggered by Large Load

Cost-causation principles are already reflected in ERCOT’s interconnection procedures for dedicated facilities, but those rules should be extended and clarified so that any transmission upgrade whose primary driver is a large-load interconnection is directly assigned to that customer rather than socialized across the rate base. Financial security requirements should be structured to make that assignment enforceable even if a data center subsequently reduces its load or exits the market. Transmission and distribution utilities should also receive clear regulatory guidance on stranded asset recovery procedures for network infrastructure associated with large-load customers, thus reducing the uncertainty that currently produces conservative, inefficient planning decisions.

The PUC has moved substantially toward this framework already. Proposed 16 TAC §25.194 in Project No. 58481 requires large load customers to fund all direct interconnection costs through a contribution in aid of construction, bars recovery of those costs under any regulated rate, and applies forfeited security as a rate base offset when a customer withdraws (PUC, 2026b). The pending amendments in Project No. 58000 exclude post-effective-date interconnection costs from a TSP’s cost of service and establish a twenty-year minimum billing demand for large load customers (PUC, 2026a).

What remains unresolved is the treatment of network upgrades beyond the interconnection facilities themselves. The Foundation’s comments in Project No. 58481 support the non-refundable interconnection fee but raise two concerns with its structure: the $50,000 per megawatt value appears arbitrary and untethered to any clear cost-causation framework, and routing those payments straight into the rate base dilutes the fee’s purpose of recovering project-specific interconnection costs and protecting against stranded infrastructure risk (PUC, 2026c). The Commission should extend direct assignment to the network upgrades large loads actually trigger, with a per-megawatt cap to prevent excessive allocation in low-interconnection years.

Recommendation 4: Incentivize Grid-Connected Data Centers Near Existing Infrastructure

Hyperscalers seeking expedited grid interconnection should be required to integrate a minimum quantity of firm capacity into the ERCOT system as a condition of that expedited interconnection (a “bring your own capacity” requirement) that benefits all ratepayers rather than just the interconnecting facility. The minimum is best expressed as a performance standard—e.g., firm capacity, verifiable by ERCOT and deliverable during scarcity events—rather than a fixed percentage of nameplate load, which invites gaming through paper capacity and penalizes configurations that deliver equivalent reliability through different mixes of generation and storage. This priority status should also be focused on data centers that site within existing high-capacity transmission corridors rather than requiring new greenfield transmission builds. Where facilities locate should remain a private decision, but policymakers should make the grid-beneficial choice the more economically attractive decision.

This is not a novel proposal. PGRR134, filed in November 2025, would have allowed a large load electing Controllable Load Resource status to be authorized for earlier energization where constraints could be mitigated by dispatching down to its Low Power Consumption level, while still being studied for full capacity on its Load Commissioning Plan timeline and subject to any reliability limits ERCOT specified (Sharma Frank, 2025). It was tabled and withdrawn in May 2026, weeks before the Commission approved the Batch Zero framework, which absorbed part of the same logic by permitting a Provisional Controllable Load Resource election and allowing on-site generation to offset a project’s transmission capacity requirement. But Batch Zero is a one-time transitional process, and its accommodations expire with it; the question PGRR134 raised should be settled as standing policy, not left to the design of each successive batch. The August 2026 suspension of Batch Zero makes the point concrete: the accommodations that let on-site generation offset a project’s transmission requirement are now paused along with the batch that created them.

The model here is Texas’s own refining industry: large industrial loads strengthened the grid for everyone by creating dense, efficient load centers that justified and financed transmission investment. No other state can match Texas’s combination of locally accessible natural gas supply, flexible industrial siting, and an independent market structure purpose-built for large industrial customers, making a broader BYOC framework not just sound policy, but commercially viable in a way it simply would not be elsewhere.

Making this workable requires preserving the regulatory plumbing that now exists. Specifically, ERCOT and the PUC should preserve and expand the Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network framework so that co-located generation can net against facility load; extend expedited study treatment to bring-your-own-generation configurations; and ensure co-located generation is not penalized in transmission cost allocation relative to standalone plants. The refining-industry model only works if the rules make participation cheaper than exit.

The same siting logic unlocks a second stranded asset: generation Texas has already built but cannot use. As documented earlier, ERCOT curtailed more than 8 TWh of wind and solar in 2024—roughly the annual consumption of a gigawatt-scale data center campus. A substantial amount of wind and, particularly, solar is also forcing the curtailment of gas generation that could be operating more efficiently, while suppressing prices and preventing the financing of new gas generation that is sorely needed for reliability. Critically, much of that curtailment reflects renewable generation concentrated in export-constrained zones far from load, a geographic mismatch that transmission projects—including the $33 billion 765-kV STEP—relieve only slowly and partially, but that well-sited demand can absorb directly, where the surplus already is. Ratepayers financed the transmission serving these resources; today the energy is a sunk cost producing nothing.

A data center sited at these pockets of stranded capacity completes the grid-asset loop this paper describes. It absorbs output that would otherwise be curtailed through schedulable workloads and storage, anchors its reliability with on-site gas, balances the entire stack behind a single interconnection, and returns surplus firm capacity to the grid during scarcity. None of this requires building more intermittent generation; it requires putting demand where the existing overbuild already sits. Financing should follow the user-pays principle of Recommendation 3. Interconnection and network upgrades tying stranded generation to large loads can be funded through revenue bonds serviced by the facilities themselves—at no cost to ratepayers or taxpayers.

Recommendation 5: Demand Volatility Management

The ERCOT grid’s ability to maintain reliability depends on matching supply and demand in real time. Data centers—if properly integrated—can reduce demand volatility rather than exacerbate it. By shifting interruptible computing tasks, primarily AI training, to periods of high renewable generation and low grid stress, data centers can absorb supply volatility rather than amplify it. They can reduce the need for residential conservation calls during peak summer hours by providing a large, dispatchable demand resource that operators can draw on before residential demand becomes a reliability concern. With appropriate technical agreements, data centers can also provide ancillary services such as frequency response, functions currently supplied almost exclusively by thermal generation and energy storage. A larger grid with more diverse, flexible load lowers per-unit costs for all consumers—a direct benefit to residential ratepayers that grows as data center load scales.

What converts these capabilities from contractual promises into operating reality is orchestration: software-driven, physics-aware coordination of a facility’s on-site generation, battery storage, cooling systems, and schedulable workloads as a single dispatchable resource. An orchestrated campus can shift training load into hours of renewable surplus, discharge storage into evening ramps, and shape its draw against real-time grid conditions automatically and verifiably—rather than through phone calls during an emergency.

The technology exists today; what lags is the market plumbing. ERCOT’s demand response and ancillary service qualification frameworks were built around industrial loads that curtail slowly and manually, and they should be updated to recognize and compensate large loads that can respond in seconds. ERCOT already has the building blocks: Controllable Load Resources can provide ancillary services today, and the Real-Time Co-optimization market design launched in December 2025 makes fast, verifiable response more valuable than ever—qualification simply needs to scale to gigawatt campuses. A gigawatt-scale campus operated this way is not merely a smaller burden on the grid; it is one of the largest fast-responding resources on the system—serving its own load, absorbing surplus the grid cannot otherwise use, and returning firm capacity to it when scarcity hits.

Conclusion

The question before policymakers is not whether AI data centers will have a large impact on our grids. They are already doing so at a scale and pace without precedent in modern American history. The question is whether Texas will capture the full benefits of this investment surge, or whether regulatory missteps will saddle the grid with socialized transmission and reliability costs, leaving ordinary ratepayers exposed to the financial and reliability risks. Under the right policy conditions—conditions Texas is uniquely positioned to create—data centers will become assets to the ERCOT grid: sources of firm load, catalysts for reliable generation investment, and a long-term subsidy for residential electricity costs.

The evidence assembled here cuts sharply against the popular narrative that data centers drive up electricity bills and strain the grid. Texas and Virginia have seen the steepest increases in data center load yet have recorded minimal electricity rate increases in recent years, while California and New York, which added minimal large industrial load, saw the largest residential price hikes. The culprits behind rising bills are elsewhere: mandated retirements of reliable generation, expensive transmission buildout to support intermittent wind and solar, aging distribution infrastructure, and broader inflationary trends.

Conflating those cost drivers with data center growth obscures the diagnosis and the cure. The environmental picture is similarly distorted. Data centers’ water and land footprint, while real, is modest relative to agriculture, steel manufacturing, and semiconductor fabrication—industries that face nothing approaching the level of public alarm directed at hyperscalers. Managing these externalities is achievable within existing regulatory frameworks, applied evenhandedly and without double standards. Management of far more intensive industries and consumers has existed for decades, if not centuries.

The central grid challenge is not only the data center load itself but where the power to serve it comes from and if it can provide it reliably. ERCOT’s interconnection queue now tracks more than 474 GW of large load seeking connection, with 90% of it from data centers (ERCOT, 2026b). Meanwhile, less than 20% of new generation requests are firm thermal generation, including natural gas (ERCOT, 2026c). If that imbalance persists, Texas will have invited the largest industrial load growth in its history onto a grid increasingly dependent on weather-driven generation that will be especially vulnerable to unpredictable winter storms like Winter Storm Uri.

The alternative is available and within reach. Hyperscalers usually prefer grid interconnection as it offers reliability and cost advantages over building private power plants. As discussed above, the on-site generation-and-storage layer that a grid-connected facility adds runs roughly $1.5–7 million per MW, depending on generation mix and reliability target—a modest increment against the roughly $35–40 million per MW all-in cost of a large AI data center, which is dominated by GPUs and cooling. Fully islanded, renewable-heavy configurations sit at the high end of that range; the gas-anchored, grid-connected builds hyperscalers actually favor sit at the low end.

The economics of interconnection already favor the grid, but grid planners, transmission utilities, and policymakers are not keeping up with the speed of development that hyperscalers need. Hence the need for the private grid option. Policy needs to preserve and reinforce the advantage of grid economics, not undermine it through slow queues, uncertain cost assignment, and curtailment frameworks that do not account for the $74,000 per MWh economics of AI inference load (Royal, 2026, p. 10).

Texas has the tools to lead, and the five recommendations in this paper can help extend Texas’s leadership.

ERCOT should refine its load forecasting methodology using project-specific feasibility indicators to avoid overbuilding for projects that never materialize, while planning for full utilization of facilities that do get built.

The PUC and the Texas Legislature should work together to reform the wholesale market to adequately compensate firm, dispatchable thermal generation while allowing data centers to self-manage grid stress through on-site generation and storage; aligning private investment incentives with public reliability needs is more effective than curtailment.

Transmission costs triggered by large-load interconnection should be directly assigned to the customers that cause them, with financial security requirements that keep that assignment enforceable if a facility reduces its load or exits, preventing cost shifting onto ratepayers.

Hyperscalers seeking grid interconnection who agree to co-develop a minimum quantity of firm generation should receive expedited permitting and queue priority. A bring-your-own-power incentive like this is commercially viable in Texas in a way that it is not in many other places. Siting incentives should point these facilities toward existing corridors and the state’s stranded generation, funded on a user-pays basis.

Data centers should be integrated as active grid participants that shift interruptible workloads to periods of low grid stress, provide ancillary services such as frequency response, and reduce demand volatility. Orchestrating on-site generation, storage, and workloads as a single resource lets these facilities absorb surplus energy and return firm capacity to the grid, ultimately lowering per-unit costs for all consumers in the process.

The companies building AI are making trillion-dollar bets on where the power will be, and Texas has a unique opportunity to be a global leader in the most consequential technology of the 21st century. The question is whether this surge of investment can be done in such a way that all Texans will benefit from it, instead of benefiting only a few while imposing costs on many. Setting the right policies, particularly regarding the ERCOT grid, is essential to enable Texas entrepreneurs, workers, and taxpayers to all flourish from this wave of innovation and investment.

title: Acceleration of benefits for solar and ESS sectors as U.S. Senate passes energy permitting reform bill
description:
Expectations are growing that domestic solar and battery industries will benefit from the passage of the energy permitting reform bill by the U.S. Senate.
According to industry sources on the 24th, the U.S. Senate passed the "Energy Permitting Reform Bill" on the 19th (local time).
The increase in ESS demand accompanying the expansion of solar power generation is a positive factor for domestic battery companies.
As the share of renewable energy in power generation increases, demand for ESS installations to ensure the stability of power supply may also rise.
SK On is also converting some of its electric vehicle battery production lines at its Georgia plant into LFP battery production lines for ESS, and will commence mass production in the second half of the year.
text:
Expectations are growing that domestic solar and battery industries will benefit from the passage of the energy permitting reform bill by the U.S. Senate. The bill includes provisions to impose the costs of power supply for data centers and grid expansion on operators, as well as to simplify the permitting procedures for renewable energy generation projects.

Analysts suggest this could lead to an expansion of power generation and Energy Storage System (ESS) projects in the U.S., along with increased demand for equipment.

According to industry sources on the 24th, the U.S. Senate passed the "Energy Permitting Reform Bill" on the 19th (local time). The bill stipulates that operators must directly bear the costs associated with power supply or grid expansion caused by data centers.

Environmental review procedures for ESS will also be simplified. The bill will be finalized after receiving House approval and the President's signature.

The solar industry expects that once the bill is enacted, construction starts and equipment orders for pending power generation and ESS projects, which have been delayed due to permitting issues, will be accelerated. This is because the bill aims to minimize project delays by specifying deadlines for processing permits for renewable energy generation projects and simplifying procedures.

In fact, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) estimated that under a medium-to-long-term scenario assuming the introduction of the bill, net new solar capacity in the U.S. from 2028 to 2035 would increase by 167 gigawatts compared to the current system.

Hanwha Solutions' Q-Cells division (hereinafter Hanwha Q-Cells) expects benefits centered on its local production facilities in the U.S. Hanwha Q-Cells began commercial production of solar cells at its Cartersville plant in Georgia, U.S., last May.

Following the establishment of a domestic solar value chain in the U.S., ranging from ingots to wafers, cells, and modules, the company has also established a product manufacturing system that meets the Domestic Content Act (DCA) requirements for U.S.-made components.

The increase in module demand due to the expansion of solar projects in the U.S. is expected to strengthen the supply competitiveness of Hanwha Q-Cells, which possesses local production infrastructure.

OCI Holdings is also expected to benefit from the expansion of the U.S. solar market. It is projected that the company will be able to expand supply contracts with U.S. customers based on non-Chinese polysilicon produced in Malaysia.

OCI Holdings' annual polysilicon production capacity is approximately 35,000 tons, and it is expected that most of its production volume from next year onward will be sold through long-term supply agreements (LTAs) with U.S. customers.

The increase in ESS demand accompanying the expansion of solar power generation is a positive factor for domestic battery companies. As the share of renewable energy in power generation increases, demand for ESS installations to ensure the stability of power supply may also rise.

The battery industry plans to respond to such demand based on local production facilities in North America. LG Energy Solution aims to secure a production capacity of over 50 GWh by the end of this year by establishing five major ESS complex manufacturing hubs in North America, including its Michigan Holland and L-H Battery Company Ohio plants, Ultium Cells Tennessee and Michigan Lansing plants, and NextStar Energy Ontario plant in Canada.

Samsung SDI will begin producing Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS from the fourth quarter of this year by converting part of its electric vehicle production line at its Indiana plant, a joint venture with Stellantis called Star Plus Energy (SPE). SK On is also converting some of its electric vehicle battery production lines at its Georgia plant into LFP battery production lines for ESS, and will commence mass production in the second half of the year.

title: Tanzania Falls Behind Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda in Africa's Electric Vehicle Race
description:
Electric two wheelers accounted for 94% of registered electric vehicles, while the country had also registered 168 electric buses and approximately 1,600 electric three wheelers by March 2026.
The Kenyan experience demonstrates why electric vehicle adoption cannot be explained solely by the purchase price or availability of electric models.
The figures relate to electric two-wheeler sales during 2025 and should not be confused with the total number of electric vehicles registered or currently operating in Uganda.
Legislation approved in late 2025 and implemented from January 2026 removed the previous 20% customs duty on vehicles powered exclusively by electric motors, while additional tax reforms reduced the excise burden on selected electric vehicles.
Zambia has similarly introduced incentives for qualifying electric vehicles and components, while pursuing discussions on electric bus deployment.
text:
Tanzania is becoming an exception in a regional electric mobility market that is expanding rapidly, as neighbouring Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda introduce policies, financing arrangements and infrastructure that are moving electric motorcycles and buses from demonstration projects into commercial transport. The International Energy Agency's 2026 Global EV Outlook reports that Uganda sold more than 30,000 electric two-wheelers in 2025, while Kenya recorded more than 25,000 sales, accounting for approximately 15% of new motorcycle registrations. Rwanda has gone further in regulatory terms by prohibiting the registration of new petrol-powered motorcycle taxis in Kigali since January 2025. Tanzania, meanwhile, has an emerging electric motorcycle and three-wheeler market but continues to face regulatory uncertainty, limited investment and difficulties establishing the commercial infrastructure necessary to expand adoption.

The differences are especially consequential because Tanzania has many of the conditions that should make electric mobility commercially attractive. It has one of East Africa's largest markets for motorcycles, three-wheelers and other commercial passenger vehicles; a growing electricity system; substantial demand for affordable urban transportation; and an extensive network of small transport operators whose daily earnings are influenced by petrol prices and maintenance costs. Dar es Salaam alone provides a substantial potential market for electric boda bodas, bajajis, delivery motorcycles and buses, while growing cities such as Dodoma, Mwanza, Arusha and Mbeya present additional opportunities. Yet the scale of the market has not translated into investment and adoption comparable with the more developed commercial electric motorcycle markets in Kenya and Uganda.

The explanation is more complicated than the absence of electric vehicles on Tanzanian roads. The Africa E Mobility Alliance estimated in its 2025 industry report that Tanzania had approximately 10,000 electric two and three-wheelers, more than Kenya's estimated 8,421 and Uganda's 3,200 at the time. However, it cautioned that most of Tanzania's estimated fleet consisted of lead acid battery scooters, a different market from the more commercially developed lithium ion electric motorcycle fleets increasingly used by professional riders in neighbouring countries. Those estimates also predate the extraordinary growth recorded in Kenya and Uganda during 2025 and 2026, making them unsuitable as a current ranking of national electric vehicle fleets.

Kenya's Ministry of Roads and Transport reported in November 2026 that the country had registered more than 50,000 electric vehicles by June 2026, predominantly motorcycles, following the formal launch of its National Electric Mobility Policy in February. Uganda has developed a substantial battery swapping network supporting electric commercial motorcycles, while Rwanda has established tax incentives, electricity pricing arrangements and regulatory restrictions intended to accelerate the transition. Burundi, despite possessing a much smaller economy and substantially weaker electricity infrastructure than Tanzania, has adopted legislation requiring certain passenger vehicles ordered for import from January 2027 to be electric or hybrid. The direction of policy across the region suggests that governments increasingly regard vehicle electrification as an issue involving transport costs, fuel import dependence, industrial development and energy policy rather than environmental protection alone. al gas reserves, increasing electricity generation and a large commercial transport sector, has not attracted a comparable level of electric vehicle investment. They also reveal an unusual competition between different national approaches to reducing transport fuel costs. While Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda have concentrated on electric motorcycles and buses, Tanzania has devoted substantial policy attention and investment to compressed natural gas as an alternative to petrol and diesel. Both approaches can reduce dependence on imported petroleum products, but they require different infrastructure, financing arrangements and long term industrial capabilities.

Kenya Has Turned Electric Motorcycles Into a Commercial Financing Market

Kenya's electric vehicle market has expanded through the combination of supportive regulation, dedicated electricity pricing, commercial financing and the rapid growth of companies supplying electric motorcycles to boda boda operators. According to the International Energy Agency, more than 25,000 electric motorcycles were sold in Kenya during 2025, compared with approximately 4,862 in 2024, taking their share of new motorcycle registrations to around 15%. The growth was driven principally by commercial motorcycle operators, whose relatively high daily mileage makes the cost of fuel and maintenance a major consideration when selecting vehicles.

A November 2026 study published by the Africa E Mobility Alliance, Popular Transport and Electrification: Kenya Baseline Study, reported that cumulative electric vehicle registrations increased from 1,378 in 2022 to 39,324 by the end of 2025. Electric two wheelers accounted for 94% of registered electric vehicles, while the country had also registered 168 electric buses and approximately 1,600 electric three wheelers by March 2026. The study estimated that Kenya's popular transport sector includes approximately 1.5 million boda bodas, 70,000 matatus and 55,000 tuk tuks, illustrating the size of the market available to companies capable of providing affordable electric alternatives.

Kenya's expansion has been supported by companies including Spiro, Roam and Ampersand, which have developed vehicle supply, battery swapping infrastructure and financing arrangements designed around the earnings of commercial motorcycle riders. Rather than requiring every rider to purchase a motorcycle and an expensive battery upfront, some companies offer arrangements under which the vehicle is financed separately from the battery, with riders paying for battery access or swaps as they operate. Others work with asset financing institutions to recover vehicle costs through daily or weekly payments, reducing the difficulty of obtaining a conventional bank loan.

These arrangements address an economic constraint affecting many East African transport operators. A motorcycle taxi rider may depend on daily fares to meet fuel, maintenance and loan repayment costs and may not possess the savings required to purchase a substantially more expensive electric motorcycle outright. A lower operating cost therefore provides limited benefit if the initial purchase price remains inaccessible. Financing that follows the operator's cash flow can allow the rider to obtain the vehicle while using savings on fuel and maintenance to support repayment. The International Energy Agency estimates that conventional motorcycle operators in Kenya can spend approximately 40% to 60% of daily earnings on petrol, while electricity costs for commercial electric motorcycles are typically below $2 a day, depending on vehicle use and commercial charging arrangements.

Government policy has reinforced the commercial case. Kenya Power operates a dedicated electric mobility tariff of approximately KSh 16 per kilowatt hour during peak periods and KSh 8 during off-peak periods, although eligibility rules and consumption thresholds apply. The National Electric Mobility Policy, officially launched on February 3, 2026, provides a framework for developing charging infrastructure, promoting investment and coordinating public institutions. The government has also maintained selected tax exemptions for domestically assembled electric vehicles, while the International Finance Corporation signed a cooperation agreement with the State Department for Transport in August 2026 to support implementation of the national policy.

The Kenyan experience demonstrates why electric vehicle adoption cannot be explained solely by the purchase price or availability of electric models. Private companies have developed businesses around vehicle ownership, battery management, maintenance and financing, while the public sector has provided a clearer regulatory framework and electricity pricing arrangements. The market remains exposed to challenges involving charging access, limited financing, import duties on certain vehicle categories and the cost of expanding electricity distribution infrastructure. Nevertheless, the combination has been sufficient to attract investment and expand the number of vehicles operating commercially.

Uganda Has Built a Battery Swapping Industry and Begun Manufacturing Electric Buses

Uganda's electric mobility market has developed even faster in some commercial segments. The International Energy Agency reports that sales of electric two-wheelers exceeded 30,000 during 2025, making Uganda one of Africa's fastest-growing markets for electric motorcycles. The expansion was supported by investment from companies including Spiro, Zembo and Gogo, which developed motorcycle financing arrangements and battery swapping facilities serving commercial riders. The figures relate to electric two-wheeler sales during 2025 and should not be confused with the total number of electric vehicles registered or currently operating in Uganda.

The scale of the supporting infrastructure is also increasing. A World Bank study published in September 2026 reported that Uganda's battery swapping network expanded from approximately 150 stations in mid-2024 to more than 350 by late 2025. The Bank estimated that an electric boda boda could save its operator approximately UGX 1 million, equivalent to about $255, annually compared with a petrol motorcycle, although actual savings depend on vehicle utilisation, energy pricing, maintenance and financing arrangements. The study also identified limitations involving the cost of purchasing vehicles, access to credit, grid connections and uncertainty over the treatment of imports and incentives.

Uganda's strategy is distinguished by its attempt to develop local automotive manufacturing alongside vehicle adoption. Kiira Motors Corporation, supported by the Ugandan government, has developed the Kayoola electric bus programme and established an automotive production facility in Jinja. During 2026, Uganda introduced locally manufactured electric buses into commercial transport services in Kampala and surrounding urban areas. The Uganda Media Centre reported that eight electric buses began operations in May, followed by the launch of another 15 buses serving routes around Kira Municipality later in the year. These deployments remain modest relative to the country's total public transport fleet, but they represent an operational market for vehicles assembled through a domestic manufacturing programme.

The country's industrial ambitions extend beyond the manufacture of complete vehicles. Uganda has pursued battery assembly, charging equipment, training and the development of local suppliers, aiming to capture a greater share of the value associated with vehicle electrification. The government's 2026/27 budget speech reported that Kiira Motors had recorded bus sales worth UGX 21.6 billion and orders for 450 buses from Uganda and regional customers. Orders and production targets should be distinguished from vehicles already delivered, but they indicate the scale of the commercial and industrial ambitions attached to the programme.

The World Bank's analysis also shows that vehicle adoption creates new responsibilities for the electricity sector. Under a moderate expansion scenario, electric vehicles could increase peak electricity demand in Greater Kampala by approximately 99 megawatts without substantial charging coordination, compared with 60 megawatts under better managed charging conditions. The Bank estimated that coordinated charging could reduce the additional annual cost of electricity distribution losses in its model from about $21 million to $10 million. These figures are scenario estimates rather than observed costs, but they demonstrate why large electric vehicle fleets require planning involving utilities, transport authorities, charging operators and electricity regulators.

Uganda's progress is therefore commercially and institutionally relevant to Tanzania. Both countries possess substantial commercial motorcycle markets, growing urban populations and expanding electricity infrastructure, but Uganda has begun connecting vehicle sales, battery services, financing and domestic manufacturing through a more identifiable national programme. Tanzania also shares an electricity interconnection development agenda with Uganda, supported by the World Bank's June 2026 regional power trade initiative, which creates opportunities for cooperation in electricity supply even as the countries pursue different approaches to transport electrification.

Rwanda Has Used Regulation and Electricity Pricing to Accelerate Adoption

Rwanda has pursued a more interventionist approach by introducing regulations intended to direct specific parts of the transport market towards electric vehicles. Since January 2025, Kigali has prohibited the registration of new petrol powered motorcycle taxis, requiring new entrants into that commercial category to use electric models. The restriction does not mean every motorcycle operating in Kigali is already electric, nor does it constitute a nationwide ban on all petrol motorcycles. It is a targeted measure affecting new registrations within a commercially important transport category.

The policy has been supported by other measures intended to reduce the cost of adoption. Rwanda has introduced exemptions and favourable tax treatment for qualifying electric vehicles, arrangements for charging facilities and an electricity tariff cap of RWF 110 per kilowatt hour for electric mobility charging. The Africa E Mobility Alliance's 2026 implementation assessment also identifies government support for land access, charging infrastructure and battery safety rules as part of Rwanda's relatively developed regulatory framework. These measures are intended to make the financial conditions for electric transport more predictable while creating demand for vehicle suppliers and battery service operators.

Companies such as Ampersand have developed battery swapping services for motorcycle taxi operators in Rwanda, allowing riders to exchange depleted batteries rather than waiting for vehicles to recharge. Financing initiatives supported by international development partners have also targeted the additional upfront cost of electric motorcycles, including subsidies and credit guarantees. Rwanda's comparatively small domestic market means that the scale of adoption differs from Kenya and Uganda, but the policy approach demonstrates how government decisions can create a defined market for private investment.

The distinction matters because an investor considering a vehicle assembly facility, charging network or battery service operation needs some confidence that demand will develop over several years. Rwanda's registration restriction provides a direct indication of future demand within Kigali's motorcycle taxi market, while tax incentives and regulated electricity pricing help companies estimate operating costs. The approach also involves economic risks, particularly where riders cannot afford qualifying vehicles or charging and battery services fail to expand sufficiently. Nevertheless, Rwanda has established a clearer direction for commercial electrification than Tanzania's more fragmented arrangements.

Burundi, Malawi and Mozambique Are Changing Tax Rules Even Without Large EV Fleets

The regional comparison becomes more revealing when countries with smaller markets and weaker infrastructure are considered. Burundi's 2026/27 Finance Law introduces exemptions for electric vehicles and related equipment and, under Article 221, requires certain passenger cars and jeep type vehicles ordered for import from January 1, 2027 to be electric or hybrid. The requirement does not apply to every vehicle category, and the law provides exceptions for specified institutions. According to a November 2026 policy brief by the Africa E Mobility Alliance, qualifying electric vehicles receive exemptions from import duty, value added tax and excise duty, while hybrid vehicles remain subject to a customs duty of 25%.

Burundi's decision is economically unusual because the country faces substantial electricity access constraints and recurring shortages of petroleum products. Its policy is motivated partly by the desire to reduce the cost of importing fuel, which exposes the economy to foreign exchange shortages and international price fluctuations. The Africa E-Mobility Alliance estimates that Burundi imported approximately $255.8 million in mineral fuels in 2023, equivalent to 22% of its total imports and approximately 68% of exports of goods and services. These figures provide context for the government's willingness to adopt an unusually restrictive vehicle import policy despite the country's relatively limited charging infrastructure.

However, Burundi's legislation should not be confused with evidence that it has achieved higher electric vehicle adoption than Tanzania. Available reporting indicated that the country had only a few hundred electric and hybrid vehicles by May 2026, and the policy brief itself identifies major uncertainties concerning charging infrastructure, battery standards, implementation and the affordability of qualifying vehicles. Burundi has established an aggressive future policy direction, but the commercial results remain to be demonstrated.

Malawi has taken a different approach through fiscal incentives. Its 2023/24 budget removed import duties and certain taxes on electric vehicles and charging equipment, while subsequent measures extended relief to electric motorcycles. These decisions indicate that the government has sought to reduce the cost of adopting electric vehicles, partly to address petroleum import dependence and related foreign exchange pressures. However, reliable national statistics demonstrating commercial adoption comparable with Kenya or Uganda are not readily available, and the existence of tax incentives alone is insufficient to establish that Malawi's electric vehicle market has expanded faster than Tanzania's.

Mozambique has also moved to change import taxation. Legislation approved in late 2025 and implemented from January 2026 removed the previous 20% customs duty on vehicles powered exclusively by electric motors, while additional tax reforms reduced the excise burden on selected electric vehicles. Finance Minister Carla Loveira presented the customs exemption as part of efforts to encourage cleaner transport and reduce barriers to adoption. Mozambique nevertheless remains an early stage electric vehicle market, and available national vehicle statistics do not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that it has achieved a higher adoption rate than Tanzania.

Zambia has similarly introduced incentives for qualifying electric vehicles and components, while pursuing discussions on electric bus deployment. In December 2025, the Zambian government announced plans to work with Uganda on the introduction of electric buses after officials inspected and tested a Kiira Motors vehicle. This suggests increasing policy interest and potential regional industrial cooperation, but it does not establish that a large electric bus fleet has been deployed or that Zambia currently leads Tanzania in adoption.

The Democratic Republic of Congo presents another distinct case. Its principal attraction to electric mobility investors includes its large motorcycle transport market, extensive population and position within the global supply chain for battery minerals. Spiro identified the DRC among the markets it intended to enter following a $215 million financing announcement in June 2026, while local companies have introduced electric motorcycles and vehicle assembly initiatives in Kinshasa and other cities. The DRC remains at an early stage of commercial deployment, however, and investment announcements should be distinguished from motorcycles actually sold, charging facilities constructed and vehicles operating on public roads.

These differences demonstrate why Tanzania's position cannot be accurately described as falling behind every neighbouring country in actual electric vehicle adoption. Kenya and Uganda have clear evidence of rapidly expanding commercial sales, Rwanda has introduced a more directive regulatory framework, and Burundi has adopted an ambitious import policy that has yet to take effect. Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and the DRC have taken various policy or investment steps, but the available evidence is insufficient to establish that all four have larger or faster growing operational electric vehicle markets than Tanzania.

Tanzania's Problem Is Increasingly About Regulation, Financing and Commercial Scale

Research conducted by the Africa E Mobility Alliance, with support from UN Habitat and the Urban Electric Mobility Initiative, identifies several obstacles affecting Tanzania's electric mobility industry. Its report, Barriers to E Mobility in Tanzania, documents inconsistent treatment of electric vehicles by customs and registration authorities, uncertainty concerning applicable standards, high import costs, limited access to investment capital and inadequate coordination among institutions responsible for transport, taxation, standards and electricity. The research drew on consultations with Tanzanian companies and public institutions, including the Tanzania Revenue Authority, Tanzania Bureau of Standards, TANESCO and Dar es Salaam Rapid Transit.

The report records cases in which companies experienced difficulty registering electric vehicles or obtaining licence plates and insurance, while others faced import charges exceeding 50% of the value of their products. It also documented uncertainty concerning customs classifications for batteries, electric motorcycles and imported vehicle components. These findings are important because an electric vehicle supplier must be able to establish the total landed cost of its products before committing capital, setting prices or offering financing to customers. Where the tax treatment changes according to the classification applied or the interpretation of individual officials, companies face additional uncertainty that can undermine their willingness to invest in assembly, distribution and charging infrastructure.

The regulatory situation has evolved since the original research. Tanzania's 2023 amendments to the Motor Vehicle Registration and Transfer Tax legislation recognised electric vehicle categories, while subsequent regulations gazetted in June 2025 established registration fees for different classes of electric vehicles. The Energy and Water Utilities Regulatory Authority also published guidelines for electric mobility charging stations and battery swapping in April 2026. These developments mean it would be inaccurate to describe Tanzania as having no laws or rules addressing electric vehicles. The more specific difficulty concerns the absence of a sufficiently coordinated national market development strategy and continued problems implementing existing rules.

Reporting by The Citizen in February 2026 documented concerns that some electric motorcycles and three wheelers operating in Dar es Salaam and Arusha remained unregistered despite the existence of legal provisions governing their registration. The report identified uncertainty among operators and distributors, as well as difficulties concerning licensing, safety and enforcement. Some electric vehicle businesses reported completing registration successfully, while others continued encountering delays. The difference indicates that Tanzania's problem cannot be reduced to the legal recognition of electric vehicles; it also involves consistent administrative procedures and clear responsibilities for the institutions required to apply them.

Financing presents another substantial constraint. The Africa E Mobility Alliance's Tanzania study found that companies operating in the sector had secured only slightly more than $1 million in funding at the time of its assessment, compared with more than $5 million in Uganda and $50 million in Kenya. These figures describe historical funding conditions rather than current national investment totals and should not be used as a definitive ranking for November 2026. They nevertheless illustrate the financing gap that confronted Tanzanian firms during the market's early development. The report also identified shortages of trained technicians, limited access to suitable vehicles and weak customer awareness as obstacles restricting the expansion of electric transport businesses.

The investment consequences have become visible in decisions made by regional companies. In June 2026, The EastAfrican reported that Spiro had prioritised expansion into Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo over the full commercial rollout previously announced for Tanzania. Raymond Kitunga, the company's deputy country head for Kenya, attributed the decision partly to the absence of a sufficiently developed national electric mobility policy and weaker market readiness in Tanzania. The company had previously announced plans involving battery swapping stations, local assembly and collaboration with youth organisations, but the full programme had not materialised at the time of the report.

The comments are commercially revealing because electric vehicle companies require several connected investments before customers can adopt their products at scale. A motorcycle supplier may need battery swapping facilities before riders are willing to purchase vehicles, while swapping stations require sufficient motorcycle demand to operate profitably. Lenders need confidence that vehicles can be registered, insured, maintained and resold if borrowers default. Electricity companies must understand where charging demand will arise and what infrastructure is required to serve it. Without coordination, each participant may delay investment while waiting for the others to establish the conditions necessary for the market to function.

Tanzania's relatively large transport market does not automatically resolve this problem. It creates demand potential, but the conversion of that potential into a commercially attractive investment proposition depends on predictable regulation, financing arrangements and an effective network of suppliers and service providers.

Natural Gas Has Become Tanzania's More Visible Transport Energy Strategy

Tanzania's slower electric vehicle expansion also needs to be examined alongside its considerable investment in compressed natural gas. Unlike Kenya and Rwanda, Tanzania possesses commercially developed domestic natural gas resources, including production from Songo Songo and Mnazi Bay. The government has promoted the use of natural gas in vehicles as a means of reducing the cost of transport, creating additional domestic demand for Tanzanian energy resources and lowering dependence on imported petrol and diesel.

The strategy has produced measurable results. The Bank of Tanzania's October 2026 Consolidated Zonal Economic Performance Report recorded an increase in the number of vehicles using compressed natural gas from approximately 7,000 in 2024/25 to 16,354 in 2025/26. Other official statements during 2026 referred to more than 20,000 vehicles using natural gas, although differences in reporting periods, vehicle categories and definitions mean those figures should not be treated as directly interchangeable. The government and private investors have also expanded refuelling stations and vehicle conversion facilities, particularly in Dar es Salaam, with additional projects planned or under development in Morogoro, Dodoma and other locations.

The economic logic of compressed natural gas differs from that of electric mobility. Tanzania produces natural gas domestically and can use it directly as a transport fuel after appropriate processing and distribution, while electric vehicles rely on electricity generated through a mixture of natural gas, hydropower and other sources. Both approaches can reduce the amount of imported petrol or diesel consumed by transport operators, although their relative costs, emissions and infrastructure requirements differ. Natural gas remains a fossil fuel, while electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions and their wider environmental benefits depend partly on how electricity is generated and how batteries are manufactured and managed.

The availability of domestic natural gas creates a commercial reason for Tanzania to support compressed natural gas vehicles, particularly where conversions allow existing petrol vehicles to continue operating with lower fuel costs. Converting a vehicle may also be financially easier than replacing it with a new electric model, depending on the vehicle, installation cost and availability of refuelling facilities. For taxi operators and owners of existing vehicles, this can make natural gas an attractive immediate option.

However, the development of compressed natural gas does not inherently prevent investment in electric motorcycles or buses. The two technologies can serve different transport categories, and a diversified transport energy strategy could support both. Electric motorcycles may be particularly competitive for riders travelling predictable daily distances with access to battery swapping, while compressed natural gas can offer a lower cost fuel alternative for owners of existing petrol vehicles. Electric buses may be suitable for organised urban routes where fleet operators can finance vehicles and operate centralised charging depots, while the economics of gas powered vehicles may differ according to their size, routes and fuel consumption.

The policy question for Tanzania is whether support for natural gas has become the practical default for reducing transport fuel dependence while electric mobility remains without a comparably coordinated commercial development programme. The existence of a successful natural gas conversion industry does not demonstrate that the government has deliberately excluded electric vehicles. It does suggest that investors in the two sectors are operating within different levels of policy attention, financing coordination and supporting infrastructure.

Zanzibar Is Already Demonstrating a Different Tanzanian Approach

The most important domestic qualification to Tanzania's slower electric mobility development is Zanzibar, which began operating its first electric public bus service in 2026. President Hussein Ali Mwinyi officially launched the ZanBus programme on July 23, with an initial fleet of 15 electric buses serving two corridors between Stone Town, the international airport, Chukwani and Buyu. The project is financed through an arrangement involving the Zanzibar Social Security Fund and private sector partners, with the buses supplied by India's EKA Mobility. The programme includes charging infrastructure, terminal development and a digital fare payment system.

The Zanzibar government has outlined ambitions to expand the service substantially, ultimately targeting a fleet of 500 electric buses. Those figures are policy targets rather than vehicles already in operation, and the programme's financial performance will depend on passenger demand, fleet utilisation, fares, maintenance and the cost of electricity and financing. The initial rollout also encountered operational challenges, including shortages of passenger cards, long waiting times and limited bus availability, illustrating the difficulties of introducing a new transport system even when vehicles and charging infrastructure have been secured.

Nevertheless, the project is relevant because it demonstrates that Tanzanian institutions can organise electric public transport through coordinated financing, fleet procurement and infrastructure planning. Zanzibar's relatively compact geography, high concentration of passenger movement and dependence on imported liquid fuels make it a distinct market from mainland Tanzania, but its experience provides a practical example of how a public institution can establish an initial fleet and supporting operating arrangements.

Dar es Salaam presents a substantially larger opportunity because of its population, extensive network of daladalas, boda bodas and bajajis, and the existence of an organised bus rapid transit system. However, the commercial structure is more complicated. Large numbers of vehicles are owned by individuals or small operators, while routes, financing and operational arrangements differ across the sector. Electrification would therefore require financing arrangements suited to different categories of owners, charging or swapping locations close to operating routes and coordination with existing transport regulations.

The Zanzibar experience also highlights the difference between purchasing electric vehicles and establishing an operational transport service. A fleet requires maintenance, spare parts, trained technicians, predictable electricity supply, ticketing arrangements and sufficient passenger revenue to support operating costs. The success of electrification should therefore be assessed through actual vehicle availability, passenger numbers, costs and financial performance rather than announced fleet targets alone.

Tanzania Could Lose More Than Vehicle Sales as Regional Manufacturing Expands

The economic consequences of slower electric vehicle adoption extend beyond the number of vehicles operating on Tanzanian roads. Kenya and Uganda are attracting investment in vehicle assembly, charging equipment, batteries, maintenance services, software systems and financing products, creating opportunities for domestic suppliers and technical employment. As these industries grow, companies are likely to make investment decisions based on existing production facilities, the availability of skilled workers, market size, supplier relationships and the stability of government policy.

Tanzania has the potential to participate in these activities because of its domestic transport market, industrial infrastructure, access to ports and regional trading position. Dar es Salaam could support the importation and assembly of electric motorcycles and components for domestic use and neighbouring markets, while industrial areas in Pwani, Morogoro and other regions could accommodate supporting manufacturing and maintenance activities. However, the commercial viability of such investments will depend on costs, demand, finance and predictable regulation rather than the availability of industrial land or policy announcements alone.

The country's wider mineral and energy resources provide additional opportunities, but they should be treated separately from vehicle assembly. Tanzania possesses deposits of graphite and other minerals relevant to battery supply chains, while domestic electricity generation can support charging and industrial processing. Developing a battery manufacturing industry, however, requires substantial capital, technology, specialised skills, reliable electricity and access to international markets. The presence of minerals does not automatically establish that battery cell manufacturing would be commercially competitive in Tanzania.

An electric motorcycle assembly programme may therefore be a more immediate industrial opportunity than attempting to establish a complete battery manufacturing industry. Firms could initially concentrate on importing components, assembling vehicles, adapting products to local operating conditions and developing maintenance capabilities, while expanding local production where scale and costs justify it. The same principle applies to battery swapping services, where commercially viable operations require a large enough fleet to recover investment in batteries, charging equipment and station infrastructure.

The regional experience indicates that financing is likely to determine whether these opportunities materialise. Vehicle manufacturers and battery service companies need working capital and long term investment, while riders and small transport operators require affordable means of acquiring vehicles. Partnerships involving banks, specialised asset financiers, development finance institutions and established transport operators could reduce some of these constraints, although lenders will need reliable vehicle registration, insurance, service support and mechanisms for managing credit risk.

A National Electric Mobility Strategy Would Need to Begin With Commercial Transport

The evidence from Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda suggests that the earliest large scale opportunities in Tanzania are more likely to emerge in commercial motorcycles, three wheelers and organised bus fleets than in the immediate replacement of privately owned passenger cars. Commercial vehicles generally operate more frequently than privately owned cars, allowing the financial benefits of lower energy and maintenance costs to accumulate more quickly. Their routes and operating patterns can also make it easier to locate battery swapping stations and charging depots where demand is concentrated.

For electric boda bodas, the central issue is whether the cost of purchasing or financing a vehicle, together with battery access charges, is lower than the cost of acquiring and operating a comparable petrol motorcycle over the repayment period. A commercially viable model must include vehicle purchase costs, financing charges, batteries, maintenance, insurance, registration, downtime and eventual replacement. Fuel savings are relevant, but they cannot be evaluated independently of the overall ownership arrangement.

For electric bajajis, Tanzania already has an emerging market that could support greater expansion. Three wheelers are widely used for urban passenger transport, cargo delivery and short distance trips, while some operators travel predictable routes over substantial distances each day. Dedicated charging facilities and financing arrangements could improve the commercial case, particularly where vehicles are operated intensively and electricity is priced competitively. However, the durability of batteries, the availability of spare parts and the ability to repair vehicles locally will influence whether owners are willing to replace familiar petrol models.

Bus electrification involves different considerations. An organised operator can potentially charge vehicles at a central depot, negotiate electricity supply arrangements and plan routes according to battery range and charging requirements. However, electric buses generally require greater upfront investment than conventional alternatives, making financing, fleet utilisation and operating revenue crucial. Zanzibar's programme demonstrates one approach involving institutional investment, while Kenya's BasiGo model and Uganda's Kiira Motors programme provide different examples of private fleet financing and domestic manufacturing.

A practical Tanzanian strategy would therefore need to establish clear institutional responsibilities, predictable customs treatment, safety and battery standards, functioning registration and insurance procedures, and a coordinated approach to charging infrastructure and electricity pricing. It would also need to address the economic incentives facing transport operators rather than assuming that the environmental benefits of electric vehicles are sufficient to create demand.

The existing work by EWURA on charging and battery swapping guidelines provides a starting point, while the legal recognition of electric vehicles in registration regulations creates an administrative foundation. The next challenge involves ensuring that the different institutions responsible for transport, energy, taxation, standards, investment and licensing apply compatible rules and provide investors with sufficient clarity to commit capital.

Tanzania's Delay Is Becoming an Industrial and Economic Policy Question

The evidence from neighbouring countries indicates that electric mobility is increasingly being treated as a commercial transport industry rather than an isolated technology initiative. Kenya has demonstrated how financing, battery swapping and electricity pricing can support rapid motorcycle adoption. Uganda has expanded commercial electric motorcycles while investing in domestic bus manufacturing and the supporting electricity infrastructure. Rwanda has created a regulatory direction for motorcycle taxis, while Burundi is preparing a major intervention in its passenger vehicle import market. Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia and the DRC are developing incentives or investment programmes at different stages of maturity, although they have not all achieved comparable commercial adoption.

Tanzania is operating within the same regional market, with substantial demand for affordable transport and an expanding electricity system. Its slower development of commercially financed electric motorcycles and larger electric vehicle fleets cannot be explained simply by a lack of suitable geography or technology. Research identifies specific constraints involving policy coordination, customs treatment, registration, standards, financing, customer awareness and technical capacity. Those constraints affect whether companies can establish supply networks, whether lenders can finance vehicles and whether operators can achieve sufficient savings to justify adoption.

The country's investment in compressed natural gas provides a rational response to the availability of domestic energy resources and the cost of imported petroleum products. However, natural gas and electricity offer different opportunities within the transport sector, and the growth of one does not eliminate the potential economic value of the other. Tanzania's infrastructure and energy advantages could support a broader strategy covering both technologies, with commercial choices determined by operating costs, vehicle categories and the availability of suitable services.

Zanzibar's electric bus programme demonstrates that domestic institutions are already capable of pursuing electrification when financing, procurement and operational responsibilities are coordinated. The wider challenge is whether mainland Tanzania can establish comparable conditions for private businesses and commercial transport operators across a much larger and more varied market.

As Kenya and Uganda continue expanding electric motorcycle fleets and attracting assembly and battery investment, the cost of delayed policy coordination for Tanzania may increasingly be measured through investment decisions made elsewhere in the region. The country has the transport demand, electricity resources and commercial scale to participate in the transition. Whether it captures the associated investment, manufacturing and operating opportunities will depend on how quickly its institutions establish the conditions that allow businesses and transport operators to adopt the technology competitively.

title: Democrats Want to Make Life More Affordable. They Could Begin With Permitting Reform.
authors: Jason Bordoff, Josh Busby, Greg Pollock, Cameron Abadi, Adam Tooze, Cullen Hendrix, Chkhikvadze, Deng Yuwen, David Milne, Howard W. French
