text:
The Democratic wave that shook the U.S. political landscape this month delivered a striking rebuke to President Donald Trump and put affordability squarely at the top of the political agenda. A bill that passed the Senate last week to reform the nation’s permitting laws offers Democrats—who voted two-to-one against the bill in the Senate—an early test of whether they can make daily life more affordable for Americans, even before taking control in January. Permitting reform may seem like a narrow or technical topic, but this is the most important piece of energy legislation in years. By speeding up environmental reviews, limiting litigation delays, and easing transmission siting, it would expand clean energy, lower energy prices, strengthen our energy system, and make future climate action more effective.

The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would make it easier to build transmission lines and other energy infrastructure, including both clean energy and oil and gas projects. That breadth has delighted advocates of abundance, the movement that argues that shortcomings in public infrastructure stem from regulatory bottlenecks, and enraged many environmentalists. Some supporters have been too quick to dismiss legitimate concerns, while some climate activists have drowned out substantive but highly technical legal objections with reflexive anti-fossil fuel rhetoric. As the bill heads to a House vote, a careful assessment of its provisions should lead members to support it while pursuing opportunities where possible to address credible objections in the final stages of the legislative process.

Objections to the permitting reform bill fall into several broad categories. First, some Democrats and environmental groups argue that the blue election wave gives them leverage to secure a better deal next year, yet that misreads both the politics and the policy. A larger Democratic majority does not necessarily mean a majority for blocking fossil fuel infrastructure. The incoming caucus includes members who support oil and gas development alongside clean energy—in states such as Texas, Mississippi, Kansas, South Carolina, and Alaska. Nor does 56 Senate seats eliminate the need for Republican votes to overcome a filibuster. And Trump will still be president, with the power to veto the bill.

Second, some environmental groups oppose the bill because it weakens tools of environmental review and permitting often used to block fossil fuel projects such as oil and gas pipelines. Yet ample evidence demonstrates that trying to “keep it in the ground”—stymying fossil fuel supply by blocking infrastructure—does little to reduce global oil and gas use, which ultimately is what matters for greenhouse gas emissions, and can trigger backlash to climate action if energy security and affordability are perceived to suffer as a result.

In a global market, supply restrictions in one location merely lead to increases elsewhere unless demand falls. Higher prices can curb demand, but this year’s energy crisis offers further evidence that political and economic pressures push elected leaders to use every available tool to bring prices back down. The Iran war led to the closure of much of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil flowed, yet oil demand this year will drop only 2.5 percent, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

While it is possible—and necessary—to reduce the need for oil and gas over the long term, today fossil fuels still supply roughly four-fifths of the world’s energy, a figure that has barely changed in decades. While reducing that dependence is urgently needed to address the rapidly escalating threats of climate change, the hard reality is that keeping energy affordable and reliable during a multidecade transition still requires investment in oil and gas. According to the IEA, around $490 billion a year would still be needed by 2035 even in a scenario where countries meet their climate pledges—which the collapse of United Nations climate talks in Turkey made plainly clear is far from being true today.

Moreover, the same strategies used against high-profile pipelines such as Keystone XL and Mountain Valley have often proved effective at obstructing clean energy projects as well. As the New York Times editorial board argued this month in endorsing permitting reform, essential laws protecting the environment, communities, and Indigenous peoples “have become so complex and restrictive that the country cannot build the future it needs.”

To be sure, the BAAJA is not a substitute for climate policy, nor are its emissions benefits assured. Analysis by Rhodium Group, a consultancy, projects that the bill could reduce U.S. power-sector emissions in 2040 by as much as 18 percent compared with current policy, or by as little as 1 percent, depending on energy prices and technology costs. At the same time, climate policy cannot be effective without a bill such as the BAAJA that allows for the rapid buildout of the generation, transmission, storage, and transit infrastructure required for cleaner energy solutions.

A third area of concern involves weakened tribal consultation under the National Historic Preservation Act. Faster permitting should not undermine tribes’ ability to meaningfully influence decisions that affect sacred sites and other places central to their history and traditions. A set of revisions to the bill would have expanded the projects subject to tribal consultation and authorized additional money to support tribal and state historic-preservation work, yet Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley prevented those amendments from being considered, which may make it harder for some House Democrats to support the bill.

Finally, some opponents worry that specific provisions could protect improperly approved projects, require the government to pay companies large sums in damages, and constrain future administrations’ ability to issue or enforce environmental protections. Because these objections involve detailed, often technical, legal objections to the bill’s drafting, they have failed to garner the same attention as absolutist rhetoric about fossil fuels or misleading claims about data center buildout, which is unfortunate because many of these legal concerns have merit, even if they do not ultimately justify opposing the bill.

At the heart of critics’ concerns is a mistrust of how a conservative judiciary hostile to environmental regulation will interpret the bill’s ambiguities. Key areas of concern include new limits on National Environmental Policy Act lawsuits and potential unintended consequences of provisions to limit an administration’s ability to revoke existing permits. Those so-called permit certainty provisions, which the New Yorker’s Elizabeth Kolbert called the most “dangerous” in the bill, were designed to prevent just the sort of harm the Trump administration has done to offshore wind.

Yet subsequent revisions to the bill, known as the “manager’s amendment,” made meaningful improvements to address those concerns. Kolbert writes that the bill could “tie the hands of any future Administration that wants to responsibly promote green energy over fossil fuels,” yet the revisions specifically added an exception to address this concern for agency actions taken under applicable law or regulation and a clause intended to preserve existing legal authorities. They responded to concerns that restrictions on government interference with a permitted project’s operation at “full capacity” could be used to block new environmental rules—for example, emissions standards under the Clean Air Act that would induce a coal plant to curb its output. The amendment also extends from five to 10 years the permitting-data lookback used to assess claims of disparate treatment. That longer time period addressed concerns that Trump’s preferential treatment of fossil fuels and obstruction of renewables would become the benchmark against which a future administration’s permitting decisions are judged.

The changes also require a showing of bad faith for the additional damages available under the bill, addressing concerns that an agency could face enormous payouts for an action a court finds unlawful. And the amendment expressly allows the government to offer lawful explanations for differences in permitting outcomes and extends the requirement that applicants seeking relief demonstrate technical and financial capacity to all of their pending projects.

But the changes do not eliminate every risk. For example, an expansive interpretation of what counts as a “permit” or “authorization” could, critics fear, extend protections beyond formal agency approvals to informal assurances from the Trump administration. Critics also worry that because nearly every agency action invokes some legal authority, a broad reading of the exception for actions “taken pursuant to any applicable law or regulation” could render the permit protections meaningless. To avoid that result, judges could read the exception narrowly, limiting future administrations’ ability to curb pollution.

Another round of revisions—the one blocked by Merkley—would have made modest improvements, such as to the concern about private assurances counting as authorizations. The legal risks identified about how hostile judges could interpret ambiguity merit attention and should be remedied to the extent possible as the current bill moves through Congress. Although the bill is unlikely to be amended in the House, one of its architects in the Senate has suggested the House might attach amendments to other pieces of must-pass legislation.

Even without those revisions, however, the bill’s benefits outweigh the risks. The current permitting system simply makes it too difficult and costly to expand the grid, build a stronger energy system, connect cleaner generation, and lower energy costs.

Later this week, Americans will gather for Thanksgiving, with energy costs weighing on the price of traveling to see family, heating homes, and cooking the holiday meal. The annual national observance of Thanksgiving started with President Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation in 1863—the same year construction began on the transcontinental railroad. Six years later, the two lines met in Utah, connecting nearly 1,800 miles of track. By contrast, California today aims to begin high-speed rail service between Merced and Bakersfield—a distance of less than 200 miles—in 2033, a quarter-century after voters approved the project. When members of Congress return from their Thanksgiving celebrations, their first order of business should be to make it easier to build again in this country—starting with the infrastructure needed for a cleaner, more affordable, and more reliable energy system.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

title: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained | Council on Foreign Relations
description:
Global construction of data centers is accelerating as the race to lead in AI development heats up.
AI data centers, however, rely mostly on graphics processing units (GPUs)—specialized processors that can run thousands of calculations simultaneously, making them well suited to building and running large-scale AI models.

text:
Global construction of data centers is accelerating as the race to lead in AI development heats up. These facilities have the computational and physical infrastructure needed to train and run large-scale AI models, making them a critical part of countries’ efforts to drive AI expansion. However, while technology companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into building these facilities, countries’ approaches to their construction differ, shaped by energy supply, land availability, and economic capital.

Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, and communities have pushed back over concerns about rising power bills and strained resources. In response, some countries have restricted new construction, while others have taken action to fast-track projects with the goal of attracting investment.

These differing approaches reflect broader uncertainty about AI proliferation. “It’s not really about energy or water so much as people’s concerns about AI,” David Hart, CFR senior fellow for climate and energy, said of the backlash to data center construction. “It’s very hard to tackle that directly because it’s a very abstract, amorphous thing, but if the data center is right there, then it’s a much easier target.”

Data centers are large facilities filled with servers that store and process the data behind nearly everything people do online. Traditional data centers run mainly on central processing units and were built to supply roughly five to ten kilowatts of power per rack—the cabinet that holds a stack of servers. These centers use air cooling systems to prevent servers from overheating.

AI data centers, however, rely mostly on graphics processing units (GPUs)—specialized processors that can run thousands of calculations simultaneously, making them well suited to building and running large-scale AI models. These systems require substantially more power: A single rack of Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 system, for example, draws approximately 120 kilowatts per rack, equivalent to the average electricity demand of one hundred American homes. To manage the added heat, AI facilities primarily use liquid cooling systems that pipe coolant directly to the chips.

AI’s growing power demands are driving a rapid consumption of electricity. Data centers consumed an estimated 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024—about 1.5 percent of all electricity consumed worldwide that year—and the International Energy Agency estimates that figure will more than double by 2030, primarily due to the increase in AI use.

Much of that electricity demand is a result of how AI models are built and used. Before an AI model can be deployed, it needs to be trained, a process that involves feeding enormous amounts of data through many thousands of GPUs at once. Because these models run around the clock, AI data centers require a reliable, continuous power supply that renewables such as wind and solar alone cannot provide, causing developers to look increasingly to natural gas and nuclear energy.

The United States has more data centers than any other country, with more than five thousand operational and planned facilities of varying sizes listed across the country, according to Data Center Map. Globally, more than 13,000 planned or operational data centers are listed across over 180 countries. Beyond the United States, these centers are clustered primarily in major European economic hubs, such as France and Germany, as well as large Asian markets such as China and India.

Data centers use water directly to cool their servers and indirectly through the power plants that generate their electricity. Many still rely on evaporative cooling, which requires a constant water supply because lost water cannot be immediately reused. In 2025, global data centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water, according to a report [PDF] by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment, and Health—enough to meet the annual basic household water needs of more than six hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa.

AI expansion could drive water consumption much higher. By 2030, the UN report projects that AI-related water consumption could reach nearly 2.5 trillion gallons annually. Where data centers are built also matters: S&P Global estimates that 43 percent of data centers worldwide face high water stress, including 38 percent in the United States and roughly 60 percent in China.

Environmental. In addition to concerns over water usage, AI data center growth is driving up carbon emissions and increasing demand for coal and natural gas, which still power many facilities. AI-related carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030—roughly what the entire United Kingdom emitted in 2025. AI’s expansion is also challenging tech companies’ climate goals. Microsoft, which has promised to become carbon negative by 2030, saw its emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025, largely because of data center development.

Data centers can also pose health risks to nearby communities. Harvard University researchers estimated that the power supply for a single data center in Loudoun County, Virginia—dubbed the data center capital of the world—could cause between $53 million and $99 million in annual health damages from related air pollution. These facilities also take up sizable portions of land. By 2030, the land needed to generate electricity for AI data centers globally could exceed 14,500 square kilometers (more than 5,500 square miles).

Economic. Building AI infrastructure requires significant investment, and tech companies are betting that the payoff will be worth it. For example, Alphabet (the parent organization for Google), Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft collectively plan to spend roughly $725 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, with most of that money funding AI infrastructure. However, a growing share of the AI build-out is financed by debt, which experts warn could make lenders more cautious as it becomes less clear when AI’s economic gains will materialize. “There’s just too much uncertainty in the market,” Connor Martin, a CFR international affairs fellow, said.

A large share of the capital powering the AI boom in the United States also comes from abroad, particularly Gulf countries. The United Arab Emirates (UAE), for example, committed in 2025 to a ten-year, $1.4 trillion framework to boost investment in AI infrastructure, semiconductors, and other areas of the U.S. economy. Saudi Arabia also struck a nearly $1 trillion investment deal with the United States last year.

But Martin noted that those commitments were made before the outbreak of the Iran war. “It would be totally reasonable for the Saudi or Emirati governments to cut back at least some of that committed money to focus on their own defense and oil infrastructure,” he said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if some of their commitments don’t end up materializing, or at least take longer to materialize than we thought.”

For many countries, however, the AI boom represents a major economic opportunity. Africa’s data center market is expected to attract $10–20 billion in investment by 2030, while in Southeast Asia, Malaysia has attracted billions of dollars from major tech companies with its relatively cheap land and electricity. But these investments can come with trade-offs. Data centers have so far used an average of 7 percent of Malaysia’s electricity in 2026, and that share is projected to climb to roughly one third by 2035.

United States. In the United States, private companies decide where and how to build, while the federal government has focused on facilitating expansion. In July 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to fast-track permits for construction of AI data centers and power plants and support related projects through federal loans, grants, and tax incentives. “The private sector leads, and that’s the source of our strength,” Martin said. “But it also means that the federal government has less leverage to strategically plan where these data centers should go. As a result, they go where the economics say they should.” Most U.S. data centers are heavily concentrated in Georgia, Texas, Virginia, and major metropolitan hubs like Silicon Valley.

Hart argued that the United States’ patchwork of utilities, state regulators, and regional grid operators “is falling short as a whole,” and described the Trump administration’s energy policy as “sort of contradictory,” as it is fast-tracking data centers while also blocking wind and other sources that could come online quickly and cheaply.

China. China has taken a more centralized approach. In 2022, Beijing launched a national project called East Data, West Computing, which directs new data centers to be built away from the eastern provinces—where land is expensive and energy supplies are tight—and in the country’s western provinces, where large solar and wind farms are located. Although China still gets roughly half of its electricity from coal, Hart said its massive renewable build-out means power isn’t what’s holding it back. “Their big constraint on AI is chips,” he said, adding that although the United States has the necessary chips, it is constrained by an aging power grid.

The Gulf. Gulf states are using their vast energy resources and sovereign wealth funds to build AI infrastructure as quickly as possible. Following strikes by Iran, the UAE is reassessing the design and layout of Stargate UAE, a U.S.-backed AI data center infrastructure project projected to cost more than $30 billion. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia plans to invest tens of billions of dollars through HUMAIN, an AI company backed by the country’s public investment fund, which manages over $1 trillion in assets.

Europe and Southeast Asia. Given limited land space and grid capacity, some European and Southeast Asian governments have leaned on moratoriums and rationing, slowing down data center development. The Netherlands, for example, imposed a nationwide ban on new hyperscale data centers in 2024, and Ireland now requires newly constructed facilities to supply their own power. Meanwhile, Singapore, Southeast Asia’s original data center hub, halted new approvals from 2019 to 2022 over concerns about energy use, and now only admits facilities that meet strict efficiency standards.

Rebuilding trust and showing that the U.S. can be a reliable partner in addressing climate change going forward was top of mind for a group of House Democrats who attended a United Nations climate conference in Turkey last weekend, Rep. Dave Min, D-Irvine, said.

And though the delegation focused on exploring ways the U.S. could strengthen relationships to address climate issues, Min said they also felt some skepticism from others in attendance. Min said there is some worry that the U.S. cannot commit to climate issues long-term, because of how the political winds of the federal government can change quickly.

“You could feel the lack of trust they have in the United States these days, and that trust is going to take a long time to earn back,” Min said.

“That being said, I think everyone also agrees that the future is here,” he continued. “We can catch up. People still believe in the innovation economy of the United States. They believe we can catch up, but right now we’re way behind.”

Min said the delegation was met with “legitimate excitement” when they arrived because the U.S., under President Donald Trump, has not sent an official delegation to the conference in previous years.

Min said he and other members of Congress were set to attend last year’s conference in Brazil, but their trip was canceled amid the 43-day federal government shutdown.

One of the big issues Min said he is motivated to address once the 120th Congress convenes at the beginning of next year is to cut carbon emissions in the U.S., and even before the new Congress is sworn in, the House may be voting on new legislation that aims to speed up review processes for energy infrastructure.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which the Senate passed Thursday, would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects, like building power plants and other infrastructure, while also forcing data centers to pay for their own energy costs.

The bill was set to receive a vote from the House this week, but a lack of House Republican attendance delayed any action, Min said.

Though in principle, Min is in favor of the bill, he said he will ultimately be a no-vote when the time comes. Min argued that if enacted, the law would strip localities of control over their own backyard and limit their ability to prevent major infrastructure, like data centers, from being built, he said.

“This is a topic we discussed extensively at (the conference). When you’re talking about data centers, it’s not just the energy costs, although that’s a big part of it. It’s also the other ways in which they impact local communities — noise and heat, water usage — that should be part of any package we’re talking about,” Min said. ” At the end of the day, localities should be the ones deciding whether or not they want to put up a data center … with that being said, we should be pushing forward with permitting reform, for all of the above.”

text:
What if the same work truck used for daily maintenance could also provide backup power during an emergency? That's part of the thinking behind ZMD Motors' planned acquisition of Inventev, a company developing technology that allows electrified vehicles to supply power to external equipment and facilities.

Ad Loading...

Detroit-based ZMD Motors is developing zero-emission medium-duty Class 4-6 work trucks under its EQUIPD brand, starting with the Ram 5500 Class 5 chassis cab. The company is targeting a potential launch around the 2027 model year, with future plans to incorporate Inventev's export power technology as an optional feature.

Ad Loading...

The acquisition is underway as part of ZMD Motors' startup capitalization plan. The companies intend to develop their technologies together, although the electric trucks and export power capabilities will follow separate commercialization timelines.

Why ZMD Motors Is Acquiring Inventev

According to Sharon Dudley-Parham, chief marketing officer for ZMD Motors, the decision grew out of the companies' shared interest in making commercial vehicles more useful across different operating conditions.

"Simply, the synergies were too strong to pass up with both ventures in early stages of development," Dudley-Parham told Work Truck.

Inventev initially focused on plug-in hybrid vehicle conversions, with export power offered as an additional capability. The company later shifted its primary focus toward providing commercial-grade mobile power.

Meanwhile, ZMD Motors has been developing electrified medium-duty work trucks designed around the operational needs of utility, government, and vocational fleets.

Ad Loading...

The acquisition would bring those efforts together, allowing ZMD Motors to plan for export power integration while developing its electric truck architecture.

Starting With the Ram 5500 Chassis Cab

ZMD Motors has identified the Ram 5500 chassis cab as the starting platform for its EQUIPD electric work trucks. Rather than developing an entirely new vehicle from the ground up, the company plans to integrate its electrification systems into newly manufactured internal combustion chassis after they leave the OEM production line.

Under the proposed ship-through manufacturing approach, new chassis would be routed to a specialized facility for electrification before being prepared for fleet deployment.

The approach is intended to preserve familiar chassis configurations and vocational upfitting options while replacing conventional propulsion systems with electric power.

As previously reported by Automotive Fleet, ZMD Motors is targeting a potential launch around the 2027 model year, depending on development progress.

Ad Loading...

The company's initial focus includes municipal, state, utility, and other vocational fleets that operate medium-duty trucks with predictable daily routes and centralized operations.

For those customers, maintaining familiar vehicle platforms could help reduce some of the operational changes associated with transitioning to electric trucks.

How Could Export Power Change Work Truck Operations?

For many fleet operators, emergency power requires additional equipment, whether that's a dedicated generator, a trailer-mounted unit, or a rental secured when the need arises. ZMD Motors sees an opportunity to make that capability part of the truck itself.

When commercialized, Inventev's technology could allow appropriately equipped EQUIPD trucks to provide electricity for temporary operations, emergency response, and work in locations without access to the power grid.

Dudley-Parham described the technology as a selectable feature rather than something every customer would necessarily need.

Ad Loading...

"Think of export power as a 'bolt-on' feature or selectable option," she explained.

Potential applications include powering emergency lighting, water pumps, temporary shelters, and traffic control equipment during outages. Utility fleets could also use mobile power during planned maintenance or restoration work.

Outside emergency response, construction crews, agricultural operations, and other vocational fleets working in remote locations could benefit from having a mobile power source available without bringing a separate generator.

The idea is not necessarily to replace every dedicated generator. Instead, the technology could give fleets another option when temporary power is needed.

"The broader value is flexibility and efficiency…a work truck that is already part of the fleet can become an additional mobile power resource when and where circumstances demand it," Dudley-Parham said.

Ad Loading...

Looking Beyond Traditional Vehicle TCO

One of the more interesting aspects of the acquisition is how ZMD Motors is approaching fleet economics. Traditional total cost of ownership (TCO) calculations focus on expenses such as vehicle acquisition, maintenance, energy, insurance, and depreciation. ZMD Motors is also considering how additional vehicle capabilities might affect the need for other equipment.

For example, a municipal fleet might maintain dedicated generators for emergency response, even though those units spend much of their time in storage. If an electric work truck can perform its normal maintenance duties and provide temporary power when needed, that could change how the fleet evaluates its equipment requirements.

There are still important questions to answer, including the cost of the optional technology, available power output, operating duration, and how using a truck for backup power would affect its availability for other assignments.

However, the acquisition reflects ZMD Motors' interest in developing trucks that can support multiple operational needs rather than focusing exclusively on vehicle propulsion.

What's Next for EQUIPD and Inventev?

ZMD Motors said the acquisition will not change its initial plans to introduce zero-emission work trucks under the EQUIPD brand. The Ram 5500-based electric truck remains the company's starting point, with a potential 2027 model-year launch. Inventev's export power technology is being developed separately and is not confirmed as a feature on the initial production vehicles.

Ad Loading...

As EQUIPD engineering progresses, ZMD Motors plans to incorporate provisions into the vehicle architecture that could accommodate future export power integration.

Inventev is currently focused on work associated with a Federal Transit Administration Temporary Emergency Power research grant. ZMD Motors also sees potential applications for the technology on other manufacturers' electrified commercial vehicle platforms.

The company has not announced a firm date for completing the acquisition or introducing export power-equipped EQUIPD trucks.

For fleet managers considering electric medium-duty trucks, the Ram 5500 platform provides a more specific starting point for evaluating ZMD Motors' plans. Questions about vehicle range, payload, upfit compatibility, charging requirements, and cost will be important as the company moves toward commercialization.

The proposed Inventev integration adds another consideration: whether an electric work truck could eventually handle its regular vocational assignments while also serving as a mobile power source when needed.

text:
Actor and progressive activist Mark Ruffalo warned his social media followers about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act being considered in Congress, saying the bill to loosen the permitting process for major energy projects, including data centers, would harm the environment.

This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

In the Nov. 18 video that’s been viewed 22 million times, Ruffalo said, “Democrats in the United States Senate are on the verge of handing Trump, Republicans and the fossil fuel industry a major legislative win by passing a bill that would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants, and ICE camps, while sacrificing our clean water, tribal rights, public lands, and endangered species. If it passed, it would be the most severe and devastating rollback of environmental laws in American history.”

A day after Ruffalo’s post, the bill cleared the Senate, 62-33, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans in support. The vote sharply divided Senate Democrats: 30 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against it.

The legislation, which President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for in a Nov. 20 news conference, must win approval in the House to advance. The House could amend the bill, which would require the Senate to approve the new text.

The uncertainty over the bill’s fate, the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know with any certainty whether the scenario Ruffalo predicts will come to pass.

As written, the bill would ease the process of building major infrastructure — including data centers — by limiting laws historically used to block such projects.

It would also accelerate the adoption of low-emission renewable energy and require data centers to pay for their increased energy use.

“There are priorities that both sides want — it is not perfect,” said Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy.

Ruffalo’s representative did not respond to an inquiry for this article.

What does the bill do, and who supports and opposes it?

The bill’s sponsors — Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia — designed it to speed up the process of securing approval for major infrastructure projects, particularly those for energy production and transmission.

The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts. With energy demand growing and electricity prices rising, supporters said a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs.

Critics of the bill say it effectively guts tools to prevent local governments and citizens, Native American tribes, and other local interests from blocking the harms caused by such projects. They also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure.

It has the support of some renewable energy groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association and the AFL-CIO labor union, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute, which represents utilities.

Groups opposing the bill include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union.

Why are environmentalists concerned?

Certain laws that have long been used to oppose big projects — including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act — would be pared back if the new law is enacted.

The Natural Resources Defense Council’s analysis concluded that under the bill, a court “can never invalidate a permit” based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act, “no matter how severe it finds a legal violation to be.” It also found that the bill would exclude certain types of environmentally harmful activities from review and limit who can bring a case.

In most cases, the bill would prevent federal agencies from canceling, suspending or changing federal permits for projects that have received all necessary permits.

“It is reasonable to be concerned that the development of each of the kinds of projects (Ruffalo) mentioned could be facilitated by this bill,” said Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning.

Opponents also worry the bill could allow the Trump administration to lock in fossil fuel projects or data centers without enough opportunity for opponents to challenge them.

“If the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits,” the NRDC analysis says.

As for Ruffalo’s reference to detention facilities for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the bill does not directly address those, but opponents of the bill say their concerns stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida.

How does the bill advance environmentalists’ goals?

Although the Natural Resources Defense Council opposes the bill in its current form, its analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill’s positive features, including:

The bill would improve the nation’s electric capacity in two ways: by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and by enabling construction of new lines. The bill could cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

While fossil fuels and data centers could benefit from the bill’s changes, renewable energy — including solar, wind and geothermal energy — would benefit more. “Approximately 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage.”

The bill includes a provision that requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. (Critics say this response is insufficient if the new rules promote data centers being built in the first place.)

One of the bill’s highest-profile supporters is The New York Times columnist Ezra Klein, who is considered left of center politically.

In a recent column, Klein said he was “unnerved” by conflicting interpretations over what certain provisions of the bill mean, but still supported it.

“The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand — whether from data centers or electric vehicles or heat pumps or anything else — with renewables,” Klein wrote. “What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels. And the absence of that system describes our reality today.”

The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, Klein wrote, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access.

Ultimately, Henderson said, the bill’s impacts “are highly uncertain, depending on a mix of political outcomes (who controls the federal government and what decisions they make), market outcomes (competition between electricity sources domestically), geopolitical outcomes (such as global demand for the United States’ oil and gas exports), and legal outcomes (courts’ interpretation of the law).”

This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

Seven episodes, each lasting several days, affected at least 30% of the region.

text:
November 23, 2026

SAN FRANCISCO (Nov. 23, 2026) – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced eight settlements with eight companies operating California and Arizona facilities, resolving alleged violations of chemical safety requirements under the Clean Air Act. The settlements involve the companies’ anhydrous ammonia and chlorine gas handling at various facilities, all of which will come into compliance with the safety regulations.

“Too many companies handling large quantities of dangerous chemicals are not fully aware of federal safety requirements and the serious consequences of accidental releases,” said EPA Pacific Southwest Regional Administrator Mike Martucci. “These EPA actions will ensure facilities are working to keep our communities safe by meeting standards required by law.”

EPA’s action is enforcing the Risk Management Plan (RMP) chemical safety requirements of the Clean Air Act’s Section 112(r). In addition to returning to compliance, the companies have collectively agreed to pay penalties totaling over $1.3 million.

Background

The goal of Section 112(r) of the Clean Air Act is to reduce the risk of chemical accidents. Facilities that house over 10,000 lbs of anhydrous ammonia or over 2,500 lbs of chlorine gas must comply with RMP requirements designed to prevent and prepare for accidental chemical releases.

Anhydrous ammonia presents significant health and safety hazards as it is corrosive to the skin, eyes, and lungs. Exposure to 300 parts per million is immediately dangerous to life and health. Ammonia is also flammable at concentrations of approximately 16% to 25% by volume in air and can explode if released in an enclosed space with a source of ignition present, or if a vessel containing anhydrous ammonia is exposed to fire.

Chlorine is a gas used in the production of thousands of products and for water disinfection. Exposure to 10 parts per million is immediately dangerous to life and health and can result in changes in breathing rate, coughing, and lung damage.

For more information about Section 112(r) of the Clean Air Act, visit EPA’s Risk Management Program Rule websiteExit EPA’s website.

text:
Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections.

The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition.

“There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board.

The gas plant in question is an 800-megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted.

“This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution.

Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution.

On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81% of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX.

Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours.

That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case.

“In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email.

In this decision and those pertaining to renewable energy, critics take issue with the Power Siting Board’s deference to local governments, even when evidence shows they are not necessarily reflecting the wishes of the broader public.

In 2025, for example, the Power Siting Board’s staff recommended against the Grange Solar project in Logan County on the basis of pushback from local governments. But a majority of individuals who submitted comments wanted the solar farm. The developer ultimately withdrew its plan and opted to pursue projects elsewhere.

And earlier this year, regulators nixed the Crossroads Solar farm in Morrow County because all nearby local governments opposed the project. Although that ruling noted the ​“presence of strong, united opposition” among the local population, dozens of comments were apparently fake, and an analysis by the developer found that the number of verifiable individuals against the project was not overwhelming in comparison with its supporters.

The board’s staff also did an about-face from supporting Crossroads Solar to opposing it after one township changed its position from neutral to opposed.

“Ultimately, the Ohio Power Siting Board has demonstrated its hypocrisy,” Tavenor said, ​“by approving a natural gas facility for a data center where it has denied renewable energy projects with less significant opposition.”

Regulators, for their part, acknowledged the Ashville vote in their decision but asserted that they have authority to issue the permit regardless of the outcome of the election. The 108-page opinion also says that conditions agreed to by the village, the developer, and the board staff were enough to deal with public concerns.

The board also gave short shrift to opponents’ argument that the gas plant proposal fails to meet a separate legal requirement that projects have minimal environmental impact. Its take stems from the fact that the developer opted for reciprocating internal combustion engines and simple-cycle natural gas turbines over less-polluting combined-cycle turbines or fuel cells, which are more expensive right now.

Regulatory staff argued that ​“minimum” doesn’t demand the lowest environmental impact but depends on a plant’s purpose, available technology, and economics. The board decided that the project meets the requirement, basically punting to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency’s expected issuance of air permits for the facility.

Project opponents have 30 days to ask for reconsideration of the ruling. Unless the Power Siting Board changes its mind, an appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court could follow.

As written, the bill would ease the process of building major infrastructure — including data centers — by limiting laws historically used to block such projects.

text:
Actor and progressive activist Mark Ruffalo warned his social media followers about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act being considered in Congress, saying the bill to loosen the permitting process for major energy projects, including data centers, would harm the environment.

This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

In the Nov. 18 video that’s been viewed 22 million times, Ruffalo said, “Democrats in the United States Senate are on the verge of handing Trump, Republicans and the fossil fuel industry a major legislative win by passing a bill that would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants, and ICE camps, while sacrificing our clean water, tribal rights, public lands, and endangered species. If it passed, it would be the most severe and devastating rollback of environmental laws in American history.”

A day after Ruffalo’s post, the bill cleared the Senate, 62-33, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans in support. The vote sharply divided Senate Democrats: 30 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against it.

The legislation, which President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for in a Nov. 20 news conference, must win approval in the House to advance. The House could amend the bill, which would require the Senate to approve the new text.

The uncertainty over the bill’s fate, the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know with any certainty whether the scenario Ruffalo predicts will come to pass.

As written, the bill would ease the process of building major infrastructure — including data centers — by limiting laws historically used to block such projects.

It would also accelerate the adoption of low-emission renewable energy and require data centers to pay for their increased energy use.

“There are priorities that both sides want — it is not perfect,” said Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy.

Ruffalo’s representative did not respond to an inquiry for this article.

What does the bill do, and who supports and opposes it?

The bill’s sponsors — Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia — designed it to speed up the process of securing approval for major infrastructure projects, particularly those for energy production and transmission.

The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts. With energy demand growing and electricity prices rising, supporters said a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs.

Critics of the bill say it effectively guts tools to prevent local governments and citizens, Native American tribes, and other local interests from blocking the harms caused by such projects. They also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure.

It has the support of some renewable energy groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association and the AFL-CIO labor union, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute, which represents utilities.

Groups opposing the bill include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union.

Why are environmentalists concerned?

Certain laws that have long been used to oppose big projects — including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act — would be pared back if the new law is enacted.

The Natural Resources Defense Council’s analysis concluded that under the bill, a court “can never invalidate a permit” based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act, “no matter how severe it finds a legal violation to be.” It also found that the bill would exclude certain types of environmentally harmful activities from review and limit who can bring a case.

In most cases, the bill would prevent federal agencies from canceling, suspending or changing federal permits for projects that have received all necessary permits.

“It is reasonable to be concerned that the development of each of the kinds of projects (Ruffalo) mentioned could be facilitated by this bill,” said Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning.

Opponents also worry the bill could allow the Trump administration to lock in fossil fuel projects or data centers without enough opportunity for opponents to challenge them.

“If the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits,” the NRDC analysis says.

As for Ruffalo’s reference to detention facilities for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the bill does not directly address those, but opponents of the bill say their concerns stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida.

How does the bill advance environmentalists’ goals?

Although the Natural Resources Defense Council opposes the bill in its current form, its analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill’s positive features, including:

The bill would improve the nation’s electric capacity in two ways: by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and by enabling construction of new lines. The bill could cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six.

While fossil fuels and data centers could benefit from the bill’s changes, renewable energy — including solar, wind and geothermal energy — would benefit more. “Approximately 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage.”

The bill includes a provision that requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers. (Critics say this response is insufficient if the new rules promote data centers being built in the first place.)

One of the bill’s highest-profile supporters is The New York Times columnist Ezra Klein, who is considered left of center politically.

In a recent column, Klein said he was “unnerved” by conflicting interpretations over what certain provisions of the bill mean, but still supported it.

“The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand — whether from data centers or electric vehicles or heat pumps or anything else — with renewables,” Klein wrote. “What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels. And the absence of that system describes our reality today.”

The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, Klein wrote, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access.

Ultimately, Henderson said, the bill’s impacts “are highly uncertain, depending on a mix of political outcomes (who controls the federal government and what decisions they make), market outcomes (competition between electricity sources domestically), geopolitical outcomes (such as global demand for the United States’ oil and gas exports), and legal outcomes (courts’ interpretation of the law).”

This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.

It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

name: Indiana Environment
title: COP31 ends with no deal after negotiators fail to reach an agreement on fossil fuels - WVXU
authors: Rachel Waldholz, Steve Inskeep, www.wvxu.org, steve-inskeep
description:
Nearly 200 nations typically commit to some statement on the next steps to address climate change.
But oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia blocked any mention of fossil fuels in the final agreement.
Ultimately, the EU decided that getting no deal at this summit was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels at all.
And wealthy countries, who are most responsible for climate change, agreed to provide funding as part of the Paris Climate Agreement.
But given how key fossil fuels are still to most economies, that's a big shift.
text:
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:

Delegates from around the world walked away from a climate summit over the weekend after failing to agree on a plan.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Yes, this annual meeting has taken place since 1995. Nearly 200 nations typically commit to some statement on the next steps to address climate change. This time, even going overtime did not lead to an agreement.

INSKEEP: NPR's Rachel Waldholz also went into overtime. Is that right, Rachel?

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: Yes, indeed, Steve.

INSKEEP: OK. She's still in Turkey. What caused the talks there to break down?

WALDHOLZ: Well, countries came into these talks with a lot of disagreements, but the issue that really pushed this conference over the edge was the question of how to address fossil fuels. Many countries wanted a final agreement that explicitly called for a global transition away from coal and oil and natural gas as the primary drivers of climate change. And that included especially many small island states - Panama, the European Union. But oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia blocked any mention of fossil fuels in the final agreement. Ultimately, the EU decided that getting no deal at this summit was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels at all. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DARRAGH O'BRIEN: It fails to meet the moment. The moment that our world faces, the crisis that our world faces.

WALDHOLZ: And he said that's especially true in a year that has seen climate-fueled disasters all over the globe, from heat waves and wildfires in Europe to the massive flooding in Nepal.

INSKEEP: Was the mention of fossil fuels the only thing they disagreed about?

WALDHOLZ: Oh, it is never only one thing, Steve. And the other big sticking point at the summit was money. Developing countries want more help dealing with climate change. They point out that they've contributed very little to global warming but are often dealing with some of the worst impacts. And wealthy countries, who are most responsible for climate change, agreed to provide funding as part of the Paris Climate Agreement. Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner - she represents the Pacific Island nation of the Marshall Islands, and she called on rich countries to follow through on their promises.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KATHY JETNIL-KIJINER: We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises. People are dying. Seas are rising. Ecosystems are collapsing.

WALDHOLZ: And, of course, one big, wealthy country that wasn't at the climate talks is the U.S. The Trump administration has withdrawn from the international climate negotiations.

INSKEEP: OK. So what does it mean when the various countries of the world can't seem to agree on anything big, even if the U.S. - which has its own issues - is not there?

WALDHOLZ: Yeah. It certainly raises questions about how effective the U.N. process can be for dealing with an issue like climate change. But actually, you know, what's interesting is that some of the biggest defenders of this COP system are the smaller countries and developing countries. They see it as one of the places where they can have a say and be heard. Mohamed Adow leads the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, which is based in Nairobi.

MOHAMED ADOW: It's the only process we have where the least developed countries, the small island states, have a voice and are able to provide that much-needed moral leadership.

WALDHOLZ: You know, one interesting development at these climate talks is that countries have begun forming these side deals, these kinds of coalitions of the willing. Countries including France and Germany and Spain have rolled out these roadmaps to leave behind fossil fuels entirely. These are voluntary. A lot of them are pretty squishy. They don't have that many specifics. But given how key fossil fuels are still to most economies, that's a big shift.

INSKEEP: OK. NPR's Rachel Waldholz in Turkey. Thanks so much.

WALDHOLZ: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

title: California Needs Science And Politics Free From Corporate Influence
description:
Leading up to the 2026 midterms, a small number of powerful people spent staggering amounts of money to influence the election.
Industrial agribusinesses are more concerned with protecting their bottom lines and maintaining California’s resource-intensive and unsustainable agricultural system, while communities, public health, and local economies pay the price.
What must come next: science-based policymaking free from corporate influence To help see past the disinformation and deliberate deception on such complex issues, UCS works to ensure that independent science, free from corporate or political bias, can guide decision-making.
Even with these new opportunities, issues like climate change, energy affordability, and sustainable land use remain complex.
When we put science at the center of the policy process, we can build a California that is more affordable, healthier, and fairer.
text:
My daughter, 6 years old, likes to sit with me as I fill in my mail-in ballots. Maybe she’s motivated by the beautifully designed “I voted” sticker from the City and County of San Francisco’s Department of Elections. Maybe filling out the circles on the ballot looks like the worksheets that she’s used to doing at school. But I also hope she’s curious about what the adults are doing around Election Day.

I try to bring her into why we vote, understanding who the candidates are, what the issues are, and how we vote. Living in San Francisco, I start with an issue that is local and easy to explain to a 1st grader. I explain how some people want to use an area next to the ocean as a highway for driving cars, some people want to use it as a park for playing, and San Franciscans choose between the two options by voting.

Which has happened three times in her lifetime, in 2022, 2024, and 2026.

Many San Francisco voters are probably exhausted by this issue coming back again and again on our ballots, but I have some appreciation that a lesson is easier to teach to your kid when you can repeat it a few times.

Who else showed up?

But my explanation of how we vote left out who else showed up in the election.

Leading up to the 2026 midterms, a small number of powerful people spent staggering amounts of money to influence the election. The top 20 megadonors spent $2 billion on federal races in this year’s election. In California, ultra-wealthy donors spent $378 million to defeat a proposition that would have taxed the state’s few hundred billionaires to fill the gap left by federal Medi-Cal cuts. There’s no sticker to record their participation in the election. If there were, it would say, “We spent billions to influence votes.”

The influence extends beyond elections, as those with extreme wealth and power are using disinformation to influence the policy fights. Oil companies try to shift the blame for the affordability crisis away from their own sky-high markups to California regulations designed to keep people safe and preserve a healthy environment. After decades of fossil fuel companies misleading the public about their products’ contributions to climate change and blocking climate action, we now know that 94% of industrial CO2 emissions since 1959 trace to just 122 oil, gas, coal, and cement companies.

Tech companies are resisting protections for children and consumers, while forcing data centers on communities where the pollution, noise, and energy costs are not welcome. Industrial agribusinesses are more concerned with protecting their bottom lines and maintaining California’s resource-intensive and unsustainable agricultural system, while communities, public health, and local economies pay the price.

What must come next: science-based policymaking free from corporate influence

To help see past the disinformation and deliberate deception on such complex issues, UCS works to ensure that independent science, free from corporate or political bias, can guide decision-making. The midterm elections opened up opportunities with the 120th Congress and with states to prioritize the public good over distortion of facts and to continue the work to protect democracy, science and public institutions.

Even with these new opportunities, issues like climate change, energy affordability, and sustainable land use remain complex. In California, leaders including the newly elected Governor Becerra will have to tackle challenging questions.

Addressing energy affordability in California needs to include reducing risk of future wildfires, paying for the costs of wildfires that have already ravaged communities, and transitioning to an electricity system that no longer exacerbates climate change. Read my colleague Mark Specht’s piece on the seven energy priorities for our Governor-Elect.

We can—and must—tackle unfair gas prices without sacrificing environmental progress. Read my colleague Jeremy Martin’s piece outlining a path to taking on the oil monopoly and restoring fair competition.

Despite federal attacks on California’s authority to regulate air pollution, we have effective options to transition to clean transportation to save Californians money at the pump, while avoiding the worst public health and climate impacts. My colleague Don Anair lays out a bold agenda for California’s new governor to target the most polluting vehicles on the road and make electric cars more affordable for more people.

As California transitions away from unsustainable agricultural practices, communities need to be in the driver’s seat, leading a coordinated transition towards thriving and resilient local economies. Read my colleague Erin Wooolley’s piece to hear more about the multiple benefits that can be achieved with a just cropland transition and how to focus resources and coordinate planning to achieve transformational change.

These are all hard problems with no easy solutions. In each of these linked posts, my colleagues at UCS sift through the noise of unfounded claims to understand real trade-offs and feasible solutions. When we put science at the center of the policy process, we can build a California that is more affordable, healthier, and fairer. Whether in Sacramento or Washington, DC, decisions should be grounded in evidence, not in the interest of the biggest donors.

description:

But the outcome shouldn’t obscure an important point of consensus: Nations are not divided on the need to electrify.

text:
Like many, The Rockefeller Foundation is disappointed that countries were unable to reach consensus at COP31. Global consensus matters, especially when people around the world are feeling the effects of extreme weather, pollution, and rising food and energy costs. But the outcome shouldn’t obscure an important point of consensus: Nations are not divided on the need to electrify. The disagreement lies in how, and how quickly, economies move away from fossil fuels.

That distinction is important. Climate negotiations at COP have historically focused on subtraction — which emissions are cut, by whom and how much. That is a difficult conversation to resolve amongst 200 nations. Building clean power for people is different because it’s additive. It means new grids, new jobs, and new businesses–as well as lower emissions. It is a policy of economic growth, and growth is a goal that communities and leaders can align behind.

Today, 655 million people still live without access to reliable electricity. Energy poverty rarely exists on its own — most energy-insecure people experience another form of poverty, such as in health, education, or food security. Our research shows that if today’s energy-poor countries are left behind, their share of global emissions could rise from 25% in 2020 to 75% by 2050. How the world brings electricity to these communities is not a side issue in the climate debate; it is central to it.

Progress on electrification will not come from negotiated text alone. It will come from capital, most importantly from lowering its cost and increasing accessibility. Clean energy projects in emerging economies often cost more to finance than in wealthier countries. Closing that gap will unlock investment at the scale that electrification goals require.

The Rockefeller Foundation will continue to deploy grants and catalytic finance that take on early risk so others can follow, in particular supporting grid finance that makes larger-scale investment possible. Philanthropy cannot fund the energy transition alone, but it can help make it investible.

We are grateful to everyone who worked toward an agreement at COP31. The consensus on electrification is strong, and the task is now to finance it.

text:
The first cells are being shipped to Louisville Assembly Plant for use in Ford Fathom prototypes. Ford said the milestone makes it the first company to manufacture LFP batteries in the US for mainstream consumer automotive applications while also building expertise that can be applied to its growing energy storage activities.

LFP Focus for Lower-Cost EVs

According to Ford, the development programme centred on identifying an LFP prismatic battery technology that could help reduce EV costs while supporting large-scale manufacturing.

The company selected technology from CATL, whose batteries are used in millions of vehicles globally. Ford highlighted LFP chemistry’s lack of nickel and cobalt as a key factor in lowering costs, while also pointing to the chemistry’s durability through years of charging and use.

Battery durability is expected to play a role in vehicle-to-home energy applications. Ford noted that AC bidirectional power can enable a vehicle to receive electricity from a suitably equipped home and supply power back when required.

Prismatic Cells and Structural Pack Design

Ford engineered the Fathom platform around battery efficiency, using prismatic cells and incorporating the battery pack as a structural part of the vehicle. Rather than acting solely as an enclosure, the pack contributes to the vehicle chassis.

The company said the rectangular cell format allows cells to fit directly into the structure, helping to reduce structural costs. Electrical and sensing connections have also been combined into a flexible circuit board, while compact power electronics have been integrated into the pack.

Scaling Battery Manufacturing

Beyond cell design, Ford is focusing on high-volume production. The assembly lines at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan are capable of producing 40 cells per minute, making the facility one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly operations outside China.

To support quality control, employees use AI-powered image recognition and other inspection tools to identify defects during production.

Ford said the experience gained in Michigan is also being applied to preparations for battery energy storage production in Glendale, Kentucky. While the end products and customer base will differ from the automotive sector, the company believes the manufacturing expertise, controls and battery know-how developed through the programme will support both businesses in the future.

text:
Although the NRC issued the project’s initial license in 1998, facility construction never began. The project has faced opposition since the license approval; most recently, in July of this year, the New Mexico Department of Justice filed a petition to intervene in the CUP license renewal process with the NRC, noting that the project sites extend into Navajo Nation land and calling for assurances that the project will meet the state’s standards for groundwater protection. That petition is still being adjudicated as of this writing.

History of the CUP: The license for the CUP was initially held by another company, Hydro Resources, which filed its application with the NRC in 1988. The NRC issued the construction and operation license for the CUP a decade later, after which, according to NRC documentation, the project stalled because of ongoing litigation, fluctuations in the market for uranium, and negotiations regarding the facility between Hydro Resources and the Navajo Nation.

Hydro Resources submitted its first license renewal request for the project in 2002; however, delays persisted for similar reasons. The CUP license was transferred to NuFuels in 2018, and in 2024, the NRC requested a revised license renewal application from the current license holder.

Recent regulatory actions: NuFuels submitted the revised renewal application for the CUP in January 2025. Along with providing an updated environmental report, it also incorporated parts of the previous licensing history into its application as allowed by 10 CFR Part 51. The NRC published its notice of the application on May 27, 2026.

Two months later, the NMDOJ filed its petition to intervene, listing 10 environmental contentions and three safety contentions. Among its environmental contentions, the state claimed that NuFuels’ environmental report failed to demonstrate the feasibility of restoring the Westwater Canyon aquifer below the project areas, relied on outdated hydrogeological models, and lacked any references to the Navajo Nation’s legal prohibitions. In its safety contentions, the state claimed that NuFuels’ mine design and characterization, assessments of existing boreholes, and financial guarantees were inadequate.

NuFuels and the NRC both submitted their responses to New Mexico’s petition on August 21. While NuFuels argued that none of the state’s contentions were admissible, the NRC stated that it found six of the environmental contentions and two of the safety contentions admissible and recommended that the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board grant the petition in part.

A panel from the board held a hearing with representatives from NuFuels and the NMDOJ as well as NRC staff on October 5. During the session, it was noted that the NRC had amended its position on one of the safety contentions and no longer considered the claim regarding NuFuels’ financial guarantees admissible.

This was not the only change potentially made regarding the contentions in New Mexico’s petition. At the end of the hearing, panel chair Michael Gibson confirmed that the November publication of the draft EA would give the NMDOJ 30 days to submit new and amended contentions. The state has yet to file such contentions as of this writing.

A ban and a moratorium: NuFuels’ license renewal application comes as New Mexico and the Navajo Nation continue to deal with the legacy of uranium mining in the Southwest, going back to the first such activity on Navajo land in 1944.

In August of this year, New Mexico land commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard issued a ban on new uranium mining projects and related activities on state lands, calling on the State Land Office to direct its attention instead to cleaning up and restoring the state’s legacy uranium mine sites, which total more than 1,000.

More recently, at the 2026 ANS Winter Conference & Expo, the panel “Uranium Mine Remediation: Past, Present, and Future” examined the history of uranium mining on Navajo land in New Mexico and Arizona, which saw approximately 30 million tons of uranium ore extracted between 1944 and 1986. As a result of this activity, Navajo land now contains 523 abandoned uranium mines, where uranium waste rock sits on the surface; 230 of these sites have not been provided funding for cleanup.

The Diné Natural Resources Protection Act, which the Navajo Nation Council passed in 2005, stands as a response to this history. The act established a moratorium that prohibits uranium mining and milling on Navajo land—including land where NuFuels seeks to establish the CUP.

text:
The $7,500 federal tax credit for electric vehicles expired on September 30, 2025, after U.S. EV market share peaked at nearly 12% that month. Market share has since fallen to under 6%, and EV sales dropped 20% in January compared with December.

Why it matters

Without the credit, EVs cost roughly $5,000 more than comparable petrol cars, pricing out many buyers. Automakers that invested heavily in EV factories and technology are absorbing billions in write-offs as demand softens.

U.S. EV market share peaked near 12% in September 2025 and later fell below 6%, while the federal credit was $7,500 per vehicle. Analysts expect 2026 EV sales to be flat, and it remains unclear how much of the drop is tied to the credit's expiry alone.

The players

Tesla

Tesla is an American electric vehicle and clean energy company, and a leading EV maker that is offering 0% financing on its Model Y.

General Motors

General Motors is a Detroit-based automaker that has continued to prioritize hybrid vehicles as its EV demand softens.

Ford

Ford Motor Company is a Detroit-based automaker that remains committed to hybrids and plans a smaller electric truck.

The details

The Biden-era goal of having half of new vehicles be electric by 2030 was revoked under a tax-and-spending bill signed by President Trump. Tesla is offering 0% financing on its Model Y, while General Motors and Ford remain committed to hybrids.

Timeline

September 30, 2025: The federal $7,500 EV tax credit expired.

September 2025: EV market share peaked near 12%.

January 2026: EV sales dropped 20% from December.

2026: Analysts expect EV sales to remain flat for the year.

2028: Ford plans a smaller electric truck reportedly priced around $30,000.

Electric Vehicles

Electric Vehicles
