Roadmap

The expiration of the $7,500 federal credit, once a central pillar of U.S. EV adoption under the Inflation Reduction Act, has exposed how dependent demand was on subsidies. The shift marks a sharp reversal from the Biden-era goal of electric vehicles making up half of new vehicle sales by 2030.

Without the $7,500 credit, buyers face roughly $5,000 more in upfront cost compared with petrol cars, making EVs harder to afford. Shoppers weighing a purchase may find deals such as Tesla's 0% Model Y financing more relevant than the removed federal incentive.

The takeaway

Buyers considering an EV should compare total cost after the credit's expiration, including financing offers, rather than relying on pre-September 2025 pricing.

text:
Nevada’s Democratic US Senators were split on a controversial bill that would make it easier to build large-scale infrastructure projects on public land.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed the Senate on November 19, 62–33.

The federal permitting reform bill is designed to speed up environmental reviews and approvals for energy, transmission, and infrastructure projects across the United States by changing the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and preservation laws meant to protect the country's natural and tribal history.

The bill is more than 400 pages long and drastically modifies the process for approving large-scale development on federally owned land across the country.

According to one of the bill's sponsors, Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico, all of it is part of an effort to make energy development cheaper.

"[Voters] want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable," said Heinrich. "And that's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do. BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so families have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm. This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers. That one provision is worth $35 billion to American households. That's pretty remarkable. BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project's completion. BAAJA will cut emissions in the power sector by up to 20% over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and lower healthcare costs.

Nevada’s Senior Senator Catherine Cortez Masto voted against the bill. In a statement, she said it contains harmful changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that undermine Tribal sovereignty and fail to protect government-to-government Tribal consultation.

Senator Jacky Rosen, on the other hand, voted for the legislation. She says it will, among other things, strengthen American energy independence.

“As the state with the most solar jobs per capita and an abundance of geothermal and other clean energy sources, Nevada stands to greatly benefit from increased investments in renewable energy projects that create good-paying jobs and lower energy costs, all while reducing carbon emissions," said Rosen in a statement. "Unfortunately, current government red tape has made it nearly impossible to bring these clean energy projects online, which is why sensible reforms like this bipartisan bill are needed. While further improvements can and should be made to strengthen this bill, we cannot squander the opportunity to deliver results and lower costs for families.”

But what do conservation and environmental groups make of the legislation?

"This kind of eliminates many of the options we have to weigh as a public on whether that's the right place for a transmission line or a data center," said Jocelyn Torres, chief Conservation officer, Conservation Lands Foundation. "All of those right decisions that our community really has been facing here in the last couple of months, [this bill is] just eliminating the processes to have that science-based information to make those decisions, weakening or removing options for public engagement within that, and really eliminating that tribal consultation piece."

The bill now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives.

title: COP31: Will the Push for Electrification Survive the Collapse of Climate Talks? - PassBlue
description:
It was rejected by the European Union, Panama and highly vulnerable nations like the Marshall Islands, on the grounds of being “‘unconscionable” and failing to especially address fossil fuels.
The omission of fossil fuels in draft agreements became common practice in COP talks until just a few years ago.
After pushback from Saudi Arabia, the Arab Group and Russia, all mention of fossil fuels were removed.
The omissions raised concerns that fossil-fuel-generated electricity could still count toward the 35 by 35 electrification goal without a corresponding roadmap to phasing out fossil fuels.
Hard red lines Although the tendency during COP31 was to push for faster phaseout of fossil fuels, both the first and the second draft proposals generated major political divisions.
text:
The clearest message from the recent United Nations annual climate change conference was that the world must increase its use of electricity in global energy consumption from its current level of 23 percent to 35 percent by 2035, under a “35 by 35 Global Electrification Pledge.”

The 31st Conference of the Parties, or COP31, officially wrapped up in the southern city of Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, but the negotiations ran two extra nights, making it the longest COP ever. The conference ended without a mutual agreement to meet the electrification pledge, among other issues.

In the early hours of Nov. 22, the Turkish climate minister and COP31 co-president, Murat Kurum, announced that COP31 had failed to reach a final “cover decision,” the overarching political statement adopted at the end of every COP. COPs meet annually to focus the world on implementing the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

In Antalya, Australia’s climate minister and COP31 co-president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, pointed to “unbridgeable red lines” and called the geopolitical environment around this COP “the most complicated and fraught in living memory.”

He said, “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time.”

During the 12-day gathering, negotiations on the electrification goal were deadlocked mainly over omission of references to fossil fuels and climate finance obligations.

A third and 94-paragraph draft deal, technically the final version, was published in the early hours of Nov. 22. It was rejected by the European Union, Panama and highly vulnerable nations like the Marshall Islands, on the grounds of being “‘unconscionable” and failing to especially address fossil fuels. Although the co-presidents attributed the omission of the language “transition from fossil fuels” to and that the global commitment to it was established in the COP28 Dubai agreement, Saudi Arabia and other large oil producers reportedly blocked any mention of phasing out coal, oil and gas in the final COP31 draft.

Every COP decision requires consensus from the nearly 200 participating nations and territories, meaning they can abstain from active support without blocking the decision, provided they do not formally object. The omission of fossil fuels in draft agreements became common practice in COP talks until just a few years ago. The omission this year, which led to the breakdown of talks, laid bare a basic impediment to UN climate negotiations, which rely on decision-making by consensus, according to the Washington-based Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL).

While acknowledging the need for COPs and their multilateral nature to manage global warming, Nikki Reisch, the director of the climate and energy program at CIEL, said in a statement that “because those with the money won’t pay, those with the oil won’t give it up, and those most responsible refuse to answer for the harm they’ve caused.

The fact that any one of them can hold collective action hostage is part of the problem. . . . Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency.”

Pushing an electric future

Backed by analysis from the International Energy Agency (IEA), a Paris-based intergovernmental organization established in 1974 after the 1973 oil crisis, and the Abu Dhabi-based intergovernmental organization International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which supports countries to transition to sustainable and renewable energy, the pledge on electrification was seen as much-needed progress and glimmer of hope for the Antalya COP.

As of Nov. 22, around 90 countries and 180 business and civil society organizations had taken the voluntary 35 by 35 electrification pledge regardless of a final agreement.

The UN says the pledge’s implementation initiative, COP31 Electrification Delivery Package, announced on Nov. 19, covers action by 150-plus countries and the European Union, 37 cities and over 260 businesses. Electricity grids of 21,000-plus kilometers were deployed in 2025 by members of the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance. Annual investment plans totaling $156 billion were announced for grids, renewables and energy storage by the alliance.

In some rural parts of Africa, cooking with fossil fuels, such as coal, firewood and dung, emit as much carbon yearly as the world’s entire airline and shipping industry combined, according to the IEA, leading to 2.5 million premature deaths worldwide of mostly women and children.

Electrification initiatives such as Clean Cooking Africa use renewable-powered high-efficiency appliances like induction stoves, electric pressure cookers, hot plates powered by national grids, solar mini-grids and rooftop solars. Pairing smart electrification directly with new clean power would nearly double global greenhouse gas cuts — jumping from roughly seven to nearly 14 percent (7.9 billion tons annually) — at 20th the cost, according to Climate TRACE, an independent greenhouse emissions tracking platform.

Language on ‘fossil fuels’

A major controversy from the onset of the COP31 negotiations was whether global electrification could deliver genuine climate progress without any binding commitments to clean, renewable electricity and a meaningful reduction in fossil fuel dependence.

The COP31 co-presidents Türkiye and Australia released an 18-page, 144-paragraph first draft of the cover decision on Nov. 16, which didn’t mention a “clean electricity” obligation but instead used the phrase “electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix.” The draft mentioned “fossil fuel(s)” six times.

A second, nine-page draft was unveiled three days later. After pushback from Saudi Arabia, the Arab Group and Russia, all mention of fossil fuels were removed. The omissions raised concerns that fossil-fuel-generated electricity could still count toward the 35 by 35 electrification goal without a corresponding roadmap to phasing out fossil fuels.

The text also positioned COP31 as the first climate summit to formally acknowledge that the world is overshooting the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold established in the Paris climate agreement.

Despite the voluntary nature of the electrification proposal, the broader issue still needed to clear significant political friction during the decisive second week of negotiations due to the fossil fuels loophole behind it.

The fact that the 35 by 35 target concerns electricity’s share of energy consumption rather than renewables’ share of electricity generation means countries can expand gas- and coal-fired power plants while still claiming progress toward the 35 percent goal.

Voluntary electricity pledge

To reach an overall agreement, the so-called COP31 Divan, an informal ministerial gathering based on the old Turkish “divan,” a council of deliberation and collective judgment, was held on Nov. 18.

To avoid setting an unachievable COP target, the conference co-presidents had noted at the opening of the summit, on Nov. 10, that the electricity pledge was voluntary. They also did not specifically describe whether low-carbon renewables (solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and nuclear) or high-carbon fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal), were required to power the additional electricity production.

Faith Birol, the head of the IEA, described during a Nov. 13 press conference at COP31 how further electrification would reduce carbon emissions even under countries’ current national energy policies. Birol also hinted that the IEA was being pragmatic by recommending that the COP31 presidency not attach a rigid clean energy condition to the 35 by 35 pledge.

“To have as many countries as possible signing this pledge is extremely important,” Birol said. “It is high time that we see that many countries come together behind an international target, which could have a reflection on the market trends.”

Yet the clean route to electrification was repeatedly noted as a requirement throughout the conference by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on Dec. 31, 2026, and by countries like Portugal, Spain and Denmark through the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance (BOGA) initiative.

Hard red lines

Although the tendency during COP31 was to push for faster phaseout of fossil fuels, both the first and the second draft proposals generated major political divisions.

Panama said after the second draft that it would block any outcome that failed to meet its demands, including a cap on oil production. The Arab Group and Russia rejected the first draft text almost entirely over its fossil fuel phase-out language and the electrification targets or anything they argued would interfere with their national priorities.

Similarly, the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc — a subset of the G77-plus China coalition, including India and Saudi Arabia and representing over 50 percent of the world’s population with low economic development — stated that setting a 35 percent electrification goal and fossil fuel roadmaps as well as singling out methane, which has a warming impact 80 times stronger than CO2, crossed their red lines.

Rich countries, including those in Europe, as well as Switzerland, generally embraced the 35 by 35 initiative but criticized its broad approach. The European Union’s climate envoy, Wopke Hoekstra, described the first draft as “a shopping list” that reopened issues such as climate finance.

As the only G7 leader participating in Antalya, Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain, which officially endorsed 35 by 35, was the front-runner European leader to back it.

Small island states and developing nations, led by Pacific Island nations and Brazil, insisted that the global electrification target sources be strictly tied to renewable energy and explicitly exclude fossil fuels to ensure a genuine climate impact rather than just shifting emissions elsewhere.

China stayed out of the heated battle over fossil fuel wording — saying it had decided on its own clean energy transition to dominate green energy manufacturing and deployment in the world — and focused instead on pushing against green tariffs.

Civil society objections

Guterres of the UN expressed disappointment over the collapse of the COP31 talks but was adamant in his message to civil society: “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we. Keep spreading the facts. Keep demanding action. Keep turning up the heat.”

Climate advocacy organizations also criticized the COP31 drafts, which they feared would give the fossil fuel industry cover to carry on as usual, raking in profits.

Climate Analytics, a global science and policy institute based in Berlin, warned that electrification without binding clean-power conditions could add at least 0.1°C to global warming by midcentury. Its research found that under current policies, gas-fired electricity generation could increase, while energy-related carbon-dioxide emissions would decline by only 20 to 25 percent from 2025 to 2035.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the grassroots environmental movement 350.org, said in a statement: “They have reduced one of the defining challenges of our time to an inconvenient paragraph they would rather delete, while leaving the door open for fossil fuels to masquerade as clean electrification.”

Meanwhile, the world has produced 38 billion tons of emissions so far this year. Based on the same IEA modeling of energy production, of all the new power plants installed in 2026, 79 percent came from renewable sources, according to the IEA.

“With the current settings, which means, if we don’t put a [clean energy] condition to the ‘35 by 35’ . . . [the figure] will go down to 30 billion tons of emissions. So there’ll be a strong decline in the emissions coming from the energy circle,” Birol said.

US no-show

As the world’s historically largest polluter, and now the second-largest after China, US government officials were notably absent from COP31, the biggest UN event of the year, drawing more than 100,000 attendees. The Trump administration withdrew from the Paris climate agreement in its first presidency and again last year as it continues to boycott UN climate summits. (The Biden administration rejoined the Paris agreement in 2021.)

Instead, a 120-member “observer” delegation, mostly Democrats and headed by Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and the highest-profile American official to participate in COP31, showed up to support international allies of mitigating climate change and save America’s face at Antalya with the motto “America Is All In.”

Newson reminded the COP31 participants that as the world’s fourth-largest economy, California had achieved climate goals at scale, cutting greenhouse gas emissions by over 20 percent since 2000, while growing its economy by more than 80 percent.

Meanwhile, in Shenzen, China, around 4,956 miles and a 900-metric-ton flight away from Antalya, the world’s biggest polluters, the US, China and Russia, met on Nov. 18-19, where they agreed to pump more oil into the world, among other matters.

As to the three powers’ pledge to boost oil production at the trilateral summit in China, Kurum, the COP31 co-president, said that countries could not be forced to do anything unless voluntarily, using a Turkish proverb, “You cannot force beauty.”

title: Honda's Radical Fix for EVs' Biggest Flaw - Banyan Hill Publishing
description:
Every owner that I’ve talked to absolutely LOVES their Tesla.” There’s just one thing I wish I could change about owning an electric vehicle (EV).
I always thought it would be amazing if you could charge your electric vehicle without ever having to stop driving.
And overseas, a company called Electreon has already demonstrated even greater charging power on France’s A10 motorway.
One Indiana feasibility study estimated that a wireless charging lane could cost more than $6 million per mile.
Here’s My Take What excites me the most about Honda’s announcement is that it offers a potential solution to one of the biggest headaches of owning an electric vehicle.
text:
I love my Tesla Model Y.

And apparently a lot of my readers do too. Like Bruce C. who messaged me: “I own a 2026 Tesla Model Y. I LOVE IT! Every owner that I’ve talked to absolutely LOVES their Tesla.”

There’s just one thing I wish I could change about owning an electric vehicle (EV).

Charging.

If you’re driving around town and can plug in at home every night, charging isn’t usually much of an issue.

But what happens when you want to take a long road trip?

You have to think about how far your battery will take you, where you’ll stop to recharge and how long you’ll have to wait before getting back on the road.

And if you’re driving an electric truck carrying thousands of pounds of cargo across the country, those problems compound exponentially.

I always thought it would be amazing if you could charge your electric vehicle without ever having to stop driving.

And today, Honda is developing a technology that could make this dream possible.

The Road Charger

Last month, Honda announced it’s developing a technology that could fundamentally change how electric vehicles get their power.

And it’s based on something we use every day.

The roads we drive on.

Working with Japanese construction companies Taisei and Taisei Rotec, Honda has developed a system that can wirelessly transfer electricity from equipment buried beneath the pavement to vehicles driving overhead.

The technology uses electromagnetic induction, the same basic principle behind the wireless charging pads you can use for your smartphone.

Coils embedded in the pavement create a magnetic field that transfers electricity to a receiver mounted underneath a vehicle.

And the vehicle doesn’t have to stop for any of this to happen. It can keep driving while its battery receives electricity.

Honda plans to begin testing the technology on a public highway during Japan’s fiscal year 2027. The company wants to demonstrate that it can deliver up to 150 kilowatts of power to moving vehicles.

That’s roughly as much power as you can get from a typical highway fast-charging station, without ever having to stop to use it.

But this technology isn’t unique. Engineers around the world have already demonstrated that charging vehicles while they drive is possible.

And some of the most impressive work is happening right here in America.

Earlier this year, researchers at Purdue University revealed they’d successfully charged an electric semi-truck while it was traveling down a public highway at 65 miles per hour.

Working with the Indiana Department of Transportation and commercial vehicle manufacturer Cummins, the researchers installed wireless charging equipment beneath a quarter-mile stretch of highway in West Lafayette, Indiana.

As the specially equipped truck drove over the pavement, the system transferred electricity directly to its battery.

And we’re not talking about a mere trickle of power.

It delivered between 50 and 190 kilowatts of electricity while the truck was moving, with power-transfer efficiency approaching 85%. In other words, it received enough electricity to significantly extend its driving range, with very little energy lost in the process.

Other entities are also working on this technology.

In Detroit, Israeli technology company Electreon helped build America’s first public wireless charging roadway in 2023. The quarter-mile installation uses coils embedded beneath the pavement to charge specially equipped vehicles as they drive over it.

Meanwhile, Florida is developing a three-quarter-mile wireless charging section of State Road 516, a new highway being built near Orlando. That project is designed to deliver up to 200 kilowatts of power to compatible vehicles, roughly as much as a powerful public fast-charging station.

And overseas, a company called Electreon has already demonstrated even greater charging power on France’s A10 motorway. During testing, its system delivered more than 200 kilowatts on average to a heavy-duty truck, with peak power exceeding 300 kilowatts.

Of course, these are still small-scale tests. But they prove that the technology can work on real roads.

Even the federal government is getting involved.

The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is supporting research into wireless charging roads, including the project in Indiana.

But the reality is that installing charging equipment beneath existing highways is expensive. One Indiana feasibility study estimated that a wireless charging lane could cost more than $6 million per mile.

Still, there may be a practical way to introduce the technology without rebuilding the entire highway system.

And it starts with America’s trucking industry.

Electric semi-trucks need enormous batteries to haul heavy loads over long distances. These batteries are expensive, heavy and take up valuable space.

But if trucks could recharge while driving, they wouldn’t need nearly as much battery power onboard.

That could mean smaller, lighter and cheaper batteries, more room for cargo and a much more practical way to power long-distance trucking.

Commercial trucking could also make the technology more affordable to roll out.

Unlike passenger vehicles, which travel all over the place, commercial trucks often follow the same shipping routes. That means we wouldn’t need to electrify every highway.

We could simply start with the busy trucking routes where thousands of vehicles travel the same roads every day.

Here’s My Take

What excites me the most about Honda’s announcement is that it offers a potential solution to one of the biggest headaches of owning an electric vehicle.

Instead of building bigger batteries or faster charging stations, we could make charging part of the driving experience.

It’s the kind of breakthrough that could give the EV market a much-needed jolt.

Regards,

Ian King

Chief Strategist, Banyan Hill Publishing

description:
Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06) released the following statement regarding the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act: “America desperately needs permitting reform to spur the deployment of clean, affordable, and reliable energy that fuels the American economy.
While the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes many provisions from EBRA, I cannot support BAAJA in its current form.
Instead, we consistently struggle to build cheaper, cleaner energy sources that would successfully compete against existing fossil fuel assets but are blocked by the incumbent interests.

“Climate change and permitting reform are too important to settle for anything less than a deal that unleashes our economy and protects our communities.
text:
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06) released the following statement regarding the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act:

“America desperately needs permitting reform to spur the deployment of clean, affordable, and reliable energy that fuels the American economy. I have worked extensively on this issue, most notably with Congressman Mike Levin on the Energy Bills Relief Act (EBRA, H.R. 7977). While the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes many provisions from EBRA, I cannot support BAAJA in its current form. The House must be given the opportunity to improve the legislation.

“The United States does not struggle to build data centers, LNG export facilities, natural gas pipelines, or electricity assets that are owned, operated, and controlled by regulated utilities. Instead, we consistently struggle to build cheaper, cleaner energy sources that would successfully compete against existing fossil fuel assets but are blocked by the incumbent interests. BAAJA fails to eliminate the economic disincentives stacked against cheaper energy and weakens critical environmental laws that keep dirtier energy sources offline.

“Those problems in BAAJA can be fixed, specifically by overhauling sections 1401 and 1402, which make it impossible for a future administration to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent, and by adding provisions to create incentives for utilities to deploy lower-cost, cleaner energy sources. While the manager’s amendment improved BAAJA in these areas, it still falls far short of what’s necessary.

“Climate change and permitting reform are too important to settle for anything less than a deal that unleashes our economy and protects our communities. If we are compelled to vote only on the Senate-passed text, I will vote No, with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”

text:
Despite the recent attention on new electric demand created by data centers, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries sees greater potential for long-term growth in the utilities sector, MHI President and CEO Eisaku Ito said earlier this month.

Utilities and independent power producers accounted for 94% of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ new gas turbine orders in 2024 and 2025, Ito said.

Although many U.S. data center operators say they intend to install their own off-grid generation, Ito argued that these plans rely on smaller gas-fired power plants that cost more to run than the larger plants utilities and IPPs are pursuing.

In the long-term, Ito said, the cost differential will push data centers to connect to the grid, ultimately supporting utilities’ expansion plans.

His comments, made during a call with analysts on Nov. 6, according to a translated transcript, come as fallout from the U.S. midterm elections and stock market volatility raise questions about the future of the artificial intelligence buildout in North America. Ito expressed confidence in utilities’ long-term expansion plans, arguing that growing demand for electricity does not rely solely on data centers.

“Electricity demand from data centers is expected to grow rapidly in the United States, but data centers still account for only around 10% of the country’s total electricity demand,” Ito said. “If some of the anticipated growth in demand does not materialize, there will be some impact, but we believe the effect on our overall GTCC business would be limited.”

MHI booked 8 GW in orders for large frame gas turbines in the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, compared to 16 GW of orders in all of FY 2025. Profit for the company’s Energy Systems segment rose 80% on account of increased orders and shifts in the value of the yen, according to the company’s financial statements.

“We are also beginning to see the benefits of improved pricing on new unit projects, lower loss-related costs and greater production efficiency,” MHI CFO Hiroshi Nishio said.

Company executives said they continue to take a conservative approach to forecasting demand and expanding manufacturing capacity. The company expects global demand for gas turbines at all manufacturers and makers to average about 70 GW per year over the next five years — somewhat lower than the 100 GW MHI expects will sell across all manufactuers this year amid what Ito characterized as “exceptionally strong” demand he does not anticipate will continue.

But Ito said he remains confident in MHI’s company backlog, noting that the company vets new orders carefully and hasn’t had any order cancellations in the past two years.

The company plans to double its gas turbine production capacity by 2030, though most of the additional capacity will come from improved processes and automation at existing plants in the U.S. and Japan.

“We are improving productivity and driving other initiatives at a pace that outstrips the growth in orders,” he said.

MHI also signaled that it’s exploring opportunities to expand into other infrastructure-related markets.

Ito said MHI will release additional details in May, but suggested the company is interested in expanding its gas turbine service and repair capabilities, as well as investing in unmanned systems that can operate in harsh environments. At the same time, MHI plans to divest some of its aerospace business, he said.

“These examples may seem quite different, but they all share a common theme: resilience,” Ito said. “We aim to identify new business opportunities in infrastructure and industrial machinery through the lens of resilience and turn them into future growth.”

text:
The City Council is nonpartisan and comprises eight district representatives who annually set a tax rate, adopt a budget, make wide-ranging policy decisions and appoint a city manager and city attorney. They serve four-year terms and are paid $72,800 a year. District 8 represents South El Paso, Downtown and neighborhoods around the University of Texas at El Paso.

Who’s running for this seat?

Candidate Questionnaires

Candidates were asked to limit their responses to 100 words. Responses have been lightly edited for grammar. (These Q&As are from the November general election responses and republished here.)

Looking ahead 10 years, what do you want El Paso to look and feel like, and what are the most important decisions the city needs to make now to get there?

Chris Canales: I want El Paso to be an affordable and welcoming city where people of all backgrounds can build a good life. That means investing in the city we already have: expanding housing choices, strengthening neighborhoods, creating good paying jobs, managing finances responsibly, and maintaining streets, infrastructure and public facilities. We also need to grow sustainably, directing development where existing infrastructure can support it and protecting our clean air, water and natural resources.

Matthew Guzman: I want El Paso to be ripe with job opportunities for young professionals seeking a city on the rise. I want the region to recognize El Paso as a destination for the arts, food and culture. And I want residents to be proud of where they live and happy with their quality of life. To get there we have to capitalize and execute on the economic development opportunities ahead of us. Namely the buildout of the Advanced Manufacturing District and creating sustainable energy capacity to support growth.

El Paso relies heavily on residential property taxpayers to fund city services. What specifically should the city do to attract more commercial and industrial development and broaden the tax base?

Chris Canales: We should diversify our economy by targeting industries that fit our strengths, including renewable energy and advanced manufacturing. I supported creating the new Business One Stop Shop to help local businesses and entrepreneurs access resources and assistance. We must also streamline permitting and inspections, invest in infrastructure, infill, and redevelopment, and focus resources on projects that create quality jobs, substantial taxable value and lasting benefits for El Pasoans.

Matthew Guzman: We need to align educational institutions and workforce development with high wage sectors like aerospace, advanced manufacturing, robotics and skilled trades so we can provide the workers these companies need when they look to relocate. We need to create shovel-ready sites to lure companies looking to expand. And, as companies begin to recognize the benefits of our location and the quality of our workforce, incentive packages should be based on performance and job creation.

Police and fire make up a significant share of the city’s budget. How should the city balance competitive compensation and staffing with the need to control public safety costs and fund other city priorities?

Chris Canales: We must provide competitive compensation and adequate staffing to keep up with public safety needs. I have supported funding three police academies annually to address vacancies while investing in programs like the Crisis Intervention Team for mental health that best match resources to community needs. Public safety spending must also receive the same scrutiny as every part of the budget, including efficient use of personnel and overtime, so we can adequately fund other essential City services.

Matthew Guzman: We have been training recruits with our tax dollars then watching them leave for other cities. We need to take a look at contract minimums for new fire and police recruits to ensure they have a stable workforce and aren’t forced to go over budget on overtime hours that eventually burnout their existing workforce. Safety services are an increasing part of the overall budget, which brings us back to our need to grow the commercial and industrial tax base to fund these expanding services.

El Paso is attracting interest from data centers and related developments. What standards or conditions should the city require of these projects regarding infrastructure and economic benefits to the community?

Chris Canales: I don’t want hyperscale data centers, particularly those supporting AI, in El Paso. They require huge amounts of scarce land, energy, water and infrastructure. I led council action to not incentivize them moving forward. If private projects go ahead anyway, they must be made to pay their full infrastructure costs, protect ratepayers from higher utility rates, meet strict water and energy standards and provide enforceable community benefits commensurate with their enormous resource demands.

Matthew Guzman: We need to ensure these companies are creating jobs, attracting industry, and growing our commercial/industrial tax revenue. There needs to be contract language in place that ensures the responsible use of our resources, and investment from these companies into our energy and water infrastructure that creates new capacity, or improves efficiencies. Legally binding community benefit agreements need to be executed that ensure El Paso extracts as much from these companies as they extract from us.

When the city offers tax breaks, grants or other incentives to attract businesses and development, what should taxpayers expect in return, and how should the city determine whether those incentives are worth the cost?

Chris Canales: Taxpayers should receive a clear, measurable return for economic development incentives. During my term, I have approved stronger requirements for projects receiving city incentives, including performance standards and clawbacks. We should prioritize projects that create quality jobs, expand the tax base and produce lasting benefits that justify the public investment, while accounting for infrastructure and resource needs and publicly tracking whether promised benefits are actually delivered.

Matthew Guzman: Taxpayers should expect that the revenue derived from these deals will have a real effect on their tax bills. Transparency is paramount, and when a deal is finalized we should be able to provide a visual projection showing what was given up in incentives versus the tax revenue expected, the new jobs created, and the services the new tax revenue can cover. Taxpayers want to know where their money is being spent and spared.

title: Mecklenburg County urges residents to recycle lithium-ion batteries ahead of landfill ban
description:

The rechargeable batteries are commonly found in cellphones, laptops and power tools.
Mecklenburg County officials say improperly discarded lithium-ion batteries cause an average of two fires per week at county waste facilities.
County officials are encouraging residents to recycle rechargeable batteries instead of throwing them away.
Residents can drop off rechargeable batteries at Mecklenburg County recycling centers.
text:
North Carolina will ban lithium-ion batteries from landfills statewide beginning Dec. 1.

The rechargeable batteries are commonly found in cellphones, laptops and power tools.

Mecklenburg County officials say improperly discarded lithium-ion batteries cause an average of two fires per week at county waste facilities. The batteries can ignite when they are crushed or damaged during the disposal process.

County officials are encouraging residents to recycle rechargeable batteries instead of throwing them away.

Residents can drop off rechargeable batteries at Mecklenburg County recycling centers. More information is available at MeckNC.gov/batteries.

title: Democratic Clean-Tech Leaders Mike Levin and Sean Casten Oppose BAAJA | Hill Heat
description:
Reps. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) and Sean Casten (D-Ill.), both clean-tech businessmen before joining the House of Representatives, announced their rejection of the industrial-expediting bill known as BAAJA today.
Here’s why: “I’ve spent my career as a clean energy advocate and an environmental attorney.
I want us to build clean energy, and to build it far faster than we do now.
Will it help clean energy grow?
“There’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment.
text:
Reps. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) and Sean Casten (D-Ill.), both clean-tech businessmen before joining the House of Representatives, announced their rejection of the industrial-expediting bill known as BAAJA today.

Levin and Casten are two of the five vice chairs of the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition, a large Democratic caucus focused on climate and energy policy. The office of fellow vice chair Don Beyer (D-Va.) also confirmed today that Beyer opposes BAAJA, as did the office of SEEC co-chair Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.).

Rep. Levin:

“I can’t support the energy permitting bill the Senate just sent to the House, known as BAAJA, at least not as it’s written today. Here’s why:

“I’ve spent my career as a clean energy advocate and an environmental attorney. I want us to build clean energy, and to build it far faster than we do now. So I’ve measured this bill against three questions. Will it lower costs for families? Will it protect our clean air and water? Will it help clean energy grow?

“There’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment. The bill would modernize a power grid that too often can’t carry affordable clean energy to the homes that need it, and it would require data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades instead of passing the cost on to families. Many of those reforms are similar to legislation I wrote with Sean Casten and Kathy Castor, and I want to see them become law. I believe the emissions reductions and cost savings may be smaller and less certain than supporters suggest, however.

“Other parts of the bill raise concerns. The bill would limit California’s ability to protect its own water, weaken the science behind endangered species decisions, and keep courts from halting a project even when an agency skips the review the law requires. It would also make this administration’s fossil fuel approvals, offshore leases included, extremely hard for a future president or a judge to undo. For those of us who have spent years fighting to keep new oil rigs off the California coast, that’s a serious threat.

“Tribal nations have warned that the bill’s changes to historic preservation law could endanger sacred sites and undercut Tribal sovereignty, and they deserved a far bigger voice in writing it.

“Those harms would be permanent, while the clean energy gains would rise or fall with whoever happens to be carrying out the law.

“I’ve thought hard about the old saying that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon. That risk is significant. But in the end, taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.

“Since the Senate released the bill, I’ve worked with my colleagues in the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition on targeted fixes to permitting certainty, clean water, endangered species, judicial review, and historic and Tribal protections. None of our major concerns have been addressed. I’ve also heard from hundreds of people across our district, and they oppose this bill by roughly two to one.

“Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, who helped write this bill, are my friends and have long been champions of climate action. Many allies I deeply respect support it, and I know they want the same future I do.

“There’s still time to get this right. If House and Senate leaders from both parties sit down together and negotiate sufficient changes, I’ll be ready to vote yes.

“We can and we must find a better balance that protects communities and the clean air and water they rely on. I believe this is possible this Congress and I urge my colleagues to be responsive to the concerns of Americans across the country and fix this bill before it becomes law.”

Rep. Casten:

“America desperately needs permitting reform to spur the deployment of clean, affordable, and reliable energy that fuels the American economy. I have worked extensively on this issue, most notably with Congressman Mike Levin on the Energy Bills Relief Act (EBRA, H.R. 7977). While the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes many provisions from EBRA, I cannot support BAAJA in its current form. The House must be given the opportunity to improve the legislation.

“The United States does not struggle to build data centers, LNG export facilities, natural gas pipelines, or electricity assets that are owned, operated, and controlled by regulated utilities. Instead, we consistently struggle to build cheaper, cleaner energy sources that would successfully compete against existing fossil fuel assets but are blocked by the incumbent interests. BAAJA fails to eliminate the economic disincentives stacked against cheaper energy and weakens critical environmental laws that keep dirtier energy sources offline.”

text:
INDIANA — As 2026 draws to a close, state conservation leaders are urging Hoosiers to consider a simple but impactful resolution for the new year: protecting Indiana’s natural heritage through the purchase or renewal of the iconic blue Environmental License Plate.

First introduced in 1992 as Indiana’s inaugural specialty plate, this effort has quietly generated substantial funding for land preservation for over three decades.

Proceeds from the sale and renewal of the plate directly fund the President Benjamin Harrison Conservation Trust. Since its inception, this funding has helped protect more than 74,000 acres of critical natural habitats, including state parks, nature preserves, and forests across the state.

Where Your Money Goes

When a Hoosier purchases the blue plate for $40, the transaction is split:

$15 goes to the Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV) for administrative processing.

$25 goes directly to the President Benjamin Harrison Conservation Trust Fund, dedicated solely to acquiring land.

The tangible results of these contributions are visible in nearly every corner of Indiana. To date, Trust funds have supported the following acquisitions and projects:

Fish & Wildlife Areas: More than 36,000 acres protected.

Nature Preserves: More than 19,000 acres protected.

State Forests: More than 11,000 acres added.

State Parks: Over 3,000 acres acquired as additions to 24 state parks and recreation areas.

Local Parks and Trails: Over 3,000 acres protected in local park systems and recreational trails.

State Historic Sites: 23 projects benefiting 10 historic sites.

With the new year approaching, conservation advocates hope to see the trend of environmental stewardship continue. Residents interested in purchasing or renewing the Indiana Environmental License Plate can find more details and start the process online through the BMV or local license branches.

text:
There’s a group of congressional lawmakers I affectionately refer to as the “oddball caucus.” These are members who are known for their idiosyncratic ways on Capitol Hill, with lengthy records that suggest they tend to march to the beat of their own drum.

In the wake of the midterm elections, it’s fair to say this was not a great year for the oddball caucus.

It started several months ago, when then-Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia resigned from Congress, and continued soon after when Republican Rep. Troy Nehls of Texas announced his retirement. It wasn’t long before the list grew, as Rep. Thomas Massie lost in a GOP primary in Kentucky.

Election Day made matters worse for the contingent, as voters defeated several more oddball caucus members, including Republican Reps. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, Victoria Spartz of Indiana and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin.

Over the weekend, another notable figure in the faction joined the club. MS NOW reported:

Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx conceded in her race to represent North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District to Chuck Hubbard on Sunday, delivering Democrats another surprise midterms win and further strengthening their grip on the House of Representatives in the upcoming Congress. […]

The race was close, with Foxx losing by a fraction of a percentage point and less than 400 votes after a recount. The AP called the race Sunday afternoon.

Foxx called Hubbard to concede on Sunday, though the outgoing incumbent has already indicated that she intends to run again in two years, when she’ll be 85 years old.

The congresswoman’s defeat wasn’t exactly likely. This is, after all, a district that Donald Trump won two years ago by 17 points. Indeed, Foxx herself won re-election in 2024 by 19 points — and at the time, she ran against Hubbard, the same Democrat who narrowly defeated her this year.

So what happened?

In every race, there are a variety of factors that determine the outcome, and Foxx faced all kinds of headwinds: the collapse of the Republican Party in North Carolina, an anti-GOP-incumbent sentiment, the president’s unpopularity dragging down Republican incumbents, etc.

More articles

But when looking at Foxx’s record, it’s probably fair to say one piece of correspondence helped tip the scales in her opponent’s favor.

Six months ago, a 10-year-old boy was given an assignment in school: Write a persuasive essay and send it to someone in a position of authority. He wrote a letter to Foxx, encouraging her to support rebates for electric vehicle purchases.

The good news, the GOP lawmaker received and responded to the child. The bad news is, Foxx’s response was obnoxious. She wrote, among other things, “Please ask your teacher to explain propaganda to you. My guess is that your teachers will not give you a good educational experience and help you learn to think as they are too interested in indoctrinating you.”

The boy’s mother called the letter “horrific” and addressed Foxx on Facebook, writing, “Reprehensible response. You crossed a line when you attacked a child and attacked teachers. You don’t deserve to be on a Committee for Education when you talk to children like this and think so lowly of teachers.”

All of this generated quite a bit of attention, locally and nationally, and reminded voters about Foxx’s intemperate and mean-spirited ways.

It may be a stretch to say this one story sealed her fate, but it certainly did not help.

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey — Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations, but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.

The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.

Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

ASSOCIATED PRESS

Nations demand fossil fuel cuts as UN climate talks COP31 wrap up

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.

For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

text:
Expectations were low heading into COP31. But at the very least, it was anticipated that Türkiye, the host nation, and Australia in its role of President of Negotiations would deliver some form of consensus on tackling climate change. Even this low bar wasn’t achieved.

Talks on the proposed Antalya Pact had begun with some promise. Targets for achieving 35% electrification of final energy by 2035, agreeing just transition provisions, tripling climate finance and deploying carbon capture and storage technologies seemed realistic. But deep divisions around the text to “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” proved unbridgeable, despite protracted negotiations. The result was no consensus and no final draft, and the first COP since 2009 to conclude without a core agreement.

I asked VP Prakash Sharma and our Energy Transition team for their initial thoughts.

First, mounting challenges this decade have progressively weakened the collective resolve to tackle global warming.

The fragmentation of the rules-based international order, trade disputes and ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran have elevated energy security above climate change as many governments’ primary focus.

Fossil fuels remain the backbone of the energy system in virtually all countries, meeting 80% of global energy demand. Eleven years on from the Paris Agreement, it is (almost) universally acknowledged that transitioning to a low-carbon energy system can’t happen overnight, especially with global demand rising faster than supply. Supply disruptions and spiralling oil and LNG prices triggered by the Iran war may have underlined the vulnerability of countries that depend heavily on imported hydrocarbons, but neither has fundamentally changed the outlook.

Second, resource-rich oil and gas exporters are on the front foot.

An acceleration of electrification, most likely to take hold in oil and gas importing countries, threatens their economic future.

Fossil fuel producers seized their opportunity in Antalya. By keeping any reference to phasing out fossil fuels from the final text, producers sidestepped any renewed impetus to the goals of the Paris Agreement. With or without those words, the reality is that fossil fuels will continue to play a critical part in energy security for decades to come as we forecast in our Energy Transition Outlook earlier this month.

Ultimately, what matters is competitiveness. Renewables, competitive in most power markets, will continue to grow along with other low-carbon technologies, not least batteries and electric vehicles. Oil and gas at current elevated prices can’t compete, but our expectation is that prices could soon fall – and sharply. And with power demand rising at pace due to data centres, electric vehicles and advanced manufacturing, some countries may take a pragmatic view, soften their anti-fossil fuels stance and allow the current energy mix to persist.

Third, some oil and gas importers – Europe included – may actually benefit from the omission of the text on fossil fuels.

While Europe is at the vanguard of climate policy and decarbonisation, it remains a major importer of oil and gas. Moreover, some European countries, including the UK, are in a quandary over whether to approve new investment in domestic production. The failure of talks in Antalya may smooth the path for these governments to greenlight new upstream projects.

Fourth, there is a global leadership vacuum on tackling climate change.

The absence of the US from both COP30 and COP31 has undoubtedly weakened the ability to achieve consensus. The Democratic party has signalled its intention to take the US back into the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, but even with majorities in both chambers of Congress following this month’s midterms, it will take victory in the 2028 presidential election for this to become a realistic prospect. With affordability top of the political agenda, curtailing investment in oil and gas doesn’t look a vote winner.

China, meanwhile, has chosen not to grasp a climate leadership role that was there for the taking. Its position as the global pacesetter in manufacturing and exporting low-carbon technologies and dominance of critical minerals for the transition may be proving a sufficient prize.

Leadership and cooperation are essential if multilateral climate goals are to be achieved. The lack of consensus on display at COP31, however, is further evidence of the growing failure of global institutions to act decisively on areas such as climate, conflict and trade.

Waga Energy, Randolph Farms Landfill, and Best Way Disposal Launch Second RNG Project in Indiana

Philadelphia (USA), November 23, 2026. Waga Energy (EPA: WAGA), a specialist in renewable natural gas (RNG) production from landfill gas, has signed an agreement with Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal, both part of The Balkema Companies, a family-owned group of businesses, to build an RNG production unit in Modoc, Indiana. The new unit will upgrade the gas naturally emitted by landfilled waste into clean, local, and renewable energy.

This project is the second collaboration between Waga Energy and The Balkema Companies, following the successful commissioning of the Decatur Hills RNG Facility in Greensburg, Indiana (August 2026).

Under the agreement, Waga Energy will finance, build, own, and operate the RNG facility for at least 20 years. Randolph Farms will manage the landfill gas collection system and support the civil works for the project. Waga Energy and Randolph Farms will share the revenues generated by the sale of the RNG.

The facility will utilize Waga Energy’s patented WAGABOX® technology to process up to 2,000 scfm (3,200 m³/h) of raw biogas and produce up to 407,000 MMBtu (120 GWh) of RNG per year at full capacity. Commissioning is scheduled for early 2028. The WAGABOX® unit will replace the existing landfill gas upgrading technology at Randolph Farms, where renewable natural gas is currently produced for Best Way Disposal's onsite fueling facility. The new project will allow Randolph Farms to continue making productive use of landfill gas by converting it into a valuable energy resource. RNG produced by the new facility will be delivered to a nearby interstate pipeline for distribution to natural gas markets, including transportation fueling. By substituting fossil natural gas, the unit will avoid the emissions of approximately 31,700 tons of CO₂ equivalent per year, equal to the emissions from burning 2.8 million gallons of diesel[1].

With many years of remaining disposal capacity, Randolph Farms Landfill provides a reliable, long-term source of landfill gas, making it well suited for continued renewable natural gas production.

RNG, a pillar of the energy transition, can replace fossil fuels in transportation, industry and heating. The result of 15 years of development, the WAGABOX® technology recovers landfill gas through cryogenics. It optimizes the energy production of landfill sites and delivers high-quality RNG, which can be injected directly into gas grids, regardless of the biogas composition.

“At Randolph Farms and Best Way, we're always looking for practical ways to improve our operations and manage costs,” said Jessica Routley, CEO of The Balkema Companies. “Landfill gas is a natural byproduct of our operations, and this project allows us to turn that resource into something valuable rather than letting it go to waste. We've had a successful partnership with Waga Energy at Decatur Hills, and we're pleased to build on that relationship at Randolph Farms.”

“We are proud to build on our successful collaboration with The Balkema Companies through this new project at Randolph Farms Landfill, alongside Best Way Disposal. Their commitment and long-term vision made our first collaboration at Decatur Hills a success. It is the trust we built together on that project that makes this new unit possible. This second facility strengthens our footprint in Indiana, where we are creating a true renewable energy hub,” said Guénaël Prince, CEO of Waga Energy Inc.

About Randolph Farms Landfill & Best Way Disposal

Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal are part of The Balkema Companies, a family-owned group of businesses with operations in waste management, construction, aggregates, and related industries. Located in Modoc, Indiana, Randolph Farms Landfill has been operated by The Balkema Companies since 1986 and provides waste disposal services to communities throughout eastern Indiana and neighboring counties in Ohio. Best Way Disposal provides residential, commercial, and industrial waste collection and disposal services throughout Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, and Ohio. The company focuses on reliable service, continued investment in its operations, and practical, cost-effective solutions for its customers and the communities it serves.

About Waga Energy

Waga Energy produces competitively priced renewable natural gas (RNG, also known as biomethane) by upgrading landfill gas using a patented purification technology called WAGABOX®. The RNG produced is injected directly into gas grids that supply homes and businesses, providing a substitute for fossil natural gas. Waga Energy currently operates 38 RNG production units in France, Spain, Canada, and the USA, representing an installed capacity of more than 7.1 million MMBtu (2.1 TWh) per year. To date, WagaEnergy has 22 RNG production units under construction worldwide. Each project initiated by WagaEnergy contributes to the fight against global warming and helps drive the energy transition. Waga Energy is listed on Euronext Paris (FR0012532810 – EPA: WAGA).

text:
Highlights

Ucore Rare Metals Inc. received a minor source air permit from the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality for its Strategic Metals Complex in Alexandria.

The permit covers construction, testing, commissioning and operation from the enhanced Machine A line through the planned full build-out of the facility.

Ucore Rare Metals Inc. (TSXV:UCU) Basic Materials Ucore Rare Metals Inc (TSXV:UCU) 1.67 CAD +0.170 ↑ 11.333% said that the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality has issued a minor source air permit for its Strategic Metals Complex in Alexandria, Louisiana. According to the release, issued from Halifax, Nova Scotia, the permit is not limited to the opening phase of the project. It covers construction, testing, commissioning and operation of the complex from the enhanced first processing line, known as Machine A, all the way through the company's planned full build-out of rare earth separation capacity.

The announcement marks a regulatory step for a company that has positioned its Louisiana site as the first of several planned processing hubs for heavy and light rare earth elements outside Asia. Ucore stated that the permit is the final permit required from the state environmental regulator before enhanced Machine A can be installed.

Scope of the Louisiana Permit

The permit authorises processing at the complex up to the full planned throughput of contained total rare earth oxide, commonly abbreviated as TREO. That scope matters because it means the company does not need to return to the state air regulator for a fresh authorisation each time a later phase is added, provided operations remain within the permitted parameters. The release explains that the processing metrics used in the application were derived from mixed rare earth carbonate and mixed rare earth oxide feedstock planned for the complex.

Those feedstock materials were tested at the company's RapidSX Commercialization and Demonstration Facility in Kingston, Ontario. Ucore has used that Ontario facility to demonstrate its separation technology on representative material, and the release links the permitting data directly to that demonstration work. In other words, the figures submitted to Louisiana regulators were grounded in pilot-scale data generated in Canada.

The release also clarifies a point of terminology. A minor source permit applies to facilities whose emissions fall below the levels that would trigger a federal Title V operating permit. Ucore noted that the phrase describes the emissions category of the facility, not its physical size or its processing capacity.

Machine A and the Phased Construction Plan

The complex is designed to grow in stages. The first phase is built around enhanced Machine A, which the company plans to operate at an initial commercial capacity of TREO. Ucore is targeting installation, testing and commissioning of enhanced Machine A next year. Subsequent phases are intended to scale the facility toward the full build-out now covered by the permit.

Mike Schrider, the company's Vice President and Chief Operating Officer, thanked the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality and the State of Louisiana for what he described as an efficient permitting process built on the demonstration work completed in Kingston. He added that each milestone achieved is a building block toward commissioning enhanced Machine A next year, and that the facility is intended to serve the United States, Canada and allied nations.

Beyond the air permit, the release notes continued coordination with the State Fire Marshal and with England Airpark, the property in Alexandria where the complex is located. The company's website describes the site as a brownfield facility within the airpark and states that the complex will be commissioned in stages.

Planned Product Slate and Feedstock Sources

Ucore plans to produce separated rare earth products including neodymium-praseodymium oxide, often shortened to NdPr, as well as samarium, gadolinium and yttrium. NdPr is a key input for permanent magnets used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and a wide range of industrial and defence equipment. Samarium is associated with high-temperature magnet applications, while gadolinium and yttrium serve specialised roles in electronics, medical imaging and advanced materials.

The company has said it intends to supply medium and heavy rare earth oxides to Western markets, drawing feedstock from multiple Western sources. That multi-source approach is designed to give the complex flexibility in the type of concentrate it processes, which is consistent with the testing of both carbonate and oxide feedstock at the Kingston facility.

Ucore's broader corporate plan extends beyond Louisiana. According to the company description in the release, it intends to follow the Louisiana complex with similar facilities in Canada and Alaska. Over the longer term, the company fully controls the Bokan-Dotson Ridge rare heavy rare earth element project on Prince of Wales Island in Alaska.

Rare Earth Supply Chains and the Canadian Listing

The permit arrives at a time when governments in North America and Europe continue to focus on domestic processing of critical minerals. Rare earth separation, the chemical step that turns mixed concentrates into individual oxides, has historically been concentrated in a small number of jurisdictions. Projects that can add separation capacity in the United States or Canada have drawn attention from policymakers, manufacturers and the broader market.

Within the wider group of Canadian growth stocks, companies working on processing technology and critical mineral supply chains have become a recognisable theme, and permitting milestones are among the operational markers the market tends to track.

The company's website also references support at the state and local level. It describes an incentive package outlined by the State of Louisiana that includes a grant for infrastructure upgrades, along with a grant from the Greater Alexandria Economic Development Authority to offset early facility costs, and notes public support from state and federal elected officials. The site further states that the project is expected to create family-wage jobs in Central Louisiana.

What the Permit Changes for the Timeline

From a project management perspective, securing an air permit that already covers the full build-out removes a regulatory workstream from the critical path of later expansion phases. Ucore has framed the approval as clearing the way for the next physical step, which is the installation of enhanced Machine A at the Alexandria site. The release did not provide a capital cost update or a revised production schedule beyond the commissioning target.

As with any development-stage processing project, the company's release includes forward-looking statements and lists assumptions such as continued support from governmental partners and the ability to qualify for further government funding in the United States or Canada. The timelines described represent company targets rather than completed outcomes, and progress will depend on construction, commissioning and feedstock arrangements proceeding as planned.

Key Points from the Announcement

The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality issued the permit for the Strategic Metals Complex in Alexandria, Louisiana. The approval covers construction, testing, commissioning and operation from enhanced Machine A through the planned full build-out. Application data came from feedstock testing at the RapidSX facility in Kingston, Ontario. The company targets commissioning of enhanced Machine A next year, with products planned to include NdPr, samarium, gadolinium and yttrium.

The next disclosures of interest are likely to centre on equipment installation at the airpark site, coordination with the State Fire Marshal and further feedstock and offtake arrangements. Each of these steps will shape how quickly the Louisiana complex moves from a permitted facility to an operating separation plant serving North American magnet and advanced materials supply chains.

title: Q&A: Can Dems turn midterm gains into environmental wins? | Seaside Signal
authors: Chuck Thompson/Columbia Insight, Chuck Thompson, Columbia Insight
description:
What can you actually accomplish in regards to environmental legislation with control of two-thirds of the levers of power?
