On data centers, I have introduced legislation that would ban the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands to build new data centers and associated infrastructure in Oregon and nationwide.
I also have unveiled a comprehensive proposal that would ensure data centers start paying for disruptions caused to communities like higher energy costs and water usage.
CI: Senate Bill 5653 (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026) would weaken, perhaps fatally, the foundation of U.S. environmental laws.
text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

In an exclusive Columbia Insight interview, Sen. Ron Wyden assesses Trump’s war on the environment.

The Democrats’ recapture of the U.S. House and Senate as a result of national successes in the midterm elections has many in the Pacific Northwest optimistic about clawing back Trump administration reversals of environmental protections.

But how much can opponents of the Trump administration’s war on the environment really accomplish? And how will they balance such efforts against promises to end the war in Iran, make healthcare more affordable and investigate White House corruption?

Following the dramatic electoral gains by progressives, Columbia Insight reached out to Ore. Sen. Ron Wyden, the second senior-most Democratic lawmaker in the Senate and incoming chair of the Senate Finance Committee.

Sen. Wyden responded this week via email.

Columbia Insight: The Democrats have recaptured Congress. What can you actually accomplish in regards to environmental legislation with control of two-thirds of the levers of power?

Sen. Ron Wyden: There’s a blueprint for this situation where a Democratic Congress can achieve huge and lasting environmental gains with a Republican in the White House.

In the 1970s, significant achievements with that dynamic included creation of the EPA in 1970 and passage of major bills during the 1970s like the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Air Act, the Marine Mammal Protection Act and the Endangered Species Act.

Voters in Oregon and nationwide sent a clear message in this most recent election that it’s a new day. And that new day includes a big “No” to the pathetic litany of Trump attacks on the environment like unchecked data centers, and dangerous backtracking on proven protections for our land, air and water.

I am ready to work with anybody who recognizes that message is the need to stop reversing environmental safeguards and to resume the proven path of building robust protections for public health and natural habitat.

CI: The Trump administration wants to rescind the Roadless Rule; has proposed slackening EPA emissions regulations on pollutants from oil and gas industries; eased environmental rules for data centers; changed wording in the Endangered Species Act to make it easier for developers to degrade habitat where endangered species live. How will Democrats prioritize combatting these and other Republican-led attacks on the environmental protections?

RW: Here’s how I am combatting these attacks on protections we hold dear as Oregonians: On the roadless rule, I have always worked to achieve balanced and responsible public land stewardship that protects natural treasures with well-maintained roads, trails and parks. The roadless rule is essential to that work. And I will never stop battling Trump schemes to undo these proven protections and to press for protection of current access points by addressing growing maintenance backlog across the Forest Service’s existing road network.

On emissions regulations, I am proud that major pieces of my Clean Energy for America Act were part of the Inflation Reduction Act and I will be relentless in battling any administration ploy like anti-science emissions increases that would hurt public health and increase America’s dependence on foreign oil.

On data centers, I have introduced legislation that would ban the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands to build new data centers and associated infrastructure in Oregon and nationwide. I also have unveiled a comprehensive proposal that would ensure data centers start paying for disruptions caused to communities like higher energy costs and water usage.

CI: Senate Bill 5653 (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026) would weaken, perhaps fatally, the foundation of U.S. environmental laws. It has bypassed many of the usual protocols for new legislation and seems to be getting rushed into law behind the support of fossil fuel and data center companies. Do you agree with the Columbia Insight board that this legislation presents an existential threat to the environment of the Pacific Northwest and that it must be defeated at all costs? Or is SB 5653 fait accompli?

RW: I cannot support a bill that relies on a pinky-swear promise from Donald Trump’s minions after they’ve dedicated every waking moment since taking office to oppose clean energy projects. And I cannot support a deal that strips Oregonians and Tribes of their most important tools to hold Trump and his cronies accountable.

I continue to believe Democrats have a unique opportunity to reach an agreement that reduces red tape for green energy projects that lower costs without ongoing dangers of political interference.

While I have been working to defeat it, I am not the last word on this bill—YOU, the reader, are and you should make your voice heard on this issue.

CI: What is your position on HB 655 (Dalles Watershed Development Act), which would transfer 150 acres of federal land to the City of The Dalles, and which critics say is being proposed primarily as a way to gift attached water rights to the owners of data centers, Alphabet/Google specifically?

RW: Congress shouldn’t be in the business of helping Donald Trump sell public lands, and HB655 would put his scheme in the express sell-off lane. I oppose this legislation as it’s currently written.

CI: The Department of Energy is actively promoting the construction of new nuclear power facilities at the Hanford Site, which many assume is a way to provide power for data centers. Where do you stand on this issue?

RW: Hanford has more than enough on its to-do list without this out-of-left-field notion that does nothing to fulfill the federal government’s long-overdue responsibility to manage millions of gallons of hazardous and radioactive nuclear waste.

Management of that waste threatening families, farmlands, fisheries and more along the Columbia River demands the federal government’s full attention, not doubling down on nuclear in this already heavily contaminated part of the Northwest.

CI: In late 2025, the Bureau of Land Management green-lit exploratory lithium mining projects on 7,200 acres near the McDermitt Caldera in southeastern Oregon. Is this something you support?

RW: Exploratory mining is exactly that—exploratory—and thus should come with minimum environmental disruption. I will be watchdogging the development of this mining interest to ensure that the disruption is minimal and that there’s a balanced approach.

With the ongoing growth of Smartphones and other technologies, it’s clear we can no longer be exporting critical minerals and rare earths to countries with less stringent environmental laws than ours. America knows how to extract and refine these critical materials better, safer and with more respect for the planet and the people involved in the mining of them than anywhere else.

And that brings us back to the balanced approach of using these talents to get us what we need while also protecting our planet, water and communities.

CI: The Bureau of Land Management is moving forward with a number of controversial timber sales in Oregon. For just two examples, the 42 Divide Timber Project near Roseburg and Last Chance Timber Sale near Grants Pass include mature and old-growth logging approved by questionable federal environmental assessments. Can and will the Democrat-controlled Congress exercise more oversight and restraint on the massive increase in logging of Oregon’s forests ordered by President Trump?

RW: I have already drafted a letter with my priorities for the upcoming Congress to the incoming Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Martin Heinrich, and the incoming Chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Resources Committee, Jared Huffman. Ending old-growth timber sales is at the top of that list to my two fellow Democrats.

Also topping my list is oversight into the old-growth sales the Trump administration has already jammed through and probing just which special interests profited from those sales.

CI: Columbia Insight has been using the phrase “Trump’s war on the environment” for the past couple of years because that’s what the sum total of his environment-related executive orders and other pronouncements feels like to us. Would you agree with this assessment or are we being a little too dramatic?

RW: Unfortunately, Trump’s deplorable record does add up a “war” on the environmental priorities Oregonians hold so dear. I also believe that there are battles to be won, thanks to the recent elections results. And I am committed to winning them.

There is nothing “overly dramatic” about our need, as people, for clean air to breathe and clean water to drink.

In a sentence, “Trump puts the robber back in robber baron” because Trump obviously doesn’t care about the environment one way or another. What he does care about is lining his pockets and the pockets of his friends.

The old saying goes: Follow the money and that adage is certainly true here.

CI: When you were elected to Congress more than 45 years ago, environmental issues seemed less partisan. Richard Nixon established the EPA in 1970; Ronald Reagan signed the Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area Act in 1986. How might Democrats and Republicans be persuaded to adopt a less partisan mindset when it comes to environmental issues and regain political consensus on important conservation issues?

RW: As we have both pointed out, history shows that working together on green-friendly policies doesn’t need to be a red or a blue thing.

There’s no Republican or Democrat way to enjoy hiking in the woods, fishing in a stream or just marveling at our state’s world-renowned natural treasures. There’s just the Oregon Way, and that’s a value always worth employing as a lodestar for smart and lasting policies.

The key here is that the environment is all about public health—because without clean air and clean water, without a place to hike or a view to take in—our lives are less rich and less healthy.

Chuck Thompson is editor of Columbia Insight.

title: You Won't Believe How Little This Autopian Reader Paid For A Slightly Used $120000 Car
description:
Autopian reader Henry Y. recently purchased a 2022 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ and has some thoughts.
Luckily for Henry, he was paying nowhere near the $120,000 sticker price for his car.
The car had done about 44,000 miles and was certified pre-owned (CPO).
For interested car shoppers out there, the best part is that there are many deals like this one.
A cursory search online reveals over 70 CPO EQS sedans at the moment with several around the same price Henry paid.
text:
It is a truth universally acknowledged that large luxury sedans depreciate faster than mere gravity would allow. That is not Jane Austen satire, but a real true fact. Such an inescapable fact that not even Lexus – a brand noted for its strong resale value – and its LS flagship could defy it.

Modern EVs, whose out-the-door prices have been distorted by a mix of federal tax credits, local incentives, and generous lease deals, have also demonstrated notoriously poor resale value. So, at the intersection of those two groups, you have luxury EV sedans, which exhibit crater-deep levels of depreciation. Exhibit A: this Lucid Air, which depreciated over $50K (47%) in 9 months and 1800 miles. Exhibit B: this Audi e-tron GT, which depreciated $71K (70%) in 25K miles. To a smaller extent, C: this Polestar 2, which depreciated $37K (72%) in 4 years. I could go on and on.

Though we (or at least David) may pity the first owners who suffer the insidious and colossal cuts of depreciation, perhaps there is more to these cars’ story than the middling reviews they received at launch. As happens with the passage of time and in the hands of second and third owners, maybe the public image of some of these EVs can be resuscitated. If cars like the Pontiac Aztek, Fiat Multipla, and Ssangyong Rodius could go from zero to (anti)hero, then there is hope for any car, right?

Enter the Mercedes-Benz EQS. Much meh’d when new, could it now be a pre-owned hidden gem? Autopian reader Henry Y. recently purchased a 2022 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ and has some thoughts.

For its first model year, Car and Driver noted as highs of the EQS 450+: “Impressive real-world range, luxurious appointments, generous cargo capacity.” And for lows: “Polarizing design, wonky brake pedal, merely adequate acceleration.”

Edmunds was more direct in its review and noted the EQS was “[n]ot as quick or as sporty as other luxury EVs” while being “[m]ore expensive than some rivals”. Two points that generally do not form a compelling value proposition.

Luckily for Henry, he was paying nowhere near the $120,000 sticker price for his car. He picked up his Selenite Grey Magno sedan for $40,000 out the door. The car had done about 44,000 miles and was certified pre-owned (CPO). Mercedes CPO means an additional year (with unlimited miles) was added to what was left of the factory warranty, and a fresh set of tires was fitted. Beyond the Magno paint (Mercedes speak for matte), other options on Henry’s specific model include rear-wheel steering, AMG styling package, diamond-quilted Nappa leather seats, and augmented-reality head-up display. Doing out some math, that is roughly 67% depreciation or $1.36 per mile driven. Gaudy numbers in their own right.

If you walked into a Mercedes-Benz dealership today and asked for a brand-new 2026 EQS, they would ask you for at least $101,000 of cash or credit. While that car would have some changes (namely to the grille and a switch over to the NACS charging port) and improvements (slightly larger battery pack and improved highway efficiency), it would still be on the same platform as Henry’s first-year EQS and have the same flowing aero design that has come to define an entire generation of Mercedes EQ vehicles.

Six months into his ownership, things are going well with no glaring faults. An EV veteran who has previously owned Teslas, Audi e-tron GT, and BMW i3, Henry says the EQS has been “probably my favorite of the bunch.” The most appealing attributes of the experience have been comfort and cabin quietness. In his time with it so far, the air suspension makes for a soft ride, and minimal cabin noise has been ideal for lulling a newborn to sleep.

One of the benefits of a sedan body style is aerodynamics and better range. Car and Driver got 400 miles out of the EQS on the highway going 75 mph. Henry is not quite seeing those numbers, but it sounds like 350 miles is achievable:

I drive almost exclusively in Eco mode, and the cluster shows 3.33 mi/kWh. The range is great. I can drive from Pasadena to Las Vegas on one charge comfortably, with the A/C on and the massage seats running. I leave at 100% and arrive on the Strip with about 25%.

Concern over battery degradation should be low at this point as well. Mercedes covers all EQE and EQS models with a 10-year/155K mile battery warranty, which is longer than the typical 8-year/100K most of other EVs offer.

Ownership has resulted in some slight niggles though. Once again, in Henry’s own words:

The rear bench is steeply sloped, so our infant car seat sits at an awkward angle. I get occasional software glitches, and sometimes the flush door handles don’t present. There are some creaks around the cabin, and the fit and finish feel a bit lacking for a car with such a high original MSRP. The 12V battery also drains quickly if the car sits for more than about two weeks. None of these have been deal-breakers, and at what I paid, they’re easy to live with.

Those certainly sound like the types of complaints that taking $80K off the MSRP helps assuage.

For interested car shoppers out there, the best part is that there are many deals like this one. A cursory search online reveals over 70 CPO EQS sedans at the moment with several around the same price Henry paid.

So long as you have access to easy charging or are willing to install it, a heavily depreciated used luxury EV could be a lovely daily driver.

text:
Severe weather, high energy costs and thin margins go hand-in-hand for many small business owners in the Philippines – and the recent energy crisis has accentuated their problems. Women-led businesses, especially in rural and hard-to-reach areas, often face additional difficulties in accessing finance, technology, information and business support. A United Nations initiative has set out to change that and has already provided over 16,700 women business owners with support, including over $2 million in clean energy loans.

“When clean energy financing is intentionally designed to reach women-led small businesses, it can unlock a powerful pathway toward climate resilience, economic security and local development,” said Parimita Mohanty, Programme Management Officer at the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).

The EmPower: Women for Climate Resilient Societies initiative, a joint programme led by UN Women and UNEP, supported by the Governments of Germany, New Zealand, Sweden and Switzerland, is breaking down the financial barriers faced by women, supporting green livelihoods and jobs, and offering a roadmap for more inclusive climate action.

Unlocking Renewable Energy Entrepreneurship in Iloilo

In Iloilo, the first province in the country to pass a renewable energy ordinance with its own budget allocation, clean energy is directly transforming local public services. Through a strategic collaboration under EmPower, provincial officers are embedding gender equality into local energy efficiency plans. In practice, this means ensuring women's needs and priorities are reflected in renewable energy investments, from more reliable health services to safer public spaces and new green job opportunities. The lessons from Iloilo are now informing EmPower's support to 31 other provinces across the Philippines as they advance a more gender-responsive clean energy transition.

EmPower, through the Microfinance Council of the Philippines, Inc., partners with microfinance institutions, including Ahon sa Hirap, Inc. (ASHI) and the Negros Women for Tomorrow Foundation (NWTF), giving rural women entrepreneurs access to financing specifically for renewable energy technologies, combined with practical business training.

“Our goal with this joint initiative is to show how we can stimulate resilient and inclusive grassroots economic growth through supporting women entrepreneurs,” said Rosalyn Mesina, Country Programme Coordinator at UN Women Philippines. “Truly, we are seeing that women are proving to be viable clients for green finance when products and tools are designed according to their realities, needs and constraints – and once addressed, the impact goes beyond their businesses, but the communities where they belong.”

Here are the stories of four entrepreneurs who benefitted from EmPower support.

Mary Grace Moreno: Livestock Farming With Solar Energy

In the town of Maasin, Mary Grace runs a small livestock business of over 20 pigs, an enterprise easily hurt by intense summer heat and unpredictable power outages. “We need to run the fans to keep the animals cool during the day, and we need to feed the pigs at night, so our energy costs are high,” said Mary Grace. For years, her business relied on an unstable electricity supply, including a low-cost solar system she bought online but which could provide power for only an hour. Through EmPower’s partnership with NWTF, Mary Grace secured a small loan to install a higher quality solar home system. This gave her energy independence, cutting her monthly electricity bills and enabling her business to be more sustainable.

Avelina Simpia: Pastry and Online Food Vending With a Rooftop Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Home System

In nearby Zarraga, Avelina faced an energy bottleneck for her pastry production and food vending business, which she runs with her daughter, Cherile. For her, electricity is a necessity for food preparation, keeping her products fresh and operating her online store. Rising power rates kept her profit margins thin, making it difficult to save money or expand her shop.

Partnering with ASHI under EmPower, Avelina took out a clean energy loan to install a rooftop solar PV home system last year. Generating her own electricity has dropped her operating costs, increasing profits, which she plans to re-invest in growing her business.

Rosenne Baco Fiscal: Hog and Poultry Farming With a Solar PV Home System

Rosenne operates a hog and poultry business in Zarraga. In livestock farming, heat mitigation and consistent ventilation are critical to animal health and survival. Relying on an unpredictable local grid meant that sudden power failures during extreme heatwaves put her entire livestock population at risk, while high electricity prices stunted her ability to grow even when power was available.

Through EmPower, Rosenne integrated a reliable solar setup into her farming infrastructure. This clean energy alternative provides continuous and reliable energy for an egg incubator, lighting and ventilation systems. Rosenne has improved animal safety, increased her production capacity and strengthened her business in a historically male-dominated sector.

Beyond Small Businesses: Commercial Solar Energy in Batangas

While the solutions in Iloilo demonstrated how clean energy helps micro-businesses, the model scales up to power larger women-owned operations in Batangas as well. Through the technical assistance provided by MCPI under EmPower, local thrift banks, such as Bangko Kabayan, can support larger-scale green infrastructure investments.

Mary Rose Bathan Buen: Commercial Solar-Powered Ice Plant

In the town of Balayan, Mary Rose runs an industrial business for the local fishing community. Backed by a pioneering, clean energy loan from Bangko Kabayan, she installed Balayan’s first ice production plant, which works using solar power.

Mary Rose’s plant serves as an economic anchor for the coastal community. For local fisherfolk, quick access to affordable ice is crucial to bringing their catch to market, preventing post-harvest food waste, protecting incomes and creating local green jobs.

Sparking Commitments to Accelerate Gender-Responsive Actions

EmPower looks to build on tested local solutions and scale them through stronger partnerships with Government, financial institutions and women entrepreneurs.

“By helping to reduce the perceived risks of green technology, supporting financial institutions to design products that respond to women’s realities and demonstrating strong demand from women-led businesses, EmPower is helping build an investment-ready model for energy transition in the Philippines,” said UN Women’s Mesina.

The experiences of Mary Grace, Avelina, Rosenne, Mary Rose and more than 16,000 women business owners prove that financial barriers can be broken and, in their place, a greener and more inclusive future are possible.

title: Alternative-fuel vehicle inquiries rise as buyers seek options beyond petrol: FADA - ET Auto
description:
In October, alternative fuels again edged past petrol, accounting for 41.83 per cent of passenger vehicle retail against petrol's 41.60 per cent, according to FADA's latest retail data.
So as and when we see more options and more variants across segments for consumers, definitely customers will adopt these new energy vehicles,” Giridhar added.
At present, WagonR is the only passenger vehicle available in flex fuel, while Hero Deluxe and Xtreme are in two-wheelers.
The shift towards alternative powertrains comes even as electric vehicle retail continues to expand.
FADA expects total vehicle retail sales could cross three-crore annual milestones by the year's end.
text:
Rising fuel prices and geopolitical uncertainties are prompting Indian consumers to explore alternative powertrains, with auto dealers reporting an increase in inquiries for flex-fuel, mild-hybrid and strong-hybrid vehicles, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA).

However, limited model availability and a lack of choices across vehicle segments remain key constraints in converting consumer interest into purchases.

“Definitely the inquiries are there, but as of today, there is not much availability, and there is not much choice with the consumer,” Sai Giridhar, President, FADA, told ETAuto in an interview.

According to the body, consumers are showing an appetite for new-energy vehicles, with purchase decisions being influenced by the overall cost of ownership, including its initial cost, running expenses and servicing requirements.ETAuto earlier discussed how petrol is losing its market share, while there is an uptake in fuels such as CNG and electric vehicles (EVs). In August 2026, the combined share of CNG, hybrid and EVs crossed 41 per cent, surpassing petrol and ethanol vehicles at 40.85 per cent for the first time.

While, in the alternative-fuel share aspect, CNG stood at 25.28 per cent, hybrids at 9.04 per cent and electric vehicles at 7.63 per cent. Petrol, which has remained the dominant fuel category, has seen its lead over the combined alternative-fuel categories narrow significantly. The onset of the festive season in September saw alternative fuels accounting for 41 per cent of passenger vehicle retail, compared with petrol's 41.27 per cent. Hybrid vehicles contributed 9.44 per cent, while EVs accounted for 8.45 per cent and CNG for 23.11 per cent.

In October, alternative fuels again edged past petrol, accounting for 41.83 per cent of passenger vehicle retail against petrol's 41.60 per cent, according to FADA's latest retail data. This pattern demonstrates that consumers are increasingly considering powertrain alternatives.

“It is probably the same at the start of the electric revolution, I should say. There were only a couple of OEMs, only one or two models which were available. So as and when we see more options and more variants across segments for consumers, definitely customers will adopt these new energy vehicles,” Giridhar added.

At present, WagonR is the only passenger vehicle available in flex fuel, while Hero Deluxe and Xtreme are in two-wheelers. Toyota Kirloskar Motor is soon going to bring its Hycross flex fuel in India. The shift towards alternative powertrains comes even as electric vehicle retail continues to expand. During the 42-day festive period in 2026, electric passenger vehicle retail rose 72.91 per cent year-on-year to 52,104 units, while total electric vehicle retail across categories increased 52.62 per cent to 5,09,667 units, FADA data showed.

EV demand rises, but availability remains a concern

OEMs, along with FADA, have been advocating for more demand than supply in the EV market. Electric passenger vehicle retail grew by nearly 73 per cent year-on-year during the 42-day festive period, while the overall EV industry expanded by around 53 per cent to close to five lakh units. Despite this growth, EV penetration in passenger vehicles remained below 7 per cent, due to the unavailability of vehicles. Giridhar said buyers were increasingly confident about adopting new-energy vehicles with respect to the economics of buying, using and servicing them, becoming an important consideration. Though strengthened, charging infrastructure remains essential.

Retail growth seen as structural

On the broader market, Giridhar said the growth was no longer merely a seasonal increase following the GST 2.0 reforms but had become more broad-based across vehicle segments and regions. FADA expects total vehicle retail sales could cross three-crore annual milestones by the year's end. Looking ahead to December, Giridhar expects discounts to remain available in the market but does not anticipate the unusually high promotional offers seen in some previous years.

text:
Philadelphia (USA), November 23, 2026. Waga Energy (EPA: WAGA), a specialist in renewable natural gas (RNG) production from landfill gas, has signed an agreement with Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal, both part of The Balkema Companies, a family-owned group of businesses, to build an RNG production unit in Modoc, Indiana. The new unit will upgrade the gas naturally emitted by landfilled waste into clean, local, and renewable energy.

This project is the second collaboration between Waga Energy and The Balkema Companies, following the successful commissioning of the Decatur Hills RNG Facility in Greensburg, Indiana (August 2026).

Under the agreement, Waga Energy will finance, build, own, and operate the RNG facility for at least 20 years. Randolph Farms will manage the landfill gas collection system and support the civil works for the project. Waga Energy and Randolph Farms will share the revenues generated by the sale of the RNG.

The facility will utilize Waga Energy’s patented WAGABOX® technology to process up to 2,000 scfm (3,200 m³/h) of raw biogas and produce up to 407,000 MMBtu (120 GWh) of RNG per year at full capacity. Commissioning is scheduled for early 2028. The WAGABOX® unit will replace the existing landfill gas upgrading technology at Randolph Farms, where renewable natural gas is currently produced for Best Way Disposal’s onsite fueling facility. The new project will allow Randolph Farms to continue making productive use of landfill gas by converting it into a valuable energy resource. RNG produced by the new facility will be delivered to a nearby interstate pipeline for distribution to natural gas markets, including transportation fueling. By substituting fossil natural gas, the unit will avoid the emissions of approximately 31,700 tons of CO₂ equivalent per year, equal to the emissions from burning 2.8 million gallons of diesel[1].

With many years of remaining disposal capacity, Randolph Farms Landfill provides a reliable, long-term source of landfill gas, making it well suited for continued renewable natural gas production.

RNG, a pillar of the energy transition, can replace fossil fuels in transportation, industry and heating. The result of 15 years of development, the WAGABOX® technology recovers landfill gas through cryogenics. It optimizes the energy production of landfill sites and delivers high-quality RNG, which can be injected directly into gas grids, regardless of the biogas composition.

“At Randolph Farms and Best Way, we’re always looking for practical ways to improve our operations and manage costs,” said Jessica Routley, CEO of The Balkema Companies. “Landfill gas is a natural byproduct of our operations, and this project allows us to turn that resource into something valuable rather than letting it go to waste. We’ve had a successful partnership with Waga Energy at Decatur Hills, and we’re pleased to build on that relationship at Randolph Farms.”

“We are proud to build on our successful collaboration with The Balkema Companies through this new project at Randolph Farms Landfill, alongside Best Way Disposal. Their commitment and long-term vision made our first collaboration at Decatur Hills a success. It is the trust we built together on that project that makes this new unit possible. This second facility strengthens our footprint in Indiana, where we are creating a true renewable energy hub,” said Guénaël Prince, CEO of Waga Energy Inc.

About Randolph Farms Landfill & Best Way Disposal

Randolph Farms Landfill and Best Way Disposal are part of The Balkema Companies, a family-owned group of businesses with operations in waste management, construction, aggregates, and related industries. Located in Modoc, Indiana, Randolph Farms Landfill has been operated by The Balkema Companies since 1986 and provides waste disposal services to communities throughout eastern Indiana and neighboring counties in Ohio. Best Way Disposal provides residential, commercial, and industrial waste collection and disposal services throughout Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, and Ohio. The company focuses on reliable service, continued investment in its operations, and practical, cost-effective solutions for its customers and the communities it serves.

About Waga Energy

Waga Energy produces competitively priced renewable natural gas (RNG, also known as biomethane) by upgrading landfill gas using a patented purification technology called WAGABOX®. The RNG produced is injected directly into gas grids that supply homes and businesses, providing a substitute for fossil natural gas. Waga Energy currently operates 38 RNG production units in France, Spain, Canada, and the USA, representing an installed capacity of more than 7.1 million MMBtu (2.1 TWh) per year. To date, WagaEnergy has 22 RNG production units under construction worldwide. Each project initiated by WagaEnergy contributes to the fight against global warming and helps drive the energy transition. Waga Energy is listed on Euronext Paris (FR0012532810 – EPA: WAGA).

Ashok Leyland's e-mobility subsidiary OHM Mobility has secured an order to deploy more than 200 trucks for cement distribution on fixed routes under its electric mobility-as-a-service (e-MaaS) model.

The development was disclosed by Ashok Leyland Managing Director and CEO Shenu Agarwal during the company's Q2 FY27 earnings conference call on November 16, 2026. The company did not disclose the name of the customer, order value or deployment timeline.

The order expands OHM Mobility's operations beyond its electric bus fleet and comes as Ashok Leyland continues to develop its electric commercial vehicle business and associated mobility services.

OHM Mobility expands fleet operations

OHM Mobility had an operating fleet of approximately 2,100 electric buses at the end of September 2026, according to the company's management. The subsidiary is also progressing towards its profitability objectives.

Separately, Ashok Leyland's other electric mobility subsidiary, Switch Mobility India, delivered 439 electric buses and 732 electric light commercial vehicles during the first half of FY27. Its electric bus order book stood at approximately 2,800 units at the end of September 2026.

Ashok Leyland expands electric mobility investments

Ashok Leyland is also investing in battery manufacturing to support its electric commercial vehicle operations. The company has received the necessary approvals for its battery pack manufacturing facility at Pillaipakkam, near Chennai, and construction has commenced.

The first phase is planned with an initial capacity of approximately 4 GWh, intended to meet captive requirements across Ashok Leyland and Switch Mobility. The facility is designed to allow future expansion to 8 GWh or 12 GWh. Production is expected to commence in Q3 of the next financial year.

The company is positioning electric mobility as an important part of its commercial vehicle strategy, with management expecting electric vehicle adoption to progress across light commercial vehicles, buses and, subsequently, heavy-duty trucks.

Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn has begun production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic batteries at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, east of Battle Creek. The batteries will power Ford Fathom truck prototypes being built in Louisville, Ky.

“Today represents more than the start of production in Marshall,” says Dave Carroll, president of Ford Energy. “It represents Ford officially becoming a battery manufacturer.

Ford Energy also is building up battery energy storage system production at Ford Energy Systems in Glendale, Ky.

name: Indiana and Evs
title: Slate Truck review: the clever, cut-price, electric pick-up that makes basic cool
description:
Its truck is designed around a single basic specification, with personalisation taking place through accessories rather than a conventional ladder of trim levels.
I drove a pre-production Slate Truck in and around Pasadena, California, on roads I know particularly well.
My phone already does the things I’d want it to do, and the Slate gives it somewhere to sit.
Phone charging is provided, and an accessory bracket is available if you’d prefer a tablet.
I was seriously impressed by the way the pick-up drove, particularly its settled ride, direct steering and smooth electric drivetrain.
text:
Slate is a new American vehicle maker backed by investors including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Its truck is designed around a single basic specification, with personalisation taking place through accessories rather than a conventional ladder of trim levels. The company sells directly to customers, and assembly is planned at a former printing plant in Warsaw, Indiana, with first deliveries scheduled for next year.

Buying a Slate starts with a two-seat electric pick-up. What happens after that is rather more open-ended: you can keep the standard grey body and wind-up windows, change the colour with a wrap, add equipment as you need it or turn the whole thing into a five-seat SUV. You can even change it back again. The starting point is called the Blank Slate, which gives you a fair idea of what the company has in mind.

Every truck begins with unpainted grey body panels. Leaving out the paint shop helps keep manufacturing costs down, while owners can choose full or partial wraps, stripes and other graphics – as my prototype test car did. More than 200 accessories cover everything from extra storage and different cabin finishes to audio systems and the kits that change the body style. You can order equipment at the beginning or add it later.

The same approach continues inside, where a phone takes on the navigation and entertainment duties that would normally fall to a central touchscreen. Heating and air conditioning have physical controls, and the standard window winders can be replaced with powered windows if that’s what you want.

Underneath, the Slate has a single motor driving the rear wheels, a 65kWh battery and a maximum claimed range of 205 miles. US prices start at $24,950 before delivery, taxes and other fees. Sales are currently restricted to the United States, so there’s no British price to put beside that figure, although it currently equates to around £19,000. My introduction to the driving experience came in a pre-production pick-up around Pasadena in California.

I drove a pre-production Slate Truck in and around Pasadena, California, on roads I know particularly well. My route took in the freeway, bumpy city streets and roads up in the hills, before parking outside a trendy coffee shop. Along the way, I assessed the ride, steering, acceleration and braking, including regeneration, as well as noise levels. I also tried the phone mount and optional stereo, and reacquainted myself with those wonderfully simple wind-up windows.

Independent rating: 9/10

The first pleasant surprise was the ride. I’m used to pick-ups that bounce around when there’s nothing in the back, but the Slate felt settled on the bumpy streets around Pasadena. There was none of the constant bobbing about I’d been half expecting, and I found myself enjoying the drive rather than bracing for the next rough patch. The battery helps tie everything down, and I was impressed by how settled it felt.

The steering helped, too. There’s a nice weight to it and a directness that some pick-ups miss. It didn’t have that woolly feel where you turn the wheel and wait for the rest of the vehicle to catch up. Up in the hills, that made the Slate an enjoyable companion, while its compact size meant it never felt like too much truck for the road.

I was just as pleased with the electric drivetrain. The accelerator brings a smooth response, without the jerkiness that can make some EVs unnecessarily awkward at low speeds. The brakes have a decent feel, too, and the regeneration blends into the way the car slows down naturally. Everything felt really well integrated.

The prototype did have some wind noise, but I was still surprised by how quiet the Slate felt overall. For such a rudimentary little truck, it went about its business with rather less fuss than I’d expected.

The single rear motor produces 181bhp and 264Nm. Slate estimates 0–60mph in 8.0 seconds and a top speed of 90mph, while the pick-up’s kerb weight is 1,836kg, rising to 1,966kg with the SUV body configuration.

I liked the way the car rode on the standard steel wheels, although Slate also offers different wheel and suspension options for owners who want to change the look – you can beef up your Slate if that’s your wish.

The battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry and has an overall capacity of 65kWh. Slate’s maximum claimed range of 205 miles applies to the Blank Slate pick-up and is the company’s projection based on an approximation of the American EPA test, rather than a certified European test result. Temperature, driving style, and chosen accessories will all affect the distance between charges.

For a rapid top-up, the Slate accepts up to 120kW DC, with the company estimating around 30 minutes to go from 20 to 80 per cent. The onboard AC charger handles up to 11kW, and the truck can also charge from a slow 1.9kW AC supply. The American charging socket is the NACS type, and the truck can use compatible Tesla Superchargers. A charging cable is included, so a new owner has something to plug in with from the start.

There’s something about the Slate’s simple shape and steel wheels that reminds me of an old Defender. I think it looks really cool, and I like the fact that you can keep that plain, purposeful appearance if it suits you. Nobody is making you cover it in stickers or bolt on half the accessories catalogue, although there’s plenty of scope to do both.

The size is a big part of the appeal. At 4,435mm long, 1,793mm wide without the mirrors and 1,984mm with them, this is smaller than many pick-ups sold in Britain. It certainly didn’t feel too big on my drive surrounded by Cybercabs and other giant pick-ups, and I could see it fitting into life on UK roads really well.

There were plenty of unfinished plastics in the prototype I drove, although what caught my attention most was the return of wind-up windows. Remember those? You turn a handle and the window goes down; I loved having them back. Slate will sell you the kit to power them if you must, although I’d be quite happy keeping the winders.

There’s scope to change the interior in much smaller ways, too. Dashboard panels, armrests, seat covers and storage accessories let you alter the colour and usefulness of the cabin without replacing the vehicle. Some seat covers simply zip into place. Slate’s online tutorials explain accessory fitting, while its service partners can do the work for owners who’d prefer to hand over the tools.

The load bed provides about 994 litres of space. It’s 1,537mm long with the tailgate up, extending to 2,050mm with it lowered, and measures 1,115mm between the wheelarches or 1,499mm above them. The sides are 495mm high, with the top of the closed tailgate sitting about 1,201mm above the ground. There’s another 198-litres of storage under the bonnet, giving you an enclosed place for smaller belongings alongside the open load area.

That SUV conversion is a substantial change, adding a rear bench, protective structure and rear airbags, as well as enclosing the back. The Squareback has a more upright shape and the Fastback a sloping rear, with five seats in either. There’s also an Open Air configuration without a hard rear roof or rear windows, and a Cargo version for enclosed load carrying. You can have a conversion fitted before delivery or make the change later.

The phone mount worked just fine. That might sound like faint praise in a world of vast touchscreens and elaborate digital dashboards, but I really didn’t feel this truck needed a big screen in the middle. My phone already does the things I’d want it to do, and the Slate gives it somewhere to sit. It’s an approach that fits the rest of the vehicle rather neatly.

There’s no built-in infotainment system or Apple CarPlay/Android Auto interface: navigation and entertainment run through the apps on your own device. Phone charging is provided, and an accessory bracket is available if you’d prefer a tablet. The heating and air conditioning have physical controls, so you don’t have to involve the phone when you want to change the temperature – and yes, air con is one creature comfort that comes as standard.

Music is where I’d choose carefully. The added stereo in my test car sounded no more than okay, and at around $300 I’d be tempted to find a way of fitting a decent Bluetooth speaker of my own, such as a Sonos Play. I’d want a suitable mount, of course, and I’d be surprised if somebody didn’t come up with one with their own 3D printer.

Slate offers portable-speaker mounting and its own accessory audio, including speakers that can turn the dashboard into a soundbar. There’s also an optional steering-wheel controller for connected devices. You can add equipment later, so you don’t need to decide on the final sound system at the same moment you choose the truck.

The same thinking runs through the wider accessories programme, and I think it’s brilliant. Slate encourages outside companies and individual makers to develop products for the truck. Its Collective programme gives approved businesses the design information and attachment-point details they need, while letting them keep their own branding and ideas. When I describe the Slate as an open-source car, it’s this approach to accessories I’m talking about.

If there’s a bracket, storage solution or other extra that Slate hasn’t made, there’s a good chance somebody in that community will tackle it. The car has been designed with attachment points from the outset, and the online marketplace brings the company’s own products together with those from other makers. You can personalise it when you buy it and keep making changes afterwards.

The basic approach doesn’t leave out the usual safety equipment. The Slate gets traction and stability control, forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking, pedestrian detection, a reversing camera and automatic high-beam headlights. There are front, seat-side and curtain airbags, plus remote keyless entry – and the key just slots into a space in the dash for you to start the car.

A free Slate app is also planned, with charging status, battery-health information and help finding a charger – it won’t be required to drive the truck. That leaves you free to use the phone for the jobs it does well without making every part of owning the vehicle depend on it.

The Blank Slate starts at $24,950 in America, but you need to add the mandatory $1,450 destination charge. That makes $26,400 before taxes, registration and other fees, or any accessories.

Slate also quotes prices from $29,950 for its Squareback and Fastback SUVs, before delivery and other charges. The truck and accessories are only available to buy in the United States. A $300 preorder deposit counts towards the purchase price, with the vehicle bought directly from Slate rather than a traditional dealer.

How far you wander through the accessories catalogue is up to you. Slate says more than 80 per cent of its accessories cost less than $500. Full wraps start at around $500, with professional installation targeted at a similar amount, and there are more than 100 colours as well as partial wraps and decals. The wrap material is made for Slate’s unpainted panels, so this isn’t simply a case of assuming any film intended for painted bodywork will do the same job.

You can fit many accessories yourself, using Slate U’s free guides, or pay someone to do it. You can also spread the purchases over time. I like that flexibility, although I’d still keep an eye on the total; the roughly $300 stereo I tried is a good example of an extra I wouldn’t automatically choose.

For servicing, Slate is working in the US with a company called RepairPal’s nationwide network and making repair manuals and diagnostic information freely available. The truck still needs attention to tyres, brakes, filters and fluids, but there are no engine oil changes or spark plugs to budget for. High-voltage battery work belongs with an appropriately qualified workshop, rather than on the driveway accessory-fitting list.

I came away seriously impressed. The Slate’s smooth electric drivetrain, weighty steering and settled ride make it a fun thing to tool around in, while its simple looks and scope for personalisation add to the appeal. My prototype had wind noise and unfinished plastics, and the optional stereo was only okay, but I really enjoyed my time behind the wheel. If its range and charging fit your life, I’d happily recommend this cool little truck.

Slate estimates around 30 minutes for a 20 to 80 per cent top-up using a suitable DC rapid charger, with a maximum charging rate of 120kW. The onboard AC charger accepts up to 11kW, and Slate describes a full overnight charge from a suitable higher-powered home supply. From a standard US household socket, it quotes roughly three to four miles of range added per hour. The truck uses a NACS charging socket and can use compatible Tesla Superchargers. A home charging cable is included.

The US starting price is $24,950, plus a mandatory $1,450 delivery charge, making $26,400 before taxes, other fees and extras. Squareback and Fastback SUVs start at $29,950 before those additional charges. I was seriously impressed by the way the pick-up drove, particularly its settled ride, direct steering and smooth electric drivetrain. I also loved its simple appearance and the scope to personalise it. If the claimed range of 205 miles fit your needs, I’d recommend it on the evidence of this drive.

Slate provides a battery and powertrain warranty for 10 years or 110,000 miles, whichever comes first, with protection for retaining 70 per cent battery capacity. The standard vehicle limited warranty lasts four years or 50,000 miles, whichever comes first, and roadside assistance runs for the same period and mileage.

Our team of motoring experts have decades of experience driving, reviewing and reporting on the latest EV cars, and our verdicts are reached with every kind of driver in mind. We thoroughly test drive every car we recommend.

name: Clean Energy
title: Ossoff and Warnock Vote No on BAAJA As Senate Passes Sweeping Permitting Reform Bill
description:
Georgia’s two Democratic senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, were not among its supporters.
Both had voted to advance the bill at earlier stages of the Senate debate.
At its core, BAAJA is a permitting reform bill.
Days before the final vote, about 100 environmental and energy law scholars warned Senate Democratic leaders that the bill would do lasting damage to the nation’s core environmental laws.
Ossoff and Warnock both voted to advance BAAJA when the Senate first took it up.
text:
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Image

By Colleen Hamilton, Courier Georgia

The US Senate passed the most sweeping overhaul of federal permitting in decades late Thursday night, voting 62-33 to send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to the House.

Georgia’s two Democratic senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, were not among its supporters. Both had voted to advance the bill at earlier stages of the Senate debate. On final passage, they joined 28 other Democrats, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and two Republicans in voting no.

Ben Prater, director of the Southeast field conservation program at Defenders of Wildlife, called their votes “a strong indication both for the power of their leadership and their willingness to listen to their constituents.”

What is BAAJA?

At its core, BAAJA is a permitting reform bill. It would rewrite how federal agencies review and approve energy and infrastructure projects, from power lines and solar farms to pipelines, mines, and data centers.

The bill would change several of the nation’s foundational environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.

Prater said those laws have protected Georgia’s wildlife and public lands for decades. Weakening them, he said, “leaves the door wide open” to potentially harmful development.

Who supports BAAJA?

Nearly every Republican voted for the bill. They were joined by 15 members of the Democratic caucus, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

Proponents say permitting reform is urgently needed, especially as Americans struggle with rising costs. They argue that faster approvals will let companies bring new power online sooner, driving down energy prices. An analysis by the research firm Rhodium Group projected the bill would cut household electricity bills by an average of $50 to $78 a year by 2040.

The American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s largest trade group, has been a strong supporter of the legislation. It argues that “permitting delays and uncertainty can drive up the cost of building infrastructure and postpone projects that could help make energy more affordable.”

The bill is also supported by some of the largest artificial intelligence companies in the world like Nvidia, Meta, Amazon, Google, and OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. The Information Technology Industry Council, the trade group that represents these companies, called the bill “essential to America’s ability to build, compete, and lead—especially in the AI era.”

Who opposes BAAJA?

Opponents say the bill fails to distinguish between clean energy and fossil fuel projects. By speeding approvals for everything from solar farms to fracking, they argue, it would worsen the climate crisis while limiting communities’ ability to fight developments they don’t want.

“This deregulatory deal further eviscerates the National Environmental Policy Act, rips apart key provisions of the Clean Water Act, weakens the Endangered Species Act, and codifies the highly problematic Mining Regulatory Clarity Act that gives mining companies free rein over public lands, all while simultaneously preventing ordinary people from challenging harmful projects in court,” the Climate Justice Alliance wrote in a statement.

Environmental law groups have zeroed in on the bill’s limits on lawsuits. Earthjustice argues that the bill significantly restricts access to the courts at a time when judges are an important check on the executive branch. Days before the final vote, about 100 environmental and energy law scholars warned Senate Democratic leaders that the bill would do lasting damage to the nation’s core environmental laws.

Tribal nations have been among the most vocal opponents. The National Congress of American Indians called on both chambers to reject the bill outright, saying the bill would undercut their right to decide what gets built on their land and in their neighborhoods.

What impact could BAAJA have in Georgia?

Prater described the legislation as “written by industry, for industry.” He noted that the Southeast is already developing rapidly, and said the bill would strip away guardrails that have protected Georgia’s endangered species and wild places for decades.

The bill would require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to serve them. But critics say its limits on environmental review and lawsuits could also speed data center construction. That could matter a great deal in Georgia: metro Atlanta has more data center capacity under construction than any other US market, according to the real estate firm CBRE.

Why did Georgia’s senators vote no on BAAJA?

Ossoff and Warnock both voted to advance BAAJA when the Senate first took it up. By final passage on Thursday, both had flipped.

title: Congress Has 14 Days Left and A Lot To Do
description:
Others want a bipartisan bill capping the cost of insulin at $35 a month to be included with the spending bill.
In total, the House is only set to be in session for 12 more days this year; the Senate is scheduled for 14.
The annual lame-duck session was supposed to be abolished by the 20th Amendment, ratified in 1933, which pushed the first day of Congress up from March to January.
Since the 20th Amendment shortened the lame-duck session, but failed to end it completely, there have been some attempts to finish the job.
Unless and until the Constitution is amended, the lame-duck session is likely to continue — though perhaps it should be renamed.
text:
Now that campaigning is over, the real work can begin.

No, I don’t mean the next Congress, which will convene in January. I mean that age-old tradition, the lame-duck session, where members of Congress (including those who are retiring or were rejected at the ballot box) float around Washington like ghosts for the two months between Election Day and the end of their terms.

Ghosts who often get a lot done, that is.

Here’s a fun fact for you: more bills became law in the final two months of the last Congress (168) than in its first 22 months combined (106). The brief period after Election Day — after some of them had already been voted out of office! — turned out to be the most productive of that entire Congress. Not so lame after all, huh?

This year, one major piece of legislation has already started inching towards the president’s desk during the lame-duck. Lawmakers are hoping more will follow.

In a 62-33 vote on Thursday night, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, also known as BAAJA. The measure would overhaul the lengthy process for approving new energy projects in the U.S., which can currently stretch on for years.

This push (known as permitting reform) has been a white whale for policymakers for years now. Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — the chairs and ranking members of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) and Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) committees — ultimately inked an agreement by giving something to everyone. BAAJA would speed the permitting process for fossil fuel and clean energy projects alike, while also making it harder for presidents to stop both, whether it’s Joe Biden blocking the Keystone XL pipeline or Donald Trump blocking wind farms.

The bill was backed by all but two Senate Republicans and about one-third of Senate Democrats. Advocates argued that the measure will boost energy supply, thereby lowering energy prices; supportive Democrats also pointed to analyses finding that the net impact of the bill would favor clean energy projects. Progressive critics argued that the bill would make it difficult to block environmentally harmful projects and pointed to concerns raised by Native American tribes. The measure now heads to the House, where Republican leadership has signaled support.

Lower-profile bills have also been moving through the legislative pipeline. Since the election, about a dozen bills have been sent to the president’s desk, including measures requiring veterans’ benefits to keep pace with inflation and bolstering the fight against child sexual exploitation.

The Senate has also passed bills banning prediction markets from offering bets on war, terrorism, assassination, or individual deaths and ensuring that parents who work for the same employer receive the same amount of family leave as other parents. (Currently, parents who work for different employers are guaranteed 12 weeks of unpaid family and medical leave each, while parents who work for the same employer — including many military families — are only legally guaranteed 12 weeks combined.) The House also passed a long-stalled veterans bill that I covered back in September.

Lawmakers face several year-end deadlines that will force movement on other fronts. Most notably, government funding is set to expire on December 11; some Democrats are pushing the party to spark a shutdown unless they secure language cutting off funding for the war in Iran. Bipartisan negotiations that could choke off war funding have already begun, although it is unclear if President Trump would sign any eventual agreement into law.

Various farm, transportation, and health programs also expire in December; plus, the annual defense policy bill remains unfinished, as do talks over extending a key surveillance authority.

These major packages that have to get out the door before the end of the year are sometimes known as Christmas tree bills, a nod to the season — and the fact that everyone tries to hang their own priorities on them like ornaments. If only a few pieces of legislation are absolutely guaranteed to get a vote before the Congress comes to an end, then oftentimes your best bet is to push for your bill to be added to one of those must-pass bills as an amendment.

This year is no exception, which means a flurry of bipartisan legislating is possible in the next month. Some lawmakers are pushing for child online safety legislation to get tacked on to the defense policy bill. Others want a bipartisan bill capping the cost of insulin at $35 a month to be included with the spending bill. A deal to ban Chinese cars from the U.S. is in the works. So is a bipartisan tax package. It’s also possible that a continuing resolution to extend government funding and the defense bill themselves could be packaged together, creating a massive mega-bill.

President Trump had been hoping to use these final few weeks of Republican control of Congress to bypass Democrats and push through a $350 billion defense spending package, using the party-line reconciliation process one last time. However, Republican lawmakers appear unlikely to bow to his request; several of his more controversial nominees are also facing roadblocks getting confirmed in the last days before Democrats retake the Senate.

No matter the priority, time is running out: both chambers of Congress are on recess all week for Thanksgiving, and they are set to take off the last two weeks of December as well. In total, the House is only set to be in session for 12 more days this year; the Senate is scheduled for 14. (Then again, this can often provide a forcing mechanism of its own: no one wants to be stuck in Washington for Christmas!) Complicating matters further, both chambers were plagued with attendance issues last week: with a record number of members headed for the exits — about 20% of lawmakers will not be returning next Congress, either because of retirement or defeat — many seem to have already checked out.

It’s sort of like a case of senioritis, except with senior citizens instead of high school seniors — and with the entire budget of the U.S. federal government on the line. No biggie.

What does it say about our government that so much crucial policymaking happens in such a mad dash in the last few weeks, when some lawmakers have already been voted out and many are barely even paying attention?

The annual lame-duck session was supposed to be abolished by the 20th Amendment, ratified in 1933, which pushed the first day of Congress up from March to January. Although that still left the potential for a year-end meeting, at the time, it was widely assumed that Congress would simply not convene between November and January, ending lame-duck sessions once and for all.

Instead, senators and congressmen quickly realized that — without those pesky elections to be afraid of — lame-duck sessions could actually be a nifty time to get stuff done.

Lawmakers have given themselves a pay raise during lame-duck sessions. They’ve impeached a president. And installed a new vice president. Many bipartisan efforts have snuck through during lame-duck sessions, often as part of large “omnibus” packages. After the 2010 elections, the outgoing Congress repealed “Don’t Ask Don’t Tell,” approved a bipartisan tax deal, expanded health care benefits for 9/11 first responders, and ratified an arms control treaty with Russia.

The bipartisan First Step Act criminal justice reform deal was passed after the 2018 elections. The aftermath of the 2022 elections saw approval of the Electoral Count Reform Act, Ukraine aid, and the Respect for Marriage Act.

These legislative bonanzas pit two of our most prized American values against each other. From a small-d democratic perspective, it seems pretty strange that members of Congress who have already been ousted by the voters continue to make major policy decisions for two more months. There are many other countries that don’t do this: in the United Kingdom, for example, there’s often a brief “wash-up period” lasting a few days after new elections are called, but then the outgoing parliament is completely dissolved until a new one is chosen. Then, less than a week generally passes between the elections taking place and the new parliament convening.

“I think it is an outrage upon public sentiment and a disgrace to our system that the representatives of a party which has been repudiated at the polls should afterwards defy the will of the people by legislating in accordance with the policy that had been adopted before their repudiation,” one congressman said as far back as 1891, railing against what was then an even lengthier lame-duck session.

However, from a small-r republican perspective — focused less on direct rule by the people, and more on reasoned decisions being made by representatives on their behalf — lame-duck sessions might look a bit more appealing. This is as far from electoral pressure as any members of Congress will ever get: some because they will literally never face the voters again, and others because they won’t have to do so for two more years. Elections are never as far away as they are now. This might allow lawmakers to exercise a bit more of that reasoned judgment, striking deals that might be politically unpopular during the campaign season.

“This is one time in the life of a member of Congress when he can vote his real convictions without the hope of reward or the fear of punishment,” another congressman argued in 1932, battling against the 20th Amendment. “I defy successful contradiction of the statement I am about to make: that some of the best legislation that has ever been passed by any Congress has been passed in the [lame-duck] session, and often when a considerable number of men have been defeated.”

Does this hew to the will of the people? Oftentimes, no. Does a lot get done that might be in their best interest? Oftentimes, yes. Our country was founded on both democratic and republican principles (here, these value systems have nothing to do with the competing political parties that took their names); reasonable minds can differ on how best to strike that balance, and whether the anti-democratic, often-quite-productive lame-duck session falls on the right or wrong side of that line.

According to a 2016 study, members are ever-so-slightly more likely to break with their parties during lame-duck sessions — though they are also much more likely to miss votes entirely.

Since the 20th Amendment shortened the lame-duck session, but failed to end it completely, there have been some attempts to finish the job. In 1970, a Democratic congressman from California proposed a constitutional amendment that would have set the start of a new Congress to be “the Tuesday following the third Monday in November,” two weeks after Election Day. It was never voted on. (For one thing, we would have to count ballots faster: we are now three weeks after Election Day, and a handful of House races remain uncalled.)

More recently, in 2010, then-Rep. Tom Price (R-GA) introduced a resolution that would have barred the House from meeting for a lame-duck session, except to respond to an “unforeseen sudden emergency.” It was voted down.

These proposals deserve consideration. Although new members of Congress need some time to staff up and get ready, they might not need two months — which means those members should arguably be seated sooner, since they (not their predecessors) are the representatives with a democratic mandate from the American people. That said, that would probably prevent some substantive pieces of bipartisan legislation from becoming law. These are the trade-offs of democratic and republican systems of government.

Unless and until the Constitution is amended, the lame-duck session is likely to continue — though perhaps it should be renamed. If around half (or more!) of Congress’ legislative output is being produced in these last two months, maybe it’s really the rest of a two-year term where lawmakers are “lame,” cowering in fear of elections and getting little done.

name: Clean Energy
title: Riding the blue wave: Why corporate advocacy is safe again | Trellis
description:
Clean energy has been decisively reframed in the political conversation, and I’m seeing renewed interest from countless business leaders in constructive policy advocacy.
It also helps them bring the clean energy message home to voters.
With dozens of new lawmakers in both the House and Senate, now is the time to explain why clean energy and a modern grid matter to you.
States are engines of innovation State energy policy is hugely important and ripe for sustainability leaders to maximize their impact.
By explaining how that policy impacts operations, business leaders can help them see the bigger picture.
text:
The opinions expressed here by Trellis expert contributors are their own, not those of Trellis or its editors.

The U.S. midterm election results have provided a defining moment for corporate sustainability leaders. We’ve survived serious headwinds over the past two years — against clean energy projects, climate goals and the very notion that businesses should care about the environment. Now, we have a major tailwind.

Clean energy has been decisively reframed in the political conversation, and I’m seeing renewed interest from countless business leaders in constructive policy advocacy.

Responsible business voices are crucial to making that a reality. We have momentum, majorities and a mandate for change. It is a real chance to curb actions from the current administration and to build a more affordable energy system for businesses across the economy.

Companies should engage with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle and make their individual and collective interests heard. I offer four opportunities below:

Bipartisan permitting reform

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) offers an immediate opportunity for direct engagement on permitting and transmission reform. To quote Tom Steyer, the bill is “the best chance we’ve had to build clean energy at scale.”

The legislation would make important changes to the siting and permitting processes for long-distance transmission lines, making it easier to build the infrastructure we need to transport clean energy around the country. It also includes provisions that would ensure federal permits cannot be arbitrarily revoked once they are issued, which would put a stop to the administration’s ongoing attacks on wind and solar projects.

It’s important that lawmakers pass it before the end of the year because waiting until the next Congress would effectively restart the negotiations. We can’t afford to keep waiting while projects keep getting stuck in bureaucratic and political fights.

Companies have joined Ceres for more than 70 meetings on Capitol Hill this fall to support the bill. More than 80 organizations also joined Ceres and other sustainability advocates in a letter thanking congressional negotiators for their work on the legislation.

We still have some concerns about the bill’s proposed changes to key environmental laws. While the bill has passed the Senate, we anticipate that there will be opportunities to improve its impact and prospects as it moves to the House in the weeks to come.

Meet the new members on Capitol Hill

The 120th Congress will be a more favorable environment to build a robust, clean economy. Nothing beats meeting directly with lawmakers to tell them your individual needs, challenges and vision.

Responsible businesses were key voices when Congress enacted sweeping investments in clean energy, electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure and clean manufacturing in 2021 and 2022. Although many have since been repealed, they still spurred some $185 billion in private investment in clean energy manufacturing, and the vast majority of those projects are still moving forward. More recently, they have helped build bipartisan support for the permitting and transmission provisions in BAAJA, as well as novel trade policies like carbon tariffs that could capitalize on America’s clean manufacturing advantage.

Ceres’ signature annual advocacy day, LEAD on a Clean Economy, is a big opportunity to hit Capitol Hill in person. As always, our goal is to build a bipartisan coalition to pass and enshrine durable policy wins. We’ll be talking to members of Congress about five critical areas:

New clean energy policy and programs using tax credits, federal appropriations and engagement with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

Leveraging data centers to pay for grid upgrades and clean energy deployment

Trade policies that reward clean manufacturing and industrial products

Preserving investors’ ability to consider climate and environmental risk factors as part of their decision-making

Advocating for transportation and domestic battery policy to drive EV adoption

Across hundreds of meetings at our annual advocacy days, by far the most popular person in any congressional office is a business leader operating in that member’s state or district. Lawmakers and their staff love to hear about jobs and opportunities in the places they represent. Telling them about why a particular energy project matters to your operations is the most effective way to direct their attention to the policy issue at hand. It also helps them bring the clean energy message home to voters.

With dozens of new lawmakers in both the House and Senate, now is the time to explain why clean energy and a modern grid matter to you. Joining like-minded companies across sectors to get the message across is both effective and low risk.

States are engines of innovation

State energy policy is hugely important and ripe for sustainability leaders to maximize their impact. Newly elected state legislators will be thrust into complex, parochial debates about the electric grid. By explaining how that policy impacts operations, business leaders can help them see the bigger picture.

Electric transmission is the major opportunity here. It’s the key that unlocks a more affordable grid over the long term. Business leaders can join advocacy efforts at the state level to ensure policymakers know that expanding the transmission system is critical for reliability, affordability and the broader economy. They need to hear from diverse businesses like ski resorts, retailers and manufacturers that increased transmission will benefit all sectors.

More than 25 companies and business organizations have signed a letter asking policymakers to enact commonsense solutions to modernize the electric grid, accelerate clean energy deployment and expand energy efficiency programs. California, Virginia, Illinois and others have made some of these ideas a reality over the past year, and more will follow suit when legislatures convene in 2027.

In Georgia, which just elected new leaders across state government, Ceres is bringing together companies and policymakers for a discussion on electricity load growth and sustainability. We’re partnering with Siemens and Advanced Energy United for a similar event in Pennsylvania featuring the governor’s staff and the chair of a key committee in the legislature. Showing up to events like these is a great first step to having your voice heard.

Support regulatory certainty

Companies need stability and regulatory certainty to invest. They should stand up for it, as EPA seeks to roll back its 2009 Endangerment Finding, which underpins all of the agency’s climate pollution standards. An easy way for companies to get involved is to join the business amicus brief Ceres and EDF are joining in the ongoing lawsuit against EPA’s rollback.

Being a “friend of the court” is a simple way to join a group of peer companies and investors who understand the financial and business risk of climate change and the need for EPA’s authority to address it.

For nearly 20 years, forward-thinking companies have built a movement for responsible businesses to create a more sustainable world. If the last two years have taught us anything, it is that our movement needs supportive public policy and the rule of law.

In the coming months, smart companies will ride new waves of advocacy opportunities and abandon the undertow of despair.
