text:
Ashok Leyland is preparing to introduce new products based on liquefied natural gas (LNG) as part of its alternative-fuel strategy for commercial vehicles, with the company identifying LNG as a viable option for long-haul applications.

Speaking during the company's Q2 FY27 earnings conference call on November 16, 2026, Managing Director and CEO Shenu Agarwal said the company was working across electric, LNG and hydrogen technologies, with different priorities and timelines for each.

Agarwal indicated that Ashok Leyland would provide further details on its LNG product development at its next investor interaction, adding that new products were being prepared for the segment. However, the company did not disclose specific models or a confirmed launch date.

LNG positioned for long-haul applications

Addressing the potential of alternative fuels in heavy-duty commercial vehicles, Agarwal said LNG was a viable option for long-haul transportation, while hydrogen would take longer to develop commercially.

The company expects electric mobility to gain traction earlier, particularly in the light commercial vehicle and bus segments. Adoption in medium and heavy commercial vehicles is expected to take longer, although the company is also preparing electric truck technologies.

Ashok Leyland is pursuing all three technology pathways rather than relying on a single alternative fuel. The company's approach involves developing products and preparing the supporting supply chain in line with the expected adoption timelines for each technology.

Battery manufacturing forms part of EV strategy

As part of its electric mobility investments, Ashok Leyland is establishing a battery pack manufacturing facility at Pillaipakkam near Chennai. The facility has received the necessary approvals, and construction work has commenced.

The first phase is planned with an initial manufacturing capacity of approximately 4 GWh, which is expected to cater to the captive requirements of Ashok Leyland and Switch Mobility. The facility is being designed for potential expansion to 8 GWh or 12 GWh.

Production is expected to commence in Q3 of the next financial year. Management also indicated that battery cell manufacturing could form the second phase of its battery strategy, with a decision on the investment likely to be considered during the next financial year.

Hydrogen development continues

Ashok Leyland is also continuing its work on hydrogen-powered commercial vehicles. Agarwal said the company has the country's largest fleet of hydrogen trucks and has deployed hydrogen-powered buses in partnership with NTPC.

While the company is pursuing hydrogen as a longer-term technology option, its immediate focus remains on electric mobility, particularly in LCVs and buses, alongside preparations for LNG-powered products for long-haul applications.

The multi-fuel strategy reflects the company's approach to addressing different commercial vehicle applications through multiple propulsion technologies rather than adopting a single alternative-fuel pathway.

text:
WASHINGTON — A sweeping permitting bill winding through Congress has divided California Democrats, reigniting a debate over preserving environmental protections versus expediting energy projects.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would shorten the review process for energy projects by overhauling landmark federal environmental legislation, potentially shaving years off the timeline for building new infrastructure.

It would expedite permitting for clean energy like wind and solar, as well as fossil fuel infrastructure and data centers. And it would make it easier to build housing and public transportation, along with upgrading existing power lines and building new ones to allow electricity to flow more freely across state lines.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The Senate passed the bill Thursday evening in a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one independent joining Republicans. It now heads to the House for final approval before the end of year. President Donald Trump signaled he would sign the bill once it reached his desk, calling it in a November social media post a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.”

There is also a lot for Democrats to like.

Rep. Josh Harder, D-Stockton, hailed BAAJA as a long overdue measure to help states like California meet high energy demands and address an affordability crisis by lowering costs for ratepayers.

“This is a huge win for the American people and I’m incredibly excited it’s finally moving,” Harder told the Chronicle.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Other Democrats see the bill as causing more harm than good. BAAJA opponents have painted it as a giveaway to the fossil fuel and AI industries that throws tribes and other marginalized communities under the bus.

The Dem-on-Dem battle is the latest flash point in a years-long clash between environmentalists and followers of the YIMBY-adjacent Abundance movement, which argues that environmental laws have been weaponized to stifle American progress at the expense of workers and consumers.

“The sort of YIMBY-Abundance crowd started out about housing, and I’m all for housing,” said Rep. Jared Huffman, D-San Rafael, who is opposed to the bill. “If this whole YIMBY-Abundance thing is now being hijacked for data centers and refineries and pipelines, then I think there’s a little bit of a distortion there and I think these terms have really kind of ceased to mean much.”

Democrats supporting BAAJA do not deny it has unappealing parts. But they contend it’s their party’s best path forward to cleaner, cheaper energy and upgraded infrastructure nationwide.

Harder chairs the bipartisan Build America Caucus, founded last year amid the Abundance movement to “advance federal pro-growth policies and make it easier to build the things we need in America.” He sees the bill as the best way to level a playing field that finally gives clean energy the chance to compete with fossil fuels.

He said California could be “one of the biggest winners under this bill,” noting that electricity rates have risen “so much faster than many other states” in part because of monopolies like Pacific Gas and Electric. Harder is particularly excited about how the bill would possibly bring relief for consumers via new transmission lines to deliver clean energy from other states to California.

“It’s just almost impossible to build new energy projects across California or to get the transmission across state lines to make sure that California’s energy needs are met by some of the rest of the country,” Harder said. “And so that’s exactly what this bill is intended to fix.”

Supporters of BAAJA, including labor unions, business interests, pro-housing YIMBY groups and clean energy organizations, have focused on its potential to unlock a backlog of renewable energy projects. But several analyses of the original bill anticipate fossil fuels would also benefit.

Even so, the nonpartisan Rhodium Group estimates the bill could lower household electricity bills by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, while reducing cumulative greenhouse emissions by as much as 1.5 gigatons. The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions estimates that wind and solar energy would provide up to 40% of electricity by 2035 under the bill, while natural gas would lower to about 36%. Residential utility bills could fall by $2.5 billion, it noted.

“Clearly this is a bill about hopefully improving a broken system,” Tom Steyer, the billionaire climate philanthropist, told the Chronicle about why he’s supporting BAAJA. “It’s not like we are trying to change something that is working fine. We are trying to revive a system that is effectively broken and make it possible to get things done and bring down costs.”

Opponents want Democrats to wait until the new Congress begins in January, when their party will take control of both chambers and have the chance to negotiate a new measure and address outstanding concerns.

“It’s just really kind of mind-boggling to see so many Democrats right now, on the eve of claiming all this power, wanting to unilaterally give it to Donald Trump,” Huffman said.

Critics have accused Huffman and other opponents in recent weeks of NIMBY idealism that could ultimately tank a long-overdue, bipartisan bill that took years to negotiate.

Huffman chalked up those charges as an “empty trope” by the “oil and gas folks and the Big Tech bros and the Trump administration” to push Democrats into a bad deal.

“There are things in this bill that Donald Trump and Big Tech and the oil and gas industry and the mining industry desperately want,” Huffman said. “I mean, not just a little bit, but a lot. They really want these things.”

Environmentalists opposed to the bill say there is a long list of issues that make it a nonstarter. Chief among them is tribal concerns with how the bill would change the National Historic Preservation Act and therefore weaken their consultation rights over construction in sacred places, including burial sites or religious monuments.

That provision is part of why California Sens. Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff voted against the bill on Thursday, after unsuccessfully pushing to strike those changes from the measure.

“I strongly believe we need permitting reform and to build new infrastructure quickly and efficiently,” Schiff said in a statement. “But I also believe that this can be done in a way that does not needlessly degrade clean water, endanger wildlife or disrespect tribal nations.”

Padilla similarly said he supported “commonsense permitting reform,” but that he could not vote to “sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.”

Environmentalists are also worried about a “project certainty” provision that could make it harder for future administrations to revoke approved permits, including for unlawful fossil fuel projects in states like California.

“Any decisions happening under this administration, which has a very specific agenda related to public lands, will be locked in for generations,” said Helen O’Shea, the California state director for The Wilderness Society. “Instead of moving forward with California’s clean energy future, it’s going to lock in really backwards-facing infrastructure.”

Padilla pointed out in his statement that Trump recently said he would not approve any wind projects, raising concerns that the bill “lacks the enforceable safeguards to ensure renewable energy projects will be judged and approved fairly by the Trump administration and that oil and gas drilling will not resume off the coast of California.”

Supporters see that portion of the bill as a way to protect projects from what they described as political retaliation by Trump, who has led a crusade against renewable energy projects during his second term in office. They say that while Trump may disproportionately favor fossil fuel projects, it’s more likely that future presidents prioritize clean energy, including wind farms, both for their business and climate benefits.

“I think if you’re a Democrat who doesn’t like Trump’s war against clean energy, then the best thing to do is pass this bill and make sure that we have legal protections for those projects,” said Harder, who noted the Trump administration canceled funding for a hydrogen project in his district last year.

Democrats backing BAAJA say it would be foolish to bank on a better deal in the new year. Even with their majorities, it’s likely they will need Republicans to pass a new package. And it’s unlikely Trump would approve a bill without Republican support, they argue, which could mean waiting another three years — if a Democrat wins in 2028 — to get something signed.

In his statement, Schiff said it was his hope that the bill would be considered in the new Congress, and that Democrats can use their majority to “pass a more balanced work product.”

Proponents say that’s not an option.

Rep. Scott Peters, D-San Diego, said he knows BAAJA is flawed. But he also sees it as Democrats’ best chance to act on their newfound power and respond to what they’ve described as a mandate by voters in the Nov. 3 election to get things done in Congress and make their lives better.

“I don’t think there is going to be a better deal,” he said. “We have to recognize that even after next year, we need Republicans.”

In the meantime, Peters said, climate change is only becoming more of an emergency.

“You have to make compromises to do something as big as this,” he said. “It sure as hell beats the status quo.”

text:
Lithium-ion batteries, like those found in cars, cell phones and cameras, often have anodes made of graphite. During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite anode. How quickly they can move through the graphite is one of the key factors limiting how fast a battery can charge. James Tour’s lab at Rice University has recently developed a new kind of synthetic graphite, one that supports much faster charging and can be produced in a fraction of a second.

“This method could help make future electric vehicle batteries charge faster while reducing the cost and environmental impact of battery manufacturing,” said Tour, the T.T. and W.F. Chao Professor of Chemistry and corresponding author on this study. “Our analysis suggests it could reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions by more than 80% compared with conventional graphite production.”

The study, recently published in Advanced Materials, describes a method that uses a small amount of a nickel compound and an extremely short, powerful electrical pulse. The nickel compound is added to petroleum coke, a low-cost carbon residue from oil refining. A single electrical pulse then briefly heats the mixture to about 2,500 C, triggering its rapid transformation into graphite — the same form of carbon found in pencil leads. But in this case, the process produces highly ordered, low-defect graphite with promising properties for fast-charging battery anodes.

Graphite is a two-dimensional material, meaning that it is created from layers of horizontal structures only one atom thick stacked on top of each other. In graphite, each layer is comprised of carbon atoms neatly ordered into hexagons. When the research team added a little bit of nickel compound to the petroleum coke, the carbon atoms were able to quickly organize around the tiny nickel particles.

“The nickel acts almost like a temporary construction worker, helping the carbon atoms organize themselves into a highly ordered, layered graphite structure,” said Haojie Zhu, postdoctoral associate and first author of the paper. “Usually, creating graphite requires prolonged heating at extremely high temperatures for long periods, but this method allows us to do it in just two-tenths of a second.”

The nickel slightly expanded the interlayer spacing in the graphite, providing greater access for subsequent lithium entry during charging. When the team tested this nickel-formed graphite on a lithium-ion battery, they found it significantly outperformed conventional graphite for charging, tolerating a rate equivalent to a four-minute charging time. And it retained 80% of its capacity after 1,000 charge and discharge cycles, where the battery was fully drained and then charged up again.

“This method addresses two major challenges simultaneously: improving battery fast-charging performance and simplifying the production of a key battery material,” Tour said. “Imagine charging your battery in four minutes.”

The team found that the benefits of nickel-assisted graphite production remained even after more than 99% of the residual nickel was removed. This suggests that the main advantage comes from how nickel helps build the graphite structure rather than simply from nickel remaining in the material.

Surprisingly, more heat did not necessarily mean better graphite: At excessively high temperatures, much of the nickel was lost, while lower temperatures resulted in less ordered graphite.

“We identified the Goldilocks region for graphite preparation,” Tour said.

“What I find especially exciting is that a process lasting just 0.2 seconds can produce graphite with such impressive fast-charging performance,” Zhu said. “Making better materials is not always about using more energy or processing them for longer but about applying the right conditions at exactly the right moment.”

This work was funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (FA9550-22-1-0526), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, ERDC (W912HZ-21-2-0050, W912HZ-24-2-0027), the Department of Energy NERSC award (BES-ERCAP0027822, B.I.Y.) and the Welch Foundation (C-2065).

title: One Year After OBBBA: What The New Energy Incentive Landscape Means For Investment Strategy
description:
A year after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) reshaped the federal energy incentive landscape, businesses have a clearer view of which opportunities have narrowed, which remain available and which have become more significant.
For companies investing in energy infrastructure, manufacturing, carbon capture, hydrogen, clean fuels or renewable energy, these changes can influence project timing, sourcing decisions and overall economics.
Energy efficiency credits such as Sections 179D and 45L were set to expire, along with wind energy manufacturing credits.
Looking Ahead As businesses plan for 2027 and beyond, the energy incentive landscape continues to present both new considerations and meaningful opportunities.
Considering an energy, manufacturing, carbon capture, hydrogen or clean fuel investment?
text:
A year after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) reshaped the federal energy incentive landscape, businesses have a clearer view of which opportunities have narrowed, which remain available and which have become more significant.

For companies investing in energy infrastructure, manufacturing, carbon capture, hydrogen, clean fuels or renewable energy, these changes can influence project timing, sourcing decisions and overall economics.

The opportunity now is to understand where the current incentive environment intersects with investments already underway or being planned for 2027 and beyond.

Some Incentive Windows Have Narrowed

Several provisions were reduced, restricted or accelerated under OBBBA.

Energy efficiency credits such as Sections 179D and 45L were set to expire, along with wind energy manufacturing credits. Wind turbine manufacturers that expected to rely on Section 45X credits into the 2030s have had to adjust to a different incentive environment. The impact has been significant, with 54 GW of wind energy projects reportedly cancelled since OBBBA was enacted.

Solar energy remains credit eligible through 2030, although Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) requirements introduce additional supply chain considerations.

Large manufacturers have reported that the sale of 45X credits accounts for more than 25 percent of their revenue, even under the new restrictions. At the same time, solar manufacturing has continued to expand, albeit at a more moderate pace.

Renewable energy purchasers have also been affected. Section 48 was replaced by Section 48E, narrowing the window for certain wind and solar projects.

Solar and wind projects that either begin construction by July 4, 2026, or are placed in service by the end of 2026 may still have an opportunity to claim 30 percent of project costs as a direct credit.

For businesses with projects already in development, these timelines may influence sequencing, procurement and investment decisions.

Eligibility Is More Closely Connected to Operations

The new PFE requirements also demonstrate how closely tax incentives can intersect with operating decisions.

Supplier relationships, component origin, manufacturing structure, sourcing strategy and project design may all influence eligibility for certain incentives.

As a result, the analysis often extends beyond the tax function. Procurement, operations, finance and technical teams may each contribute information that helps determine whether a project is positioned to benefit from an available incentive.

For business leaders, this creates an opportunity to view tax incentives within the broader context of how projects are structured and executed.

Some Technologies Emerged in a Stronger Position

Sections 45Q, 45V and 45Z, covering carbon capture, hydrogen production and clean fuel production, were preserved or enhanced.

These incentives can also interact in ways that influence project economics. Carbon capture can improve the carbon intensity of hydrogen and biofuel production, while hydrogen itself is often used as a feedstock for next-generation biofuels.

Section 45V continues to carry a credit value of up to $3.00 per kilogram for the first 10 years of operation, with a placed-in-service deadline of December 31, 2027.

Section 45Q remains an important component of the economics surrounding carbon capture.

Section 45Z emerged in a particularly strong position. Induced Land Use Change (ILUC) was removed from the carbon score for ethanol plants, meaning that virtually all domestically produced ethanol now qualifies. Earlier this year, the IRS published regulations for Section 45Z, providing additional clarity around the credit.

With values of up to $1.00 per gallon of gasoline equivalent, Section 45Z remains a significant consideration for biofuel producers.

Four Questions Leadership May Want to Consider

As organizations plan for 2027, a few practical questions can help frame the conversation.

1. Which planned investments are time-sensitive?

Some incentives now operate within shorter construction or placed-in-service windows. Understanding those timelines can help leadership assess project sequencing and planning considerations.

2. Could sourcing or project structure affect eligibility?

PFE requirements illustrate how supplier selection, component origin, manufacturing location and project design may influence certain incentives.

3. Could more than one incentive affect the same investment?

Carbon capture, hydrogen and clean fuel projects demonstrate how multiple credits may interact within the same operating model.

4. Would earlier visibility improve the planning process?

Understanding available incentives before major project decisions are finalized can provide leadership with a more complete view of potential project economics.

What This Means for Business Strategy

The post-OBBBA environment is more selective.

Some opportunities have narrowed, while others remain significant or have become more favorable. For business leaders, the value lies in understanding which current or planned investments may be materially affected by the incentives that remain.

That could mean evaluating a project against an approaching deadline, reviewing supply chain considerations or understanding how multiple credits may influence the same investment.

The objective is not to build business strategy around tax incentives. It is to ensure that potentially meaningful incentives are considered alongside the broader investment case.

Looking Ahead

As businesses plan for 2027 and beyond, the energy incentive landscape continues to present both new considerations and meaningful opportunities.

Working collaboratively with leadership, finance, tax and technical functions to assess eligibility, timing, technical requirements and how multiple incentives may interact within the same investment.

text:
The North Wales Clean Energy Fund, led by Ambition North Wales and designed to support green energy projects across the region, has agreed to a $2 million investment for tidal energy developer HydroWing Ltd. The investment will support the construction and installation of a tidal turbine scheme at Menter Môn Morlais, the largest consented tidal stream energy scheme in Europe, situated off the coast of Anglesey.

With the first devices expected to be deployed in 2027, the funding brings Morlais a step closer to generating clean electricity, marking a significant step forward for the scheme. The HydroWing project will be Wales’ first and largest consented tidal stream energy project.

Richard Parkinson, CEO of HydroWing, the tidal energy division of Inyanga Marine Energy Group, said: “Securing this funding from Ambition North Wales is a major milestone, enabling us to deploy our first HydroWing tidal energy device at Morlais in 2027. This investment lays the foundation for our planned 30MW commercial development and our ambition to establish Wales as a global center for tidal energy technology and manufacturing, creating highly skilled jobs, strengthening the Welsh supply chain and opening up significant international export opportunities.”

Cllr Gary Pritchard, Ambition North Wales Lead Member for Low Carbon Energy and Leader of Ynys Môn Council, said: “Our Clean Energy Fund is going from strength to strength and I am delighted that it has been possible to support HydroWing to further progress Morlais, marking another important milestone for the North Wales low-carbon economy. Ambition North Wales has already supported Morlais through the North Wales Growth Deal’s Cydnerth project to strengthen the local grid infrastructure. So, to build on that is fantastic.”

John Idris Jones, Chair of Menter Môn Morlais Ltd, added: “This investment is an important contribution in order to bring HydroWing’s technology into operation at Morlais and demonstrates the value of partnership in developing the tidal energy sector. Morlais already has the infrastructure in place to support tidal energy devices, and projects like this will help turn that potential into clean electricity, skilled jobs and opportunities for communities and businesses across North Wales.”

Adam Price, Welsh Government Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, said: “If we’re serious about raising productivity and growing the Welsh economy, we need to back sectors where Wales can genuinely lead. With some of the best tidal energy resources in the world, Wales is well placed to play a leading role in this growing industry, and this investment will help bring that ambition closer to reality. Working alongside the UK Government through the North Wales Growth Deal, we’re investing in projects that create new opportunities and support long-term economic growth across North Wales.”

Anna McMorrin MP, Wales Office Minister in the UK Government, said: “This $2 million investment brings clean tidal power off Ynys Môn a step closer. The UK Government is backing North Wales’s clean energy sector through the Growth Deal, creating skilled, well-paid jobs and growing the local economy.”

The North Wales Clean Energy Fund forms part of the North Wales Growth Deal, which is backed by the Welsh Government and the UK Government and delivered by Ambition North Wales.

Louisiana Will Pay You $6 for Every Nutria Tail You Bring In

If you've spent any time around the bayous, marshes, and waterways of South Louisiana, chances are you've spotted a nutria or two...or 12.

But Louisiana isn't exactly interested in making friends with these furry little troublemakers. In fact, the State is willing to pay you $6 for every qualifying nutria tail you bring in this season.

The annual program is back for the 2026-2027 season, and its mission is to protect Louisiana's coastal wetlands from an animal that causes some serious environmental damage.

Louisiana's Nutria Control Program Is Back for 2026-2027

The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries has opened another season of its Coastwide Nutria Control Program.

The program officially runs from November 20, 2026, through March 31, 2027. Registered participants can collect $6 for every qualifying nutria tail they turn in at an approved LDWF collection location.

READ MORE: Beneficial Reasons Why Louisiana Should Be Eating Nutria

Louisiana's goal is to remove as many as 400,000 nutria during the season.

That might sound like a whole lot of rodents, but Louisiana has a pretty big problem to deal with.

Why Does Louisiana Pay People to Catch Nutria?

Nutria are an invasive species that can cause considerable damage to coastal marshes.

Originally brought to Louisiana for the fur industry during the 1930s, nutria eventually spread throughout the state's coastal wetlands.

The problem is their appetite.

Nutria feed on marsh vegetation, often eating plants down to their roots. Those roots are important because they help hold marsh soil together.

READ MORE: Louisiana Couple Cooks Fresh Nutria Over Rice for YouTuber

When nutria destroy the vegetation, the exposed soil becomes more vulnerable to erosion. Over time, that damage can contribute to the loss of valuable coastal wetlands.

Louisiana's marshes provide important habitat for wildlife, support fisheries, and help protect communities from storm surge and coastal erosion. Keeping those wetlands healthy is an important part of protecting South Louisiana.

How Do You Qualify for the $6 Nutria Bounty?

This is probably the Louisiana way to earn extra money this Holiday Season, and we're here for it, Just don't forget that you'll need to follow the program's rules before turning those tails into cash!

Participants must have a valid Louisiana trapping license and complete the Coastwide Nutria Control Program application.

They must also identify the property where they intend to trap or harvest nutria. Those planning to use private property need the landowner's information and permission.

Only nutria harvested from approved properties within the program's designated boundaries qualify.

Participants must bring their qualifying tails to designated collection locations and follow the program's submission requirements.

ou can find program details, applications, and additional information through the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries at wlf.louisiana.gov/page/nutria.

text:
Bentley's 2025 UK operational carbon-neutrality declaration independently verified by LRQA against ISO 14068-1:2023

Crewe site amongst the early adopters of ISO 14068-1 within the automotive sector

Latest milestone complemented by renewed ISO 14001 and ISO 50001 certifications

Amongst the first UK drone-lifted rooftop solar installation

New 2.8MW solar installation spans four rooftops at Bentley’s new Paint Shop

2,030 panels lifted into position, with drone technology more than halving installation time, bringing the total to over 35,000

(Crewe, 23 November 2026) Bentley Motors has marked two significant milestones in the continued development of its Crewe manufacturing operations: achieving independent verification of the carbon neutrality of its UK operations and being amongst the first to use heavy-lift cargo drone technology, for onshore rooftop construction logistics, to support the installation of rooftop solar panels at an automotive manufacturing site.

Together, the achievements combine independently assessed environmental standards with practical innovation at Bentley’s Crewe campus. ISO 14068-1 verification provides external assurance of Bentley’s carbon neutrality declaration for its UK operations during 2025, complemented by renewed ISO 14001 and ISO 50001 certifications, while a new 2.8MW rooftop solar installation demonstrates another innovative approach to expanding renewable energy infrastructure at the site.

Andreas Lehe, Member of the Board for Manufacturing at Bentley Motors, said:

“These achievements reflect the continued evolution of our manufacturing operations in Crewe. Independent certification recognises the progress we are making in reducing our operational impact, while innovations such as cargo drones demonstrate how we are finding safer, smarter and more efficient ways to expand our renewable energy infrastructure. Our focus remains firmly on what comes next, embracing new technologies and ideas as we continue to transform our manufacturing site, supporting Bentley’s longer-term decarbonisation ambition.”

Bentley’s UK operations have been independently verified by LRQA in accordance with ISO 14068-1:2023 Climate Change Management – Transition to Net Zero – Part 1: Carbon Neutrality for the 2025 calendar year. The achievement is among the early adopters within the automotive sector, providing external assurance, assessed against internationally recognised requirements.

ISO 14068-1 is the standard for demonstrating carbon neutrality. It specifies principles, requirements and guidance relating to achieving and demonstrating carbon neutrality in a credible, transparent and consistent way.

Importantly, the standard prioritises reducing emissions and enhancing carbon removals within an organisation's value chain, with offsetting used to address the remaining carbon footprint rather than as a substitute for emissions reduction.

The verification applies to Bentley’s main campus in Crewe, associated UK operations in the Chesire region, and follows the company’s transition from PAS 2060, against which Bentley first achieved certification in 2018. The standard requires applicable Scope 1, Scope 2 and relevant Scope 3 emissions within the defined operational boundary to be quantified and reported.

Bentley recorded market-based residual emissions of 9,326 tonnes CO₂e for the 2025 reporting period and 9,326 Verified Emissions Reductions Carbon Offset Credits were retired to address these emissions.

Alongside its market-based emissions, Bentley reduced its directly comparable Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from 17,482 tonnes CO₂e in 2018 to 1,907 tonnes in 2025, an absolute reduction of 89 per cent.

The verification is complemented by Bentley’s renewed certification to ISO 14001:2015 for environmental management and ISO 50001:2018 for energy management. The recertification applies across Bentley’s Pyms Lane headquarters and Orion Park operations in Crewe, with both standards certified until October 2029.

Alongside the certification milestone, Bentley has supported a pioneering new approach to renewable-energy infrastructure at its Crewe campus. Cargo drones have been used to lift solar panels into position as part of an automotive manufacturing-site installation, providing a faster and lower-impact alternative to conventional lifting equipment.

Delivered by Push Power Limited in partnership with Finlight, the 2.8 MW rooftop installation covers four rooftops and comprises 515-watt JA Solar panels. A total of 2,030 panels were lifted to roof level, bringing the site total lto over 35,000, using XAG P150 Max cargo drones, with each panel weighing approximately 30 kg.

The drones positioned approximately one panel per minute, enabling the rooftop lifting activity to be completed in just over one week. By lifting the panels individually rather than transporting them in large pallets, the approach also reduced loading risk to the new Paint Shop roof.

The use of cargo drones more than halved the installation time compared with the conventional approach, allowing a direct decant to each installation position. It also reduced manual handling, created a safer working environment for installation teams and removed the need for fuel-powered telehandlers to move panels to roof level, reducing construction-vehicle emissions during this stage of the project.

Andy Khan, Managing Director of Push Power Limited, said:

“At Push Power, we’re always looking for innovative solutions to optimise and streamline our technical operations. Devising this new technique of using cargo drones as a faster, safer, cleaner and more efficient way to position rooftop PV panels, we were eager to implement this at the Bentley Motors site, and we’re very satisfied with the results.

“Together with the Government’s pledge to tackle National Grid reform, and the speed at which solar panels can now be installed using drone technology, we’re optimistic that the UK’s potential for reaching Net Zero is accelerating.”

The new solar array adds to Bentley’s established renewable-energy infrastructure and demonstrates how innovation in construction methods can support the expansion of on-site renewable electricity generation at Bentley's Crewe operations.

Together, these achievements mark another step in Bentley’s transformation of Crewe, where innovation and renewable energy continue to drive measurable environmental progress.

text:
ZANZIBAR has invited investors in the mining sector to explore opportunities in heavy mineral sands following geological mapping that identified mineral deposits across Unguja and Pemba, opening up prospects for investment in resources used in advanced technologies and electronics manufacturing.

Othman Masoud Othman, Zanzibar’s First Vice-President of Zanzibar said the geological mapping exercise, conducted by the Geological Survey of Tanzania (GST) in collaboration with Zanzibar's Ministry responsible for water, energy and minerals, had produced geological maps showing different rock formations and mineral deposits across the islands.

He said the findings presented opportunities for further exploration and investment, particularly in heavy mineral sands, which are important raw materials for aerospace technologies and electronic equipment.

Speaking during the closure of the Seventh Tanzania International Mining and Investment Conference, Othman urged mining stakeholders to visit Zanzibar and explore opportunities in mineral exploration and the development of related industries.

He said the discovery of mineral resources should be accompanied by investment in local processing facilities to ensure that Tanzania captured greater economic value instead of continuing to export raw materials.

Othman said Tanzania was endowed with several strategic minerals, including graphite, nickel, copper, rare earth elements, niobium, gold, tanzanite, diamonds and rubies, which could support industrial development if properly exploited and processed.

He called for the establishment of industries capable of transforming minerals into finished products, citing battery manufacturing for electric vehicles and equipment for storing electricity generated from renewable energy sources as important investment opportunities.

He said developing such industries locally would generate greater economic returns than exporting unprocessed minerals, while creating employment opportunities and facilitating technology and skills transfer to Tanzanians.

The First Vice-President also highlighted the challenges facing small-scale miners, particularly limited access to modern technology for mineral extraction, processing and environmental management.

He said providing miners with appropriate technology, capital and geological information could significantly improve productivity, increase their incomes and strengthen the mining sector.

He urged the State Mining Corporation (STAMICO) and the Geological Survey of Tanzania to continue supporting small-scale miners through geological exploration and drilling services to reduce speculative mining and improve knowledge of mineral deposits.

Othman further called for stronger cooperation between governments and the private sector to address challenges facing mineral value addition in Tanzania and across Africa.

He said the government would carefully consider recommendations and resolutions arising from the conference, with the objective of improving the investment environment and increasing the mining sector's contribution to employment and the national economy.

The conference, held under the theme, “Value-Added Minerals as a Catalyst for Industrialisation and Economic Growth”, discussed 10 papers covering mineral processing challenges, access to capital, human resource development, legal and regulatory frameworks, and environmental protection amid the global transition to clean energy.

Othman also urged investors to consider establishing mineral-processing industries within the country, saying stronger domestic industrial capacity would benefit the national economy and support private-sector growth.

He thanked participants for attending the three-day meeting and officially declared the Seventh Tanzania International Mining and Investment Conference closed.

By EVWorld.com AI Editorial Team

When COP31 ended in Antalya without a consensus climate agreement, headlines understandably focused on what was missing: no agreed language on moving away from fossil fuels, no breakthrough on climate finance, and no overarching deal acceptable to both developed and developing nations.

For Asia, however, the more important story may not be what happened inside the negotiating halls, but what continues to happen outside them.

The Limits of Climate Diplomacy

The collapse of COP31 underscored a growing reality in global climate politics. The annual COP framework remains politically important and symbolically powerful, but increasingly struggles to reconcile the competing interests of oil exporters, industrial powers, developing economies, and climate-vulnerable nations.

For developing Asia, climate finance remains the central fault line. Countries across Southeast Asia, South Asia, and the Pacific face escalating costs from extreme weather, sea-level rise, heat waves, and agricultural disruption. Many arrived at COP31 hoping for stronger commitments to adaptation funding and support for clean-energy deployment.

Those expectations largely went unmet.

The result leaves unresolved questions about who will pay for both climate resilience and the transition to lower-carbon energy systems across some of the world's fastest-growing economies.

Electrification Moves Ahead Anyway

Yet diplomatic failure should not be mistaken for a loss of momentum.

Across Asia, investments in renewable energy, battery storage, electric transportation, and grid infrastructure continue expanding. Governments are increasingly viewing electrification not merely as climate policy but as economic and industrial strategy.

China remains the dominant force in global solar manufacturing, battery production, and electric vehicle exports. India is rapidly expanding domestic clean-energy supply chains. Indonesia hopes to leverage its vast nickel resources into a battery-manufacturing hub. Vietnam and the Philippines continue attracting investment in solar generation, energy storage, and grid modernization.

These developments are being driven by market realities as much as emissions goals.

Climate Policy Is Becoming Industrial Policy

The most important shift may be conceptual. Climate action is increasingly being folded into national industrial policy.

Governments are pursuing electrification because it creates jobs, reduces fuel imports, improves energy security, and strengthens economic competitiveness. Electric vehicles, batteries, and renewable energy technologies are now strategic industries, not simply environmental initiatives.

This evolution means progress is becoming less dependent on the outcome of annual climate summits.

The Financing Challenge Remains

The greatest risk highlighted by COP31 is not a slowdown in technology deployment but a shortage of capital where it is needed most. Developing nations still require significant investment to strengthen electrical grids, build resilient infrastructure, and adapt to worsening climate impacts.

Without stronger financial support mechanisms, some countries could find themselves trapped between rising energy demand and growing climate vulnerability.

The Center of Gravity Has Shifted

COP31 will likely be remembered as a summit that failed to produce consensus. But history may ultimately judge it differently.

The conference exposed a reality that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: the future of decarbonization is being determined less by diplomatic communiques and more by factories, transmission lines, battery plants, renewable power projects, and electric vehicle assembly lines.

The negotiations stalled. Asia's energy transition did not.

text:
The American Public Power Association and the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association recently sent a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in which the groups urged House passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) before the end of the 119th Congress.

“This legislation presents an important opportunity to reform the federal environmental permitting process, increasing reliability and reducing costs for electric utilities and the people they serve,” the letter noted.

APPA is urging its members to contact their representatives to ask them to support BAAJA.

The Senate passed the legislation on Nov. 19. The House returns on November 30 and is scheduled to recess for the year on December 18, leaving a very small window to consider and pass BAAJA before the 119th Congress ends.

“BAAJA represents a meaningful and balanced effort to improve the efficiency and predictability of federal permitting while preserving necessary environmental protections and opportunities for public engagement,” wrote Scott Corwin, President and CEO of APPA, and Jim Matheson, CEO of NRECA, in the letter.

“The bill includes common-sense reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), including greater clarity regarding agency responsibilities, more predictable review timelines, and a timelier framework for judicial review,” the letter noted.

“The legislation also contains important improvements to Clean Water Act permitting, Endangered Species Act consultation, and National Historic Preservation Act reviews to promote better interagency coordination, reduce duplicative requirements, and establish clearer timelines for decision-making. These changes will help our members more efficiently construct, maintain, and modernize the infrastructure necessary to deliver reliable and affordable electric service,” wrote Corwin and Matheson.

The letter said that expanding and strengthening the nation's transmission system “will also be critical to meeting future electricity needs and supporting our country’s economic growth. The Senate-passed legislation finds the right balance of facilitating the construction of new transmission infrastructure while recognizing the essential role of local governance and accountability built into our not-for-profit business models without adding new, burdensome Federal Energy Regulatory Commission regulation over electric cooperatives and public power utilities.”

text:
MUSCAT, NOV 23

US technology company Tesla has applied for trademark protection in Oman for its Tesla Terafab brand, covering semiconductor technology, as the Sultanate of Oman prepares to expand battery storage capacity to support its growing renewable energy sector.

The application, published in the Official Gazette on November 15, comes as Tesla seeks to protect its technology brands in international markets. Although the filing does not establish plans for investment in Oman, it coincides with growing demand for batteries, power conversion equipment and related technologies in the country's electricity sector.

Tesla filed the application on September 29, 2026, under number 202343. It covers integrated circuits, semiconductor chips, microchips, memory chips and related components. The notice identifies Tesla, Inc., headquartered in Austin, Texas, as the applicant, represented locally by Alyafi Intellectual Property.

Best known for its electric vehicles, Tesla also operates a major energy storage business. Its Megapack systems store electricity on a large scale, helping power networks manage fluctuations in supply and demand.

Separate notices in Oman's Official Gazette list the Megapack, Megablock and Powercore trademarks, covering battery storage equipment, power conversion systems, electronic controls and related services. Tesla has also applied to protect Megapack and Megablock internationally, although ownership of the corresponding Omani applications has not been independently confirmed.

The filings come as Oman moves beyond developing solar and wind farms towards building the storage infrastructure needed to make greater use of renewable electricity.

A notable example is the Ibri III project in Al Dhahirah Governorate, which will combine a 500-megawatt solar power plant with a battery energy storage system capable of storing 100 megawatt-hours of electricity. The project, estimated to cost around $300 million, reached financial close in January 2026.

It is being developed by a consortium led by Abu Dhabi's Masdar, alongside Al Khadra Partners, Korea Midland Power and OQ Alternative Energy. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2027.

Oman's battery storage ambitions extend well beyond Ibri III. Nama Power and Water Procurement Company is pursuing five standalone battery storage facilities with a combined power capacity of 950 megawatts and storage capacity of 3,800 megawatt-hours, according to an October report by industry publication MEED.

The largest proposed facility is in Suhar, with a planned capacity of 500 megawatts. Other locations include Al Mabellah in Muscat Governorate, Ayjah and Jalan Bani Bu Ali in South Al Sharqiyah, and Sadah in Dhofar.

Earlier this month, Nama Holding, a subsidiary of Oman Investment Authority, also signed a framework agreement with China's State Grid International Development for two battery storage projects in Duqm and Ibri.

The proposed facilities would have a combined capacity of 1,000 megawatts, representing an estimated investment of RO 384.5 million. The agreement establishes a framework for their development, although it does not confirm that construction has commenced or that the full investment has been committed.

These projects, currently at various stages of planning, procurement and development, underscore Oman's efforts to strengthen its electricity infrastructure in preparation for a significantly greater contribution from renewable energy sources.

The Sultanate aims to generate 30 per cent of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030, supported by major investments in utility-scale solar and wind power projects.

Unlike conventional power plants, solar and wind facilities depend on weather conditions. Battery energy storage systems can store surplus electricity when generation exceeds immediate demand and release it when required, helping stabilise the grid and maintain reliable power supplies as renewable capacity expands.

text:
What it is and who runs it

The regulation designated as 2 CFR Part 910 bears the formal title Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards. Promulgated under the authority of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 as amended, the Department of Energy Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7101 et seq.), and the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPACT 2005), 2 CFR 910 gives regulatory effect to OMB guidance while reinstating specialized rules previously housed under 10 CFR Part 600.

The system is administered by the United States Department of Energy through its Office of Management, specifically overseen by senior procurement executives, financial assistance policy divisions, and designated Contracting Officers across headquarters secretariats, field operating offices, and operations centers such as the Golden Field Office and the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL). Program offices issuing awards subject to 2 CFR 910 include the Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE), the Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED), and the Office of Science.

A core foundation of federal grant law is the legal distinction between acquisition contracts and financial assistance agreements. While procurement contracts are governed by the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) at 48 CFR Chapter 1 to acquire goods or services for the direct benefit of the government, financial assistance awards under 2 CFR 910 transfer funds or property to accomplish a public purpose of support or stimulation. Under 2 CFR 910.127, financial assistance agreements establish legally binding reciprocal obligations. Contracting Officers possess exclusive legal authority to obligate federal funds, approve deviations under 2 CFR 910.133, and adjudicate disputes pursuant to 2 CFR 910.128.

Eligibility rules and covered entities

The primary innovation of 2 CFR 910 lies in its explicit expansion of entity eligibility. Under standard Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR 200.1, the definition of a non-Federal entity is restricted to state governments, local governments, Indian tribes, institutions of higher education (IHE), and non-profit organizations. In contrast, 2 CFR 910.122 and 2 CFR 910.350 formally expand the definition of a non-Federal entity for DOE financial assistance to include for-profit organizations.

Under 2 CFR 910.122(b), a for-profit organization is defined as any entity that distributes any profit not reinvested into the business as profit or dividends to its employees or shareholders. This expansion ensures commercial technology developers, early-stage clean energy startups, corporate joint ventures, and manufacturing corporations can serve as direct prime recipients or subrecipients of DOE federal grants and cooperative agreements without ad-hoc legislative exemptions.

Eligibility to receive a DOE financial assistance award is established through specific Funding Opportunity Announcements (FOAs). Under 2 CFR 910.124, eligibility determinations must conform to statutory authorities and competitive merit review procedures outlined in 2 CFR 910.126. Key entity categories regulated under 2 CFR 910 include:

Domestic Commercial Entities: For-profit corporations, LLCs, and partnerships subject to Subpart D post-award rules, commercial cost principles, and Subpart F audit requirements.

Higher Education and Research Institutions: Universities and non-profit laboratories subject to 2 CFR 200 and DOE-specific cost sharing and patent rules under 2 CFR 910 Subpart B.

State, Local, and Tribal Governments: Public entities funded for regional energy resilience, state energy programs, or public infrastructure demonstrations.

Foreign Entities: Organizations outside the United States requiring a formal foreign entity waiver from the Contracting Officer prior to award execution.

Consortia and Teaming Arrangements: Multi-entity structures where a prime recipient manages partners subject to subrecipient monitoring checklist obligations.

Applicants must satisfy pre-award criteria established under 2 CFR 200 Subpart C pre-award requirements, including active registration in SAM.gov and financial risk reviews conducted prior to selection.

What it funds or requires

To accommodate technology development and commercial scaling, 2 CFR 910 introduces specialized post-award requirements diverging from baseline federal grant standards across four operational domains: statutory cost sharing, commercial cost principles, property encumbrances, and governance controls.

Statutory cost sharing under EPACT 2005 (2 CFR 910.130)

Unlike civilian agencies where cost sharing is discretionary unless specified by program statute, DOE financial assistance for research, development, demonstration, and commercial application is subject to mandatory statutory cost sharing enacted under Section 988 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. Codified at 2 CFR 910.130, these baselines establish strict financial ratios:

Research and Development (R and D): Requires a non-Federal cost share of at least 20 percent of total allowable project costs. Basic research may be excluded only upon formal determination by an Under Secretary.

Demonstration and Commercial Application: Requires a non-Federal cost share of at least 50 percent of total allowable project costs. Reductions require Secretarial approval evaluating technological risk.

Exempt Programs: Awards under the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs are statutorily exempt pursuant to 2 CFR 910.130(a)(1).

Recipients must provide non-Federal funds derived from cash outlays, personnel commitments, or third-party in-kind contributions. Under 2 CFR 910.130(d)(3), recipients are prohibited from counting future commercial revenues, proceeds from asset sales, or other federal award funds as allowable cost share.

Commercial cost principles for for-profit entities (2 CFR 910.352)

While non-profit organizations and universities calculate allowable costs under 2 CFR 200 Subpart E, 2 CFR 910.352 mandates that for-profit entities must follow commercial cost principles in Federal Acquisition Regulation 48 CFR 31.2 (FAR 31.2) in lieu of 2 CFR 200.400 through 200.476. This applies to commercial prime recipients and subrecipients. In addition, 2 CFR 910.352 establishes that patent prosecution costs are unallowable for for-profit entities unless specifically authorized in advance within the written award agreement.

Property, equipment, and UCC encumbrance filings (2 CFR 910.360)

Under 2 CFR 910.360(a), recipients purchasing real property or equipment with an acquisition cost per unit of $5,000 or more in whole or in part with Federal funds must obtain prior written approval from the Contracting Officer. Title vests conditionally in the recipient with the government retaining an undivided reversionary interest. Crucially, 2 CFR 910.360(b)(4) mandates that recipients record Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) financing statements (UCC-1 filings) for all equipment purchased with Federal funds whenever the Federal share exceeds $1,000,000. These UCC filings must be approved in writing by the Contracting Officer before equipment reimbursement can occur.

Change of control and U.S. manufacturing (2 CFR 910.366, 910.368)

Under 2 CFR 910.368, any corporate transaction transferring more than 50 percent voting power, merger, or asset sale requires written notice to the Contracting Officer within 30 days and affirmative Contracting Officer authorization. Failure to obtain authorization permits award termination or payment suspension. Furthermore, under 2 CFR 910.366, recipients must execute a binding U.S. Manufacturing Plan committing to manufacture products embodying award technologies substantially in the United States, with waivers requiring formal DOE approval.

Application or compliance steps

Successfully navigating a DOE award governed by 2 CFR 910 requires strict adherence to sequential administrative steps throughout the project lifecycle:

Entity Registration: Secure an active Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) in SAM.gov and register credentials in Grants.gov, FedConnect.net, and agency portals such as EERE Exchange.

Cost-Share Verification: Model total project costs and calculate mandatory 20 percent research or 50 percent demonstration cost-share commitments under 2 CFR 910.130. Execute commitment letters incorporating mandatory 2 CFR 200 Appendix II provisions.

Accounting Setup: Configure general ledger systems to track award costs separately, align job costing with FAR 31.2, and segregate unallowable costs like unapproved patent fees.

Award Negotiation: Finalize the Statement of Project Objectives, milestone schedules, Go/No-Go stage gates, and special award conditions under 2 CFR 910.372 with the Contracting Officer.

UCC-1 Equipment Filings: When the federal share exceeds $1,000,000, prepare UCC-1 financing statements for equipment valued at $5,000 or greater, obtain Contracting Officer approval, and record filings with the state.

Reimbursement Invoicing: Under 2 CFR 910.354, submit reimbursement requests for actual disbursements through VIPERS using SF-270, typically processed within 30 days.

Subrecipient Oversight: As a pass-through entity, conduct risk assessments, monitor commercial partner invoices against FAR 31.2, and enforce flow-down clauses.

Subpart F Audit Submission: When annual DOE expenditures reach or exceed $750,000, engage an independent CPA firm to complete a compliance audit under 2 CFR 910 Subpart F within nine months of fiscal year-end.

Typical timeline phases

A financial assistance award governed by 2 CFR 910 unfolds across four distinct lifecycle phases, enabling recipients to anticipate operational milestones without relying on calendar dates:

Phase 1: Solicitation, merit review, and selection

Following FOA release, applicants submit technical volumes, budget justifications, and cost-share plans. Proposals undergo peer review against published criteria, culminating in formal selection notifications authorizing award negotiations.

Phase 2: Award negotiation and baseline establishment

The recipient and Contracting Officer reconcile budgets, complete NEPA environmental reviews, finalize the Statement of Project Objectives, and review draft UCC filings before executing the binding assistance agreement.

Phase 3: Budget period execution and milestone reviews

Performance proceeds across twelve- to twenty-four-month budget periods. Invoicing occurs on a reimbursement basis through VIPERS. Formal Go/No-Go stage gate reviews determine whether technical progress and cost-share ratios justify continuation into subsequent periods.

Phase 4: Closeout and audit reconciliation

Upon completion, recipients submit final technical reports to the Office of Scientific and Technical Information (OSTI), resolve property disposition under 2 CFR 910.360(g), file patent utilization reports, and submit final financial reports (SF-425) alongside any required Subpart F audits.

Common mistakes

Audits and legal disputes under 2 CFR 910 frequently stem from misunderstandings regarding DOE divergences from academic grants. Common compliance pitfalls include:

Applying University Cost Principles to Commercial Entities: Evaluating commercial expenses under 2 CFR 200 Subpart E rather than FAR 31.2, leading to questioned costs during audits.

Claiming Unapproved Patent Expenses: Incurring patent prosecution costs without prior written authorization in the financial assistance agreement under 2 CFR 910.352.

Omitting UCC-1 Equipment Filings: Failing to record UCC financing statements on equipment when the federal share exceeds $1,000,000, resulting in suspended reimbursements.

Unannounced Change of Control: Executing mergers or transferring over 50 percent voting stock without 30-day notice and Contracting Officer approval under 2 CFR 910.368.

Improper Cost-Share Sourcing: Using unallowable federal funds or anticipated commercial revenues to meet Section 988 cost-share obligations.

Overlooking the Subpart F Audit Threshold: Failing to commission an independent compliance audit when annual DOE expenditures reach $750,000 under 2 CFR 910.501.

Incomplete Flow-Down Terms: Failing to bind commercial subrecipients to FAR 31.2 cost principles, audit rights, and U.S. manufacturing covenants.

Related programs

Compliance under 2 CFR 910 requires understanding its position within federal administrative law. The lookup table below illustrates how 2 CFR 910 interacts with related regulatory frameworks across federal assistance and procurement domains.

Regulatory Framework Governing Authority Covered Entity Types Primary Application to Energy Programs 2 CFR 200 (Uniform Guidance) Office of Management and Budget Universities, Non-Profits, State and Local Governments Baseline federal grant rules adopted by DOE in 2 CFR 910.120; governs academic recipients. 2 CFR 910 Department of Energy For-Profit Entities, Clean Energy Grantees, Consortia Agency-specific rules, FAR 31.2 cost principles, EPACT cost share, and for-profit audit rules. 48 CFR 31.2 (FAR Part 31) Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council Commercial and For-Profit Contractors and Grantees Cost principles governing allowable costs for commercial entities under 2 CFR 910.352. 10 CFR 600 Department of Energy (Historic) Historic DOE Financial Assistance Recipients Legacy DOE financial assistance regulations superseded by 2 CFR 910 in December 2014. 48 CFR Chapter 9 (DEAR) Department of Energy Procurement Direct Procurement Contractors, M and O Contractors Department of Energy Acquisition Regulation governing direct federal contracts, not grants. 35 U.S.C. 200-212 (Bayh-Dole Act) United States Congress (Statutory) Small Businesses, Non-Profits, Contractors Governs patent rights and technology commercialization incorporated into 2 CFR 910.362.

The data table below compares key structural distinctions between baseline Uniform Guidance and DOE Part 910 across nine core regulatory dimensions.

Frequently asked questions

What is 2 CFR 910?

Title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 910 (2 CFR 910) is the Department of Energy’s agency-specific regulation that formally adopts and supplements the Office of Management and Budget’s Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200) for federal financial assistance awards. It establishes specialized administrative rules, commercial cost principles, mandatory cost-sharing standards under EPACT 2005, and compliance audit guidelines for recipients of DOE grants and cooperative agreements.

Who does 2 CFR 910 apply to?

2 CFR 910 applies to all recipients and subrecipients of Department of Energy financial assistance awards. While non-profit organizations and institutions of higher education are subject to general Uniform Guidance provisions supplemented by Part 910, 2 CFR 910 explicitly expands the definition of a non-Federal entity to include commercial for-profit entities, applying specialized post-award requirements under Subpart D and audit standards under Subpart F to private sector energy technology developers.

What cost principles apply to for-profit entities under 2 CFR 910?

Under 2 CFR 910.352, for-profit entities that receive DOE financial assistance must follow the commercial cost principles set forth in the Federal Acquisition Regulation at 48 CFR 31.2 (FAR 31.2) rather than the standard non-profit and academic cost principles in 2 CFR 200 Subpart E. In addition, 2 CFR 910.352 establishes that patent prosecution costs are strictly unallowable for commercial entities unless specifically authorized in advance within the written award agreement.

What are the audit requirements for for-profit entities under 2 CFR 910?

Under 2 CFR 910 Subpart F (specifically 2 CFR 910.501), any for-profit entity that expends $750,000 or more in DOE financial assistance awards during its fiscal year is required to undergo an independent compliance audit. The compliance audit evaluates financial records, internal controls, and compliance with specific award terms and DOE program requirements in accordance with the audit scope defined in 2 CFR 910.514.

How does 2 CFR 910 handle payments to for-profit recipients?

Pursuant to 2 CFR 910.354, reimbursement is the required standard method of payment for for-profit entities receiving direct funding from the Department of Energy. Unlike universities and non-profits that may qualify for advance payment under 2 CFR 200.305, commercial recipients must disburse organizational funds first and submit electronic reimbursement requests through the VIPERS system, which are paid within 30 calendar days of receipt.

Is profit or fee allowed under DOE financial assistance awards?

Under 2 CFR 910.358, the payment of fee or profit is strictly prohibited across all Department of Energy financial assistance programs, with two specific statutory exceptions: awards issued under the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program and the Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program. For all other grants and cooperative agreements, financial assistance transfers only allowable, allocable project costs without commercial markups.

text:
The North Wales Clean Energy Fund, led by Ambition North Wales and designed to support green energy projects across the region, has agreed to a $2 million investment for tidal energy developer HydroWing Ltd. The investment will support the construction and installation of a tidal turbine scheme at Menter Môn Morlais, the largest consented tidal stream energy scheme in Europe, situated off the coast of Anglesey.

With the first devices expected to be deployed in 2027, the funding brings Morlais a step closer to generating clean electricity, marking a significant step forward for the scheme. The HydroWing project will be Wales’ first and largest consented tidal stream energy project.

Richard Parkinson, CEO of HydroWing, the tidal energy division of Inyanga Marine Energy Group, said: “Securing this funding from Ambition North Wales is a major milestone, enabling us to deploy our first HydroWing tidal energy device at Morlais in 2027. This investment lays the foundation for our planned 30MW commercial development and our ambition to establish Wales as a global center for tidal energy technology and manufacturing, creating highly skilled jobs, strengthening the Welsh supply chain and opening up significant international export opportunities.”

Cllr Gary Pritchard, Ambition North Wales Lead Member for Low Carbon Energy and Leader of Ynys Môn Council, said: “Our Clean Energy Fund is going from strength to strength and I am delighted that it has been possible to support HydroWing to further progress Morlais, marking another important milestone for the North Wales low-carbon economy. Ambition North Wales has already supported Morlais through the North Wales Growth Deal’s Cydnerth project to strengthen the local grid infrastructure. So, to build on that is fantastic.”

John Idris Jones, Chair of Menter Môn Morlais Ltd, added: “This investment is an important contribution in order to bring HydroWing’s technology into operation at Morlais and demonstrates the value of partnership in developing the tidal energy sector. Morlais already has the infrastructure in place to support tidal energy devices, and projects like this will help turn that potential into clean electricity, skilled jobs and opportunities for communities and businesses across North Wales.”

Adam Price, Welsh Government Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, said: “If we’re serious about raising productivity and growing the Welsh economy, we need to back sectors where Wales can genuinely lead. With some of the best tidal energy resources in the world, Wales is well placed to play a leading role in this growing industry, and this investment will help bring that ambition closer to reality. Working alongside the UK Government through the North Wales Growth Deal, we’re investing in projects that create new opportunities and support long-term economic growth across North Wales.”

Anna McMorrin MP, Wales Office Minister in the UK Government, said: “This $2 million investment brings clean tidal power off Ynys Môn a step closer. The UK Government is backing North Wales’s clean energy sector through the Growth Deal, creating skilled, well-paid jobs and growing the local economy.”

The North Wales Clean Energy Fund forms part of the North Wales Growth Deal, which is backed by the Welsh Government and the UK Government and delivered by Ambition North Wales.

title: Indonesia's Just Energy Transition and Carbon Market opportunities: How Can the Private ...
description:
Indonesia’s carbon market framework is taking shape with the issuance of Presidential Regulation No.
“In recent years, Indonesia’s carbon market framework has developed rapidly, including the start of international carbon trading through the Indonesia Carbon Exchange and stronger cooperation under Article 6.
So, how can the private sector contribute to Indonesia’s just energy transition?
Early engagement can help ensure that REDI4JET’s activities reflect market realities and that future carbon market initiatives have the support needed to progress.
“We aim to bring just energy transition activities and carbon markets together, so that the transition creates more jobs and supports sustainable development across the country.
text:
The shift to clean energy infrastructure that is fair for workers, communities, and the economy requires significant investment. As Indonesia advances its Just Energy Transition (JET), carbon markets can provide an additional source of financing for credible and well-designed projects, as well as benefiting the communities involved.

Through the Redirecting Investments for an Inclusive Just Energy Transition (REDI4JET) project, the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), together with its consortium partners Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) and Perspectives Climate Research (PCR), brought together private sector stakeholders for a webinar exploring how private stakeholders can take part in just energy transition projects and carbon market opportunities. The discussion focused on opportunities to align Indonesia’s JET initiatives with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, as well as ways for the private sector to participate in REDI4JET’s inception phase focused on capacity needs assessment and other activities in 2027.

Indonesia’s carbon market framework is taking shape with the issuance of Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on carbon pricing. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement adds another route, allowing countries to cooperate on carbon markets through the international transfer of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and a Paris Agreement crediting mechanism (PACM). The voluntary carbon market continues alongside it, with growing attention to credit integrity. The opportunity for Indonesia is to align these mechanisms with just energy transition activities, such as clean energy projects that create jobs and benefit local communities, so that carbon market finance supports the transition.

“In recent years, Indonesia’s carbon market framework has developed rapidly, including the start of international carbon trading through the Indonesia Carbon Exchange and stronger cooperation under Article 6. These developments open up new opportunities, but also require technical and institutional readiness from all market participants. The private sector has a key role to play in this process.” Retno Setianingsih, Energy Lead, GGGI Indonesia

Within REDI4JET, carbon markets are a tool to support the just energy transition, not an end in themselves. The project’s carbon markets work includes an assessment of Article 6, voluntary and domestic carbon markets, policy recommendations, the identification and prioritization of a pipeline of mitigation activities, and the development of two pilot Mitigation Activity Design Documents (MADDs) together with the private sector. A just transition also means that projects respect workers and communities, which is why civil society organizations are part of the survey, including on safeguards, free, prior and informed consent, grievance mechanisms and benefit sharing.

So, how can the private sector contribute to Indonesia’s just energy transition?

The private sector is at the forefront of markets and production and can therefore help shape the policies and projects needed to advance the transition. Project developers and financial institutions, for example, can share insights on technology costs, grid constraints, and buyer preferences. Private sector involvement can help ensure that proposed projects are technically sound and commercially viable. They can also help validate potential projects and explore co-investment opportunities, supporting efforts to move projects from design towards implementation.

Under REDI4JET, private sector stakeholders will have opportunities to contribute to policy recommendations that encourage investment in the energy sector, provide input into approaches such as de-risking instruments, receive technical assistance to improve the transaction readiness of energy projects, and participate in training on carbon finance and project development. This includes learning how to develop bankable projects, reach financial close, and access financing.

“Private sector stakeholders can actively contribute to policy recommendations and help shape approaches that improve the investment environment, including de-risking instruments. With REDI4JET, the private sector can also benefit from technical assistance, for example, training on carbon finance and developing bankable projects, and reaching financial close,” Ardian Candraputra, Senior Energy Officer and REDI4JET Project Manager, GGGI.

Building the capacity to participate in carbon markets is another important part of Indonesia’s JET.

“We want to make sure that the support we develop responds to actual needs. The feedback from participants gives us a useful starting point for identifying where further training and capacity building are needed. We are keen to develop activities that address these gaps and make the process as participatory as possible.” Debi Nathalia, Investment Unit Lead, GGGI

REDI4JET’s training program is planned to run over the next two to three years. The program will also bring public and private sector participants together, rather than having them learn separately, creating opportunities to exchange knowledge and clarify regulatory requirements while building the capacity needed for effective participation.

For private sector stakeholders, this is an opportunity to contribute to investment, sector expertise, feedback, and participation in developing projects and strengthening the wider investment environment. Early engagement can help ensure that REDI4JET’s activities reflect market realities and that future carbon market initiatives have the support needed to progress.

“We aim to bring just energy transition activities and carbon markets together, so that the transition creates more jobs and supports sustainable development across the country. We can only do that by working hand in hand with the private sector.” Sebastian Hernandez, Carbon Finance Officer, GGGI

That partnership starts with understanding the needs of the private sector, and the survey is the first step. Interested private sector organizations working on JET can share priorities, challenges, and capacity-building needs through the REDI4JET survey: click here

About REDI4JET

REDI4JET is an IKI-funded project, with Indonesia’s Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs (CMEA) as its main partner. The project is implemented by the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) as the lead consortium partner, together with the Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) and Perspectives Climate Research (PCR).
