title: IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 looks at nuclear power's future amid global turmoil
description:
Construction started on eight reactors in the first half of 2026, one of the highest levels of nuclear construction the IEA has seen in 40 years.
In addition, more than 50 countries have some form of plans in place or under discussion for nuclear power; many of these countries are interested in small reactors.
Countries and regions like China, the United States, the European Union, and Japan have demonstrated a commitment to expanding nuclear energy through efforts like new nuclear construction, reactor operating license extensions, policy, and restarts.
“Nuclear power expansion reflects growing policy momentum and construction activities at their highest level in over 35 years,” the report said.
The report also takes into account that global demand for electricity has grown at a faster rate than the world economy and twice as fast as overall energy demand.
text:
“This World Energy Outlook looks past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” IEA executive director Fatih Birol said in a statement. “By providing multiple scenarios—none of which are forecasts—and analysis of unparalleled scope, it can serve as a reference as countries consider their next steps. It also brings into focus the difficult trade-offs they face.”

Outlook on nuclear: According to the report, nearly 90 GW of new nuclear capacity was under construction in 17 countries in 2026, the highest level in more than 35 years. This includes small reactor construction in Argentina, Canada, China, and Russia. Construction started on eight reactors in the first half of 2026, one of the highest levels of nuclear construction the IEA has seen in 40 years. In addition, more than 50 countries have some form of plans in place or under discussion for nuclear power; many of these countries are interested in small reactors. As a result, the IEA has had to revise its projections from prior reports and analyses.

Countries and regions like China, the United States, the European Union, and Japan have demonstrated a commitment to expanding nuclear energy through efforts like new nuclear construction, reactor operating license extensions, policy, and restarts. The report at times singles out China and its nuclear growth, noting, for example, that rapid growth in renewables and nuclear has impacted the country’s demand for coal and shifting “China’s coal-fired fleet from providing bulk electricity towards meeting peak demand and providing flexibility.”

The IEA projects renewables and nuclear power will “expand strongly” in all scenarios now through 2035, although the pace varies by scenario. These scenarios include the following:

the Current Policies Scenario (CPS), which is based on energy policies and regulations that are already in place.

the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which adds to CPS by considering specific policy measures that have formally been put forward but not yet adopted because of the global crises.

the Additional Response Case Scenario (ARC), which is based on supply-and-demand actions that are under consideration by governments and ponders what would happen if these actions were implemented.

and the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE), which models under the assumption if global emissions were on track for net zero by 2050.

“Nuclear power expansion reflects growing policy momentum and construction activities at their highest level in over 35 years,” the report said.

For example, the CPS projects that nuclear electricity generation will more than double by 2050 and its share of the global energy market will increase up to 10 percent.

“The current geopolitical and energy security environment could further boost nuclear power, which can diversify energy mixes and reduce exposure to market volatility while supporting reliability in increasingly electrified economies,” the report said. “As part of the response to the 2026 energy crisis, many countries have confirmed or strengthened plans for nuclear power or extended the lifetimes of existing reactors, and some are reconsidering restrictions on nuclear development. In addition, new demand drivers, including electrification, AI, and data centers, are strengthening the case for firm power sources such as nuclear.”

The IEA weighs in: Overall, the IEA’s global outlook said the current crises—resulting in “the largest energy supply shock in history,” as the agency described it—has led countries all over the world to revise and review their energy strategies in order to keep their resources stable, secure, and affordable.

“Although national responses to the crisis vary, the WEO-2026 sees some common directions emerging: greater diversification of energy supplies, trade routes, fuel mixes, and technology supply chains; a stronger preference for domestically available energy resources; and a push for faster progress on electrification,” the IEA said.

The report also takes into account that global demand for electricity has grown at a faster rate than the world economy and twice as fast as overall energy demand. This growth is attributed to greater increased electrification in industry, appliances, air conditioners, vehicles, heat pumps, and data centers. According to the report, electricity’s share in final energy consumption globally will close in on 30 percent by 2035 under all scenarios.

“The pressures of the current crisis must not obscure the choices that will shape energy security, sustainability, and prosperity for the decades to come,” Birol said in a statement. “Countries will pursue different pathways, reflecting their resources, circumstances and priorities. But all have a stake in building a more secure, affordable and sustainable energy system—and in effective cooperation to achieve that goal.”

The core purpose of the bill is to overhaul federal review and permitting mechanisms to reduce delays for major infrastructure.

text:
Senate Bill 5653, officially titled the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, includes a comprehensive federal permitting reform package aimed at expediting energy and infrastructure projects across the United States. Introduced on September 30, by Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), the legislation passed the U.S. Senate yesterday (November 19), by a vote of 62 to 33, and has subsequently been sent to the House of Representatives for consideration.

The core purpose of the bill is to overhaul federal review and permitting mechanisms to reduce delays for major infrastructure. Under its environmental and permitting provisions, the bill establishes strict deadlines for permit decisions, limits the scope and alternatives required under National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews, and creates specific exemptions for selected project types. Regarding clean water, wildlife, and historic preservation, the measure narrows state water quality certification reviews under the Clean Water Act, extends National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit durations, shortens Endangered Species Act consultation periods, and modifies triggers for reviews under the National Historic Preservation Act.

In the energy sector, the legislation significantly expands the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC) authority to approve interstate electricity transmission lines and mandates ratepayer protections related to high-consumption energy loads such as data centers.

Additionally, it eliminates federal permitting requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal lands while accelerating the development pathways for renewable, geothermal, hydropower, and offshore energy initiatives.

During the Senate vote, Wisconsin's delegation was divided. Senator Ron Johnson (R) voted in favor of the bill, while Senator Tammy Baldwin (D) voted against it.

description:

text:
Copyright © 2026 Boston Neighborhood News, Inc. This content may not be re-published or re-used without written permission.

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has reached agreements with Massachusetts conservation officials and 54 other involved parties to advance a long-awaited, $78.6 million cleanup of the Lower Neponset River, a major milestone in efforts to remove decades of industrial pollution from the waterway that flows through Boston and Milton.

The agreements, announced last Wednesday (Nov. 18), set the stage for engineering and construction work on the first mile of the 3.7-mile Superfund site, including the removal of the deteriorating Tileston and Hollingsworth Dam, which has trapped large quantities of contaminated sediment in the river near the Hyde Park-Milton line.

“This is great news for the Lower Neponset River and the communities it flows through,” said EPA Regional Administrator Mark Sanborn in a statement. “These agreements work together to allow cleanup efforts in the Lower Neponset River Site to begin and are a truly important first step to address PCBs and other contaminants in the most contaminated reach of the Site.”

In an interview with The Reporter, Sanborn said the agreements represent a breakthrough in a complicated process involving dozens of parties with potential responsibility for historic pollution.

“When you’re dealing with more than one entity, it gets complicated, never mind more than 50,” he said. “With Superfund projects, the early logistical work and organizing parties to get everyone on the same page is usually part of the challenge.”

Sanborn credited EPA staff and the companies involved for reaching the agreement, which he said would advance the cleanup under the agency’s Superfund Solutions Initiative.

“These settlements are a major step forward for the cleanup,” he said. “They allow design work for the first phase of the project to move forward and ensure that responsible parties are contributing to the cleanup.”

Under one agreement, 54 settling parties identified as contributors to the river’s contamination will undertake the engineering and design work needed to remove polluted sediment and floodplain soil from the river’s uppermost mile, beginning where Mother Brook joins the Neponset in Hyde Park.

The parties, which include property owners and operators, waste generators, and transporters, will continue negotiations with EPA over responsibility for carrying out and financing the actual cleanup.

Sanborn declined to discuss whether additional companies or other potentially responsible parties might eventually join the effort, citing ongoing legal negotiations.

“What I can say is that EPA is going to look for every opportunity to have as many potentially responsible parties involved as possible in the ultimate funding agreements and contributing to the cleanup activities,” he said.

A separate agreement with the state’s Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR) commits the state agency to designing, financing, and carrying out the removal of the Tileston and Hollingsworth Dam, a critical component of the overall project.

Removing it will allow for a more natural river flow in that section of the Neponset, Sanborn said. “It’s also a critical part of the cleanup because the dam currently impounds contaminated sediment. Its removal will support both environmental restoration and the long-term cleanup of the river.”

The agreements follow EPA’s November 2025 approval of a comprehensive cleanup strategy that calls for dredging contaminated sediment, excavating polluted riverbank soils, installing protective caps along portions of the riverbed, and restoring the river channel.

The project is expected to require approximately four years to complete, with construction previously anticipated to begin in 2027 and conclude around 2031. The new agreements do not establish a firm construction start date.

The Lower Neponset was designated a federal Superfund site in March 2022 following years of advocacy by residents, environmental organizations, and elected officials concerned about contamination from centuries of industrial activity along the river.

Among the principal pollutants are polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, toxic chemicals widely used in industrial manufacturing until they were banned in 1979. EPA investigations have also identified pesticides, heavy metals, dioxins, and other hazardous substances in river sediment and adjacent floodplain soils.

Federal investigators documented PCB concentrations as high as 11,000 milligrams per kilogram in sediment immed iately upstream of the Tileston and Hollingsworth Dam. EPA has determined that the contamination poses unacceptable risks to human health and wildlife.

The dam itself presents an additional threat. A 2021 inspection found it to be in poor condition, with significant structural, mechanical, and operational deficiencies.

According to the newly signed settlement, contaminated sediment trapped behind the dam has continued moving downstream during normal river flows and storms. The maximum thickness of sediment behind the structure declined from 9.7 feet in 2002 to 4.8 feet in 2021, evidence that polluted material continues to migrate toward Mattapan and Dorchester.

EPA officials have warned that a dam failure could release large quantities of contaminated sediment downstream.

The settlement also documents the role of the former Lewis Chemical Corporation facility on Fairmount Court in Hyde Park, which operated as a hazardous waste processing operation from 1963 until an explosion and fire forced its closure in 1983. Federal investigators found evidence of releases from the property into the river. EPA completed a separate cleanup at the former facility in 2024.

An EPA staff member said on Thursday that several parties associated with the Lewis Chemical property are participating in the settlement.

The new agreement requires DCR to conduct additional engineering investigations, prepare detailed construction plans, arrange for the removal and off-site disposal of contaminated material associated with the dam, and restore disturbed portions of the river channel and banks.

DCR must also coordinate its work with the other responsible parties and comply with EPA requirements governing air quality, dust, noise, traffic, and public safety during construction.

Although the agreement does not assign a specific dollar figure to the state’s share of the $78.6 million project, it requires DCR to finance its assigned work and seek legislative appropriations to reimburse EPA for eligible future oversight costs.

The first phase is intended to reduce the most serious pollution risks and prevent contaminated sediment from continuing downstream. A second phase will eventually address the remaining stretch of the Superfund site, extending from the Tileston and Hollingsworth Dam through Mattapan and Lower Mills to the Walter Baker Chocolate Dam.

Asked whether EPA might eventually seek removal of the Baker Dam, which has been the subject of past discussions about river restoration, Sanborn said that question remains open.

“I want to be careful not to get ahead of ourselves in terms of what that will look like exactly,” he said. “But as you mentioned, the Baker Dam is where Phase 2 would end. Obviously, consideration of its future will be part of the discussion about what’s needed for the next steps in the cleanup.”

For now, Sanborn said, EPA is focused on moving ahead with the most contaminated section while continuing investigations downstream.

“With these agreements in place, the next step is to complete the design work and move toward implementation,” Sanborn said. “At the same time, EPA will continue studying the rest of the river to support future decisions.”

“We also want to look for opportunities for reuse and repurposing spaces so they can have a new legacy and a new path forward,” he said. “That might mean contributing through economic development or community development or simply creating new spaces that can be used for recreation and enjoying parts of our community.”

The Neponset River Watershed Association, which has closely monitored and supported the Superfund’s progress, called the agreements a significant milestone.

“We are excited to see this next phase get underway and to continue working toward a healthier, cleaner, and more accessible Neponset River,” the association said in a Nov. 19 statement.

More information is available at epa.gov/Neponset.

name: EVs
title: New gas station display puts EV charging costs beside fuel prices - Yahoo Autos
description:
The display has attracted attention by placing EV charging rates alongside traditional fuel prices.
The display attracted attention in 2021 as an early example of a petrol station publicly advertising EV charging prices alongside traditional fuel rates.
Renewed media coverage in November 2026 shows that the long-standing display continues to attract interest in electric vehicle charging costs.
However, charging prices and vehicle efficiency can vary depending on the station, vehicle, and charging conditions.
What do you think about displaying EV charging prices alongside gas prices at every station?
text:
Depositphotos

A sign that catches attention

Most drivers are used to seeing gas prices displayed outside a station. Unleaded, diesel, and premium usually get their own lines. But one gas station in Australia has attracted renewed attention for displaying something unexpected on its sign: the price of electricity for electric vehicles.

The display has attracted attention by placing EV charging rates alongside traditional fuel prices. While the figures use different units and cannot be compared directly, they give drivers useful information for estimating potential savings based on their vehicles' energy consumption.

pavelyar105@gmail.com/Depositphotos

Where the sign appeared

The unusual sign was spotted in Toowoomba, a city in Queensland, Australia. It caught the attention of Sam Evans, who runs the popular YouTube channel The Electric Viking and regularly covers developments in the electric vehicle industry.

Evans shared the discovery in a video, drawing attention to a feature most gas station signs do not include. Instead of showing only traditional fuel prices, the station also displays an EV charging rate, allowing drivers to see the advertised electricity price alongside petrol and diesel prices.

Depositphotos

An extra line on display

At first glance, the sign looks much like the ones drivers see at gas stations every day. It lists prices for unleaded, diesel, and premium fuel, allowing motorists to check costs before pulling in.

However, one additional line makes it stand out. The station also displays the price of electricity for EV charging. This small change gives drivers a clearer picture of what it costs to power different types of vehicles without having to search for the information elsewhere.

arvydele.gmail.com/Depositphotos

The price of electricity

According to reporting published in November 2026, the sign showed an EV charging rate of 35 Australian cents per kilowatt-hour, approximately 24 US cents at the exchange rate used in the report.

The figure was reported at the time and should not be treated as a guaranteed current charging rate.

For electric vehicle owners, the figure offers a useful starting point when estimating charging expenses. Unlike traditional fuel prices, electricity costs are measured by the amount of energy used. Displaying the rate publicly makes it easier for drivers to understand what they are paying to recharge their vehicles.

BeritKessler/Depositphotos

Gas prices tell another story

The same sign also showed the cost of traditional fuel. The cheapest unleaded petrol was listed at A$2.30 per liter, while premium fuel was around A$2.70 per liter.

For American readers, those prices were approximately US$6 per gallon for unleaded petrol and US$7 per gallon for premium fuel, based on the exchange rate used in the original report.

Although fuel prices change over time and vary by location, these figures help explain why the comparison attracted attention.

Drivers could see petrol and electricity prices on the same sign, making it easier to estimate running costs once vehicle fuel consumption and energy efficiency are taken into account.

amor7/Depositphotos

Comparing the same journey

The most interesting part of the comparison comes when looking at how much energy different vehicles need to travel the same distance. The figures shared by Evans use an SUV as an example, making the difference easier to understand.

A petrol-powered SUV using eight liters of fuel per 100 kilometers would cost approximately A$18.40 to travel that distance at the reported unleaded petrol price of A$2.30 per liter.

fransz/Depositphotos

Electric driving costs less

An electric SUV consuming around 17 kWh per 100 kilometers would have an estimated energy cost of A$5.95 for the same journey at A$0.35 per kWh, before accounting for charging losses. Actual costs may be higher depending on the vehicle's efficiency and charging conditions.

That creates a noticeable difference between the two vehicles. Under these assumptions, the electric SUV's energy cost would be approximately one-third of the petrol SUV's fuel cost for the same 100-kilometer journey.

Actual savings depend on vehicle efficiency, energy prices, and driving conditions. Even with these limitations, the comparison illustrates how EV energy costs can be lower than petrol expenses over the same distance.

Fun fact: EVs can recover some energy normally lost during braking and send it back to the battery through regenerative braking.

blinow61/Depositphotos

Evans shares his reaction

Sam Evans was impressed by the way the station presented the information. He argued that more petrol stations should display electricity prices alongside traditional fuel rates, especially those that already provide EV charging.

His point was simple. Drivers should be able to see the costs for themselves and make their own comparisons. Rather than relying on advertisements or complicated calculations, a single sign could give motorists a clearer idea of what different vehicles cost to run.

andreadelbo/Depositphotos

More stations could follow

Evans believes this approach could make everyday conversations about electric vehicles more practical. Many drivers focus on the purchase price of a vehicle, but the cost of keeping it on the road also matters.

Putting electricity prices on familiar gas station signs could help people understand one part of EV ownership more easily. It would also make charging costs visible to drivers who may not regularly visit EV charging websites or use electric vehicle apps.

Depositphotos

Four stations in Toowoomba

The station operates under the Pacific Fuels name. A November 2026 report identified four fuel station locations associated with Pacific Fuels or Pacific Petroleum in the Toowoomba area and noted that Google Maps images showed electricity prices at two of them.

According to the original report, Google Maps images showed electricity prices on signs at the Anzac Avenue and North Street locations.

However, the images do not establish whether both stations continue displaying those prices today. The visible rates allowed passing motorists to compare the advertised prices of petrol and electricity.

Little-known fact: Australian EV owners can charge their vehicles using an ordinary 240-volt household power outlet.

info.grabowski-foto.pl/Depositphotos

Not every location shows it

The same information was not confirmed at every Pacific Fuels location. A recent Google Maps image of the Brisbane Street station, dated April 2026, did not appear to show an electricity price on its sign.

There was also no recent image available for the Pacific Petroleum location in Newtown. Because of that, the original report could not confirm if the electricity pricing information was displayed there. The available images offered only a partial picture of how widely the feature had been introduced.

Depositphotos

The idea dates back years

Although the sign may look like a new development, the idea has been around for several years. The practice was documented as early as June 2021, when Australian EV publication The Driven described the Toowoomba station's display as a possible first for the country.

The display attracted attention in 2021 as an early example of a petrol station publicly advertising EV charging prices alongside traditional fuel rates. Renewed media coverage in November 2026 shows that the long-standing display continues to attract interest in electric vehicle charging costs.

Depositphotos

Could this become common?

The Pacific Fuels sign raises an interesting question for the wider fuel industry. As electric vehicles become a more familiar sight, showing electricity prices beside petrol and diesel could help make running costs easier to compare.

However, charging prices and vehicle efficiency can vary depending on the station, vehicle, and charging conditions. The figures displayed in Toowoomba are only one example. Still, the idea is straightforward, and more stations may consider adopting it as drivers look for clearer information about their transportation costs.

title: RE+ 2026 recap: Facing an uncertain future, clean energy industries focus on addressing ...
description:

Nearly every extant residential solar installer has pivoted to serving commercial clients or transferred their offerings to third party ownership models — or both.

text:
The annual RE+ flagship trade show is a vast and unknowable beast, as broad and varied as the industries represented within it. A single mind cannot apprehend its totality.

RE+ (née SPI) has long since eclipsed its origins as a show about solar and energy storage technology, now encompassing grid-scale power management, AI compute infrastructure, industrial automation and manufacturing design, advanced robotics, construction labor management (those last two are related), and — last but absolutely not least — national and global politics.

At any given moment, a hundred experts were speaking on stages and in conference rooms spread across the 4.6 million square feet of the Las Vegas Convention center, holding forth on the latest changes in policy and technology, while thousands more entertained guests at their booths in the hopes that those guests would soon be ready to work up their next multimillion-dollar deal.

The show is virtually impossible to cover in a single article with anything that resembles a unifying theme or certainty about the future, so thankfully, the USA and Global teams from pv magazine have been working hard to bring you coverage of the latest and greatest announcements from the show. Go to the home page to read more of that coverage.

For now, I have the unenviable task of synthesizing all I saw and heard into a unifying narrative. So here goes. The first theme:

People are paramount

Every year, trade shows like RE+ remind us that there is truly nothing like being face-to-face with your friends and customers in the solar industry. Being together provides opportunities to understand each other in a much richer way than is usually possible through a phone call or video chat.

My first stop on Tuesday morning at the booth for C&I solar monitoring platform Stem reminded me just how powerful that connection can be. The company’s RE+ booth hosts what they call a “Technical Expertise Center,” which their VP of marketing Tatjana Legans described as a place their customers can chat with experts about all the things that get left unsaid during an ordinary support call.

Legans said the center was a big hit with Stem’s clients the last time the company attended the show and they decided to keep it going for 2026. Customers get a chance to ask questions they don’t have time for during the daily grind, or learn about new solutions and features of products they haven’t used before.

Elsewhere in the show, it was the same story. The most effective sales pitch is one that comes from a live person, and that’s a big reason nearly 40,000 of us keep coming back to this place every year.

The RE+ show writ large may be unknowable to a single mind, but the personal connections that can be forged between people at the show are the invaluable currency that continues to carry us through hard times.

This brings us to the second theme:

Uncertainty remains

The mid-term elections will usher in a new-look congress, which has some solar advocates very excited for the future. But relying on the blue tsunami to deliver wins for the solar industry isn’t a strategy that can provide certainty, with president Trump still in office and vowing to become “Mr. Veto” for bills he doesn’t like.

Accordingly, experts at the conference expressed tempered optimism for outcomes favorable to solar and storage in the coming congressional term. For instance, at the “Hot takes, Hard numbers” module manufacturing roundtable, analysts agreed that there is legislative support for an extension to 45X manufacturing tax credits — though it might take until 2029 to get it — but seemed much less sure of whether support for a Section 48E extension exists.

In a lunchtime discussion hosted by Wood Mackenzie, new SEIA president Tim Pawlenty said he wants to move past the idea of solar as a partisan issue among lawmakers. “Our hope and our aspiration in the intermediate and long term is to make SEIA purple so that we can make credible, compelling, persuasive arguments in policy regardless of what combination of red or blue is in charge of the White House,” he said.

Looking ahead to the end of the current congress, Pawlenty said he gives the Bipartisan Affordable American Jobs Act permitting reform bill a 50/50 chance of passing in the lame duck session before the end of the year.

Moving forward, Pawlenty says his goal is to keep advocating for solar on terms lawmakers in each party can understand, but pointed out that some further education is necessary. “We’ve still got serious policymakers at senior levels of government who think solar only works when the sun is shining,” he said.

Pawlenty explained that despite what the advent of commercially-viable energy storage technologies means to energy markets, the aforementioned policymakers “seem to have no modern or contemporary understanding of it.”

“That’s just one example of how much work we have to do to bring policymakers up to speed,” he told the crowd of the SEIA/Wood Mackenzie lunch, noting that when policymakers are presented with good information about the modern application of solar and storage technologies, they understand the benefits.

“Eventually, the policymakers catch up to the facts,” he concluded. “And we’ve got good facts.”

Data centers are a major reason we’re all still here

Following the Pawlenty interview, Wood Mackenzie analysts outlined their predictions for the next 20 years, with analysts expecting to see load growth of 3.5% per year over that time, compared to an average of 0.8% between 2016 and today. The analysts further predicted that energy demand from data centers will represent 25% of the U.S. total in 2036.

With the clean energy industry facing a cliff as developers complete safe harbored projects in the coming years, the conversation at every level is about how solar and (especially) energy storage can best be positioned to serve much of that load growth.

Huge developers like Cypress Creek are putting in multi-gigawatt utility-scale installations and signing offtake agreements with hyperscalers, and module makers and battery firms from around the globe are vying to supply these projects, with or without tax credits.

A dozen companies, from Delta and Enphase to SolarEdge and Tesla are working on equipment designed to take medium-voltage AC power from the grid and deliver low-voltage DC to the server rack, and firms like FlexGen are designing integrated software and hardware solutions that directly serve clients, providing blazing fast speed to power for data center operators who don’t want to wait for the grid, and outpacing the interconnection queue by several years.

Even at the residential and small commercial level, the most exciting players are developing virtual power plants of thousands of distributed batteries, delivering a way for the grid to absorb the shocks of spikes in the use of inference computing near urban centers while adding a measure of resilience for everyday users of energy with a side helping of goodwill from data center skeptics.

Energy advisor Hans Royal has developed a metric known as “Compute Heat Rate” (CHR), which measures the maximum electricity price AI workloads can economically sustain. The CHR for Q3 2026 is $5,630 per MW — more than 100 times the cost of gas.

With hyperscalers able to pay that much for electricity, the future of all the solar, energy storage, and power electronics industries can provide lives and dies by the accuracy of that 3.5% per year load growth figure. For now, it looks as though growth in data centers’ demand for power stands to protect the market once the safe-harbored projects are gone.

The role of innovation

In years past, the show floor at RE+ teemed with companies offering their latest and greatest products that seemed like revolutionary new inventions. In many ways, new products in the modern solar industry are merely iterations on the previous versions with slight tweaks and design changes.

But there are still a few standouts.

On the small side, I was impressed to see the new partnership between Every Electric and Jackery, featuring simple portable power stations given to 1,000 New Yorkers to be plugged in between a wall outlet and a window air conditioner. With Every Electric’s software embedded inside, Con Edison can control the batteries as a virtual power plant that doesn’t require any interconnection agreements or complicated changes to wiring. All that’s needed is a wi-fi connection and a load to shift. Imagine 100,000 of these kinds of power stations responding to peak demand events in apartments across every major city.

The most interesting innovation at the next step up in size is the EG4 Homestead 60, a pre-assembled, pre-wired solar and energy storage system on wheels that can be deployed in short order, anywhere the road can take the tilt-bed semi trailer upon which it is delivered. With 14 kW of solar and a 60 kWh battery on a U.S. steel frame at a retail price of just $37,700, the total cost is $2.62 per watt — even with the battery.

EG4 representatives told us the Homestead 60 is designed for permanent installation at rural residential sites, and not necessarily for temporary deployment in use cases like disaster recovery. It consists of two separate large units with 12 solar modules each that can be deployed facing east/west, as shown in the image above, or split into halves so all the solar modules can be deployed south-facing.

Homestead 60 systems are expected to be available in December from EG4’s Sulphur Springs location, and a company rep said EG4 is looking at a broader range of manufacturing sites in the future.

As for solar modules, the latest technology is perovskite tandem glass. Heliene and Sirius PV both brought modules featuring glass from perovskite thin-film company Caelux.

Heliene’s booth showcased their take on the HybridTandem module architecture just a few days after the company announced the start of commercial-scale production for perovskite/silicon tandem modules.

Sirius PV surprised the residential solar industry at the booth of distributor BayWa r.e., showcasing both perovskite tandem glass and the new EPIC frame design from IronRidge, which enables quick mounting and unmounting of can generate 525 W in the same space as the company’s existing 450 W offerings.

Perovskite solar cells and modules are a space we will be watching closely, as the technology promises to add greater efficiencies in tandem with silicon. Perovskite technology companies will be featured at our pv magazine Solar Manufacturing USA 2027 event in Austin, Texas.

In a similar vein to the EG4 solution (but another step larger) is the Voltage Microgrid System (MGS), which is also pre-assembled and pre-wired, but comes with 70 kW of solar and 140 kWh of energy storage built in. Voltage says the system can be unfolded and fully installed by three people in less than a day. The system is designed to be leased by solar construction teams as they build huge utility-scale solar and BESS installations as an economical alternative to diesel generators.

And then, of course, comes the solid-state transformers and power electronics being developed by Delta, Enphase, SolarEdge and Tesla. As AI compute operations demand ever-increasing amounts of power, AC power distribution inside data centers is quickly becoming impractical. Based on specs by NVIDIA, the industry is coming up with new ways to provide 800 V DC power directly to server racks. These companies are leveraging long histories of developing silicon-based power electronics to answer NVIDIA’s call.

Whither residential solar?

Residential solar installers seemed to account for a much smaller set of the overall crowd this year, and the number and size of booths that cater to them did, as well. For better or worse, the industry has been changed completely by the end of the Section 25D solar tax credit.

“Diversify or die” seems to be the name of the game. Nearly every extant residential solar installer has pivoted to serving commercial clients or transferred their offerings to third party ownership models — or both. Many have begun focusing on a service-first model, or now prioritize energy storage and backup generator installations over solar.

Manufacturers and B2B service providers with a historical focus on residential solar have also gotten on board. Booths from Lunar Energy and EG4 showcased new commercial battery offerings, and Solar Insure’s big launch at the show was a commercial battery extended warranty product. Well-known residential company enphase premiered its new stackable residential battery alongside an 80 kWh commercial offering and a data center transformer. Several well-known residential brands without a large commercial presence didn’t exhibit at the show at all.

In mid-2025, experts predicted “holes in the market” for residential solar in 2026 in places without existing third-party ownership offerings, and that has largely come true. State legislatures haven’t really done much to step into the hole left by expiring federal incentives, and net metering protections continue to erode.

Brands like Climate First Bank/Bodhi and Atmos Financial are working hard to serve the residential market with solid financing offerings, and while there’s a place for homeowner ownership of solar and storage, that place is largely in the same markets that support third-party ownership economics, which tend to have high retail electric prices or novel monetization models like VPPs.

Wrapping it up

The solar and energy storage industries have been transformed at nearly all levels by wild swings in legislative and trade policy over the past two years, and no one can predict with 100% accuracy what will happen in Washington in the coming biennium.

What we know is the companies in these industries can offer expertise and value where it counts. The well-oiled utility scale firms are built for serving the broader needs of the grid. The power electronics specialists can pivot to delivering modern solutions to modern problems. The systems integrators know how to deliver speed to power via all-of-the-above microgrid solutions, and they have paying customers who can afford it any seemingly any cost.

The coming year may bring permitting reform, new energy bills in congress, new breakthroughs in perovskite technologies and novel battery chemistries. The best place to learn about it is from the people making it happen; face to face at RE+.

text:
Green hydrogen technology company Hysata has made 17 staff redundant two months after receiving a $49 million Commonwealth grant to expand its operations.

The company, based in Port Kembla, builds energy-efficient electrolysers, which are used to produce hydrogen.

In September, it received a $49 million grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) as part of a $98 million expansion into commercial manufacturing.

At the time, the government said the expansion would create 40 skilled jobs.

The company's CEO, Paul Barrett, confirmed the redundancies in a statement on Friday.

They include 12 research and development roles and three administration roles from the Port Kembla site, as well as two remote roles.

Dr Barret said the cuts reflected the "different mix of staff" needed as the company scaled up manufacturing.

"This week's changes reflect a shift in the skills we need as we move from technology development to commercial-scale manufacturing," he said.

"We remain committed to Port Kembla as our global headquarters and continuing to create jobs.

"Our workforce is evolving, not contracting."

He said the company had simplified the systems it used to produce hydrogen, in part by sourcing more components from established suppliers.

"These advances change the capabilities required within Hysata," he said.

"As a result, some roles at its Port Kembla facility are no longer required."

Mr Barret said the expansion was proceeding, and the company would announce more new orders in the near future.

Government funding

Hysata has been awarded tens of millions of dollars in Commonwealth grants.

In 2023 it secured $20.9 million to build its first commercial-scale demonstration plant next to the Stanwell coal-fired power station near Rockhampton.

But that plan collapsed in 2025 after the Queensland LNP government withdrew support for Stanwell's hydrogen projects, and Stanwell confirmed the test site would not go ahead.

Hysata said the demonstration had since moved to another location.

The latest ARENA grant contributed to a new manufacturing line to produce components for Hysata's first commercial export order.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen, Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres and Member for Cunningham Alison Byrnes announced it at the Port Kembla site in September.

Ms Byrnes said the timing of the redundancies was unfortunate, but she defended them as a necessary.

"This is about the next phase of Hysata, which is expanding their manufacturing base," she said.

"They've [already] done a lot of the research and development work, which has unfortunately reduced the need for a lot of those positions."

She said she remained confident the company would deliver new jobs in the area.

"They are a growing team, and they are growing that business," she said.

Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan disputed the rationale provided for the job cuts, calling on the Mr Bowen to explain them.

"It seems bizarre to me that the Federal government would give [Hysata] … nearly $50 million to see a company shrink in size," he said.

"Chris Bowen needs to explain how this has occurred."

Mr Bowen declined to comment when approached by the ABC.

— Trishan Peruma, CEO of Hubject North America

LOS ANGELES , CA, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Hubject, the global leader in eMobility interoperability, and Cal EPIC (California Energy, Power, and Innovation Collaborative), a Sacramento-based organization advancing clean energy, transportation and manufacturing innovation, today announced that Hubject has become an official member of Cal EPIC. Hubject is also now a strategic testing partner for Cal EPIC’s Capital Charge Yard, a $4 million effort funded by the California Energy Commission (CEC) to build and operate California’s first publicly accessible EV Charger Testing and Interoperability Lab.

“Cal EPIC is a place where innovators and industry leaders can come together to test their technologies and ensure California customers get the best experience with clean tech,” said Orville Thomas, CEO of Cal EPIC. “We want EV charging to be easy and work the first time you plug in. There’s no better partner to help make that happen than Hubject.”

“Plug&Charge is already how many Californians choose to charge, and every new vehicle and charger that comes to market has to work reliably from the start. As a member of the Capital Charge Yard advisory board, Hubject can help make sure that testing keeps pace with the growing number of products drivers depend on,” said Trishan Peruma, CEO of Hubject North America.

The CEC awarded the grant to Cal EPIC in partnership with CharIN North America, the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute (KERI) and Momentum. The publicly accessible testing and demonstration facility gives electric vehicle and EV charger manufacturers a place to validate interoperability, develop future charging standards and explore vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technologies. Alongside technical testing, the facility will host annual policy conferences and public demonstration events for regulators, industry leaders and other stakeholders.

Plug&Charge, based on ISO 15118, allows a compatible EV to start charging automatically when plugged in, with no app, card or manual step. It relies on digital certificates that allow the vehicle, the charge point and the mobility service provider to authenticate one another securely. Hubject’s PKI issues and validates these certificates, giving vehicle and charger suppliers at the Charge Yard the certificate infrastructure they need to test Plug&Charge between their implementations.

Accelerating Plug&Charge capability is one of the benefits the CEC expects the Capital Charge Yard to deliver. As a member of the advisory panel, Hubject will contribute its global experience in eMobility interoperability to support the Charge Yard’s work on reliable, standards-based charging.

Hubject’s North America team attended the Testival in Sacramento on November 17-18.

About Cal EPIC

California has set the most ambitious clean energy goals in the nation. Cal EPIC exists to make them real. Our 33,000-square-foot Innovation Hub in Sacramento brings together startups, manufacturers, and workforce talent to build the energy and transportation technologies that get us there — with an EV and charger testing lab, manufacturing and prototyping facilities, and programs designed to move innovators from concept to commercial scale. This is where California’s zero-carbon future gets built.

About Hubject

Hubject simplifies the charging of electric vehicles. Through its eRoaming platform intercharge, the eMobility specialist connects Charge Point Operators (CPOs) and eMobility Service Providers (eMSPs) to provide standardized access to charging infrastructure. Hubject operates the world’s largest cross-provider charging network, connecting over 1,100,000 charge points and more than 3,500 B2B partners across more than 75 countries. Hubject is also a leader in Plug&Charge technology, reaching 5,000,000 PnC-ready EVs and using the ISO 15118-2 and -20 standards to deliver secure, seamless EV charging experiences. text:
During her time on the campaign trail, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa promised to freeze Texas electricity rates on her first day in office, as affordability became akey concernfor many voters.

In September, after the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) initially approved amultimillion-dollar contractfor its CEO, Hinojosa criticized the agency and took aim at her opponent, Republican governor Greg Abbott.

"Abbott let his billionaire donors cash in after Winter Storm Uri, and now people are paying more per month for their electricity bills in the middle of a high-cost economy," Hinojosa said in astatementat the time. "On Day One as governor, I'll freeze residential electricity rates and make corporations finally pay their fair share."

But exactly how Hinojosa could freeze electricity rates remains unclear.

"This would have to be something that she would push through the Public Utility Commission," University of Houston Energy Fellow Ed Hirs said. "The actual mechanism is not clear."

Hinojosa's campaign did not respond to requests for comment. In aninterviewwith theTexas Tribune,she pledged to work with state regulators to make her campaign promise a reality.

"[T]he state regulates electricity rates through the Public Utility Commission, and so working with them, I think that's something that we can accomplish," she told the nonprofit news outlet.

Generally speaking, Texans' electric bills can be divided into two main parts.

The first part is the rate that a customer is charged per kilowatt-hour of energy used. Those prices are set by private electric companies, so they're not regulated by the state or subject to oversight from the governor.

The second part of Texans' electric bills is made up of transmission and distribution charges. That's the costs that customers pay for upkeep of electricity poles, wires and other infrastructure needed to deliver power to their homes.

Those charges are regulated by the Public Utility Commission (PUC), and University of Texas energy researcher Joshua Rhodes said Hinojosa could have some say in how those rates are set.

"Those charges are set through a process at the Public Utility Commission and so, that in theory, could also be paused or stopped," he said.

Energy consultant Karl Rábago, who served on the commission under Texas Gov. Ann Richards, said Hinojosa could invoke her emergency powers to pause these rate increases. It's not uncommon for governors to use their executive powers to intervene in utility rate policymaking, he added.

"We've done that after hurricanes. We've done that after winter storms, in many parts of the country," Rábago said. "This is not unique and many people would say, it's an appropriate flexing of gubernatorial powers in the face of the economic crisis that many citizens find themselves in."

Energy consultant Eric Goff said he views Hinojosa's campaign promise as more of a rhetorical pledge to lower bills.

"So I don’t expect her to freeze rates in a direct way," he said. "But I do expect there's stuff [she] can do on day one to lower consumer costs."

Goff said Hinojosa could work with the legislature to pass new laws that would favor consumers. The governor-elect could also encourage state regulators to adopt new rules that would require large energy users — like data centers — to bear the costs of new electric infrastructure.

While all members of the current Public Utility Commission have been appointed by Abbott, Goff said he's optimistic that they would be willing to work with Hinojosa to find ways to lower rates.

I want us to build clean energy, and to build it far faster than we do now.
“There’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment.
text:
Washington, D.C.—Today, Rep. Mike Levin (CA-49) announced that he cannot support the Senate-passed energy permitting bill, known as BAAJA, as currently written. While the legislation includes important reforms to modernize the electric grid and accelerate clean energy deployment, Rep. Levin raised concerns about its impacts on the environment, Tribal sovereignty, and future fossil fuel development. He urged House and Senate leaders to negotiate changes that address these concerns before the bill moves forward in the House. Rep. Levin released the following statement:

“I can’t support the energy permitting bill the Senate just sent to the House, known as BAAJA, at least not as it's written today. Here’s why:

“I’ve spent my career as a clean energy advocate and an environmental attorney. I want us to build clean energy, and to build it far faster than we do now. So I’ve measured this bill against three questions. Will it lower costs for families? Will it protect our clean air and water? Will it help clean energy grow?

“There’s real promise on costs and clean energy deployment. The bill would modernize a power grid that too often can’t carry affordable clean energy to the homes that need it, and it would require data centers to pay for their own grid upgrades instead of passing the cost on to families. Many of those reforms are similar to legislation I wrote with Sean Casten and Kathy Castor, and I want to see them become law. I believe the emissions reductions and cost savings may be smaller and less certain than supporters suggest, however.

“Other parts of the bill raise concerns. The bill would limit California’s ability to protect its own water, weaken the science behind endangered species decisions, and keep courts from halting a project even when an agency skips the review the law requires. It would also make this administration’s fossil fuel approvals, offshore leases included, extremely hard for a future president or a judge to undo. For those of us who have spent years fighting to keep new oil rigs off the California coast, that’s a serious threat.

“Tribal nations have warned that the bill’s changes to historic preservation law could endanger sacred sites and undercut Tribal sovereignty, and they deserved a far bigger voice in writing it.

“Those harms would be permanent, while the clean energy gains would rise or fall with whoever happens to be carrying out the law.

“I’ve thought hard about the old saying that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon. That risk is significant. But in the end, taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.

“Since the Senate released the bill, I’ve worked with my colleagues in the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition on targeted fixes to permitting certainty, clean water, endangered species, judicial review, and historic and Tribal protections. None of our major concerns have been addressed. I’ve also heard from hundreds of people across our district, and they oppose this bill by roughly two to one.

“Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, who helped write this bill, are my friends and have long been champions of climate action. Many allies I deeply respect support it, and I know they want the same future I do.

“There’s still time to get this right. If House and Senate leaders from both parties sit down together and negotiate sufficient changes, I’ll be ready to vote yes.

“We can and we must find a better balance that protects communities and the clean air and water they rely on. I believe this is possible this Congress and I urge my colleagues to be responsive to the concerns of Americans across the country and fix this bill before it becomes law.”

description:

text:
DTE Energy is opening its checkbook for more Michigan sunshine, launching a competitive solicitation for up to 150 megawatts of new solar generation across the state. Developers have until January 19, 2027 to submit proposals, and the utility expects to sign contracts sometime in the second or third quarter of that year.

What Developers Need to Know

According to Solar Power World, projects accepted into the program must be located in Michigan, connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE's own distribution network, and reach commercial operation by June 30, 2030. Interested bidders can register and pull additional details through PowerAdvocate, the platform DTE is using to manage the procurement, the outlet reports.

The push is not a standalone idea. It fulfills terms of a settlement agreement approved by the Michigan Public Service Commission on May 15, 2025, in Case No. U-21662. That settlement lays out a schedule for DTE Electric to issue solar solicitations in 2026, 2028, and 2030 totaling up to 150 MW, according to the commission's order. The settlement also sets specific conditions for power purchase agreement projects: those must sit within an incorporated Michigan city, on a brownfield site, or qualify as agrivoltaic developments, and if the utility receives conforming build-transfer bids, it may accept PPA projects capped at 5 MW each — no more than 50 MW total — at a 2:1 build-transfer-to-PPA ratio. Notably, the commission's filing specifies that any projects accepted through these solicitations are incremental additions, separate from DTE's broader Integrated Resource Plan build-out.

Why DTE Says This Pays Off for Customers

DTE frames the economics in straightforward terms: solar doesn't need fuel, so locking in these projects is meant to insulate the company from swinging fuel prices over the facilities' operating lives, per the same Solar Power World account. The utility also argues that generating more power inside Michigan reduces its reliance on energy sourced from outside the state, which it says can help lower what customers ultimately pay. Beyond the balance sheet, DTE points to construction jobs, fresh capital investment, and increased local tax revenue as community benefits tied to the build-out — claims the company itself is making about projects that haven't yet been sited or selected.

This 150-MW push follows a much larger solicitation DTE launched earlier in 2026. As DTE Energy announced in May, the utility sought 1,000 MW of Michigan wind and solar projects to support its CleanVision Integrated Resource Plan, with bids due August 13, 2026 and contract execution targeted for the first quarter of 2027. That earlier RFP required projects to interconnect with MISO or DTE's distribution system and reach commercial operation by December 31, 2029 — a tighter and earlier deadline than the new 150-MW solicitation's June 2030 target.

The Bigger Renewable Picture

DTE's broader ambitions are sizable, though the exact figure depends on which account you read. Solar Power World reports that DTE's 2026 Integrated Resource Plan calls for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042, while pv magazine USA describes the same plan as targeting 15.4 GW of new wind and solar assets alongside 1.83 GW of energy storage by that year. Either way, the scale dwarfs the current 150-MW ask. Per pv magazine USA, DTE's plan also calls for deploying 4.4 GW of solar and 1 GW of wind during an initial 10-year development block running through 2032.

DTE already operates 20 wind parks and 37 solar parks across Michigan, generating enough clean energy to power nearly 1 million homes, according to Solar Power World's reporting on the utility's renewable footprint. One recent example is the Fish Creek Solar Park near Sheridan, Michigan — a 132-MW facility that cost $268 million and was funded entirely by customers who voluntarily enrolled in DTE's MIGreenPower program, the outlet notes. That project alone can power roughly 30,000 homes, and Bushnell and Evergreen townships each received $330,000 through Michigan's Renewables Ready Communities Award in connection with the development.

A new engineering alliance aims to accelerate the global rollout of compact, round-the-clock nuclear power plants. Sargent & Lundy has partnered with ENTRA1 Energy to provide design and engineering support for ENTRA1 Energy Plants.

“The plants intend to use NuScale Power Corporation’s proprietary small modular reactor technology,” said Sargent & Lundy in a press release.

Their emergency planning zone is also limited strictly to the site boundary. Operators can build plant capacity in stages as power needs grow. This modular approach allows a first reactor unit to generate electricity while crews install additional modules nearby.

“The NuScale Power Module design is based on proven pressurized water-cooled reactor technology, and was developed to supply energy for electrical generation, district heating, desalination, commercial-scale hydrogen production, and other process heat applications,” highlighted Sargent & Lundy.

Multi-purpose industrial applications

description:

The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA.
The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.

text:
The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects.

The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.

The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA.

The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.

Opponents voiced concern that NEPA, a bedrock federal statute for environmental protection, would be too severely weakened and that tribes would lose power over the consultation process.

Just two Republicans — Missouri Senator Josh Hawley and South Dakota Senator Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor.

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee’s leaders — GOP Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — along with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair, GOP Senator Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat, Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, negotiated the measure.

In a statement celebrating the bill’s passage, Capito said the upper chamber “took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people.”

Capito said she has “spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building,” adding that the bill “is the culmination of those efforts.”

In his own statement, Heinrich said the measure would bring down electricity costs while preserving environmental standards.

The bill “will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” the New Mexico Democrat said.

President Donald Trump has backed the measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. In a statement of administration policy this month, the administration said the bill would “deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and economic growth across the United States.”

‘Deeply disappointing’

But the bill has drawn sharp criticism from many environmental organizations, including the Center for Western Priorities, a public lands group.

The Center’s executive director, Aaron Weiss, described the vote as “deeply disappointing,” adding that senators “who promised Westerners they would stand up for our public lands just voted for a bill that sells them out to Big Oil and Big Tech.”

Weiss urged the House to reject the bill and allow the next Congress beginning in early January to craft “a permitting bill that builds clean energy without sacrificing America’s public lands.”

In the lower chamber, House Natural Resources Committee Chair Bruce Westerman said the Senate vote marked “a strong step forward in fixing our nation’s permitting challenges,” in a statement Friday.

The Arkansas Republican said he looks forward “to working with my colleagues in the House to swiftly pass this bipartisan bill that will unleash the full force of American innovation.”

title: How data centers can help bring solar and batteries to homes | Latitude Media
authors: Lisa Martine Jenkins, Latitude Studios, Open Circuit, Maeve Allsup, Catherine Boudreau, Shayle Kann
description:
In the first quarter of 2026, at least 75 U.S. data center projects collectively worth approximately $130 billion were blocked or delayed amid local opposition, according to Data Center Watch.
Developers face another constraint at the same time: securing enough grid capacity to bring facilities online without waiting years in interconnection queues.
A March 2026 Gallup survey found that 71% of Americans opposed construction of an AI data center in their local area.
Paying for residential solar and batteries would give data center developers a practical way to address local concerns about rising electricity bills.
Sunrun says it’s already in discussions with hyperscalers about putting this model into practice, including financing new residential solar and battery installations near planned data centers.
text:
This is partner content, brought to you by Sunrun.

Opposition to new data centers is starting to carry a serious price tag.

In the first quarter of 2026, at least 75 U.S. data center projects collectively worth approximately $130 billion were blocked or delayed amid local opposition, according to Data Center Watch. Developers face another constraint at the same time: securing enough grid capacity to bring facilities online without waiting years in interconnection queues.

Sunrun thinks the homes surrounding proposed data centers could help developers address both challenges.

“Rather than spending the money you would spend to build [on-premises] or fund some new development of generation, subsidize a consumer offering for people around the data center,” Sunrun president and chief revenue officer Paul Dickson said at Latitude Media‘s Flex Summit in Austin in October.

The idea is to use hyperscaler investment to bring solar and batteries to households in the region, creating distributed capacity that could accelerate grid connections while giving residents lower energy costs and greater resilience.

Tapping into residential capacity to accelerate interconnection

Much of the data center industry’s search for speed to power has focused on building or buying new generation. Sunrun proposes using residential resources to ease the capacity constraints holding up large-load interconnections. Those resources can be deployed incrementally, potentially faster than conventional infrastructure.

Here’s how Sunrun envisions it working: Hyperscalers would subsidize solar and battery installments in homes connected to the same grid as their developments. Sunrun would aggregate those systems into dispatchable capacity that utilities could draw on to manage grid constraints. Then, the key to accelerating large-load interconnection is convincing utilities and regulators to recognize that flexibility as a dependable planning resource.

“If we can get regulators to recognize this resource as planned capacity, you instantly lift the peak capacity headroom, can interconnect more, and have more comfort in controlling costs for consumers,” Dickson said.

Giving communities a stake in AI growth

At the same time, hyperscalers face a community pushback problem. A March 2026 Gallup survey found that 71% of Americans opposed construction of an AI data center in their local area. While data centers may bring regional investment and tax revenue, those benefits can feel distant to residents worried about what new electricity demand might mean for their bills.

“We believe that Americans should participate in the AI boom,” Dickson said.

Sunrun’s pitch to hyperscalers would offer communities tangible benefits. A resident in the same region of a proposed data center could receive a solar-plus-storage system subsidized by the company creating the new demand. The household could benefit from lower electricity bills, backup power, and reduced installation costs, while the developer could gain access to distributed capacity that helps accelerate its grid connection.

Paying for residential solar and batteries would give data center developers a practical way to address local concerns about rising electricity bills. The subsidized systems would give participating residents something more immediate and personal than regional tax revenue, while potentially helping utilities avoid or defer costly infrastructure investments.

Of course, much depends on how the deals are structured. One potential model would have a hyperscaler contract with Sunrun to install and service thousands of solar-plus-storage systems and manage distributed power plant dispatches, which would create headroom on the grid. While communities have other concerns about data center development, electricity costs are among the biggest — and Sunrun’s proposal could give developers a tangible way to address them.

Turning battery dispatches into planning capacity

Sunrun already has substantial experience aggregating residential energy resources. As of September 30, 2026, it had installed more than 284,000 solar-plus-storage systems, with roughly 5.0 gigawatt-hours of networked storage. In October, Sunrun and Tesla delivered a combined 745 megawatts of peak power to California’s grid during a coordinated residential battery dispatch.

The companies, alongside Everyday Electric, have also announced a nonbinding plan to market 16 gigawatts of flexible capacity from existing and new distributed resources to utilities and hyperscalers.

These deployments demonstrate the scale and responsiveness of aggregated residential batteries. Translating this capability into faster interconnections will require commercial agreements and regulatory frameworks that allow utilities to count the resources toward their capacity requirements.

Dickson said Sunrun could negotiate directly with a hyperscaler in some markets. In others, the local utility would also need to be involved, with regulators potentially playing a role. Sunrun says it’s already in discussions with hyperscalers about putting this model into practice, including financing new residential solar and battery installations near planned data centers.

For Sunrun, the opportunity is to turn the AI industry’s enormous appetite for electricity into an investment in the communities hosting that growth. If the model works, hyperscalers could bring projects online faster while helping more residential customers gain access to solar, storage, and the financial benefits that come with them.

"We've done that after hurricanes. We've done that after winter storms, in many parts of the country," Rábago said. "This is not unique and many people would say, it's an appropriate flexing of gubernatorial powers in the face of the economic crisis that many citizens find themselves in."

Energy consultant Eric Goff said he views Hinojosa's campaign promise as more of a rhetorical pledge to lower bills.

"So I don’t expect her to freeze rates in a direct way," he said. "But I do expect there's stuff [she] can do on day one to lower consumer costs."

Goff said Hinojosa could work with the legislature to pass new laws that would favor consumers. The governor-elect could also encourage state regulators to adopt new rules that would require large energy users — like data centers — to bear the costs of new electric infrastructure.

While all members of the current Public Utility Commission have been appointed by Abbott, Goff said he's optimistic that they would be willing to work with Hinojosa to find ways to lower rates.

"The PUC and ERCOT are interested in outcomes that are good for the state," Goff said. "And I’m sure there are some versions of that where they’d be happy to cooperate with her on everyone’s mutual interest to make the grid more affordable and more reliable."
