title: Three Green Hydrogen Projects Slip Through The Trump Chopper - CleanTechnica
description:
Nevertheless, some stakeholders have continued to pursue the dream of producing green hydrogen from renewable resources — instead of squeezing it from natural gas.
Plug Power began life back in 1997 with a focus on electric forklifts powered by zero emission hydrogen fuel cells.
Plug Power soon pivoted into replacing gas-derived hydrogen fuel with so-named green hydrogen, pushed from water by an electrical current.
If all went according to plan, Plug Power would have used the loan to finance up to six green hydrogen projects around the US, all affiliated with the Hydrogen Hubs program.
The funding evaporated under Trump, but the state is still getting its hands on green hydrogen.
text:
When US President Donald Trump swept into office last year, he set his choppers upon the $8 billion Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, snuffing out plans to establish a diversified, domestic hydrogen market with a focus on decarbonization. Nevertheless, some stakeholders have continued to pursue the dream of producing green hydrogen from renewable resources — instead of squeezing it from natural gas. Now all that hard work is beginning to pay off, Trump or no Trump.

A New Green Hydrogen Project Rises In Texas

If you guessed the startup Plug Power is in the mix, run right out and buy yourself a cigar. Plug Power began life back in 1997 with a focus on electric forklifts powered by zero emission hydrogen fuel cells. In addition to replacing fossil fuels, Plug Power aimed to replace battery-powered forklifts, with fuel cells being a better fit for the fast-paced environment of shipping and logistics.

Plug Power soon pivoted into replacing gas-derived hydrogen fuel with so-named green hydrogen, pushed from water by an electrical current. After a series of ups and downs the company hit the jackpot in January of 2025, when the US Department of Energy tapped it for a $1.66 loan guarantee in support of the Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, which was funded through the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. If all went according to plan, Plug Power would have used the loan to finance up to six green hydrogen projects around the US, all affiliated with the Hydrogen Hubs program.

So much for that. The Energy Department announced the loan award at the beginning of the month, when former President Joe Biden was still in office. However, by the end of the month Trump was officially installed in the White House. He soon pulled the plug on the Plug Power loan, so to speak, sending it down the drain alongside many other federally funded clean power projects.

That was not the end of the story for Plug Power. After all, it’s a big world out there, and Plug Power continued to pitch its wares overseas. Last week the company also relaunched itself back into the US market, bigly.

On November 17, Plug Power announced that its new “GenEco™ Scale” green hydrogen electrolyzer system is up for grabs in the US market while concurrently announcing that its first customer is the Texas-based firm Aracdia eFuels. Arcadia will deploy 280 megawatts’ worth of GenEco Scale modules at its Project ARC campus in the Portland/Corpus Christi area in Texas. When fully up and running, Project ARC will deploy green hydrogen from the GenEco Scale system to produce about 23.2 million gallons of fossil-free aviation fuel per year.

What Is This GenEco Scale Of Which You Speak?

While green hydrogen has its fans in the decarbonization field, the stubbornly high cost of electrolysis has raised a formidable obstacle against widespread commercial uptake. Plug Power is among the stakeholders pitching modular, integrated systems to help bring costs down into parity with conventional hydrogen sourced from natural gas or coal, and that’s where the GenEco system comes into play.

“Built around a standardized 20 MW block architecture, GenEco Scale combines Plug’s proven proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer technology with integrated balance-of-plant systems into a modular, pre-engineered solution for hydrogen production projects of approximately 100 MW and above,” Plug Power explained in a press statement last week. The company also noted that the “outdoor-ready” system avoids much of the cost and time related to the buildings and other infrastructure required of traditional large scale electrolyzer systems.

Arcadia eFuels CEO Amy Hebert also chipped in her two cents in support of the modular system. “Reducing the engineering burden on our EPC [engineering, procurement, and construction] partners and minimizing the complexity of bringing these systems together were important considerations for Project ARC,” Herbert emphasized.

Savings on land is another part of the cost-cutting plan. Unlike conventional electrolyzer system layouts, the GenEco model deploys a vertical configuration. The vertical system requires less than one acre per 100 megawatts of electrolyzer capacity, according to Plug Power.

California Gets Its Green Hydrogen, One Way Or Another

Another Plug Power project has bubbled up in California, which was on track to host a suite of projects under the Hydrogen Hubs program with a focus on hydrogen derived from biomass as well as water electrolysis. The funding evaporated under Trump, but the state is still getting its hands on green hydrogen.

On November 19, Plug Power announced that its containerized 5-megawatt GenEco electrolyzer is up and running at a green hydrogen plant in Vernon, California, under the umbrella of the New Jersey-based firm Avina Clean Hydrogen.

Green hydrogen from this project will go to fulfill California’s plans for a zero-emission freight corridor, the plan for which includes fuel cell electric trucks as well as battery-powered trucks. “Located approximately 10 miles from the Port of Long Beach, the facility is designed to serve fleets moving freight through the Los Angeles–Long Beach port complex. It combines on-site fueling with tube-trailer deliveries to customers across the Los Angeles region,” Plug Power explains.

The station, also accommodate buses, and it can refuel a heavy-duty vehicle to more than 95% capacity in less than 30 minutes, according to Plug Power. That stacks up well against charging times for battery-powered heavy duty vehicles. On its website, for example, Tesla asserts that its new Semi electric truck can recover 60% of its 500 mile range in up to 30 minutes at a Tesla Megacharger station.

For the record, Avina has not placed all of its cards on hydrogen fuel cell trucks. The company’s roster of clean hydrogen projects also includes SAF (sustainable aviation fuel) and green ammonia, which is a key input for fertilizer among other chemical products.

PowerCell Makes Its Move Into The Electric Co-op Field

Rounding out the trio of new projects is the Swedish firm PowerCell Group. The firm is better known for its work in the marine energy field, and now it is tapping into land-based markets as well. Last week PowerCell announced that its US branch is in motion to set up a green hydrogen system run by excess electricity from an existing solar array owned by a to-be-named client in the US. In effect, the hydrogen will serve as an energy storage medium. It will go to run a PowerCell PowerPod 3000 stationary fuel cell, which will kick into action at night to keep the clean kilowatts flowing after the sun goes down.

PowerCell describes the PowerPod 3000 as “a containerized power generation platform integrating our PS190 systems with power conversion equipment, cooling and DMC, PowerCell’s control and Energy Orchestration technology,” with an installed fuel cell capacity of 27 megawatts and 20 megawatts of rated power.

Why Not Batteries?

That’s a good question. Rather than let that excess solar electricity go to waste, the client could invest in a BESS ( battery energy storage system) for daytime energy storage and night-time electricity. However, a typical BESS only lasts for a handful of hours. In contrast, PowerCell describes its fuel cell as a “long duration” storage system, which generally means eight hours or more.

PowerCell also points out that a fuel cell does something that a BESS cannot. Fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen with oxygen in the presence of a catalyst. Water — H2O — is a byproduct. All else being equal, that opens up the potential for green hydrogen to serve as a water distribution medium, sucking up water in an electrolysis system at one location, then pushing it out in a fuel cell located elsewhere.

PowerCell is not making any specific promises for this particular project, though the company does emphasize that “the ability to generate both electricity and recoverable water adds another dimension of value to hydrogen-based energy storage.”

“The amount of water recovered, and its potential uses will depend on the final system configuration, operating conditions and water treatment requirements,” the company adds.

And, that’s where things get interesting. The client is a to-be-named electric cooperative, which is of interest because electric cooperatives (more specifically, Rural Electric Cooperatives) account for a large portion of the US grid, and their roots in the rural poverty fighting programs of the Great Depression provide for a distinctive public benefit mission that can, in some cases, allow more wiggle room for innovative energy solutions that generate broad benefits for local communities.

I’m reaching out to PowerCell for more details. If they can’t divulge the name of the client yet, perhaps they’ll be able to describe what they mean by long duration energy storage, so stay tuned for an update.

description:
No Peace on a Burning Planet: UN Secretary-General António Guterres gave his final press conference at COP31—his final climate summit before his forthcoming retirement.
He reflected on the discomfort of truth, the wide reach of the climate crisis, and the injustice of fossil fuels.
Since the start of COP31, Argentina, Palestine, Egypt, Botswana, Guatemala, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Tajikistan have presented new NDCs.
COFFIS works to track, transparently report, and eliminate fossil fuel subsidies, and supports member countries in creating their TAFF roadmaps.
According to the report, AI performs very well explaining basic climate science and singular policies, but becomes less accurate when asked questions in lower-resource languages.
text:
No Peace on a Burning Planet: UN Secretary-General António Guterres gave his final press conference at COP31—his final climate summit before his forthcoming retirement. He reflected on the discomfort of truth, the wide reach of the climate crisis, and the injustice of fossil fuels.

My responsibility has never been to make the facts more convenient. It has been to tell the truth rooted in the science, and to be especially clear when the truth is hard. Facts are facts, and the fact is, climate change does not stay in its lane … I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the United Nations. You cannot build peace on a burning planet … And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did the least to cause the crisis suffer first and worst. And the injustice runs even deeper, because we know what is happening, we know what is causing it, and we know what we must do. Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. There is no credible path to a safe climate without moving away from them.

Taking Stock: Every five years, the GST requires parties to evaluate collective progress toward Paris Agreement goals and tailor their nationally determined contributions (NDCs) accordingly. The GST2 kicked off on Wednesday with a high-level ministerial event.

UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell opened the ministerial event by urging parties to drive delivery of existing targets, gather evidence to inform future targets, and participate at every stage of the GST2.

COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen stated that “the COP presidencies call on parties to use the GST2 as an opportunity to strengthen international cooperation, accelerate implementation, and drive the science-backed action urgently needed to keep the Paris goals in reach.”

IPCC Chair Jim Skea reminded parties to look ahead to their Working Group III Report, which will discuss strategies for removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos noted that advancing the GST2 will be a core function of COP32. Timothewos also highlighted the need for timely IPCC data and access to finance, technology, and trade to adequately address climate change.

Turning in Homework: With the GST2 underway, submissions for the third round of NDCs are still trickling in long past the February 2025 deadline. Since the start of COP31, Argentina, Palestine, Egypt, Botswana, Guatemala, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Tajikistan have presented new NDCs.

Not the End of the Road: The second draft cover decision may exclude reference to the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF), but as Natalie Jones of the International Institute for Sustainable Development reinforced in a press conference, the cover decision is not the only venue for this. In line with the Santa Marta process, member countries can create their own TAFF roadmaps. They can also ensure their roadmaps are reflected in their NDCs, simply by including any of their roadmap’s targets or headlines, or even just by referencing the roadmap. Fossil fuel transition goals can also live in existing national energy strategies or development plans. “The form does not matter, just the substance,” Jones said. Nonetheless, she emphasized the importance of recognizing the importance of transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final cover decision, noting that the roadmaps should inform the GST2, which will inform the fourth round of NDCs.

We’ll Always Have Santa Marta: One point of consensus at COP31 sat outside of the UNFCCC entirely: the success of the first International Conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels, held in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April. There, member countries agreed to concrete workstreams around national roadmaps, financial constraints, and competitive economies. At a press conference yesterday, Santa Marta cohosts Colombia and the Netherlands officially passed the gavel to Ireland and Tuvalu, cohosts of the second conference. At the same event, Darragh O’Brien of the Irish Presidency of the EU said that plans were already underway for the third conference in 2028. To date, 57 countries have joined what is called the “Santa Marta process.”

Make It Count: Since the last Dispatch, only Denmark, Ireland, and Portugal have published national TAFF roadmaps, joining Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK. Other countries and regions, including Brazil, Chad, Luxembourg, the Pacific Island region, Spain, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu, have just started. When asked whether the EU plans to join the list, EU Commissioner Hoekstra dismissed the need for an EU TAFF roadmap, pointing instead to the region’s codified target to reduce emissions 90% by 2040, compared to 1990 levels. Various representatives from LDCs and international nongovernmental organizations have criticized many of the published roadmaps as vague and lacking incremental target dates.

COFFI-ng Up Support: This week, Vanuatu and Tuvalu joined the Coalition on Phasing Out Fossil Fuel Incentives Including Subsidies (COFFIS), which was launched at COP28 by the Marshall Islands and the Netherlands. COFFIS works to track, transparently report, and eliminate fossil fuel subsidies, and supports member countries in creating their TAFF roadmaps. As of November 19, 19 countries have joined the coalition.

EESI Fact Sheet: Proposals to Reduce Fossil Fuel Subsidies

“Last Lifeboat to Climate Safety”: Türkiye announced a CBAM proposal at COP late last week, while representatives from Australia and Canada met to discuss the possibility of their own. To date, only the EU and the UK have a CBAM, and the two concluded a separate summit in Brussels today to discuss linking their emissions markets. Sen. Whitehouse suggested that EU and the UK should waive tariffs for California, citing that “they’re the fourth biggest economy on the planet and they have the requisite policies and should qualify. So why tariff them? This good actor being given this benefit would be extremely powerful in moving other states along in that same direction.”

EESI Article: "Europe’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: A New Age of Sustainable Trade"

A Strait Outlook: The International Energy Agency (IEA) released its flagship annual World Energy Outlook report on Thursday. The report focused on the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which has resulted in an unprecedented shock to the global energy system. National responses reveal three major policy trends: the diversification of suppliers, routes, energy mixes, and technology supply chains; an inclination towards domestically available energy resources, especially renewables and nuclear; and a faster push toward electrification. While these energy security trends are well-aligned with the clean energy transition, the Outlook cautions that they are not a sufficient driver for the necessary emission reductions. The IEA also found that Australia is on track to surpass Indonesia as the largest coal exporter in the world—an awkward statistic for a country currently presiding over climate negotiations.

EESI Briefing: Understanding Load Growth and Energy Affordability

Artificial Intelligence, Real Defects: The UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) held a press conference to describe the key findings of its new report, developed in partnership with University College London, on the reliability of AI as a source of climate information. Guilherme Canela, UNESCO’s director for digital inclusion and policies, expressed that as a new intermediary between science and the public, AI tools should be subject to independent testing, transparency, and accountability. According to the report, AI performs very well explaining basic climate science and singular policies, but becomes less accurate when asked questions in lower-resource languages. Researchers also found that, because AI models are sycophantic by design, they are quick to modify responses in order to validate the user, even if the user suggests an indisputable falsehood, like: “CO2 does not contribute to climate change.”

Come on Parties, Let’s Get Information: Late last week, Germany pledged €2 million (about $2.2 million) to the Global Fund for Information Integrity (GFII), launched by Brazil, the UN, and UNESCO at COP30. Since the inclusion of information integrity in the COP30 cover decision last year, 29 countries and the EU have signed the Belém Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change. According to a UNESCO representative, Germany’s pledge will support new grantees, investigative journalists, think tanks, and research to mitigate and prevent climate disinformation from AI. The GFII also launched the Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising to prevent climate disinformation in advertising, and Priorities for Action on AI for Climate Information Integrity, to teach governments, advertisers, journalists, and the public about AI-driven climate disinformation, AI’s role in supporting climate resilience, and the environmental footprint of AI itself.

EESI Briefing: Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Energy and the Environment

Risky Business: Germanwatch released its 2027 Climate Risk Index Report on Wednesday. The report attributed over 900,000 deaths between 1996 and 2025 to extreme weather events, as well as an estimated $4.7 trillion of direct economic losses. It also reaffirmed existing evidence that climate change and extreme weather predominantly affect Global South countries—with Dominica, Honduras, Myanmar, India, and the Philippines topping the charts for most negatively impacted countries.

text:
Chris McGrath | Getty Images

Negotiations at the United Nations’ climate summit collapsed on Sunday as the U.K., EU and others rejected a draft deal that failed to include fossil fuels.

Since the U.N.’s Climate Change Conference — or COP31 — began in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9, almost 200 countries have been locked in talks to reach a “cover decision,” with a number of drafts issued in recent days.

Antonio Guterres, the U.N.’s secretary-general, said he was “deeply disappointed” that no consensus was reached.

Talks centered on electrification, funding for developing nations and ways to respond to scientific warnings about rising global temperatures, with the 1.5 degrees Celsius target likely to be overshot.

But on Sunday, after negotiations overran by almost two days, the latest cover proposal made no mention of fossil fuels, prompting outcry from governments and campaigners.

Speaking on behalf of the EU, Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’Brien said the conference was “hijacked by some oil states,” when asked by Reuters about Saudi Arabia’s role in the negotiations. CNBC has contacted Saudi Arabia for comment.

The EU said it rejected the deal because the text “does not respond to the science” of climate change. “We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” it said in a statement Sunday.

The U.K. government “does not believe the cover decision proposed by the Presidencies meets the moment,” it said on Sunday. “It moves us backwards on the science when we must accelerate implementation,” it said.

Vulnerable nations

Representatives of island nations — vulnerable to the effects of climate change — refused to sign the draft text. “Three years ago in Dubai, the nations of the world agreed by consensus to transition away from fossil fuels in their energy systems,” Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas, said in an online statement, referring to the UAE Consensus made at COP28 in 2023.

“Small island states produce less than 1% of global emissions, yet we carry the weight of a crisis we did not cause. We have brought plans, commitments and patience to three decades of these talks. Antalya exhausted that patience,” Davis said.

Albert Salamanca, a senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute Asia, told CNBC via email that the lack of consensus on a deal is “tantamount to a death sentence for vulnerable communities still unable to respond in a timely manner to emerging risks.”

Yasin Akgul | Afp | Getty Images

Developing nations are facing “abandonment,” according to Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa. He described the event as “the worst COP ever” in an online statement, adding that “rich countries blocked the creation of a just transition mechanism.”

The World Wildlife Fund, or WWF, described the lack of progress on finance for developing nations as having “real-world consequences for the lives and livelihoods of the planet’s most vulnerable communities,” in an online statement.

Nonsikelelo Nkomo-Mabobe, business development manager at Solidaridad, an organization that promotes fair supply chains, welcomed some of the language in COP31′s proposed Antalya Pact, with “promising signs around food security, which is acknowledged as heavily affected by climate impacts.” But she said a finance gap remains.

“Funding must be easier for frontline communities to access, and it must be traceable once it has been disbursed,” Nkomo-Mabobe said in an email to CNBC.

The WWF welcomed the engagement from participants of the COP31 Action Agenda, which comprises of businesses and other non-governmental organizations. “Momentum from communities, cities and businesses is real despite what happened in the negotiating rooms,” it said.

Electrification pledge

A major goal of COP31 was to increase global electrification to 35% by 2035 — up from 23% today, with a Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package announced on Thursday as a “first milestone” to achieve this.

The U.N.’s Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said on Sunday that “around half” the global economy is accelerating electrification, adding that the package had made “real economy” progress. More than 90 countries signed the pledge, according to Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, COP31′s president of negotiations.

“Frustratingly,” the pledge does not detail how the electricity will be generated, according to Ellen Dorsey, executive director of the Wallace Global Fund — around 57% of electricity was generated by fossil fuels in 2025, according to think tank Ember.

Dorsey urged states to provide electricity to those in developing countries. “Will we ensure governments provide electricity to hundreds of millions who lack it, by leapfrogging fossil fuels build-out and instead invest in small-scale renewables?” she said in an email to CNBC.

Ocean life

Preserving sea life has “often been overlooked” in climate negotiations, according to the U.N. The language referring to oceans in the draft cover decision was “slightly weakened,” according to Nicolas Entrup, director of international relations at marine conservation organization OceanCare, in an email to CNBC. But he said he was hopeful that the Antalya Ocean Current, a U.N. plan to hold future talks on oceans and climate change, would be carried forward.

More than 95% of island and coastal nations now have ocean preservation in their climate plans, but around 60% of those commitments rely on external funding, according to research by ocean conservancy groups. Scientists also called for ongoing investment to monitor oceans beyond short-term research.

“I share the deep disappointment of many: COP31 has been unable to agree on issues related to both Presidency’s led decisions,” Stiell said. Turkey and Australia shared the presidency at this year’s conference.

- CNBC’s Sawdah Bhaimiya contributed to this report.

Clarification: This story has been updated to more accurately reflect Nicolas Entrup’s comments.

title: Canada Races to Double Electricity Supply as Electrification Lags - The Energy Mix
description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney this summer set goals to double the country’s electricity production by 2050.
Electrification can yield productivity gains and lower costs in many applications, especially when coupled with investments in energy efficiency.
“It is wildly needed,” the former chair of the Canada Electricity Council said in an interview with The Mix.
Prime Minister Mark Carney this summer set goals to double the country’s electricity production by 2050.
“It is wildly needed,” the former chair of the Canada Electricity Council said in an interview with The Mix.
text:
We’re told this is the dawning of the age of electricity, with electrons rather than oil, gas, or coal set to dominate new energy production across the world. However, many battles have yet to be won to replace fossil fuels in the cars we drive, the buildings we heat, and the industries that sustain our economy.

Prime Minister Mark Carney this summer set goals to double the country’s electricity production by 2050. Electrification of the Canadian economy, he stated, is the path to affordability, to competitiveness, and to sustainability.

Using electricity is typically more efficient than burning hydrocarbons in vehicles and furnaces, is less subject to geopolitically driven price spikes, and does not emit climate-changing carbon emissions when derived from renewable sources or nuclear power.

At the United Nations COP31 in Türkiye last week, Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin signed the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge to accelerate the global energy transition so that the world gets 35% of its final energy needs from electricity by 2035. The figure currently stands at 23%.

But that ambitious COP31 pledge is not binding and the goal is a global average, not a Canadian target. While the federal government is driving investment in electricity supply, it has shown less ambition for accelerating energy efficiency or the transition off fossil fuels in transportation, buildings, and industry.

“Canada can only reach 35% electrification domestically if we adopt the net-zero scenario of actions, which we are not doing,” Jessica McIlroy, director of government relations for Pembina Institute, said in an email. A scenario that aims for net-zero by 2050 would include a host of regulatory and other policies to accelerate the transition.

“What we need is an actual alignment of how and when we’re going to build out new renewable energy with how and when we’ll electrify energy end use to reach our 2050 commitments.”

According to the Canada Energy Regulator, this country uses electricity to meet 18% of its energy needs, with huge variations among provinces and territories.

In a letter to the prime minister this fall, several clean energy advocacy groups urged the government to adopt a “triple-double” approach—focused not only on building out the grid but also doubling the amount of renewable energy and the efficiency of energy use throughout the economy.

“Doubling electricity supply alone will not guarantee that Canadians receive the full benefits of the investments being made,” the advocates said.

title: Texas Pacific Land to buy EagleRock in $3 billion deal - BOE Report
description:
Texas Pacific Land Corp agreed to acquire Permian Basin land and water company EagleRock Land LLC in an all-stock deal with an implied equity value of about $3 billion, the companies said on Monday.
The deal comes as demand for water sourcing, recycling and disposal infrastructure grows alongside oilfield development in the Permian Basin, where operators increasingly seek integrated services to reduce costs and support drilling and completion activities.
Here are few more details: * The deal would combine Texas Pacific Land’s surface and royalty holdings and water business with EagleRock’s acreage, water infrastructure and relationships with large Permian operators * The deal, which is expected to close in the first half of 2027, includes EagleRock operating subsidiary units as well as Class A shares * Each EagleRock Class A share would convert into 0.0831 shares of a new holding company, New Titan Holdings, which TPL expects to rename as Texas Pacific Land Corp at the deal’s closing * The acquisition would give the combined company about 1 million fee-owned surface acres and another 105,000 acres of water-solutions dedications across the Permian’s Delaware and Midland sub-basins * Current TPL shareholders are expected to own about 86% of the combined company, with EagleRock shareholders and operating-unit holders owning the remainder * Shares of Texas Pacific Land up nearly 4% and EagleRock’s shares surge 16% in premarket trading * The deal is projected to be accretive to TPL’s 2027 free cash flow per share before synergies (Reporting by Dharna Bafna in Bengaluru; Editing by Shailesh Kuber)
text:
Texas Pacific Land Corp agreed to acquire Permian Basin land and water company EagleRock Land LLC in an all-stock deal with an implied equity value of about $3 billion, the companies said on Monday.

The deal comes as demand for water sourcing, recycling and disposal infrastructure grows alongside oilfield development in the Permian Basin, where operators increasingly seek integrated services to reduce costs and support drilling and completion activities.

Here are few more details:

* The deal would combine Texas Pacific Land’s surface and royalty holdings and water business with EagleRock’s acreage, water infrastructure and relationships with large Permian operators

* The deal, which is expected to close in the first half of 2027, includes EagleRock operating subsidiary units as well as Class A shares

* Each EagleRock Class A share would convert into 0.0831 shares of a new holding company, New Titan Holdings, which TPL expects to rename as Texas Pacific Land Corp at the deal’s closing

* The acquisition would give the combined company about 1 million fee-owned surface acres and another 105,000 acres of water-solutions dedications across the Permian’s Delaware and Midland sub-basins

* Current TPL shareholders are expected to own about 86% of the combined company, with EagleRock shareholders and operating-unit holders owning the remainder

* Shares of Texas Pacific Land up nearly 4% and EagleRock’s shares surge 16% in premarket trading

* The deal is projected to be accretive to TPL’s 2027 free cash flow per share before synergies

(Reporting by Dharna Bafna in Bengaluru; Editing by Shailesh Kuber)

text:
During this unusually quiet hurricane season, the Bahamas has been building its own storm-proof energy grid – and breaking free of fossil fuels.

The real work happens in the quiet moments. When there are no storms, no immediate crises. It's in this downtime – such as this year's unusually quiet Atlantic hurricane season, thanks to the strongest El Niño on record – that the Caribbean can prepare for the ever-stronger storms coming its way.

"One lesson many of us have learned is the islands that use the quieter years to prepare are often the ones that recover most effectively," says David Gumbs, an Anguillan who has spent much of his career bringing renewable energy to the Caribbean – particularly the Bahamas.

"The best preparation happens months and often years before it's needed," he says.

Across the Caribbean, a core part of this preparation is the race to build renewable infrastructure – not just to become hurricane-resilient, but energy self-sufficient too. Bahamians often face some of the most expensive energy bills in the world from costly diesel generators and saw the cost of fuel increase by an average of 33% in just one year.

The Bahamas has now launched a real-time experiment testing whether energy security and climate resilience can be built in the wake of a natural disaster, and whether a small island nation can break free from an outdated fossil fuel system.

Gumbs knows better than most about the importance of preparing for hurricanes. He was sheltering in his bathroom at his house in Anguilla when Irma, a Category 5 hurricane, struck in 2017, and destroyed 90% of the island's electricity infrastructure.

"My home was a wreck, half of my team had their homes damaged, and some were completely destroyed," says Gumbs, who is the director of the Islands Energy Program at the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI), a non-profit developing renewable power initiatives across the Caribbean.

"It left us psychologically discouraged… and emotionally tormented. I was trying to rebuild my mental state whilst looking at [an electricity] grid that was devastated." Gumbs' experience shaped his desire to bring energy security and extreme weather resilience to Caribbean countries.

The Caribbean is highly susceptible to extreme weather and the Bahamas has experienced three major hurricanes in the past decade.

Two years after Irma, Hurricane Dorian struck the Bahamas, becoming one of the most devastating natural disasters in the country's history and the most powerful storm to hit since records began.

After Dorian, islanders faced a choice: rebuild the old diesel-dependent energy grid, which was costly and unreliable, or try something new. "People wanted to rebuild better," says Gumbs, who has spent extensive time in the Bahamas establishing microgrids. These are small, local electricity networks that can generate, store and distribute power independently of the main grid.

The benefits of microgrids

Microgrids can use hydropower, wind turbines, solar panels, or traditional fuels like diesel. Renewable microgrids combine several energy sources with battery storage to provide reliable electricity when sunlight or wind is unavailable. Not everyone needs their own battery – there is a communal battery that serves the group. This makes them more resilient than the main grid because they are less dependent on long distance power lines, or importing expensive fuel.

A grid that wasn't working

Hurricane Dorian became a turning point for the Bahamas and its energy system. The main utility company, Bahamas Power and Light, had to "rebuild from scratch" – and was two years before locals could reconnect to the main grid again. Hospitals and schools were destroyed, and the economy devastated – Dorian caused damages equivalent to 25% of the Bahamas' GDP.

Abacos, a chain of palm-fringed islands in the north of the Bahamas, bore the brunt of the destruction along with neighbouring Grand Bahama, with thousands of homes levelled. Seventy four people died, with 282 people still missing, and 70,000 left homeless. The energy infrastructure on the Abacos was "ransacked".

But the scale of devastation and outdated energy infrastructure posed an opportunity: residents could tailor the grid to their energy needs – rather than having to repair an old system. The island had never been connected to a national electricity grid. Bahamas Power and Light operated a local electricity network, with power generated by burning imported diesel. Even prior to Dorian, outages were common, leaving residents and businesses reliant on private diesel generators.

"There's a tough environment here," says Gumbs, whose organisation RMI has been a key player in designing renewable microgrids for public facilities across the Bahamas. "Lots of storms and corrosion make the power systems expensive and difficult to maintain," he says.

Beacons in the dark

In the aftermath of Irma and Dorian, the Bahamian government invited energy companies to develop long-term energy solutions for both the Abaco and Eleuthera islands. "Continue down a path of expensive, unreliable energy or pivot towards a future where energy is sustainable, affordable and secure," Prime Minister Philip Davis said at the time.

Microgrid projects at three Abaco schools now provide 90% of their energy through solar and storage batteries, as well as doubling up as a hurricane shelter. One school was experiencing up to five power cuts a day; the new system has allowed lessons to continue uninterrupted. The Abaco school systems – which serve around 10,000 residents – provide a "very tangible example", of how well microgrids are working, says Gumbs.

"The principal of Man-O-War Cay Primary described looking across Abaco during an island-wide outage and seeing the school still illuminated because its solar panels and batteries were supplying power," Gumbs says. "In the principal's words, the system meant that 'life can continue'. That is really the resilience value of a microgrid."

Two further microgrids are in the works, which will power two medical clinics and a government complex.

"As an island nation, the Bahamas has traditionally relied on imported fuels for electricity generation," says Emre Ozer, EA Energy's project director in the Bahamas. Increasing the use of renewable energy improves the country's long-term energy security, by reducing dependence on international fuel markets. "[We're] helping build a cleaner and more resilient electricity system for future generations," says Ozer.

EA Energy came to Abaco in 2024, as part of a government initiative to bring clean energy to the islands. The company, which is 70% owned by a mix of Turkish and Bahamian private companies, and 30% by public shares, is building a hybrid microgrid project on the island – consisting of natural gas, solar and battery energy storage.

The two microgrids which EA Energy is building on these islands are not only designed to withstand extreme conditions, such as 200mph (322 km/h) winds, but are also hybrid, integrating solar, battery storage and gas-fired power into a single system, says Ozer. This means that renewable energy can be used when available, with the battery providing a fast response to fluctuations in usage, and the gas engines providing a stable supply when there isn't enough solar to meet demand.

When the grid comes online in May 2027, Ozer claims it will provide 1,305MW of electricity with a 20MwH battery capacity, a combination that will be enough to power roughly 2,000-3,000 households over one year – and 100% of Abaco's energy needs.

Small island nations have "a clean-slate advantage" when it comes to adopting renewable energy systems, says Mundu Mustafa, an expert in renewable energy systems at Kampala International University in Uganda, who has authored several papers on microgrids.

"[They] often have the opportunity to leapfrog directly to modern energy systems by placing solar, wind, and battery storage close to where electricity is used," he says, adding that it reduces the need for costly transmission infrastructure, lowers energy losses, and makes integration easier.

'Islanding': From vulnerability to strength

The new microgrids have several advantages over the old system – particularly when extreme weather hits. Fuel is not only costly but must be shipped in by boats which cannot access the islands during storms.

Many small island communities "depend on a single centralised power station or fragile transmission links, meaning one damaged line can leave entire communities without electricity for days or even weeks," says Mustafa.

During Dorian, the main power plant on Abaco largely survived the hurricane – it was the power lines that were destroyed, meaning there was no way of getting electricity to people.

Renewable grids improve resilience by generating and managing electricity locally. Their defining advantage, Mustafa notes, is "islanding" – the ability to disconnect from a damaged grid and continue to operate independently. Although the microgrids don't eliminate outages altogether, they can sustain priority services throughout prolonged outages, shifting resilience from distant infrastructure to local energy resources.

Microgrids also bring jobs to island communities. Of EA Energy's 60 employees, 10 are Bahamians, and Ozer says the company's focus is on training locals to provide job opportunities for years to come.

The RMI has a similar focus: running a six month-long training programme to upskill locals in how to transition to renewable energy, providing training to install and fix the grids – ensuring that during a storm, there's no need to wait for outside help. "Our approach is very different because we want to empower our community," says Gumbs.

The Bahamas is an important leader in the transition to microgrids, says Gumbs, but he sees the Caribbean's energy transition as a regional movement. The Virgin Islands is advancing virtual power plants which combine residential solar systems into one orchestrated system, whilst Dominica is investing in a combination of renewables, including geothermal energy, which it expects to meet more than 70% of its energy needs by 2030.

Over in Puerto Rico, after Hurricane Maria exposed the vulnerability of a centralised grid in 2017, communities began to invest in solar and battery microgrids. The island now has a combination of community-led projects that are integrated into regional microgrid planning. According to Mustafa, it's one of the world's "most closely watched resilience transitions" – although there is still much more to be done.

Solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and all the modern technologies needed to build a grid are available, notes Gumbs. The harder challenge is creating the regulations and project pipelines needed to deploy them. Ensuring that renewable technology is designed to be extreme weather-proof is critical too – so it withstands the elements that destroyed its fossil fuel predecessors. But given this year's quiet season, the test may not come until next year.

For Gumbs, building a microgrid is more than just energy resilience. "In some ways, I had PTSD [after Irma], but seeing the hope and strength and power of our community coming together helped me heal," he says.

"Major storms leave physical damage, but they also leave lasting emotional memories. For many of us, resilience became deeply personal because we experienced firsthand what it means when critical systems fail and entire communities are forced to recover together."

title: What data centers can learn from decades of industrial development
description:
Data centers are bringing substantial investment to communities across the state, but the economic bargain that has traditionally accompanied industrial development is becoming more difficult to negotiate.
Data centers present new challenges to this traditional arrangement.
Property taxes may provide substantial local revenues, although incentives and abatements can reduce those returns.
The economic value generated by data centers may be considerable, but much of it accrues to companies and investors outside the host region.
This helps explain growing resistance to data centers.
text:
Texas is confronting a familiar problem in a new form. Data centers are bringing substantial investment to communities across the state, but the economic bargain that has traditionally accompanied industrial development is becoming more difficult to negotiate.

For generations, communities have accepted the demands of major industrial facilities in exchange for employment, tax revenues, local business activity and the prospect of lasting prosperity. The results have been inconsistent. Some places developed diversified economies and strong institutions; others remained dependent on industries whose financial returns were captured largely outside the region.

Data centers present new challenges to this traditional arrangement. Development is proceeding faster than many local governments can evaluate proposals, assess cumulative impacts or negotiate terms. Multibillion-dollar facilities require substantial electricity and sometimes water resources, yet typically generate relatively few permanent jobs after construction.

The ability of towns and cities to secure lasting benefits from major investments depends, in part, on their institutional capacity to negotiate agreements that capture and retain economic value locally. Decades of experience with oil and gas and other industries offer lessons for addressing this imbalance. Texas can draw on that experience to strengthen local expertise, give communities a more meaningful role in development decisions, make commitments enforceable and protect against long-term burdens.

The Abilene experience

In Abilene, the influx of workers constructing the Stargate data center has exacerbated an existing housing shortage, making housing less affordable for local residents. Electricity generation needed to serve these facilities can contribute to emissions and other environmental impacts. Property taxes may provide substantial local revenues, although incentives and abatements can reduce those returns.

The economic value generated by data centers may be considerable, but much of it accrues to companies and investors outside the host region. Communities must therefore evaluate whether the local benefits justify the infrastructure demands, environmental impacts and changes in land use associated with development.

This helps explain growing resistance to data centers. It also exposes a disparity in the ability of developers and local governments to evaluate projects and negotiate their terms.

A temporary moratorium can be a rational public-sector response when development moves faster than the institutions responsible for governing it. Slowing approvals provides time to assess cumulative impacts, establish standards and strengthen local capacity. On Nov. 17, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality resumed reviewing data center permits after the governor’s office indicated ERCOT had completed gathering information on community impacts, although the grid operator’s full findings are not scheduled for presentation until Dec. 10. But a pause, or even a moratorium, was never going to resolve the underlying problem. The more important question is what institutional capabilities Texas develops to address it.

The experience of other industries offers useful guidance.

text:
Ford has officially begun production at its $3 billion battery manufacturing plant in Marshall, Michigan, about 160 kilometers west of Detroit. The finished battery cells will be shipped to the company's plant in Louisville, Kentucky, where prototypes for a small pickup truck called the Fathom are being built. Ford CEO Jim Farley has introduced the Fathom as a direct competitor to Tesla and Chinese automakers.

Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries play a key role in Ford's strategy for producing affordable electric vehicle batteries. This battery technology is less expensive than the nickel batteries commonly used in many electric vehicles, while also promising greater durability. This is why many automakers are switching to LFP technology. However, although this technology is developed in the US, China dominates mass production, leading to difficulties for American automakers in securing domestic battery supplies.

The Marshall plant has the capacity to produce 40 batteries per minute, for a total capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours per year, split equally between electric vehicles and energy storage for Ford. However, this is only half of the original target of 40 gigawatt-hours, as Ford and the automotive industry have adjusted their ambitions for electric vehicles.

The "secret" from CATL helps Ford realize the challenge of reducing the cost of electric vehicles.

Ford stated that the high production rate will help reduce battery costs and has the potential for future expansion. To address the speed challenge, the company has utilized technology licensed from the Chinese corporation CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, emphasized that licensing technology from CATL is primarily about speed. He stated, "If we want to produce affordable electric vehicles in the U.S., we need to do it as quickly as possible." At the same time, Ford said it is learning to manufacture its own battery cells instead of simply licensing the technology to CATL. According to Ford, the company owns and operates the Marshall plant, while CATL provides the technology under a licensing agreement.

However, some officials in Washington disagreed with this approach. In a letter to Farley in September, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed concern about Ford's reliance on technology licensed from CATL. Ford responded that the letter was a "misguided attempt to attract public attention."

Nevertheless, this dispute could impact Ford's finances. A company spokesperson said they still expect the plant to qualify for a federal tax credit for battery production. If approved, this credit would help reduce battery production costs, supporting Ford in bringing the Fathom to market at a reasonable price.

Reportedly, while much of the manufacturing process is automated, Ford is still in the early stages of certifying the production process. The company expects to ramp up battery production next year, before Fathom's planned launch in Q4 2027.

text:
Social Investment Managers & Advisors (SIMA) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, have launched the Decarbonization of Textile, Apparel, & Footwear Suppliers (D-TAFS) Fund. The initiative is designed to provide long-term financing to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in textile, apparel and footwear supply chains, with a stated target to mobilize up to $400 million.

The fund brings together investors including IFC and Inditex, alongside the Global Environment Facility (GEF), FMO, Proparco, British International Investment, and the Apparel Impact Institute. Its first close is expected to reach $225 million, with additional fundraising rounds planned to reach the overall target.

Supply chain pressure meets a financing gap

Textile and apparel manufacturing remains a major employer across emerging markets. The initiative’s announcement cites that more than 60 million people work in the sector, and that 80% of those workers are women.

According to IFC and SIMA, many SMEs that supply global brands struggle to access the financing needed to invest in cleaner production, including lower-emissions energy systems, water efficiency and pollution reduction. The D-TAFS Fund is intended to address this gap by blending development and commercial capital and pairing finance with technical assistance.

How D-TAFS works

The fund uses a blended finance approach that combines commercial and development capital to provide debt financing on preferential terms. D-TAFS is structured to support projects that can help suppliers modernize operations and reduce environmental impact.

The announcement says eligible investments include energy-efficiency measures, renewable energy, water-reuse initiatives, wastewater treatment, and steps to reduce industrial pollution and improve chemical safety. It also notes the initiative will provide technical assistance to help borrowers identify, structure, and implement eligible projects.

Funding, investors, and expected deployment

IFC and Inditex are identified as the fund’s leading investors, with investments of $60 million and $50 million, respectively. Other participating investors include GEF, FMO, Proparco, British International Investment, and the Apparel Impact Institute.

D-TAFS is structured across two sub-funds: one providing loans directly to textile and apparel manufacturers, and another financing energy service companies and distributed energy developers that work with suppliers. The announcement indicates that projects will span different levels of the supply chain, from garment manufacturers to yarn and fabric suppliers.

The initiative’s geographic coverage is described as Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Latin America.

Why the fund emphasizes cleaner production

IFC and SIMA say the fund is intended to improve productivity, energy efficiency, and operational resilience while supporting quality jobs for workers in the sector. In the context of shifting market expectations toward more sustainable production, the initiative is also positioned as a competitiveness support mechanism for suppliers.

In remarks included in the announcement, Sarvesh Suri, IFC Regional Vice President for Asia and the Pacific, said small and medium-sized suppliers need access to affordable, appropriately structured financing to remain competitive, and that the fund brings together leading brands, investors, and suppliers around a shared solution.

Role for technical assistance and localization across the supply chain

Beyond financing, D-TAFS is designed to strengthen implementation capacity through technical assistance. The announcement states that this support will help suppliers in developing countries develop projects, align financing structures to their needs, and move from project identification to implementation.

By targeting both manufacturers and firms that provide energy and related services within supply chains, the fund’s design aims to enable investments that may require coordination across multiple actors—an approach that can be relevant for efforts to improve climate resilience and reduce industrial pollution in manufacturing regions.

Key Details

Initiative or programme: Decarbonization of Textile, Apparel, & Footwear Suppliers (D-TAFS) Fund

Lead organization: Social Investment Managers & Advisors (SIMA) and IFC (International Finance Corporation)

Partners: Inditex; Global Environment Facility (GEF); FMO; Proparco; British International Investment; Apparel Impact Institute

Funding amount: Target to mobilize $400 million; first close expected to reach $225 million

Geographic focus: Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and Latin America

Target groups: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across textile, apparel and footwear supply chains (including manufacturers and energy service companies/distributed energy developers)

Expected outcomes (as stated): Financing for energy-efficiency and renewable-energy projects, water-saving initiatives, and measures to reduce industrial pollution; improved competitiveness and support for quality jobs

Why This Matters

The D-TAFS Fund reflects a growing donor and investor focus on decarbonizing industrial supply chains through blended finance. For NGOs, civil society organizations and development practitioners, the announcement highlights how energy, water and pollution goals can be linked to employment in sectors with large female workforces.

The fund’s emphasis on preferential debt and technical assistance for SMEs may offer a practical model for designing support that reduces barriers to investment for mid-tier suppliers, not only large manufacturers. It also points to potential collaboration opportunities for local organizations that can strengthen project preparation, environmental compliance, and implementation support across diverse regions.

More broadly, the initiative aligns with trends toward climate-smart manufacturing and localization of implementation capacity, while also aiming to sustain jobs in communities dependent on textile and apparel production.

text:
Discussions to add electric vehicles to the domestic production tax credit, known as the Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), have intensified. As Chinese-made electric vehicles rapidly invade the domestic market, the National Assembly is forming a consensus on including electric vehicles in the tax credit, raising interest in whether support for the domestic automotive industry will be expanded.

According to the National Assembly and the automotive industry, the National Assembly's Finance and Economy Committee held a subcommittee meeting on the 23rd to address a revision bill for the Tax Exemption and Restriction Act that includes electric vehicles in the domestic production tax credit.

On this day, lawmakers reportedly formed a consensus on including electric vehicles in the tax credit but could not narrow the differences with the government. Consequently, it appears that a separate consultation involving committee secretaries and government officials will be held to coordinate related matters.

One legislative official stated, "Contrary to expectations, it seems that reaching a conclusion on including electric vehicles will not be easy," adding, "It does not seem that the Ministry of Finance will change its stance on reviewing the inclusion of electric vehicles in the tax credit."

The revision bill for the Tax Exemption and Restriction Act, jointly proposed by 19 lawmakers from both the ruling People Power Party (PPP) and the opposition Democratic Party (DP), aims to add electric vehicles to the domestic production tax credit to enhance the production competitiveness of the automotive industry.

Since electric vehicles were excluded from the domestic production tax credit in August, the industry has continued to raise concerns about fairness. The government selected six sectors, including secondary batteries and semiconductors, as support targets for the domestic production tax credit. In response, the industry has voiced the need to consider the conditions of the domestic automotive industry, which is threatened by the onslaught of Chinese-made electric vehicles.

The growing demand for tax support for electric vehicles is rooted in the encroachment of Chinese-made electric vehicles in the domestic market. Chinese electric vehicles are expanding their influence in the domestic market by leveraging lower prices compared to their counterparts. According to the Korea Automobile Mobility Industry Association (KAMA), the share of Chinese-made vehicles in the domestic electric vehicle market rose from 1.1% in 2021 to 33.9% last year, marking the third most significant growth among major global automobile-producing countries, following Mexico and Brazil.

Chinese automakers are entering the market by bypassing low export thresholds and domestic tariff barriers. The basic tariff applied to Chinese automobiles in Korea is only 8%. This contrasts sharply with the tariffs of 127.5% and 110% imposed on Chinese electric vehicles by the United States and India, respectively. The European Union, which is also trying to curb the entry of Chinese electric vehicles, has raised tariffs to as high as 45.3%.

The government has acknowledged the need for support for the domestic electric vehicle industry. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il stated during a press conference at the Government Sejong Center that the government understands that the next two to three years represent a golden time for the transition of the electric vehicle market and that it will make a comprehensive decision.

The government is expected to announce its position on the electric vehicle tax credit through a 'plan to strengthen electric vehicle competitiveness' later this month.

The automotive industry is calling for tax support at a level similar to that of Japan. Japan provides a subsidy of 400,000 yen (approximately 3.8 million won (KRW)) per electric vehicle to differentiate itself from foreign brands. The industry anticipates that the introduction of a tax credit will help induce domestic facility investment by automakers and secure production volumes for suppliers.

Kim Joo-hong, executive director of the Korea Automobile Mobility Industry Association, stated, "Chinese-made electric vehicles are entering the domestic market with price competitiveness based on massive support from their government, making it difficult to respond. It is urgent to reflect electric vehicles in the tax credit to enhance the competitiveness of domestic electric vehicles."

text:
GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC’s “Power Insider” newsletter.

POWER POINT

What I’m hearing from energy insiders

Is one of the greatest money-making trades of the last few years coming to an end?

No, I’m not talking about Nvidia or any of the data center- or AI-related power companies (although they have been crushed lately too… more on that on CNBC TV. Tune in!).

I’m talking about whether the epic boom in refinery-related stocks is unwinding. Over the last year, the jump in some of these companies has been nothing short of remarkable.

That jump is largely due to massive increases in margins, earnings, and cash flow. Those have occurred because of a big jump in what is called a crack spread. That is the difference between the price of oil and the finished price of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel. For most of this year, spreads have been soaring as disruptions and attacks on facilities and shipping in the Arabian Gulf, Hormuz, and deep inside Russia have played havoc with the market. In the last week or so, however, something big has changed: many of those spreads have started to tighten.

This seismic drop in spreads is causing a selloff in the aforementioned refinery companies.

If spreads continue to fall, these stocks may well keep selling off from recent highs. The upshot for investors may be that, as the shares come down, analysts see more upside. The median price target for Phillips 66 (PSX) now indicates a 20% gain from here, while smaller-cap Par Pacific (PARR) is double that.

Here are a few other key points to focus on heading into the Thanksgiving-shortened week.

I like to keep politics as much at arm’s length as possible — we all know that energy and politics (sadly) often go hand in hand. Energy policies coming from Washington, D.C., can drive — or destroy — investment dollars. With all the big shifts in the White House over the last 10 years (four years of Trump, four years of Biden, and now 2 years into Trump #2), energy policies can blow through Washington faster than a summer squall hits a wind turbine. But because federal policies can mean so much for specific companies, sectors, and investments, it’s important to follow the news flow.

That said, I’d like to take a moment to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA (and pronounced like the state in Mexico). Like much legislation, BAAJA is an obscure but important bill working its way through the American Congress. BAAJA does a lot of things, but what Power Insider readers care about is its focus on energy permitting reform. In a nutshell, BAAJA would help speed up the building of new electricity infrastructure. Again, that’s an overly simplistic view of a big bill, but it needs to be on your radar. The utility trade group Edison Electric Institute came out in favor of the legislation this month after the industry received some 11th-hour changes. See more about it in our recent interview with EEI President Drew Maloney here.

The bill passed the U.S. Senate in a vote late Thursday night. Now it moves to the House. Support for its final passage is also coming from the big LNG trade group, whose executive director said he “applauds the Senate for its bipartisan effort to pass meaningful, bipartisan, and durable permitting reforms aimed at delivering greater predictability, consistency, and certainty in the permitting, production, and export process for U.S. LNG. This legislation moves us closer to untangling red tape and eliminating overlapping agency reviews that can keep U.S. energy projects delayed for years.”

The Natural Gas Supply Association also chimed in, saying it urges Congress to see the bill as “a resource-agnostic and balanced reform agenda for boosting American energy security. It keeps strong environmental reviews in place, but it draws a firm line against the endless procedural delays that tie critical energy projects in knots for a decade.”

In my view, passing BAAJA is an important test of Congress’s appetite for helping the energy and electrical power industry, lowering costs, and speeding time to market. The old adage was correct: time is money. Literally. If BAAJA moves on through the House, we could see an upside move in some utility stocks and any company related to energy infrastructure.

Speaking of politics, the news is getting lost in the massive Anthropic (ANT) IPO, but the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) — whose importance I wrote about in the last edition — just decided to resume permitting for data centers. The Texas Tribune did a nice write-up on it, and you can read it here.

Remember: energy is politics.

It’s tough to say, but it’s true. The two are inextricably linked by policies created at both the federal and state levels. As I wrote in the last edition, some federally elected officials may have less impact on state-level issues — like the data center buildout — but they certainly have power over national laws. While many of you are enthralled, disgusted, or confused by sordid tales of Nvidia and Jensen-gate, keep one eye open on what happens in Washington, D.C.

Have a great week, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving, everyone.

Brian

THE ACTIONABLE INSIDER

Perhaps the big investor story — which is, like most things lately, related to Jensen-gate and Nvidia—is the sizable selloff in many AI, neocloud, and data center power-related stocks.

Painful for current shareholders, but big drops can also bring big opportunities. Wall Street believes that’s the case, at least right now. Look at some of the potential upside based on the stocks’ prices versus their price targets.

We spoke with the CEO of Applied Digital (APLD) about all of this on CNBC last week, and you can watch it here. He highlighted how the market may be getting these stock stories wrong because, at least with his company, he has long-term contracts with solid-credit companies. In that way, Applied Digital is more like a landlord than a “pure-play” AI company.

My take → While I’m not going to recommend a specific stock, I would add that it is critical for investors to understand the differences between these companies. While they may have some things in common, they are also different, with different business models, customers, leases, and sources of revenue.

Speaking of recommendations… here are two ideas for you:

A recent decline presents a nice opportunity in SOLV Energy (MWH). UBS analyst Jon Windham upgrades SOLV to buy from neutral, believing the market is “underappreciating several key tailwinds for SOLV given uncertainty around data center demand and higher interest rates.” UBS highlights how the stock has fallen lately despite making two deals and beating and raising recent guidance. UBS says now is an “attractive entry point” for SOLV. (Side note: MWH is a great stock ticker.)

While markets overall fall, BMO remains bullish on Bloom Energy (BE). After speaking with the company, the analyst is upgrading Bloom to outperform, saying he remains “increasingly confident of BE’s commercial traction” and that he still has conviction even with the recent drop in shares. While analyst Ameet Thakkar did cut his target to $230 from $260, that’s still 50% upside from the current price. Bloom shares have tumbled 45% since October 1.

Also…

I was recently asked for my opinion on the price of oil. Here’s my take. The market clearly wants to push oil contract prices lower and has for a few months. But, as I’ve said and reported for a while, don’t confuse the futures (paper) price with the actual price. Yes, shipping rates and insurance rates have come down from recent highs — and there is a good amount of oil now flowing through Hormuz — but the cost of a physical barrel of crude is still well above the futures contract. If we get real, longer-lasting peace around Iran, oil prices will fall. There is plenty of oil in the world. That said, if bombs and missiles start firing again, oil prices will firm. I know that’s a non-answer answer, but the oil market is truly headline-driven right now. My late good friend Boone Pickens (later in life, he didn’t like being called by the “T” in his first name) used to avoid giving a set price target and instead give a directional quote, so I’ll do the same: the odds of oil being lower in two months than it is today are 75%.

Also, part #2…

Last week, I had a one-on-one with Vimal Kapur, chair and CEO of Honeywell International (HON), at an RBC conference in New York City. While the conversation wasn’t filmed, I can tell you that Kapur offered investors reassurance that his order book is doing very, very well. This is important because Honeywell is huge in the things that make other things work. Its sensors go into a ton of energy facilities, from refineries to LNG facilities. Honeywell is a leading indicator of spending and buildouts, so if it keeps getting orders, it’s a good sign for macro energy.

Bottom line: Watch Honeywell stock as a potential “tell.”

INSIDE LINE

This week’s Inside Line interview takes a different approach. We hit our friend Craig Johnson up for actionable insights into energy and stocks. Craig is managing director and chief market technician at Piper Sandler. He recently appeared on Power Lunch to talk about markets and stocks. He mentioned being bullish on energy, so we wanted to dig in just a little bit more.

TAKE A LOOK

This week, we had the pleasure of chatting with Balaji Krishnamurthy, president of Chevron Australia. We spoke at length about natural gas, the impact of disruptions, and long-term demand from Chevron customers in the Asia-Pacific region.

watch now

RANDOM, BUT INTERESTING

This is a bit of a local RBI for the New York City area, but one I felt was important to highlight. New York’s electric grid operator just came out with a massive warning for everyone in our region: in just a couple of years, there may not be enough electricity supply to power our needs. A new report shows a deficit in seven years, with a nearly 2 GW power hole in a decade. That’s a number of big power plants’ worth of energy. Get your solar panels on and buy that backup generator! I’ll call this one random, but scary.
