text:
ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. – The east side of Orange County doesn’t have a skyline. It has smokestacks.

The Stanton Energy Center, run by the Orlando Utilities Commission, sits a few miles from the restaurants and homes of Avalon Park. It burns natural gas and coal, and it has solar panels on site. Most people nearby say they rarely think about it.

“From zero to 10?” Avalon Park resident Manouchka said when asked how often she thinks about the plant. “Minus five. It does not register.”

But what happens at Stanton is changing, and not in the direction OUC had previously planned.

OUC initially planned to put one of Stanton’s two coal-fired units into an extended shutdown at the end of May 2026, part of the utility’s long-running move away from coal.

Then the federal government stepped in. On June 4, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed an emergency order requiring OUC to keep that coal unit, known as Stanton Unit 1, available to run. The Department of Energy later extended the order through Nov. 30. Click here to see the order.

“The Department of Energy said, hey, let’s pump the brakes on this and ensure that we have enough capacity to meet our current needs,” said Orlando Alancastro, OUC’s vice president of transmission.

The emergency order points to the growth of data centers. It says that in Florida, “projections for resource and transmission growth lag behind what is needed to support new data centers and other large loads.”

“As of April 2026, eight data centers are planned for construction in Florida,” the order says.

OUC’s CEO, Clint Bullock, raised the same concern at a public workshop earlier this month.

“The size of these hyperscalers is like nothing we’ve ever seen. You can’t forecast it into your traditional forecasting. That’s why this is a concern,” Bullock said. Hyperscalers are the massive data centers run by companies such as Google and Amazon.

OUC says data centers are only part of the picture. The utility points to faster-than-expected growth in electric vehicles, more manufacturing, and a lack of new power generation across Florida.

“There hasn’t been a whole lot of new generation that has been built in the last several years,” Alancastro said.

Recent winter and summer weather events have also increased peak energy demand. As a result, OUC is increasing its reserve margin from 15% to 20% to help ensure reliable service during periods of high demand.

At the workshop, OUC proposed its Electric Integrated Resource Plan, a 20-year roadmap, which does not take coal off the table. The workshop presentation is posted on OUCFuturePlanning.com.

Under the plan, Stanton Unit 1 comes back online in 2028, converted so it can run on either coal or natural gas. Stanton Unit 2 gets the same conversion in 2029. The plan does not set an end date for burning coal at Stanton.

“It leverages existing infrastructure. The cost to convert those units are far more economical than building a new resource,” Alancastro said.

The plan also adds 150 megawatts of solar and 100 megawatts of battery storage by 2035. A gas plant with carbon capture and 345 megawatts of nuclear power are penciled in for the 2040s. Castro described those as placeholders that could change as technology develops.

OUC says the plan still meets its goals of cutting carbon emissions 50% by 2030 and 75% by 2040, compared with 2005 levels.

Coal’s share has already shrunk. According to OUC, coal made up 41% of its generating capacity in 2019 and 27% in 2025. Solar grew from less than 1% to 11% over the same period.

What it means for your bill

OUC says the plan would raise bills by about 1% a year for the next 5 years.

There is some short-term relief. OUC is proposing a fuel charge cut that would lower a typical residential bill, based on 1,000 kilowatt-hours a month, by about $5 starting in April 2027.

Avalon Park resident Jenna Egensteiner said she supports cleaner energy but wants the details. “Cleaner energy is obviously where you want to go. It’s just how, when, how much, for what,” she said.

name: Indiana Environment
title: Solar vitriol engulfs Indiana counties, keeping power off the grid - IndyStar
description:
When solar projects come to town, some landowners sign leases that promise financial security.
Across Indiana, solar opposition can turn ugly.
After inheriting the land, Harrington and McCay continued to lease it, generating a small income.
At first glance, solar projects seem like a win-win for rural counties and Indiana’s electric grid alike.
Anti-solar signs have cropped up along Indiana county roads, and in several Indiana counties, the pushback against solar has led to bullying and harassment, threats and intimidation and a slew of county-wide bans or restrictions on solar development.
text:
When solar projects come to town, some landowners sign leases that promise financial security. But sometimes those projects are halted in their tracks, at the last minute.

Across Indiana, solar opposition can turn ugly. Landowners say they've faced harassment, bullying and threats.

County government has the authority to green light or stop energy projects, but some energy experts believe the the state needs to provide more resources as counties wade into uncharted territory.

When Jim McCune passed away on Aug. 6, 2014, he left nearly 800 acres of Indiana farmland and forest to his two adult daughters. Darla Harrington and Rhonda McCay, both married with families of their own, named the Marshall County farm in honor of the man who taught them how to pick rock and love thy neighbor.

The sisters, however, can’t farm it.

As their father developed health issues and medical bills piled on, he retired, sold much of the pricey equipment necessary for modern farming and rented out the land to a close friend. After inheriting the land, Harrington and McCay continued to lease it, generating a small income. But they worry a time will come when it won't be easy for their children, who will one day split the land six ways, to hold on to it.

In 2019, Harrington thought she had found a lifeline that would preserve McCune Farm's future. A solar company came knocking. Geenex, a utility-scale solar developer, wanted to lease several hundred acres of the land in a multi-decade agreement. Harrington and McCay hoped the lease would bring in more than enough revenue to persuade their children to keep the land.

Then the rest of Marshall County found out.

That's when "all hell broke loose," Harrington said. Anti-solar sentiment quickly devolved into harassment, threats and ostracization. The dream of steady solar income that could have sustained the farm for upwards of 30 years evaporated almost overnight.

At first glance, solar projects seem like a win-win for rural counties and Indiana’s electric grid alike. Through lucrative leases that often span decades, solar farms have helped rural farmers retire, pay down medical debt and keep land in the family as the agricultural industry faces staggering declines.

Solar power, which converts sunlight into electric currents, is the cheapest form of electricity for ratepayers. It's also a timely solution to meeting rising electricity demand. Solar is considered the fastest form of power to deploy, from breaking ground to putting additional megawatts on the grid.

Despite the charms of sunshine-fueled electricity, utility-scale solar farms can be difficult to build in some parts of Indiana. Multiple projects across several counties have been shut down abruptly, sometimes after vicious fights that leave communities bruised and weary.

When two solar developers in Marshall County, including Geenex, worked through the county zoning process in 2024, anti-solar opposition erupted with vehemence. Crowds showed up at county meetings, which were eventually held in auditoriums and church sanctuaries to accommodate everyone (and inspire respectful language, one pastor said before a nearly four-hour meeting at the Plymouth Wesleyan Church).

In 2025 the county voted to ban solar projects for two years, dashing the McCune sisters' hopes. But they lost more than money; relationships with many of their community members, including one of their father's closest friends, were left fractured.

“The things they said about my sister and I, how we’re just wanting money and our dad is rolling over in his grave. It’s very hurtful. We admired our dad. We love him. And people were saying we were making decisions that would have hurt him,” Harrington said, shaking her head in disbelief. “Every time we made a decision or did research, it was, ‘How can we honor him? How can we keep the land?’”

Concern over solar often stems from unverified claims, disagreement over property rights and deeply personal feelings regarding how rural Indiana counties are changing. Anti-solar signs have cropped up along Indiana county roads, and in several Indiana counties, the pushback against solar has led to bullying and harassment, threats and intimidation and a slew of county-wide bans or restrictions on solar development.

Unlike Wisconsin and Michigan, where state government has substantial control over where and when large energy projects can set up shop, the power of zoning in Indiana largely sits with county officials, some of whom have been forced to make consequential decisions about Indiana's electricity grid while staring down community in-fighting.

"We're in a time of growing energy demand, and we needed megawatts on the grid yesterday," said Topher Anderson, the director of programs and operations at the Indiana Conservative Alliance for Energy. "These local fights that are all being regulated at the county level determine the future of our state. It's a huge opportunity and roadblock right now that's made it really difficult."

Vitriol and acrimony abound statewide

Utility-scale solar energy boomed across Indiana in 2025, but not every county is amenable to this form of energy generation. Threats of violence cropped up after local government meetings in Noble County last year, prompting County Commissioner Anita Hess to vote against a county-wide solar moratorium. Because the moratorium would likely bring more public debate, Hess said she voted against the measure to avoid creating an "arena for more of these types of threats." Solar opposition led to death threats against county commissioners in Knox County, according to a local news station. As the solar debate heightened in Clark County, a Board of Zoning Appeals member, Bob Ellison, resigned one month after taking the role, citing personal attacks against his family. Harrington said one person threatened her physical safety one night after a county meeting.

'Everyone is just nasty'

Kerri Vaughn, a landowner in Clark County, understands the skepticism about renewable energy. What she doesn't quite comprehend is how the debate becomes quite so ugly.

A solar company approached Vaughn and her husband before the pandemic. The lease they offered to sign would provide nearly $80,000 annually, which could help pay off nearly $300,000 that the family accrued in medical debt after Vaughn went through treatment for breast cancer.

Still, Vaughn said, they were not interested: "We've always been conservative. We have always felt like the Green New Deal was kind of shoved down our throats."

Plus, Vaughn had heard that solar could be dangerous for human and environmental health, lower nearby property values and harm agricultural communities. But when the pandemic left Vaughn and her husband with plenty of time on their hands, they decided to do some research – just to make sure they were right. They read about solar's positive economic impact on rural economies and how the projects can let farmland rest, leaving the soil in better shape.

Vaughn's research, however, did not prepare her for how her county would respond to the proposed project. As anti-solar opposition grew, she saw neighbors get bullied online, watched videos targeting her directly and learned to brace for county meetings.

"When you go into these meetings, and I've had to stand in front of their group because there weren't any seats, you could hear them whispering, 'What a piece of' – you know. About me," Vaughn said.

And the outcry didn't just impact her, Vaughn said; she thinks it swayed county officials.

“Everyone is just nasty, trying to scare you out of it. Most of these [zoning officials] are appointed. They did not sign up for this, and it scares them. And they just fold,” she said.

The county passed an ordinance in 2025 that restricted how developers could design solar projects. It included a setback that disqualified nearly half of Vaughn's farm from the solar lease. She was bewildered.

“If this was turned down for a legitimate reason, okay. That’s totally fine. But I have yet to hear anything legitimate,” Vaughn said.

Solar opponents explain their stance in a variety of ways.

Some worry about the future of Indiana farmland, despite a clause in many leases guaranteeing thorough removals after the life of the project. Others theorize about chemical leaks and property right infringement. And some detractors cite their frustration with the aesthetic effect of solar panels.

Counties have the authority, but do they have the right resources?

Despite Indiana's desire to increase energy generation and keep electricity affordable, solar projects that could address both goals have gotten harder to build.

The state does not keep data on how many solar projects or megawatts have been kept off the grid by county bans or ordinances, according to Indiana Energy Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski.

The projects abandoned by developers in Marshall County would have brought 350 megawatts on the grid. Orion's Idlewild Project, which would have leased the Vaughns' land, was designed to produce nearly 500 megawatts. With renewable energy off the table, power generation that is slower to build and more dangerous for human and environmental health – such as coal, natural gas and backup diesel generators – becomes the fallback.

State officials say they want to see more solar energy on the grid, which would mean fewer moratoriums.

“As energy demand grows, we need more generation on the grid, not less,” Jaworowski wrote in a statement to IndyStar. “Moratoriums on solar or any other energy source undermine reliability, create unnecessary barriers to investment, limit future supply, and can ultimately increase costs for consumers. The path to energy affordability is growth, competition, and investment in new generation, not bottlenecks.”

But the energy secretary demurred when asked if the power of siting should be in the hands of the state, not the counties.

“The state respects local decision-making and does not impose a one-size-fits-all mandate,” Jaworowski said.

In both 2021 and 2025, legislation attempting to consolidate state authority over siting failed to become law. Nor do most energy experts endorse handing this power entirely to the state and taking away local control. Still, many believe the current system isn't serving Indiana farmers or the grid.

Anderson, of ICAE, doesn't want to see authority stripped away from counties, but he's not sure that every county is governing appropriately. To thread the needle of supporting local government and supporting landowner rights, Anderson would like the state to compile a database of research and relevant information that county commissioners with little or no energy expertise can lean on to make sound zoning decisions.

Brian Flory, a program director with Solar United Neighbors, has traveled across Indiana, sitting in zoning meetings and meeting with landowners. He's seen communities struggle with overwhelming decisions about siting solar and wind, as well as battery storage and data centers. Despite witnessing some contentious debates, Flory said he and his colleagues don't want to see authority stripped from county government. Rather, they want counties to have more resources.

"Local control definitely needs to be a part of the solution. I think that is also a place where the state needs to step in and provide more clarity for counties and developers and for local groups, chambers of commerce, just for everybody to have a clear sense of the rules of the road," Flory said. "Currently we don't have that."

When counties erupt into chaos, the noise may also drown out a very real concern of some opposed to solar farms, Flory said. The pain of watching rural life transform as solar becomes the preferred crop is not easy to express in a county zoning meeting.

“There is a deeply held emotional concern to a changing way of rural life, and there is a way to honor and acknowledge that experience,” Flory said. “But then there’s the social media stuff. And the derision. Those things all intermix really easily.”

For Harrington and her sister, solar power was a way to hold on to that heritage longer, even as the modern world encroaches. Now, the sisters are not entirely sure what they will do. They discussed selling the land after losing the prospect of the solar lease but ultimately decided to keep holding on to it for their father's sake. At least for now.

“His name ends with us,” Harrington said. “We just feel that if we sell, that’s the end of his legacy. His name will be gone. And that saddens me. I want it to go on.”

Booth: N3554, Las Vegas Convention Center | Show dates: November 16–19, 2026

AGM focuses on the R&D and industrialization of advanced materials, with businesses spanning GaAs concentrator photovoltaics, zinc-nickel batteries, zinc-air flow batteries, and PEO solid-state batteries, while advancing an integrated solar-storage-charging architecture. description:
Multiple countries rejected a proposed text that failed to deliver climate justice, particularly by not mentioning fossil fuels as the primary driver of climate change.
Furthermore, industry lobbyists heavily promoted risky and unproven technologies, which arguably include carbon capture and storage, that could prolong the use of fossil fuels.

They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use.
text:
Multiple countries rejected a proposed text that failed to deliver climate justice, particularly by not mentioning fossil fuels as the primary driver of climate change. Furthermore, industry lobbyists heavily promoted risky and unproven technologies, which arguably include carbon capture and storage, that could prolong the use of fossil fuels.

High-income countries, the most responsible for global warming, obstructed progress on climate finance, adaptation and just transition. The co-presidencies, Türkiye and Australia, failed to secure an outcome that responded to the demands of lower-income countries, Indigenous Peoples, civil society and communities most affected by climate change.

Türkiye prioritised increasing global electrification, but the proposed outcome neither committed to this being produced by renewable energy nor addressed profound inequalities in energy access. For example, more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still live without electricity. Electrification must support a just transition and serve people, not power artificial intelligence and data centres with fossil fuels to boost the profits of Big Tech and fossil fuel companies in high income countries while hundreds of millions remain without affordable and reliable renewable energy.

Lobbyists from polluting industries and their financial backers attended in record numbers, while human rights defenders and climate activists faced barriers to participation and restrictions on peaceful protest and expression, including within the UN-controlled venue. Although the People’s Climate March passed without incident, COP31 took place amid a wider crackdown in Türkiye, particularly against LGBTI+ people and organisations.

“Countries from across regions were right to reject the colossal betrayal that the COP31 co-presidencies tried to pass off as climate action” said Ann Harrison, Climate Justice Policy Advisor at Amnesty International, responding to the conclusion of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, without the adoption of a cover decision. “They resisted a polluters’ charter designed to protect corporate profits while sacrificing people and the planet. They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use. Rejecting the dangerous ‘cover decision’ text was an important act of resistance. It prevented a predatory world order imposing a terrible outcome while hiding under the mask of consensus. But COP31 itself was a colossal failure. After two weeks of obstruction by high-income historically high emitting states, COP31 failed to deliver progress towards the fossil fuel phase out, finance for adaptation and loss and damage and just transition measures urgently needed to protect people’s rights and survival. Responsibility lies with the high-income, historically high-emitting states that blocked climate justice and the co-presidencies that tried to force through an outcome serving corporate interests. The rejection of a bad deal must not obscure the political failure that produced it. Communities already facing deadly floods, wildfires, droughts, displacement and hunger have been abandoned yet again. From the devastation in Nepal to deadly extreme weather across the world, the climate crisis is not waiting for governments to overcome their divisions. Governments must now deliver what COP31 failed to provide. The route from Antalya must lead to the Pacific in July 2027, where Tuvalu and Ireland will co-host the Second International Conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels, and then to COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. These meetings must move beyond red lines and obstruction to deliver a full, fast, fair and funded phase-out of fossil fuels, backed by massively scaled up grant-based and non-debt-creating climate finance to meet the actual level of need. People facing deadly floods, wildfires, droughts, hunger and displacement cannot wait through another cycle of broken promises. COP32 must not repeat this betrayal. It must put the rights, demands and leadership of the people most affected by climate change ahead of the interests of polluters.”

Amnesty International has repeatedly called on states to deliver a full, fast, fair and funded phase-out of fossil fuels during the COP process, as well as urging the provision of grants-based and non-debt-creating climate finance at the scale to match need; the scrapping of fossil fuel subsidies; taxing fossil fuel and other polluting companies’ profits; and ensure that all climate measures respect, protect and fulfil human rights.

Commenting on the conclusion of COP31, Climate Analytics's CEO Bill Hare said that the lack of an agreement on the main document should not be seen as a failure of the COP process but as a “successful defence of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change - UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels.”

“Countries committed to a safer future drew a line in the sand and refused to sign up to a document that did not include any reference to phasing out fossil fuels yet did include a target for massive amounts of carbon capture and storage” Mr Hare said. “That was clearly unacceptable, and countries that refused to accept it were right to do so. The 35 by 35 electrification target would have been a step forward but was compromised through its failure to specify clean sources of electricity, but scores of countries are moving to accelerate electrification anyway. On finance, the clear failure of wealthy countries including the European Union to come up with believable and solid proposals to triple adaptation finance cast a pall over the negotiations. Looking ahead to next year's COP in Ethiopia, the EU clearly has to do a lot better on climate finance, as do other wealthy countries. What the non-agreement here means for the COP process will be worked out in the coming few months, but three lessons are already clear.

One is that the experiment where two countries share the presidency should not be repeated.

The second is that if the world is to move forward with a transition away from fossil fuels, many countries need to come prepared to push back against Saudi Arabia. This country has been the most implacable opponent of climate action for over 30 years and has had an outsize influence on three of the last five COPs - Sharm El Sheikh, Baku and now Antalya - and the international community has to stop that happening again.

Thirdly, with momentum building for countries to compile fossil fuel transition roadmaps, many more need to join this in 2027 so that by the COP in Ethiopia a large number of countries have roadmaps prepared or underway, to spur a global transition away from fossil fuels.”

Dr Jeni Miller, Executive Director of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a consortium of more than 300 health professional and health civil society organisations and networks from around the world addressing climate change, said that the COP31 process has “betrayed people’s health by failing to deliver a clear plan for transitioning away from fossil fuels or providing the finance countries need to protect lives and prepare their health systems for escalating climate shocks.”

“COP31 and its presidents Australia and Türkiye did not deliver the necessary protection for people’s health and lives” added Dr Miller. “The rightly rejected ‘Antalya Pact’ comes as climate change compounds this year’s super El Nino, causing severe droughts in Fiji and Bolivia, extreme flooding in the western US, and wildfires in Southeast Asia, and putting millions of additional people at risk of hunger or famine.”

text: India is eyeing a revamp of its framework for special economic zones (SEZs) to boost manufacturing, including the exemption of factories located in them from minimum alternate tax (MAT), seen as a key factor that has stunted the zones. Other ideas include slashing the category of deemed exports besides reducing minimum area requirement for smaller and special category states. The proposals are likely to be considered during budget talks, but a final call will be taken keeping in view revenue considerations and government’s intent to cut corporate exemptions. The revamp has been necessitated by the switchover to the goods and services tax (GST), but the government is keen to go beyond this to spur private investments, particularly in manufacturing. GST was implemented across the country on July 1. “Imposition of MAT had a huge negative impact on exports from SEZ,” said a person aware of the recommendations of a panel set up to draft a plan for the revamp of the zones, conceived as areas of enterprise that would drive jobs and growth as in China. The SEZ Act of 2005 exempted the zones and units located within them from MAT without any sunset clause. But the government changed the law again to impose MAT on SEZs and their units at the rate of 18.5% from 2012. Experts welcomed the proposals. “Focus seems to be on making the entry, exit as well as operations within SEZ easier and incentivising exports by simplifying the procedures and removing operational restrictions such as manufacturing for domestic units,” said Pratik Jain, indirect tax leader, PwC. The ministry of commerce and industry had set up a panel comprising Noida SEZ development commissioner LB Singhal and his counterparts at Kandla SEZ, Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (Seepz) and Madras Export Processing Zone (MEPZ) to suggest changes in the framework to align it with the GST regime. The panel has also identified access to cheap finance as an issue and sought incentives for setting up overseas banking units in these zones. It has mooted a reduction in the minimum area needed to 4 hectares from 25 hectares for establishment of sector-specific SEZs such as biotechnology, non-conventional energy equipment, agro-based food processing and services in the North-Eastern states, Goa, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and the Union Territories. “Land requirement has to be tailored in line with the size of the state,” an official said. The move on deemed exports will make it necessary for units to sell goods overseas to get benefits available to them. A long and more flexible list for activities qualifying as deemed exports made it easy for the units as even without actually exporting they could get the benefits. The panel has also suggested that units of a company within the same SEZ should be allowed to merge subject to conditions. In line with this, net foreign exchange earning computation and income tax exemption of the merged units should be with effect from the date when the first unit commenced operation, according to the report. The panel has suggested that duty and tax benefits on goods needed for setting up a unit be extended to sub-contractors as well. This is currently limited to contractors. It has suggested that subcontracting for Domestic Tariff Areas (DTAs) be allowed subject to conditions as well as a change in computation for net foreign exchange earnings. It will be computed on the basis of exports and supply of goods manufactured or services provided in the SEZ but will exclude traded goods.

description: Here’s the latest in automotive sales and strategy: Eighth-generation vehicle highlights automaker’s commitment to affordable sedans… Genesis to introduce first hybrid powertrains in G80 and GV80… Volkswagen revives Rabbit name
text:
Here’s the latest in automotive sales and strategy:

Hyundai unveiled the redesigned Elantra at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show last week, seeking to attract buyers who like the styling and functionality of SUVs but prefer the affordability of a compact sedan. The North American debut included the 2027 Elantra and 2028 Elantra Hybrid . Hyundai highlighted several features under the theme “affordability is standard.” The 2027 Elantra represents the eighth generation of the sedan and underscores Hyundai’s commitment to the compact car segment despite the growing popularity of SUVs and crossovers in the U.S. market, according to Car Dealership Guy .

Genesis will introduce its first gasoline-electric hybrid powertrains next year, offering the technology in the G80 sedan and GV80 crossover, Automotive News reports. The automaker said the 347-horsepower hybrid systems will deliver performance comparable to its turbocharged V-6 models while improving fuel economy by as much as 30%. Both vehicles, which will be sold as 2028 models, were presented to the media ahead of their public debuts at the Los Angeles Auto Show .

Volkswagen is bringing back its Rabbit nameplate with a limited-edition version of the GTI scheduled to go on sale next year. The 2027.5 Volkswagen GTI Rabbit Edition , unveiled at the Los Angeles Auto Show , will be available exclusively in the U.S. and positioned between the GTI S and SE models, Autoweek reports. The special edition combines retro styling elements with hardware from higher-priced versions of the current GTI. Volkswagen has not announced pricing, but the Rabbit Edition is scheduled to reach U.S. dealerships in the second quarter of 2027.

Ford Motor has begun producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technology licensed from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL . The automaker said last week that production began last month at its $3 billion battery plant in Marshall, MI, about 100 miles west of Detroit. The cells are now being shipped from the facility. CNBC reports the batteries will initially be used in prototypes of Ford’s Fathom small electric pickup. CEO Jim Farley has promoted the vehicle as a potential competitor to offerings from Tesla and Chinese automakers.

Wholesale used-vehicle prices were unchanged in the first half of November, as seasonal declines offset gains vs. a year earlier, according to data from Cox Automotive . The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index stood at 206.8 during the first 15 days of November, unchanged from October’s full-month reading and up 0.7% from November 2025, CBT News reports. On a non-adjusted basis, prices declined 0.7% during the first half of November, a seasonal pattern Cox Automotive said is typical for the month. The index had reached 207.4 in mid-October before settling at 206.8 for the month. Jonathan Gregory , Senior Director at Cox Automotive, said the year-over-year increase narrowed from 2% in October because weakness in October flattened the comparison.

name: Clean Energy
title: From ambition to execution: is the energy system ready for the next phase of the clean ...
description:
Across the clean-energy landscape, the discussion is shifting from ambitions for individual technologies towards the challenge of making the wider energy system work together.
Where electricity can perform the task efficiently, direct electrification should play a central role.
And optimise the energy system connecting them all.
Optimising an integrated industrial energy system requires visibility.
And major industrial investments require confidence that sufficient energy will remain available throughout the lifetime of the asset, a clean energy system must also be a resilient, affordable and competitive energy system.
text:
A year can be a long time in the energy transition. When many of us gathered in Copenhagen twelve months ago, hydrogen was still surrounded by enormous ambition: new projects, capacity targets, hydrogen valleys, electrolyser factories and increasingly bold national strategies. Returning to Copenhagen in 2026, the conversation feels different. Not less important, more mature. Hydrogen is perhaps one of the clearest examples. Projects are increasingly being tested against harder questions: Where will the electricity come from? Is there a credible long-term offtaker? Who carries the market risk? And is hydrogen actually the best decarbonisation pathway for that particular application? But this change is bigger than hydrogen.

Across the clean-energy landscape, the discussion is shifting from ambitions for individual technologies towards the challenge of making the wider energy system work together. Perhaps the biggest change over the past twelve months is therefore not simply that hydrogen has become more selective. The energy transition itself is moving from technology ambition towards system execution.

One thing seems increasingly clear: there will be no single technology that decarbonises industry. Where electricity can perform the task efficiently, direct electrification should play a central role. Where industrial processes require a molecule rather than simply an electron, hydrogen and its derivatives may provide part of the answer. Steel, chemicals, refining, ammonia, methanol and synthetic fuels illustrate some of the applications where clean molecules could play important roles. And there are industrial processes where emissions cannot be fully eliminated through electrification or fuel substitution alone. Cement is perhaps the clearest example: part of its CO₂ emissions comes from the chemical transformation of limestone itself. Here, carbon capture, utilisation and storage may have an important role. The transition is therefore not necessarily about choosing between electrification, hydrogen and carbon management. It is about understanding where each creates the greatest value and how they interact within the same industrial system.

A simple way to think about it might be:

Electrons where possible.

Molecules where necessary.

Manage carbon where unavoidable.

And optimise the energy system connecting them all.

This becomes particularly important because industrial decarbonisation is happening at the same time as electricity demand itself is changing. Industrial electrification requires more power. Renewable hydrogen requires substantial amounts of electricity. Power-to-X processes add further conversion demand. Carbon capture systems themselves consume electrical and thermal energy. Meanwhile, another rapidly growing electricity consumer has entered the conversation: data centres and artificial intelligence. A future electrolyser may therefore find that one of its greatest competitors is not another electrolyser manufacturer, it may simply be another electricity consumer. Producing more renewable electricity remains essential, but so do grid capacity, connection availability, storage, flexibility and the ability to coordinate supply and demand. For an industrial customer, the question therefore becomes much bigger than “How much renewable energy can I procure?”

It becomes:

“How do I get the right energy, to the right process, at the right time, at a competitive cost and with the lowest possible carbon footprint?”

That is fundamentally an energy optimisation challenge.

Hydrogen provides a particularly good illustration. An electrolyser should not be considered in isolation from the industrial process it ultimately serves. A hydrogen project may sit alongside renewable generation, grid supply, battery storage and downstream processes producing steel, ammonia, methanol or synthetic fuels. Depending on the application, carbon capture, CO₂ handling and utilisation may become part of the same value chain. Each element has its own energy requirements, operating constraints and economics. And optimising each element independently does not necessarily optimise the whole. The challenge becomes coordinating grid supply, local generation, storage, flexible industrial loads and production schedules against changing electricity availability, cost and carbon intensity, the objective changes.

We stop trying to maximise the performance of individual technologies and start optimising the economic, energy, carbon and operational performance of the complete industrial system.

This is also the underlying logic behind integrated approaches combining renewable generation, storage, grid infrastructure, industrial loads and digital energy management. Hitachi Energy's work on integrated industrial energy systems already considers renewable electricity, hydrogen, storage, carbon capture and utilisation, multi-energy-vector control and digital certification as parts of the same architecture.

Once we start looking at industry this way, digitalisation stops being an additional layer and becomes part of the infrastructure itself. Optimising an integrated industrial energy system requires visibility. We need to understand what electricity is available, what it costs, where it comes from and when it should be consumed. Forecasting, storage, flexible industrial loads and production requirements increasingly need to be coordinated. And there is another question becoming more important:

Can we prove the environmental impact we claim?

As definitions of renewable hydrogen and low-carbon industrial products become more rigorous, energy provenance becomes increasingly relevant. Regulatory frameworks are already moving towards more granular matching between renewable electricity generation and consumption. For energy-intensive industrial facilities, this is far more than a reporting challenge. It creates a need to connect metering, energy management, renewable generation, storage, operational data and carbon accounting through trusted and auditable digital information flows. The same data that helps an industrial operation decide when to consume electricity may increasingly be needed to demonstrate what electricity was consumed and how that translates into the carbon intensity of the resulting product. This is already becoming tangible in industrial energy management applications. Hitachi-related work around steel, for example, identifies verified CO₂ per tonne, Digital Product Passport information, energy reporting, real-time monitoring and auditable data trails among capabilities required for greener industrial production. The next phase of industrial decarbonisation is therefore not only about producing clean energy, It is about connecting it, optimising it and proving its impact.

There is another force reshaping the conversation: energy security.

Recent years have reminded industry that sustainability, affordability and security of supply cannot be separated. Renewables, grids, electrification, storage, hydrogen and alternative fuels can help diversify energy supply and reduce exposure to imported fossil fuels. But when energy becomes scarce or expensive, reliability and industrial competitiveness quickly move up the political agenda. At the same time, increasing electricity demand means industries may compete for access not simply to clean electricity, but to reliable and affordable electricity full stop. Governments want to decarbonise. Industries need to remain competitive. Digital infrastructure requires rapidly increasing quantities of power. Electricity networks need to expand and modernise. And major industrial investments require confidence that sufficient energy will remain available throughout the lifetime of the asset, a clean energy system must also be a resilient, affordable and competitive energy system.

Over a longer horizon, this systems perspective might also create new roles for technologies such as hydrogen. As renewable penetration increases, hydrogen could eventually complement batteries, interconnection and demand flexibility by providing longer-duration or potentially seasonal energy storage, with renewable electricity converted into hydrogen and, where the economics justify it, ultimately returned to the electricity system. The conversion losses mean this is unlikely to compete with batteries for frequent daily cycling. Its potential value may instead emerge at longer timescales where duration, scale and resilience become as important as efficiency.

Perhaps this is the real change we have witnessed over the past twelve months. Success in the energy transition cannot be measured only by gigawatts of announced electrolyser capacity, renewable projects, tonnes of captured CO₂ or the number of projects in development. We increasingly need to ask harder questions:

Is clean energy available when and where it is needed?

Is the chosen technology really the right pathway for this application?

Can the wider industrial process operate flexibly and efficiently around it?

Can the resulting carbon impact be measured and verified?

And, ultimately, does the complete system remain competitive?

Those are more difficult questions than setting technology targets. But mature industries are built by answering difficult questions.

Perhaps that is what makes this year's Horizons Clean Energy Expansion Week particularly timely. The next phase of the clean-energy transition will not be defined by one winning technology. It will be defined by how effectively we turn technological potential into competitive, resilient and measurable industrial outcomes. For companies developing technologies, for industries investing in decarbonisation and for those of us working on the energy infrastructure connecting everything together, this requires a different way of thinking.

We need to move from optimising individual assets towards optimising complete energy ecosystems.

And perhaps that leaves us with a good question for Copenhagen:

If the next phase of industrial decarbonisation is also an energy optimisation challenge, are we designing individual technologies first, or the energy system that will allow them to succeed together?

That is a conversation I am looking forward to continuing with customers, partners and colleagues at Horizons Clean Energy Expansion Week.

text:
Americans could save around $250 a year on their energy bills following the Senate's passage of a bipartisan permitting reform package, a U.S. senator told Newsweek.

The Senate approved the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) in a 62-33 vote Thursday—a measure aimed at speeding up environmental reviews and federal permitting for energy, infrastructure and industrial projects.

Speaking to Newsweek before the vote, Senator Alan Armstrong, an Oklahoma Republican who helped champion the legislation, said easing permitting bottlenecks could reduce costs for households by making it easier to build power generation, transmission lines, and other energy infrastructure.

Read More on Politics

"The estimates I've seen are around $250 per year on people's utility bills," Armstrong said. "But for areas with really constrained energy, I think that's way too low."

The legislation marks a significant victory for Armstrong, who entered the Senate earlier this year pledging to make permitting reform his top legislative priority and who is now preparing to leave office on Friday.

In a farewell address delivered after the bill's passage, Armstrong said he wanted to be remembered for helping the country overcome longstanding barriers to building projects.

"If there was one lasting contribution I could make during my brief time in the Senate, I wanted it to be helping America recover its ability to build," Armstrong said.

Backers of the permitting reform have argued for years that lengthy reviews and legal challenges can delay projects such as new transmission lines, power plants, mines, roads, and manufacturing facilities. Those delays in turn increase costs and discourage investment.

Armstrong told Newsweek that the effects are visible in electricity prices across different regions of the country.

"People think when they block a pipeline or transmission line, it's the big bad corporation that's getting hurt and not really themselves," he said. "But as you start to see the disparity in utility prices in the U.S., where prices in the Northeast are almost three times what they are in a state like Oklahoma, that's coming from the fact they've refused to let new infrastructure get built."

The senator argued that expanding transmission capacity would allow lower-cost energy to reach markets where power is more expensive.

"If you can build the infrastructure where the energy is cheap and move it to where it's expensive, consumers are going to benefit from that," he said.

The debate comes as the United States faces a growing demand for electricity. According to a report by global solutions and technology provider ICF, demand is projected to increase by 21 percent in the U.S. by 2030 driven largely by artificial intelligence and data centers.

Grid operators and utilities have increasingly warned that additional generation and transmission infrastructure will be needed in coming years to maintain reliability and meet rising demand.

Armstrong said part of the solution will require ensuring that large new electricity users pay the costs associated with connecting to the grid.

"The data center has to pay for all the incremental improvements required for the power grid, plus pay the full tariff," he said.

"If that occurs, the retail consumer is going to be a big beneficiary of that."

Following Senate passage of the legislation, Armstrong described the vote as a "historic moment."

"For years, America has been slowly strangling our own ability to build, allowing a broken permitting process to delay critical infrastructure, drive up utility bills for hardworking families, and threaten our national competitiveness," he said in a statement.

Opponents of the Bill have argued that streamlining reviews could reduce opportunities for public input and legal scrutiny.

They also suggest it erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities.

The measure now heads to the House, where lawmakers will decide whether to advance the bipartisan bill.

title: Want 24/7 clean power for data centers? Try giant heat batteries. - Canary Media
description:
Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities.
But for large data center developers, ​“the issue right now isn’t so much cost, but speed to power,” Gimon said.
By comparison, thermal energy storage systems are relatively new technologies whose producers are eager to scale up, he said.
Arpit Dwivedi, founder and CEO of thermal energy storage startup Cache Energy, agreed that the industry could scale up quickly.
Data center developers could also look to hybrid thermal systems to streamline their path to securing a grid interconnection, he said.
text:
Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities. Some are building their own fossil gas power plants. But that comes with tradeoffs — sky-high equipment costs, yearslong waits for backlogged turbines, and growing public backlash against their polluting plans.

A new report from think tank Energy Innovation proposes a faster, cheaper, and cleaner route for powering off-grid data centers: giant heat batteries that are fueled by low-cost solar and wind.

This ​“hybrid thermal power” approach can be cost-competitive with fossil gas in many parts of the country, said Eric Gimon, the report’s author and an Energy Innovation senior fellow. Even more important, it can deliver power within a year or two in places where renewable energy is under development, he said — much faster than the wait for a gas plant.

“It’s a pretty simple solution that hyperscalers and developers can pursue,” Gimon said. ​“You can do off-grid that’s fast, clean, reliable, and affordable.”

Nevertheless, Gimon said he’s unaware of a U.S. data center taking this approach today. That’s despite the availability of heat batteries from a number of different companies, including Antora, Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, and Rondo Energy.

These energy storage systems use electricity to heat rocks, bricks, or other materials to temperatures exceeding 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit). The systems can retain that heat for hours, days, or even weeks at a time, and then dispatch it later.

Most thermal storage systems installed today supply industrial process heat for everything from food processing to cement production. But they can also use that heat to boil water, spin a steam turbine, and produce electricity.

Storing heat to make electricity has its drawbacks. The process recovers only about 40% of the total energy that’s been put into it, mainly because of losses in converting heat to steam and then to power, Gimon said. That’s not great, compared with the typical low-to-mid-90% ​“round-trip efficiency” rate for lithium-ion batteries.

“But when I started modeling it, I realized TES [thermal energy storage] is cost-effective,” he said.

Data centers that want to run independently of the grid and on clean energy will need to store enormous amounts of power for when solar and wind aren’t available. As long as the solar and wind power is cheap enough, and the value of the electricity being generated from the steam turbines is high enough, the efficiency losses are tolerable. In fact, thermal batteries would be cheaper than conventional lithium-ion storage over longer durations, Gimon said.

Gimon also looked at how fossil-fueled boilers could run on fuel stored on-site, to give the thermal storage and gas turbines emergency backup power, much like data centers rely on emergency backup diesel generators today. This graphic shows how all the pieces fit together.

All told, Gimon estimated that these ​“hybrid thermal power brick” systems can deliver reliable, round-the-clock power at a cost of about $120 per megawatt-hour — a figure that includes the cost of developing the renewables that deliver their primary power.

Depending on where a data center is located, that can be competitive with building a dedicated gas-fired power plant. References range from about $72 per MWh for a data center in West Texas to the $140 to $165 per MWh that investment bank Jeffries estimated Meta is paying for an off-grid gas power plant in Ohio.

But for large data center developers, ​“the issue right now isn’t so much cost, but speed to power,” Gimon said. Data center developers have proposed hundreds of gigawatts of gas-fired power plants across the country, but those plans are constrained by the gas-turbine supply chain, workforce availability, and pipeline capacity.

By comparison, thermal energy storage systems are relatively new technologies whose producers are eager to scale up, he said. And while demand for steam turbines is beginning to tick up, those manufacturers are not nearly as backlogged, he said.

Arpit Dwivedi, founder and CEO of thermal energy storage startup Cache Energy, agreed that the industry could scale up quickly. His company’s technology uses standard steel components and stores heat in limestone-derived pellets coated in a proprietary binder. Those components are ​“simple and abundant,” which makes it easier to ​“build things faster,” he said.

The startup has enough manufacturing capacity today to build about a gigawatt-hour of its systems per year, ​“and we haven’t made a big deal about it,” Dwivedi said. He estimated the company could scale up to 10 GWh per year in 12 months and 100 GWh per year in 24 months without much trouble.

Cache Energy has already deployed its technology to store on-site wind power for industrial heating and space heating, Dwivedi said. The company has been talking with data center developers about using its heat batteries for electricity generation, though he declined to share more information. For data center developers to adopt thermal energy storage at scale, ​“we need one or two real projects that show it really works” in that setting, he said.

Hybrid thermal systems also open opportunities for solar and wind developers. Gimon estimated that a renewables-only project could boost its value threefold by adding a thermal battery and steam turbine that can deliver reliable ​“clean, firm” power. Landing an off-grid data center client could help them avoid the risk of yearslong wait times to connect to the grid, and would give them enough time to secure federal tax credits before they expire.

Data center developers could also look to hybrid thermal systems to streamline their path to securing a grid interconnection, he said. Utilities and grid operators are increasingly pressuring data centers to build or pay for their own power, so the facilities don’t overload the grid during heat waves, winter storms, and times of peak power demand.

And while many data centers are building gas power plants for that explicit purpose, more and more states are demanding that they bring clean alternatives to the table. Batteries are one such option, and thermal energy storage could play a similar role, Gimon said

text:
Highlights

Cybertruck production to wind down next year

Cybercab output expanding in Texas and Berlin

Robotaxi service launches in a new city

Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) Consumer Cyclical Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA) 346.00 USD -28.410 ↓ 7.588% is reshaping its vehicle lineup around autonomous driving. The electric vehicle maker plans to wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of next year to make room for more Cybercab output, and it reportedly plans a large investment to expand Cybercab production at its Berlin-Brandenburg plant. Tesla also launched robotaxi rides in San Antonio this month.

For readers who follow Automobile Stocks, Tesla remains the most closely watched electric vehicle company in the world. The company is a member of the Russell 1000.

What Is the Cybercab?

The Cybercab is Tesla's purpose-built robotaxi, designed without a steering wheel or pedals. It is intended to operate on Tesla's ride-hailing network using its autonomous driving software. Tesla believes robotaxis may eventually generate recurring revenue from rides rather than one-time vehicle sales.

By shifting factory capacity toward the Cybercab, Tesla is signaling that autonomous transportation is now its top priority.

Why Is Tesla Ending Cybertruck Production?

The Cybertruck, Tesla's angular stainless-steel truck, attracted strong attention when it launched but received mixed reactions due to its unusual design and pricing. Tesla said it would wind down production at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to focus that capacity on the Cybercab.

This decision may open opportunities for other electric truck makers, as Cybertruck customers look for alternatives.

Where Is the Robotaxi Service Expanding?

Tesla began offering robotaxi rides in San Antonio this month, adding to its earlier service areas. Expanding to new cities is an important step in proving that its autonomous technology can operate safely at scale and in different environments.

Regulatory approval, safety records and customer acceptance will determine how quickly the service can grow nationwide and internationally.

What Is the Berlin Investment?

According to media reports, Tesla plans a multibillion-dollar investment to expand Cybercab production at its factory near Berlin. A European production base would allow Tesla to supply robotaxis to markets outside the United States and reduce shipping costs and trade barriers.

How Has Tesla's Stock Performed?

Tesla shares have fallen this year and trade well below their recent high. The stock dropped further during the recent broad technology downturn, which hit electric vehicle stocks particularly hard as the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year.

Speculation about a possible combination between Tesla and SpaceX has also influenced trading. Tesla's leadership has not ruled out such a deal, and some analysts have noted that this speculation is supporting the share price regardless of current fundamentals.

How Is Tesla's Core Car Business Doing?

Tesla's core vehicle sales have faced pressure from increased competition, especially from Chinese automakers, and from changes in electric vehicle incentives. Model updates and lower-cost versions of its popular vehicles aim to support demand.

Tesla's energy storage business, which supplies large battery systems to utilities and businesses, has been growing and adds diversity to its revenue.

Why Do Automobile Investors Follow Tesla?

Tesla is viewed not only as a carmaker but also as a technology company with ambitions in autonomous driving, robotics, artificial intelligence and energy. Its strategic shift toward robotaxis may change how investors value the business if the technology succeeds at scale.

How Does Tesla's Autonomous Software Work?

Tesla's driving software uses cameras and artificial intelligence trained on large amounts of real-world driving data collected from its fleet. Unlike some competitors that rely on lidar sensors and detailed maps, Tesla uses a vision-based approach, which it says can scale more easily and at lower cost.

The company continues to release software updates to vehicle owners and its robotaxi fleet. Improving safety and reliability in complex city environments is essential for wider regulatory approval and public trust.

What Is Tesla's Energy Business?

Tesla's energy segment produces large battery storage systems for utilities and businesses, as well as home batteries and solar products. Demand for grid storage has grown as utilities add renewable energy and need to balance supply and demand. This business has become an increasingly important source of revenue and profit diversity for Tesla.

How Do Competitors Compare?

Chinese automakers have expanded aggressively in electric vehicles, offering lower-cost models with advanced features. Traditional automakers continue to adjust their EV plans based on demand and policy. In autonomous driving, Tesla faces competition from dedicated robotaxi operators already running services in several cities.

What Risks Should Readers Consider?

Risks include delays or setbacks in autonomous driving, regulatory restrictions on robotaxis, safety incidents, weaker vehicle sales, intense competition, high valuation and uncertainty around possible corporate transactions. Heavy investment in new production may also pressure cash flow.

What Should Readers Watch Next?

Key indicators include robotaxi expansion to new cities, Cybercab production progress, fourth-quarter deliveries, energy storage growth, regulatory decisions and any developments regarding a SpaceX combination.

Final Thoughts

Tesla is redirecting factory capacity from the Cybertruck to the Cybercab and expanding its robotaxi service, showing a clear focus on autonomous transportation. The strategy carries high upside and significant execution risk. Robotaxi progress and vehicle demand remain the key areas to watch.

Tesla has filed a tax-incentive application under Texas's Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act for a polysilicon refinery in Nueces County, with an estimated cost of USD 3.1 billion. The filing is not a final investment decision.

Why it matters

The refinery would form the upstream step of a vertically integrated solar manufacturing platform in the United States, where China currently dominates polysilicon production. For Texas, the project signals a potential expansion of advanced manufacturing and skilled jobs in the state.

Tesla's application estimates a USD 3.1 billion cost, with about USD 1.5 billion for engineering and construction, USD 1.4 billion for equipment and USD 183 million for utility infrastructure. The company is seeking a ten-year limit on the taxable value of the property, and the project's final investment decision remains pending.

The players

Tesla

Tesla is an American electric vehicle and clean energy company led by Elon Musk, which is expanding into solar cell and polysilicon manufacturing.

The details

The refinery would produce ultra-high purity, solar-grade polysilicon from trichlorosilane for high-efficiency N-type solar cells. Tesla's application seeks a ten-year limit on the property's taxable value, with spending projected across 2027 to 2030.

Timeline

Spending on the refinery is expected to be spread over 2027 to 2030.

The refinery is expected to employ 515 people by 2032.

The refinery would be filed under the Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act, a state incentive program that the application uses to support a domestic supply chain for solar manufacturing. text:
Drax Group expects its full-year adjusted EBITDA for 2026 to be significantly above analyst consensus, after a strong run of system support and generation in September and October.

The UK power generator told investors at its Capital Markets Day that it had added around £50 million to its net contracted power position for 2026 over those two months, with further gains from activity in the Balancing Mechanism. It said the result showed how the dispatchable nature of its portfolio, together with its trading and optimisation capabilities, allowed it to respond flexibly to the needs of the power system.

Since its last update in September, Drax has added 2.5TWh (net) to its forward position at an average price of around £158/MWh between 2026 and 2028. This includes about 2TWh of merchant biomass generation in summer 2027, on top of the volume set out in its new low-carbon dispatchable Contract for Difference (CfD) agreement.

As of 19 November, the group had more than £1 billion of contracted forward power sales across its Renewables Obligation biomass, pumped storage and hydro assets for 2026–2028, along with more than £800 million of associated ROCs.

Biomass becomes a smaller part of the group

Drax will combine its pellet production in the US South with biomass generation at Drax Power Station into a single Biomass Operations reporting segment. The segment also includes its Canadian operations, which are under strategic review.

In 2025, Biomass Operations made up more than 80% of group adjusted EBITDA. Drax expects its Solar & Wind and Flexgen businesses to account for most of its earnings by 2029, giving it a larger share of contracted revenue while keeping exposure to merchant power prices.

Drax increased its capacity under management from 4GW to 6.2GW between 2025 and 2026 through the acquisitions of Bluefield Solar Income Fund (BSIF) and Flexitricity and the commissioning of its first open-cycle gas turbine. It now plans to reach 7.6GW by 2029, and potentially around 9GW by 2031.

In October, the company took a final investment decision on three solar projects in northern England. The projects total around 130MW, represent an investment of about £120 million, and are backed by 15-year CfDs.

Future of the power station site

Drax Power Station covers more than 1,000 acres and has around 4GW of grid access, including 2.6GW of active dispatchable generation. Drax said it is looking at long-term options for the site that would use several generation technologies alongside its existing biomass units, and it has formally requested 1.2GW of import capacity from the system operator.

The company is also developing an option to provide non-generation grid stability services, such as inertia, from two units that no longer operate. Work on this will continue through 2027.

Drax has signed an agreement to develop a strategic partnership with Brookfield and its AI infrastructure platform Radiant to build a GW-scale AI data centre on the estate, with capital provided through a Brookfield-Qai joint venture. The agreement provisionally values the site's powered land at around $1 million/MW across all three phases. The first phase still needs planning, regulatory and network approvals, a tenant and final investment decisions.

Financial targets

Drax is targeting adjusted EBITDA of £800–900 million in 2029 and more than £1 billion in 2031. That represents average annual growth of more than 12% between 2027 and 2031, with dividend per share expected to grow by more than 10% a year over the same period. The group is raising its long-term leverage target from around 2x to around 2.5x net debt to adjusted EBITDA.

Will Gardiner, CEO of Drax Group, said: "Starting from a strong foundation of system critical assets in Drax Power Station and Cruachan Pumped Storage Hydro, the Group is building a scalable portfolio of flexible and renewable generating assets in the UK, designed to benefit from the growth in renewable power and resulting need for flexible assets to support the system."

text:
ASEAN as a Science Region maps the strengths and gaps of all eleven member states, from industry translation and semiconductors to sustainability and the ASEAN University Network

LONDON, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Researchers in Southeast Asia published approximately 228,000 papers in 2025, almost 20 times the 2000 figure, on research and development investment of just 1.03% of GDP, compared with 1.92% worldwide and 2.72% across the OECD, according to ASEAN as a Science Region: The Strength of Diversity and Collaboration, a new report released by Elsevier, a global leader in advanced information and decision support.

The report, launched at the QS Higher Ed Summit: Asia Pacific in Bali, is part of Elsevier's Science Nations and Regions series. It covers all eleven ASEAN member states, including Timor-Leste, which joined in October 2025, and the 30 core universities of the ASEAN University Network (AUN). It draws on Scopus and SciVal data, mainly for 2021–2025, and on Overton data on policy citations. It arrives as the ASEAN Plan of Action on Science, Technology and Innovation (APASTI) 2026–2035 begins, and offers a baseline against which progress can be tracked.

Key findings

Fast growth, above-average impact. Output grew by about 31% between 2021 and 2025, compared with 14.9% globally, and ten of the eleven member states recorded growth. ASEAN's field-weighted citation impact (FWCI) is 1.11, meaning its research is cited about 11% more than the world average.

Collaboration is the impact multiplier. Around 43% of ASEAN's output is internationally co-authored. Those papers have an FWCI of 1.61, roughly double the 0.79 of nationally co-authored work. Over 2021–2025, China, the United States and the United Kingdom were ASEAN's three largest research partners by co-authored output, followed by Australia and India. China alone accounted for the equivalent of 12.4% of ASEAN's output in 2025. China and India, growing at 19.1% and 16.1% a year since 2021, are the only two of the five largest partners growing faster than ASEAN's own research base. India passed the United Kingdom in 2024 to become ASEAN's third-largest partner by annual output.

The ASEAN University Network anchors the system. Its 30 core universities produce 42% of ASEAN's research output, with an FWCI of 1.41. Of about 40,000 co-publication links among them, 63.8% are between institutions in the same country. The cross-border 36.2% is, the report says, where the network adds collaboration that might not otherwise occur. Members in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar remain lightly connected.

Translation into economic value is the gap. Academic–corporate co-authorship stands at 2.5% of output, close to the 2.7% world rate, but only about 1% of ASEAN research is cited in patents, against 1.9% worldwide. Singapore reaches around 4%. Artificial intelligence output nearly tripled between 2020 and 2024 to about 60,000 publications, with an FWCI of 1.87, and clean energy and climate technology research grew by about 50%. Semiconductor and advanced manufacturing output, by contrast, was essentially flat at around 21,000 publications, even as ASEAN plays a major role in chip assembly, testing and packaging.

Climate risk is rising, but climate action is less researched. ASEAN is among the world's most disaster-prone regions, and the number of people killed, missing or affected by climate-related disasters per 100,000 population more than doubled between 2016 and 2023. Of the 68 Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets ASEAN tracks, only 15 are on track for 2030. Research is concentrated in good health and well-being (SDG 3), peace, justice and strong institutions (SDG 16) and responsible consumption and production (SDG 12), but is comparatively less concentrated in climate action (SDG 13), life below water (SDG 14) and life on land (SDG 15).

Quotes

Dr. Anders Karlsson, Vice President Asia Pacific, Global Strategic Networks, Elsevier, said: "ASEAN has become one of the world's fastest-growing research regions on barely 1% of GDP. Collaboration is what doubles the impact of that research, and the next step is to build it deliberately, across borders and with industry. Understanding the diversity is what makes the commonalities actionable."

Distinguished Professor Tan Sri Dr Zakri Bin Abdul Hamid, Founder Chairman of the International Institute for Science Diplomacy & Sustainability (IISDS) at UCSI University, Malaysia, said: "Co-authored research functions as a powerful instrument of science diplomacy, bridging geopolitical divides […] By synchronizing national policy and establishing deep regional consortia, member states can assert a strong and collective impact."

Prof. Dr. Thanapan Laiprakobsup, Executive Director of the ASEAN University Network, said: "Together, these findings highlight the value of connecting expertise across institutions and countries, supported by lasting academic relationships."

The report closes with five observations for the ASEAN Committee on Science, Technology and Innovation (COSTI) and the AUN, including tracking intra-ASEAN co-authorship annually and linking microelectronics research with the region's fast-growing clean energy research. The full report, with country-level analysis of all eleven member states, is available at: ASEAN as a Science Region: The Strength of Diversity and Collaboration

Notes to editors

In this release, "ASEAN" refers to the collective of all eleven member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which together make up Southeast Asia. Timor-Leste joined in October 2025 and is included retrospectively across the whole period.

FWCI compares the citations a publication receives with the world average (1.0) for the same field, publication type and year. Collaboration figures use whole counting, so country totals include intra-ASEAN co-authorship and exceed the regional total. Data for the four technology areas (artificial intelligence, biotechnology and health, clean energy and climate technologies, and semiconductors and advanced manufacturing) cover 2020–2024. The report notes that internationally co-authored papers can differ in team size, subject mix and participation in large consortia, and that co-authorship and patent citations capture only some forms of knowledge exchange.

Myanmar was the only member state where output fell between 2021 and 2025 (from 897 to 574 publications). The report notes that publication data alone does not establish the cause.

The ASEAN University Network, established in 1995, comprises 30 core member universities and more than 300 associate members. The analysis covers the 30 core members.

About Elsevier

Elsevier is a global leader in advanced information and decision support. For over a century, we have been helping advance science and healthcare to advance human progress. We support academic and corporate research communities, doctors, nurses, future healthcare professionals and educators across 170 countries in their vital work. We help impact makers achieve better outcomes with research and clinical-grade solutions built on three foundational capabilities: a leading scientific and medical knowledge base of evidence-based content, precision AI designed specifically for the complexities of research and healthcare, and expert human assessment and oversight to ensure accountability at every step. We champion inclusion and sustainability, working with the communities that we serve. The Elsevier Foundation supports research and health partnerships around the world.

text:
Written by Martin Lynch, European News Editor for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

Leading German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has announced that it is stopping further investment in German car plants due to high production costs and deadlocked talks with worker's unions.

No New Investment

The future of some Mercedes-Benz German car manufacturing plants is under threat following a decision by the company to halt further investment in Germany.

The decision was revealed via an internal company memo following a management board meeting that cited the ongoing deadlock with the works council and the IG Metall union on reducing labour costs. The possible closure of two unnamed plants is now being considered. According to Industrial Info Resources data, there are three Mercedes projects in Germany worth US$1 billion in investment. The German car industry is one of the most important parts of the country's economy, accounting for roughly 5% of GDP and employing 691,000 people. It is also the country's top export industry at almost 17% of the total, worth 262 billion euro (US$284 billion) in 2024.

Meeting Outcome

The internal memo from Mercedes Production Chief Michael Schiebe said that management had "jointly decided to suspend all further investments in our German operations," while citing high production costs and the failure of talks with worker's councils and unions to reduce them. The company stated that an hour of labour in German plants can cost up to five times more than sites in Eastern Europe. The luxury carmaker wants longer working hours without extra pay to boost productivity but there has been no agreement reached despite four months of negotiations. In the memo, Schiebe admitted that the management board could not find a way forward on a solution "despite numerous intensive discussions," with the union. "We are now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."

Possible Plant Closures

Schiebe had previously told the media that if cost reductions could not be agreed, then two plants - an assembly plant and a powertrain plant - in Germany could be closed. According to Die Zeit, the company has assembly plants in Sindelfingen, Rastatt and Bremen. Powertrain plants, where components for the cars are manufactured, are located in Stuttgart-Untertürkheim, Affalterbach near Stuttgart, Berlin, Hamburg, Kamenz in Saxony, as well as Kölleda and Arnstadt in Thuringia. The company's Chief Executive Officer Ola Källenius defended the cost-cutting measures, speaking to Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung. "Locations outside Germany sometimes offer both: lower costs and longer annual working hours. This also influences the awarding of future product contracts and investments. Europe has become too expensive and too complex as a location for investment and production," he added. "High energy and production costs, lengthy approval processes, and increasing regulatory burdens are impairing our competitiveness. We need more pragmatism and speed in implementation."

VW and Audi Also in Trouble

Mercedes-Benz is not the only other German carmaker suffering, as Volkswagen AG (VW) and Audi are looking to make major cuts due to growing competition, higher production costs and the shift to electric vehicles (EVs). In September, Volkswagen's supervisory board green-lit a plan to eliminate an additional 50,000 jobs, doubling its planned cuts announced in late 2024 to 100,000 job cuts by 2030. It represents roughly 15% of the group's global workforce of 650,000 employees. It also plans to halve its product lineup across all of its brands, including Audi, Porsche, Bentley, Skoda, Seat, Cupra and Lamborghini. Following a deal with union IG Metall for the proposed cuts, the threatened closure of four German assembly plants, including Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Audi's Neckarsulm facility, has been set aside. Production at the plants will be phased out between 2031 and 2034. Last year, Audi confirmed that it would cut 7,500 jobs in Germany by 2029 - 14% of its global workforce - mostly in administration and development. Earlier in the year, it shut a car assembly plant in Belgium with the loss of 3,000 jobs. The German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) said that passenger car production fell to just over 3 million vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 4% year-on-year, and down 15% from 2019. Foreign orders for German cars also fell by 16% in September alone while sales of German cars in China dropped 25% in the first six months of 2026.

Key Takeaways

Carmaker Mercedes-Benz has announced that it is stopping further investment in German car plants due to high production costs.

The potential closure of two plants is also possible, according to management.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking three Mercedes projects in Germany worth US$1 billion in investment.
