title: UN climate conference ends without its signature agreement as countries clash over fossil ...
authors: Matthew Glasser, Dan Peck, ABC News
description:
Countries and blocs including the European Union, the United Kingdom, Belize, the Marshall Islands, Norway, Panama and Vanuatu objected to the proposed agreement.
Many cited the omission of fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate finance commitments, with some delegates arguing that those responsible for climate change should pay for it.
It also says that "every increment of warming above current levels will increase the frequency and intensity of loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change."
Support for the proposal and electrification Not every country was opposed to the draft agreement.
The proposed agreement instead calls for the "greatest possible use of clean energy."
text:
After two extra days of deliberations, multiple drafts and late-night and early-morning negotiations, the nearly 200 participating countries ended COP31, the annual U.N. climate conference, without agreeing on the cover decision, the conference's overall summary of what was decided.

Scientists overwhelmingly agree that fossil fuels are the primary driver of climate change, but the final draft of the agreement presented to the delegates meeting in Antalya, Turkey, contained no references to oil, natural gas or coal, and no call to phase out fossil fuel use.

Countries and blocs including the European Union, the United Kingdom, Belize, the Marshall Islands, Norway, Panama and Vanuatu objected to the proposed agreement. Many cited the omission of fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate finance commitments, with some delegates arguing that those responsible for climate change should pay for it.

"I want to clearly state that the European Union and its member states object to this cover decision,” said Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's climate minister, on behalf of the EU, adding that the decisions "go nowhere near the level of action or ambition that are required for us to tackle climate change."

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either, and it is for that reason and those reasons that the European Union strongly objects to this text,” O'Brien said.

A delegate from Panama told the assembled representatives, “Panama believes that we must tell the truth about the collective failure to keep within 1.5 degrees Celsius, and Panama believes that those who have most contributed to this crisis must shoulder a proportionate responsibility to resolve this crisis.”

Many participating countries and climate groups insisted on language calling for a fossil fuel phase-out and were unwilling to accept an agreement that didn't address the primary cause of climate change head-on. That demand was one reason negotiations headed into overtime after the two-week conference was scheduled to conclude.

But instead of mentioning a fossil fuel phase-out, the proposed agreement referenced the United Arab Emirates Consensus, an outcome of the 2023 COP28 summit, when, for the first time, the attending countries formally agreed to transition away from fossil fuels for energy.

A first draft of the COP31 cover decision called for phasing out fossil fuels "through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems," but the language was removed from the second draft after opposition from several oil-producing nations, according to reporting by the Guardian.

While the COP31 draft text doesn't mention the primary cause of climate change, it does include details about its potential impacts, such as noting "deep concern that peak global warming is expected to exceed 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels in the next few years." It also says that "every increment of warming above current levels will increase the frequency and intensity of loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change."

'Most disappointing COP'

Some climate organizations also objected to the proposed agreement's language.

"Country after country has called on the COP31 presidencies to build on the Dubai commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, and they have looked the other way,” said Sara Shaw, Campaigns and Networks Director at 350.org, a climate advocacy organization focused on transitioning the world to renewable energy. “This text isn't a climate plan. It's a license to keep polluting.”

A first draft of the COP31 cover decision called for phasing out fossil fuels "through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems," but the language was removed from the second draft after opposition from several oil-producing nations, according to reporting by the Guardian.

On the evening that COP31 was supposed to conclude, a coalition of 100 climate nonprofits and community organizations sent a letter to the COP31 leadership, saying they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had."

They listed several objections to the draft agreement, including that "The major cause of the climate crisis – coal, oil and gas – fails to rate a mention."

Countries push back on climate financing

Global South countries and their allies pushed back on the funding pledged by wealthier nations for adaptation and loss and damage, saying it was too little and too slow to arrive.

While an earlier draft of the agreement called for "efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035" and included a goal of $120 billion, that amount didn’t make it into the proposed text. Instead, the text said it “Agrees to discuss … implementation pathways for tripling adaptation finance by 2035” and “encourages continued efforts to scale up” funding for the loss and damage sustained as a result of climate change.

Carbon capture singled out?

Some delegates also objected to including carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) language in the proposed agreement, saying it was being used in place of a plan to eliminate the source of greenhouse gas emissions. Vanuatu Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu told AFP that CCUS "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

Saudi Arabia defended the inclusion of CCUS in the proposal, saying "we believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances."

Support for the proposal and electrification

Not every country was opposed to the draft agreement. Ghana expressed concerns about the text but said it would support the proposed agreement because “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.” China said it supports the proposed agreement and called on all of the parties “to show necessary compromise.”

Also, not every issue in the proposal was as divisive as the fossil fuel phase-out or climate financing.

Electrification found broad support, with at least 75 countries backing the new 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, according to the U.N. The voluntary pledge aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from an estimated 23% in 2026.

But even with broad support for the pledge itself, some countries objected to including it in the cover decision draft because it did not include a mandate requiring the use of emission-free renewable energy to meet the electrification goal. The proposed agreement instead calls for the "greatest possible use of clean energy."

In the end, however, the final draft wasn’t enough to get the deal past the finish line. Decisions at COPs are made by consensus, not by majority vote, so the objections from the EU and others were enough to block it.

COP31 fall short of expectations

Going into this year's conference, climate organizations and experts told ABC News that they didn't expect significant breakthroughs and that much of the work gets done during small meetings. Despite the failure to reach a big agreement, delegates did pass a number of the 160 agenda items on a variety of technical matters.

But the final draft of COPs signature agreement fell far short of the expectations of many delegates, environmental groups and nongovernmental organizations.

“The hollow outcome at COP31 was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement. When narrow national interests override collective responsibility to confront the climate crisis, the entire world pays the price," said Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO of World Resources Institute. "Climate summits are not stages for posturing; they require every country to roll up their sleeves and do the hard work of finding ambitious common ground.”

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the morning session urging delegates to support the agreement, telling them they "stand on the threshold of a historic opportunity." But after several countries objected to the text, he acknowledged that COP31 would end without an official agreement.

“We did our best,” Kurum said. “This text was not imposed on anyone. We did not force people to accept it. But it seems that there are parties that object to this text. I understand that there is no agreement on this text.”

The countries will try again next year. COP32 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from Nov. 8 to 19, 2027.

description:

We will provide more specific guidance on the EBIT margin once deliveries to the Data Centers segment have reached a consistently high level.
2G company portrait The 2G Energy AG Group is an internationally leading manufacturer and system provider of decentralized energy supply systems.
text:
Energy supply company orders combined heat and power plant in the mid-double-digit megawatt range

Revenue expanded by 28% in the third quarter, total output boosted by 72%, while the EBIT margin stood at 1.4%

The Management Board confirms its revenue forecast of up to EUR 490 million for the current year, as well as its forecast for an EBIT margin of 9.5 to 10.5%.

Heek, November 23, 2026 – 2G Energy AG (ISIN DE000A0HL8N9), one of the world’s leading manufacturers of sustainable power plants and CHP systems, as well as a producer of heat pumps, has secured the largest single order in the company’s history for the German market.

Energy supply company orders combined heat and power plant in the mid-double-digit megawatt range

In November 2026, 2G gained the largest single order in the company’s history to date for its German home market. The contract covers several combined heat and power plant modules delivering an electrical output in the mid-double-digit megawatt range. As is common practice, the contractually agreed-upon down payment has already been received.

“This contract is further confirmation of our diversification strategy,” as CEO Pablo Hofelich stated. “Our North American business is heavily driven by data centers. However, if we take a look at the other markets worldwide, they have also shown significant growth of 68% year-over-year since the beginning of the year – even without data center orders.”

This latest major contract in Germany, along with the promising projects in the biogas, mining, gas-fired reserve power plants, and heat pump sectors, clearly underscores the positive momentum in the various markets. Just a week ago, 2G reported on a major contract to supply power plants designed to increase the flexibility of biogas plants (see CN, November 16, 2026).

Revenue grew by 28% in the third quarter, total output climbed by 72%, while the EBIT margin stood at 1.4%

In the third quarter just ended, the Services segment drove growth, exceeding the same quarter of the previous year by 59% (EUR 44.9 million, prior year: EUR 28.3 million).

Although overall output increased by 72%, revenue from new installations barely reached the previous year’s level (EUR 29.6 million; prior year: EUR 30.2 million, -2%). The recognition of revenue from new equipment and systems, however, is significantly influenced by the customer’s final acceptance and can only be accelerated to a limited extent by 2G.

“In connection with the growing number of multi-module projects, we will see revenue recognition to become significantly more consistent,” as CFO Martin Laux stated. “This is due to the fact that in the case of these large-scale projects, the transfer of risk generally occurs as soon as the individual power plant arrives at the customer’s warehouse.” The Management Board therefore expects revenue recognition to be much more steady in the future.

Against the backdrop of record-high order intake and order backlog, 2G is working full steam ahead on expanding capacities, which is reflected in the significant increase in total operating revenue in the third quarter (EUR 132 million, prior year: EUR 76 million). As a result of these efforts, the quarter closed with an EBIT margin of 1.4% (previous year: -1.5%).

The Management Board confirms its revenue forecast of up to EUR 490 million for the current year, as well as its forecast for an EBIT margin of 9.5 to 10.5%.

The Management Board reaffirms its revenue forecast of up to EUR 490 million for the full year. In order to reach this figure, fourth-quarter revenue must total EUR 279 million. This represents a gain of approximately EUR 109 million compared with the same quarter of the previous year.

For the first time, revenue from three new business segments is expected to contribute to this growth: With regard to the Data Centers segment, revenue recognition is expected from the first significant partial shipments, most of which have already been produced. In addition, new demand-response systems are being delivered in significant numbers for the first time. Initial partial deliveries are also planned for the mining sector, a market holding a promising future. All three segments are contributing to revenue growth right from the outset and, as a result, are generating additional revenue compared to last year.

Based on this revenue surge, the Management Board continues to expect an EBIT margin of 9.5–10.5%.

The forecasts for 2027 (revenue of EUR 600 to 650 million, EBIT margin in excess of 11%) and for 2028 (revenue of EUR 750 to 850 million, EBIT margin also above 11%) remain unchanged. We will provide more specific guidance on the EBIT margin once deliveries to the Data Centers segment have reached a consistently high level.

2G company portrait

The 2G Energy AG Group is an internationally leading manufacturer and system provider of decentralized energy supply systems. The company develops, produces and installs comprehensive solutions in the structurally growing market for highly efficient CHPs, large heat pumps and peak-load gensets. Digital grid integration and plant control for these types of energy generators, as well as service and maintenance, are further decisive performance criteria.

The product portfolio comprises three types of energy generation: CHP plants in the output range from 20 kW to 4,500 kW for operation with hydrogen, natural gas, biogas and other lean gases, large heat pumps in the range from 100 kW to 3,200 kW as well as peak-load gensets with an electrical output of 500 kW or more. CHP plants operate with efficiencies of 90 percent and more, while large heat pumps achieve efficiencies of 300 to 500 percent, depending on the general conditions. With its products and services, 2G is at the interface to a decentralized, secure and largely decarbonized energy supply. More than 10,000 2G systems have already been installed worldwide in various applications, supplying electrical and thermal energy to a wide range of customers from the housing industry, agriculture, commercial and industrial companies, energy suppliers, municipal utilities and local government authorities.

2G is positioned worldwide as a system provider for decentralized energy solutions with its combination of CHP plants, peak-load gensets and large heat pumps. The company benefits from far-reaching synergies of these plant categories, ranging from project development, procurement, production and the predominantly containerized design to the largely identical customer base and regulatory framework as well as sales channels and digital control and service.

2G is consistently expanding its technological leadership through continuous research and development work, both in power plant and pump technologies as well as in specific software development for service and maintenance activities. The digital grid integration consistently implemented by 2G is an indispensable, system-relevant element in the future electricity market design and represents a high market entry hurdle for competitors. The sector coupling required for the success of the energy transition is reflected in 2G’s portfolio.

2G employs more than 1,000 people in Germany, North America, and at additional locations across Europe. The company is active in more than 60 countries and generated net sales of EUR 398.4 million in the 2025 financial year with an EBIT margin of 6.6%.

2G was founded in 1995. The shares of 2G Energy (ISIN DE000A0HL8N9) have been listed on the stock exchange market since 2007 and are included in the “Scale” segment of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and listed in the Scale30 index.

title: Will EV tax credits exclude exports? Focus turns to eligibility details and deduction amounts
description:
The government announced in its tax reform plan released last August that it would introduce a domestic production tax credit, which reduces income and corporate taxes based on production volume for items with weak domestic production bases.
However, contrary to expectations, electric vehicles were excluded from the scope, sparking controversy.
The government calculates the total deduction amount by multiplying the production volume by the base deduction amount.
The base deduction amount is set in the enforcement decree, taking into account production costs, selling prices, and other factors.
The automotive industry maintains that the base deduction amount should be at least 4 million won, considering the 'ultra-low-price offensive' of Chinese brands.
text:
As the government and the National Assembly build consensus on including electric vehicles in the scope of the domestic production tax credit, fierce debate is expected over the future 'deduction amount' and whether 'exported vehicles' will be included.

According to the automotive industry on Monday, even if the government's 'Electric Vehicle Competitiveness Enhancement Plan,' to be released this week, includes electric vehicles in the domestic production tax credit, significant friction is anticipated in coordinating the details between the government's proposal and bills introduced by both ruling and opposition parties.

The government announced in its tax reform plan released last August that it would introduce a domestic production tax credit, which reduces income and corporate taxes based on production volume for items with weak domestic production bases.

However, contrary to expectations, electric vehicles were excluded from the scope, sparking controversy. As the automotive industry and both parties argued for including electric vehicles, citing the rapid penetration of Chinese brands into the domestic market, the government moved to re-examine the issue, and the results of this review are expected to be reflected in the current Electric Vehicle Competitiveness Enhancement Plan.

The biggest point of interest is the 'base deduction amount,' which is likely to be finalized during the revision of the Enforcement Decree of the Special Tax Restriction Act (Tax Restriction Act) in early next year. The government calculates the total deduction amount by multiplying the production volume by the base deduction amount.

The base deduction amount is set in the enforcement decree, taking into account production costs, selling prices, and other factors. The automotive industry maintains that the base deduction amount should be at least 4 million won, considering the 'ultra-low-price offensive' of Chinese brands.

Rep. Lee Eon-ju of the Democratic Party of Korea also explicitly stated "base deduction amount for electric vehicles: 4 million won per unit" in the Tax Restriction Act amendment bill she introduced as a representative sponsor last September.

However, considering the decrease in national tax revenue resulting from the implementation of the system, there is a possibility that the government will set the base deduction amount lower than this.

The Tax Restriction Act amendment bill jointly introduced by Reps. Yoon Hu-deok (Democratic Party) and Yoon Han-hong (People Power Party) includes the base deduction amount as a matter to be stipulated in the enforcement decree, thereby strengthening the government's discretion.

Some observers speculate that, given that Lee Hyoung-il, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Ministry of Economy and Finance, emphasized the automotive industry's 'self-rescue efforts' during a press conference held on the 23rd, the determination of the base deduction amount will comprehensively consider investment, employment, and mutual benefit plans of major domestic companies.

Attention is also being paid to whether export-oriented electric vehicles will receive benefits. The government stated in its tax reform plan that benefits would only be available for vehicles directly produced and sold domestically.

However, Rep. Lee specified "domestic sales or exports" as the scope of application for the system. The automotive industry also takes the position that exported units should be included in the support targets, given that the ultimate goal of this system is to secure price competitiveness in the global electric vehicle market. However, in this case, the scale of tax exemptions would increase significantly, leaving the government with no choice but to proceed cautiously.

On the other hand, opinions are emerging that the issue of fairness with other industries struggling due to the 'Chinese offensive' could become a last-minute variable in introducing the system.

Oh Jong-hyun, Director-General of the Korea Institute for Public Finance, pointed out at a recent meeting of the Fiscal and Economic Planning Committee, "Not only electric vehicles, but also in other industries such as steel, if price competitiveness declines in competition with China, these (support targets) will continue to increase, and fiscal costs will skyrocket," adding, "We must consider what kind of ripple effects this will have."

text:
JAKARTA, INDONESIA (23 November 2026) — The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved the second subprogram of the Affordable and Sustainable Energy Transition Program, supporting Indonesia’s efforts to strengthen energy security and economic resilience while accelerating the shift to cleaner energy.

As Indonesia’s shift to sustainable energy evolves toward a more integrated, intersectoral approach, the program broadens reforms beyond the power sector to support critical minerals and manufacturing, industrial decarbonization, carbon markets, just transition, and regional electricity connectivity.

The program builds on reforms initiated under the first subprogram, approved in 2024, and reflects Indonesia’s efforts to build a more secure, affordable, and sustainable energy future. Together, these reforms are designed by the government to make the shift to cleaner energy work for the people and businesses.

“A successful shift to sustainable energy is not only about cleaner energy. It is also about creating the conditions for businesses to invest, grow, and create jobs,” said ADB Country Director for Indonesia Bobur Alimov. “These reforms can help attract investment into sustainable industries while ensuring that the benefits are shared more widely.”

Key reforms under the program include strengthening carbon market frameworks and mineral traceability, improving electricity subsidy targeting, broadening risk mitigation for clean energy investment, supporting electric vehicle ecosystem development, and mainstreaming measures to protect women and girls and just transition practices in state-owned enterprises. The program also promotes energy conservation and supports bilateral cooperation in exploring opportunities for electricity connectivity and related carbon-crediting arrangements.

The program, supported with an equivalent of $500 million in ADB financing, complemented with cofinancing support from JICA, KfW, AFD and AIIB, emphasizes energy independence, private sector-driven downstream industrialization, and equitable development, while ensuring that its reform agenda remains aligned with Indonesia’s national priorities, as reflected in the National Medium-Term Development Plan 2025–2029 and Golden Indonesia Vision 2045.

ADB is a longstanding partner of Indonesia and ASEAN. As the region’s main bank, ADB supports countries in advancing the shift to clean energy while strengthening institutions, financing, and systems needed to deliver sustainable and resilient growth.

ADB is a leading multilateral development bank supporting sustainable, inclusive, and resilient growth across Asia and the Pacific. Working with its members and partners to solve complex challenges together, ADB harnesses innovative financial tools and strategic partnerships to transform lives, build quality infrastructure, and safeguard our planet. Founded in 1966, ADB is owned by 69 members—50 from the region.

title: IFC announces $175 million in Jordan deals to strengthen water resilience, clean energy ...
description:
The initiatives target water resilience, clean energy, support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and trade, high-tech investment conditions, and manufacturing and women’s employment.
Water resilience through climate and water finance A central component of the package is an IFC investment of $100 million into Arab Bank’s adaptation and resilience blue bond.
Unlocking new capital for SMEs and trade IFC also announced a $50 million financing package for Safwa Islamic Bank.
In addition, the partnership includes a $50 million trade line under IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program.
The mix of Jordan-specific measures and regional clean energy investments also suggests opportunities for partnerships with local stakeholders working across water, energy, and enterprise development.
text:
On 19 November 2026, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, announced five investment and advisory agreements at the EU-Jordan Investment Conference to expand access to finance and mobilize private capital in Jordan. The initiatives target water resilience, clean energy, support for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and trade, high-tech investment conditions, and manufacturing and women’s employment. Together, the agreements are designed to support private-sector growth and job creation while aligning with Jordan’s Economic Modernization Vision.

Water resilience through climate and water finance

A central component of the package is an IFC investment of $100 million into Arab Bank’s adaptation and resilience blue bond. According to the IFC announcement, the bond—described as the first issued by a commercial bank in Jordan—will finance measures to improve water efficiency, reduce non-revenue water, expand wastewater treatment and agricultural reuse, and strengthen water systems in water-stressed areas.

IFC said the bond supports Arab Bank’s strategy to embed environmental, social and governance (ESG) considerations in its business operations to support long-term value for stakeholders and communities.

Unlocking new capital for SMEs and trade

IFC also announced a $50 million financing package for Safwa Islamic Bank. The package includes $30 million from the OPEC Fund and will support lending for SMEs and sustainable projects, including initiatives led by SMEs. IFC noted that the arrangement marks Jordan’s first Sharia-compliant financing dedicated to sustainability.

In addition, the partnership includes a $50 million trade line under IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. The aim is to help facilitate trade flows and narrow financing gaps facing underserved SMEs, building on work described by IFC as linked to the Central Bank of Jordan’s efforts on green finance.

IFC said the support is connected to the Global SME Finance Facility (GSMEF), a blended-finance partnership funded by the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the Netherlands’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which focuses on financial inclusion and reducing the financing gap for underserved SMEs in emerging markets.

Scaling clean energy across MENA with a focus on Jordan

Under the clean energy pillar, IFC is investing $25 million in Catalyst MENA Climate Fund 2. The fund includes $10 million in blended finance equity from IFC’s Frontier Opportunities Fund, which IFC said has already helped mobilize $127 million from companies and entities based in Australia, Europe, and the Gulf Cooperation Council.

IFC said the fund will provide equity for projects including solar, wind, energy efficiency, energy storage, and water treatment. The investment focus will cover Jordan, Egypt, Tunisia, and Morocco, with the stated objectives of improving energy access, resilience, and energy diversification. IFC also said it advised the fund on integrating a gender and a forced displacement lens into its operations and investments.

Advisory to position Jordan for high-tech investment

The agreements also include an advisory engagement intended to strengthen Jordan’s high-tech investment environment. IFC said it is advising the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship to assess Jordan’s semiconductor investment landscape, specifically focusing on chip design and assembly, testing and packaging (ATP).

IFC said the partnership also aims to strengthen conditions for high-tech investment, and includes training to build the Ministry’s capacity in collaboration with its investment promotion arm, Jordan Source, to attract and support investors. This advisory engagement is delivered in partnership with the Government of the Netherlands through the MENA PSD program.

Textile manufacturing support and women’s employment

IFC said it is partnering with Jerash Holdings to support the company’s expansion program. The project is expected to support the creation of more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs, including for women, who already make up about 74% of the workforce, according to IFC. IFC added that the support is also intended to help enhance the company’s production capacity.

IFC further stated it will support Jerash Holdings through EDGE Gender Certification, a standard used to improve working conditions, employability, and career progression opportunities for women.

Link to IFC’s broader Jordan portfolio

IFC described the five agreements as reinforcing its long-term commitment to private investment, sustainable growth, jobs, and financial inclusion in Jordan. The announcement states that Jordan is one of IFC’s largest portfolios in the Middle East, with $919.7 million committed across 31 projects.

Why the development package matters beyond the projects

The announcement reflects a program approach that combines financing instruments—such as blue bonds, blended finance equity, and trade lines—with sector-specific advisory support. By targeting water efficiency, wastewater and reuse, clean energy investment, SME access to capital, and job-rich manufacturing expansion, IFC’s package is positioned as contributing to multiple development priorities, including climate resilience, gender equality, and inclusive economic growth.

Key Details

Initiative or programme: Five IFC investment and advisory agreements announced at the EU-Jordan Investment Conference (water resilience, SME finance and trade, clean energy, high-tech advisory, and textile manufacturing and women’s employment)

Lead organization: International Finance Corporation (IFC), member of the World Bank Group

Partners: Arab Bank; Safwa Islamic Bank; OPEC Fund; Catalyst MENA Climate Fund 2; Frontier Opportunities Fund (IFC); Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship; Jordan Source; Government of the Netherlands (via MENA PSD program); Jerash Holdings; Global SME Finance Facility (GSMEF) funded by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the Netherlands’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Funding amount: $175 million total stated across five investments: $100 million (Arab Bank blue bond) + $50 million (Safwa Islamic Bank financing package) + $25 million (Catalyst MENA Climate Fund 2)

Geographic focus: Jordan; and clean energy investments across MENA including Jordan, Egypt, Tunisia, and Morocco (for Catalyst MENA Climate Fund 2)

Target groups: SMEs (including underserved SMEs), trade actors using trade finance, communities in water-stressed areas (via water systems and reuse investments), investors and workforce in high-tech and semiconductor-adjacent activities, and women workers in textile manufacturing

Expected reach or outcomes (verified): More than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs expected from Jerash Holdings expansion, including for women (women already make up about 74% of the workforce, per IFC)

Timing: Announced on 19 November 2026

Why This Matters

IFC’s Jordan package illustrates how development finance is increasingly combining commercial financial instruments with development objectives such as water resilience, SME inclusion, energy transition, and gender-focused employment outcomes. For NGOs and development professionals, the announcement highlights several practical areas to watch: the use of blue bonds to channel private capital into water systems; blended finance and trade lines to address SME financing gaps; and sector-linked advisory support tied to investment promotion and workforce capacity-building.

The gender emphasis in both the textile manufacturing component (via EDGE Gender Certification) and the clean energy fund (through integration of a gender and forced displacement lens) may offer reference points for program design, particularly where private-sector investment is expected to generate jobs and access to services. The mix of Jordan-specific measures and regional clean energy investments also suggests opportunities for partnerships with local stakeholders working across water, energy, and enterprise development.

text:
A Sierra Club attorney said Sunday it remains unclear whether a court order temporarily putting on hold the Army’s EPA permit would prevent the Army from detonating nearly five tons of lead azide this week at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an administrative stay of the EPA’s emergency permit Thursday, pending its ruling on the groups’ emergency motion. That prompted the federal government to say it would use its emergency authority to continue with its plan to destroy the chemicals being stored south of the Quad-Cities and near the Mississippi River.

The detonation is set to take place Wednesday for optimal weather conditions, the Army said in a post on X. The Army had originally planned to detonate the material Friday, then announced a delay until Monday before pushing it to Wednesday.

In a notice filed late Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department said the Army intends to invoke a separate emergency exclusion under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate the material without a permit from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency EPA permit no later than Nov. 24.

The federal government argues the court’s administrative stay of the EPA permit does not prevent the Army from acting under a separate RCRA emergency exclusion. The government said colder weather and continued delays could increase the danger.

Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter, said the groups fighting to halt the detonation believe the court’s stay should stop the demolition, while the Army argues the order does not apply to action under the separate authority its invoking.

“I guess a lawyer’s answer is we don’t know. It’s a little up in the air,” Taylor said.

The Sierra Club is still asking the court to extend the stay, he said, though he is not confident the court can prevent the Army from acting.

” It’s been really discouraging that the Army has not been more transparent about what they’re doing and when they let people know,” Taylor said. “We didn’t know about this until just a few days ago, and the Army apparently has known about this for quite some time, but they haven’t been very good about notifying the public.”

He said his group and others want the demolition to be done safely and be followed by adequate cleanup if it proceeds.

The environmental groups said in a Sunday statement that declarations filed with the court challenged the Army’s public notice and questioned whether it had properly considered alternatives.

The groups have urged consideration of chemical neutralization, though the Army says that option would require prolonged handling of the 68 drums and increase the risk of an accidental explosion, the AP reported.

Cody Smith, program director at the Iowa Environmental Council, said the council had not received updated plume maps or modeling and was urging the Army to release them.

“We are less than 48 hours from their planned date of detonation according to the filing today, and we have yet to see any of that information,” Smith said. “It’s critical for Iowans and community leaders at every level to be able to protect themselves and their families from lead exposure, of which we know there is no safe level for humans.”

Smith said the filings led the environmental council to believe detonation may now be the best treatment option, but he blamed the Army’s handling and storage of the material for creating the crisis.

He said the Army had not directly confirmed a date or time. Although the filings indicate a plan to act by Tuesday, he said the timing remained unconfirmed.

” I think it’s really important that folks continue to call on the Army and on federal officials for transparency as soon as possible,” Smith said. “If folks are looking for something to do, reaching out to their elected federal officials is probably the most helpful at this point.”

text:
Premier Roger Cook to visit Japan to strengthen Western Australia's biggest energy partnership and back local jobs

WA LNG and renewable energy sectors to be showcased to major Japanese investors and energy companies

Mission focused on attracting investment, supporting trade, and strengthening long-term energy security

Premier Roger Cook will travel to Japan next week to strengthen one of Western Australia's most important economic partnerships, support local jobs, and reinforce WA's role as a reliable energy supplier to the region.

The Premier will be in market from 24 November to 28 November, with engagements focusing on deepening government-to-government engagement with Japan and progressing shared priorities across trade, investment, energy, critical minerals, defence, and manufacturing.

The Premier will lead the Western Australian LNG Investment Forum & Business Luncheon in Tokyo, a government initiative delivered in partnership with the Australian and New Zealand Chamber of Commerce in Japan.

The forum will bring together senior Japanese LNG buyers, energy companies, trading houses, investors, financiers, and government representatives with proponents of the State's next generation LNG projects, including Chevron, Equus Energy, and Woodside.

WA's pipeline of LNG projects will be on display at the forum, highlighting opportunities for Japanese companies to secure long-term LNG supply agreements, invest in projects, and participate in project financing.

These projects reinforce WA's commitment to secure, long-term LNG supply to Japan, supporting its energy security through to 2050 and beyond, while also providing domestic gas to support growth in the State's advanced manufacturing sector.

The Premier will also tour Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and visit a JERA thermal power station, as well as sign a separate Memorandum of Cooperation with the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and engage with Japanese financial institutions on future cooperation.

Japan remains one of WA's most important and enduring economic partners and was the State's second-largest trading partner in 2024-25, with $28.2 billion in two-way goods trade, including $24.9 billion in Western Australian goods exports.

The Premier's engagements in Japan will highlight WA's competitive energy advantages, including its world-class natural gas resources and growing renewable energy sector, and its commitment to delivering affordable, reliable and cleaner energy.

Through investment in renewables, energy storage, and infrastructure, Western Australia is building a stronger energy future while continuing to support the energy security of key trading partners such as Japan.

The mission builds on the Cook Labor Government's ongoing engagement with Japan, including a recent visit led by Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson last month.

Comments attributed to Premier and Tourism, Trade and Investment Minister Roger Cook:

"Japan has been one of Western Australia's closest and most important partners for decades, supporting thousands of local jobs and billions of dollars in investment.

"This visit is about making sure WA remains the partner of choice as Japan looks for secure, reliable energy supplies into the future.

"We're building a stronger economy by backing the industries that create jobs today while investing in the cleaner energy technologies and industries of tomorrow.

"Our State has everything the world needs to power the energy transition, from natural gas and critical minerals through to renewable energy, and we'll continue working closely with partners like Japan to deliver it."

text:
The government has decided to evaluate industrial competitiveness and the potential for mutual growth with the parts industry while considering whether to include electric vehicles (EVs) in domestic production tax credits. It has adopted a cautious stance on revising income tax brackets due to concerns over potential tax revenue losses, and is preparing a compromise proposal that incorporates parliamentary feedback regarding the so-called "anti-stock price suppression bill."

Support for EV Production, Plan to be Announced This Week

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il stated at a press conference with the press corps at the Government Complex Sejong on the 23rd that the decision on whether to include EVs in domestic production tax credit eligibility would be made "after a comprehensive assessment." The government plans to announce measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry this week.

Domestic production tax credits are a form of corporate tax support designed to reduce the tax burden on companies producing goods domestically. The industry is calling for EVs to be included in the credit scheme, which offers corporate tax relief, to counter the influx of low-priced Chinese EVs. This system differs in its purpose and scope from the acquisition tax exemptions applied at the vehicle purchase stage.

“The Next 2–3 Years are the Golden Time for Transition”

Deputy Prime Minister Lee explained that he views the next two to three years as a critical period for the transition in the electric vehicle market. However, his position is that rather than making an immediate decision on tax credits for finished vehicles, the government must examine the effects on overall industrial competitiveness and the ecosystem.

He presented the potential for sufficient competitiveness of EVs themselves and the industry's efforts to create a structure that fosters mutual growth with parts suppliers as criteria for determining support. The intention is to look at the entire supply chain, including parts and charging systems, rather than just finished vehicles when reviewing support for the EV industry.

The current system already provides some tax credits and tax exemptions for technologies, parts, and charging facilities related to electric and hydrogen vehicles. If finished EVs are added to the list for domestic production tax credits, the government may also review whether the scope of application overlaps with existing support.

Cautious Stance on Income Tax Reform

Regarding demands to adjust income tax brackets amid criticisms that inflation has increased the actual tax burden, the Deputy Prime Minister expressed a cautious view. The tax base refers to the income standards used to apply tax rates; adjusting this can change both the tax burden on individual workers and government tax revenue.

Deputy Prime Minister Lee said there are significant concerns that the tax base could be weakened and that the impact on tax revenue must be considered comprehensively. He explained that the appropriateness of such changes must be examined carefully over time, taking into account trends in workers' tax burdens, deduction levels, and changes in taxation by income bracket.

In this year's tax reform bill, the government is also pushing to significantly expand the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) to boost work incentives and support income. This approach aims to strengthen support for low-income workers separately from adjustments to income tax brackets.

Compromise Proposal Prepared for Listed Stock Valuation Adjustments

Regarding the government's push for what is known as the "anti-stock price suppression bill," a compromise proposal incorporating opinions from the National Assembly is being prepared. The core of the discussion involves expanding the scope of listed stock valuations and increasing minimum premiums.

Deputy Prime Minister Lee stated that he views the feedback suggesting the government's initial proposal was too narrow and had room for higher tax burdens positively. However, he added that safeguards are needed to prevent the system's design from leading to constitutional disputes.

The government plans to adjust the scope and level of tax burden during the parliamentary discussion process while developing a plan that avoids constitutional controversy.

The U.S. Senate passed legislation late Thursday that would overhaul federal permitting, with Minnesota’s Democratic senators casting opposing votes.

Coined the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the bill passed the Senate 62-33. It is meant to speed the approval of power plants, transmission infrastructure and other large projects.

Supporters maintained it would speed the development of renewable energy projects and protect electricity ratepayers from data centers. But critics argued it would instead spur a build-out of data centers and fossil fuel projects while paring key aspects of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws.

While Sen. Tina Smith opposed the bill, Sen. Amy Klobuchar was among 14 Democrats who voted for it.

“I have long supported modernizing our permitting process to lower costs, get more affordable clean energy onto the grid, and create good-paying jobs,” Klobuchar, who will become governor in January, said in a statement to the Duluth News Tribune on Friday. “But I have also been clear that this legislation needed improvements to strengthen tribal and environmental protections. I voted for the bill because I believe it will help address longstanding permitting challenges, but there is more to do to ensure stronger protections are included in law in the future.”

In a statement late Thursday, Smith said she opposed the bill because it would make it easier for Twin Metals to build a copper-nickel mine in the same watershed as the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, and it would violate tribal sovereignty.

“I have always said, and I still believe, that we need permitting reform,” Smith said. “We need to update our outdated permitting process so we can lower energy costs by getting cleaner, cheaper power connected to the grid, but this bill is a bad deal that Democrats should not take.”

The bill similarly divided some environmental groups.

Citizens’ Climate Lobby said it “applauded” the bill’s passage and said it could reduce greenhouse gases, but was disappointed that amendments addressing tribal concerns were “obstructed” during the Senate’s debate.

“The bill makes meaningful progress toward unlocking clean energy development and transmission infrastructure, which are desperately needed nationwide,” the group said Thursday.

The Sierra Club said the U.S. House of Representatives should reject the bill.

“While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the build-out of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife,” Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford said in a news release Thursday.

The bill has the support of President Donald Trump and now heads to the Republican-controlled House.

Rep. Pete Stauber, R-Hermantown, said he planned to vote yes on the bill.

“This is the most significant permitting-reform package in U.S. history,” Stauber said on social media. “Once it clears the House, America will build again, and American families will save thousands of dollars a year.”

title: Tesla's $3.1 Billion Solar Polysilicon Bet: Musk Is Back, But Needs Washington's Help Again
description:
Elon Musk appears to be making another serious attempt at entering the solar manufacturing business.
The proposed facility would manufacture ultra-high-purity polysilicon, a critical raw material used in the production of solar ingots, wafers and cells.
Tesla's proposed $3.1 billion investment in just one upstream manufacturing facility is an indication of the capital involved.
That raises an obvious question: if Tesla's manufacturing ambitions are commercially competitive, why is such substantial public support necessary?
The proposed polysilicon facility is still at the application stage, and the $10.1 billion solar manufacturing project is also dependent on significant incentives and execution milestones.
text:
Elon Musk appears to be making another serious attempt at entering the solar manufacturing business. Tesla has proposed a $3.1 billion investment in a solar-grade polysilicon facility in Nueces County, Texas, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and commercial operations targeted for 2030.

But there is an important qualification to the announcement. Tesla has told authorities that it would not make the investment in Texas without a property-tax incentive agreement under the state's Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) programme. In other words, one of the world's most valuable companies is looking for government assistance to make its latest manufacturing ambition commercially viable.

The proposed facility would manufacture ultra-high-purity polysilicon, a critical raw material used in the production of solar ingots, wafers and cells. Tesla has not disclosed the proposed plant's production capacity, although industry estimates suggest it could be in the range of 30,000-40,000 tonnes annually.

The project is expected to employ 260 people when operations begin in 2030, rising to 515 by 2032. More than 80% of the proposed investment is expected to be spent in 2028 and 2029.

The facility is part of a much larger ambition. Tesla has separately proposed a $10.1 billion vertically integrated solar manufacturing facility in Fort Bend County, Texas, which would cover several stages of the solar supply chain. Together, the proposals represent a significant attempt to build a domestic manufacturing ecosystem rather than rely on imported Chinese components. With its history of solar manufacturing and now Megapack Battery making as well, Tesla remains the most promising large firm in the US capable of taking on Chinese competition. Yet the economics remain the biggest question.

The China problem cannot be wished away

China accounts for more than 90% of global solar-grade polysilicon production, according to Tesla's own filing. Its dominance extends across virtually the entire solar manufacturing chain, supported by years of investment, enormous manufacturing scale, established supply networks and intense competition between producers.

Replicating that ecosystem in the US is an expensive proposition. Tesla's proposed $3.1 billion investment in just one upstream manufacturing facility is an indication of the capital involved.

The US is attempting to change this equation through tariffs, import price mechanisms and incentives for domestic manufacturing. New Section 232 trade measures targeting polysilicon and its derivatives are also scheduled to take effect in December 2026.

These measures could make imported Chinese material more expensive, improving the relative economics of domestic production. But they do not automatically make US-produced polysilicon competitive with Chinese supply on an unsubsidised basis.

Tesla's own application is revealing. It describes the tax agreement as a compelling factor in its site-selection decision, adding that the investment would not be made in Texas without it.

That raises an obvious question: if Tesla's manufacturing ambitions are commercially competitive, why is such substantial public support necessary?

A familiar Musk business model

This is hardly the first time Musk's businesses have depended on government support to get large investments off the ground.

Tesla's early expansion was helped by a $465 million US Department of Energy loan, which the company subsequently repaid. Its growth also benefited from federal electric-vehicle tax credits, state-level manufacturing incentives and the sale of regulatory credits to other automakers.

SpaceX, meanwhile, received crucial early support through NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services programme and subsequent cargo and crew transportation contracts. Government procurement helped create a market for its launch services and provided a revenue base for developing technologies that eventually found wider commercial applications.

SolarCity, which Tesla acquired in 2016, also benefited from substantial public backing for its Buffalo, New York manufacturing facility, including a reported $750 million state investment.

More broadly, a Washington Post investigation published in 2025 estimated that Musk's businesses had received at least $38 billion in government contracts, loans, grants, subsidies and tax credits over more than two decades. This figure includes commercial government contracts, which should not be confused with outright subsidies, but illustrates the scale of the public-sector relationship.

There is little unusual about governments supporting strategically important industries. What is more interesting is how frequently the success of Musk's businesses has depended on a combination of public investment, policy support and private execution.

Tesla's latest solar ambitions appear to be following a similar path.

Who ultimately pays for the solar ambition?

The larger question is whether the US can create a competitive solar manufacturing industry through this approach. Tesla is not simply competing against Chinese manufacturers. It is attempting to recreate an entire supply chain in a country where labour, energy, construction and financing costs can be significantly higher.

Tax incentives can help bridge part of that gap. Tariffs can protect domestic producers from cheaper imports. Government procurement and domestic-content policies can create a market for their output.

But all of these interventions have costs, whether borne by taxpayers, electricity consumers or businesses purchasing the resulting products. For solar, that creates a particularly awkward contradiction. The technology has become globally competitive largely because manufacturing costs have fallen dramatically, led by China. Rebuilding capacity at substantially higher costs in the US could undermine some of the very economics that made solar attractive in the first place.

Tesla's bet is that vertical integration, automation, domestic supply security and supportive policy will eventually make the numbers work.

That remains to be demonstrated. The proposed polysilicon facility is still at the application stage, and the $10.1 billion solar manufacturing project is also dependent on significant incentives and execution milestones.

Musk may be back in solar with an ambitious plan. But this time, as on several previous occasions, the route to commercial success appears to run through government offices as much as factory floors.

Renewable energy refers to energy generated from naturally replenished sources like sunlight, wind, water, plants, and geothermal heat. It includes established technologies such as hydropower, bioenergy, and geothermal energy as well as emerging sources like solar photovoltaics (PV), wind turbines, and ocean energy (IRENA, 2019). Renewables offer energy security as they utilize domestic resources, unlike importing fossil fuels. Solar, wind, hydro, and other renewables also produce negligible greenhouse gas emissions during operations, helping address climate change (IPCC, 2022). The Philippines has abundant renewable energy resources such as solar, geothermal, hydro, and biomass that can meet and even exceed domestic demand if fully tapped (Gulagi et al., 2021).

As one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change, investing in renewables will help the country mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and adapt to the effects of climate change. Within the green economy, renewable energy stands out as a key sector requiring massive workforce skilling and reskilling globally (IRENA, 2019). At the same time, the growth of the renewable energy sector presents opportunities for decent and green job creation. The IEA (2021) projects renewable energy to account for over 90% of global power generation by 2050, with solar and wind constituting nearly 70%. This exponential growth will require corresponding labor. IRENA (2019) estimates the renewable energy sector to employ 43 million people by 2050. The Philippines provides a microcosm of this global trend. However, significant skills gaps exist. The recent Skills Audit Survey by the Green Jobs Human Resource Council revealed occupational shortages, lack of green credentials, and mismatches between industry needs and training programs (TESDA, 2022).

Jeff Wyden Merkley and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) introduced an amendment to the bill that would ban data centers on public land.
The effort to streamline federal permitting to benefit clean energy has been underway for decades.
It’s one thing to build a big wind or solar installation on a patch of BLM land or private land, quite another to permit a 300-mile transmission line that crosses a dozen different jurisdictions.
Earlier this week, Heinrich sat down for an interview with The Hill’s Alex Bolton and they got to talking about the SunZia transmission project.
text:
Heinrich and other pro-BAAJAers hold up the SunZia transmission project’s 17-year permitting journey as evidence of why permitting reform is needed. Yet it is now under construction, for better or worse. Meanwhile, other major lines were also approved, including TransWest Express, Ten West Link, Gateway South, and Boardman-to-Hemingway.

The anti-BAAJA crowd has said the legislation will “gut” and “eviscerate” bedrock environmental laws (I may have used similar language) and would “supercharge” the data center boom, leading to “environmental catastrophe.”

In fact, the legislation would tweak and weaken NEPA, NHPA, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and make the General Mining Law even more permissive than it already is. Michael B. Gerrard, Andrew Sabin Professor of Professional Practice at Columbia Law School, described it as pulling “NEPA’s principal teeth,” by precluding the possibility of a court order blocking a project. While losing one’s teeth isn’t as bad as losing one’s guts, it does suck, and these changes would rob the public of their say over how its lands are managed.

BAAJA’s only data center-specific provision would require that data centers pay the full cost of associated grid and infrastructure upgrades to ensure that utility ratepayers are not stuck with the tab; even the most vehement anti-BAAJA groups like this aspect of the legislation.

Beyond that, it’s not clear that BAAJA would have much effect on data center development. So far, the Big Data Center Buildup has occurred largely outside the federal permitting system. The huge projects going up or being proposed all over the West, from Project Stratos to Project Jupiter to Valar Atomic’s Raceway Energy, are all on private or state land, and don’t have a federal component, meaning they are not subject to NEPA, meaning BAAJA would have no or little effect on them. Unless, that is, the facility requires a transmission line or gas pipeline or some other infrastructure that crosses federal land or affects Waters of the United States, and would therefore be subject to NEPA, NHPA, the CWA, and/or the ESA. In that case, the associated infrastructure, and therefore the data center itself, would benefit from BAAJA.

And, of course, if a developer were to formally propose a data center on public land, BAAJA would limit the public’s ability to block it. Only one data center project has formally been proposed for public lands, and the Trump administration simply ignored NEPA and any environmental review requirements and secretly gave it the go-ahead (which was later revoked). But other developers have expressed interest in public lands, and the administration has signaled its desires to hand those lands over to the developers, so this certainly could become an issue in the future, which is why Sens. Jeff Wyden Merkley and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) introduced an amendment to the bill that would ban data centers on public land. It did not pass.

Et tu, Martin?

The internecine feud over the bill risks eroding environmental support for Democrats like Heinrich, who previously were known to stand up for public lands and tribal sovereignty. One Land Desk reader, in a comment, wondered what Heinrich’s motivations were, adding: “ … it seems like he is blowing up his previous environmental record with this … .”

I certainly can’t speak for Heinrich, nor do I have any desire to be an apologist for him, but from my perspective it seems that support for this bill is not only sincere, but is in line with his previous record on these issues.

The effort to streamline federal permitting to benefit clean energy has been underway for decades. During the early days of the energy transition, wind and solar developers in places like Wyoming and eastern New Mexico ran up against a lack of transmission capacity to get the energy from the windy and sunny spaces to the places it is needed, such as the urban Southwest. It’s one thing to build a big wind or solar installation on a patch of BLM land or private land, quite another to permit a 300-mile transmission line that crosses a dozen different jurisdictions. While the federal Natural Gas Act gives companies certain bludgeons to build interstate pipelines — including the power of condemnation, it doesn’t do the same for big transmission, and permitting a major project can take a decade or more.

That difficulty — and the need not only for more transmission, but also for an integrated Western power grid — spawned a movement aimed at developing long-distance power lines to facilitate solar and wind development. New organizations such as Americans for a Clean Energy Grid sprung up to support the effort, while some existing environmental groups got on board in a more limited fashion, such as the National Resources Defense Council and Western Resource Advocates. Heinrich, who was elected to the Senate in 2012, was one of the few federal lawmakers to really embrace this concept and to advocate for a 100% clean energy grid. He was a big proponent of the SunZia transmission line that carries wind power from New Mexico to the Phoenix area, and uses its interminable route to approval as evidence that permitting reform is necessary to achieve a clean energy transition and tackle climate change.

Heinrich has introduced and backed other legislation aimed at encouraging transmission development and grid modernization. The Biden-era Infrastructure and Jobs and Inflation Reduction acts allocated billions of dollars to transmission lines, and in September Heinrich introduced a bill that would incentivize new transmission development. Now some Biden administration officials have said that permitting delays prevented some of the subsidized projects from getting built before the Trump administration clawed back much of the funds, killing the projects altogether.

If one believes that a major and rapid transmission buildout is necessary to bring more clean energy online to tackle the climate crisis (and to keep the grid from collapsing under increased energy demand), and if one believes that the primary hindrance blocking these projects is an outdated and overly rigorous permitting process that favors lawsuit-filing advocacy groups, then it would logically follow that streamlining the process would require weakening or partially dismantling the legal framework governing that process. Or to mix some metaphors: You’ve got to pull some teeth, or at least file them down, to keep the beast from killing your project (even if it ultimately harms the beast).

I imagine Heinrich, an old-school, pragmatic Democrat who prides himself on bipartisanship, felt he was signing onto the best chance at reform he could get in a Republican-dominated Congress, even if it was deeply compromised. He was able to get the GOP to sign on to decent provisions on transmission, including the one requiring data centers to pay their own way, despite strong objections from the utility industry. He had been on this path for so long that when he reached a destination — even if it wasn’t the one he originally had in mind — he immediately and stubbornly staked his flag there, largely ignoring constituents’ and colleagues’ protests.

Heinrich and his colleagues introduced amendments aimed at making the legislation more palatable to tribal nations. While one made it into the bill, it was not enough, according to the National Congress for American Indians, which still called on the Senate to kill the entire legislation. A later effort to further amend the bill was blocked, sparking yet another conflict between environmental and tribal advocates.

In doing so, he basically threw his lot into the same bet all of the environmentally minded, pro-BAAJA side is making: That the climate benefits of a clean energy buildout under a reformed permitting system will offset resulting direct harms to front-line communities, the landscape, the water, and the air. It’s a gamble, maybe even an act of faith, faith that when put on a level playing field, clean energy will always win out over fossil fuels, and a faith that even a weakened, toothless system will continue to protect the nation’s natural and cultural resources, even though it’s overseen by an ethically compromised administration. It’s a big and perilous leap, and we’ll all be forced to pay if Heinrich loses the bet.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Quaise Energy has signed a purchase agreement with Google to develop superhot geothermal energy near Bend, with electricity expected to begin flowing as early as 2030.

The agreement marks big step for Project Obsidian, which Quaise is developing on Bureau of Land Management land south of Newberry National Volcanic Monument, 20 miles south of Bend.

The project aims to tap deep underground heat to generate electricity for Google’s data center operations in The Dalles.

The agreement also provides a major customer for the project’s initial phase, which Quaise has been developing around a planned 50-megawatt power plant.

The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement.

Harry Kelso, a spokesperson for Quaise, said a power plant will bring economic benefit to Central Oregon.

“To date, we’ve injected more than $6 million into Deschutes County businesses as part of Project Obsidian, and we expect that local impact to continue as the project advances,” Kelso said.

The project is expected to support 200 to 400 construction jobs and create more than 50 permanent positions in engineering and operations, according to Quaise.

Earlier this year, Quaise drilled its first well at the site, a confirmation well expected to reach a depth of about 15,000 feet. The company is using conventional drilling methods for initial development, with plans to introduce its experimental drilling technology in a later phase.

The technology uses concentrated electromagnetic energy to break through hard rock and is designed to reach extreme underground temperatures that could make geothermal power more viable.

Quaise estimates superhot systems could produce up to 10 times more electricity per well than traditional geothermal systems.

Google has operated in The Dalles since 2006 and now has three data centers in the area. The company said its Oregon data centers use 83% carbon-free energy and that the new agreement will expand its investment in clean energy.

Google also said it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon over the past 20 years.

Data centers have come under fire in recent months amid public backlash against their massive energy and water needs. Around 75% of Americans now say they oppose data center construction near them.

Deschutes County Commissioner-elect Jamie Collins, a climate scientist and former environmental emergency response official, said in a statement on Tuesday that “transparent and deep engagement with our community” is needed.

Collins is calling on Obsidian for public outreach and engagement with tribal nations and community organizations. He also wants to learn if some of the energy will be available for residents and businesses in Central Oregon.

I’m excited that Central Oregon could become a net exporter of clean energy, but right now our county doesn’t have enough energy of any kind — or enough of the basic infrastructure like power lines — to meet our own needs over the next five years,” Collins said.

Project Obsidian is separate from the geothermal development being pursued by Mazama Energy in another part of the Newberry area. Both companies are pursuing enhanced geothermal systems, which use engineered underground reservoirs to extract heat from rock rather than relying on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs.

Quaise announced a $180 million Series B financing round in August, including a $35 million investment from drilling contractor Nabors Industries.

The company ultimately hopes to expand Project Obsidian beyond its initial 50-megawatt capacity, potentially reaching 250 megawatts or more if the geothermal resource supports further development.

text:
An electric vehicle (EV) charger manufacturer is bringing its first South Carolina operations to Fort Mill.

According to a Post and Courier report, Alpitronic, the Italian EV-charging equipment maker — whose chargers are used by companies including Ionna, Walmart, Mercedes-Benz, BP Pulse, and Electrify America — plans to establish a major manufacturing operation in Fort Mill.

Located at 3560 Stateview Blvd., the company will use a 173,315-square-foot facility to assemble its Hypercharger DC fast chargers. The facility will include the HYC400 and HYC1000, along with warehousing, testing, repair, logistics, and office operations.

Production is expected to begin in February 2027. Alpitronic bought the property for $28.4 million in September. The project is part of a redevelopment of the former Wells Fargo Home Mortgage site near Interstate 77 and Carowinds, according to a report by The Herald.

According to the Post and Courier, the $33.94 million project is expected to create 70 jobs, with roles focused on quality, purchasing, production, and customer experience.

Alpitronic said the assembly operation will use no industrial chemicals or batteries, and will not require significant water or utility consumption.

The Fort Mill site builds on Alpitronic's North American headquarters in Charlotte and its first local production site, which opened in Wisconsin in 2024. Its global headquarters is in Bolzano, Italy.

“We're pleased to welcome Alpitronic to York County and to see the company choose our community for its new manufacturing operation,” said Christi Cox, chairwoman of the York County Council, in a statement shared with the Post and Courier. “With its North American headquarters already in the Charlotte region, this is a natural fit as the company expands its U.S. operations. We appreciate Alpitronic's investment and look forward to the new jobs and opportunities it will bring.”

Alpitronic CEO Patrik Herrnegger said the company expects demand for fast charging to rise as electric and driverless vehicles become more common.

“Our Fort Mill facility will put U.S. production under our direct control, bringing us closer to our customers and enabling us to serve them more efficiently. We thank South Carolina and York County for their partnership as we prepare to begin production in early 2027,” he said in a statement.

South Carolina's Coordinating Council for Economic Development approved job development credits for the Alpitronic project and awarded York County a $200,000 grant for building improvements, according to the Fort Mill Sun.

Individuals interested in employment opportunities with the company can visit Alpitronic's careers page.

title: Europe could lose billions in battery investment under proposed Franco-German car deal
description:
T&E argues that the Franco-German deal would secure a smaller share of the market than existing conditions, as more than 50% of battery cells used in electric vehicles sold in the EU are already manufactured in Europe.
Under the proposed agreement, EU-made battery cells would be required in only 10% of eligible vehicles in 2028 and 2029, rising to 20% in 2030 and 2031, before reaching 70% from 2032.
The potential effects extend beyond battery cell manufacturing to the production of key components.
T&E identifies facilities such as Lyten, formerly Northvolt, in Sweden, PowerCo Salzgitter in Germany and Verkor Dunkirk in France as projects whose prospects could be affected by the proposed changes.
In response, T&E is calling on EU policymakers to reject the Franco-German proposal on batteries and maintain the timelines and battery requirements included in the European Commission’s IAA proposal.
text:
A proposed Franco-German agreement on the automotive sector could secure only 13% of Europe’s planned battery cell production by 2030, putting the region’s battery manufacturing ambitions at risk, according to an analysis published by Transport & Environment (T&E) on 19 November 2026. The organisation warns that weaker EU local-content requirements and proposals to ease vehicle emissions targets could shift demand towards foreign suppliers and undermine investment in Europe’s battery value chain.

The analysis estimates that around 100 GWh of battery cell demand, equivalent to approximately 1.5 million electric vehicles, and 250 GWh of cathode active material demand could move outside Europe by 2030 under the proposed rules. T&E argues that the Franco-German deal would secure a smaller share of the market than existing conditions, as more than 50% of battery cells used in electric vehicles sold in the EU are already manufactured in Europe.

Under the proposed agreement, EU-made battery cells would be required in only 10% of eligible vehicles in 2028 and 2029, rising to 20% in 2030 and 2031, before reaching 70% from 2032. T&E estimates that this framework would secure cell production equivalent to around 900,000 electric vehicles in 2030, compared with 4.6 million under a stricter Made-in-EU approach within the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).

The organisation also highlights the potential impact of changes to EU vehicle emissions rules. According to its analysis, proposals by the European Parliament to weaken emissions reduction requirements could reduce demand for EU-made battery cells by 247 GWh between 2027 and 2032, equivalent to the batteries needed for approximately 3.7 million electric vehicles manufactured in the EU. T&E compares this volume with almost three times the annual production capacity of LG Energy Solution’s plant in Poland, which it identifies as Europe’s largest battery factory.

The potential effects extend beyond battery cell manufacturing to the production of key components. T&E says that a broad scope for free trade agreement (FTA) partners under the IAA could allow lower-cost countries to capture demand before European manufacturers. By contrast, the organisation estimates that stricter Made-in-EU requirements could generate 323 GWh of additional demand for EU-made cathode active materials, bringing total demand to 407 GWh and securing 94% of expected EU supply by 2032.

The report also raises concerns about projects that have yet to begin production, as most of the battery cell capacity expected in Europe by 2030 comes from factories still in the development or ramp-up stages. T&E identifies facilities such as Lyten, formerly Northvolt, in Sweden, PowerCo Salzgitter in Germany and Verkor Dunkirk in France as projects whose prospects could be affected by the proposed changes.

In response, T&E is calling on EU policymakers to reject the Franco-German proposal on batteries and maintain the timelines and battery requirements included in the European Commission’s IAA proposal. It also advocates for a strict Made-in-EU scope, or a limited list of trusted partners comprising the EU27, the European Economic Area (EEA) and the UK, alongside maintaining the existing vehicle CO? reduction standards without further weakening them.
