text:
DTE Energy is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports requirements of a settlement agreement approved by the Michigan Public Service Commission in Case No. U-21662.

Why it matters

The projects are intended to create construction jobs, support local communities, and save customers money on fuel costs, while reducing the company's exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. For Michigan, the procurement adds to the state's shift toward renewable generation.

DTE is seeking up to 150 megawatts of solar, a fraction of the 15 gigawatts of additional renewable energy its 2026 Integrated Resource Plan calls for by 2042. Selected projects must reach commercial operation by June 30, 2030, and final contract volumes remain unset until bids close January 19, 2027.

The players

DTE Energy

DTE Energy is a Detroit-based utility holding company serving electric and natural gas customers across Michigan.

Michigan Public Service Commission

The Michigan Public Service Commission is the state agency that regulates utilities and approved the settlement agreement in Case No. U-21662.

The details

Projects must be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE's distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate, with proposals due January 19, 2027.

Timeline

May 15, 2025: Michigan Public Service Commission approved the settlement agreement in Case No. U-21662.

January 19, 2027: Competitive solar proposals are due.

Second or third quarter of 2027: DTE expects to execute contracts.

June 30, 2030: Deadline for projects to reach commercial operation.

2042: Target year for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy.

Utilities Landscape

The solicitation implements the obligations set out in the settlement approved in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, which requires DTE to procure new in-state solar capacity. It fits DTE's 2026 Integrated Resource Plan, which calls for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042.

Michigan residents and customers may see fuel-cost savings over the operating lives of the new projects, according to DTE's stated expectations. The procurement is tied to projects that must be built in Michigan and connect to the MISO transmission system or DTE's distribution system.

The takeaway

The procurement shows how a state settlement can translate into concrete renewable capacity, with contracts and in-state construction following a multi-year timeline. Readers tracking Michigan's energy transition can watch the January 2027 proposal deadline as the next milestone.

What happens next

DTE Energy's competitive solar proposals are due January 19, 2027, and the company expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks fizzled out Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable. Nations' negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word “disappointing” to characterize the discussions.

Though the talks, called COP31, failed to reach a main agreement, known as a cover decision, the meeting had already made progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night, after running more than 50 hours overtime at the resort town of Antalya.

This all happened as global warming accelerates with ever-worsening heat waves, floods, storms and droughts. The U.N. said it is now inevitable that the world will soon blow past the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. And there is also a global energy shock due to the war in Iran. On top of that, a strong El Niño amplifies human-caused warming and causes more weather disasters.

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

Upset youth representative Oumnia Anfer told the negotiators “you have let us down.”

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn’t mention fossil fuels. A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks.

Previously, fossil fuels went unmentioned in COP final decisions for more than 25 years, said Alden Meyer, with the think tank E3G. Then, three years ago in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai agreement in its entirety, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

“Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis,” said Guterres. “The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks and undermining energy security. We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it.”

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would undermine efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of COP31 is an outrage — it is outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels," said former U.S. Vice President Al Gore .

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations.

Bowen said the Dubai agreement's explicit call to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

Other climate issues weren’t settled, and many were deferred to next year’s negotiations in Ethiopia. They include details on transitioning away from fossil fuels, financial help for poorer nations to adapt to the warming world and action on gender and climate.

For this year's negotiations, Turkey made global electrification its signature issue. A proposal introduced separately from the main agreement calls for countries to increase the share of electricity in total final energy consumption from about 21% today to 35% by 2035. This would require nations to commit to measures such as switching transportation — including cars, trucks and planes — from fossil fuels to electricity and using electricity instead of coal to make industrial products. Nearly 100 nations signed up for this goal as part of the separate pledge.

Meyer, with E3G, also hailed progress on global adaptation goals and on a program that helps countries achieve their emissions-cutting goals fairly.

In negotiations over the main agreement, the final proposal was distributed after 3 a.m. and negotiators had little time to register their objections. Many observers and countries blamed the two-headed leadership of Turkey and Australia for the failure to reach an overarching agreement.

Speaking at the meeting, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, said, “With all due respect, Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter.” Kurum later publicly apologized.

Confusion ensued at the meeting. Kurum was caught on a hot mic telling U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell “to sit down,” as Stiell tried to advise him on proceedings onstage.

Earlier this week, Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and needed to be reformed.

Manuel Pulgar-Vidal, president of COP20 and now climate energy lead at the World Wildlife Fund, said “COP31 left too much undone.”

“Too many once again shied away from the toughest decisions, including how to turn their commitment to transition away from fossil fuels into real action," he said. "The climate will not wait for governments to find their courage.”

Earlier this year, the United Nations Environment Program announced that the world will blow past the Paris Agreement temperature threshold of limiting long-term warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial times. The goal should now be to limit how much the world exceeds that threshold and then somehow come back down using systems to suck carbon out of the air, U.N. officials said.

The world is heading for between 2.7 C and 3 C (between 4.9 F and 5.4 F) of warming by the end of the century, scientists estimate. October 2026 had the largest temperature increase above preindustrial temperatures of any month on record at 1.8 C (3.2 F), according to Berkeley Earth, which said there’s a 97% chance that 2026 will end up as the warmest year on record. Friday saw the most above normal temperature on record, according to the European climate monitor Copernicus.

“Mother Nature decided to comment on the collapse of #COP31 climate negotiations in failure by setting a new record,” University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann said on X.

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland; Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

text:
Updated November 22, 2026 at 5:02 PM CST

ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.

Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.

As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035.

During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.

"Vulnerable countries from Africa and elsewhere are quite angry about that outcome," he says.

Earlier this year, countries requested $2.8 billion to help with damages, but only $342 million in funding was available.

At the COP31 summit, only $142 million in additional funding was pledged, far less than in other recent COP summits.

text:
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

But Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, who called it “the worst Cop ever”, said: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create ... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations. Pakistan told the conference that just because a few items in the pact were objectionable to some, the rest should not be sacrificed: “Climate action is not a menu from which we can select only what suits us.”

Ghana also had criticisms of the process but did not reject the final text: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

The Cop co-president, Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, defended his leadership. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines the presidencies had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.

Asked about the consensus-based system that broke down at the talks, Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN framework convention on climate change, said: “It certainly fell short today,” while emphasising that a significant number of agenda items were passed, with “real progress and concrete results”.

But for many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis.

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

text:
South Korea's electric vehicle market is being overtaken by Chinese-made models at a faster pace than in any other major auto-producing country. The share of Chinese-made vehicles in the domestic EV market surged from 1.1% in 2021 to 33.9% last year, a 32.8-percentage-point increase in just four years, according to the Korea Automobile and Mobility Association. Among the world's 10 largest auto-producing nations, the increase was the third-largest, behind only Mexico and Brazil. Among countries with their own domestic auto manufacturing industries, South Korea recorded the steepest rise.

South Korea's defenses are rapidly eroding as Chinese automaker BYD steps up its push into the market and Tesla adds China-made models to the competition. The country's trade deficit with China in automobiles reached $4.23 billion, or approximately 5.7 trillion won, through October, already far exceeding the deficit for all of last year. The shortfall is on track to hit a record high, extending an annual run of deficits that began in 2017.

China's advance can no longer be dismissed as a simple price-driven effort to undercut competitors. South Korea's revealed comparative advantage (RCA) index, a measure of export competitiveness, plunged from 2.92 in 2023 to 1.48 last year. China's index, meanwhile, climbed to 1.49, overtaking South Korea's for the first time. In a separate assessment of connected-car readiness by Germany's Center of Automotive Management, seven Chinese automakers ranked among the top 10, while Hyundai Motor Group came in 13th. The competitive pressure is mounting as other major Chinese manufacturers, including Zeekr, Leapmotor and Changan, accelerate their efforts to enter the South Korean market, adding to the challenge posed by BYD.

Governments around the world are moving to protect their domestic auto industries through tariffs and tax incentives. South Korea, by contrast, has little to shield its automakers beyond an 8% basic tariff. The immediate priority should be to fast-track legislation already introduced in the National Assembly that would provide tax credits for EVs manufactured in South Korea. Without swift and decisive action, the country risks ceding even its home market to foreign competitors.

This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.

COP31 ended Sunday in collapse, with negotiators unable to deliver an overarching climate deal after failing to agree on language about fossil fuels and climate funding.

The talks ran into overtime and became the longest U.N. climate conference on record, but the final draft did not directly mention coal, oil, or gas. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, and other countries rejected the text, saying it was too weak to address climate change.

COP31 President Murat Kurum said there was no consensus on the text.

Climate finance was another major sticking point. The draft called for efforts to at least triple funding to help countries adapt to climate impacts by 2035, but it did not specify a dollar amount or a baseline for measuring the increase.

According to the reports, the breakdown marked the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that a COP failed to reach its main political agreement.

The collapse came as the world is expected to exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5-degree Celsius warming limit. Current government policies put projected warming at about 2.8 degrees by 2100, the U.N. says.

Many cited the omission of fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate finance commitments, with some delegates arguing that those responsible for climate change should pay for it.

"I want to clearly state that the European Union and its member states object to this cover decision,” said Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's climate minister, on behalf of the EU, adding that the decisions "go nowhere near the level of action or ambition that are required for us to tackle climate change."

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either, and it is for that reason and those reasons that the European Union strongly objects to this text,” O'Brien said.

A delegate from Panama told the assembled representatives, “Panama believes that we must tell the truth about the collective failure to keep within 1.5 degrees Celsius, and Panama believes that those who have most contributed to this crisis must shoulder a proportionate responsibility to resolve this crisis.”

Many participating countries and climate groups insisted on language calling for a fossil fuel phase-out and were unwilling to accept an agreement that didn't address the primary cause of climate change head-on. That demand was one reason negotiations headed into overtime after the two-week conference was scheduled to conclude.

But instead of mentioning a fossil fuel phase-out, the proposed agreement referenced the United Arab Emirates Consensus, an outcome of the 2023 COP28 summit, when, for the first time, the attending countries formally agreed to transition away from fossil fuels for energy.

A first draft of the COP31 cover decision called for phasing out fossil fuels "through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems," but the language was removed from the second draft after opposition from several oil-producing nations, according to reporting by the Guardian.

While the COP31 draft text doesn't mention the primary cause of climate change, it does include details about its potential impacts, such as noting "deep concern that peak global warming is expected to exceed 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels in the next few years." It also says that "every increment of warming above current levels will increase the frequency and intensity of loss and damage associated with the adverse effects of climate change."

'Most disappointing COP'

Some climate organizations also objected to the proposed agreement's language.

"Country after country has called on the COP31 presidencies to build on the Dubai commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, and they have looked the other way,” said Sara Shaw, Campaigns and Networks Director at 350.org, a climate advocacy organization focused on transitioning the world to renewable energy. “This text isn't a climate plan. It's a license to keep polluting.”

A first draft of the COP31 cover decision called for phasing out fossil fuels "through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems," but the language was removed from the second draft after opposition from several oil-producing nations, according to reporting by the Guardian.

On the evening that COP31 was supposed to conclude, a coalition of 100 climate nonprofits and community organizations sent a letter to the COP31 leadership, saying they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had."

They listed several objections to the draft agreement, including that "The major cause of the climate crisis – coal, oil and gas – fails to rate a mention."

Countries push back on climate financing

Global South countries and their allies pushed back on the funding pledged by wealthier nations for adaptation and loss and damage, saying it was too little and too slow to arrive.

While an earlier draft of the agreement called for "efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035" and included a goal of $120 billion, that amount didn’t make it into the proposed text. Instead, the text said it “Agrees to discuss … implementation pathways for tripling adaptation finance by 2035” and “encourages continued efforts to scale up” funding for the loss and damage sustained as a result of climate change.

Carbon capture singled out?

Some delegates also objected to including carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) language in the proposed agreement, saying it was being used in place of a plan to eliminate the source of greenhouse gas emissions. Vanuatu Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu told AFP that CCUS "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

Saudi Arabia defended the inclusion of CCUS in the proposal, saying "we believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances."

Support for the proposal and electrification

Not every country was opposed to the draft agreement. Ghana expressed concerns about the text but said it would support the proposed agreement because “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.” China said it supports the proposed agreement and called on all of the parties “to show necessary compromise.”

Also, not every issue in the proposal was as divisive as the fossil fuel phase-out or climate financing.

Electrification found broad support, with at least 75 countries backing the new 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, according to the U.N. The voluntary pledge aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from an estimated 23% in 2026.

But even with broad support for the pledge itself, some countries objected to including it in the cover decision draft because it did not include a mandate requiring the use of emission-free renewable energy to meet the electrification goal. The proposed agreement instead calls for the "greatest possible use of clean energy."

In the end, however, the final draft wasn’t enough to get the deal past the finish line. Decisions at COPs are made by consensus, not by majority vote, so the objections from the EU and others were enough to block it.

COP31 fall short of expectations

Going into this year's conference, climate organizations and experts told ABC News that they didn't expect significant breakthroughs and that much of the work gets done during small meetings. Despite the failure to reach a big agreement, delegates did pass a number of the 160 agenda items on a variety of technical matters.

But the final draft of COPs signature agreement fell far short of the expectations of many delegates, environmental groups and nongovernmental organizations.

“The hollow outcome at COP31 was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement. When narrow national interests override collective responsibility to confront the climate crisis, the entire world pays the price," said Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO of World Resources Institute. "Climate summits are not stages for posturing; they require every country to roll up their sleeves and do the hard work of finding ambitious common ground.”

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the morning session urging delegates to support the agreement, telling them they "stand on the threshold of a historic opportunity." But after several countries objected to the text, he acknowledged that COP31 would end without an official agreement.

“We did our best,” Kurum said. “This text was not imposed on anyone. We did not force people to accept it. But it seems that there are parties that object to this text. I understand that there is no agreement on this text.”

The countries will try again next year. COP32 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from Nov. 8 to 19, 2027.

And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.

"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."

Disagreements on fossil fuels

The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.

The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.

At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.

Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.

These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.

Increasing electrification

This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.

Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas.

COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.

The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.

The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.

An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.

Billions of dollars still needed

While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.

"The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.

text:
23 November 2026

A First Nations-led plantation forestry project that has sown more than two million seedlings in its first year is delivering training opportunities, local jobs and ongoing economic benefits to the Tiwi Islands people.

The carbon plantation project exceeded its first-year planting target by more than 20 per cent, with 1,798 hectares planted in since January 2026, marking an important step in the development of sustainable forestry on the Tiwi Islands.

As well as supporting training, employment opportunities and economic activity for Traditional Owners, the project is building a future source of Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs), expected to be available from 2027.

The first-year progress of this project demonstrates how investment in natural capital can deliver practical outcomes on the ground, from large-scale plantation establishment to jobs, skills and direct economic benefits for Tiwi communities.

Rory Lonergan

CEFC CIO - Investment Alternatives

The project’s benefits are already flowing through to the local economy, with Tiwi workers representing almost 60 per cent of the workforce, contributing more than 33,000 work hours and earning more than $1.4 million in direct wages. It also delivered 196 formal Tiwi training sessions, supporting pathways into long-term roles in forestry, fire management and land stewardship.

CEFC CIO – Investment Alternatives, Rory Lonergan said: “The first-year progress of this project demonstrates how investment in natural capital can deliver practical outcomes on the ground, from large-scale plantation establishment to jobs, skills and direct economic benefits for Tiwi communities. This is the kind of achievement that improves investor confidence in the long-term potential of plantation forestry to support high-integrity carbon abatement, sustainable timber supply and First Nations economic participation.”

Tiwi Plantations Corporation Chairman, Gibson Farmer Illortaminni said: “Tiwi people have always worked with wood for our culture, tools and fire. We’ve had forestry trials and plantations on the Tiwi Islands since the 1960s. We are really proud and happy to now be seeing the Eucalyptus Pellita being planted. We’ve worked hard for this and we are creating jobs for our people here at home for the next 35 years”.

Midway Limited CEO and Managing Director Tony McKenna said: “This is a significant long-term investment in the future of the Tiwi Islands - in people, skills, economic opportunity and regional resilience. We are incredibly proud to partner with the Tiwi people and Tiwi Plantations Corporation to deliver a high-quality, sustainable plantation and carbon project at significant scale. The outstanding first-year results demonstrate the capability of our team and give us great confidence in the long-term benefits and opportunities this investment will deliver for the Tiwi people.”

As planting activities continue, the project is expected to play an increasing role in Australia’s natural capital investment landscape, with a strong focus on ACCU delivery, First Nations economic empowerment, and community outcomes.

The CEFC has committed $40 million alongside a $41 million investment from River Capital to finance the planting and operation of a 30,000-hectare plantation estate in the Tiwi Islands, expected to generate up to five million ACCUs over its lifetime. Midway is managing the carbon forestry operations for the Tiwi Plantations, including the plantation establishment, carbon registration, ongoing forestry management and marketing of ACCUs generated by the project.

Forecast to increase Australia’s total plantation area by around 2 per cent, the planting of 30,000 hectares of Eucalyptus pellita on Melville Island also supports meeting international demand for high-quality timber products for construction, as well as reducing reliance on native forests.

text:
The Nov. 3 elections changed the political balance of state attorneys general, who play a central role in disputes over the division of power between states and the federal government. Democrats won Republican-held attorney general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, winning 21 of the 30 directly elected attorney general offices on the ballot.

Nationwide, Democrats will hold or control 29 attorney general offices, compared to 21 for Republicans. Before the election, Democrats held 23 offices and Republicans held 27.

State attorneys general serve as their states’ chief legal officers, representing state governments in litigation and defending state laws against legal challenges. That places them at the center of federalism disputes over federal regulations, funding conditions, and the boundaries of state authority.

How the elections affect federalism litigation

The attorney general's role in challenging federal policies was also an issue in the 2026 elections. As of Nov. 18, 2026, states had filed at least 95 multistate lawsuits against the second Trump administration. In Wisconsin, Attorney General Josh Kaul (D) defeated Eric Toney (R) after a campaign in which the candidates disagreed over the office's participation in lawsuits against the Trump administration. In Nevada, Nicole Cannizzaro (D) defeated Adriana Guzmán Fralick (R) in a race where the candidates differed over whether to continue the state's participation in lawsuits against the administration.

Immigration enforcement is another area where the change in leadership is particularly relevant. Texas and Iowa are defending state laws — Texas Senate Bill 4 (2023) and Iowa Senate File 2340 (2024) — in federal court against challenges brought by immigrant advocacy organizations and individuals. These laws authorize state authorities to arrest and prosecute certain individuals suspected of entering the country unlawfully. Both cases raise questions about whether federal immigration law preempts state enforcement efforts, and the incoming attorneys general will inherit their states’ positions.

During the second Trump administration, state attorneys general have also challenged federal grant conditions, education policies, election policies, and public-assistance requirements. These disputes raise questions about federal authority to impose requirements on states and the extent of state discretion in implementing federal policies.

The elections also bring new leadership to states involved in litigation over environmental, social, and governance (ESG) policies. Texas and Kansas are among the states suing asset managers, including BlackRock, alleging that coordinated climate-related investment activities restricted coal production and increased energy prices. BlackRock has denied wrongdoing. Vanguard settled claims against it for $29.5 million in February 2026 without admitting wrongdoing. Litigation against other defendants continues as of Nov. 19.

Attorneys general have also brought ESG disputes to federal regulators and courts. On Sept. 24, Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen (R) and 21 other Republican attorneys general asked the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to scrutinize the use of ESG considerations in credit ratings by Moody’s, a credit rating agency. Twenty Democratic attorneys general had written the SEC in August to dispute the Republican attorneys general’s claims. A federal judge also blocked New York’s climate superfund law — which would require certain fossil fuel companies to contribute toward climate adaptation costs — on Aug. 31 after 22 Republican attorneys general challenged it. New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) appealed the ruling on Oct. 26.

What happens to existing lawsuits?

The incoming attorneys general will inherit litigation initiated or defended by their predecessors. In Texas, Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson (D) said he would review lawsuits brought by outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton (R). He said, “Everything will be examined.” These cases include disputes involving immigration, abortion restrictions, and financial institutions. In Kansas, Attorney General-elect Chris Mann (D) will assume responsibility for the state’s participation in several multistate lawsuits.

Changes in leadership have already affected at least one pending case. In Georgia, a federal judge paused proceedings in litigation over the state’s congressional maps, citing the impending transition in the attorney general’s office. In other states, ongoing litigation involves abortion medication, transgender rights, voting rights, and religious expression in public schools.

Newly elected attorneys general will decide whether to challenge federal actions, defend state laws, join multistate lawsuits, or continue litigation begun under their predecessors. Changes in leadership do not automatically alter state laws or end existing lawsuits, particularly when other states or federal agencies remain involved.

“The failure to adopt a cover decision and several other key decisions also leaves important areas of near-term climate action without the backing they deserved.
That includes electrification, methane and other super pollutants, the ocean-climate link, and a credible path to scale adaptation finance for the countries that need it most.
Between now and COP32, we need to accelerate action, show what is working and build the case for countries to go further.”
text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye — COP31 concluded today without agreement on key decisions on mitigation, finance and adaptation.

“We are disappointed by the outcome of the negotiations in Antalya and the failure to agree key decisions on mitigation, finance and adaptation.

“Outside the negotiating rooms, governments, businesses, cities and communities came ready to act. There was energy and commitment across the action agenda and the Blue Zone. But that was not reflected in the negotiations.

“That gap is a problem. The climate process should respond to what is happening on the ground and use it to push countries further. In Antalya, it did not.

“The failure to adopt a cover decision and several other key decisions also leaves important areas of near-term climate action without the backing they deserved. That includes electrification, methane and other super pollutants, the ocean-climate link, and a credible path to scale adaptation finance for the countries that need it most. These are among the fastest and most cost-effective ways to slow warming and protect people now.

“But action on these issues does not have to wait. Around 90 countries have already backed the 35% electrification goal. Countries and other partners are already working together on methane, clean energy and ocean action.

“EDF will keep working with partners to turn commitments into results. The road to Addis Ababa starts now. Between now and COP32, we need to accelerate action, show what is working and build the case for countries to go further.”

Toyota Reworks Sienna Steering and Braking Hardware Handling changes center on a new electric power steering system.

text:
PLANO, Texas — Toyota Motor North America announced on November 20, 2026, a broad set of updates to the 2027 Sienna minivan, led by the debut of the company’s sixth-generation hybrid system. The changes reach nearly every part of the vehicle: the powertrain, steering and braking hardware, driver-assistance suite, infotainment, and the trim lineup. Toyota said the Sienna, which carries a standard hybrid powertrain and offers available all-wheel drive, is expected to reach dealerships across the United States by early 2027, with full-line pricing to be announced at a later date.

Toyota’s Sixth-Generation Hybrid System Reaches the Sienna

The centerpiece of the update is Toyota Hybrid System 6, which the company describes as engineered for larger vehicles that need higher-capacity hybrid hardware. The system uses new electric motors built with silicon carbide conductors and replaces the previous battery with a 1.15 kWh lithium-ion unit. Toyota lists a 124-kW drive motor on all models and a 40-kW rear motor on those equipped with all-wheel drive. A gear set has been engineered to handle added weight and reaction torque, and the inverter is now integrated into the hybrid transaxle, a change Toyota said makes the system more compact, lowers the center of gravity and reduces overall unit weight.

Total system output rises to 251 horsepower from 245, while engine torque holds at 176 lb.-ft. Toyota’s estimates put the zero-to-60 mph time at 7.5 seconds for front-wheel-drive models and 7.6 seconds for all-wheel-drive models, down from 7.9 seconds for the prior model year.

Fuel economy improves as well. The manufacturer-estimated city rating climbs by three miles per gallon on front-wheel-drive models and four on all-wheel-drive models, producing a rating of 39 city, 35 highway and 37 combined mpg on both drivetrains. To reduce friction and maximize output, the system adopts a lower-viscosity e-transaxle fluid and 0W-8 engine oil.

Toyota’s engineers also retuned the 2.5-liter engine to rev at lower speeds, which the company said produces quieter operation in the low and mid-speed range, such as when maneuvering in a parking lot or accelerating between 50 and 70 mph.

Toyota Reworks Sienna Steering and Braking Hardware

Handling changes center on a new electric power steering system. Toyota replaced the steering column, steering gear box, motor control unit and torque sensor, and a new steering wheel is included. The system was retuned to reduce steering effort at low speeds for easier parking while adding on-center definition for stability at highway speeds.

The Sienna also receives an Electronically Controlled Brake System that debuted on the 2026 RAV4. The system uses a master cylinder configuration with on-demand pressurization intended to deliver optimal brake feel and response. It also includes Vehicle Braking Posture Control, which applies braking inputs at select wheels to slow the rate of body roll when turning into a corner. Toyota’s list of new features additionally cites vehicle posture control with an AHB-C actuator.

Toyota Safety Sense 4.0 Arrives on a New Electrical Platform

A new electrical platform, covering the vehicle’s electronic control units and software, enables the move to Toyota Safety Sense 4.0. According to Toyota, the Sienna becomes one of the earlier models to adopt the suite, following the 2026 RAV4 and the 2027 Tundra and Sequoia. The update consolidates the ECU architecture to reduce complexity and brings upgraded sensors and hardware intended to improve detection.

Features cited by Toyota include Emergency Driving Stop System, Proactive Driving Assist, Safe Exit Assist and trailer sway control, along with improved performance from Lane Trace Assist and Adaptive Cruise Control. The standard suite also covers the Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Road Sign Assist and Automatic High Beams. Blind Spot Monitor with Rear Cross-Traffic Alert and the Toyota Star Safety System are also listed. Every grade now includes a drive recorder dash cam as standard. Toyota noted that the safety systems are not a substitute for safe and attentive driving.

Toyota Audio Multimedia Brings Larger Screens to Every Grade

Inside, all grades receive a 12.3-inch touchscreen running the latest version of Toyota Audio Multimedia, developed by the Toyota Connected team. The LE grade previously had an 8-inch display. A 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster with customizable settings also becomes standard, replacing a 7-inch multi-information display on the LE and XLE. The cluster shows integrated multimedia information, the speedometer, an energy monitor and battery charge meter, drive mode indicators and charging information.

The system includes eight speakers and supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. A JBL Premium Audio system is standard on the XSE and Platinum grades. Qi wireless charging and multiple USB-C ports are standard, and the XSE, Woodland and Platinum grades include a 1,500-watt inverter with two 120-volt outlets. For Woodland, XSE and Platinum models equipped with the optional rear seat entertainment center, the screen grows to 12.9 inches from 11.6 inches and gains touch functionality with a new user interface.

Connected services include five-year trials of Safety Connect and Service Connect, a five-year trial of Remote Connect, and a 30-day Wi-Fi Connect trial with unlimited data. Toyota said Wi-Fi Connect depends on 5G network availability and requires a subscription after the trial.

Toyota Sienna Cabin Space and Noise Reduction

The Sienna rides on the Toyota Next Generation-K platform, which Toyota said is engineered to resist noise and vibration entering through the steering, floor and vehicle structure. For 2027, a new higher-density dash silencer reduces the noise entering the cabin by 1.6 decibels, according to the company.

Passenger space figures are unchanged in the announcement: 39.9 inches of second-row legroom and 38.7 inches in the third row. Cargo volume measures 101.0 cubic feet behind the front seats and 75.2 cubic feet behind the second row with the third row folded. The LE and some XLE models come in eight-seat configurations with a stowable middle seat. In some seven-seat models, Super Long Slide second-row captain’s chairs move 25 inches, and an available ottoman is standard on the XSE and Platinum grades.

Toyota Consolidates the Sienna Lineup Around Five Grades

The 2027 lineup spans the LE, XLE, XSE, Woodland Edition and Platinum grades. Toyota said the XSE’s expanded feature content removes the need for a Limited grade, which it described as grade simplification.

The XSE adds standard ventilated driver and passenger seats, a seat memory function, a panoramic view monitor, a black headlight interior and a 10-inch color head-up display showing speed, navigation and hybrid system indicators. The Woodland Edition now includes the Panoramic View Monitor as standard, alongside a towing hitch receiver, all-weather mats and a 1,500-watt inverter. XLE grades and above gain an eight-way power-adjustable front passenger seat, while the LE adds a rear liftgate kick sensor, standard when a towing hitch is not equipped. New interior LED cabin lighting is included across the range.

On the exterior, Storm Cloud joins the paint palette and Cypress is discontinued.

Toyota Sienna Production, Availability and Warranty Coverage

The 2027 Sienna is assembled in Princeton, Indiana. Toyota’s new-vehicle coverage includes a 36-month/36,000-mile basic warranty and a 60-month/60,000-mile powertrain warranty, along with 60-month coverage against corrosion perforation with no mileage limit. Hybrid-related components are covered for eight years or 100,000 miles, and the hybrid battery is covered for 10 years or 150,000 miles, whichever comes first, with coverage transferable across ownership. ToyotaCare covers normal factory-scheduled maintenance for one year or 10,000 miles, and two years of roadside assistance is included regardless of mileage.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.

Toyota launched Scion by Toyota on November 9 with three vehicles at simultaneous events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas. Among them, the BKE Concept folds in roughly 30 seconds and fits in the trunk of a GR86 sports car.

Why it matters

The launch positions the brand as a platform for experimental mobility, with Toyota describing it as a freedom lab for new ways to move. Production commitments for the concept vehicles have not been made, so the lineup's path to showrooms remains uncertain.

The KEI-01 uses a 660cc three-cylinder engine with a CVT and a three-way fold-down cargo bed rated for up to 600 pounds. Toyota has not disclosed the BKE Concept's motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed or weight.

Toyota Motor North America

The North American arm of Toyota Motor Corporation, responsible for sales, marketing and operations across the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Akio Toyoda

The chairman of Toyota Motor Corporation who has long championed the company's diversification into niche and experimental vehicle segments.

The details

Toyota plans to start selling the KEI-01 through a fleet-focused pilot program at selected Scion by Toyota dealers. The BKE Concept can be recharged from 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles and has no pedals.

November 9, 2026: Scion by Toyota launched with three vehicles at two events.

Second half of 2027: The KEI-01 kei truck is expected to arrive in the US.

title: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making - WRAL
description:

So, even though fossil fuels are the cause of climate change, and the annual climate summits are convened to confront climate change, it’s become all but impossible to have even the words “fossil fuels” show up in a final agreement, much less any detailed transition plan.
During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn't a strong agreement on fossil fuels.
Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.
Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change?
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

The science has been clear for decades

The burning of these fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases, which go up into the atmosphere and raise global average temperatures, creating havoc on ecosystems and leading to more, and more intense, extreme weather events.

In simple terms, the solution is to burn less of these fuels over time and instead use sources of energy that don’t release greenhouse gases, like solar, wind and geothermal. But there is nothing simple about getting countries to agree on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, particularly major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States, or major coal users like China and India.

So, even though fossil fuels are the cause of climate change, and the annual climate summits are convened to confront climate change, it’s become all but impossible to have even the words “fossil fuels” show up in a final agreement, much less any detailed transition plan.

In the 30 years of climate negotiations, the one exception was the U.N. climate conference three years ago in Dubai, COP28, where the final decision encouraged countries to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Fossil fuels were not mentioned in the final agreements in the following two conferences, and the current one, of course, had no final agreement.

Emerging fault lines finally cracked

The backdrop to the climate talks had become a split-screen reality, with the world being hammered by costly and deadly extreme weather events while the top international body set up to deal with the crisis could only nibble around the edges. It ultimately became too much to sustain.

During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn't a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they would voice their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately get in line, figuring there was always next year and ultimately the overall negotiating process needed to be preserved.

But by the final week of this year's conference, which would go into overtime and become the longest on record, it was clear that many nations, including the European Union bloc, were no longer willing to do that.

Earlier this week, Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s minister of environment, seemed to encapsulate what many frustrated participants were thinking when he said the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Navarro likened the situation to “Stockholm syndrome,” when captives, in this case people worried about the future of the planet, were “in love with our kidnappers,” or the oil industry.

The “petroleum guys” have convinced us that “they destroy nature to help us,” said Navarro.

The mention of carbon removal was also a sticking point

The collapse didn't happen just because the cause of climate change was left out of a final agreement, but also because of what was in it. Draft agreements, including the final text released early Sunday, included language encouraging the world to scale up technologies that remove carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, and store it.

Such technology, heavily supported by the oil industry, is energy intensive, expensive and far from being deployed at scale. To date, it only captures and stores much less than 1% of the estimated 60 billion tons of global greenhouse gases produced each year. For many at the climate talks, including carbon removal in the agreement was at best a misguided attempt to produce a small solution, and at worst a pass for carbon polluters to simply continue with business as usual. After all, why stop spewing carbon pollution when it can just eventually be scooped up?

In the months ahead, there will be many recriminations and reflections about what happened in Turkey, and what it may all mean for the next round of talks, scheduled in Ethiopia next year. Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.

Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change? Reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size. Indeed, in recent years it's ballooned so much that on the ground it feels more like a trade fair than a summit to confront one of humanity's most pressing challenges.

Wherever the process ultimately goes, extreme weather events will continue and intensify as global temperatures rise. Many scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest on record.

“Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high," said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, reacting to the outcome. "And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

After all, why stop spewing carbon pollution when it can just eventually be scooped up?

In the months ahead, there will be many recriminations and reflections about what happened in Turkey, and what it may all mean for the next round of talks, scheduled in Ethiopia next year. Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.

Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change? Reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size. Indeed, in recent years it's ballooned so much that on the ground it feels more like a trade fair than a summit to confront one of humanity's most pressing challenges.

Wherever the process ultimately goes, extreme weather events will continue and intensify as global temperatures rise. Many scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest on record.

“Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high," said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, reacting to the outcome. "And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”
