title: The Worst UN Climate Conference Ever: No Deal Was Better Than a Bad Deal
description:
The words “fossil fuels” did not show up in the final draft declaration presented by the COP co-presidents from Türkiye and Australia.
“What are we to call a system in which those who have contributed least to the crisis suffer its worst consequences, while those with the greatest responsibility protect fossil fuel profits?
In the end, the unconscionable failure of the COP negotiations delivered the message that no deal was better than a bad deal.
We need real commitments to a fair and financed phaseout of fossil fuels that delivers on the Paris Agreement, not collapses it.
Mitchell Beer traces his background in renewable energy and energy efficiency back to 1977, in climate change to 1997.
text:
After a year of wildfires and heat waves, storms and flooding, months of build-up and positioning statements, and two weeks of negotiations, the COP31 climate summit wrapped up just hours ago by delivering…nothing of substance.

The words “fossil fuels” did not show up in the final draft declaration presented by the COP co-presidents from Türkiye and Australia. Instead, it called for greater reliance on discredited carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies meant to give fossil companies political cover to keep on expanding production—even though wind and solar avoided at least 65 times more carbon dioxide emissions last year, according to Berlin-based Climate Analytics.

All the other priorities that countries brought into the negotiations—from climate adaptation finance, to a firm commitment to clean electricity, to mechanisms for a just transition off fossil fuels, and more—were lost or watered down.

Chalk it up as the latest in a series of big wins for the “petroleum mafia”, as Panama Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro described the legion of fossil fuel lobbyists, including 700 dedicated specifically to pushing CCUS, who descended on the conference venue in Antalya, Türkiye.

Call it a kick in the teeth to people in Nepal still trying to comprehend, much less cope with, the results of a devastating glacier collapse and rampaging flood earlier this year, later clearly linked to climate change.

Recognize it as a death sentence to the small island states and countries in Asia and Africa that have been warning for years that they won’t survive global warming above 1.5°C—the limit from which we are now in overshoot.

Read it as the deepest of deadly affronts to the developing countries that have been negotiating long, hard, and in good faith for the financing mechanisms that will give them a fighting chance of adapting to the climate change they’re already enduring—but pay out more in interest on climate finance loans than they’re actually investing in front-line climate solutions.

And call it the best, most visceral argument for the fossil fuel phaseout and just transition that 30 countries in the Global South have already endorsed.

“We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia,” Panama’s Navarro said, and “they’re so smart that they have convinced us that they are actually doing this for our own good. They torture us for our own good. They destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love.”

But for Panama, “climate change is a risk to our very survival as a nation. For us, this is not a game. We understand where we are. Mind you, we are a carbon-negative country, yet we are suffering the ravages of climate change.”

“Imagine Alcoholics Anonymous spending 30 years negotiating and producing a statement that never mentions alcohol. Now imagine the alcohol industry turning up as the largest delegation and helping shape the outcome,” veteran South African campaigner Kumi Naidoo, now the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, wrote on LinkedIn.

“What are we to call a system in which those who have contributed least to the crisis suffer its worst consequences, while those with the greatest responsibility protect fossil fuel profits? Is this climate apartheid?” he added. “History will judge these talks by whose lives were protected, whose interests were defended, and whose future was sacrificed.”

No Deal

All of those factors made COP31 “the worst COP ever,” Climate Action Network International Executive Director Tasneem Essop said this morning, echoing earlier remarks by Power Shift Africa founder Mohamed Adow.

“We are witnessing human suffering on an unimaginable scale, and we had hoped this COP would take steps to protect people from the worsening climate crisis. Instead, rich nations gutted the very measures that could have made a difference,” Essop added. In “negotiating room after negotiating room, developed countries systematically blocked measures that would require them to provide finance to protect people’s lives and address the climate crisis.”

[Energy Mix Productions is a member of CAN International’s Canadian note, Climate Action Network Canada.]

Adow said the denial of public finance was not just a betrayal of commitments at last year’s COP30 negotiations in Belém, Brazil, but amounted to renegotiating a key pillar of the 2015 Paris Agreement.

In the end, the unconscionable failure of the COP negotiations delivered the message that no deal was better than a bad deal.

“This collapse is better than a half-hearted final document would have been,” said Johan Rockström and Ottmar Edenhofer, scientific directors of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. “It forcefully brings home to the world just how dramatic the situation is. The COP process remains indispensable; what Antalya has exposed is the widening gap between agreed climate goals and credible implementation.”

“We don’t celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity, and the law. The world needs this multilateral space, and the countries that make it up, to deliver,” said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate & energy program at the U.S. Center for International Environmental Law.

“But the rejected text would have done more harm than good. The proposed cover decision did not advance the provision of climate finance, said nothing about the root cause of the crisis, and made no mention of States’ legal obligations to prevent and repair climate harm, as clarified by the International Court of Justice.” And “without so much as a whisper about fossil fuels,” the draft decision “would have been a massive giveaway to polluters.”

Nobody Asked for This

And after all that, the cover decision itself was an unforced error, said Stela Herschmann, international policy lead at Brazil’s Observatório do Clima, or Climate Observatory.

“Nobody asked for a cover decision,” she said in a release. “It was announced by the Presidencies to serve their own interests and ended up diverting time and attention away from the negotiating rooms. It is a relief that it was not adopted, because the text opened the door to CCUS and would have represented a step backwards. But the damage has been done: we leave Antalya without significant progress in the process. It was a wasted opportunity and a disservice by the Turkish and Australian presidencies.”

Other deeply flawed proposals that were lost or misplaced when the cover decision went down in flames:

• Türkiye’s highly-touted 35 x 35 electrification pledge that called for countries to shift 35% of their economies from fuels to electricity by 2035, but gradually devolved into a voluntary commitment that would have allowed for power generated from methane super-polluter natural gas—with turbine producer Siemens Energy avidly promoting gas plants as part of the solution, according to the Beyond Fossil Fuels campaign;

• A continuing fight over the timing of the next authoritative science assessment by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which is due in 2028 but has been running behind schedule, amid warnings that (shockingly) “fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization,” the New York Times reported.

What You Saw Depended on Where You Sat

As happens so often with the annual climate COP, parts of the story we heard at home differed a great deal from what veteran COP-watchers and negotiators saw on the ground.

The common denominators were the same. With fossil fuel companies reportedly sending a lobbying force larger than any national delegation, the latest in a long series of COPs controlled by petrostates gave a free pass to the industry that has caused the lion’s share of the crisis. An early version of the decision included a reference to the fossil fuel phaseout that negotiators adopted at COP28 three years ago, in the petrostate megalopolis of Dubai. But that language was expunged in later drafts, with usual suspects like Saudi Arabia identified as key influencers behind the scenes.

The intensive lobbying push was “completely orchestrated” and “definitely worse this year”, COP veteran Alden Meyer, a senior associate with climate think tank E3G, told The Financial Times. “You see the Saudis come in and 40 [countries] raise their flag with the same message. It’s clearly meant to wear people down.”

Then there was the dead-hand influence that wasn’t in the room. “Trump and the U.S. may not be here, but the rest of the rich world are doing his dirty work,” said Power Shift Africa’s Adow, a 15-year veteran of COP negotiations. “And that is what we’ve seen, facilitated and enabled by the two [COP] co-presidents.”

But behind those cornerstone realities lurked a stunning difference in perspective—or, according to observers in Antalya, a colossal gap between spin and substance.

The closing days of the COP saw several news reports about the 130 countries, including the European Union, that were agitating to include support for the COP28 text on a fossil fuel phaseout in the COP31 decision. But that story looked a lot different to people who’d spent two weeks slogging through the details of the negotiations.

Here’s Dr. Amiera Sawas, the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s head of research and policy:

While Global North countries rejected the outcome on the basis that there was no language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, these same countries have not themselves presented serious or credible phaseout plans, nor do they intend to support others in their transitions. Many wealthy countries continue expanding fossil fuel extraction despite their international legal obligations, while developing countries carrying unpayable debt can’t plan an exit at all….

With the EU and some of its most powerful countries obstructing progress or going back on past commitments, Sawas added:

Demanding the words ‘fossil fuels’ in the cover text while blocking mandated agenda items and pointing fingers at developing countries is acting in bad faith. We need real commitments to a fair and financed phaseout of fossil fuels that delivers on the Paris Agreement, not collapses it.

“Developed countries demanded that developing countries move faster away from fossil fuels while denying them the resources to do it,” agreed Climate Action Network International. “Some developed countries dressed up existing policies as ambitious fossil fuel transition roadmaps, even as they continued to expand fossil fuel production at home.”

Then, after blocking efforts to support a just transition off fossil fuels, those countries “tried to pin the failure of COP31 on developing countries,” CAN wrote. But “without climate finance from developed countries, the entire architecture of international climate cooperation is undermined.”

The Same Old Chokepoint

All of which pointed to the same, very old chokepoint that always derails COP negotiations—while everyone in the room (well, most everyone not affiliated with a fossil company or a petrostate) wants to see climate change addressed, nobody is prepared to pay their fair share to get climate finance done.

On a visit to Ottawa just ahead of the COP, the former UN high commissioner for human rights, Mary Robinson, called for “new ways of raising finance” to cover the tripling of climate adaptation finance and other commitments that rich countries have adopted in theory, but keep slow-walking in practice. But even on an adaptation finance pledge that countries arrived at just last year, those negotiations quickly bogged down.

Which does nothing to shift the searing reality that the Treaty Initiative described in its release this morning:

With low- and middle-income countries paying record levels to service debt and interest repayments, many are being pushed to expand [fossil fuel] extraction simply to service debt to wealthier nations. Without predictable grant-based finance, lower costs of capital for renewables, and access to investment, many developing countries cannot make the transition happen.

It’s an age-old dynamic, and an age-old result. Developing countries are already bearing the brunt of the climate emergency. They’re on the front lines of the crisis: geographically, economically, environmentally, socially. The same economic history that brought climate change to their doorsteps left them without the resources to address it. So they don’t need anyone from the wealthy North lecturing them about the reality they see bearing down on them every day.

Especially not when the world’s richest countries got that way in large part by being the main beneficiaries of the fossil fuel era. It’s an essential facet of this fight we don’t hear much about in most climate or energy discussions in Ottawa or Toronto, Calgary or Montreal. But it’s front and centre from the moment you set foot at a COP.

“We didn’t come here to beg,” said Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, chair of the Africa Group of Negotiators, as COP31 ground down to its final conclusion. “We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

How Does This Even Happen?

It’s been nearly a decade since I’ve attended a UN climate conference in person, but you don’t have to be in the room to share the sense of utter betrayal, this year from eight time zones away.

The pattern is almost invariably the same: a year of escalating climate impacts with warnings of worse to come, followed by months of optimistic pledges and program offerings. The conference itself opens with all the right words, but the tell is in the generalities. Everyone’s happy enough to hold forth about what we need to do to finally get climate change under control, and when they aren’t touting the fossil industry agenda, they often make sense. Just don’t ask anyone to commit too substantively to the how. And for goodness’ sake, stop being so rude as to ask who’s going to pay for it!

Once in a while, COP delegates adopt something at least somewhat substantial, as they did in Belém and Dubai, even if it’s just a preliminary step that needs to be fleshed out in future negotiations. But have no fear, because the tentative nature of those gains is the other tell—you can pretty much count on them being rolled back as soon as the fossil industry and its enablers have a chance to regroup.

In the latest edition of the Outrage+Optimism newsletter, climate strategist Tom Rivett-Carnac makes a familiar case for keeping at it. “Anything that has 198 countries and a whole host of other interested stakeholders participating is going to be complicated,” he writes. “It’s going to be frustrating, it’s going to be slower than what we’d like, but I am still extremely grateful that it happens.”

While it’s hard to endorse Rivett-Carnac’s gratitude just now, he has a point. The other predictable moment in the annual COP calendar—you can set your watch by it—is the parade of climate deniers who point to the carbon footprint of getting everyone to and from the conference, as though it’s the delegates and the process, not the fossil fuel obstructionists flooding the zone, that lack legitimacy.

But we can adapt that gratuitous attack line into something useful. I’ve long believed that a healthy way to assess any air travel is by weighing its cost against its benefit, then committing to make that benefit as real in practice as it looks in theory. If a big conference has a defined purpose that will measurably make things a lot better if it’s achieved, it doesn’t justify getting there by private jet—but it’s a carbon choice most of us would endorse ahead of an incentive trip for high-producing cryptocurrency sales reps or another starship launch by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

And far ahead of a luxury trip to the latest fossil industry mega-conference.

We should all want to avoid the slippery slope that comes along with this line of thinking. But there are also two ways to quantify whether the COP is earning the share of the carbon budget that it consumes.

First, as so many others have suggested, limit attendance onsite to actual negotiators by keeping fossil interests out of the room and cracking down on the carnival and trade show that boosted the carbon footprint of the COP’s air travel 25-fold in its first three decades, according to public health researchers.

Then, far more important, measure the remaining footprint against the emission reductions the negotiations achieve, and judge the outcome accordingly. Measuring the footprint itself (including lodging, food, and onsite transport as well as air travel) is relatively straightforward, but interpreting it is a judgement call. Should we expect a COP’s results to exceed its climate impact 1,000-fold, 10,000-fold, or more to be declared a success? Should we weight that calculation by how effectively the decision is weighted down by petrostate politics, or by rich countries obstructing the climate finance results we so desperately need?

Take these calculations literally or metaphorically, as you see fit. Never forget that international diplomacy is absolutely essential, and in an era when it’s under severe, ideological attack, we need to defend it. But that doesn’t mean giving the COP a free pass. The crisis is too big and immediate, and the stakes are too high, to permit the kind of travesty we’ve just seen in Antalya.

title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels | Wyoming Public Media
authors: Lauren Sommer, Julia Simon, Rachel Waldholz, www.wyomingpublicmedia.org, lauren-sommer

text:
Updated November 22, 2026 at 1:13 PM MST

ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.

Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.

Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.

Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.

"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."

Disagreements on fossil fuels

The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.

The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.

At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.

Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.

These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.

"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."

Increasing electrification

This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.

Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas.

COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.

The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.

The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.

Lack of U.S. Presence

The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.

An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.

Billions of dollars still needed

While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.

Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.

"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."

In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.

As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035.

During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.

"Vulnerable countries from Africa and elsewhere are quite angry about that outcome," he says.

Earlier this year, countries requested $2.8 billion to help with damages, but only $342 million in funding was available.

At the COP31 summit, only $142 million in additional funding was pledged, far less than in other recent COP summits.

NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.

title: The Watch: Data Center Boom Could Hurt Progress Fighting Air Pollution

The Watch is written by Michele Late, who has more than two decades of experience as a public health journalist.
text:
Data center boom could hurt progress fighting air pollution

Fifteen years of progress combating climate change in the U.S. could be wiped out in three years as new gas-fired plants are built to power data centers, a new report from the Sierra Club warns.

The U.S. has made substantial progress in reducing pollution from electricity generation in recent years, largely by closing coal-fired power plants and expanding renewable energy, according to the Nov. 16 report. Between 2015 and 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from power plants serving the electrical grid fell 22%, for example.

That progress is now threatened as large data centers are being built to support artificial intelligence. While some facilities draw electricity from the existing grid, others are developing their own generating stations.

More than 550 gas-fired power plants are planned or under construction nationwide, representing a nearly 40% increase in generating capacity, the report said. At least one-third of that new capacity is expected to serve data centers.

Just a dozen data center projects with on-site gas plants could annually release nearly 180 million tons of carbon dioxide — a major driver of climate change — along with fine-particle air pollution linked to asthma, heart attacks and strokes.

Many data centers operate under permits that limit public review and require little pollution reporting. A bill now making its way through Congress, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, would further weaken review requirements so data centers and their energy sources can be built faster, a move that has been condemned by health advocates.

A new poll by the Environmental Protection Network found 88% of U.S. adults support equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers and believe their expansion should not cost Americans their health.

High heat linked to premature births, dementia, traffic crashes

As climate change increases temperatures across the U.S., new research shows heat is posing risks to health throughout the lifespan.

The dangers of heat to human health come even before birth, a Nov. 18 study in JAMA Network Open finds. Exposure to high temperatures during pregnancy was linked with an increased risk of premature birth.

Researchers examined more than 12 million births in Brazil between 2015 and 2019, finding high temperatures during the week before delivery were associated with a 14% higher risk of premature birth. Heat exposure earlier in pregnancy also was linked to premature delivery.

Researchers suggested that high temperatures may trigger processes involved in labor or interfere with early fetal and placental development.

High temperatures also can pose risks to health later in life, an October analysis in Alzheimer’s & Dementia shows.

Researchers examined two decades of data on U.S. older adults, finding people who were exposed to more days of dangerously high heat had a 23% higher risk of developing dementia than those with little exposure. People who experienced an average of seven or more days annually in which the heat index reached at least 103 degrees faced the highest risk.

The link between extreme heat and dementia was stronger among people in communities with greater socioeconomic disadvantage and less access to central air conditioning.

Socioeconomic disadvantage also can play a role in whether people exposed to high heat die from cardiovascular disease, Nov. 18 research in PLOS Climate says.

People with heart-related conditions face a greater risk of death when exposed to hotter summers and repeated heat waves, according to an analysis of nearly 64,000 people in the U.K. Risks were greater among people without college degrees and those living in poorer neighborhoods or areas with less green space.

For every 1-degree Celsius increase in average summer temperature, the risk of death rose 15%. People exposed to four or more heat waves annually had a 24% higher risk of death than those experiencing two or fewer.

Higher temperatures also can influence whether someone dies in a car crash, a new study in the Journal of Urban Health finds.

Researchers examined 10 years of data from California, linking extreme heat with increases in the number of crashes and injuries. The most intense heat events were linked to about 180 additional crashes and 100 injuries annually statewide, they estimated.

Policies could have long-term consequences for U.S. health

Recent federal policy changes could cause lasting damage to the health of the nation, weakening public health agencies and worsening health disparities, a recent study warns.

Cuts to healthcare, research, food assistance and public health programs under the Trump administration are impacting U.S. health, with further harms ahead, according to the study in The Lancet Regional Health–Americas.

Vulnerable Americans are at highest risk. People with low incomes, rural residents, people of color, immigrants and people with disabilities are expected to face the greatest impacts, researchers said. The policy changes could lead to more illness and preventable deaths, long-term losses in public health capacity and damage to science.

Among the most significant recent changes are cuts to Medicaid and new eligibility requirements that could leave millions of Americans without health insurance. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program changes could increase the number of uninsured people by 7.5 million by 2034.

Medicaid enrollment had already fallen by 4.8 million people between April 2025 and April 2026, before most of the new requirements took effect. Meanwhile, the expiration of federal subsidies that allowed people to afford health insurance has increased costs and fueled declining enrollment.

Rural communities face particular risks as Medicaid funding reductions threaten hospitals and healthcare providers already struggling with financial pressures and workforce shortages.

Federal public health agencies also have experienced major staffing and funding reductions, which could weaken disease surveillance, vaccination services and the ability of health departments to respond to emergencies, researchers said.

Other recent public health news of note includes:

• Babies may be ingesting microplastics shed by their feeding bottles, new findings in the Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering says. Researchers tested baby bottles made of polypropylene and polyamide —plastics commonly used in the products — finding they released microplastics during sterilization and exposure to hot water. Hotter water and longer exposure tended to increase the risk of particles. Infants may ingest as many as 20 microplastic particles per kilogram of body weight daily from feeding bottles, drinking water and infant formula combined, the researchers estimated.

• New research in JAMA Network Open shows storms and power outages can increase death risks for seniors. Researchers examined the effects of Winter Storm Uri, which caused widespread power outages across Texas in February 2021, leaving millions without electricity during freezing temperatures. Using Medicare data, they found that during the week of the storm, about three additional people died for every 10,000 beneficiaries. Among low-income beneficiaries, that rose to more than five additional deaths per 10,000.

• High prices for directly paid medical services are linked to greater medical debt, a new study in JAMA Network Open says. Researchers examined healthcare prices and medical debt between 2020 and 2023. They found increasing prices for professional services — such as doctor visits, diagnostic tests and outpatient procedures — were linked to a greater share of people having medical debt of more than $500 that was sent to collections. Professional services often require patients to pay deductibles, copayments and other out-of-pocket costs, which can add up, researchers said.

The Watch is written by Michele Late, who has more than two decades of experience as a public health journalist.

title: The collapse of UN climate talks, over fossil fuels, was years in the making - Audacy
description:

During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn't a strong agreement on fossil fuels.
Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.
Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change?
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

The science has been clear for decades

The burning of these fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases, which go up into the atmosphere and raise global average temperatures, creating havoc on ecosystems and leading to more, and more intense, extreme weather events.

In simple terms, the solution is to burn less of these fuels over time and instead use sources of energy that don’t release greenhouse gases, like solar, wind and geothermal. But there is nothing simple about getting countries to agree on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, particularly major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States, or major coal users like China and India.

So, even though fossil fuels are the cause of climate change, and the annual climate summits are convened to confront climate change, it’s become all but impossible to have even the words “fossil fuels” show up in a final agreement, much less any detailed transition plan.

In the 30 years of climate negotiations, the one exception was the U.N. climate conference three years ago in Dubai, COP28, where the final decision encouraged countries to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Fossil fuels were not mentioned in the final agreements in the following two conferences, and the current one, of course, had no final agreement.

Emerging fault lines finally cracked

The backdrop to the climate talks had become a split-screen reality, with the world being hammered by costly and deadly extreme weather events while the top international body set up to deal with the crisis could only nibble around the edges. It ultimately became too much to sustain.

During previous conferences, nations frequently threatened to walk away if there wasn't a strong agreement on fossil fuels. Instead, in the end, they would voice their disagreements in closing plenaries and ultimately get in line, figuring there was always next year and ultimately the overall negotiating process needed to be preserved.

But by the final week of this year's conference, which would go into overtime and become the longest on record, it was clear that many nations, including the European Union bloc, were no longer willing to do that.

Earlier this week, Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s minister of environment, seemed to encapsulate what many frustrated participants were thinking when he said the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Navarro likened the situation to “Stockholm syndrome,” when captives, in this case people worried about the future of the planet, were “in love with our kidnappers,” or the oil industry.

The “petroleum guys” have convinced us that “they destroy nature to help us,” said Navarro.

The mention of carbon removal was also a sticking point

The collapse didn't happen just because the cause of climate change was left out of a final agreement, but also because of what was in it. Draft agreements, including the final text released early Sunday, included language encouraging the world to scale up technologies that remove carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, and store it.

Such technology, heavily supported by the oil industry, is energy intensive, expensive and far from being deployed at scale. To date, it only captures and stores much less than 1% of the estimated 60 billion tons of global greenhouse gases produced each year. For many at the climate talks, including carbon removal in the agreement was at best a misguided attempt to produce a small solution, and at worst a pass for carbon polluters to simply continue with business as usual. After all, why stop spewing carbon pollution when it can just eventually be scooped up?

In the months ahead, there will be many recriminations and reflections about what happened in Turkey, and what it may all mean for the next round of talks, scheduled in Ethiopia next year. Inevitably, long-standing questions about the entire U.N. climate process will be raised and likely get much more attention than in years past.

Has the process run its course, or can major reforms turn it into a credible way to confront climate change? Reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size. Indeed, in recent years it's ballooned so much that on the ground it feels more like a trade fair than a summit to confront one of humanity's most pressing challenges.

Wherever the process ultimately goes, extreme weather events will continue and intensify as global temperatures rise. Many scientists expect 2026 to be the hottest on record.

“Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high," said United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, reacting to the outcome. "And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

___

Peter Prengaman has been AP's climate and environment news director since 2021 and be followed here.

Shifting to clean electricity will provide a competitive advantage in terms of lower energy costs and energy security by shielding countries, businesses, investors, and consumers from volatile fuel prices.
Countries that move fastest will capture the benefits: lower energy costs, more jobs, a more secure energy supply, and cleaner air.

text:
“It is disappointing that our world leaders could not meet this critical moment and reach an international agreement that would help transition away from fossil fuels or provide the necessary support to scale climate finance and advance a clean energy economy.

We need leadership and collaboration to move forward in the right direction. This setback will certainly make our collective work more challenging. But the calls were clear, and momentum is on our side, with many countries supporting efforts to increase clean electricity and clean energy investment, particularly in emerging and developing economies.

Shifting to clean electricity will provide a competitive advantage in terms of lower energy costs and energy security by shielding countries, businesses, investors, and consumers from volatile fuel prices. It is critical for economic growth and a healthier economy. That’s why more than 180 companies with more than $1.7 trillion in combined annual revenue called on global leaders to make clean electrification a central pillar of economic and industrial strategy.

Without an agreement in place, nations are left to move at their own pace. Countries that move fastest will capture the benefits: lower energy costs, more jobs, a more secure energy supply, and cleaner air. But leaders must commit to the conditions that make clean electrification work, from modernizing grids and connecting clean energy faster to promoting and enacting policies that unlock private investment.

Electrification delivers its full benefits only if electricity comes from clean energy, not fossil fuels. That means enacting national policies that accelerate, scale up, and support the expansion of clean power. Such measures are essential to delivering on the promises of past climate pledges and advancing the calls that came out of this international summit.”

text:
Alabama Power customers are likely to pay lower electric rates in 2027, the company announced Friday.

The state’s largest utility submitted a $160 million rate reduction to the Alabama Public Service Commission. Alabama Power attributed the reduction to increased revenue from large-load data centers.

In its filing to the PSC, the company said the reduction “demonstrates the ability of large load data centers to promote positive benefits to all other customers.”

If a customer uses 1,000 kilowatt-hours each month, the company estimates that person will save about $50 annually, or about $4 per month. For households using 2,000 kilowatt-hours a month, customers could save $106 per year or about $9 per month.

Rates will continue to heavily depend on how much electricity a household uses and the weather.

“In January, our customers will see their rates go down because of the growth we’re seeing across the state,” Jeff Peoples, Alabama Power’s chief executive officer, said in a news release. “Alabama is growing and we’re making sure that growth works for all of our customers.”

Power rates will remain at or below the new lower level through 2028, according to the company.

The PSC previously approved a two-year rate freeze for Alabama Power customers last year.

A WBRC analysis in 2025 found that Alabamians paid more on their electricity bills than residents in neighboring states.

U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., took credit for the reduction Friday, saying she “successfully led this charge” to put “more money back in hardworking Alabamians’ pockets.”

“I asked Alabama Power to find a way to lower rates — not just freeze them, but achieve lower power bills for Alabama households. Today, I am excited to say that is happening,” Britt said in a statement.

Gov.-elect and U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., had been a strong proponent of building data centers in the state while campaigning for governor but he softened his stance closer to Election Day, pushing for companies to get community input before starting construction on the projects.

He praised Alabama Power’s announcement even though “it should have come months ago when we first proposed this to the power company.”

“As I’ve said before, allowing data centers to invest in Alabama’s communities is only going to generate more revenue for local schools, hospitals, and law enforcement—and REDUCE power rates,” Tuberville said in a statement.

As he prepares to enter the governor’s mansion, Tuberville said his team is working on legislation to “remove energy taxes on residential customers” and is talking with other utilities in the state to get them to lower their rates.

Energy Alabama, a clean energy nonprofit, said Alabama Power customers “should not be fooled” by the company’s rate reduction.

“The company credits data centers, but its own numbers show there would be no cut without a roughly $180 million drop in its tax bill, which the company ties to nuclear tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act. Even after this action, the company’s own filing shows its return on equity, a marker for its profits, remaining above the national average,” Daniel Tait, the group’s executive director, said in a statement.

“The rate freeze isn’t a gift either, because Alabama Power wants to pay for it with more of your tax credits and a 2026 refund you’re likely owed. Alabamians want real relief on their electric bills, and that comes from a cut to what Alabama Power is allowed to profit. Sure, people will take the $4 per month but shuffling tax credits around doesn’t cut it.”

In October, the PSC adopted a procedure to automatically approve Alabama Power’s contracts with large load data centers if the commission fails to take a vote within 90 days of submission.

Under the Power to the People Act, signed into law this year, the PSC board will expand from three members to seven based on congressional districts starting next year.

text:
Marshall County residents are expressing opinions on proposed revisions to an existing ordinance that would regulate the installation of battery cells, solar panels and wind turbines, said Tyler Kelley, Marshall County Planning & Zoning director, sanitarian and weed commissioner.

And he wants more, he said Friday in a telephone interview with the Times-Republican. Residents are encouraged to share their opinions with him and the three P&Z commissioners, Will Hobson, Pat VonAhnen and Will Wears.

Work on the revised renewable energy ordinance began in 2024, and Kelley said there is still more work to do. The existing ordinance was drafted a number of years ago and Kelley said it is outdated.

He previously told the T-R that a surge in recent years of renewable energy development and resulting new technology were at issue. Kelley said he did not want to set a timeline for when the revised ordinance would be reviewed and approved by the P&Z Commission.

That will happen only after they have heard and read all public comments. That ordinance will then be sent to the Marshall County Board of Supervisors for their review, which will also allow for public comments.

In previous statements to the T-R, supervisors Christian Goodman, Jarret Heil and Carol Hibbs have commended Kelley for his efforts to hold work sessions open to the public and attended by county department heads.

Setbacks from County Conservation property at issue

After the most recent work session of Nov. 13, Marshall County Conservation Board (MCCB) Director Emily Herring told the T-R in an interview Wednesday she had concerns about proposals that would significantly reduce "setbacks" to 1,400 feet.

For example, in the revised ordinance a wind turbine could be installed on private property only 1,400 feet from a MCCB park or campground.

"There have been suggestions about removing all setbacks from county conservation areas, the river, the floodplain ... putting them closer to people's houses," Herring said. "We are concerned about those changes ... quite a bit of cutting ... it is disconcerting."

Herring said she is "very uncomfortable" with only a 1,400-foot setback of wind turbines from MCCB properties such as the Green Castle Recreation Area between Ferguson and Gilman.

"I think we will lose income from people who want to camp there," she said. "There is a pond - we get migrating birds ... we did a bat study and have multiple species of bats."

Herring said Green Castle is one of the most heavily used of the numerous MCCB properties open to the public.

"We do not have exact numbers (of visitors), as we count cars," she said. "But from January to September, 26,771 cars visited. The Department of Energy reports the average vehicle occupancy is 1.5 (probably low for people who visit GCRA) ... so we say we have had about 40,157 visitors from January to September. Since July 1, GCRA has brought in $23,000 - that does not include income from the shelter house. Nor does it include money spent at local businesses."

The nearly 117-acre property was purchased by the MCCB in 1977. Its attractions include a 16-acre lake accessible by carry-in canoes and kayaks. There are 16 campsites with electric and water hook-ups. Several are ADA accessible according to the MCCB website.

MCCB seeks compromise

"From the very beginning ... every conversation I have had ... is that we (MCCB) want to try to find a compromise ... we want to find something in the middle. We understand the importance of 'renewable energy' (and that) climate change will have a negative effect on wildlife anyway. We have to find something in the middle that is not detrimental to our county's environment and economic possibilities as well," Herring said. "A lot of people think we are against windmills coming in, and that is not the case. We have had discussions with ScoutCleanEnergy (one of three renewable energy companies exploring Marshall County properties as development opportunities). We have told them on several occasions we are willing to work with them to make their projects successful while protecting county areas. The company has been open and honest with us."

MCCB Board Vice ChairmanTom Deimerly, a local businessman, agreed with Herring on the setback issue.

"Yes, I think a setback of that size (1,400 feet) would hurt our conservation and recreation areas," he wrote in an email to the T-R Friday. "The board looked for a middle ground that’s fair to taxpayers, business and conservation. We feel our proposed setbacks do that ... they should be with limited special permit reviews that aren't overly cumbersome ... that is the goal. Unfortunately, no decision will meet everyone’s needs."

He added: "I like where taxpayer dollars meet conservation and recreation. I studied natural resources conservation and economics and spent years in economic development, and I’m still pro-business. Projects like this pull me both ways."

Deimerly has served on the MCCB board since 2020. He and other directors are appointed by the Marshall County Board of Supervisors.

MCCB board members are volunteers who determine policy and delegate to staff to carry-out their directives. Rich Naughton of Marshalltown - a retired businessman - is chairperson. The board meets monthly at the Grimes Farm Conservation Center, 2349 233rd St., Marshalltown. The meetings are open to the public, and the organization's budget and staff hiring decisions are reviewed and approved by the supervisors.

For additional information or to comment on the revised ordinance, contact Kelley at 641-844-2707 or tkelley@marshallcountyia.gov, or Hobson - 641-752-3894, VonAhnen - 641-751-5385, and Wears - 641-485-8892.

For additional information about MCCB, contact 641-752-5490 or mccb@marshallcounty.ia.gov.

title: Scientists in China print lithium anodes that keep test batteries stable for over 260 cycles
description:
Scientists in China have printed ultra-thin lithium anodes that kept test batteries stable for more than 260 charging cycles.
These ultra-thin anodes could make EV batteries more powerful, expand their energy storage capacity, and lessen their mass.
The resulting reaction produced lithium-magnesium alloys along with lithium sulfide, lithium nitride, and lithium fluoride.
The same benefit could extend to portable electronics, as battery weight and space affect the devices people carry every day.

text:
Scientists in China have printed ultra-thin lithium anodes that kept test batteries stable for more than 260 charging cycles. The approach could help electric vehicles carry more energy without heavier batteries, and it could also benefit portable electronics and energy storage systems.

Here's what to know

The mask-assisted screen-printing process deposits lithium microdiscs on copper, Interesting Engineering reported. These ultra-thin anodes could make EV batteries more powerful, expand their energy storage capacity, and lessen their mass.

The Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led the research team that developed it. Researchers from Southern University of Science and Technology and Guilin University of Technology also participated. They published their findings in the journal Nano-Micro Letters.

Previously, producing thin, uniform anodes was difficult because molten lithium tends to form droplets on copper rather than coat the surface evenly. The screen-printing process developed by the researchers uses a patterned mask to place the lithium onto the copper, producing evenly spaced lithium microdiscs.

The team produced lithium arrays with equivalent thicknesses of 10, 20, and 28 micrometers by controlling and adjusting the discs' dimensions and the gaps between them.

Lithium can react with a battery's electrolyte and develop uneven deposits, including needle-like structures called dendrites that affect performance. To help protect the anode, the team introduced a magnesium-based compound into the molten lithium.

The resulting reaction produced lithium-magnesium alloys along with lithium sulfide, lithium nitride, and lithium fluoride. Together, these materials formed a more stable protective layer intended to reduce unwanted chemical reactions and lithium loss during repeated charging.

More background

Conventional lithium metal battery designs often use thick foils. Lithium metal's appeal, though, is its ability to store substantial energy at low weight. With that extra material, a battery stores less energy for its weight.

The researchers' tests suggested a battery stack could store 504 watt-hours per kilogram by weight and 1,071 watt-hours per liter by volume. Those results came from pairing a printed 20-micrometer anode with high-loading, nickel-rich cathodes.

The same benefit could extend to portable electronics, as battery weight and space affect the devices people carry every day.

What's being done?

When paired with lithium iron phosphate cathodes, the modified 10-micrometer anodes maintained stable performance for 260 cycles, demonstrating durability as well as a specific capacity above 130 milliampere-hours per gram. They also achieved Coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.8%, a measure of how effectively charge is recovered.

The approach also showed promise in gel-electrolyte solid-state battery tests, extending the team's testing beyond the nickel-rich cathode design.

title: Cop31 failed but in 'the real world' the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable - The Guardian
authors: Fiona Harvey, Graham Readfearn, www.theguardian.com, fiona-harvey, graham-readfearn
description:
“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network.
Irene Vélez Torres, a former Colombian environment minister who earlier this year chaired a conference of 57 countries on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said this was the right outcome.
Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition.
Commitments on finance to help the poor and vulnerable cope with the impacts of the climate crisis were sidelined.
For that, what is happening outside the windowless air-conditioned conference halls of Cop may be far more important than any Cop decision, or lack of one.
text:
The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned.

“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.”

The Australian president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, did not quite apologise for the failure. “Unfortunately we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision,” he told journalists outside the hall. “And that’s disappointing, very disappointing.”

For two weeks, ministers and high-level officials from 190 countries laboured over a few pages of convoluted text, only to produce, at the end, almost nothing. What was proposed as the main outcome, the prematurely named “Antalya pact”, inviting countries to electrify their economies and address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond 1.5C above preindustrial levels, was abandoned after a lengthening roll call of countries rejected it, during the final dramatic meeting on Sunday afternoon.

The collapse was almost unprecedented in the long history of Cops, because it was so clearcut. Other conferences have produced mediocre outcomes, but usually tried to salvage some face-saving semblance of unity at the end. But after a marathon final negotiating session that carried on more than 40 hours beyond its scheduled end, a small group of countries led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept an outcome that mentioned the need to “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Normally, as Cops proceed by consensus and even a few holdouts can change the outcome, that refusal would have been enough to force through a weakened final compromise that excised such commitments in favour of the presidencies’ preferred wording, referring only to an “irreversible transition towards lower greenhouse gas emissions”.

Instead, a large group of other countries led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries, decided they would not accept such a weak deal. When it came their turn to take the microphone, each in turn declared their objections – close to 40 countries registered objections or refusals.

Irene Vélez Torres, a former Colombian environment minister who earlier this year chaired a conference of 57 countries on the phaseout of fossil fuels, said this was the right outcome. “This Cop has failed, not because there are no pathways to advance climate action, but because there has been an attempt to erase from the final decision a reality that science has demonstrated and a growing number of countries already recognise: there is no way to confront the climate crisis without ending our dependence on fossil fuels,” she said.

Yet the developed countries that led the charge are riven with contradictions over the issue, as Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, pointed out. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow.”

In place of the cover decision, there was agreement on some side issues, including a “just transition mechanism” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to the low-carbon economy, which was decried as toothless by campaigners. Commitments on finance to help the poor and vulnerable cope with the impacts of the climate crisis were sidelined.

Tasneem Essop, the executive director of Climate Action Network, cried foul. “This was the worst Cop ever,” she said. “We are witnessing human suffering on an unimaginable scale, and we had hoped this Cop would take steps to protect people from the worsening climate crisis. Instead, rich nations gutted the very measures that could have made a difference. Negotiating room after negotiating room, developed countries systematically blocked measures that would require them to provide finance to protect people’s lives and address the climate crisis.”

The result also threatens the “multilateralism” on which Cops depend, which is crucial for many of the smallest nations and disadvantaged groups. For them, Cops are the only forum in which they can confront the authors of the fossil fuel crisis – the rich nations and petro states which have benefited from coal, oil and gas up to now.

“Despite the discouragement we feel today, we will keep betting on multilateralism,” said Juan Carlos Jintiach Arcos, the executive secretary of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities. “We start from a clear premise: multilateralism is not built by political leaders alone. We remain hopeful that the world’s governments will find the courage to join us in this fight.”

The question now is how the world can put this right. For that, what is happening outside the windowless air-conditioned conference halls of Cop may be far more important than any Cop decision, or lack of one.

Renewable power has overtaken coal in China, reaching 60% of generation capacity, investment in clean energy around the world is twice that into fossil fuels, and electric vehicles have taken off, making up a third of new car sales in Europe and a majority in many other countries around the world, from China to Vietnam, Singapore and Iceland.

title: NEWSWIRE: Senate passes #BAAJA; Plus some thoughts on U.S. Senator Heinrich's ...
description:
Beyond that, it’s not clear that BAAJA would have much effect on data center development.
So far, the Big Data Center Buildup has occurred largely outside the federal permitting system.
In that case, the associated infrastructure, and therefore the data center itself, would benefit from BAAJA.
And, of course, if a developer were to formally propose a data center on public land, BAAJA would limit the public’s ability to block it.
The effort to streamline federal permitting to benefit clean energy has been underway for decades.
text:
Heinrich and other pro-BAAJAers hold up the SunZia transmission project’s 17-year permitting journey as evidence of why permitting reform is needed. Yet it is now under construction, for better or worse. Meanwhile, other major lines were also approved, including TransWest Express, Ten West Link, Gateway South, and Boardman-to-Hemingway.

The anti-BAAJA crowd has said the legislation will “gut” and “eviscerate” bedrock environmental laws (I may have used similar language) and would “supercharge” the data center boom, leading to “environmental catastrophe.”

In fact, the legislation would tweak and weaken NEPA, NHPA, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and make the General Mining Law even more permissive than it already is. Michael B. Gerrard, Andrew Sabin Professor of Professional Practice at Columbia Law School, described it as pulling “NEPA’s principal teeth,” by precluding the possibility of a court order blocking a project. While losing one’s teeth isn’t as bad as losing one’s guts, it does suck, and these changes would rob the public of their say over how its lands are managed.

BAAJA’s only data center-specific provision would require that data centers pay the full cost of associated grid and infrastructure upgrades to ensure that utility ratepayers are not stuck with the tab; even the most vehement anti-BAAJA groups like this aspect of the legislation.

Beyond that, it’s not clear that BAAJA would have much effect on data center development. So far, the Big Data Center Buildup has occurred largely outside the federal permitting system. The huge projects going up or being proposed all over the West, from Project Stratos to Project Jupiter to Valar Atomic’s Raceway Energy, are all on private or state land, and don’t have a federal component, meaning they are not subject to NEPA, meaning BAAJA would have no or little effect on them. Unless, that is, the facility requires a transmission line or gas pipeline or some other infrastructure that crosses federal land or affects Waters of the United States, and would therefore be subject to NEPA, NHPA, the CWA, and/or the ESA. In that case, the associated infrastructure, and therefore the data center itself, would benefit from BAAJA.

And, of course, if a developer were to formally propose a data center on public land, BAAJA would limit the public’s ability to block it. Only one data center project has formally been proposed for public lands, and the Trump administration simply ignored NEPA and any environmental review requirements and secretly gave it the go-ahead (which was later revoked). But other developers have expressed interest in public lands, and the administration has signaled its desires to hand those lands over to the developers, so this certainly could become an issue in the future, which is why Sens. Jeff Wyden Merkley and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) introduced an amendment to the bill that would ban data centers on public land. It did not pass.

Et tu, Martin?

The internecine feud over the bill risks eroding environmental support for Democrats like Heinrich, who previously were known to stand up for public lands and tribal sovereignty. One Land Desk reader, in a comment, wondered what Heinrich’s motivations were, adding: “ … it seems like he is blowing up his previous environmental record with this … .”

I certainly can’t speak for Heinrich, nor do I have any desire to be an apologist for him, but from my perspective it seems that support for this bill is not only sincere, but is in line with his previous record on these issues.

The effort to streamline federal permitting to benefit clean energy has been underway for decades. During the early days of the energy transition, wind and solar developers in places like Wyoming and eastern New Mexico ran up against a lack of transmission capacity to get the energy from the windy and sunny spaces to the places it is needed, such as the urban Southwest. It’s one thing to build a big wind or solar installation on a patch of BLM land or private land, quite another to permit a 300-mile transmission line that crosses a dozen different jurisdictions. While the federal Natural Gas Act gives companies certain bludgeons to build interstate pipelines — including the power of condemnation, it doesn’t do the same for big transmission, and permitting a major project can take a decade or more.

That difficulty — and the need not only for more transmission, but also for an integrated Western power grid — spawned a movement aimed at developing long-distance power lines to facilitate solar and wind development. New organizations such as Americans for a Clean Energy Grid sprung up to support the effort, while some existing environmental groups got on board in a more limited fashion, such as the National Resources Defense Council and Western Resource Advocates. Heinrich, who was elected to the Senate in 2012, was one of the few federal lawmakers to really embrace this concept and to advocate for a 100% clean energy grid. He was a big proponent of the SunZia transmission line that carries wind power from New Mexico to the Phoenix area, and uses its interminable route to approval as evidence that permitting reform is necessary to achieve a clean energy transition and tackle climate change.

Heinrich has introduced and backed other legislation aimed at encouraging transmission development and grid modernization. The Biden-era Infrastructure and Jobs and Inflation Reduction acts allocated billions of dollars to transmission lines, and in September Heinrich introduced a bill that would incentivize new transmission development. Now some Biden administration officials have said that permitting delays prevented some of the subsidized projects from getting built before the Trump administration clawed back much of the funds, killing the projects altogether.

If one believes that a major and rapid transmission buildout is necessary to bring more clean energy online to tackle the climate crisis (and to keep the grid from collapsing under increased energy demand), and if one believes that the primary hindrance blocking these projects is an outdated and overly rigorous permitting process that favors lawsuit-filing advocacy groups, then it would logically follow that streamlining the process would require weakening or partially dismantling the legal framework governing that process. Or to mix some metaphors: You’ve got to pull some teeth, or at least file them down, to keep the beast from killing your project (even if it ultimately harms the beast).

I imagine Heinrich, an old-school, pragmatic Democrat who prides himself on bipartisanship, felt he was signing onto the best chance at reform he could get in a Republican-dominated Congress, even if it was deeply compromised. He was able to get the GOP to sign on to decent provisions on transmission, including the one requiring data centers to pay their own way, despite strong objections from the utility industry. He had been on this path for so long that when he reached a destination — even if it wasn’t the one he originally had in mind — he immediately and stubbornly staked his flag there, largely ignoring constituents’ and colleagues’ protests.

Heinrich and his colleagues introduced amendments aimed at making the legislation more palatable to tribal nations. While one made it into the bill, it was not enough, according to the National Congress for American Indians, which still called on the Senate to kill the entire legislation. A later effort to further amend the bill was blocked, sparking yet another conflict between environmental and tribal advocates.

In doing so, he basically threw his lot into the same bet all of the environmentally minded, pro-BAAJA side is making: That the climate benefits of a clean energy buildout under a reformed permitting system will offset resulting direct harms to front-line communities, the landscape, the water, and the air. It’s a gamble, maybe even an act of faith, faith that when put on a level playing field, clean energy will always win out over fossil fuels, and a faith that even a weakened, toothless system will continue to protect the nation’s natural and cultural resources, even though it’s overseen by an ethically compromised administration. It’s a big and perilous leap, and we’ll all be forced to pay if Heinrich loses the bet.

text:
The U.S. Senate passed S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) by a 62–33 vote Thursday, to speed federal permitting for energy and infrastructure projects.

According to the President, BAAJA aims to accelerate $2 trillion worth of energy projects, which are held up by a labyrinth of government permitting.

“It’s one of the biggest things that you will see. It’s a big deal… It’s projected to put at least $1,300 a year back in the pockets of hardworking Americans,” said President Donald J. Trump.

So naturally, the Washington Post headline had this to say: “Senate votes to weaken environmental laws to speed up energy projects.”

Infrastructure and energy capital expenditures currently stuck in the federal permitting pipeline, have unrealized economic activity estimated in the $1.7–2.4+ trillion range. The bill is intended to move many of those projects forward more quickly.

“By modernizing the federal permitting system, this legislation would make it easier to build critical energy projects, roads, ports and other much-needed infrastructure. The benefits would flow to Americans in the form of lower utility bills, new good-paying jobs and more private-sector investment in communities across the country,” Business Roundtable CEO Joshua Bolten summarized.

BAAJA is a major bipartisan overhaul of federal permitting aimed at speeding up energy and infrastructure projects including pipelines, power plants, transmission lines, mines, data centers, and renewables.

BAAJA amends core laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and Federal Power Act.

Major provisions include:

Faster reviews and tighter deadlines for environmental analyses and agency decisions (targeting roughly 2 years for major projects in many cases).

Shorter litigation windows (often 150 days) for challenges to NEPA reviews, certain Clean Water Act actions, ESA biological opinions, and other authorizations.

Limits on remedies — preference for remanding deficient reviews for fixes rather than vacating/approving projects.

Permit certainty — makes it much harder for agencies to revoke, suspend, or arbitrarily alter already-issued permits (with remedies for developers if they do).

Stronger FERC backstop authority for interstate transmission lines (easier to approve major lines when states delay or reject them).

Data center cost allocation — large new loads (commonly referenced around 20 MW+) must bear more of the transmission and infrastructure costs they impose, protecting other ratepayers.

Technology-neutral treatment covering renewables, fossil fuels, nuclear, geothermal, mining, pipelines, storage, and related infrastructure, plus some categorical exclusions and process streamlining.

Supporters argue delays in permitting power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure raise costs for consumers and businesses. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated the bill could increase annual economic output by $82 billion to $164 billion and reduce average household ​electric bills by roughly $178 to $251 per year, Reuters reports.

The bill would lower costs and significantly expand transmission capacity, as well as generating an estimated $350 billion in savings through 2050.

President Trump’s Executive Order 14154 from January 2025, “Unleashing American Energy,” underscores the national interest in maximizing the use of affordable, reliable domestic energy. The order establishes U.S. policy to “encourage energy exploration and production on federal lands and waters, including the Outer Continental Shelf, to meet the needs of our citizens and solidify the United States as a global energy leader long into the future.”

President Trump’s order was done not only to eliminate the “electric vehicle mandate” and promote true consumer choice, but to “protect the United States’s economic and national security and military preparedness by ensuring that an abundant supply of reliable energy is readily accessible in every State and territory of the Nation.”

The order continues:

“America is blessed with an abundance of energy and natural resources that have historically powered our Nation’s economic prosperity. In recent years, burdensome and ideologically motivated regulations have impeded the development of these resources, limited the generation of reliable and affordable electricity, reduced job creation, and inflicted high energy costs upon our citizens. These high energy costs devastate American consumers by driving up the cost of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing, while weakening our national security.

“It is thus in the national interest to unleash America’s affordable and reliable energy and natural resources. This will restore American prosperity—including for those men and women who have been forgotten by our economy in recent years. It will also rebuild our Nation’s economic and military security, which will deliver peace through strength.”
