text:
Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx is projected to lose her House seat to Democrat Chuck Hubbard, ending her more than two decades representing North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District.

Foxx’s loss cements another fall for long-serving Republican incumbents this cycle, which has seen Democrats reclaim control of both chambers of Congress. Cook Political Report changed Foxx’s district rating from “solid R” to “likely R” shortly before Election Day.

“Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process,” Hubbard said in a statement Sunday. “Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices. I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District.”

Foxx has already said she would run again for the seat in 2028.

Trending

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, The Associated Press reported, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.

Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

The North Carolina race, which the AP called Sunday morning, remained separated by a margin of less than 100 votes for a significant period following Election Day. Ultimately, a drop of close to 2,500 provisional ballots, which can be cast when a voter’s eligibility is not immediately clear on Election Day, turned the race in Hubbard’s favor.

As House Rules chair, Foxx was responsible for setting the procedures and schedule for any legislation to be considered — which made her a key part of the Republican leadership structure.

Hubbard focused his campaign on combating the rising cost of living, expanding access to health care, protecting women’s rights and calling on Congress to help North Carolina recover from the devastation of Hurricane Helene in 2024. Foxx’s platform included a focus on anti-abortion and religious liberty issues, reducing federal spending and supporting Trump’s immigration enforcement policies.

Trump won North Carolina in 2024, but Democrats made significant gains in the state during the 2026 midterms.

text:
US EV sales fell 20% in January compared with December, according to Cox Automotive data cited in an ABC News report that asks whether electric vehicles are about to become too niche. The same data puts EV market share at 6% in January, roughly half the nearly 12% recorded in September, which Cox described as a record high.

The swing is large enough to change the conversation around electrification. In September, EVs hit a record share. Four months later the question is whether the segment can hold its ground at all. Two forces sit behind the shift in the report: the end of the $7,500 federal tax credit in September, and a buyer preference for hybrids over higher-priced EVs.

This analysis separates what the data confirms from what the headline implies. EV owners already face new costs in some states, as our look at Pennsylvania’s EV road charge of $250 a year shows, so the policy backdrop matters as much as sticker prices. Where the sources stop, this article stops too, and it labels every forecast as analysis rather than fact.

The Core Numbers Behind the EV Sales Drop

Only a handful of figures anchor this story, so it pays to list them plainly. Cox Automotive’s data shows EV sales in the United States dropping 20% from December to January. Market share, which had touched nearly 12% in September, slid to 6% in January. The $7,500 federal tax credit for EVs expired in September, the same month the share peaked.

The report adds two more points. Automakers have booked billions of dollars in write-offs tied to factories, battery technology and new models. And consumers who still wanted an electrified vehicle picked hybrids more often than higher-priced EVs. Everything else in this piece builds from those facts.

Note what the table does not contain. There is no automaker-level breakdown, no unit counts and no price list. The available material names no specific model and no individual speaker, so nothing below attributes an opinion to a person.

From a Record 12% to 6%: Reading the Market Share Swing

Share is a ratio, so it moves when either side changes. A falling EV share can mean EV sales dropped, total vehicle sales rose, or both. The Cox data gives a direct measure for the first piece, a 20% month-over-month decline in EV sales, which is steep for a single step. The ratio then fell by about half between September and January.

The arithmetic of a halved share

Going from nearly 12% to 6% is a drop of close to six percentage points, or roughly half in relative terms. That is our own arithmetic on the reported figures, not a number Cox published. The sources give no unit volumes, so we stop at the percentages instead of converting them into vehicle counts.

One month is a data point, not a trend

A December-to-January comparison can mix a real demand change with ordinary seasonal patterns, and the report does not say how Cox adjusts for that. Treat the 20% figure as a strong signal that needs follow-up months to confirm.

Why the September peak is the right reference

September’s record share gives the comparison its drama. A peak reached in the same month the federal credit expired suggests that buyers may have moved purchases forward to capture the $7,500. That reading is our interpretation of timing, and the sources do not state it as cause. If it holds, part of the September high was borrowed from later months, and the January slump reflects the repayment.

Why the $7,500 Tax Credit Expiry Matters

A $7,500 credit changes the math on a car purchase more than almost any other incentive. For a buyer comparing a mid-priced EV with a hybrid, $7,500 can close the monthly payment gap entirely. When the credit disappears, the EV’s price relative to its alternatives jumps overnight, and the buyer’s decision resets.

The report links the share decline to the credit’s end in September and to consumers choosing hybrids over higher-priced EVs. Those two facts sit naturally together. Remove a subsidy from the pricier option and some buyers move to the cheaper one. Cox’s data shows that movement in aggregate even without naming a model.

Sellers can offset some of that loss with their own money. Our Black Friday EV deals roundup lists customer cash of $10,000 or more from Kia, Volkswagen and Lucid, which shows how aggressively brands are working to replace a government incentive with a manufacturer one. Whether that spending lifts volume in the coming months is the open question, and it is a costly one for any company already carrying write-offs.

Buyers Chose Hybrids Over Higher-Priced EVs

The most useful detail in the report is the direction of the substitution. Shoppers did not abandon electrified powertrains. They moved from higher-priced EVs toward hybrids. That distinction separates a collapse in interest from a price-driven reshuffle inside a category buyers still want.

Hybrids ask less of a household. They need no home charger, no change in routine and no range planning for road trips. They also usually cost less than the pricier EVs the report says buyers passed over. When the tax credit vanishes, those trade-offs tilt the decision toward the hybrid, which is consistent with what the data describes.

There is a practical angle for shoppers too. A buyer who wants lower fuel use but cannot justify a premium price now has a clear middle option. That option keeps the engine as a backup and trims running costs, and it asks nothing of the driveway or the wall socket. For households without home charging, the case is stronger still.

The report does not give hybrid sales numbers, so we cannot size the gain. Readers should hold that gap in mind whenever someone claims hybrids “won” the quarter. The direction is confirmed, the magnitude is not.

Billions in Write-Offs: The Automaker Balance Sheet Problem

Automakers have recorded billions of dollars in write-offs tied to investments in factories, battery technology and new models. The report gives no company-by-company breakdown and no combined total, so the word “billions” is as precise as the record gets.

A write-off is an accounting admission that an asset is worth less than the books said. For factories, that usually means capacity built for demand that did not arrive on schedule. For battery technology and new models, it means development spending that will earn back less than planned. Each category ties directly to the demand picture: when sales slow, planned output shrinks, and the assets behind that output lose value.

Investors tend to read write-offs as a lagging indicator. They record decisions made years earlier, when planners expected steeper demand curves. The more telling signal is what companies do after the charge, whether they cut shifts, pause platform work or redirect spending. The report gives no examples, so those moves remain something to watch in coming filings and announcements.

The write-offs also shape what happens next. Companies that have already taken a hit have less appetite for new EV-only programs and more reason to hedge with hybrids. That behavior would feed the same shift the sales data shows, with product plans following buyer preference instead of leading it.

Is “Plummeting” Accurate? Separating Data From Headline

The ABC News headline calls EV sales “plummeting.” That word is a summary judgment. The quantified facts are a 20% monthly drop and a share decline from nearly 12% to 6%, and those are large moves. But the headline’s characterization is not a separate measurement, and the available material gives no longer time series that would let us call it a sustained plunge.

The same caution applies to the framing question about EVs becoming “too niche.” It is a forecast, not an established fact. A 6% share is smaller than September’s high, yet it still marks a meaningful slice of the market, and nothing in the report says where the line sits between a mainstream product and a niche one.

Will EVs Become Too Niche? What the Evidence Can and Cannot Say

Evidence for the niche scenario is real. Share halved in four months, the incentive is gone, and the buyers who remain lean toward cheaper alternatives. If those conditions persist, the EV segment would settle at a lower plateau than the September peak implied.

Evidence against that scenario is also real, though thinner. A 6% share is still a substantial market, and a record share just a few months earlier shows that demand exists when prices work for buyers. The September high happened with the $7,500 credit in place. That tells us less about weakness in EVs than about how much of their appeal rested on a subsidy.

Our read: “niche” is the wrong frame for a market that sits between 6% and 12% depending on incentives. The better question is what share EVs can sustain on their own economics. The January figure is one estimate of that floor, and a single month cannot settle it.

Hardware Pressure Points: Batteries, Packs and Charging

For a hardware audience, the sales story is really a component story. The battery pack accounts for much of an EV’s cost, and the factories the report mentions, along with the battery technology investments, are where the write-offs concentrate. Lower volume hurts pack makers and cell suppliers first because their plants need steady utilization to pay off. More on our broader coverage lives in the hardware section.

Some of the industry’s response aims at cost and flexibility rather than volume. NIO’s plan to open its network to other brands is one example, covered in our piece on NIO’s battery swap opening to other brands in 2027. Swap networks try to cut the upfront battery cost for drivers, which speaks directly to the price barrier that pushes shoppers toward hybrids.

Manufacturing research targets the same pressure. A Cornell test reported a cut of up to 60% in battery formation time, a step that sits early in cell production and drives factory throughput. Our write-up of the Cornell battery formation test explains why shaving time there matters for unit cost. Lower cost per pack is the cleanest route to EVs that compete without a subsidy.

Competitive Comparison: EVs, Hybrids and Gas Cars

The report supports a qualitative comparison only, so we keep it that way. Higher-priced EVs lost ground. Hybrids gained buyers. Conventional gas vehicles are not discussed in the source material, which means any claim about their share in this period would go beyond the facts.

What the shift implies is a ranking on affordability and convenience. Hybrids score well on both, since they avoid the charger question and typically carry a lower price than the EVs shoppers skipped. EVs still own advantages on running costs and technology for owners who can charge at home, but those advantages did not offset the lost $7,500 for many buyers in the data.

Global competition adds pressure from outside the US. Our comparison of the BYD Seal 06 against the Tesla Model 3 in China shows a gap of 109,900 yuan against 235,500 yuan in that market. Prices like that illustrate how far the cost frontier can move, and they show how much room exists for lower EV prices in other markets.

Historical Context: A Record Peak, Then a Reset

The path in this data has a clear shape. EV share climbed to a record near 12% in September. The tax credit that helped support it expired that month. Four months later, share sat at 6%. A rise to a peak followed by a quick reset is common when a subsidy ends, and it usually leaves a market at a new base level rather than at zero.

We avoid comparing this episode to earlier technology cycles with specific numbers, because the sources provide none. What can be said is that the record itself matters. A market that reached nearly 12% proved that a large block of US buyers will choose an EV under the right price conditions. The January reading shows what happens when one of those conditions changes.

Market Impact: Suppliers, Dealers and Investors

The effects spread across the chain. Suppliers with EV-specific contracts face lower order flow. Dealers face a harder sell on pricier EVs, and the hybrid shift in the report hints that some may lean on a different product mix. Investors read the write-offs as proof that earlier growth assumptions ran ahead of demand.

Trade policy and tariffs add another layer. As our report on the UK and EU reset and Chinese EV tariffs of up to 45% shows, governments elsewhere are still working out how to protect domestic EV production while keeping prices attainable. A US market with weaker demand makes those choices harder for exporters looking for volume.

The sources offer no stock moves, no earnings guidance and no company names, so we do not claim any specific financial reaction. The direction of pressure is clear. The size of it is not, and readers should wait for company filings before drawing numbers.

How to Read EV Sales Reports Without Overreading Them

Headlines about car sales compress a lot of moving parts. Before drawing a conclusion from any EV report, check four things. Which months does the comparison cover? Is the figure a count or a share? Does the source name the data provider? And does the article separate measured facts from the writer’s summary?

Apply those checks here and the picture sharpens. The comparison covers December to January for sales and September to January for share. The figures mix a percentage change in sales with a market share ratio. The provider is Cox Automotive. And the “plummeting” label is the summary, while the 20% drop and the move from nearly 12% to 6% are the measurements.

One more caution applies to timing. The Cox figures describe September and January, so they are the latest quoted data points in the ABC News piece, not a live monthly feed. Anyone making a purchase or investment decision should look for newer monthly releases before leaning on them.

The same discipline helps with the “too niche” question. A forecast needs a threshold and a time frame, and the report offers neither. Without them, the phrase works as a prompt for debate rather than a claim that data can prove or disprove. Our job as readers is to ask what number would change the answer, and then track that number as it arrives.

Five Predictions for EV Sales

These are our forecasts, not facts from Cox Automotive or ABC News. We give each a reason and avoid attaching figures the sources do not support.

Share stays below September’s peak for a sustained stretch. Without the $7,500 credit, the price math for most buyers has changed, and one month of recovery would not reverse that.

Hybrids keep gaining relative to higher-priced EVs. The direction is already confirmed, and nothing in the report points to a change in buyer preference.

More automakers trim or delay EV-only programs. Write-offs reduce the appetite for further factory and platform spending.

Manufacturer cash incentives replace some of the lost federal credit. Deals like the customer cash we tracked on Black Friday point that way, though the cost lands on company margins.

Cheaper packs decide the next upswing. Progress in cell manufacturing and battery access models gives the best chance of narrowing the price gap without subsidies.

What to Watch Next

Several indicators will show whether January was a trough or the start of a slide. First, the next monthly Cox Automotive readings, which will show whether share stabilizes near 6% or keeps falling. Second, hybrid sales data, which would size the substitution the report describes. Third, automaker filings that put figures on the write-offs.

Policy is the fourth signal. A restored incentive, new state-level fees or changes to trade rules would each move the price math again. Finally, watch whether lower-cost EVs reach US showrooms, since the data suggests price is the lever that moves buyers most.

The takeaway: the confirmed facts show a sharp, incentive-linked reset in EV sales, with buyers shifting to hybrids. They do not show that EVs are headed for a niche, and the evidence for that claim has to come from the months ahead.

FAQ: EV Sales, Market Share and the Tax Credit

How much did US EV sales fall in January? Cox Automotive data shows EV sales dropped 20% in January compared with December, as reported by ABC News.

What was the EV market share at its peak? EVs reached nearly 12% of the US vehicle market in September, which the report describes as a record high.

What was EV market share in January? Cox Automotive put it at 6%, roughly half the September level.

When did the $7,500 federal EV tax credit end? The credit expired in September, the same month EV share hit its record.

Are buyers leaving electrified cars altogether? The report says consumers chose higher-priced EVs less often and bought hybrids instead, so the shift looks like a move between powertrains rather than a retreat from electrification.

Have automakers lost money on EVs? The report says automakers have recorded billions of dollars in write-offs tied to factories, battery technology and new models. It gives no company-level totals.

title: Google Backs Superhot Geothermal in 50 MW Oregon Power Deal | OilPrice.com
description:
The runaway energy demand driven by the artificial intelligence era is pushing Big Tech to pursue an all-of-the-above approach to energy generation.
Just this week, Google signed a major power purchase agreement with Quaise Energy for 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power.
The agreement indicates a huge step forward and a massive vote of confidence for the as-yet unproven form of clean energy production.
"Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power."
A report from the Rhodium Group estimates that geothermal energy could meet up to 64 percent of data center energy demand growth by the early 2030s.
text:
The runaway energy demand driven by the artificial intelligence era is pushing Big Tech to pursue an all-of-the-above approach to energy generation. At the same time that the sector is causing a natural gas boom and extending the life of fossil fuels, it is also channeling huge amounts of funding into next-gen clean energy technologies including space-based solar power, nuclear fusion, and advanced geothermal.

Just this week, Google signed a major power purchase agreement with Quaise Energy for 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power. The energy will be produced in Central Oregon at a site known as Project Obsidian. The agreement indicates a huge step forward and a massive vote of confidence for the as-yet unproven form of clean energy production.

Geothermal itself is not new, but at present commercial geothermal plants only exist in places where the Earth's heat naturally breaks through to the surface. This occurs at geologically anomalous locations like geysers and hot springs, meaning that geothermal is only viable in a very small number of locations worldwide. But in recent years, thanks to drilling technologies borrowed from the oil and gas sector and nuclear fusion research, startups have been getting closer and closer to making geothermal a viable option nearly anywhere on the planet.

By drilling deep enough, the Earth's natural heat can be tapped into from almost any location. And the temperatures accessed at those depths are often much, much hotter than those being accessed through natural thermal vents on the surface, meaning that the energy potential is huge.

"We started Quaise to make the Earth's most abundant energy source universally accessible - and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector," said Carlos Araque, CEO and President of Quaise Energy. "Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power."

Quaise is using technology originally developed at MIT in order to dig its superdeep wells to tap into enhanced geothermal technology. The method relies on a vacuum-tube gyrotron, which is able to send high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole to vaporize rock molecules. In tandem, a jet of gas clears away the ash. And while this may sound futuristic, the company claims that its technology is ready to deliver: Project Obsidian aims to begin its delivery of energy to Google as soon as 2030.

This marks a major step forward for the enhanced geothermal industry as a whole, but the technology still has a long way to go before it becomes commercially scalable. The enhanced geothermal sector as a whole is still in its infancy and continues to face high up-front and operational costs thanks to a lack of scale, among other factors. At present, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of the United States energy mix, even though the country is the global leader in installed geothermal capacity at about 3.7 gigawatts.

But geothermal energy is quickly gaining ground, as it boasts a number of critical advantages. For one, it's one of vanishingly few clean energy sectors that enjoys broad support from both sides of the aisle in the United States. Plus, it is an infinite resource capable of producing clean energy around the clock, giving it a major edge over variable renewable energy forms like wind and solar power.

The potential is massive. A report from the Rhodium Group estimates that geothermal energy could meet up to 64 percent of data center energy demand growth by the early 2030s.

Indeed, the AI boom may be just the extenuating circumstance that the sector needs to finally make it out of testing grounds and into the broader economy, as skyrocketing energy demand projections and associated greenhouse gas emissions force the public and private sector alike to seriously consider energy alternatives that had previously existed at the underfunded fringes of research and development.

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”

The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process,” he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.

“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.

“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.

But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe’s ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.

“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”

Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

DENVER — A massive bill that would change how the federal government considers environmental impacts when issuing permits for oil and gas drilling, mining and other industrial activity on public lands is being pushed through Congress amid criticism from environmentalists and Native Americans who say it would undo years of preservation and conservation work.

Advocates for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act say it would speed the nation’s transition to renewable energy by cutting red tape and would strengthen the economy by allowing companies to more quickly expand production through faster permitting. But opponents called the bill a “Trojan horse” that would also undermine the nation’s bedrock environmental protection laws, lock in controversial oil and gas projects and limit judges’ ability to intervene in projects they find violate environmental law.

“It may help some renewable energy projects move forward, but it also accelerates mining, it accelerates drilling, it will accelerate building pipelines,” Ellie Andrews, climate solutions advocate at Environment Colorado, said Wednesday at a gathering of opponents of the bill in downtown Denver.

The Senate late Thursday night voted 62-33 to pass the bill — known as BAAJA — and it will now be heard in the House. Colorado’s two Democratic senators were split on the bill, which was first introduced Sept. 30. Senators from both parties sponsored the bill, but the final vote was largely along party lines. Sen. Michael Bennet voted against the bill while Sen. John Hickenlooper joined 15 other Democrats who voted in its favor.

The business sector, including the Colorado Oil and Gas Association, the American Petroleum Institute Colorado and the Denver Chamber of Commerce, supports the bill, saying projects now are stymied by lengthy reviews, duplicative processes, unpredictable timelines and litigation. All of that red tape causes projects to be more expensive, reduces investment and delays progress.

“It takes way too long and costs way too much to build anything in our country today,” said Lynn Granger, president of the Colorado Oil and Gas Association . “That’s hurting our competitiveness.”

Heidi McIntosh, managing attorney at Earthjustice’s Rocky Mountain office in Denver, criticized the speed with which a Republican majority is trying to push the bill through the legislative process before the balance of power shifts in January. The bill would roll back measures established decades ago to protect air, water, wildlife and public lands, she said.

“This is a hugely consequential bill and it would basically allow this administration to move forward with all kinds of permits for data centers, oil and gas drilling and mining. Any kind of permitting would be exempt from many federal laws,” McIntosh said. “You would have a two-year period where the Trump administration and industry will have a smash-and-grab for public resources.”

If there are problems with the permitting system, there are other ways to amend it without erasing decades of environmental law and progress, she said.

“The environmental community would be glad to work with Congress on it,” McIntosh said.

What does the bill do?

The nearly 500-page bill aims to speed permitting by making changes to a swath of environmental regulations, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. While each law is different, they all generally require studies of a project’s potential impact before it can move forward and they create processes for public input.

The changes would apply to all large infrastructure projects, including highways, oil and gas development, solar and wind farms, dams and transmission lines.

The bill is packed with changes, including:

—Require utilities to upgrade transmission lines and reduce the time needed to construct new transmission lines – changes proponents of the bill say are critical for advancing clean energy and lowering utility costs

—Require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to create rules so that data centers pay their own way and do not shift costs to other ratepayers

—Prevent federal agencies from canceling or changing project permits once they are issued

—Restricts courts from invalidating a project permit even when a judge finds it violated federal permitting law and requires judges to allow projects to move forward even while they are facing legal challenges or a judge finds they violated law

—Relax protections for wetlands and waterways and extend the amount of time an entity can take to fix water pollution from five to 10 years.

—Eliminate required tribal participation in determining how projects impact reservations and other sacred land

Now that the Senate has passed the bill, environmental groups and business interests will begin making their cases to House members.

Ean Tafoya, state programs director for GreenLatinos, said he had urged Hickenlooper to oppose the bill, but said the senator continued to argue that it will unlock clean energy in the United States. Now that fight turns toward Colorado’s delegation in the House.

“It’s a green-washing bill,” Tafoya said. “The deal is no good. What I told him is this is going to shackle us to more fossil fuel energy.”

Hickenlooper’s office declined an interview with The Denver Post but issued a statement reiterating his support after the bill passed Thursday night.

“Bipartisan bills like this are rare,” Hickenlooper said in the statement. “Where we’ve landed isn’t perfection. But it is progress toward delivering on our promise to bring down prices, hold Big Tech accountable, and stop the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. Our work with Tribal Nations and environmental groups doesn’t end with today’s vote. We’ll keep pushing to address their concerns.”

How would it impact the energy sector?

Kevin Rennert, a fellow and director of the energy infrastructure advancement program at Resources for the Future , said the bill would make it easier to build transmission lines and energy infrastructure, which would in turn boost renewable energy.

He offered the theoretical example of a wind farm producing electricity and how a more robust, long-distance grid would push that electricity to cities that otherwise would not have access.

In the long run, that would improve reliability and encourage more renewable energy production, he said.

“You get more clean energy online sooner than if you don’t have the policy,” he said.

Rennert’s nonprofit analyzes the economic impact of energy policies through a model created at the National Laboratory of the Rockies in Golden.

“One way to think about this bill is that it’s really a down payment on future climate policy,” Rennert said. “All of the analyses show a future with far lower emissions than there are today with an expanded transmission grid.”

How would it impact Colorado’s water and public land?

The bill would make it more difficult to halt or undo development on the 24 million acres of federal public land in Colorado.

The Bureau of Land Management in June held the largest oil and gas lease sale in Colorado in more than a decade, and more large-scale leases are planned, according to a letter sent to the state’s congressional delegation by 29 Colorado organizations opposing the bill.

“In short, BAAJA could decimate the protection of Colorado’s cherished and irreplaceable public lands and leave Tribal nations and the public with no way to stop the damage,” according to the letter written by the coalition, which includes the Center for Biological Diversity, the Colorado Mountain Club, Defenders of Wildlife, the Endangered Species Coalition and Wilderness Workshop.

Environmental groups point to the Roan Plateau outside of Rifle as a prime example of a site that could be impacted by BAAJA.

In 2014, conservationists, the Bureau of Land Management and an oil and gas company agreed on a settlement that protected the top of the plateau from drilling and development. The settlement followed years of protest and litigation after the agency in 2008 auctioned off lease parcels on the plateau, which offers critical habitat for large deer and elk herds and pristine streams where rare native trout spawn.

But this December, the BLM plans to again offer 4,600 acres on top of the plateau for leases that will last at least 10 years. If passed, BAAJA would make it nearly impossible to reverse those leases or change their conditions, said Taylor Luneau, Colorado conservation manager at The Wilderness Society.

BAAJA also makes changes to the Clean Water Act, but legislation Colorado lawmakers passed in 2024 would render those changes moot, said Stu Gillespie, a Denver-based staff attorney at Earthjustice who worked on the Colorado law.

The Colorado law followed a U.S. Supreme Court decision that weakened the scope of the Clean Water Act. Now, it serves as a pre-emptive defense to further changes, he said.

“We don’t have to follow Congress off the cliff,” Gillespie said.

How would it impact tribal lands?

In 2021, Xcel Energy chose a route for its new Colorado Power Pathway transmission project that would have placed towers and electrical lines close to the Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site.

The tribes, whose ancestors were killed in the November 1864 massacre, objected, said Norma Gourneau, a Sand Creek Massacre Foundation board member and member of the Northern Cheyenne tribe in Montana.

The foundation, along with members of the Northern Cheyenne, Northern Arapaho and Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes were able to meet with Xcel executives and convince them to move their towers, she said.

Under the BAAJA, there would not be an obligation for Xcel or another utility company to do so, Gourneau said.

“It wasn’t even that far for them to move those so we could protect Sand Creek,” Gourneau said. “But that was something we had to fight for.

“We just want a seat at the table and to be able to participate in this dialogue. That’s why we are fighting so hard to keep those provisions. Leave them alone.”

An amendment added in the Senate that would have kept those tribal protections intact failed, much to the disappointment of Colorado’s tribal leaders, said Ernest House Jr., director for the Center for Tribal and Indigenous Engagement at the Keystone Policy Center .

Colorado’s two federally recognized tribes and the 50 historic tribes have developed a good working relationship on various projects such as agreeing on locations for wildlife overpasses , which allow elk and other animals to safely migrate across busy highways.

“It’s important for the Colorado delegation to know where our tribes stand,” House said. “It’s not just what people see as cultural Native American concerns, but also it’s impacts issues like clean water and wildfires.”

How would it impact historic preservation?

The bill also makes broader changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires evaluation of potential historic value in an area where a project is proposed. The changes limits public comment opportunities and narrows what kind of projects must perform a review under the law.

But the law is not the bottleneck that halts or slows down projects, said Jay Homstad, senior director of preservation advocacy at Historic Denver. Nearly all reviews under the law find no harm to historic places and are completed in about two weeks, he said. Instead, staffing shortages at federal agencies and delayed project consultation are the bottlenecks in the approval system, he said.

“The Senate permitting bill fixes none of that,” he said. “Instead, it just removes the public from the room.”

How would it impact the oil and gas industry?

Colorado’s Western Slope is rich in natural resources, including a deposit of about 200 years worth of natural gas, Granger said.

That natural gas is in demand as artificial intelligence grows and more data centers are needed to power it, she said.

“Colorado has a unique opportunity and we would love to see those natural resources being produced that could help our state but also help our nation,” she said.

Oil and gas businesses are ready to invest in Colorado, which would add jobs and tax revenue to the state, Granger said.

A letter written in support of the bill by the American Petroleum Institute and signed by four Colorado business groups, including the Denver Chamber echoed that statement.

“Businesses are prepared to invest billions of dollars in projects across the country, but investment requires predictable permitting timelines and confidence that final agency decisions will withstand judicial review,” the letter said. “A more efficient and durable permitting system can enable resources to move from production regions to homes, businesses, manufacturers, and global markets more reliably and efficiently, helping meet demand and affordability.”

text:
WEST TERRE HAUTE, Ind. — Growmark Inc. has made a minority equity investment in Wabash Valley Resources, facilitating the first advance under the company’s U.S. Department of Energy loan and supporting construction of its fertilizer facility in West Terre Haute.

The facility is designed to produce 500,000 metric tons of anhydrous ammonia annually, creating a major new domestic fertilizer source for farmers across the eastern Corn Belt. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2029.

“Our investment in Wabash Valley Resources will bring a new, independent source of ammonia closer to the farmers and cooperatives that depend on it,” said Mark Orr, CEO of Growmark. “It’s a long-term investment in reliable domestic supply and the competitiveness of our member-owners.”

Growmark’s participation reflects the strategic importance of expanding fertilizer production near the communities it serves.

As an agricultural cooperative with extensive crop nutrient and logistics operations, Growmark brings a direct understanding of farmers’ needs and the importance of reliable supply throughout the growing season.

Its investment in Wabash Valley Resources connects those priorities with the development of new domestic manufacturing capacity.

“Growmark’s investment is a pivotal milestone for WVR and a strong vote of confidence in independent ammonia production,” said Dan Williams, WVR’s CEO.

“With this investment, we move closer to turning years of development into a dependable source of American-made fertilizer. We thank the U.S. Department of Energy and its Office of Energy Dominance Financing for helping bring this transaction to fruition.

“Our focus now is on building the facility safely and delivering a dependable supply of American-made fertilizer to the farmers who feed our country.”

title: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels - WRAL
authors: SUZAN FRASER, SETH BORENSTEIN, ANTON L. DELGADO and SIBI ARASU — Associated Press, SUZAN FRASER, SETH BORENSTEIN, ANTON L. DELGADO, SIBI ARASU — Associated Press

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks fizzled out Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable. Nations' negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word “disappointing” to characterize the discussions.

Though the talks, called COP31, failed to reach a main agreement, known as a cover decision, the meeting had already made progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night, after running more than 50 hours overtime at the resort town of Antalya.

This all happened as global warming accelerates with ever-worsening heat waves, floods, storms and droughts. The U.N. said it is now inevitable that the world will soon blow past the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. And there is also a global energy shock due to the war in Iran. On top of that, a strong El Niño amplifies human-caused warming and causes more weather disasters.

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

Upset youth representative Oumnia Anfer told the negotiators “you have let us down.”

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn’t mention fossil fuels. A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks.

Impasses over draft agreements

Previously, fossil fuels went unmentioned in COP final decisions for more than 25 years, said Alden Meyer, with the think tank E3G. Then, three years ago in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai agreement in its entirety, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

“Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis,” said Guterres. “The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks and undermining energy security. We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it.”

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would undermine efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of COP31 is an outrage — it is outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels," said former U.S. Vice President Al Gore.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations.

Bowen said the Dubai agreement's explicit call to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

Other issues left unresolved

Other climate issues weren’t settled, and many were deferred to next year’s negotiations in Ethiopia. They include details on transitioning away from fossil fuels, financial help for poorer nations to adapt to the warming world and action on gender and climate.

For this year's negotiations, Turkey made global electrification its signature issue. A proposal introduced separately from the main agreement calls for countries to increase the share of electricity in total final energy consumption from about 21% today to 35% by 2035. This would require nations to commit to measures such as switching transportation — including cars, trucks and planes — from fossil fuels to electricity and using electricity instead of coal to make industrial products. Nearly 100 nations signed up for this goal as part of the separate pledge.

Meyer, with E3G, also hailed progress on global adaptation goals and on a program that helps countries achieve their emissions-cutting goals fairly.

In negotiations over the main agreement, the final proposal was distributed after 3 a.m. and negotiators had little time to register their objections. Many observers and countries blamed the two-headed leadership of Turkey and Australia for the failure to reach an overarching agreement.

Speaking at the meeting, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, said, “With all due respect, Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter.” Kurum later publicly apologized.

Confusion ensued at the meeting. Kurum was caught on a hot mic telling U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell “to sit down,” as Stiell tried to advise him on proceedings onstage.

Earlier this week, Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and needed to be reformed.

Manuel Pulgar-Vidal, president of COP20 and now climate energy lead at the World Wildlife Fund, said “COP31 left too much undone.”

“Too many once again shied away from the toughest decisions, including how to turn their commitment to transition away from fossil fuels into real action," he said. "The climate will not wait for governments to find their courage.”

Earlier this year, the United Nations Environment Program announced that the world will blow past the Paris Agreement temperature threshold of limiting long-term warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial times. The goal should now be to limit how much the world exceeds that threshold and then somehow come back down using systems to suck carbon out of the air, U.N. officials said.

The world is heading for between 2.7 C and 3 C (between 4.9 F and 5.4 F) of warming by the end of the century, scientists estimate. October 2026 had the largest temperature increase above preindustrial temperatures of any month on record at 1.8 C (3.2 F), according to Berkeley Earth, which said there’s a 97% chance that 2026 will end up as the warmest year on record. Friday saw the most above normal temperature on record, according to the European climate monitor Copernicus.

“Mother Nature decided to comment on the collapse of #COP31 climate negotiations in failure by setting a new record,” University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann said on X.

___

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland; Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

Commenting on the conclusion of COP31, Climate Analytics's CEO Bill Hare said:

“The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

“Countries committed to a safer future drew a line in the sand and refused to sign up to a document that did not include any reference to phasing out fossil fuels yet did include a target for massive amounts of carbon capture and storage. That was clearly unacceptable, and countries that refused to accept it were right to do so.

“What the non-agreement here means for the COP process will be worked out in the coming few months, but three lessons are already clear.

"The second is that if the world is to move forward with a transition away from fossil fuels, many countries need to come prepared to push back against Saudi Arabia. This country has been the most implacable opponent of climate action for over 30 years and has had an outsize influence on three of the last five COPs - Sharm El Sheikh, Baku and now Antalya - and the international community has to stop that happening again.

"Thirdly, with momentum building for countries to compile fossil fuel transition roadmaps, many more need to join this in 2027 so that by the COP in Ethiopia a large number of countries have roadmaps prepared or underway, to spur a global transition away from fossil fuels.”

text:
America's power grid faces a roadblock that threatens to put a damper on getting generated power into people’s homes and to new data centers, a new study has warned.

Researchers at Johns Hopkins University found that supplies of transformers and other critical grid equipment could fall well behind demand as early as 2027.

The study went on to forecast there could be acute shortages hitting the U.S. by 2030. Newsweek has approached the Department of Energy for comment on the report by email.

Read More on News

Why It Matters

A shortfall in the critical equipment could slow the rollout of new power plants, renewable energy projects, electric vehicle infrastructure and AI data centers.

Without enough transformers, new sources of electricity would be forced to wait to be connected to the grid.

"This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won't be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid," lead author Yury Dvorkin said in a statement. "When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry."

Dvorkin added that consumers are likely to feel the effects of the infrastructure bottlenecks through higher electric bills and more frequent power outages.

He told Newsweek: "Everyday Americans will feel the transformer shortages on their skin in two places. First, in their electricity bill and, second, indirectly by lower reliability of their power supply. In other words, they will pay more and get less, and potentially far more and far less if current expectations for load growth hold."

Many transformers already in service are decades old and approaching the end of their operational lives. Dvorkin continued: "Transformers are invisible for everyday consumers, but every unit of electricity consumed by anyone passes through several transformers on its way from where it is produced to where it is consumed.

"Electricity from renewables and battery storage also passes through converters. When there aren't enough transformers or converters to go around, utilities have to outbid other buyers to get them, including well-funded data center developers who can pay a premium for speed. This premium becomes part of the cost of delivering power, and in the end it shows up on electricity bills.

"What is important to highlight is that consumers get hit twice. Power plants need transformers to connect to the grid too, so producing electricity gets more expensive at the same time as delivering it. Consumers end up paying for both."

What are Transformers?

Transformers and converters are among the most important pieces of energy infrastructure in the country helping move electricity across transmission networks and help deliver power safely to homes and businesses.

One issue, the research published in Cell Reports Sustainability highlights, is that transformers are difficult to replace.

Large transformers often require years to manufacture because they are typically custom-built and are made using vast quantities of steel, copper and other materials.

According to the study, lead times have risen from around six months roughly four years ago to more than two years today.

Under a high-demand scenario, the U.S. could face a transformer shortfall of nearly 15 percent by 2030.

Other key pieces of grid equipment could face shortages of up to 30 percent.

The shortfall could create a roadblock for the U.S. which has seen demand for power rising faster than it has in decades–with demand projected to increase by 21 percent by 2030.

"By 2030, we're likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth," Dvorkin said.

AI Boom and Supply Chain Strain

As much as two-thirds of all the expected equipment shortages will be fueled by data centers, according to researchers.

The facilities, which power artificial intelligence systems, consume large amounts of electricity–some of the larger ones using up as much as a small country, one Harvard Study. said

Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has projected that data centers could consume nearly 12 percent of all U.S. electricity by 2030.

Grid operators and utilities have issued similar warnings amid concern the infrastructure needed to move that power around the country is lacking.

However, Dvorkin notes that international trade disruptions could mean greater shortfalls.

Transformer construction relies on materials such as copper, steel and nickel, which the U.S. relies on international partners to obtain.

The researchers concluded by saying policymakers and utilities must plan for equipment shortages years in advance as without intervention, infrastructure could become a barrier to electricity supply.

Dvorkin said: "The final point to make is that it is not only new equipment. In a stretched market, keeping existing transformers running costs more as well: parts, repairs and maintenance all go up. This industry runs on thin margins, so every one of those increases gets passed down on consumers. All these there points contribute to the cost.

"At the same time, unsatisfied demand for transformers and converters may cause problems with reliability. When electricity demand grows fast (e.g., due to data centers), it puts more stress on equipment, and existing transformers and converters wear out sooner.

"Old transformers pushed past their service life fail more often, replacement lead times have quadrupled since 2022 to more than two years, and extreme weather adds stress the system can't absorb. That means more frequent and potentially longer power outages."

text:
A new report from Ember Energy shows the enormous cost-saving potential of wind energy. While solar power and battery storage have taken off on a global level, wind power has been slower to expand. But according to the new report from the prominent energy think tank, this is a major missed opportunity for energy security, emissions goals, and economic returns.

“Solar and batteries can already deliver firm power at a competitive cost across much of the world,” reads the report, titled Harnessing the Winds. “Adding wind makes it cheaper still for the vast majority of the world, because wind and solar produce at different times of day and in different seasons,” Ember goes on to say. “Matching the different cycles of solar and wind eases the path to firm renewables.”

More specifically, Ember’s analysis finds that 90 percent of electricity demand can be met at a considerably lower cost when wind power is employed as a complement to solar and batteries on overcast days and winter days with short daylight hours. Under this scenario, the median cost per megawatt hour falls by more than 18 percent, from $105 to $86. The remaining 10 percent of electricity that these three clean energy sources could not meet would be provided by gas or diesel.

Moreover, ramping up wind energy to support solar power and battery storage systems would bring much-needed diversity to the clean energy mix, thereby improving energy security and grid resilience. According to reporting from nonpartisan global news outlet Semafor, the increased deployment of wind energy “diminishes the risk of a solar and wind lull striking at the same time — a weather phenomenon often described by the German term Dunkelflaute, which refers to a dark and windless period.”

ADVERTISEMENT

However, these benefits would not be equal for all countries and all climates. For example, the increased usage of wind power would have little impact on energy costs around the equator, where seasonal fluctuations in solar power production are not a problem like they are toward the poles, where winter days can seriously impact output. And in cash-strapped parts of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa, deploying wind energy remains a prohibitively costly endeavor.

However, costs of wind power deployment will likely continue to drop as technologies advance, supply chains become more sophisticated, and economies of scale make their mark. The technology behind wind turbines and wind power generation is slowly improving, with potentially disruptive ramifications for efficiency and efficacy of wind farms, allowing developers to get more bang per buck.

Part of the reason that wind power has been slower to take off than solar and batteries is that wind turbines have improved at a slower rate than those technologies. This is because testing new models presents a major challenge, as it’s nearly impossible to conduct a controlled experiment in constantly changing atmospheric conditions, and wind turbines aren’t going to fit inside any lab.

But a new breakthrough from MIT could change all that, potentially turbocharging wind power research and development in coming years. A new report from MIT News proclaims that “researchers closed the gap between experiments in the field and the lab by using a wind tunnel that features high pressurization to simulate the flow physics in the atmosphere.” This will allow researchers to perform much more sophisticated tests that can more closely approximate real-world conditions.

“The immediate impact of this study is that we’ve now both improved and validated models that go into wind turbine control protocols for existing farms,” Michael Howland, MIT’s Jeffrey Cheah Career Development Professor, said of the study, newly published in PNAS Nexus. “The bigger, medium-term impact, with a much larger upside, is this new experimental paradigm to rapidly prototype, validate simulation models, and test hypotheses about better designs and control strategies much faster than has been possible before.”

title: DOE Awards $117M for Clean Steel and Minerals - CASRAI
authors: Gabriel Nieves Castro, CASRAI Editorial Board
description: The DOE awarded $117 million across 56 projects for clean steelmaking and critical minerals, including a $2 million UNR grant for iron ore beneficiation.
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation announced $117 million across 56 projects nationwide to modernize key industrial sectors, including a $2,092,583 federal research award to the University of Nevada, Reno to pioneer energy-efficient iron ore beneficiation for clean steelmaking. The multi-institution project addresses critical mineral supply bottlenecks in direct-reduction ironmaking, requiring university sponsored programs offices to administer strict mandatory matching cost-share commitments, multi-party subrecipient agreements, and industry materials partnerships.

On September 1, 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation announced $117 million to strengthen America’s industrial sector , funding 56 projects across key manufacturing domains. Executed through the DOE Industrial Technologies Office, the selections target energy and cost-saving innovations to enhance domestic industrial competitiveness, lower commodity production costs, and reduce high-temperature heating and wastewater treatment burdens.

As detailed in the University of Nevada, Reno announcement of its $2 million clean steel award , researchers at UNR secured $2,092,583 under federal project number EE0011821. The three-year initiative, titled “Energy Efficient Comminution and Advanced Separation Technology for the Production of Direct Reduction (DR) Grade High-Quality Iron Ores,” develops a novel mineral beneficiation flowsheet to transform domestic low-grade hematite deposits into direct-reduction-grade iron ore.

Materials Science and Engineering Professor Mano Misra leads the project as principal investigator. He is supported by co-investigators Pradeep Menezes, professor of mechanical engineering, and Mostafa Khodakarami, assistant professor of metallurgical engineering, collaborating with the University of Utah alongside graduate and postdoctoral researchers.

Comminution—the industrial crushing and grinding of ore—accounts for substantial electricity consumption in mineral processing. The UNR flowsheet combines artificial intelligence optical sorting with high-pressure grinding rolls (HPGR) to achieve fracture size reduction while significantly cutting power demands. Subsequent beneficiation utilizes biotechnological flocculation and advanced flotation to remove non-valuable gangue rock, producing iron concentrates containing 67% to 70% iron with less than 2% gangue.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 on iron and steel , domestic apparent consumption of steel mill products reached an estimated 95 million metric tons in 2025. Although domestic mines produced 38 million metric tons of usable iron ore, existing processing flowsheets are largely optimized for traditional blast furnaces rather than low-carbon direct reduction facilities.

The table below details selected university-led projects funded under Topic Area 2 (Iron and Steel: Low Grade Ore Recovery) within the $117 million federal portfolio.

Primary steelmaking accounts for roughly 7% to 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions because traditional blast furnaces rely on metallurgical coal to chemically reduce iron oxides. The primary low-carbon alternative pairs Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) shafts with Electric Arc Furnaces (EAF). As highlighted in Canary Media reporting on direct reduced iron technology , utilizing DRI with clean electricity and hydrogen offers the clearest technical route to deep industrial emissions reductions.

Direct reduction processes, however, operate in the solid state without melting the ore, meaning all gangue minerals present in the feedstock carry over into the sponge iron. Consequently, DRI plants demand high-purity feedstocks with at least 67% iron content. Because standard U.S. taconite and hematite ores typically yield lower natural grades, advanced mineral processing is essential to prevent international supply dependence. In structuring such research partnerships, university administrators evaluate whether awards operate under standard federal grants or cooperative agreements, following principles established in grant vs contract vs cooperative agreement guidelines.

DOE Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson underscored the commercial and security goals of the program: “DOE is committed to funding innovation that positions American industry at the forefront of the global marketplace. These projects will deliver affordable, market-ready solutions that strengthen America’s energy security and support job creation and economic growth nationwide.”

UNR College of Engineering Dean Tom Weller affirmed the regional importance of the grant: “Nevada Engineering is committed to research that supports regional and national needs. Dr. Misra’s project is an example of UNR research contributing to a key national priority.”

Principal Investigator Mano Misra explained the operational mechanics of the research: “The direct reduction iron process requires extremely clean and high-quality iron-bearing ores. The process utilizes several new and existing technologies to make the clean product. These steps involve AI-enabled optical sorting, fracture mechanics using high-pressure grinding rolls and size reduction to decrease the energy consumption, followed by biotechnological flocculation and advanced flotation.”

Misra added that domestic steelmakers will provide materials: “We are working with the steel companies to use the technology for making clean steel using direct reduction iron. Steel companies will supply the raw materials and work with UNR researchers during the project implementation.”

The execution of DOE industrial decarbonization awards establishes several administrative priorities for university research operations:

Under the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPAct Section 988), applied research awards from the DOE Industrial Technologies Office typically require a 20% non-federal matching commitment. Sponsored programs offices must establish auditable accounting structures to verify third-party in-kind valuations, industry equipment donations, and unrecovered indirect costs under cost share (mandatory) rules, ensuring all contributions meet 2 CFR 200.306 documentation standards.

Because projects involve academic co-investigators and commercial materials suppliers, sponsored programs staff must establish precise partner designations under subrecipient vs contractor vs vendor classifications. Subawards to partner universities like the University of Utah require formal risk assessments, invoicing verification, and active monitoring per federal subrecipient monitoring mandates.

Working with domestic steelmakers supplying raw ore requires comprehensive Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs) and data protection protocols. University technology transfer teams must protect university background IP while defining ownership rights for newly synthesized microbial flocculants, separation flowsheets, and proprietary process software.

Pilot-scale comminution and bio-beneficiation introduce unique physical and biological hazard profiles. Campus EH&S departments must establish mechanical safety procedures, dust suppression systems for high-pressure grinding equipment, and containment protocols for microbial cultures deployed in wet separation tanks.

The three-year UNR award runs through federal fiscal years 2026 to 2029. Year one focuses on optical sensor calibration, baseline hematite ore characterization, and high-pressure roll comminution testing. Year two shifts to microbial flocculation kinetics and flotation testing at UNR and the University of Utah. The final project year will execute continuous pilot-scale beneficiation on commercial ores provided by industrial steelmakers, targeting direct-reduction hematite purity exceeding 67% iron prior to DOE stage-gate evaluations.
