text:
COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.

The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.

Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them.

"We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuel, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU in Antalya. "And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

The EU joined a group of smaller nations facing heightened threats of climate extremes and challenged oil producers, like Saudi Arabia, that staunchly rejected their views. The finale came after days of tense discussions over some of the core topics at issue during the summit, including whether to establish new rules and goals around transitioning away from coal, oil and natural gas in favor of renewable energy.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environmental minister, said in televised comments from Antalya on Sunday that a draft had not been adopted due to a lack of consensus. The conference rules require unanimous agreement to reach a deal, so even a single nation's dissent can derail the process.

"We have always emphasized that this process is one that respects the will of the parties. We did everything we could," Kurum said. "In the end, we did not impose this text on anyone. We did not pressure anyone with a take-it-or-leave-it approach. There are parties in the hall that oppose this text, and we see that there is no agreement on it. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted."

Australia's climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, who shared the COP31 presidency with Kurum as Turkey and Australia jointly hosted this year's summit, said Sunday that talks broke down because of "unbridgeable red lines" and added that "the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory," reported CBS partner BBC News.

On Friday, the scheduled final day of the conference, a coalition led by France and Panama and including countries from Europe, Africa, Latin America and the Pacific rejected the latest draft agreement as too weak, according to the U.N. The group demanded explicit language on fossil fuels and stronger commitments on climate finance.

"We cannot continue to be held hostage by petroleum producers," said Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, at a news conference last week. He also vowed that Panama would formally object to any deal omitting issues related to fossil fuels.

An initial draft of negotiators' agreement had called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels," a recurring goal at these summits, and urged an end to inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. It also resolved to bring warming back below 1.5 degrees as early as possible this century. But that language was gone days later, reflecting deep divisions over timelines and financing.

Later drafts still did not contain language about fossil fuels, although they did include proposed targets to capture billions of tons of carbon dioxide annually from the atmosphere by 2035, using technology that critics have said distracts from the need to cut fossil fuel use. They also called for electricity to supply more than a third of the world's energy by the same deadline, alongside goals around renewable energy and energy efficiency.

Negotiators had expressed "deep concern" in drafted text over global warming, which at its peak is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees. They also reaffirmed the need "for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions," warning that every increment of additional warming will increase the frequency and intensity of climate-related loss and damage. If current international climate plans were fully implemented, they noted, the world would be on track for just over 2.5 degrees of warming, down from projections of more than 4 degrees before the Paris accord.

The COP31 summit unfolded in a year marked by deadly disasters, record heat, destructive wildfires, tumultuous surf and other anomalies, which meteorologists have largely tied to a powerful El Niño. Scientists say its effects are amplified by climate change.

Speaking in Antalya last week, Guterres urged governments to move away from fossil fuels, triple adaptation funding by 2035 and tax fossil fuel companies' windfall profits to help vulnerable nations recover from disasters. "Polluters must pay," he said. At a press conference two days later, he linked the climate crisis to deeper social and political instability.

"You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," Guterres said. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause the crisis suffer first and worst."

Some environmental advocates felt the conference proposals didn't go far enough to meet the needs of communities that are already facing real consequences of the climate crisis.

Ellen Dorsey, named this month to the TIME100 climate list, told CBS News after leaving Antalya over the weekend that she hadn't expected substantial action from COP31, despite clear signs of urgency.

"The time for simply talking about phasing out fossil fuels is over. Governments need to act," Dorsey told CBS News. "That means no fossil fuel expansion, an end to fossil fuel subsidies, and an equitable phaseout that protects workers and communities."

Dorsey said fossil fuel lobbying has grown over the past decade, as has the presence of industry interests in national delegations at U.N. climate talks, including this one. Still, she sees promise in efforts pushing back, from grassroots movements to the Santa Marta process, a coalition using diplomacy to drive a transition away from coal, oil and gas.

"Momentum is building beyond the negotiations," said Dorsey, who called this "a historic inflection point" for climate policy. "The opportunity for real systemic change is here."

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.

The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions.

After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.

The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."

This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.

Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.

"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."

NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.

text:
A team led by MIT researchers has estimated that electricity demand from U.S. data centers added air pollution tied to about 650 premature deaths in 2023, with some of the highest per-person rates in Midwestern states far from the biggest data center hubs, according to a paper in Environmental Research Letters and an MIT release.

The estimate covers only power that data centers draw from the grid. The team assumed the facilities run around the clock, then simulated which power plants ramp up hour by hour to meet that demand. Many earlier studies used average grid emissions instead, the release said.

Two pollutants drive the toll: fine particulate matter (PM2.5), airborne particles small enough to reach deep into the lungs, and ground-level ozone, or smog. MIT said PM2.5 can cause heart attacks, stroke and lung disease. Of the 650 deaths, 513 were tied to PM2.5 and 137 to ozone, according to the paper.

Tracing demand to power plants

Using a grid model, the team compared hourly electricity output with and without data center demand, according to the paper. That gave nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide emissions for each power plant. A chemical transport model, which simulates how pollutants form and travel through the atmosphere, then estimated changes in PM2.5 and ozone.

The researchers converted those changes into deaths using population health research linking pollution to mortality. Data centers accounted for 3.8 percent of U.S. electricity generation but 5.3 percent of power-sector air pollution deaths, the paper said.

Virginia and Texas hosted the largest loads, but per-person death rates there were roughly half those in most Midwestern states, the release said. Iowa and Nebraska ranked among the highest, with 6.5 deaths per million people in Nebraska, the paper said. Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri and Arkansas, which have little data center load, also showed elevated rates. Noelle Selin, an MIT professor and the study's senior author, said the impacts are "very widespread across a large region."

Why the Midwest bears more

MIT's account suggests generators answering Virginia's added demand are likely in the Ohio Valley, where older coal and gas plants emit more. The paper tied Iowa and Nebraska's rates to high-emitting coal-fired units and ammonia-rich air.

The 650 figure is a modeled estimate, not a count of deaths. Its 95 percent confidence range, 559 to 740, reflects only uncertainty in the health calculation, not in the emissions or air-quality modeling. The model counts grid power only, assumes flat hourly demand and excludes backup generators, so the authors say it likely understates impacts near large facilities. Its 31-mile (50-kilometer) grid may miss local effects. Estimates also vary: the paper cites another team's figure of about 401 deaths for 2023, and an earlier projection put the toll near 1,300 a year by 2030.

The team wants to study on-site generation, where data centers add their own power plants, such as the gas-fired systems one vendor now markets.

The study appeared Nov. 19 in Environmental Research Letters.

text:
The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it.

That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too.

The grid is years behind demand

Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely.

Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom.

Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years.

The industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building new infrastructure.”

Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on.

Voters are pushing back on power bills

Public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults.

Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C.

A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%.

Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill.

Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.”

“The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms.

Big Tech is getting into the power business

Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.”

Some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations.

President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the new-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding.

On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S.

SpaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune.

It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment.

The next tests come quickly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more.

While those buildouts are planned, none are promised.

text:
PAGO PAGO, American Samoa -- Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka sat in the shallows at Fatumafuti Beach as her 4-year-old daughter, Erhys, splashed through the clear water on a Little Mermaid kickboard. Below, iridescent blue and rainbow-streaked fish wove through fields of coral.

It was a rare moment of calm before a long journey. Soon, Suluai-Mahuka would travel from American Samoa to California to protest the Trump administration's efforts to lease areas near her island for deep-sea mining. She planned to pack a bottle of seawater that would give members of the Samoan diaspora a chance to touch and connect with the waters she's fighting to protect.

The administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor. The first waters it is targeting are some of the most pristine areas of the Pacific Ocean near American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, two U.S. territories thousands of miles from where decisions for their islands are being made.

Despite its status as an experimental and controversial industry, deep-sea mining has become a pillar of President Donald Trump's campaign to expand U.S. control over minerals critical to the technology and defense industries. In April last year, the president directed his administration to expedite the search for those metals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. Auctions for the seabed near Virginia and Alaska could take place next year, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

The minerals companies are after include nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper -- useful to making everything from smartphones to electric vehicles -- that have concentrated over millions of years along the ocean floor and the volcanic crusts of seamounts. It's unclear how abundant they are near American Samoa and the Northern Marianas.

In granting a lease, the U.S. would be joining a handful of other countries that have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals. Most mining techniques involve deploying underwater vehicles thousands of feet deep to vacuum up rocks and sediment from the ocean floor. Under most proposals, those rocks are filtered and returned to a mining ship, with unwanted debris released back into the ocean.

Suluai-Mahuka and other opponents have tried to stall the auctions of the nearby ocean, rallying public comments criticizing the move. They are prepared to work against the obstacles that come with living in territories dependent on federal aid, where residents have neither a voting representative in Congress nor the right to vote for president.

"When they ask us for public comments, it always feels like we're just screaming at a moving train," said David Cabrera, who leads a group seeking to revive Indigenous forms of fishing in Saipan, the main island of the Northern Marianas.

Located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and Australia, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are two separate chains of volcanic islands that both endured occupations by colonial powers before becoming U.S. territories.

Despite economic challenges and a diaspora that is slowly shrinking their populations of 50,000 people, the territories have kept alive traditions that tie them to the ocean and remain sacred to the Indigenous peoples who first made the region's islands home.

The U.S. waters surrounding American Samoa include Rose Atoll, an uninhabited island named for the pinkish hue of its coral reefs that is an important habitat for seabirds. The U.S. waters around the Northern Marianas include parts of the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on earth. Both are protected by marine monuments that now border the proposed mining areas.

If a lease is granted, it will be difficult to undo under a different administration, said former Bureau of Ocean Energy Management Director Elizabeth Klein. The government would have to justify the cancellation at a hearing and face potential litigation.

In response to the mounting opposition, the newly formed Marine Minerals Administration has emphasized that the upcoming auctions will only grant companies the right to take initial steps to explore for seafloor minerals. Any testing or commercial mining proposals will go through further public comment and a more intensive environmental review.

"It's cold comfort," said Zeno Camacho Deleon Guerrero Jr., a resident of the Northern Mariana Islands and a board member of the Micronesia Climate Change Alliance, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region's environment and people. "Once you find what you want, you're going to get it. You're going to start mining."

American Samoans fear irreparable losses to their way of life

The first auction for deep-sea mining - in waters near American Samoa - was scheduled to take place Thursday in the Southern California city of Thousand Oaks.

Suluai-Mahuka had decided to be in California, despite the long hours it would take to get there. She and her team at Finafinau, the environmental group she founded, were working to bring people from across the Pacific community to protest alongside them.

"If these people are going to be selling our ocean, they're going to see our faces when they do these bids," she said.

A legal battle now makes it unclear whether the auction will proceed. On Monday, a judge ruled the government violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to consider the full impacts of a deep-sea mining lease. By Wednesday morning, the Trump administration had yet to delay the auction. Two other lawsuits are pending.

For an opening bid of $3 million, the administration was offering companies the chance to vie for 20-year leases granting them the exclusive right to mine commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. Two areas of the seafloor, each more than 15 million acres in size, were available for bidding.

The administration has proposed another auction for five parcels of the seafloor near the Northern Mariana Islands in December.

Deep-sea mining goes against everything Suluai-Mahuka stands for, she said, and against the Samoan way of life that revolves around the ocean -- whether it's diving among corals, swimming and relaxing, fishing for local delicacies, or the commercial tuna industry that sustains the local economy. All of that, to her, is at risk.

"We would be giving up a piece of ourselves that we cannot get back," she said. Her group, Finafinau, takes its name from the Samoan word for resilience.

In Samoan legend, the world began as only the heavens and the ocean. "The ocean is life. It's sacred to us," said Malouamaua Tuiolosega. "We lose the ocean, we lose life."

Tuiolosega represents the ancient governing council of Manu'a, a district of American Samoa that makes up the closest inhabited areas to where deep-sea mining leases could be granted, about 100 nautical miles from its shores. Populated by just 800 people across three islands, and isolated by infrequent transportation to the capital city of Pago Pago, Manu'a residents depend even more heavily on the environment for survival.

Since long before American Samoa became part of the United States, the council's chiefs have overseen the islands' resources, which they understand are in delicate balance with people.

If more is taken from the islands than is needed to survive, Tuiolosega said, "you violate the relationship and the trust between the people and its resource, and then it disappears."

He sees the same push toward exploiting the oceans behind deep-sea mining as he does the Trump administration's efforts to open up marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean to commercial fishing. The governing council, the Faleula o le Manu'atele, has joined one of the lawsuits against the Trump administration over the upcoming lease sale.

"President Trump recognizes the enormous potential of America's offshore critical minerals to drive technological innovation, economic prosperity, and national security," Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to The Associated Press.

"A lease sale is not a mandate to mine. Any future extraction would require additional environmental review and regulatory approvals, informed by engagement with local communities," Rogers said.

Although no company worldwide has started commercial mining operations in the deep sea, a crop of U.S. startups, buoyed by the president's policies, hopes to soon change that. Some supporters believe deep-sea mining could be an important income stream for American Samoa if it were to become an industry hub.

"If we don't look for some kind of manufacturing process, something that people will buy, we're going to be destitute. We're going to be broke," said John Wasko, executive director of the American Samoa Economic Development Council, a group promoting industry on the islands.

The deep-sea mining startup Impossible Metals, which has signaled interest in the upcoming auction, has offered to share 1% of any future profits with the American Samoan community.

Suluai-Mahuka and others don't buy the promises of jobs and investments.

The leases offered by the Marine Minerals Administration will ask companies to "make every reasonable effort" to hire employees from the territories and support "community well-being," but the regulations don't include any binding requirements or numeric targets.

There is also no guarantee of economic gains. While the federal government would collect the winning bid amount, along with regular rent payments and royalties over the life of the lease, there are no mandates for the government to share earnings from deep-sea mining with local territories or states. That's different from offshore oil and gas drilling, where Gulf states receive 37.5% of revenue.

Questions go unanswered for local government

A major question for local government is whether a deep-sea mining lease will hurt American Samoa's tuna fishery and force the closure of the last remaining cannery. Purse seine and longline fleets supply tuna for the local StarKist plant, with the longline fleet fishing entirely in U.S. waters -- including the areas up for leasing.

Nathan Ilaoa, director of the American Samoa Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, said his agency was hoping for a "more exhaustive" review of the potential impacts to the fishery before the auction. He said he doesn't yet have answers on whether contaminants or sediment plumes from disrupting the ocean floor will alter the tuna's migratory patterns.

"We're extremely concerned that the disappearance of our longline fleet could translate into the cannery leaving American Samoa, which would be an economic disaster for the territory," Ilaoa said.

American Samoa's leadership opposed deep-sea mining when word of company interest started reaching its shores. In 2024, the territory issued a moratorium on deep-sea mining in the waters it controls, which extend from shore out to 3 nautical miles (5.5 kms). But the territory has little say over the activities that take place in federal waters beyond that line.

When the auction was proposed last year, American Samoa Gov. Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, wrote to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management that he and all chambers of local government unanimously opposed deep-sea mining, as did the vast majority of residents. But the governor now welcomes the auction, according to a Monday statement.

"This is a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation," he said.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said it has carefully considered feedback from the governor of American Samoa, and will incorporate it into the agency's process "to the maximum extent practicable," including sharing the locations of deep-sea mining ships, coordinating with fishing vessels, and reviewing any impacts to fish habitat.

The agency said it supports sharing deep-sea mining revenues with territories, and is working with lawmakers and Department of the Interior leadership to support changes that would grant it the authority to do so.

It did not respond to questions about why the auction was arranged to be thousands of miles from American Samoa, or how it factored in local opposition to its policies on deep-sea mining.

In the Northern Mariana Islands, it's an overwhelming time to fight back

Residents of the Northern Mariana Islands are closely watching the events in American Samoa as they brace for a potential auction of the seabed near their islands. The proposal has come at a challenging time for the territory, which was battered by two super typhoons in April and July.

The territory's government is in fiscal crisis, with Gov. David M. Apatang warning of austerity measures after a five-day shutdown in October. Many public schools suffered broken windows and damaged roofs from the storms, while residents face rising electricity costs from the territory's sole energy provider.

"It's very overwhelming for everybody here in this region right now," said Cabrera, the advocate for traditional fishing. "You just want to worry about keeping your lights on and putting food on the table, so it's a challenge to get support for anything other than that."

Born and raised in Saipan, and descended from the Indigenous Carolinian and Chamorro peoples, Cabrera served in the U.S. Navy for seven years and worked in the United States mainland before returning home. He founded his group, Talaya Club, to teach people on the island how to fish with traditional fishing nets known as talayas that are cast out in the ocean surf.

His long-term goal is to help island families become less dependent on imported food through traditional fishing. Sediment plumes from deep-sea mining near the Northern Mariana Islands could endanger that mission, he said.

"That will inevitably impact our fisheries and the health of our fisheries, and thus the health of our people," Cabrera said.

Residents of Saipan have already waged many fights against the U.S. government. Most recently, islanders objected to U.S. Navy plans to turn the territory's beloved island of Pagan into a firing range for thousands of troops. The agency formally abandoned those plans in July after more than a decade of community pushback.

When the deep-sea mining auction was proposed, the Northern Marianas government initially reacted with a measured tone. Both Apatang, an independent, and Kimberlyn King-Hinds, the Republican nonvoting congressional delegate, said they neither supported nor opposed deep-sea mining.

But after the federal government doubled the leasing area in March to include waters both east and west of the territory, Apatang opposed the auction, according to Henry Hofschneider, the governor's chief of staff. The expanded leasing area is just 57 miles from Saipan and 46 miles from the U.S. territory of Guam.

Still, the governor said in a statement to the AP that he has faith in the rule of law and believes federal regulations will protect the marine environment from harm. He has asked the Marine Minerals Administration to consider pausing the auction until the various lawsuits have been heard and decided. In September, King-Hinds introduced a bill in the U.S. House that seeks to distribute 50% of federal deep-sea mining revenues to the nearest territories.

Cecilio Raiukiulipiy worries that deep-sea mining threatens another tradition in the Northern Marianas -- navigation by the sea and stars.

Raiukiulipiy was granted the title of navigator in a special ceremony in 2018. Once you accept the title, he said, "it's your responsibility to keep the knowledge, to pass it on, and to take care of your people, all the people in the islands and also the environment."

Several times per year, his voyages take him across the Mariana Trench, adjacent to where the Trump administration could green-light seabed mining. On the western side of the trench, he said, the water is colder and the waves churn like a washing machine. It's an area home to "all kinds of whales," and where seafood come to spawn, he said. He has seen baby eels swimming north toward the waters of Japan.

"Those are indicators that we are on the right course," he said. Known as seamarks, or living waypoints, they are derived from a deep-seated knowledge of the seaways in his part of the world.

Raiukiulipiy belongs to one of the groups suing the Trump administration to try to stop the auction off the Northern Marianas next month.

"They don't understand how we live," Raiukiulipiy said of the federal government in Washington. "They're looking at it with a dollar sign. Us, we look at how we're going to survive, how we are going to live, how we are going to eat."

Like many around him, the ocean is also sacred to Raiukiulipiy. His community believes their ancestors come from deep in the ocean.

"We usually do our burials in the ocean," he said. "We bury them back."

------

Wieffering reported from Washington, D.C.

text:
Carolina has enjoyed a number of groundbreaking solar projects this year, which is a testament to the state being seen as an appropriate location to pursue and successfully execute such projects. Solar energy facilities are dependent on the weather, which means developers may have identified that Carolina is a region where there is sufficient sunlight to generate consistent energy. Interestingly, the state is relying on a wide range of companies rather than a select few, which shows its willingness to have diversity in the solar facilities that exist in the state. Ultimately, the goal for Carolina, as is for all U.S. states, is to diversify the energy portfolio. On that note, INOX Solar pushed a 3 GW North Carolina cell factory toward 2027 production.

INOX Solar seeks to solidify itself among the pioneers in the solar sector

The solar energy sector is highly competitive at the moment, as there is a wide range of companies that are looking to set a new standard for what a successful project is like. Inox Solar Americas is a company founded in 2026 in the United States and has been recognized as a leading solar technology and manufacturing company specializing mainly in advanced monocrystalline PV cells and high-performance Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial PV modules.

Companies that are formed in 2026 have a massive advantage over older ones because they do not need to adapt to the latest energy generation approaches, considering that they were formed at a time when technology was already at the forefront of solar generation. However, they must still work to improve their reputation and show why they can be trusted to spearhead massive projects.

The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxion monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas’ U.S.

Delving deeper: INOX Solar pushes 3 GW North Carolina cell factory toward 2027

A recent press release from Inox Solar Americas revealed that its planned PV cell manufacturing facility in Greenville, North Carolina, with an annual production capacity of 3.0 GW, remains on track to start production in the second quarter of 2027. The enormous number of projects that have been announced to start operating in 2027 serves as an indication that 2027 is going to be yet another record-breaking year, particularly in clean energy generation.

For Inox, the continued progress that it is making on U.S. PV cell manufacturing reflects an essential step. The 515,460-square-foot facility is a key part of Inox Solar Americas’ strategy to build a more vertically integrated U.S. solar platform. When the facility becomes operational, it is expected to complement the company’s existing U.S. PV module manufacturing capabilities, providing customers with greater access to U.S. manufactured solar technology and a more transparent, resilient, and reliable domestic supply chain.

Companies adopt different strategies when it comes to how they want to pursue solar energy generation. In the case of Inox, its vertically integrated U.S. manufacturing strategy aims to provide customers with greater access to domestically manufactured PV cells and PV modules while increasing domestic content across the company’s product portfolio.

Unpacking the importance of PV solar manufacturing in the modern landscape

PV cell manufacturing is being integrated with the aim of further supporting customers in addressing evolving U.S. domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) and Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, applicable trade requirements, and federal energy policy provisions.

Unpacking how Inox is aiming to advance its position further quickly

Because Inox was established this year, it has a lot of ground to make up. The company has been making up the ground well so far, but there is still some way to go. The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxion monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas’ U.S. manufactured Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial modules.

text:
India's automotive industry witnessed several major developments between November 16 and 22, with Tata Group attracting interest from global automakers, Ashok Leyland evaluating new manufacturing capacity and electric vehicle manufacturers outlining fresh investment, localisation and product plans.

An exclusive Autocar Professional report revealed that Honda and Hyundai had engaged with Tata Group leadership to explore potential areas of cooperation. Separately, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles outlined plans to increase capital expenditure, while Ashok Leyland began evaluating a greenfield assembly plant as utilisation at its existing factories approached 90%.

Electric mobility remained a major theme. VinFast revised its near-term India strategy to prioritise passenger vehicles and electric scooters over buses, while Ola Electric outlined plans to scale battery cell manufacturing capacity to 20 GWh.

BYD crossed 20,000 cumulative electric vehicle deliveries in India, and Hero MotoCorp expects higher Production Linked Incentive (PLI) benefits for its VIDA electric scooter portfolio.

The week also saw developments in commercial vehicle electrification, auto-component manufacturing, fuel-efficiency regulations and domestic battery production.

Strategic Partnerships, Investments and Capacity Expansion

Tata Group Draws Interest From Honda, Hyundai for Potential Cooperation

The Tata Group is attracting interest from global automakers for potential partnerships spanning vehicles, engineering and technology.

According to an exclusive report by this publication, Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran met senior Honda executives in Japan in 2025, while Hyundai Motor Company President and CEO José Muñoz also met him in Mumbai.

Honda's discussions with Tata Group companies have included the possibility of selling Tata-developed vehicles, including electric vehicles, under the Honda brand in India. Potential cooperation involving vehicle platforms, engineering services and automotive components has also been explored.

However, no formal vehicle-sharing agreement, product programme or launch timeline has been confirmed.

Tata Motors PV Earmarks 6-7% of Revenue for Capital Expenditure

Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles plans to allocate approximately 6–7% of its FY27 revenue towards capital expenditure, with investments expected to rise over the next 18–24 months as it expands manufacturing capacity.

The company spent around Rs 2,700 crore on capital expenditure during the first half of FY27. Management said additional investments would support growing demand across its passenger vehicle and electric vehicle portfolios.

Tata Motors reported record quarterly volumes of approximately 2 lakh units in Q2 FY27, representing 40% year-on-year growth.

Ashok Leyland Evaluates New Factory as Capacity Utilisation Reaches 90%

Commercial vehicle manufacturer Ashok Leyland is considering a new greenfield assembly plant as capacity utilisation across its existing factories approaches 90%.

The company is also undertaking debottlenecking measures at existing facilities and coordinating with suppliers to increase production capacity.

Separately, Union Minister Sukanta Majumdar said Ashok Leyland could establish a truck manufacturing facility in Singur, West Bengal. However, the company has not confirmed a location, investment amount, production capacity or timeline for the proposed facility.

SML Mahindra Plans Rs 1,450 Crore Rights Issue

SML Mahindra has approved plans to raise Rs 1,450 crore through a rights issue, as the Mahindra Group moves to strengthen and reorganise its commercial vehicle operations.

The fundraising follows Mahindra & Mahindra's earlier approval to invest up to Rs 1,450 crore in its commercial vehicle subsidiary.

The restructuring forms part of the group's plans to build a broader commercial vehicle business covering light, intermediate and heavy trucks, along with buses.

Tata Technologies Targets Up to $1.3 Billion Revenue by 2030

Engineering and digital services company Tata Technologies has outlined plans to increase annual revenue to $1.1–1.3 billion by 2030, compared with approximately $600 million in FY26.

The company is targeting an EBITDA margin above 20%, supported by full-vehicle engineering programmes, automotive software development and expansion into aerospace and industrial machinery.

Management expects annual revenue growth of 15-20% between FY27 and FY30.

Toyota Kirloskar Auto Parts Opens Rs 460 Crore E-Drive Line

Toyota Kirloskar Auto Parts has inaugurated a new fifth-generation E-Drive manufacturing line at its Bidadi facility near Bengaluru.

The project involves an investment of approximately Rs 460 crore and adds annual production capacity of 2 lakh units, taking the company's total E-Drive capacity to 3.6 lakh units.

The expansion is intended to strengthen domestic production of hybrid powertrain technologies and support localisation of advanced automotive components.

Electric Mobility and Battery Manufacturing

VinFast Defers India Electric Bus Plans, Focuses on Cars and Scooters

Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast has put its India electric bus plans on hold, shifting its immediate focus towards expanding its passenger vehicle portfolio and launching electric scooters in 2027.

The company had earlier targeted an entry into electric buses and two-wheelers during the second half of 2026.

VinFast Asia CEO Tapan Ghosh said the company did not want to introduce too many products simultaneously and would instead concentrate on building its passenger vehicle and two-wheeler operations.

VinFast Plans VF5 Launch, More Vietnam-Developed EVs for India

VinFast plans to introduce more Vietnam-developed electric vehicles adapted for Indian conditions, including the compact VF5 SUV in 2027.

The company intends to modify existing global models for Indian customers, while the development of entirely India-specific vehicles remains a longer-term possibility.

VinFast's Thoothukudi passenger vehicle plant currently has an installed annual capacity of 50,000 units, scalable to 1.5 lakh units. Management said an intermediate expansion to 75,000-1,00,000 units could be considered depending on demand.

However, the automaker's domestic component localisation remains at approximately 15%, with higher production volumes seen as necessary for deeper sourcing from Indian suppliers.

VinFast Prepares Electric Scooters for Early-2027 India Launch

VinFast also plans to enter India's mass-market electric two-wheeler segment in early 2027. The company is preparing scooters based on the Evo, Kyo and Kinet models from its Vietnamese portfolio, with modifications to suit Indian riding conditions and customer requirements.

The vehicles are expected to support battery swapping and other charging options. VinFast is also targeting approximately 300 electric two-wheeler dealerships across 100 Indian towns by the end of 2027.

Ola Electric Targets 20 GWh Battery Cell Capacity

Ola Electric has outlined plans to expand battery cell manufacturing capacity from 6 GWh to 20 GWh.

The company commissioned additional capacity in September 2026, taking its total commissioned capacity to 6 GWh. It plans to stabilise existing operations before undertaking the next phase of expansion.

Ola expects blended capital expenditure to fall below Rs 400 crore per GWh once the facility reaches 20 GWh. The company plans to bring external equity into its battery cell subsidiary to help finance future expansion.

Separately, Ola Electric projected annual vehicle orders of 4-5 lakh units in FY28, based on an expected increase in average battery pack capacity from approximately 3.8 kWh to 5 kWh.

Hero MotoCorp Eyes 13% PLI Benefit on VIDA Revenue

Hero MotoCorp expects PLI incentives to account for approximately 13% of its VIDA electric vehicle revenue from Q3 FY27, after receiving certification for nearly its entire electric two-wheeler portfolio.

The company had recognised Rs 63 crore in PLI benefits during Q2 FY27, equivalent to approximately 6.5% of electric vehicle revenue.

VIDA retail volumes increased 74% year-on-year to around 66,000 units during the quarter. Hero is also expanding manufacturing capacity to address supply constraints and improve profitability.

BYD India Crosses 20,000 Cumulative EV Deliveries

Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD has crossed 20,000 cumulative customer deliveries in India, doubling its tally from the 10,000-unit milestone reached in September 2025.

The company currently operates 51 showrooms across 40 cities.

The Atto 3 electric SUV has surpassed 9,000 deliveries, while the Sealion 7 has crossed 5,000 deliveries, according to BYD India.

Passenger Vehicles and Two-Wheeler Market

Maruti Suzuki Raises Prices of Select Models by 0.31%

Maruti Suzuki India has increased prices of select models by an estimated 0.31% on a volume-weighted average basis, effective November 22. The company attributed the revision to higher input costs, despite continued efforts to reduce expenses.

Maruti did not disclose the individual models or variants covered by the increase. The latest adjustment follows earlier price revisions during the first half of FY27.

Tata Aeris Crosses 4,000 First-Month Sales

Tata Motors' newly introduced compact sedan Aeris crossed approximately 4,000 wholesale units in its first month.

The company is increasing production capacity to address demand and improve vehicle availability. The development comes as Tata Motors expands its passenger vehicle portfolio and invests in additional manufacturing capacity.

Hyundai Bayon Records 3,449 Units in First Month

Hyundai Motor India's newly launched Bayon SUV recorded wholesale volumes of 3,449 units in October, its first full month of sales. The model, positioned below the Creta, accounted for approximately 8% of Hyundai's utility vehicle dispatches during the month.

The launch contributed to Hyundai's record domestic passenger vehicle wholesale volume of 62,799 units in October.

TVS Motor Sees Scooters Reaching Half of Two-Wheeler Market

TVS Motor Company expects scooters to potentially account for 50% of India's two-wheeler market within two years, supported by rising demand for both petrol and electric scooters.

CEO K N Radhakrishnan said scooters currently account for approximately 41% of the market and could reach 45% next year. He also noted that electric vehicle penetration within the scooter category was approaching 22%, reflecting stronger electrification compared with the overall two-wheeler market.

Hero MotoCorp Dispatches Nearly 15,000 Flex-Fuel Motorcycles

Hero MotoCorp has dispatched close to 15,000 flex-fuel motorcycles in a little over two months since deliveries began. The company is following a limited rollout through select dealerships because E85 fuel is not widely available.

Management said customers are also purchasing the vehicles in regions where E20 petrol is available, allowing them to use the motorcycles while higher ethanol blends become more accessible.

Commercial Vehicles and Fleet Electrification

Mahindra and Uber Target 5,000 Electric Three-Wheeler Deployments

Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and Uber have partnered to facilitate the deployment of 5,000 electric three-wheelers on the ride-hailing platform over the next 12 months.

The initiative will operate under the EV Auto Advantage programme and focus on improving financing access for drivers, particularly in markets with relatively low EV penetration.

Mahindra said it currently has more than 4 lakh commercial electric vehicles operating on Indian roads.

Mahindra Expects Faster Shift From E-Rickshaws to L5 Electric Three-Wheelers

Mahindra Last Mile Mobility expects regulatory changes to accelerate the transition from e-rickshaws to L5 electric three-wheelers.

The company anticipates that tighter requirements from April 2027, including restrictions on lead-acid battery-powered models, could encourage operators to adopt higher-category electric vehicles.

Mahindra expects L5 passenger three-wheeler electrification to reach at least 70% and is evaluating additional manufacturing capacity to support demand.

Olectra Greentech Advances Electric Truck Development

Electric commercial vehicle manufacturer Olectra Greentech is developing its own electric truck platform, with plans to build around a dozen prototype vehicles for testing.

Managing Director Mahesh Babu said the company aims to undertake extensive trials before a potential commercial launch towards the end of FY27 or the beginning of FY28.mThe initiative will expand Olectra's presence beyond electric buses into the electric truck market.

Cityflo Sees Electric Bus Economics Moving Closer to Diesel

Premium bus aggregator Cityflo said the lifetime cost of operating electric buses is now only 5-10% higher than diesel buses, compared with a gap of 20-30% around two years ago.

The company operates approximately 1,300 buses across several Indian cities, including around 50 electric buses each in Mumbai and Delhi NCR.

Cityflo expects electric vehicles to account for 30-50% of its fleet within three years, supported by improving battery economics and charging infrastructure.

Auto Components, Technology and Manufacturing

Belrise Expands Into Complete Vehicle Body and Chassis Assemblies

Belrise Industries has entered complete three-wheeler body manufacturing through a new facility at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra.

The plant will manufacture complete body and chassis assemblies for a leading three-wheeler manufacturer, with production expected to ramp up from Q1 FY28. At peak capacity, the facility could generate annual revenue of Rs 100-120 crore.

Separately, Belrise is establishing a facility in Dharwad to manufacture heavy commercial vehicle chassis assemblies, with estimated annual revenue potential of Rs 150–200 crore.

The company also secured passenger vehicle sheet metal orders from Japanese and European automakers, expanding its customer base and component portfolio.

BKT Targets January 2027 Launch for Passenger Car Tyres

Balkrishna Industries plans to launch its own passenger car radial tyre range in January 2027, marking a further expansion beyond its traditional off-highway tyre business.

The company is also pursuing a separate manufacturing arrangement with Pirelli for premium passenger car tyres at its Bhuj facility. BKT aims to increase the contribution of its on-road tyre business under its Vision 2030 strategy.

Mercedes-Benz Targets Shorter Vehicle Development Cycles

Mercedes-Benz is working to reduce vehicle development time by approximately 30% as it advances its software-defined vehicle strategy.

In an exclusive interview with Autocar Professional, Mercedes-Benz R&D executive Steffen Tacke said separating software, hardware, and vehicle development cycles would allow the company to introduce technologies more quickly.

The strategy is part of the company's wider effort to improve development efficiency and respond to competition from newer automotive manufacturers.

Policy and Regulatory Developments

Automakers Seek EV-Level Benefits for Plug-in Hybrids Under CAFE-III

Indian automakers are preparing to seek regulatory benefits for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles comparable to those available to battery electric vehicles under the upcoming Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE)-III framework.

Manufacturers with substantial petrol and diesel SUV portfolios believe additional benefits for plug-in hybrids could help them comply with tighter fleet fuel-efficiency targets. The new regulations will apply from April 1, 2027, and continue until March 2032.

MoRTH Proposes Changes to PUC Certificate Validity

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has proposed revisions to Pollution Under Control certificate validity periods, linking renewal timelines to vehicle age, emissions standards and usage category.

The changes form part of proposed amendments to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules and would introduce differentiated validity periods for certain vehicle categories.

The proposal also outlines rules governing renewal before or after the expiry of an existing certificate.

India Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh Battery Manufacturing Capacity

The Ministry of Heavy Industries has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity under the government's Production Linked Incentive scheme.

The tender covers battery capacity for grid-scale stationary energy storage applications and forms part of India's wider 50 GWh domestic cell manufacturing target.

Participating companies include Amara Raja, Exide Energy Solutions, Reliance Industries, JSW Neo Energy and Waaree Energy Storage Solutions.

India Achieves 19.99% Ethanol Blending in ESY 2025–26

India recorded ethanol blending of 19.99% during ethanol supply year 2025–26, nearly achieving the government's E20 blending target.

According to data released by the All India Distillers' Association, approximately 1,134 crore litres of ethanol were blended with petrol during the period.

Grain-based feedstocks accounted for 73.52% of ethanol supplies, with maize emerging as the largest contributor.

Bombay High Court Orders Bosch to Compensate Temporary Workers

The Bombay High Court has directed Bosch to pay Rs 25 lakh each to temporary workers affected by unlawful transfers from its Nashik facility.

The court upheld findings concerning the company's transfer orders but declined to direct reinstatement at the Nashik plant.

“Enmarket Arena provides an important opportunity to expand renewable energy generation at a major public facility,” said City Manager Jay Melder in the release.
Mayor Johnson said in the press release that the savings from the city’s solar projects have amounted to around $146,000 to date.
Since Savannah’s solar initiative was launched in 2023, solar systems have been installed on 27 municipal buildings.

text:
Solar energy is coming to Savannah's Enmarket Arena, as part of the city’s effort to transition to 100% renewable energy. The 9,500-seat sports and entertainment venue, completed in 2022, is one of the largest public facilities in Savannah.

The arena’s solar system will be installed, operated and maintained under a 25-year agreement by Cherry Street Energy at no cost to the city. City representatives have not yet responded to a question about whether the agreement will renew under the same terms at the end of 25 years.

Oak View Group, the arena’s operator, can expect to save on its electric bill, while Savannah will gain renewable energy credits that move the city closer to meeting its clean energy goals, according to a news release from the city.

“Enmarket Arena provides an important opportunity to expand renewable energy generation at a major public facility,” said City Manager Jay Melder in the release. “By leveraging private-sector investment and expertise, we’re advancing our sustainability commitments, reducing operating costs at the arena, and demonstrating the value of innovative public-private partnerships.”

According to Mayor Van R. Johnson II, Savannah’s solar portfolio has produced over 5,672 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy to date. That’s roughly equivalent to the energy needed to generate electricity for about 500 average American homes for a year. Mayor Johnson said in the press release that the savings from the city’s solar projects have amounted to around $146,000 to date.

Since Savannah’s solar initiative was launched in 2023, solar systems have been installed on 27 municipal buildings. According to a tracker on the city’s website, these solar projects have offset 130,000 tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 100% Savannah Plan has two stated goals: to switch to renewable sources for all electricity consumed within the city by 2035; and to switch to renewable sources for all other energy needs within the city by 2050. City council adopted the clean energy plan in 2021, and it's currently undergoing its fifth-year review. City officials have not yet responded to a question about whether the city is still on track to meet its 2035 and 2050 deadlines.

Savannah’s Office of Sustainability is soliciting public feedback on updates to the 100% Savannah Plan on its website.

title: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels
description:
Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn’t accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.
Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.
“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.
For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.
That’s when, in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels.
text:
Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn’t accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.

For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when, in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

JOE CONCHA: AS TRUMP AND VANCE SPLIT, THE NOMINATION IS RUBIO’S TO LOSE

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

text:
The Senate approved a bipartisan permitting bill 62-33 on Thursday night, Nov. 19, sending it to the House for action before the year ends. Titled the "Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act" and shortened to BAAJA, the measure is meant to shorten approval times for energy and infrastructure projects, and the two chambers must resolve any differences before President Donald Trump can sign it.

Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee, of West Virginia and Utah, and Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, of Rhode Island and New Mexico, negotiated the text. It limits how long lawsuits can run, makes permits harder to revoke once they are issued, and trims reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act as well as the Clean Water Act. It also requires data centers to cover the grid upgrades they need and widens federal authority over the siting of certain interstate transmission lines. More than a dozen Democrats voted yes, among them Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, though more Democrats voted against the bill than for it.

Capito, one of the authors, said, "Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people." Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota said the bill would "cut through decades of red tape" and "save the average household hundreds of dollars each year." Whitehouse said Americans would "quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit." Rhodium Group, a research firm, estimates that the bill could allow 17 to 249 more gigawatts of clean energy by 2040 and lift natural gas exports 8 percent to 15 percent above levels already projected.

Industry groups on both sides of the energy divide, the American Clean Power Association for renewables and the American Petroleum Institute for oil and gas, praised the vote, and labor backing came from the AFL-CIO and a number of individual unions. Opposition came from the Sierra Club, the National Wildlife Federation and the Natural Resources Defense Council, which said the House "should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers." Several tribal organizations remain opposed even after senators amended the text in response to their objections.

Maria Cantwell of Washington, one of several Democratic senators who raised objections, urged colleagues not to "sacrifice the Clean Water Act, hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty." Jeff Merkley of Oregon called the bill "a bad deal" that "opens the gates to a flood of natural gas for data centers while leaving expanded transmission of renewable energy subject to Trump's obstruction." Ron Wyden of Oregon pushed an amendment that would have barred data center construction on public lands.

Democrats won majorities in both chambers in this month's midterm elections and take control in January. Trump urged passage on social media, calling the bill a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE." House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week that he expects enough votes to pass it in his chamber. Rep. Scott Peters, a California Democrat, urged colleagues to act before this Congress ends, while Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the likely incoming chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, urged Democrats to reject it and said, "We can produce a better deal."

The House has not yet voted on the Senate bill, and neither Rep. Andrew Garbarino nor Rep. Nick LaLota, the Republicans who represent eastern Long Island, had commented publicly on that measure as of Nov. 20. Both voted yes on Dec. 18, 2025, when the House passed H.R. 4776, the SPEED Act, 221-196, a permitting bill that would revise environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act. After that vote, LaLota said, "This past week, I voted YES on the SPEED Act to fix D.C.’s broken permitting process." Both voted yes again on Sept. 16, 2026, when the House passed H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3, which would require state utility regulators to take up a standard under which big computing facilities whose peak electric use reaches 100 megawatts or higher at one location would bear the added cost of the power-plant, power-line and local-system upgrades required to serve them.

Republican leaders and the White House back the bill, and Speaker Mike Johnson said last week that he expects enough votes to pass it in the House. Some Democrats, including Huffman, have argued they could write a better package once they control Congress next year, and some of the bill's backers in the Democratic coalition say a changed bill would leave no political path to Trump's signature.

text:
November 2026

This report was produced by the Initiative on Universal Access to Clean Water for Tribal Communities (UACW), which aims to advance the cause of access to clean drinking water for Native Americans, and the Native American Rights Fund, which focuses on applying laws and treaties to guarantee that national and state governments live up to their legal obligations.

Contributing authors include Davíd Pilz (Fluent Freshwater Insights), Amy McCoy (UACW and Fluent Freshwater Insights), Heather Tanana (UACW and University of Denver), Anne Castle (UACW and Getches-Wilkinson Center, University of Colorado Law School), Daniel Cordalis (Native American Rights Fund), Savannah Hook (Native American Rights Fund), and Keeley Joe (UACW).

UACW focuses energy and actions in the areas of policy, education, research, legislation, and outreach. More information, including a PDF version of this report and previous reports related to universal access to clean drinking water, can be found on UACW’s website: uacw.org…

Executive Summary

On the heels of the 2023 Supreme Court decision in Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency, the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers have proposed new rules redefining Waters of the United States (WOTUS), which determines the scope of the Clean Water Act. The rules significantly roll back existing safeguards for waters across the nation, with a disproportionate impact on Tribal Nations.

Tribes depend on ephemeral and intermittent streams, springs, groundwater-fed wetlands, and other hydrologically diverse waters now facing severely reduced protection under the proposed definition. Not only are Tribal waters vulnerable because of their hydrology, but Tribal water uses, including cultural, traditional, and treaty-rights-based uses, are highly sensitive to changes in water quality.

The new WOTUS definition will:

undermine water-related trust responsibilities and treaty rights;

jeopardize Tribal drinking water safety, physical health, cultural survival, economic security, and ecological resilience;

burden Tribes with increased technical complexity and costs;

limit the ability of Tribes to regulate upstream, off-reservation activities, increasing contamination risk without meaningful recourse;

require Tribal governments to conduct analyses and contest jurisdictional determinations while already faced with severe capacity constraints; and

perpetuate historical inequities and expose Tribal waters to long-term degradation.

While the impacts of rolling back the definition of WOTUS will be felt by all who value and depend on clean water, Tribes are likely to feel it first, most keenly, and with the longest-lasting effects.
