text:
Kate Gessert and her husband, Max, went looking for mushrooms and instead found an old-growth forest.

The couple spent the day driving through the Coast Range patchwork of public and private land, stopping to forage in young forests between the clear-cuts. About 10 miles from home, they stopped and got out of the car, in awe of what loomed above them.

Huge Douglas firs rose with lichen-covered trunks, moss draped from thick branches of western hemlocks. They hiked from the roadway down into a fern-covered grove, bigleaf maples flaring gold.

“We were in this completely different world,” Gessert said.

Then she noticed blue numbers spray-painted on the big trees, some wrapped in yellow tape. It quickly brought Gessert back to reality. This was a remnant, and it might not last.

That was 22 years ago. Today, Gessert still holds her breath when she travels to visit the forest — until she sees the oldest, towering trees.

On a late October afternoon, soft rain fell as she steadied herself with a cork-topped trekking pole. She leaned against a sapling and looked up.

“There they are,” she said. “The grandmothers.”

Grandmother’s Grove is a 60-acre public forest in Lane County designated as an “Area of Critical Environmental Concern,” meaning the Bureau of Land Management put it off-limits to scheduled commercial logging — at least for now.

It’s among the 2.5 million acres BLM oversees in western Oregon.

How the agency manages this land, what it cuts and what it conserves, is set by rulebooks called resource management plans. For 1.3 million of those acres, including the BLM forests around Eugene and Springfield, that rulebook is the Northwestern Coastal Oregon Resource Management Plan.

For additional policy details, read Lookout Eugene-Springfield’s explainer of BLM’s Northwestern and Coastal Oregon Resource Management Plan.

That plan is up for revision, and the agency is preparing to release a draft for public comment in the coming weeks, with an emphasis on returning to “historically higher” harvests of the 1970s and 1980s.

“The history of it is that everything got chopped up into pieces,” Gessert said of the Coast Range. “Then you take those little pieces, and you start chopping them up, too. Then you just get these little, tiny slivers left.”

She is worried about whether those slivers, the ones tucked away for conservation, will survive.

Some federal and local leaders frame off-limit forests as holding back the potential for logging dollars to help county budgets.

But federal data and policy analysis show a more complicated picture. Even at its peak in the 1970s and 1980s, BLM money was rarely steady, and since 2000, it has covered only a fraction of what counties book as timber dollars. And in recent years, as BLM’s timber receipts got bigger, many counties, including Lane, haven’t seen more money from it.

Hanging in the balance are forests like Grandmother’s Grove.

The money trees

For thousands of years, old Douglas firs anchored the Coast Range in what are now Lane and Douglas counties, part of a temperate rainforest belt stretching from Alaska to Northern California. Fog lofted, rain fell, fire burned in a shifting mosaic of old and young trees.

Some of that fire was set by Indigenous people who tended these forests in their understory for food, game and basketry materials.

White settlers moving West saw the big firs as something else: money trees.

Congress took back the unsold land and passed the Oregon and California Revested Railroad Lands Act of 1937, known as the O&C Act.

The law gave the 18 counties containing O&C lands a way to get paid for property they couldn’t tax, because it was owned by the federal government. Revenue from timber sales would substitute for property taxes and fund public services.

The system thrived during post-World War II housing development and got a boost in the 1960s when BLM doubled its harvest cap, from 500 million board feet annually to 1 billion board feet.

In 1970, a federal commission — formed to advise Congress on governing public lands — warned of a boom-and-bust cycle in a report. The report firmly supported timber production but found the revenue-sharing model problematic.

Some years the model overpaid counties. Other years, it shorted them. And, the report said, it created pressure to cut timber in ways that could “be in conflict with good conservation-management practices.”

The warnings came to pass in the 1980s, when a national recession hit, and timber payments plunged. Then in the 1990s, the system Congress designed broke for good.

The landmark Northwest Forest Plan required the U.S. Forest Service and the BLM to set aside old forests from logging and conserve them as habitat for the northern spotted owl. The harvest caps came back down.

To fill the gap, Congress began sending counties, including Lane County, “safety net” payments in 1993. This meant “timber payments” were no longer funded only by timber.

The help was meant to be temporary, as counties found other revenue streams. Instead, Congress recommitted to support in 2000 with the Secure Rural Schools Act, covering revenue from both BLM and national forest service land. National forest, which make up 48% of lands in Lane County are managed similarly to, but separate, from BLM lands, which make up about 10% of the county.

‘Timber payments’

The O&C timber payments sent to western Oregon counties no longer work the way they were first designed, with the U.S. treasury sending money to counties when timber receipts are low.

For the first 14 years of the 2000s, the U.S. Treasury sent millions of dollars annually to O&C counties. Then, timber receipts bounced back in 2016, when BLM adopted new plans for western Oregon forests, replacing direction from the Northwest Forest Plan. Also that year, Secure Rural Schools lapsed, although the program was later revived by Congress.

Counties that opt into Secure Rural Schools get a fixed amount no matter how much timber sells.

This is why some counties, including Coos and Columbia, have opted out of the Secure Rural Schools program. Lane County hasn’t, because doing so could affect its national forest payments under the same law, which fund other parts of the county budget, according to local officials.

Christine Moody, a budget and financial planning manager, has worked for Lane County over the past 25 years, starting the year Secure Rural Schools went into effect. She’s watched the spreadsheets fluctuate, trying to maximize federal dollars ever since.

She still titles a budget line item “O&C Timber Sales.” In the 2025-26 fiscal year, Lane County booked nearly $3.5 million there, about 3% of its general fund.

“The funds are critical to providing services to the community,” Moody said. “Even the cost of one deputy is going to be a benefit to the community. … It’s very important for public safety, in particular, because public safety spends most of the discretionary general fund.”

Asked why the account is still called “O&C Timber Sales” when it holds a mix of funding sources, she said, “I just never changed it.”

That nuance of what’s included in the O&C timber payments rarely comes up in public, including at meetings of the Lane County Board of Commissioners.

“These lands were designated for the good and the economic viability of every county,” said Commissioner David Loveall during a meeting March 17, when commissioners discussed whether the county should become a cooperating agency with BLM as it revises the Northwestern Coastal Oregon Resource Management Plan.

The board agreed unanimously that Lane County needed a voice in the federal process. It split over whose voice that should be.

The debate centered on the Association of O&C Counties, called the AOCC, a group that lobbies for federal timber revenues. Lane County is a member of the association and pays $80,000 a year for the group’s lobbying and legal fees.

Commissioners Loveall, Pat Farr and Ryan Ceniga voted to designate the association to represent Lane County as BLM updates its resource management plan. Commissioners Laurie Trieger and Heather Buch voted against.

“If we’re going to be a participating entity, who is in the best position to advocate for Lane County to be that representative? I argue that that would be Lane County,” Buch said. “If we give it to an outside entity such as AOCC, I wonder if their priorities and what they send and actually communicate with BLM is going to be the same as what is in the best interests of Lane County.”

Buch also questioned the group’s transparency. She told the board she has asked for years to see the group’s meeting minutes and that she doesn’t feel informed about its actions.

The Association of O&C Counties did not respond to Lookout Eugene-Springfield’s repeated requests for comment, nor did its president, Douglas County Commissioner Tim Freeman. A Douglas County spokesperson declined an interview about its O&C payments.

‘Part of life’

The BLM set a June deadline to release a draft environmental impact statement — a legally required analysis — on its “preliminary alternative” to increase timber production on its lands. June came and went.

Sarah Bennett, a spokesperson for BLM Oregon/Washington, said the draft is coming but gave no date.

“We didn’t want to rush it,” Bennett said, adding the agency is carefully considering the public comment received in February, when it shared preliminary information through a “notice of intent.”

That notice states in part:

BLM has developed a preliminary alternative that would meet the purpose of providing an increase in timber harvest levels of production to align with historically higher levels of volume on BLM-administered public lands in the decision area. The preliminary alternative would manage BLM-administered lands to provide a sustained yield of timber production consistent with the maximum productive capacity of the lands.

The BLM’s Northwestern Coastal Oregon Resource Management Plan is divided into five main management zones. Its Harvest Land Base, an allocation for timber, makes up about 20%. “Late Successional Reserves,” an allocation for spotted owl habitat, makes up 46%.

“District Reserves” include the Areas of Critical Environmental Concerns, which are reserved for conservation and cultural values. Bennett said these Areas of Critical Environmental Concerns make up 2% to 4% of the agency’s planning and have not been analyzed for commercial timber harvest.

However, she could not confirm the areas would be ruled out from potential reallocation.

Meanwhile, the Department of the Interior this month proposed new rules that would give the BLM more flexibility in how it designates and sizes Areas of Critical Environmental Concern.

“Our draft plan, that’ll lay out our first range of proposed actions,” she said, pointing to House Bill 1, the GOP-supported tax and spending bill and executive orders signed by President Donald Trump in 2025. “We think there’s more timber that could be harvested.”

The BLM’s current plan describes Grandmother’s Grove as a rare patch of mature and older forest, stands that are typically 80 to more than 200 years old. It sets the grove aside from commercial logging so it can develop through natural, ecological processes.

The agency decided at one time that the grove was worth preserving, Gessert said, and the forest “didn’t suddenly change overnight because the government’s priorities changed.”

Since she first visited in 2004, Gessert has watched nearby forest practices take a toll on the grandmothers. The original grandmothers she saw died in recent years. She noticed their rapid decline around 2019, after roadside equipment cleared the brush and young trees along Wolf Creek Road.

She turned to academic papers that described this as the “edge effect.” That’s when trees get more sunlight and wind — becoming warmer and drier — than trees inside a larger forest.

But the trees are taking on new purposes. Hollowing trunks serve as nesting places for birds. Fallen branches return nutrients to the forest floor as they decompose.

Other old trees surround them. Some could become grandmothers themselves, the dominating trees of this forest — but only if they get the chance.

Gessert, a retired educator, understands budget strains, but believes there are other values to standing forests like this grove: ecological richness and connection to nature.

It’s why she brought her students there for years.

They were adults from Lane Community College taking English as a second language, and on trip days entire families would join Gessert to see the grandmothers.

At her home in Crow, Gessert opened her laptop — letters worn off the keys from writing and researching — to look at her notes. She wrote down what her students told her when they were out together.

“This student burst out, almost shouting,” Gessert recalled, turning to read the account. “‘It’s all connected, all of it. The dead trees on the ground, the dead trees standing up, the live trees, all the little plants. They’re all part of life.'”

Top story

‘It’s a really good bill as it is’: Rep. Peters backs energy permitting reform despite opposition from California Democrats

As a San Diegan, if you hear the word Baja, it’s natural that your mind turns south of the border. But if you move in public policy circles, right now it means something else, spelled slightly differently – BAAJA.

That stands for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which deals with federal environmental review and permits for energy projects.

The Senate bill, introduced by two Democrats and two Republicans, had bipartisan beginnings, but that doesn’t mean there isn’t tension over the legislation.

Many Democrats aren’t pleased with the bill, nor are some environmental and Tribal interests. At issue are constraints that place distinct limits on challenges to future energy projects if the bill passes.

Rep. Scott Peters sees the tradeoff, though, and he’s willing to accept it. The San Diego Democrat, who once practiced environmental law, argues that BAAJA is “going to lower emissions, lower costs, and it’s going to provide jobs.”

It also will, he told our Alysa Horton, modernize environmental law and “in a way that protects the environment and even lowers emissions.”

Yet not everyone is sold, including California’s senators, Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, who voted against BAAJA when the Senate passed its version of the bill last week. One conservation advocate said “it’s just really tough to see how this bill could drive the clean energy agenda.”

Alysa has more, including why one organization contends that the bill would strip Tribes of “cultural protection and Tribal participation.”

CA, UNITED STATES, November 22, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — “Many innovative companies have adopted, at least in part, a ‘In China, with China, for the world’ strategy,” Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council (USCBC), told a reporter from Southern Finance 21st Century Business Herald in an interview during the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders’ Week. He noted that the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area is particularly attractive to US businesses, thanks to its vast market, abundant innovation opportunities and efficient investment environment.

US companies have recognized the significant potential for cooperation with Guangdong and are demonstrating their interest through concrete actions. Stein said that nearly 90% of US companies consider the Chinese market important to maintaining their global competitiveness. He also pointed to opportunities for further cooperation between businesses in the two countries in areas such as life sciences, product safety, certification and compliance with product standards.

Sustained business cooperation depends on stable economic and trade relations. Commenting on US-China trade ties, Stein said he was encouraged to see bilateral relations stabilize this year. However, he stressed that both sides still need to translate their commitment to a constructive strategic relationship of stability into concrete action. Only then can progress be made on other issues.

Stein also shared his personal connection with Shenzhen. When he first visited the city 24 years ago, he said, he did not fully understand the Chinese expression “Once you come to Shenzhen, you are one of its people.” Today, he realizes that he has been a “Shenzhen resident” for about 24 years. In his view, Shenzhen’s transformation from a relatively small place into a thriving modern metropolis has been driven by openness, innovation and cooperation. He added that hosting the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen was particularly meaningful.

Speaking about regional cooperation, Stein used the Chinese idiom “hou ji bo fa” (厚积薄发), which describes how sustained efforts and accumulated progress can eventually lead to significant achievements, to characterize APEC’s role in promoting dialogue and economic cooperation across the Asia-Pacific. He noted that APEC focuses on making incremental progress each year, with these continued efforts adding up to greater achievements over time. This year’s APEC agenda, which includes issues such as paperless trade and digital payments, reflects the practical needs of regional economic development.

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Negotiators at the United Nations climate conference are being asked to consider a last-minute proposal by Turkish officials, an attempt to reach an agreement and salvage the talks that have stretched into a second day of overtime and been characterized by sharp disagreements over how, and whether, to confront the root cause of global temperature rise.

Early Sunday, Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum, president of the two-week talks in Antalya, Turkey, called COP31, said he had “a text which all parties can agree to.” The text was not immediately made public and it was unclear if negotiators had received the wording overnight, which would give nations only a few hours to submit objections and changes.

Key issues have bogged down the negotiations. They include the amount of concerted effort by countries to wean themselves from fossil fuels including coal, oil and gas, which are the main drivers of climate change, whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants and whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewables such as wind and solar or also involve other energy sources including natural gas and coal.

“Outside of this hall there are people who are living with the effects of climate change,” Kurum told negotiators early Sunday. “The children, the parents are waiting for this.”

Talks were scheduled to end Friday and work crews boxed up the venue Saturday, although it is common for negotiations to go beyond the scheduled time.

This year’s negotiations drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in an earlier draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations.”

In the lead-up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

“No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be,” said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.

Climate talks enter overtime

Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the pavilions, where countries showcased innovations and hosted panels, workers were seen packing up electronics and boxing up belongings on Saturday.

The hallways, previously bustling with tens of thousands of participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos by deserted pavilions.

“COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.

Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters become more deadly, including this year’s heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal.

Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.

“Every year there seems to be a greater discontent, a mistrust and frustration for civil society, Indigenous people and countries that are more climate vulnerable,” Tuvalu’s Minister of Environment Maina Talia said during a Saturday press conference.

“I am still holding the line, trying to be very optimistic until we see the text,” he said.

The United States, a major polluter and the world’s largest economy, did not participate directly in this year’s talks.

The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

Criticism of COP31 grows

On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan “you are killing the future” interrupted official proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting: “You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait.”

The Global South isn’t a geographical term, but a reference to developing countries in general. As the protester was escorted out by security, he shouted: “You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now.”

The demonstration interrupted Kurum, who said “let’s try to maintain the peace in the room” before continuing with his scheduled remarks.

“Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it’s nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here, watching the negotiations,” said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.

“We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on,” he said.

text:
Australia could nearly double how long its diesel reserves last without adding any fuel to storage.

Engineer Rosemary Barnes estimated that reserves could cover 63 days instead of 36 if Australia electrified its road freight, cutting annual diesel use by about 3.7 billion gallons (14 billion liters).

Here's what to know

Barnes, an engineer and the content creator behind Engineering with Rosie (@EngineeringwithRosie), explained in a YouTube video that roughly 95% of the liquid fuel Australia uses comes from abroad.

That reliance leaves businesses that transport groceries, household goods, and other freight vulnerable to supply disruptions.

Barnes favored cutting diesel consumption as a more durable safeguard than expanding stockpiles. She described an AU$3.2 billion (US$2.1 billion) effort intended to provide enough stored diesel for 50 days.

"But a stockpile only buys time," she said. "The longer lasting fix is to need less diesel in the first place."

Barnes said mining consumes about a quarter of Australia's diesel, compared with nearly half for road freight, which includes everything from delivery vans to massive road trains.

More background

Barnes said delivery vans and trucks with predictable routes and a shared overnight depot are practical candidates for an initial switch to electric vehicles.

Buyers already pay about as much for light- and medium-duty electric trucks as for diesel models, according to Barnes. Recharging at the depot also simplifies the transition for these fleets.

Barnes cited an analysis putting the payback period for an electric prime mover's higher purchase price at three to four years for a truck traveling about 62,000 miles (100,000 kilometers) annually. These electric models cost two to three times as much upfront as diesel equivalents.

Barnes said China encouraged operators to buy electric trucks by installing chargers first, and about a quarter of China's new heavy-truck purchases are electric. Elsewhere, charging access remains a major barrier to adoption.

What's being done?

Barnes pointed to IKEA and Woolworths as examples of delivery-fleet electrification. IKEA makes most of its home deliveries with zero-pollution vehicles, while Woolworths is adding 148 electric trucks for grocery deliveries.

Janus Electric replaces diesel prime movers' powertrains with electric systems and swaps their batteries to avoid waits for recharging.

Barnes said Fortescue is developing 6-megawatt chargers for electric haul trucks. At its Pilbara operations, the company already runs 18 electric excavators that each replace roughly 264,000 gallons (1 million liters) of diesel a year.

Barnes blamed Australia's fuel tax credit scheme for making electrification more difficult, saying it artificially lowers the cost of diesel.

She called for redirecting that funding toward truck chargers and other electrical infrastructure. Barnes said the fuel tax scheme costs more than AU$10 billion (US$6.7 billion) annually, with mining receiving nearly half.

One YouTube commenter supported shifting tax-system backing away from fossil fuels and toward renewable energy.

"Strong agree," they said. "We need to uncouple our tax system from supporting fossil fuels. Diverting it all to renewable rollout is the way to go."

title: Electric vehicles powering Kenya's car industry, jobs - Business Daily
description:

text:
Kenya's emerging electric vehicle (EV) industry presents an opportunity that extends beyond cleaner transport. As the country seeks to attract investment in EVs and expand assembly and manufacturing, can the transition create sustainable jobs, particularly for its growing young population, while strengthening domestic industrial capacity?

Chinese manufacturers, who have played a role in transforming the global EV industry, could bring the investment, technology and expertise needed to accelerate this transition. For Kenya, the real opportunity is to use foreign investment to develop local suppliers, transfer technical skills and retain a greater share of the economic value generated by the industry.

China's transformation into a major global EV manufacturer was not accidental. Government support began in the early 2000s, followed by the Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles programme, launched in 2009 to stimulate electric vehicle development, particularly in public transport and government fleets.

Started initially in 10 cities, the programme then spread to 25 cities on the mainland, encouraging selected cities to adopt the new energy vehicles.

Subsequent measures included tax exemptions, charging infrastructure investment and support for battery research. The coordinated approach helped establish an extensive ecosystem of vehicle manufacturers, battery producers, component suppliers and technology companies.

The International Energy Agency's World Energy Employment 2025 report, estimates that China's EV manufacturing workforce reached 2.4 million in 2024, following the addition of approximately 570,000 jobs that year.

Kenya is beginning to establish its position in the emerging EV industry. In February 2026, Rideence Africa, an EV mobility company based in Nairobi, announced a Sh320 million partnership with Associated Vehicle Assemblers (AVA) in Mombasa to assemble Chinese-designed vehicles using completely knocked-down (CKD) kits.

The initial plan covered 132 Henrey electric taxis and 20 Joylong electric minibuses.

In May, the Business Daily reported that BasiGo had begun assembling 23 electric vans at AVA, targeting at least 120 units by the end of 2026. The local assembly line directly employs approximately 70 people on the factory floor. AVA has also announced plans to invest Sh1billion in a dedicated EV assembly line, expected to be staffed by 60 trained technicians.

These investments demonstrate the potential of existing automotive infrastructure. However, assembly and manufacturing are not interchangeable. A vehicle assembled in Kenya may still contain imported batteries, motors, electronics and other major components. The more meaningful measure of success is how much value each vehicle generates and retains locally.

The transition from semi-knocked-down (SKD) to CKD assembly can deepen local production, but CKD does not automatically mean local manufacturing. Kenya thus, needs to progressively develop capacity across various interconnected supply-chain segments.

The first opportunity lies in local industrial inputs and manufacturing of components, including metal fabrication, vehicle frames, wiring harnesses, seats, interiors, cables and battery enclosures. BYD’s dedicated wire harness division employs over 39,000 workers across more than 12 Chinese cities.

Roam, a pioneering electric mobility company in Africa, reported in October 2026 that 40 percent of the value of its Roam Air electric motorcycle was produced in East Africa, with more than 50 components supplied by over 10 Kenyan and Tanzanian companies. Local production reduced lead times for body parts from 18 weeks to 2 weeks, while the cost of a replacement body-parts kit fell by almost 40 percent. Roam is targeting 50 percent local content by 2027.

Capabilities are already present in Kenya’s automotive and engineering industries, with signs of what local supplier development can achieve.

Then there is assembly, engineering and component integration. Demand can grow for assembly technicians, structural welders, automotive electricians, quality inspectors and production engineers. Local production of vehicle frames, body structures, battery enclosures and electrical systems would expand employment beyond the assembly line and create business opportunities for Kenyan manufacturers.

BYD, for instance employs roughly 120,000 engineers alongside hundreds of thousands of frontline production workers, while Geely concentrates roughly one-third of its workforce in engineering.

Charging, software and specialised services offer another employment pathway. Charging and battery-swapping networks require electrical technicians, station operators, customer service specialists and maintenance teams. In digital fleet platforms, opportunities are for software developers, data analysts and specialists monitoring vehicle performance, battery health and energy use. Geely’s 3,000 software staff form part of its AI ventures.

Under Kenya’s 2023 EV guidelines, charging stations should be placed every 25 km on both sides of highways, fast chargers for long-range and heavy-duty vehicles every 100 km. Theoretically, that’s approximately 1,050 charging stations across the 13,089 km national paved road network, or 40 along the 482 km long Nairobi to Mombasa highway. This could generate between 750 to 2,840 long-term jobs nationwide, dependent on the use of either self-service models or requiring 12-hour daily on-site staffing.

Imported EVs can be better utilized by understanding Kenya’s driving conditions, and customizing vehicle designs to the local realities. Local manufacturers and assemblers already use real-world Kenyan driving data to modify EV vehicle designs. Local cloud facilities include Servernah Cloud, a sovereign cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure platform in Kenya developed by Atlancis Technologies Limited in partnership with Everse Technology Limited (EverseTech) and iXAfrica.

These Kenyan based and owned data centres, pair with domestic telematics platforms such as IntelliFleet 360 which builds proprietary software and iTrace Africa a vehicle tracking provider. Building such a self-sustaining EV ecosystem in Kenya, helps to create and retain high-value tech jobs locally and customize software for African roads and energy realities.

Battery manufacturing and critical-mineral processing may offer longer-term opportunities. Kenya can build capabilities in battery-pack integration, diagnostics, maintenance and recycling, capabilities that could also serve other sectors.

On October 6, 2026, President William Ruto witnessed the signing of an MoU between the government of Kenya and Endelevu Enterprise Corporation- an international enterprise operating in green mobility, clean technology and automotive manufacturing, for a proposed US$3 billion electric mobility investment with Chinese manufacturer Geely. The proposal could accelerate EV development, and position Kenya as a manufacturing and distribution base for East Africa and the wider African market.

The proposed project includes capacity to assemble 50,000 four-wheel vehicles and 100,000 two-wheelers and other light-mobility vehicles annually, alongside 1,000 solar-powered charging hubs.

Government projections indicate approximately 2,000 direct and more than 20,000 indirect jobs, with additional opportunities in fleet management, operations and services.

For Kenya’s young population, the EV industry could open new technical and professional pathways. BYD’s 2025 Sustainability Report shows that employees aged 30 and below accounted for 42.13 percent of its global workforce, demonstrating that large manufacturing companies have substantial career opportunities for young people.

World Bank/ILO estimates put youth unemployment among Kenyans aged 15–24 at approximately 15.2 percent in 2025. The Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Principal Secretary reported enrolment of 1,201,320 learners by May 2026. Connecting this training capacity to specific EV industrial needs will be essential.

China’s Field Engineer Special Cultivation Plan offers a relevant experience in connecting education and training with jobs, for Kenya to examine. Launched in 2022 by five government departments, it set targets involving at least 500 vocational institutions and 1,000 enterprises, with 200,000 field engineers to be trained in several priority sectors cumulatively by 2025.

Women can also have access to these technical and engineering opportunities, consistent with the participation priorities recognised in Kenya’s National Electric Mobility Policy.

Kenya’s ambitions can also extend beyond its domestic market. Its regional trade relationships could support a manufacturing and distribution hub serving East Africa, with manufacturing located with ease of access to ports, transport corridors, and close proximity to regional borders.

Kenya's National Electric Mobility Policy and proposed National Automotive Industry Development Bill provide an opportunity to connect foreign investment with domestic industrial development, and Chinese investment provides a starting point.

But lasting development will depend on Kenya's ability to convert foreign capital and technology into strong competitive local supply networks with domestic industrial capacity, technical jobs created, apprentices trained, technology transferred and greater local value addition per vehicle.

text:
Colorado’s senators were once again split in their vote Thursday for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. Sen. John Hickenlooper voted in favor of the bill, while Sen. Michael Bennet voted against.

Proponents of the sweeping federal infrastructure and energy-permitting legislation argue the bipartisan bill makes clean energy easier to develop and will lower electricity rates, while opponents worry the legislation weakens environmental safeguards and threatens tribal sovereignty.

The U.S. Senate voted 66-33 to pass the bill. The U.S. House will now take it up, with President Donald Trump voicing his support for its passage.

“Bipartisan bills like this are rare,” said Hickenlooper in his support. “Where we’ve landed isn’t perfection. But it is progress toward delivering on our promise to bring down prices, hold Big Tech accountable, and stop the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. Our work with Tribal Nations and environmental groups doesn’t end with today’s vote. We’ll keep pushing to address their concerns.”

Sen. Michael Bennet is concerned that the bill does very little to ensure the sovereignty of tribal governments and how they choose to steward their land. The bill also allows projects to move through with little to no public comment during permitting processes.

“Our electric grid is under significant strain and faces growing demand,” Bennet said in a statement. ‘We need to build new transmission, bring more energy, especially clean energy, onto the grid, and keep electricity affordable. We should make it easier to build new infrastructure, and I strongly support efforts to make this a reality. However, permitting reform is complex, and the details matter. I am concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico, is the leading sponsor of the bill. Native American leaders in the state have criticized him for his strong backing. Members of the All Pueblo Council of Governors in New Mexico are unanimous in their opposition.

“It wasn’t easy. But we proved that Democrats and Republicans can put politics aside and deliver meaningful results for the American people,” Heinrich said in a statement. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished. Now let’s get this bill across the finish line and signed into law.”

Here is a closer look at the bill from the National Association of Counties, which advises local county governments across the country on the legislation, its impact and how county governments should view the federal bill.

In its analysis, the bill creates “major reform” in six key areas: NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Clean Water Act, the Federal Power Act and public lands energy and mineral laws would all see changes.

On the subject of data centers, which the bill addresses, the proposed federal legislation would prevent data centers from passing grid infrastructure costs down to ratepayers, according to the National Association of Counties analysis.

County governments frequently interact with federal permitting statutes.

“The proposed changes will have significant impacts on county projects such as housing, broadband, transportation infrastructure and waterworks, as well as benefits for public lands counties,” the National Association of Counties says in its analysis.

description: United Nations climate talks in Turkey have failed to reach an overarching agreement due to disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels. The two-week negotiations known as COP31 ended Sunday without a
text:
"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" crushed the compe…

An issue with Delta Air Lines’ weight and balance automation…





COP31 President Murat Kurum, sits at center, during a closing plenary session at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra)































































ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday because of disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations, but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.

The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.

Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.

For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

text:
ALBANY — Upstate fossil fuel power plants are operating considerably more than in prior years, a trend that energy experts partly attribute to Quebec’s increased reliance on New York’s grid to help meet its electricity needs during an ongoing drought.

0:05

/

0:30

Skip Ad

Keep Watching

Quebec long served as a reliable exporter: In 2021, New York bought more clean electricity from Quebec’s powerful hydroelectric generators than a large-scale nuclear power plant produces in a year.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.

Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.

ONLY 99¢

But amid the four driest years on record, the province is now importing electricity from upstate New York to serve its needs. Even since a 339-mile power line was completed earlier this year supplying Quebec's hydro-produced electricity to New York City, the state has exported more energy than it has received from the province.

Increased fossil fuel usage could further undermine both Quebec's and New York's mandates to sharply reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Earlier this year, Gov. Kathy Hochul and the Democrat-led state Legislature delayed the 2019 Climate Act's short-term emission reduction mandates amid concerns they could not be met and over the state's surging utility costs over the last five years.

And two months ago, a federal judge struck down New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which sought to collect roughly $75 billion from companies — some controlled by foreign nations — deemed responsible for greenhouse gas emissions due to their refinement and production of fossil fuels.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Generating more energy in New York to send to Quebec creates “lots of smoke and lots of expense,” said Robert McCullough, a consultant who monitors Canadian energy markets.

Upstate fossil fuel plants ran about 38% more in 2025 than in 2021. On Nov. 17, roughly half of the electricity Hydro-Quebec, the utility serving the province, imported from New York came from natural gas facilities, according to data reviewed by the Times Union.

Lynn St-Laurent, a spokesperson for Hydro-Quebec, disputed that the province has driven up fossil fuel plant usage upstate.

“Hydro-Quebec has imported more electricity from external markets in recent years, including from New York,” Laurent said. “However, those imports cannot be characterized as purchases of fossil-fuel electricity. Electricity purchased through the (New York Independent System Operator) wholesale market is not sourced from a specific generating facility or fuel type, but rather from the generation mix (sic) available in upstate New York.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

She noted that the importation of New York's electricity to Quebec comes from “interconnections with upstate New York, where approximately 90% of electricity generation comes from low-emission sources, mainly hydropower and nuclear power. When excess energy is available in the region, it is therefore often predominantly low-emission.”

Upstate New York does get the vast majority of its electricity from emission-free sources, including four large nuclear reactors and several hydropower facilities. But the share of clean energy has declined in recent years as natural gas facilities need to be brought online more often, increasing greenhouse gas emissions.

Last week, the New York Independent System Operator, which manages New York's power grid, warned for the first time that without significantly more energy development, the state will not have enough electricity to meet its demands by 2033.

Nuclear and hydro stations run nearly nonstop, providing a baseline of power. Natural gas plants can turn on and off depending on electricity demand. As Quebec turns to New York for energy, that added demand largely forces gas facilities to ramp up to generate it, explained Tim Ennis, a market analyst for the research firm Grid Status.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Several other factors could explain some of the fossil fuel increase, including energy facilities shutting down in recent years, which puts more strain on the plants that remain. But Quebec’s shift from electricity exporter to importer has been far more meaningful, Ennis said.

Loading...

Not 'held to the same rules'

Constricted water reserves also complicate the recently completed $6 billion transmission cable that brings hydropower from Quebec to New York City. Running at full capacity, the Champlain Hudson Power Express could cover roughly 20% of the city’s power needs, helping displace old fossil fuel units.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“A million homes (will be) powered by this clean energy,” Hochul said at a June news conference touting the project. “It’s extraordinary when you think about it. Just before this past month, they had to be powered by mostly fossil fuels.”

The line has run far below full capacity as Hydro-Quebec manages its reservoirs — which serve over 90% of local electricity needs — with austerity.

“During (the Champlain Hudson Power Express’) first months of operation, delivery volumes were affected by a combination of water conditions and transmission congestion in (New York City),” said Peter Rose, a Hydro-Quebec spokesperson. “Despite these challenges, deliveries since June have saved New York $1 billion in wholesale capacity costs and displaced 400,000 tons of (carbon dioxide).”

The line delivered roughly 18% of its expected supply between June and October, according to data from Grid Status.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A contradiction is emerging, with New York City receiving clean electricity from Quebec while the state is simultaneously ramping up upstate power plants that send energy back to the province.

“The (Champlain Hudson Power Express) has allowed New York to substitute greenhouse gas emissions in New York City with greenhouse gas emissions upstate,” said Ken Girardin, a Manhattan Institute fellow who studies the state’s grid.

Girardin also objects to Hydro-Quebec buying electricity from the state without paying surcharges that, among other things, keep the four upstate nuclear power plants operating.

“When it comes to buying in New York, (Hydro-Quebec) should be held to the same rules as a New York hospital or manufacturing plant,” he said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The new power line needs to send up to 40% of its full capacity to comply with its New York contract. The agreement also created a ramp-up period before those compliance provisions take effect, which hasn’t ended yet.

“There is no requirement in the contract for Hydro-Quebec to provide continuous power on a daily basis,” said Deanna Cohen, a New York State Energy Research and Development Authority spokesperson. The contract provides “short-term energy delivery flexibility to reflect natural fluctuations in precipitation that impact Hydro-Quebec’s generation portfolio.”

Another recently completed cable between Quebec and New England has stiffer delivery requirements than the New York project and is already sending much more electricity.

The New England and New York developments “operate under different contractual structures, in different electricity markets and under different market conditions,” said Rose, the Hydro-Quebec spokesperson.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Hydro-Quebec has said they’re not economically motivated to deliver the New York line’s full capability. The utility is compensated based on power prices in Astoria, Queens, which are consistently lower than the city’s overall average. That can lead to the utility not receiving the revenue originally intended in the New York contract, a recent filing from the company explained.

Meeting both the New England and New York contracts while also relying less on imports from the U.S. “will be tense, especially if the drought persists,” said Normand Mousseau, a physics professor at the University of Montreal. “There’s a worry there, and Hydro Quebec hasn’t really answered or put numbers on to show that it can deliver. We signed two big contracts with Boston and New York. ... That’s a lot of electricity.”

Losing reliable power from Quebec comes at a challenging time for New York, as much of the state’s grid infrastructure is over 70 years old and new energy supply is struggling to keep pace with aging plants that are shutting down.

“Less dependable access to (Hydro-Quebec) imports is a concern, especially as New York’s reliability margins tighten,” said Lindsay Anderson, a Cornell University professor who studies energy policy. “The key question is whether imports are available when New York needs them most. If both systems are under stress at the same time, we can’t assume Quebec will have power to spare.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

As the drought persists, Quebec has less hydropower to export during dry summer months when New York sees peak electricity demand, Anderson explained.

But New York’s grid faces challenges in the winter, too, when the province’s demand peaks and relies most on exports from the state.

During the winter months, New York needs its natural gas system to both heat residents' homes through pipelines and supply fossil-fuel power plants. When demand rises from low temperatures, gas can become harder to source, forcing plants to use oil instead, which is usually more expensive and creates greater greenhouse gas emissions.

Quebec isn’t breaking any rules by importing energy. Electricity is often bought and sold across borders. New York benefited from the province’s ample clean power supply for years before drought conditions emerged. And it’s because of the slow development of new generating facilities, including wind and solar farms, that New York remains so reliant on fossil fuel plants.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The new power line connecting to New York City will ultimately provide substantial benefits to residents despite current challenges, said Chris Casey, utility regulatory director at the Natural Resources Defense Council.

“It’s not shocking that there’s a little bit of friction when you’re getting a brand-new resource, and especially a huge resource like that operational for the first time,” Casey said. “I would love it for the (Champlain Hudson Power Express) to be running 24/7. But that doesn’t mean that (because) they’re performing a little bit less in the early few months of the contract when there’s a number of odd factors going on that this line was a mistake.”

The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough for many nations and environmental groups.

Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would run against efforts to reduce overall emissions.

“The failure of this COP to deliver ambitious, fair, science-based outcomes falls squarely on the shoulders of richer nations, petrostates, and the disgracefully incompetent duo of the Turkish and Australian COP presidents,” said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure.

“Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that’s disappointing, very disappointing,” said Australia’s Chris Bowen, the president of negotiations in the unusual joint leadership.

Bowen said the explicit call in the Dubai agreement to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: “Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It’s happening. It’s happening at speed and it’s irreversible.”

text:
Hyundai Motor Group is teaming up with energy technology company WeaveGrid to expand smart charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services for Hyundai and Kia electric vehicle owners across North America. The partnership aims to connect EVs with the electricity grid, helping drivers reduce charging costs while supporting a more reliable and flexible energy system.

Under the agreement, WeaveGrid will power a new platform connecting Hyundai and Kia electric vehicles with energy services in the United States. The companies are developing smart charging and energy management features that will eventually be accessible through the myHyundai and Kia Access mobile apps.

The initial focus will be on smart charging, also known as vehicle-to-grid-unidirectional (V1G) charging, with bidirectional V2G capabilities planned for a later stage.

The new platform will allow drivers to manage their charging schedules directly through the mobile applications they already use.

Drivers will be able to set their preferred departure time and desired battery charge level. WeaveGrid’s technology will then automatically adjust charging schedules to take advantage of lower electricity rates and periods when demand on the local power grid is lower.

This approach could help Hyundai and Kia EV owners save money on electricity bills while reducing pressure on the power grid during peak demand periods.

WeaveGrid will provide direct, authorized connectivity between vehicles and utility companies, giving energy providers access to reliable charging and battery data across different vehicle models. The integration is also designed to maintain vehicle cybersecurity and protect customer privacy.

The companies are developing an interoperable platform that can support additional vehicle models, utility programs and more advanced energy services as the technology evolves.

While smart charging will be the first feature introduced, the longer-term goal is to expand the partnership into vehicle-to-grid technology.

Unlike conventional charging, V2G allows compatible electric vehicles to send electricity stored in their batteries back to the power grid. This could create new opportunities for EV owners to earn financial incentives while helping utilities balance electricity supply and demand.

Hyundai Motor Group already has experience with bidirectional charging technology. Most of its U.S. electric vehicle lineup is based on the Electric-Global Modular Platform (E-GMP), which was engineered with bidirectional charging capabilities in mind.

Existing examples include Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) functionality in the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Kia EV6, allowing owners to power external electrical devices using their vehicle batteries. The Kia EV9 also offers home backup power capabilities in supported configurations and markets.

The planned V2G expansion would take this technology further by allowing compatible vehicles to provide electricity to the wider energy system.

As bidirectional charging hardware, utility regulations and grid connection requirements develop, Hyundai and WeaveGrid intend to expand the platform to support these services.

For utilities, thousands of connected electric vehicles could become a distributed energy storage resource. Instead of relying exclusively on large stationary battery installations, energy providers could potentially use participating EV batteries to supply electricity where and when it is needed.

Hyundai Motor Group views the partnership as an important step toward making electric vehicles more valuable beyond transportation.

” We see our vehicles as part of a larger energy ecosystem, and our customers should benefit from that every day,” said Woong Tae Hwang, Vice President and Head of the EV Energy Strategy Group at Hyundai Motor Group.

He added that WeaveGrid’s experience working with U.S. utilities and its grid orchestration technology make it a suitable partner for developing smart charging services today and expanding into V2G solutions in the future.

WeaveGrid CEO and cofounder Apoorv Bhargava highlighted the growing demand for electricity and the potential role of electric vehicles in helping utilities manage it.

According to Bhargava, EVs represent one of the largest flexible energy resources available to utilities as electricity consumption continues to increase. The partnership is intended to give drivers a simpler charging experience while creating a path toward more advanced grid services.

The agreement also builds on Hyundai Motor Group’s strategic investment in WeaveGrid, announced in January 2025.

WeaveGrid already works with utilities serving more than 50% of electric vehicle owners in the United States. Its existing utility partnerships include Ameren Illinois, Exelon, CPS Energy, PG&E, Southern California Edison, Salt River Project, AEP and Xcel Energy.

This existing network could help Hyundai and Kia expand access to smart charging programs across multiple U.S. markets as the new platform develops.

However, availability will depend on individual utility programs. Eligibility requirements, incentives, charging features and enrollment conditions will vary depending on the driver’s location and participating electricity provider.

text:
Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

“Relying on fuel imports during an era of benign international relations and dependable strategic partners was a passable strategy. But in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, it is no longer tenable,” the report, released on Sunday, warned.

“Australia should expect the coming decades to be less stable than the past one. This means bracing, and preparing, for more oil shocks.”

Australia imports 97% of its liquid fuel. Grattan’s fuel plan report, Fuelling the Future, warns this “leaves us dangerously exposed to supply disruptions and price hikes”.

It argues that the US-Israel war in Iran has driven up inflation and cost Australians nearly $18bn, and the federal government directly at least $3bn, creating an opportunity the government “should seize” to boost fuel security.

Very little liquid fuel is produced or refined in Australia, with only two domestic oil refineries. But rather than boosting that number, Grattan says Australia should lower its reliance on imported fuels and fossil fuels generally by shifting towards EVs, including an ambitious target of 650,000 electric trucks nationwide by 2050.

That alone would cut Australia’s diesel use by 5bn litres a year, Grattan forecast. The report also calls for the fuel tax credit program – which costs Australia billions each year – to be capped at $35m per corporate group annually.

The biggest user of that program – which refunds taxes on fuel for machinery and heavy vehicles travelling on private, rather than public, roads – is the mining sector. The fuel tax credit scheme has become a political hot-button issue, with big business campaigning for it to be preserved amid calls for it to be reined in.

Tania Constable, CEO of the Minerals Council of Australia, rejected the Grattan proposal.

“Australia does need stronger fuel security, but making diesel more expensive for regional industries won’t create a single extra litre of fuel, build a refinery or improve supply-chain resilience. Instead, it would increase costs for miners, farmers, freight operators and regional businesses, with those costs ultimately flowing through to Australian households,” she said.

“If the goal is greater energy security, then Australia should be focused on increasing domestic production, expanding refining capacity and building more resilient supply chains – not making essential fuel more expensive.”

But the Grattan report says capping the scheme would save the government $3bn annually, and hasten the electrification of the mining sector – which it said would help the mining sector in the long run.

The report also recommends the government invest $1.1bn in a national network of chargers for EVs, as well as provide $2.4bn in vouchers for trucking firms to buy electric trucks. It calls for federal vehicle standards to be boosted to incentivise cleaner cars, as well as a restructuring of EV subsidies “to target people least able to afford them”.

Labor is widely expected to restrict current EV subsidies in next month’s mid-year economic update, as the government searches for budget savings.

In other areas of fuel use, Grattan notes Australia produces no “clean” jet fuel, and recommends the government direct $6bn to the first generation of so-called “clean refineries” to make that fuel.

Grattan says these refineries could provide nearly 10bn litres of clean jet fuel per year by 2050, but notes that it could cost $100bn to build them all, and that importing clean jet fuel would be cheaper.

But it argues that $6bn – the savings generated from just two years of capping the fuel tax credits to mining companies – would cover a quarter of the cost of the first five refineries, kickstarting the sector and providing fuel security in future supply shocks.

“Historically, making fuel meant making fossil fuels. But in an age of electrification and clean fuels, Australia now has more options,” the report said.

"The Board's reason for considering pausing action on legislative applications is to allow time for the county to complete the ongoing review of current data center policies and regulations," a press release from Loudoun County said.

The county said developers can continue to submit applications during the pause, and Loudoun County staff will continue to review them and schedule hearings with the planning commission. However, the board says there will be no public hearings or votes until the review is complete.

The decision could affect 33 active applications, according to the county.

Many US towns and cities have paused or outright banned large data center projects as residents debate their impact on communities. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”

The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process,” he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.

“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.

“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.

But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe’s ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.

“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”

Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”

The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process,” he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.

“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.

“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.

But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe’s ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.

“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”

Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.
