What Tesla Announced About Cybercab Personal Orders

Tesla did not hold a launch event. The company used its Robotaxi account on X to tell a small group of customers that they could now order a Cybercab for personal use. Reports dated Nov. 14 and after describe an invitation-only process, which means there is no public checkout open to everyone. Billionaires.africa, citing the same order flow, wrote that there is no public order page at this stage.

The terms that surfaced from those invitations are consistent across outlets. The listed price is $29,990 before taxes. A deposit of $1,000 is required and described as non-refundable. The vehicle seats two. It has no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla markets the personally owned version as fully autonomous, and it attaches a required monthly plan called the Autonomy Subscription, listed at $299 a month with the first month included.

Delivery timing is the other headline detail. The order page reportedly shows estimated delivery in December, in Austin, Texas. Car and Driver reported that deliveries are limited to several Texas cities and that the self-driving function is geofenced to the same areas Tesla’s Robotaxi service already covers. So the first owners will have a car that works in a defined patch of Texas, not one that can cross the country on its own.

Tesla has not published a broad ordering page or a national delivery schedule. Every figure in this article comes from the order screens and specification pages that invited customers shared, as relayed by named outlets. Anything beyond those pages stays general here.

The Tesla Cybercab Price: $29,990, Not Quite $30,000

Several headlines round the Cybercab up to $30,000. That rounding flatters the product slightly, but the actual listed number is $29,990. It sits $10 under the line Elon Musk drew at the 2024 unveiling, when he said Tesla expected the cost to be below $30,000. Kelley Blue Book wrote that the car aims to fulfill that sub-$30,000 promise, with the caveat that delivery fees and taxes were not disclosed.

That caveat is not small. A $29,990 price before taxes means the out-the-door figure will vary by state and by whatever delivery charges Tesla adds. The reports we reviewed do not say how the $1,000 deposit is applied to the final price, so we do not assume it comes off the sticker. Buyers should treat $29,990 as the starting number for the vehicle itself, not the total cost of using it.

The price also needs context against the product. A conventional new car at this price comes with a steering wheel, a license-holder at the helm, and no monthly fee to unlock the drivetrain. The Cybercab trades all three of those for a promise of autonomy. Whether $29,990 counts as cheap depends entirely on how much the autonomy is worth once the monthly bill arrives, and the next sections put numbers on that.

Why Cybercab Owners Cannot Drive It Themselves

The can’t-drive-it-yourself part is the most striking fact in the whole offer, and it is not a rumor. Two independent outlets, Digital Trends and Car and Driver, describe the car as a two-seater without a steering wheel or pedals. Any claim that a buyer can take manual control of the Cybercab is unconfirmed, because the vehicle as reported has no hardware to do it with.

Two seats, zero driver controls

Tesla built the Cybercab as a pure passenger pod. The cabin holds two people, and neither seat is a driver’s seat. There is no steering input, no brake pedal, and no accelerator. For a buyer, that removes the usual fallback of grabbing the wheel when the software hesitates. If the system cannot proceed, the car waits or asks for help through whatever remote support Tesla provides.

The design also explains the dimensions on the order page: 69.0 by 55.4 by 176.2 inches. The source that reported them noted that the page did not label which number is width, height, or length, so we do not assign them. What the figures do show is a compact, low vehicle built around two seats rather than around a driver.

What “fully autonomous” means in the listing

Tesla advertises the personally owned Cybercab as fully autonomous. That phrase deserves care. The same order terms say the vehicle will not run without the subscription, and Car and Driver reports that the self-driving ability is geofenced to Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas. In plain terms, “fully autonomous” here describes the design intent of a car without human controls. It does not mean the car can go anywhere, anytime, or without a paid plan.

That distinction is why the story resonates with readers searching for answers. People want to know whether they are buying a car or a subscription seat inside a car-shaped device. The honest answer is that they are buying both, and the second half is the part that never stops billing.

The $299 Autonomy Subscription and the Operate-or-Park Rule

Tesla’s own wording leaves little room for interpretation. As Teslarati reported, the Cybercab “will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription”. That sentence turns the subscription from an optional upgrade into the on-switch. Stop paying and the car is a parked object.

The listed rate is $299 per month, with the first month included in the purchase. Digital Trends worked out the annual figure at $3,588 a year, which matches simple multiplication. For a buyer who keeps the car for several years, that stream of payments is a large part of the real price, and it never counts toward ownership of anything.

Hardware makers have used paid unlocks before, from printers that gate ink cartridges to cars that charge for heated seats. The Cybercab pushes the idea to its limit because the paid feature is the entire driving function. Without it, a $29,990 vehicle cannot move under its own power in any way a buyer can control. That makes the subscription a different category of cost from the optional software plans on most cars today.

Tesla has not published, in anything we reviewed, what happens to the vehicle if a payment lapses mid-trip or how quickly the car would shut down. Those operational details will matter to the first owners, and they will decide whether the subscription feels like a utility bill or a leash.

Five-Year Cost of Owning a Cybercab

The headline price tells only part of the story, so we built a simple model. It uses the listed $29,990 price, the $299 monthly subscription with the first month included, and the roughly $115 monthly figure that Musk said the fee should match. It excludes taxes, delivery fees, insurance, charging, and the effect of the deposit, because those inputs are not confirmed. The arithmetic is ours and uses only the published numbers.

Over five years at the listed $299 rate, the subscription alone adds $17,641 and pushes the total to $47,631 before taxes. That means the monthly plan accounts for about 37% of the five-year spend. At the $115 figure Musk floated, the same period costs $6,785 in subscription fees and $36,775 in total, a gap of $10,856. The subscription would pass the $29,990 sticker price after just over eight years of payments.

Our earlier analysis showed how that stream compares with a conventional car, in the piece on why the Cybercab costs more than a Model 3 by month 45. The new table extends the same logic to five years and adds the lower fee scenario. The pattern holds in both cases. The sticker price is the smaller number in the long run.

Musk Says the Fee Is Too High

The most unusual detail in the coverage is that Tesla’s own chief executive appears to disagree with the fee. After orders opened, Musk wrote, as reported by Yahoo Autos: “But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That is a rare moment. A CEO publicly says his company’s listed price is wrong, on the same day it takes orders. Reports so far show the $299 listing unchanged, so the two numbers now coexist. One is what invited buyers see on the order screen, and the other is where Musk says the fee belongs.

There are two plausible readings, and both are interpretation rather than fact. The first is that the $299 figure is a placeholder that Tesla will cut before the first deliveries. The second is that Musk was commenting on a price set elsewhere in the company and pressure will build to revise it. We cannot tell which is true, and Tesla has not said. Buyers placing a non-refundable $1,000 deposit today are betting on the lower number.

The gap is also a pricing signal for the broader autonomy market. A $115 plan would sit near the cost of Tesla’s existing driver-assistance subscriptions, which Musk himself pointed to. A $299 plan prices full autonomy at about 2.6 times that level. Our table shows that difference is worth more than $10,000 over five years.

Range, Charging and Size: What the Order Page Shows

Beyond price and subscription, the specification pages that invited customers saw offer a few hardware numbers. We reviewed them against what outlets reported and kept only figures that appear in the fact record. The table below separates what is stated from what is not.

The 279-mile EPA range and the 123 miles added in 15 minutes of Supercharging come from the specification page, which we covered in detail in our look at the Cybercab spec page and its 279-mile range. One report on the charging claim noted that the 123-mile figure assumes a constant 65 mph, so real results will depend on conditions.

A conflicting range number to ignore

Not every page agrees. A market-analysis page from Admiral Markets lists a preliminary range of about 293 miles. We take the more conservative figure, which is the 279 miles shown as EPA estimated on Tesla’s own specification page. When a preliminary number and an official one disagree, the official one wins, and the lower figure is the safer one to plan around.

From 2024 Promise to 2026 Order Page

Tesla’s Cybercab story starts with a stage and a promise. At the 2024 unveiling, Musk said that you will be able to buy one, and he also said Tesla expected the cost to be below $30,000. He added a production target: “We expect to be in production with the Cybercab … in 2026. So, yeah, before 2027, let me put it that way.”

Judged against those three statements, November 2026 delivers partial results. Orders exist, which satisfies the first. The price lands at $29,990, which satisfies the second by $10. Deliveries are estimated for December, which would land inside the 2026 window if Tesla meets it. The part the 2024 remarks did not spell out is the $299 subscription and the lack of driver controls as a condition of ownership.

The timeline also shows how Tesla’s autonomy business has moved from software upgrades toward a service model. The company’s Robotaxi program in Austin already works as a ride-hailing service. The Cybercab order extends that idea by letting individuals hold the vehicle while the company keeps control of the driving layer. That shift matters more than the sticker price, because it changes who decides when a Cybercab can move.

Investors have taken note of the pace. Our earlier piece on what Tesla investors are watching, including Cybercab metros tracked how the market framed the rollout before orders opened.

How the Cybercab Compares With Robotaxi Fleets

The Cybercab arrives in a market where most driverless vehicles belong to operators, not individuals. Waymo, Pony.ai and WeRide run fleets that the public rides in. Customers pay per trip, and the company carries the cost of the vehicles, the maintenance and the software. Tesla is offering a different split, where the customer buys the vehicle and rents the software.

Scale shows how early this still is. In our coverage of Pony.ai’s third quarter, the company reported 2,768 robotaxis, a figure that framed the question of how big Tesla’s fleet really is. WeRide, in a separate report we covered, said its robotaxi revenue topped RMB 100 million, up 204%. Those fleets are measured in thousands of vehicles, and the Cybercab’s first deliveries are measured in a handful of Texas cities.

The comparison below summarizes the ownership model, not performance, since we have no verified head-to-head safety or reliability data.

The pattern is clear. In a fleet, the rider cannot drive and also owns nothing. In a conventional car, the owner drives and pays no fee to move. The Cybercab sits between them, with the owner holding the asset while the company holds the controls. Whether that bundle appeals depends on how much a buyer values having a private autonomous car on call.

Market Impact for Tesla, Rivals and the Hardware Business

For Tesla, the order opening matters more as a signal than as a volume event. Invitations to select customers in a few Texas cities will not move annual deliveries. What they do is test whether people will pay a car price plus a utility-style fee for a vehicle they cannot steer. The response will shape how Tesla prices and markets autonomy in every other product. You can find more hardware coverage in our hardware section.

For rivals, the offer sets a public reference point. Any company that plans to sell autonomous vehicles to individuals now faces a comparison with $29,990 and $299 a month. If Musk’s $115 figure becomes the real price, that comparison gets tighter. Fleet operators, who sell rides rather than vehicles, face a different test, which is whether private owners can undercut per-trip fares once the fixed costs are spread over years of use.

For suppliers and the wider hardware market, the Cybercab is a bet on the two-seat, controls-free form factor. It removes steering columns, pedal assemblies and driver displays from the bill of materials, and it replaces them with sensing and compute hardware. We do not have verified component details from Tesla, so we limit ourselves to the structural point. A vehicle without driver controls can be simpler to build in some ways and more demanding in others.

Waymo’s own regulatory record shows that autonomy remains a moving target. Our report on Waymo’s two recalls over closed freeway lanes and hand signals showed that even a mature fleet operator has to patch edge cases that humans handle without thinking. A Cybercab owner with no steering wheel has no way to handle such a case manually.

Confirmed, Reported and Unconfirmed Claims

With so many numbers circulating, a scorecard helps. The list below sorts the main claims by how well they hold up, using only the reported record.

Confirmed: Tesla is inviting select customers to buy a Cybercab for personal use. Basis: tesla Robotaxi account announcement.

Reported: The price is $29,990 before taxes. Basis: order page, relayed by multiple outlets.

Unconfirmed: The price is exactly $30,000. Basis: rounded headline figure, listed price is $29,990.

Reported: The car needs a $299 monthly subscription. Basis: tesla’s stated operating requirement.

Unconfirmed: Owners can drive it themselves. Basis: the vehicle has no steering wheel or pedals.

Unconfirmed: It runs without the subscription. Basis: terms say it will not operate without it.

Unconfirmed: The subscription will drop to about $115. Basis: musk’s comment, no Tesla price change reported.

Estimated: Deliveries begin in December in Austin. Basis: order page timing, not a guarantee.

Two lines in this table deserve emphasis. The rounded $30,000 figure appears in some headlines, but it is not the listed price. And the claim that a buyer can drive the car has no support in any reported spec. Readers who see either claim stated as fact should treat the source with caution.

Open Questions on Liability, Insurance and Service Areas

Several questions that matter to a real buyer have no public answer yet. We found none in the published coverage, and we list them as questions rather than assumptions.

Who is liable when a driverless car owned by an individual has a collision, the owner or the company that supplies the driving software?

How will insurers price a vehicle that has no human operator and a mandatory software plan?

What happens to a car parked outside the geofenced service area, and can it move at all?

Does the $1,000 deposit credit against the $29,990 price, or is it a separate fee?

Will the $299 rate hold, fall toward $115, or rise over time?

How quickly can Tesla disable a vehicle if a payment lapses?

These are not edge cases. They define what ownership means when a company controls the driving function. Early buyers will effectively write the answers through their experience, and regulators in Texas and beyond will watch closely. For the moment, buyers should read the order terms line by line and assume that anything not written down is not guaranteed.

Five Predictions for the Cybercab Rollout

The following are our own judgments based on the reported facts, not confirmed plans from Tesla.

The subscription price will draw the most pressure. With Musk on record calling $299 too high, we expect Tesla to face questions until the number changes or is explained.

The first wave will be small and local. Invitations, a geofence and Texas-only delivery point to dozens or hundreds of early buyers, not thousands, though Tesla has not given a count.

Liability and insurance will become the main story. Once cars reach owners, the first incident reports will turn on who pays when nobody is driving.

Rivals will frame their offers against the $299 figure. Any competitor that sells to individuals will be compared with Tesla’s monthly fee.

December timing will slip or stay narrow. An estimated delivery window is not a guarantee, and a late delivery would echo earlier Tesla schedules.

The takeaway: the Cybercab is a real product with a real price, but it is not yet a normal car purchase. It is an early-access subscription vehicle that happens to come with a sticker price attached.

FAQ: Tesla Cybercab Price and Ownership

How much does the Tesla Cybercab cost? The listed price is $29,990 before taxes, according to reports from Car and Driver, Kelley Blue Book and Digital Trends. A $1,000 non-refundable deposit is required to order, and delivery fees and taxes are not disclosed.

Can I drive the Cybercab myself? No. The two-seat vehicle has no steering wheel or pedals, so there is no way for an owner to drive it manually. Any claim to the contrary is unconfirmed.

Do I have to pay the $299 monthly subscription? Yes, according to the reported terms. Tesla says the car will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription. The first month is included, and the plan works out to $3,588 a year at the listed rate.

Will the subscription price drop to $115 a month? Musk said the fee should be closer to about $115 a month, but reports show the $299 listing unchanged. Treat $115 as a stated opinion, not a confirmed price.

How far can the Cybercab go and how fast does it charge? The specification page lists a 279-mile EPA-estimated range. Tesla’s page reportedly says Supercharging adds 123 miles in 15 minutes.

When and where will the first Cybercabs be delivered? The order page estimates delivery in December in Austin, Texas. Car and Driver reports that early deliveries are limited to several Texas cities, and the self-driving function is geofenced to Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas.

The world’s energy use has permanently and fundamentally changed in the wake of the oil and gas supply crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, the International Energy Agency (IEA) concludes, in a sweeping analysis that nevertheless shows only incremental reductions in fossil fuel demand across four of the five possible energy futures it presents.

Electrification, diversification of energy supplies, and a “premium on domestically available resources”, particularly solar and other renewables, all emerge as defining trends in this year’s edition of the IEA’s World Energy Outlook (WEO), the annual report the Paris-based agency previously styled as “the gold standard of energy analysis”. The report, released Nov. 19, cites geopolitical tensions, cyberattacks, and rising climate risk as elements of an “unprecedented shock to the system” that “compounds a broader sense of fragility in energy markets.”

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in a release. “In pursuit of greater energy security, countries must take care not to replace one dependency with another. But encouragingly for the future, energy security and energy transitions have never been so closely aligned.”

While the IEA followed up that statement with a series of scenarios, most of them showing only a gradual shift off fossil fuels, independent observers were rather more optimistic.

“The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” Dave Jones, chief analyst at the Ember energy think tank, said in a release. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think.”

“The key takeaway from the IEA’s latest World Energy Outlook is simple: fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures,” said David Tong, global industry lead at Oil Change International. “After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets. The IEA has yet again reiterated that there is no room for new oil, gas, and coal beyond existing fields to limit global warming to 1.5ºC.”

Biggest Energy Supply Shock Ever

The IEA describes the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, brought on by the American/Israeli war on Iran, as “by far the largest” of the oil supply shocks—BNEF founder Michael Liebreich counts 14 of them—since 1970.

“Vulnerabilities in traditional fossil fuel supply systems have again been highlighted in 2026,” and the year’s energy crisis “could have important impacts on risk perceptions and technology choices,” the report states. “It could boost deployment of a range of low-emissions technologies and speed up the electrification of end uses, especially in oil- and gas-importing countries seeking to limit import dependence,” although regions with abundant coal resources might be inclined to lean on them more heavily.

After “an extraordinarily turbulent period for oil and gas markets” right through the 2020s, the report says energy crises “can have consequences that extend beyond short-term supply disruptions and price increases,” reshaping policies, risk perceptions, and consumer choices far into the future. It notes that some regions that depend on fuel imports are speeding up deployment of solar, heat pumps, battery storage, electric vehicles, and other clean energy options, but places far greater emphasis on those trends in the most ambitious of the five projections.

However—along with the unknown duration of the Hormuz crisis, the degree to which countries like the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela will increase production, and future fossil demand and prices, the IEA identifies the pace of the energy transition as a serious uncertainty for the industry.

In the only one of the five scenarios that projects a rapid transition, “the scaling-up of clean energy technologies leads oil and gas demand to fall by an average of around 4% per year to 2035,” the agency states. “The steepness of these falls means that no new long lead-time conventional oil and gas projects would be required in this scenario, while some existing supply would need to be shut in.”

While today’s reality falls far short of that future, the report adds, “this illustrates how new oil and gas projects could face substantial commercial risks if transitions accelerate, placing sustained pressure on existing business models.”

Meanwhile, despite a “major windfall for the oil and gas industry, with exporters set to receive an additional US$700 billion from oil and gas sales in 2026 over and above the 10-year average,” fossil producers may not be in a hurry to increase their footprint. The IEA foresees only a 1% increase in oil and gas investment for this year, while an 8% increase in capital costs “will limit increases in drilling activity, equipment purchases, and new production capacity.” It will also “raise the risk of overruns and delays for projects already under development,” leading to “closer scrutiny” for new infrastructure awaiting approval.

The IEA somewhat reinforces longstanding concerns that fossil companies are on the verge of producing far more liquefied natural gas (LNG) than countries will need. Projects now under construction are on track to increase global LNG supply from 610 to 940 billion cubic metres (bcm) per day, with most of them due online by 2030, and the IEA says demand would have to grow by nearly 9% per year—twice the pace between 2020 and 2025—to absorb all the new capacity.

That happens in the Current Policies Scenario (CPS), a widely critiqued and previously abandoned “zombie scenario” that the agency restored to last year’s WEO after months of intensive bullying by the Trump administration and now allows for “continued LNG demand growth in China, Europe, India and Southeast Asia, among others.”

In the somewhat more realistic Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which factors in energy choices that governments have adopted or formally put forward, global LNG production exceeds the available supply by 70 bcm by 2035. Other projections in the report show lower LNG demand and a correspondingly larger supply glut, with the possibility that importers will take advantage of lower prices—to the detriment of producing countries like Canada.

Five Possible Futures

All told, the IEA presents five possible futures for global energy demand and supply, in a 564-page report that repeatedly and somewhat awkwardly reminds readers those outcomes are modelled scenarios, not predictions. It devotes full chapters to its Current Policies and Stated Policies Scenarios, then presents an Additional Response Case (ARC) and a Low Hormuz Case (LHC) in a single, shorter chapter titled “potential additional responses”. The Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE), first introduced in the 2021 WEO following a decisive shift in the composition of the IEA governing board, shows up in the middle of a chapter on the outlook for energy transitions.

Even as it acknowledges that “many of the energy sources and technologies that enable lower fuel imports also come with lower emissions,” the IEA presents a headline scenario that shows increased fossil fuel consumption, with subsequent analysis that suggests only minor reductions over the next decade. A longstanding concern with the WEO is that its lead scenario each year draws the lion’s share of attention from analysts and investors, potentially influencing many billions of dollars’ worth of energy decision-making around the world. In response to last year’s report, an analysis by a government-funded think tank in India showed coal consumption more than doubling through 2050, despite growing evidence that the country is pivoting rapidly to solar.

• The IEA’s lead scenario, titled the Current Policies Scenario (CPS), “has the greatest degree of continuity with pre-conflict settings, as it considers only those policies and measures that are firmly embedded in legislation,” the IEA writes. It projects energy demand rising 1.2% per year through 2035 and a total of 27% by 2050, with fossil fuels accounting for 65% of the global energy mix by mid-century. It shows no peak in fossil fuel demand, with oil consumption hitting 114 million barrels per day in 2050 while coal goes into a structural decline.

The CPS places global carbon dioxide emissions at 38 billion tonnes, “barely changed from today’s level”, producing average global warming of 2.0°C in 2050 and 2.9°C in 2100.

• The Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) shows oil demand levelling off at 103 million barrels per day around 2030 before going into a slow decline. Energy-related carbon dioxide emissions peak before 2030 then begin to gradually drop, “mainly because of lower coal-fired power generation in advanced economies and China,” the report states. “Natural gas demand grows until the mid-2030s, albeit not quickly enough to absorb the wave of new liquefied natural gas supply.”

Renewable energy sees the largest growth in demand, and the higher efficiency of renewable electricity halves the annual growth in energy demand, from 1.6% over the last decade to 0.8% in 2035. Renewables grow from 33% of global electricity generation today to 50% in 2035, and nuclear stages what the IEA calls a “comeback”, growing from 9% to 10% of total generation. Gas power plants see growth but lose market share, while coal falls from 34 to 20% of electricity production.

The report lists multiple responses to the Hormuz crisis—from adding new oil and gas export routes and increasing strategic reserves, to speeding up clean electrification and energy efficiency and turning to domestic biofuels or biomethane. “The ARC is grounded in measures that are under consideration in different countries, but it is not intended as a prediction of future government actions,” the IEA stresses. “Given the uncertainty surrounding future geopolitical developments and the duration of market disruptions, actual policy responses could differ substantially” from either the ARC or the Low Hormuz Case.

• The IEA’s net-zero (NZE) scenario has unabated fossil fuels falling to 6% of total energy supply by 2050, from 72% last year. As a result, the IEA writes, “scenarios with faster electrification and more rapid growth in renewable energy see slower growth in total energy demand.” But that potential is largely lost in the CPS, the lead scenario in the series.

Synopsis

Saraogi E-Ventures plans to explore sodium-ion battery technology for electric scooters starting in December. The company aims to capture demand in India's sub-Rs 1 lakh market segment. Currently, most electric models utilize lithium-ion technology, which is more common. The company intends to enhance its presence in states where it operates rather than pursuing national expansion. The long-term goal is to achieve profitability by 2028 with increased sales.

Kolkata: Kolkata-based Saraogi E-Ventures, which markets electric two-wheelers under the E-Went brand, sees significant growth opportunities in India's price-sensitive markets, particularly in the sub-Rs 1 lakh segment, while exploring sodium-ion battery technology as an alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries, its founder and CEO Umang Kumar Saraogi said.

The company plans to begin trials of sodium-ion battery-powered scooters around December, deploying some vehicles for testing. The technology is being explored for its potential safety advantages over conventional lithium-ion batteries, although its relatively lower energy density makes the battery packs bulkier, Saraogi said.

"It is supposed to be safer. We expect to conduct trials here starting in December and deploy some vehicles with these batteries. The economics and convenience have to be evaluated before we can deploy them in our new product launches. Currently, most of the models use lithium-ion technology," he told PTI.

If commercialised successfully, sodium-ion batteries could accelerate India's push to indigenise battery manufacturing by tapping into abundant domestic raw materials, cutting the country's heavy reliance on imported lithium-ion components.

The battery trials form part of its broader product development efforts.

Saraogi said regional electric two-wheeler manufacturers have considerable growth potential as national brands largely focus on premium models, leaving the sub-Rs 1 lakh segment and smaller towns relatively underserved.

Buyers in tier-three and smaller towns, as well as rural areas and consumers in tier I and II cities, often look for affordable mobility options, creating space for regional players that can build their businesses through local dealer networks, lower ownership costs and word-of-mouth publicity rather than expensive branding campaigns, he said.

"For someone earning Rs 30,000-50,000 a month, a high-priced electric scooter is often beyond their consideration. They are looking for a reliable, value-for-money mobility solution that fits within a budget of Rs 1 lakh, with minimum maintenance cost over the vehicle's life," Saraogi said.

"At E-Went, we believe electric mobility should be for every Indian who wants to make a smarter choice, not just those who can afford premium technology," he said.

Saraogi said national manufacturers largely concentrate on tier-one and tier-two cities with relatively expensive models, leaving considerable scope for smaller companies to cater to customers in less penetrated markets.

Rather than pursuing an aggressive pan-India expansion, Saraogi said the company plans to deepen its presence in the states where it currently operates, including West Bengal, Jharkhand, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Assam, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.

The company has increased its monthly sales from around 100 electric two-wheelers four years ago to 1,000-1,100 units currently, largely through word-of-mouth publicity, he said.

"We don't plan to go national. If we deepen our presence in the states where we are already operating, the market potential itself is very large," he said.

Saraogi E-Ventures' revenue crossed Rs 50 crore in FY26, and it is targeting Rs 65 crore in the current financial year. The company aims to become profitable by 2028, he added.

description:

During the January–October period, South Korea's auto exports to China plummeted 34.9 percent year-on-year to USD 168.77 million.

In contrast, South Korea's basic tariff rate on imported passenger cars is 8 percent, lower than China's most-favored-nation tariff rate of 15 percent.
text:
▲ Tesla

Driven by a boom in Tesla electric vehicles produced at its Shanghai factory in China, South Korea's auto imports and trade deficit with China both hit record highs this year.

As Tesla's domestic sales surged to about twice last year's level, South Korea's auto trade deficit with China reached KRW 6 trillion in the first ten months of the year, far exceeding last year's annual deficit.

The market share of Chinese-made vehicles in South Korea's electric vehicle market has also surged by nearly 33 percentage points over the past four years, marking the third-fastest increase among major global auto-producing nations.

Amid growing concerns that the expansion of Chinese-made vehicles in the domestic market could threaten the production base of South Korea's automotive industry, calls for supportive measures are growing louder.

According to the Korea International Trade Association and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy on November 22, South Korea's auto trade deficit with China totaled USD 4.23056 billion from January to October this year, up 92.7 percent from the same period last year.

This translates to approximately KRW 6 trillion.

It well surpasses last year's annual trade deficit of USD 2.51162 billion.

During the January–October period, South Korea's auto exports to China plummeted 34.9 percent year-on-year to USD 168.77 million.

In contrast, auto imports surged 79.2 percent to USD 4.39033 billion, amounting to 26 times the value of exports.

South Korea's auto trade balance with China has remained in deficit for 10 consecutive years from 2017 to this year.

The deficit widened from USD 466.05 million in 2022 to USD 1.72976 billion in 2024.

The growth in domestic sales of Chinese-made cars is being led by Teslas manufactured at the Shanghai Gigafactory.

Currently, the vast majority of Teslas sold in South Korea are made in China.

According to the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association, new registrations of Tesla vehicles in South Korea surged 105.0 percent year-on-year to 98,313 units during the first 10 months of this year.

Its market share in the imported car sector has surpassed 30 percent.

The Tesla Model Y recorded 78,631 newly registered units through October this year, making it the best-selling imported car model.

BYD, a Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer that entered the South Korean market last year, also leveraged its price competitiveness to record over 20,000 new domestic registrations between January and October this year.

Polestar, an affiliate of China's Geely Group, is also selling vehicles produced in China within the domestic market.

The penetration speed of Chinese-made electric vehicles in the South Korean market stands out even among the world's top 10 auto-producing nations.

According to statistics from the Korea Automobile Mobility Industry Association and global research agencies, the proportion of Chinese-made vehicles in South Korea's electric vehicle market jumped 32.8 percentage points from 1.1 percent in 2021 to 33.9 percent in 2025.

This is the third-highest increase among the world's top 10 auto-producing countries, following Mexico (90.7 percentage points) and Brazil (81.6 percentage points).

Unlike Mexico and Brazil, which serve as major production hubs for global automakers, South Korea has built its ecosystem centered around domestic auto brands, making the market expansion of Chinese electric vehicles a matter of significant ripple effects, analysts note.

The automotive industry attributes the differences in the penetration speed of Chinese electric vehicles across countries primarily to domestic industry protection policies.

The United States imposes tariffs of up to 127.5 percent on Chinese electric vehicles, while the European Union applies up to 45.3 percent by adding supplementary countervailing duties to a base tariff of 10 percent.

The United States is also tightening connected vehicle regulations, effectively blocking Chinese automobiles from entering its market.

India levies a minimum base tariff of 70 percent on imported cars.

France reorganized its electric vehicle subsidy system starting in 2024 to favor locally produced models.

Japan introduced a tax credit of 400,000 yen per domestically produced battery electric vehicle starting the same year.

In contrast, South Korea's basic tariff rate on imported passenger cars is 8 percent, lower than China's most-favored-nation tariff rate of 15 percent.

Under the South Korea-China Free Trade Agreement, both countries excluded passenger cars from tariff elimination, maintaining existing tariffs.

In the first half of this year, China surpassed Germany to become the largest source of imported cars in South Korea.

In response to slowing domestic market growth and intensifying competition, Chinese companies are expanding their penetration into emerging markets such as Southeast Asia, Central and South America, and the Middle East, as well as Europe.

In South Korea, following BYD, Zeekr has begun sales, and Xpeng is accelerating its domestic entry, intensifying the market offensive by Chinese firms.

Lee Hang-koo, a distinguished professor at Namseoul University, said, "China has caught up considerably in quality and is overwhelmingly superior in cost-effectiveness."

Amid the surging sales of Chinese-made vehicles, the footing of domestic cars is narrowing.

According to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's trends in the automobile industry, domestic sales by local automakers dropped 7.2 percent year-on-year to 1,043,729 units in the first 10 months of this year.

Conversely, imported car sales rose 23.3 percent to 325,542 units.

The automotive industry expresses concern that the rapid influx of Chinese electric vehicles could threaten South Korea's domestic automaker production base and parts supply chain, leading to a contraction of the overall industrial ecosystem.

Consequently, demands are mounting from the industry and the National Assembly to include electric vehicles under domestic production tax credit schemes to stimulate domestic manufacturing and investment.

In the National Assembly, successive amendments to the Special Tax Treatment Control Act have been proposed to include futuristic vehicles such as electric vehicles as targets for domestic production tax credits.

The government is also reviewing plans to include electric vehicles in the scope of domestic production tax credits.

An automotive industry official said, "Backed by astronomical support from the Chinese government, Chinese electric vehicles are securing price competitiveness across the entire supply chain, including finished cars, raw materials, parts, and batteries, and are encroaching on the global market."

The official added, "Unlike the U.S. and Europe, South Korea has an export-driven industrial structure, making it difficult to take aggressive trade measures. If policy support, including domestic production tax credits, is not implemented in a timely manner, the automotive industry ecosystem will wither away."

The justices denied the local governments’ application to appeal a May 7 decision by the Michigan Court of Appeals.
They also declined to review other issues raised in separate cross-appeals, while leaving the deadline dispute open for argument.

text:
LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - The Michigan Supreme Court has declined to hear an appeal from a group of local governments in a case involving state rules for renewable energy projects. But the court will hear arguments on a separate dispute over a deadline that could affect local review of those projects.

The case involves the implementation of Public Act 233 of 2023, a Michigan law governing the siting of certain renewable energy facilities. The court’s order does not approve or deny any specific project.

The justices denied the local governments’ application to appeal a May 7 decision by the Michigan Court of Appeals. They also declined to review other issues raised in separate cross-appeals, while leaving the deadline dispute open for argument.

What is the deadline dispute?

At issue is when a 30-day clock starts for a local official to tell a developer that the community has a qualifying renewable energy ordinance. Such an ordinance can give the community a role in reviewing a proposed project.

The Michigan Public Service Commission determined that a developer could proceed as though a community did not have a qualifying ordinance if the local official did not provide notice within 30 days of an offer to meet.

The Court of Appeals reversed that finding. Now, the Supreme Court has asked the parties to address whether the appeals court was wrong to do so.

The justices also want arguments on whether a different interpretation should apply when a meeting with a local official is never held or is unreasonably delayed.

The Supreme Court has not decided the deadline question. Its order schedules arguments on the requests for an appeal; it does not settle the dispute.

What happens next?

The case involves dozens of local governments, including Clinton County, Ionia County, Shiawassee County, Eagle Township, Ingham Township, Stockbridge Township and Watertown Township.

Arguments will be scheduled during the court’s January 2027 session. Briefs from the parties asking the court to review the deadline issue are due December 11 with responses due December 28. Reply briefs may be filed by January 4, 2027.

text:
As Chinese-made electric vehicles rapidly dominate the South Korean market, there is a growing call for prompt implementation of policy support such as domestic production tax credits. Critics argue that while countries around the world are taking action to protect their own industries, only South Korea is handing over its home market entirely to China’s offensive.

According to statistics from the Korea Automobile and Mobility Industry Association (KAMA) and major global research firms, the share of Chinese-made electric vehicles in the South Korean EV market surged by 32.8 percentage points (p) in just four years, rising from 1.1% in 2021 to 33.9% in 2025.

This ranks third among the top 10 global automobile-producing countries (China, United States, Japan, India, South Korea, Germany, Mexico, Brazil, Spain, and France) according to the Organisation Internationale des Constructeurs d’Automobiles (OICA), following Mexico and Brazil. Considering that Mexico and Brazil serve as production hubs for brands from other countries, this means that among countries with their own domestic brands, South Korea is losing its market at the most rapid pace.

The situation is even more pronounced this year. Among 258,284 newly registered domestic electric passenger vehicles from January to September 2026, the share of domestically produced vehicles was only 48.7%, falling below 50% for the first time in history. As major models from China’s BYD and Zeekr have gained popularity, other companies such as Xpeng and Chery Automobile are also swiftly moving to target the South Korean market.

The domestic automotive industry is calling for proactive government response. South Korea operates a purchase subsidy system that provides the same benefits to imported cars, but it effectively lacks defensive measures such as tax incentives or high tariffs.

In the United States, where the share of Chinese-made electric vehicles has actually decreased,

tariffs totaling 127.5% are imposed on Chinese-made EVs based on Section 301 (100%) and Section 232 (25%) of trade laws. Approaching the issue from a national security perspective, the U.S. also bans the import and sale within the country of vehicles equipped with autonomous driving software developed by Chinese companies, starting with 2027 model year vehicles.

The European Union (EU) has been imposing countervailing duties of up to 35.3% since late October 2024, based on the results of its “anti-subsidy investigation” into Chinese-made electric vehicles, taking into account factors such as each company’s cooperation with the investigation and the scale of subsidies received from the Chinese government. In France, the EV subsidy policy known as the “Green Bonus” was reformed starting in 2024 to favor locally produced models, excluding numerous Chinese-made EV models from subsidy eligibility. As a result, the market share of Chinese-made electric vehicles, which reached 31.4% in 2023, dropped to 13.4% last year.

Japan has implemented the “Strategic Sector Domestic Production Promotion Tax System” since 2024, often referred to as the “Japanese version of the IRA (Inflation Reduction Act),” providing corporate tax reductions for up to 10 years, proportional to production and sales volumes, in five strategic sectors including electric vehicles and semiconductors.

While South Korea’s defenses were left open, the comparative advantage of Korean EV exports has also deteriorated rapidly over the past two years. According to an analysis by the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI) of the Revealed Comparative Advantage index (RCA), a key export competitiveness indicator that divides a specific product’s share in domestic exports by its share in global exports, the RCA for electric vehicles plummeted from 2.92 in 2023 to 1.48 in 2025, nearly halving in two years.

In contrast, China’s EV RCA was only 0.10 in 2017 but rose to 1.13 in 2022, surpassing 1 to secure a comparative advantage, and further increased to 1.49 in 2025, overtaking South Korea (1.48).

Given these circumstances, the domestic industry has continuously requested that electric vehicles be included in the scope of the domestic production tax credit support. As both ruling and opposition parties have agreed and submitted a related bill, the industry’s position is that the government should review the matter favorably. An industry official stated, “Chinese-made electric vehicles possess price competitiveness across the entire supply chain based on astronomical support from the Chinese government, eroding the global market,” adding, “Looking at the EV market alone, even traditional top global brands are at a level where they cannot compete with Chinese brands.”

Another official warned, “If the government turns a blind eye now, China will dominate the domestic market within just a few years,” and cautioned, “If policy support is not implemented in a timely manner, the entire industrial ecosystem could wither away.”

text:
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

Deadlocked - that is the word to describe the COP31 U.N. climate talks, which are now in overtime. Delegates from nearly 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya, Turkey, to discuss international action on climate change. Negotiations were supposed to wrap up yesterday, but talks have now spilled into a second night. NPR's Rachel Waldholz is covering the talks from Turkey and joins us from the media center. Welcome.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: Hi, Rob.

SCHMITZ: You sound a little tired, Rachel. I get the sense that...

(LAUGHTER)

SCHMITZ: ...These U.N. climate conferences, they oftentimes - they go overtime, and they oftentimes end up deadlocked. Is there anything different about this time around?

WALDHOLZ: I mean, yes and no. The countries here, they're deadlocked over the two big issues that are really the two big issues at the heart of international climate action, and that is money and fossil fuels.

SCHMITZ: OK.

WALDHOLZ: Specifically this time around, some countries - they want to come away from this climate summit with an agreement that explicitly calls on the world to transition away from fossil fuels. That's because burning coal and oil and natural gas is the primary driver of global warming, and they want that called out. But other countries, especially big oil producers like Saudi Arabia and Russia, don't want language that specifically targets fossil fuels. And so that has become a big sticking point for some countries this year.

SCHMITZ: OK, which countries?

text:
The Chinese auto ‘onslaught’ has now become a source of ‘fear.’

Chinese-made Teslas, along with Chinese electric vehicle companies backed by the full support of the Chinese government, are shaking up the global auto market.

With prices far below expectations and a relentless onslaught, Europe’s auto industry, once a force to be reckoned with in the global market, is facing a fight for survival.

In Germany, the auto industry is a key industry that supports a pillar of the national economy and generates significant employment. As it begins to lose competitiveness, the threat of an economic crisis is becoming a reality, beyond the jobs crisis.

South Korea is increasingly likely to be next. Chinese-made Teslas have not only outperformed German brands such as Mercedes-Benz and BMW, but have also entered the territory of Hyundai and Kia.

As competition in China’s domestic market has intensified and made survival difficult, Chinese automakers have been actively turning their attention overseas and have begun targeting South Korea, where barriers to entry are very low.

After BYD became the first Chinese automaker to enter the South Korean market and sparked a sales boom by offering strong value for money, Chinese brands now see the country as a ‘land of opportunity.’

South Korean automakers say the Chinese onslaught, which has become a source of fear, is no mere exaggeration.

Is there evidence? Yes. Among the world’s major auto-producing countries, Chinese electric vehicles have made inroads in South Korea at the third-fastest rate, behind Mexico and Brazil.

According to statistics from the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA) and others, Chinese-made electric vehicles accounted for just 1.1% of South Korea’s electric vehicle market in 2021, but that share rose to 33.9% last year. It surged by 32.8 percentage points in just four years.

That is the third-largest increase among the world’s 10 leading auto-producing countries, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers (OICA).

Of the top 10 auto-producing countries—China, the United States, Japan, India, South Korea, Germany, Mexico, Brazil, Spain and France—only Mexico and Brazil have seen the share of Chinese-made electric vehicles rise faster than South Korea.

Mexico and Brazil are production hubs for global automakers, while South Korea has built a large automotive ecosystem centered on automakers that encompasses research and development, employment and production.

The impact of an expanding market for Chinese-made electric vehicles on the wider industry is bound to be relatively greater in South Korea than in Mexico and Brazil.

The U.S., Europe and Japan have built barriers against Chinese cars

As strong support from the Chinese government reshaped the global electric vehicle market, the nature of competition also changed. It shifted from competition between individual companies to industrial competition between nations, combining government support, trade policy, production capacity and supply chains.

The United States and Europe are raising barriers against Chinese cars to protect their domestic auto industries and economies.

Citing Sections 301 and 232 of the Trade Act, among other measures, the United States imposes tariffs totaling 127.5% on Chinese-made electric vehicles, in addition to a 2.5% base tariff.

Invoking national security and supply chain protection, the United States is also continuously tightening regulations on connected cars, effectively blocking Chinese cars from entering its market.

The European Union (EU) imposes tariffs of up to 45.3% on battery electric vehicles made in China.

Following an anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese-made electric vehicles, the EU has imposed countervailing duties of up to 35.3% since October 2024.

Companies that did not cooperate with the investigation, including SAIC Motor (SAIC), face a 45.3% tariff; Geely, 28.8%; and BYD, 27.0%.

In 2024, France revamped its electric vehicle subsidy policy, the ‘environmental bonus,’ to favor models produced domestically.

With the EU’s countervailing duties also taking effect, the share of Chinese-made electric vehicles in France fell sharply. It stood at 31.4% in 2023, before the subsidy reform, then fell to 16.4% in 2024 and 13.4% last year.

Japan also introduced a strong support policy in 2024 to boost the competitiveness of its domestic auto industry.

It is implementing the ‘Strategic Domestic Production Promotion Tax System,’ dubbed Japan’s version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

The system provides corporate tax reductions for up to 10 years in five strategic sectors, including electric vehicles and semiconductors, in proportion to production and sales volumes.

Production tax credits of 400,000 yen (3.4 million won) per vehicle apply to battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs), and 200,000 yen (1.7 million won) per vehicle to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs).

South Korea Needs Breathing Room Through Domestic Production Tax Credits

Unlike the United States, Europe and Japan, South Korea is seeing the share of Chinese cars rise rapidly. The main reason Chinese automakers have come to see South Korea as a ‘land of opportunity’ is the lack of policy tools to respond.

South Korea imposes only the 8% base tariff applied to imported passenger cars on Chinese-made electric vehicles.

Another problem is that the country’s export-oriented industrial structure makes it difficult to use proactive trade measures such as countervailing duties.

Unlike the EU and the United States, South Korea applies the lowest tariff among major countries—8%—under the Korea-China Free Trade Agreement (FTA).

Imposing additional tariffs is not easy, as the Korea-China FTA, the World Trade Organization (WTO) most-favored-nation principle and other factors must be considered together.

The auto industry has proposed including electric vehicles in the Domestic Production Tax Credit as an alternative to help overcome the crisis.

The Domestic Production Tax Credit is a key campaign pledge of President Lee Jae Myung and is dubbed South Korea’s version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

The system promotes domestic production by providing tax credits based on production performance to companies that produce and sell strategic products in South Korea.

As the Chinese onslaught began to undermine Europe’s auto industry and concern grew in South Korea, politicians also began lending their support.

At this year’s parliamentary audit, which concluded last month, lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties strongly argued that electric vehicles should be included in the Domestic Production Tax Credit.

Since the 22nd National Assembly convened, a total of 24 bills have been introduced to amend the Restriction of Special Taxation Act to include future-oriented vehicles such as electric vehicles in the Domestic Production Tax Credit.

On the 2nd, Lee Hyoung-il, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance, also visited the Hyundai Motor-Kia Technical Research Institute in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, and attended an industry roundtable on strengthening the competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry.

At the meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Lee said the government would actively participate in parliamentary discussions on support for electric vehicle production tax credits and engage in in-depth discussions.

Industry insiders are concerned that if domestic automakers give up their home market, they will inevitably struggle in global markets, negatively affecting the national economy and industry as well.

Consultant Won Jeong-hui, who advises major corporations and venture companies on the auto industry, said, “The auto industry has a direct and indirect impact not only on businesses but also on the national economy and people’s lives.”

The consultant added, “We must learn from Europe’s auto industry, which has been pushed to the brink of survival by Chinese cars backed by the full support of the Chinese government, and quickly devise measures to stimulate demand and production that will strengthen the competitiveness of domestic automakers while also benefiting consumers.”

title: Oregon has more hyperscale data centers than all but one other state, study finds
authors: Shaanth Nanguneri / Oregon Capital Chronicle, Owen Murray, Lindsay Schnell, Lilly St. Angelo, Tyson Alger, Leo Heffron, Olivia Desgrange, Wayne Parker, Shaanth Nanguneri, Oregon Capital Chronicle
description:

text:
Oregon is home to the second-highest number of hyperscale data centers in the country, according to a consortium of researchers led by Harvard University.

That means Oregon is also home to the second largest concentration of energy demand from the industry’s largest server farms.

The team published its findings Monday in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability. It focused on hyperscale data centers because they are the largest, most powerful class of data centers designed to handle the largest computing and data storage loads, and are growing in number as the era of artificial intelligence unfolds.

Analysts at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate that hyperscale data centers will account for more than 90% of all data center electricity consumption by 2028.

Researchers identified more than 400 total hyperscale facilities in the U.S. between May 2024 and April 2025, including 56 in Oregon. The researchers generally defined hyperscale facilities as housing several server-filled buildings of roughly 2,000 square meters each — about one-third of a football field — with an average energy capacity of 40 megawatts, meaning at any given hour they can use as much power as five American households use annually.

Only Virginia, with 142 facilities, had more hyperscale data centers than Oregon. Ohio is close behind Oregon with 38 facilities.

Hyperscale data centers in Oregon, almost entirely in the eastern half of the state, required 11.1 terawatt-hours of energy to operate during the 2024-25 period studied, equivalent to the amount of electricity that could power more than 1 million American homes for a year.

Oregon’s hyperscale data centers during that year contributed to 1.3 million metric tons of greenhouse gas pollution, according to the study, equal to the pollution from more than 300,000 gas-powered cars in an average year.

That’s less pollution than hyperscale data centers caused in Ohio or Iowa, which have fewer facilities but rely more on electricity powered by coal and natural gas.

Rising energy demand from data centers and rollbacks in federal clean energy policies have knocked Oregon off track on meeting state-mandated climate goals, the Oregon Department of Energy shared in March.

The study’s lead author, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University’s Department of Biostatistics, called the findings in a news release a “snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry.”

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he said. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

Data center growth became a central issue in local and statewide political races during the last year, and several communities issued temporary moratoriums on new facilities. Oregon lawmakers and Gov. Tina Kotek are expected to propose new data center regulations during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January.

Proposals could require more transparency around the facilities’ energy use, water consumption and on data centers’ access to property tax incentives meant to spur job growth in the state, according to Kotek and state lawmakers.

Kotek in October also mandated state agencies cease issuing environmental permits for new and expanded data center construction, effectively putting a halt to projects for the time being.

Umatilla County in eastern Oregon, where the state’s largest concentration of large and hyperscale data centers are located, has sued in response with the goal of restarting the permitting process. A September analysis from the consulting firm ECOnorthwest found that most of Umatilla County’s 22 data centers are hyperscale centers. Both the city of Umatilla and the county’s attorneys have asked a local judge to step in and overturn Kotek’s order pausing permitting.

The team behind the Harvard study will examine the health effects of large-scale data centers on local communities, according to the news release, given concerns over data centers’ massive energy demand driving up greenhouse gas pollution and water consumption in many states.

“When data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself,” said Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science initiative.

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Chaotic United Nations climate talks in Turkey couldn't reach an overarching agreement on Sunday amid disagreements over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations but discussions about explicitly including fossil fuels — the chief cause of global warming — and other issues including money proved irreconcilable.

The talks, called COP31, continued without a main agreement known as a cover decision. The meeting had already made progress on smaller issues that nibbled at the process and the warming problem and continued to go on after the failure on the cover decision.

Any pact approved at the talks has to be by a near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they couldn't accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australia leadership that didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations said that consensus on something was more important and accepted the decision, often reluctantly. Russia and Saudi Arabia were forces to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks, which ran nearly 48 hours overtime at the Turkish resort town of Antalya.

For most of the first 25 years of the United Nations climate talks, outcomes didn’t explicitly mention fossil fuels, until three years ago.

That’s when in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates a groundbreaking agreement called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels,” but since then there’s been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal did say it recalled the Dubai deal entirely, but that wasn’t enough to many nations and environmental groups.

___

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

text:
ANTALYA – The newest and possibly final proposed agreement to come out of United Nations climate talks doesn’t contain the words fossil fuels, the chief cause of global warming, or specifically call for transitioning away from the coal, oil and gas that spew carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.

The draft from Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, president of the two-week conference in Antalya, Turkey, called COP31, was released in the wee hours of Sunday morning. Kurum gave negotiators only about three hours to make objections or ask for changes before the wording goes before the conference plenary.

There must be near-unanimous consensus for approval and several countries earlier in negotiations made vociferous objections to omitting a call to phase out fossil fuels. But the proposal does put a specific goal on a technology, supported by the oil industry, of capturing carbon pollution and storing it.

Because the text went to negotiators and the public after 3 a.m., countries and activists did not immediately respond to the newest version. The conference was scheduled to end Friday and is now in double overtime. Organizers worry that as negotiators depart there may not be a voting quorum of 2/3 of the delegates, which would prevent passage of the draft.

Earlier in the week, Panama vowed to formally object to a final agreement that didn’t put a cap on oil production, acknowledge failing goals to limit warming and beef up finance for nations to adapt to warming’s harms. Panama Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia” and need to be reformed.

Fossil fuels also went unmentioned in final decisions for more than 25 years, mostly because of objections by Saudi Arabia, said Alden Meyer, a longtime analyst with the European think-tank E3G. He added, however, that the world agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” in Dubai in 2023.

“It would be a real setback if we come out of here with no signal that we were serious about what we agreed to do three years ago,” Meyer said.

The proposed final agreement makes a reference to the Dubai agreement in the first line, saying it is “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” but the words “fossil,” “oil” or “coal” or “phase out” do not appear anywhere in the 10-page text.

The agreement also calls for countries to increase the share of total final energy consumption, which includes switching transportation such as cars, trucks and planes to electricity from gas, to 35% from about 21% now by 2035. This has been Turkey’s signature effort.

Climate activists also have sought a provision stating the electricity should only come from renewable energy, such as wind and solar, arguing that allowing electricity powered by fossil fuel in the goal defeats the purpose of lowering emissions.

“Electrification that runs on coal and gas does not limit warming,” said climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. “Continued reliance on coal and gas risks shifting where fossil fuels are burned and locking in further emissions.”

But Turkey and the head of the International Energy Agency said because 80% of the new electricity is fueled by renewables, it will work to reduce carbon emissions just the same.

Many developing countries wanted more details on past conferences’ pledge to triple financial aid to poor countries to help them adapt to warming’s harms. Past conferences talked of tripling previous adaptation funding, but never mentioned a baseline and some nations wanted an explicit baseline. They didn’t get it.

The new proposed deal includes the controversial idea of carbon capture and storage with a specific goal of 1 billion metric tons. The proposal is aimed at industrial polluters and those that can’t easily switch to renewables, finding a way to capture the carbon dioxide in their emissions and then finding a way to bury it. The plan is more localized and different from large-scale, global carbon removal efforts.

___

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado reported from Bangkok and Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

This is also a national security issue.

With TMSRs, there is no possibility of a high-pressure explosion because they operate at atmospheric pressure. They have inherent negative temperature and void coefficients of reactivity, along with natural, fail-safe mechanisms such as freeze valves.

They could achieve twice the efficiency of converting heat into electricity compared with PWRs. They would generate less than 1% radioactive waste products, compared with approximately 95% for today’s PWRs.

They would not require high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), which many other advanced reactors need and which is in decidedly short supply.

And most importantly, they would not need to be located near water supplies — rivers, lakes or oceans. They could be used even in deserts, making them ideal for the Moon or Mars and allowing them to be distributed across the United States — anywhere those data centers need to be located.

They could be deployed as small modular reactors (SMRs) with electrical capacities of 10 to 50 megawatts, using U-233 bred from thorium at a central facility located far from population centers.

This facility would breed U-233 dissolved in molten salt, which could then be frozen into bricks at room temperature. These could be easily shipped to data center locations, as they cannot sustain fission in that form.

One such SMR design could be a compact unit measuring 5 to 10 meters (16 to 33 feet), as illustrated below. Conversion to electricity could be accomplished using closed-loop carbon dioxide or helium gas, eliminating the need for water at the reactor site. Some water might still be required, but nowhere near the amount needed for PWRs.

Rethinking nuclear energy

“Nuke” became a four-letter word because of earlier reactor designs using solid uranium-235 fuel — a wrong design pursued because of the need to produce plutonium for nuclear bombs in the 1960s.

We no longer need them to the same extent. These reactors should be phased out — surely not a pleasant proposition for today’s nuclear industry, but frankly, that should not matter.

Physics rules.

That was then. This is now.

READ: Dr. Ajay Kothari | The missed opportunity in space: How leadership gaps, priorities may cost U.S. the space race (October 22, 2024)

We face a different predicament and different priorities, particularly those related to climate change and energy security. We need a rethink.

In the 1950s, nuclear energy was touted as an incredible, almost infinite source of energy for humanity.

But even when controlled in nuclear reactors, it seemed dangerous because of the constant threat of explosions associated with the pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres needed to keep coolant water in liquid form.

This requires extensive monitoring and double or triple redundancy in safety systems, tremendously increasing costs, as is still the case with the majority of reactors worldwide, most of which are light-water or heavy-water reactors.

These fears were reinforced by the accidents at Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima.

What if this threat could be eliminated? How about addressing each problem, one by one, and finding ways to eradicate them?

Why can’t we conclude that the way we harnessed nuclear energy was wrong, rather than nuclear energy itself?

It is time to implement a better approach.

Give engineers the opportunity to engineer it.

The enormous potential of nuclear energy

The binding energy of the strong nuclear force offers almost a million times more energy per kilogram than the chemical energy released by burning fossil fuels, which involves electrons.

We have not been able to take full advantage of this potential so far. Now we can.

One ton of thorium is roughly equivalent to five million barrels of oil. It could run a 2.6-gigawatt thermal power plant for an entire year without requiring HALEU.

With a 50% efficiency rate for conversion to electricity, such a plant would provide 1.3 gigawatts of electric power.

Between 600 and 800 such plants could provide all the energy we need in this country, requiring approximately 1,000 tons of thorium annually — without adding any CO2 or pollutants to the air during operation.

READ: Dr. Ajay Kothari: We can spell, but we do not count? Asian and Indian Americans are scapegoated for the failing education system (June 1, 2019)

This vision could solve the country’s data center problem as well as our broader energy challenges, with zero CO2 emissions during operation. It may also offer the cheapest form of energy production.

The time has come for us to take advantage of this technological marvel.

It would not be fair to deny ourselves this opportunity. One hopes the administration will pay attention and find a reasonable path forward for all of us.

Soon.

Over the past 50 years, unfortunately, we have relied heavily on oil, gas, coal and other fossil fuels, adding not just CO2 but deadly pollutants to the air. China and India are particularly striking examples of the consequences.

Countries have also had to compete with one another for oil.

We do not need coal, oil or fracking.

With this solution, which offers energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week, combined with intermittent terrestrial solar power and perhaps wind energy — where it does not become an eyesore or threaten birds — we could solve our energy needs for a thousand years without adding CO2 during operation.

How does it work?

One of the forces physicists have long sought to incorporate into a unified field theory is the strong nuclear force, which overcomes the repulsive electrostatic force between protons bound within an atomic nucleus.

The binding energy residing in the nucleus is the great advantage of nuclear power, particularly nuclear fission.

About 200.1 million electron volts (MeV) of energy are released when an atom of uranium-233 (U-233) undergoes fission.

Per unit of mass, this is about a million times more energy than is released through chemical reactions such as burning fossil fuels or coal.

A thorium-232 (Th-232) atom, when bombarded by a neutron from an external source, absorbs that neutron to produce thorium-233 (Th-233). Its mass number increases by one, while its atomic number remains unchanged.

Because Th-233 is unstable, it releases an electron through beta decay, increasing its atomic number by one and transforming into protactinium-233 (Pa-233), with a half-life of approximately 22 minutes.

Pa-233 undergoes another beta decay, with a half-life of about 27 days, producing uranium-233 (U-233), which is fissile.

This atom can undergo fission into lighter elements, including strontium and xenon, releasing approximately the same energy per atom as U-235 — about 200.1 MeV.

How much do we need?

One ton of thorium is roughly equivalent to five million barrels of oil in terms of energy potential.

Consequently, total thorium resources, estimated at about six million tons worldwide, are equivalent to approximately 30 trillion barrels of oil. By comparison, total world oil reserves are approximately 1.8 trillion barrels.

The world’s electricity needs amount to about 55 billion gigajoules per year. This means approximately 667 tons of thorium annually could theoretically meet this demand.

Considering the efficiency of energy conversion, the actual requirement could be two to three times that amount. But with 6.3 million tons of thorium resources worldwide, we have enough to last several thousand years.

The United States alone has almost 600,000 tons of thorium resources. With our annual electricity needs at approximately 21 billion gigajoules — equivalent to 666 one-gigawatt power plants — we have enough to last many hundreds of years, potentially eliminating the need to import oil or gas for electricity generation.

Within that time frame, it is entirely plausible that we will have solved the problem of controlled nuclear fusion.

This vision could solve the world’s energy problems for thousands of years, with zero CO2 emissions during operation.

With substantially smaller reactor sizes and reduced pressurization requirements, thorium-based power may become the cheapest form of energy production for many poorer countries.

It would not be fair to deny those countries a future.

To summarize, here are the key advantages of thorium molten salt reactors over conventional nuclear reactors:

Abundant energy supply: Thorium resources could potentially meet global energy needs for several thousand years.

No direct CO2 emissions or air pollutants during operation.

No high-pressure coolant explosion risk.

Inherent safety features: Large negative temperature and void coefficients of reactivity, along with passive safety mechanisms such as freeze valves.

Twice the efficiency of converting heat into electricity compared with conventional pressurized water reactors (PWRs).

Less than 1% radioactive waste products, compared with approximately 95% for today’s PWRs.

No production of plutonium that could be used in nuclear weapons.

No need for proximity to major water sources: Reactors could be built even in deserts, allowing more flexible deployment across the United States and potentially on the Moon or Mars.

Continuous refueling: The potential to refuel through online chemical processing without shutting down the reactor, unlike conventional PWRs.

Nuclear waste reduction: The potential to use existing nuclear waste as fuel, helping reduce accumulated waste.
